reviewText:
Stratovarius is one of those rare bands that not only deserve ridicule, but invite it. In this review, I will carefully catalogue their shortcomings as musicians and artists. Hence I present ten reasons why Stratovarius is a band more horrible than you can imagine.
(But first, a bit of background for the uninitiated. Stratovarius is a power metal band from Europe. Uh, yeah.)
(1) Timo Tolkki, the band's guitarist, is unoriginal to the point where his solos sound like the worst, most pointlessly masturbatory moments of Yngwie Malmsteen. What makes him even less original is that he actually seems to recycle the same riffs from song to song, album to album.
(2) The keyboards and guitar solos are fast fast fast, but with nothing in the way of melody or emotion. Guitarists who can spit out 16 measures of 128th notes played flawlessly at breakneck speed are a dime a dozen these days. So, sorry Tolkki, but if you can't do anything _but_ play fast, you aren't so hot, really.
(3) Vocalist Timo Koltipelto, despite being a technically skilled singer, has real problems with English. He winds up placing the accent on the wrong syllable, making already bad lyrics sound worse.
(4) Singing at very high notes, Koltipelto sounds terrible.
(5) The lyrics are insultingly bad. The songs all feature alien grammar and fatuous rhyming that must be Tolkki's idea of poetry. Check out these lines from "4000 Rainy Nights": "These empty days are filling me with pain | After I left it seems my life is only rain [!!] | My heart is longing to the better times | When everything was still so fine [!?!]." Oh, how emotional! Such striking diction, such stirring poetry! My heart is breaking! In all seriousness, I'd rank the lyrics at about the same writing quality as the script for an Italian x-rated movie.
(6) With lyrics that are worse than bad, you are further reminded that Koltipelto is an annoying singer.
(7)The band seems to adhere the exact same drum track to every song. That is, each speedy metal cut is characterized by obnoxious abuse of double-bass drum and senseless whacking of the snare. Combined with reused riffs, fast Stratovarius songs are basically indistinguishable from one another.
(8) The drumming, which is detestable enough as is, is set so loud and overproduced in the mix that it becomes unbearable.
(9) Stratovarius' sense of melody and songwriting sounds suspiciously like bulk-rate AOR or hair metal (a genre that died for a reason).
(10) Sometimes Stratovarius is called "progressive metal." This is just false. Being progressive supplicates a certain degree of originality, which Stratovarius does not possess. They have shown zilch in terms of artistic growth over the course of their careers (which, as of this writing, covers eight studio albums). Okay, so they have a pair of 10-minute songs, but writing long songs is not a progressive quality in and of itself. Anyone considering the purchase of this album because it's been touted as "first-rate progressive metal" should NOT buy this album.
All right, I'll be fair. "Anthem of the World" is a great song...at first. A string section plays a killer riff, which is picked up by the guitar. It's intense, and it sounds killer. But when those pounding, overproduced drums settle in, and Koltipelto starts singing some vile notes, it's finished. I also admire (such a strong word, but I'll use it anyway) the band's sense of optimism and the fact that they certainly enjoy the music they're making. That's really what it's about, isn't it?
Stratovarius, ... You are abject

Firstoff I have to say ive been listening to metal for years.  But at the core of what I get out of metal, including black metal, is not the generic experience everyone expects.  In fact I have a heck of a lot I despise about the black metal archetype in its antisocial, egoism and promotion of violence.  It overt masculinity and lack of spiritual substance.  I instead have taken a lot of solace in the longtime dismissed genre of gothic and doom metal looking for a more intimate and emotionally transcendental experience.  So I am not coming here to crap upon some band for not being metal enough or sullying the good name of black metal or anything.

What I am coming here to do is speak my honest mind about this band and state some truths that are apparently not realized in an argument between fans who call this music as an emotive masterstroke misunderstood and dissenters who decry the music for being 'hipster garbage' for not carrying out the metal aesthetic.  That argument is pointless and completely asinine as both sides are very wrong.  Take it from me as a person who had long ago the experience of being far on the side of taste and fashion ridicule in the underground music world, who stood by gothic metal when it panned out and became the scapegoat for all that was commercial and valueless in metal and underground music.

The first thing that has to be said about Deafheaven is that on their first album, they were very much a part of this new tend of post-rock/black metal... blackgaze style that groups like Liturgy crystallized.  But Sunbather is a different thing altogether.  To be honest, this is straight up a screamo album.  It has no real black metal trappings.  Having blasts, trebbly gutars, and screaming vocals are not the hallmark of black metal.  Emo and screamo and punk and hardcore had for years used these elements to various degrees.  The emotive spacey guitar lines are trademarks of emo music, same with the apparently intimate lyrics about a core sense of desperate numb bitterness.  So for people to accuse the band as corrupting the genre of metal is completely inaccurate as it is not black metal at all.  Sunbather is plainly screamo.  But go on ahead anyways and moronic meatheads in Burzum shirts listening to their garbage Orthodox black superstars deserve little more than to get all pissed off over stuff like this.  Fans of Deafheaven though.... they need to know better.  They have to expand their knowledge of music and realize the proper place this album has in the genre world.  That way they know the ground their music is built upon.  They might also happen to find some more exciting and revolutionary screamo bands that existed well before Deafheaven.

I think the most compelling proof to this is when one of the band's scene's biggest figureheads cites this same detail.  The Needle Drop guy in his review of this album neglected to call this a black metal album, even called Deafheaven a loud rock outfit.  Now personally Ive chat with that guy before and found him to be a real elititst and poor at analyzing styles of music (comfortable to stick to all the bands which everyone unanimously praises, GOD stop saying 'eargasm'!!) but he definitely had a strong spot for this album.  He even cites how the band has an emo influence.

As I said before, there is a problem with black metal and its hyper masculinity.  As a gay male I never really felt like I belonged within the genre despite being into a lot of the second wave groups.  But later I found some artists who forego that posturing and open up the genre to a more intelligent and touching experience.  And that emotive experience is what fans of Sunbather have been gripping onto so much with this album.  But there is a major catch.  And that is I think that this intimacy present in the musical ideas is actually absent from the real experience of it..  Allow me to explain.

I watched a performance of this band live.  While that moronic argument goes on about how the group is either divine emotive metal music or a bunch of tend-hopping hipster whinefests, I sat throught that and noticed a few details.  I have no allegiance to that lot of spiked thugs, but Deafheaven appears to be pretty much not much different when it comes to thuggish machismo.  The singer's disposition spoke a lot to me.  He delivered his lines with a very high level of aggression tinged with an air of defiant apathy.. not far unlike traditional black metal frontmen.  As if to further enhance this, he regularly spat onto the people standing at the front of the stage.  Such a display seemed to me to be totally out of place with the apparent experience that the people who adore this music apparently are getting, claiming a current of beauty and gentle intimacy lies under the surface of this album.  It almost then seems like a cruel joke that people would rely on Deafheaven to fill them with a sense of emotional elation and consolation, then go to their shows and have the band spit upon them.  The message seems to be.. weep in your pain and isolation unloved and alone... for you are trash, and we are full of hate and violence.  Deafheaven does a good job at isolating its listener's soul.  I personally had enough of that experience when i was young, gay, and growing up in the deep south.  I don't really want to relive that.  But I do not need too because I found meaning to my life.
But I have to wonder about those who regularly listen to this release.  Particularly if it fills them with a sense of complete isolation and sorrow.  Becuase I think that is a key factor of what is so wrong with this album.  It creates a negative emotional trap whose doors are all open, but entry isolates you from everyone and subjects you to a sense of crushing numbness.  There is so much about this band that mirrors the ideas of suicidal black metal.

The lyrics come through to enforce this...

The title track is the most notable.  A white-knuckled, hand-wringing testimonial of a obsession with a beautiful divine object that once cannot possess.  In this case that object is the body of a beautiful girl from a wealthy family.  Youre the driver in the man's head as he looses sleep over and stalks circles around the home of said girl whose simple apparition is compared to being awash in the sun of heaven itself.  You know that you cannot possess her, she is only a vision you cannot escape.  And one can imagine the story points to death... more than likely of the one plagued by her beauty...
I myself know this obsession with beauty.. I get it from nature and the world of myth.  Its called a spiritual experience.  I cannot help but feel a cringe when I see this same spiritual obsession lavished over something like a rich girl's body.. a person who likely has little to no soul under that beautiful body.  But she is a fitting love interest for our hero in this song... saccharine, elite, and disconnected.

That cringe is actually part of a greater picture to Sunbather and its conceptual experience which I is the heart of my dislike of this group and this album.

My boyfriend has a much wider taste in music than I do.  He listens to a huge variety of music with a particular emphasis on traditional folk, blues, grindcore, noize, experimental, and jazz.  He was a lot less connected to the metal scene or any simplistic tastes than I was when approaching Sunbather.  But he stepped away from it unhappy.  His main complaint is he felt it was music was the product of a hypothetical individual whose experience in life was that of the self-destructive contemporary youth.  He compacted it in a scene in the film "The Comedy" where a young man from a wealthy family engages in trying to convince a taxi driver to let him drive his car, then when driving the car, he makes catcalls at a random woman out the window asking for sex, she and her boyfriend get enraged, the guy makes a run for it, and lets the taxi driver receive the beating.  His actions are not so much done for amusement, but more because he is trying to make himself 'feel' something, having lived a life of directionless apathy under a facade of ironical sarcasm.  The Needle Drop's painting of Deafheaven as a group of beautiful angels under a acid haze of pure hate and agony fits well to this image of a  person.  He hurts but wants to feel.  He lives longing for a release from interior agony, but has no way to reach out to others than to destroy them.  An angry vocalist spitting on his loving fans.  In more hasher terms.. a disenchanted rich kid sick of life who loves to ruin himself... Hell the song "Windows" features a sample of some young guy trying to buy drugs from his car window!  With interwoven biblical sermons on Hell atop it like a tasty garnish!  Couple it with longing over a beautiful rich girl in a bikini lounging on her front of her family's manor... Im sorry... but Deafheaven do little to dismiss this image, they actually do themselves a disfavor by enhancing it!  To sum it up, my boyfriend told me that the music here feels like just an outlet for such an individual to express themselves.. to themselves.  To just FEEL SOMETHING!!!  Its like attempting to resuscitate of a dying addict.

I know a lot of younger people are really responding to the music on Sunbather.  Ive listened to music all my life and I can see rather easily how the band is able to provide this emotive experience using the chord progressions and layering development keenly inspired from post-rock and emo.  To me the music is not horrible but simply predictable and not extremely exciting due to the plainness of its arrangements.  Emotive yes, but for me only a light tasting of what one could do in music.  But my feelings on Sunbather and Deafheaven are much more than that.. its in a philosophical level.  Again not some stupid metal purity philosophy but instead my own personal disdain for music focused on male machismo, apathy, and extreme individualism pushed to isolationism.  Sunbather is about all your own internal suffering.  No one else.  All your internal dialogue of misery as you starve yourself from connecting to anyone or anything around you.  If they had stripped away the lyrics and the manner of delivery, changed it into something less self indulgent, then really there is not much extremely wrong or appalling here to me to be honest, not exciting though, just a screamo album.  But no...

In the end, this is an awful album, but not in the way those who decry it most claim it is...  It feels like the music for a well off youth to ruin the lives of themselves and others around them.  HEY!  Just look at how the band claimed they were inspired by Bret Easton Ellis's books about rich screwed up teenagers who destroy everything they touch!  The fact that the group is praised by The A.V. Club!  You cant get more incriminating than that!  Thats what I dislike so much about this music (lyrics),  Its a perfect soundtrack to the contemporary comodified social isolationist life where loneliness and apathy is rampant and everyone screws over each other and all live under a facade of irony and sarcasm to hide their human emotions.  Perhaps that is why it has been such a huge success, its symptomatic of how our world is today.  Its just as bad as Watain.

Sunbather is such an appropriate title.  I would only hope that people here try and look beyond the supermodel on the lawn and find that divine glory in something much more meaningful.  I wish they would stop blanking out at just open up and be honest with their feelings... not this blinding numbness and negative posturing.
label: negative

reviewText:
Since the Beatles disbanded in 1970 a misconception has developed that they were all about Love.  Forget those songs of alienation, biting wit, loneliness, satire, and detached surrealism . . . man, those cute moptops were just all about love.  Love, Love, Love.  Their edge, the sardonic humor, the attributes I've most valued have been worn away and in the popular view that has evolved we have Saints John, Paul, George, and Ringo beatifically preaching their gospel of love.  (Can one be a saint while still alive?  I'll leave that one for the religious scholars to debate.)  The hard-edged songs - "A Day in the Life," "I'm only Sleeping," "I Am the Walrus," etc. have all been de-clawed.
The Messrs. Martin have pulled off a very clever musical feat, but when I hear the results of their labors, and imagine the unlikely contortions the Circque de Soleil performers no doubt perform while that music is playing, I give the click wheel of my iPod a quick twirl.

reviewText:
I never would have believed I'd be writing a review of a CD by one of the most famed killers in history.  Such infamous characters usually fade into obscurity but there was something a bit different about this.  It's like a macabre Edgar Allan Poe tale come to life that grew into an inexplicable phenomenon at a time when an entire generation was an inexplicable phenomenon.  And what makes this CD so unusual is it's a time capsule.  These songs came about when Charlie was riding high on a groovy (if inadvertent) commune with dedicated hipsters who saw him as a wizened guru.  From the Ken Kesey mold of mystic profundity he had answers to everything, and all the 'family' strongly tuned into his anti-Establishment vibe.  Then suddenly Manson was in the company of major music names like Dennis Wilson and Gregg Jakobson.  They too had been captivated by this enigmatic, Elf-like creature, enough that Wilson spent considerable time recording Charlie's interesting creations at his home studio, Charlie lapping up the bravado like a fish in the sea.

Essentially it's just a rough demo tape transferred to digital for posterity's sake.  It has 26 tracks, including a brief interview, and a few songs that were incomplete.  After hearing a few of these folkie-style songs it's clear that Charlie was an inexperienced amateur, just another of thousands of wanna-be 'stars' pouring into the exploding music scene who had no idea what the music business was all about.  He was in no way prepared to be an entertainer of any kind.  Charlie wasn't too bad at singing, but his guitar skills were poor (embarrasingly out of tune at times), composition skills were poor (a few were pointless jams), only one that was actually good, altogether a collection with no musical value at all.  Since Terry Melcher was a professional staff producer with Columbia Records, he was probably very embarrassed when he heard this, especially coming from experienced pro's like Wilson and Jakobson.  It's no wonder that Charlie never heard from Melcher again.  But it didn't stop Wilson from including "Never Learn Not To Love" on the Beach Boys "20/20" album that was actually a re-work of Charlie's "Cease To Exist".  It was copyrighted, licensed, and credited to the Beach Boys, done without Charlie's permission, which for musicians who have more ego than talent obviously helped light the fuse.

The only real interest in this CD is it being Charles Manson.  It's an historical, psychological study.  Song titles, lyrics, and incidental studio chat are indeed flecked with chilling hints of the horrors to come.  It's not something you'll listen to very much.  It's morbid curiosity at its fullest.  It's a glimpse into the mind of a psychopath soon to lose control.
label: negative

reviewText:
It would be too cruel to say that this disc can only be enjoyed by those with poor taste.  I don't want to disparage those listeners who find that they like this recording, which features two of the most celebrated performers of Rachmaninoff - pianist Vladimir Horowitz and conductor Eugene Ormandy, both of whom knew the composer intimately and collaborated with him.  The first time I listened to this CD as a young musician in search of inspiration, I was impressed, too.  Subjectively, the old maestros Horowitz and Ormandy can have quite an impact.  And as other reviewers have said, it is certainly more pleasant to listen to than the very shoddy original record released 3 weeks after the performance.

Objectively, though, and by the standards of piano playing today, this recording ranks among the worst ever made.  The problems are numerous and overpowering, and they compound upon one another to produce a vile concoction.  Even the sympathetic David Dubal, a good friend of Horowitz's and the editor of Remembering Horowitz: 125 Pianists Recall a Legend, wrote that this performance was "marked by excess and self-absorbed melancholy."  Some of these problems are: a crass, harsh pianistic tone that sounds like the hammers were filed to a point to sound as percussive as possible; a dire lack of either forward drive or convincing languor; only the most tenuous of connections between pianist and conductor; and wrong notes all over the place.

The severe lapse in quality, compared with his great recordings from the '30s and '50s, is characteristic of his work from the late '70s.  Horowitz was always temperamental; at the height of his fame in the '50s, he suddenly withdrew from performing.  A decade later, he re-emerged, already sixty-two years old, and re-launched his career with the same force that had come with his emergence in the '20s as a virtuoso of astonishing ability.  From there he enjoyed many productive years, but by the late '70s, he had started to decline.  He aged, as everyone does, and wrestled with health problems.  By 1982, he was a shadow of himself, heavily medicated and suffering severe memory lapses, but a period of recuperation saw him give some of the most amazing recordings of Mozart, Schumann, and Scriabin in the final years of his life.  But before that, unfortunately, he left a Liszt Sonata, some Schubert Impromptus, a Chopin First Ballade, and a Rachmaninoff Third Concerto which are deplorable.

The Horowitz of 1965 who had been so good at assimilating the entire content of the score was replaced with an artist in a fat-Elvis period, no longer able to hold his concentration and forced to compensate with fireworks. It all rings false, and does no favors to the music he plays.  Instead of this, by all means, hear Horowitz's earlier recording with Fritz Reiner.  The same performance of the Sonata from this CD is also on that disc, so you can still decide for yourself whether you agree with me.  Even if you don't like the 1980 Sonata, though, the 1951 Concerto is excellent, worlds apart from this 1978 recording, and well worth the price.  There are also some appealing encore pieces included on that disc which are absent here, so all in all, it's clearly the better choice.

I can assume this will not be a terribly popular review, because Horowitz is - rightly - one of the sacred cows of the pianistic world, but to this listener, this disc is the nadir of Horowitz's output, and its popularity is puzzling and unfortunate.
label: negative

reviewText:
Reunion albums are tricky, especially when it is in the Destiny's Child magnitude.  Not only did the overrated Beyonce conquer last year with Dangerously in Love, while the underrated Kelly received minor appreciation for Simple Deep, but the hits this time around aren't as evident.

The lead single "Lose My Breath" is a grandiose dance number - one of the best tracks the trio has ever recorded.  Aside from that breath-taking first, the rest of the album settles for a muddle of midtempo numbers.

Nothing else on Destiny Fulfilled shines.  "Soldier" is a misery and "T-Shirt" is redundant.  It comes as a surprise that Destiny's Child would release such a middle-of-the-road (MOR) R&B album when they heavily relied on strong staccato hits like "Survivor" and "Bills, Bills, Bills."

Still, there is no excuse for "Cater 2 U" and the forgettable "Girl."  Just when you think you've heard enough schmaltz, they go on with the significantly stupid "If."

Destiny's Fulfilled begins to mildly pick up with the chilled-out "Free" and the electronically enhanced "Through with Love."  However, that slight rise is not good enough to save the disgrace of this album.  Maybe that was Beyonce's way of putting an end to the group thing and getting back to being a naughty girl.
label: negative

reviewText:
Ah yes. Steve Austin and Co. So I guess I should write a positive review. One that is completely driven on the sole fact it is cool to like Today is the Day; a review that should ignore everything else about this band but that fact that Steve Austin's cult following think he is the Second Coming, which in turn results in others liking him...and so on and on and on. I should just accept it, I guess. I mean, if I don't blindly like this band, I must not be "real" with myself, or with other people. Steve Austin's music is just so real and honest, who couldn't like it?

I don't like it. I think this gun wielding, cowardly,  rotten hot dog eating (according to the liner notes of Temple of the Morning Star) is nothing but an insecure, hollowed out shell who thinks that his childish, sophomoric, poorly written and realized lyrics are passable because it "comes from somewhere real and honest". You know what I did the first time I heard "TITD"? I laughed. I laughed long and hard. "Real and honest, Real and honest, Real and honest". So what?

If you have heard one of these albums, you have heard them all. You want to know what the highlight of this album and other TITD albums is? Not Steve Austin. Dailor kills on this one. Elrod is an amazing drummer as well. And for whatever reason, Roddy has signed on to do their new one "Axis of Eden". What a clever name. Hey, no one got it Steve-O, evil and the religious right. You are a subtle one. But guess what? Even the brilliance of those three skinsmen, can't overshadow the screeching, inane, over-layered vocals of a guy who says he hates the world, but has a MYSPACE. Who continually puts Satanic images and lyrics in his songs. Yet says Jesus is one of his heroes on his MYSPACE. Are you kidding me Steve Austin? MYSPACE? How many friend requests have you received and given out in the past month? Steve, you are so evil, how can Jesus be your hero...your fans are going to hang you Steve. Ha, ha, ha.

You want to know why I haven't talked about the content of his songs? Simple, no one else does, even if they like it. Go read reviews on AMAZON, or anywhere else on the internet, all you will read is how dark and depressing this stuff is; how you will want to kill yourself. Hey, TITD fans, no one is stopping you...just go do it. Austin, you obviously are miserable...take a flying leap.

Oh, but Steven is so uncompromising. Right, which is why he has worked with the likes of Slipknot, perhaps the biggest hypocrites and liars in all of metal. Steven, if you have trouble making money, just go play bass on Britney Spears album; you've already lost all credibility. You want uncompromising? Meshuggah is probably the most uncompromising metal band you will ever hear. How about Converge? They pummel Today is the Day. And those of you who right now are about to have the thought pop into your head "Today is the Day's influence is undeniable, they paved the way...blah, blah, blah" when the taught surpasses the teacher, the teacher becomes void. You want to know the most influential band in metal music ever, who to this day arguably could out play bands that followed in their path? Death. Chuck Schuldiner, simply put, is THE true front man. An uncompromising visionary who could out play, out write, and out scream the pitiful Austin. Schuldiner signed talented musicians to compliment his immense talent. You do the math.

You want to hear a truly dark and suffocating album? Godflesh's "Streetcleaner" impales this tripe. It is a great album, with feelings and emotions that can only be described as dark and disturbing. Austin's music is empty, void, talent-less, stupid. He has to sign on far superior musicians from album to album just to hide the fact that he can't play the guitar. And he has to layer his screaming vocals to hide the fact that, really, they are weak and flaccid.

That enough from me. Your clicks of  "review was not helpful" only prove me right. While your leader continues to hide.

reviewText: It's so many years later, but I'm still bitter. Metallica, one of the original thrash metal bands, a pioneer in promoting technical excellence and superiority in music, decided to sell out. There is no better way of  putting it; our boys in black decided to simply stop the hard stuff and  write some watered-down putresence. The Black album had minimal soul, and  even that little was lost completely when "Load" was released  next. "Load" of #&@! is what I say. There was definite  evolution for a time. "Kill 'Em All" had a youthful exurberence  that had solidified into some masterful writing by the time that  "Master" came out. "And Justice" showed definite  maturity in composition.  And the Black album? Shows just a tiredness. Sort  of a, "I'm tired of doing this for myself; it's time to make some big  bucks." I'm not saying that they shouldn't have changed. Heavens  forbid; in order to improve, change is imminent. However, there are other  paths to travel other than just doing the easy thing. Pink Floyd being a  good example - their early works focused on being simply trippy, but they  grew and actually captured a pop audience while remaining true to their  sound. The simple fact that "Dark Side of the Moon" has  consistently been on the Billboard Top 200 longer than any other recording  in existence is proof enough that you don't have to sell out to sell well.  There are a few bright spots here, though. "Sad But True" has a  nice, crunchy groove that demands bootage, and "Where Ever I May  Roam" conjures up some wisps of "The Thing That Should Not  Be" (their tribute to Lovecraft and Iron Maiden). All in all, though,  for most of us who followed Metallica through their formative years,  "Metallica" was a big let-down. And "Load" just sort of  let us go completely.

reviewText:
For the ambient purist, the majority of recordings described as such simply are not ambient. Unlike the original ambient records of Eno, which are designed to seep in and out of consciousness using their subtle textures and absence of beats, Global Communication's effort is typical of ambient as defined by kids who have grown up since the rise of house/rave music.
The key failings of this album are (1) its textures are thick and unsubtle and (2) it is laden with beats. In short, it's too intrusive to be truly ambient - unlike Eno's 'On Land', Biosphere's 'Sunstrata', Thomas Koner's 'Nuuk' or John Foxx' 'Cathedral Oceans'.
However, if you like the contradiction in terms that is ambient house, you'll probably think this is the best chill out album ever...but then you probably never heard any true ambient music...

reviewText:
I've never had much of an opinion of Madonna. I've never been a huge fan, but I've never been opposed to her. I did enjoy "Ray of Light" (the album more than the song), but I personally thought that the song "Music" was one of the dumbest songs I'd ever heard. The funny thing is, it's my genre she's touching. I love electronica ----, as my friends would refer to it. Moby, Chemical Brothers, Daft Punk, et cetera...the list goes on as to the reasons why this kind of music would work for me, but "Music" rubbed me the wrong way. And dang it if "American Life" didn't rub me the wrong way with steel wool.
Madonna, I know you're talented. I've seen your videos. "Frozen" is one of my favorite songs. But what is this? First of all, I don't know how you can act like you're being introspective. The titular single "American Life" has themes that we've been hearing for years. Nothing new is touched upon. If you're trying to make a statement on the state of the nation, you're doing a very poor job of it. System of a Down made a better video, Bruce Springsteen spoke out, and all you can do is make a song where you don't say anything that 60's folk songs haven't said? Unless you're listening to the Oakenfold remix, it's not even worth the time.
However, the real thing that gets to me is the dj'ing of this album. I"m not going to begin to make guesses as to who is behind it (but I do think it wouldn't take much more than a decent Casio to pull it off). "Die Another Day" is an atrocious track that ruined the best James Bond opening made to date. Track 3 is in the same vein, and it's not any better. In fact, the only electronic track which comes out sounding particularly decent is "Hollywood," and I can say good things about it only in the same way I can make good comments around Bernie Goetz when he's surrounded by Ted Bundy and Jeffrey Dahmer.
I know you're always reinventing yourself, but honestly, I don't think going against the Material Girl image works for you, especially when you're worth more than I'll ever make in my lifetime. Maybe you have other plans for the album that I don't know of. If I could see another "Nothing Really Matters"-style video for "Nothing Fails" (the best track on this album, imo), I might be able to regain my respect for you. But, honestly, in a career full of "Sex" books and "Erotica" videos, it's kinda bothersome that this album is the most offensive thing you've produced.

reviewText: This is the first Gary Allan CD that I have bought and without question it is my last. After reading the 5 and 4 star reviews of this album, those reviews convinced me that this purchase would be a good one. Sadly, it is worth far short of the $9.49 paid.  Maybe it is the ICON producing that makes this CD so bad, or maybe it is just that Gary Allan, at least on this CD as it is delivered, plainly cannot sing. This is one CD that I was glad when it was over, Allan's voice on this CD is so grating and uncomfortable to hear, just no musicality in it at all, almost as if he is shouting the lyrics and not singing them. Again, this could be the mastering of the ICON production, I just cannot imagine original sound tracks to be produced so badly. As to the selection of songs, most of them sound much alike, the backgrounds and the accompanying band sounding like a local bar band, off more often than on, and certainly not sounding like a professional band. There are two songs on the album, selections 9 and 11 that do offer something better than the rest, and those two songs are much more listenable than the album as a whole. But for two less-than-average songs being the best that is offered here, I cannot recommend this album to anyone.

They did this repackaging, but axed what was one of the most tuneful and best highlights from the Best of OMD, Secret!!!  How could they?  This song is a hallmark of what my Asian friends affectionately call "Vietnamese New Wave" (an in-joke).  It has a great, killer hook, and is very danceable.  Every time I heard it growing up, it really lifted my spirits.
  In the age of free downloads and CD burners, the recording industry needs to learn a valuable lesson: don't cheat the fans, they are they only ones keeping you afloat!!!

reviewText: Its no use, it seems. Marvel has decided to be known as an entity that simply cannot master the musical aspect of its movies.  It should be so simple: heroes require heroic themes. As simple as that. Memorable melodies that you can whistle at the end of the show.  What will you hum after this film? Any good composer can compose something that sounds good as the images on the screen roll along. But few can actually immortalize a great theme in our head. What is so hard to comprehend? Marvel has used some great composers in the past (Silvestri, Doyle, Debney, Tyler, Elfman, Amstrong) but never cared to continue in their legacies (how can you not continue the Captain America theme from Silvestri?). Now, with Civil War, you have one of the great stories of this cinematic universe and that is what you musically come up with? Henry Jackman is a student of Hans Zimmer. A clone of his factory of scores (Remote Control).  What you hear sounds like what the other students have practiced and rejected. Generic music with occasional inspired clichs. And like all Zimmer students, they copy the Master.  You can even hear hints of the Batman V Superman score (a one-note motif that Zimmer also used in The Dark Knight for the Joker). Sure, if you have the patience to listen to this whole album and make a personal montage of all the best cues, you can come up with a good 15 minutes of enjoyable material (track 20 / 10 / 16 / 18 & 19) but theres nothing memorable here. And surely, Civil War should have been a musical masterpiece.  As far as soundtracks go, this is a musical tragedy.
label: negative

reviewText:
Pros: only KISS members writing their own songs

Cons: the sound lost and pathetic. Thayer and Singer complete the worst line up since 1985

KISS has been a band riddled with delays as far as their release dates go over the last decade or so. In this dilapidated economy, the recording business has been in decline even longer since Napster and Kazaa had come around making it legal for anyone to steal artists new albums instead of going out and buying them. KISS has been a band on a budget since their Farewell tour in 2001, holding out for the best possible record deal advances to cover the price of recording as well as line the pockets of remaining co-founders Paul Stanley and Gene Simmons. Their last release Sonic Boom was released through a deal with Wal-Mart as far as distribution was concerned. But then again KISS has always been a band on a budget, looking for a way to do things cheaper and worse than the year before. Look at their history, when original drummer Peter Criss was fired for his impossible work ethic, they replaced him with a salary player  Eric Carr. In two years, the same thing happened when original guitarist Ace Frehley quit the band to become a fulltime drunk. They replaced him with Vinnie Vincent, someone better than Ace as far as playing and songwriting taking KISSs music to new heights in 1982/1983 that haven't been reachable since 1977. When Vinnie asked for more money, he was promptly fired and replaced with another drunk, and relatively lousy guitarist Mark St John and replacement songwriters Desmond Child and Jean Beauvoir, who took over Vinnie Vincents job for writing songs and did such a lousy job, it sent KISS into a downward spiral that had a minor reprieve in 1991 when they hired Vinnie Vincent once more to write their songs. KISS then entered the mid-90s with a choice. Either change their sound to the grunge genre, or get truly retro as these were the only options that cold sell. They tried both, but after listening to the finished grunge material, they set up the KISS reunion. The KISS reunion was a success despite Ace Frehleys loser addict attitude and Paul and Gene feeling that they could steal from the not-so-smart Peter Criss more and more of his share until he was forced to quit once again. When they released Sonic Boom, I initially liked it as the band stayed with the retro KISS theme, with new guitarist Tommy Thayer mimicking and lifting Aces old licks to the backdrop of some cheap KISS party music. Now, all I know is that after listening to this album, all I can really be thankful for was that I paid no money for this, as one of my KISS-freak acquaintances bought up 20 copies the night before and distributed them for free to a bunch of KISS fans he knows.

The album opens up with the teaser track Hell or Hallelujah, a heavy rocker devoid of any valid hooks or musical cohesion, sounding like a throwback to their embarrassing mid-80s output. Even worse, it sounds like a reject from something like Asylum or Animalize. Pauls voice is post-vocal chord surgery for the first time on record and his voice sounds weaker and tired. Tommy Thayer, possibly irked by the past criticism that he can only play licks that he has stolen from Ace Frehley attempted to come off a bit less redundant which sadly translated into boring and uninteresting noise for a few bars each song. Gene Simmons first offering here is a song called Wall of Sound. This phrase is usually associated with overhyped 60s/70s producer Phil Spector, and despite reading over the lyrics its hard to decipher what Simmons is referencing here exactly. It sounds like a bunch of used KISS phrases from earlier songs like 'You cant stop the roll of thunder' and others like it.  At least Gene outdid Paul Stanleys opening song, Wall of Sound is even worse.

Paul Stanleys Freak almost resembles a song, with lyrics about teenaged angst written by a man who hasn't been a teen for almost half a century. Any kind of hopes that maybe the song could be the one okay-ish song on the album, Paul goes into this I pledge allegiance to the state of independence thing which was already used by the band back on the Psycho Circus album except Paul gives it to you in his spoken word/rap style delivery he is famous for during the live shows. For every song, the members play their respective instruments for the most part, except for this song where there is a guest musician, Brian Whelan who plays piano. To my ears though, it is impossible to hear the piano which either had been buried in the mix or its just a typo in the liner notes.  Gene Simmons comes back with an even more ridiculous track called Back to the Stone Age. Whenever Gene starts off a song with the words 'In the beginning', beware. Gene actually sings the lyrics 'Cause Im a stone age man / Im the king-yeah!'. What the heck does this mean? How can they expect any fan to pump their fists to such nonsensical drivel?

Paul Stanley comes back with Shout Mercy, a depressing song about how the singer can never attain real love with another. The intro sounds a bit like Ace Frehleys Hard Times from the Dynasty album. The verses once again verge on being passable, but the chorus is annoying with its train sounding guitars. Once again, Paul feels the need to show you how much he loves Led Zeppelin via the lyric 'Love-what is and what can never be'. Long Way Down on the other hand is a musical tribute to his favorite band.

The rest of the album is just as bad as the first part. Also, like Sonic Boom (this line-ups first album), there is a song where drummer Eric Singer sings lead, as well as a track with Tommy Thayer on lead vocals. Tommys song Outta This World is first, unashamedly taking on the Spaceman persona that Ace Frehley had created. Thayer even attempts to sound like Ace vocally. This is sacrilege and it gives me pleasure that their albums will never sell past a certain point. Paul wanted to write a song for the drummer Eric Singer, so he went back to the second album Hotter Than Hell for the first time he had done so. Paul practically rips himself off by rearranging the intro from Mainline, and then completes the song with little tidbits of Mr. Speed and lots of corny pass lyrics. The result is All for the Love of Rock and Roll, at least Singer doesnt attempt a Peter impersonation here. Everyone goes on about how great a drummer Singer is, and while this may be true his style is boring and unmemorable, especially when you compare his style to original drummer Peter Criss who managed to successfully fuse his love for Swing and the heavy rock that KISS once produced so well. Any KISS fan can tap out a Peter Criss drumbeat to any KISS song on a table, but ask them to do the same for Eric Singer, or even Eric Carr before him.

As far as I can see, as a KISS fan, the band only has two options at this point. The first is to disband and finally end the KISS brand after 20 studio albums. Choice #2 is to once again get the original band back together and record like a band should. If they could somehow put their massive egos aside and record like a real band instead of another glorified Paul Stanley solo album with special guest Gene Simmons as Monster turned out to be. It bothers me that they really bragged this album up a lot, especially since it was delayed for at least a year. This is really the worst record the band has ever put out under the name KISS. Its worse than Asylum, its even worse than Animalize. If the band needs more money, which is possible, we may see another reunion coming down the pike, sooner than later. One thing is for sure, if Ace and Peter do come back into the band, one thing they should negotiate is the firing of Tommy Thayer. This dude has been a pain in the bung hole for both of these members and should be swiftly kicked to the curb.

reviewText: Why, I wonder, would I go to the trouble of writing a review of Rieu's umpteenth potboiler? Die-hard Rieu fans, who are as blinkered as the next best al-Qaeda fanatic, and lovers of the real stuff alike couldn't care less about what I write. The first group because they will pronounce every burp and flatus that escapes from his Hirsuteness' orifices a stroke of genius, and the second group because they, well, just couldn't care less. And rightly so, because oh dear, who in their right musical minds would fall for this dehydrated, anaemic, hastily thrown together hodge-podge of musical-related material. The singers, who take pride of place here, are woefully inadequate, not only in voice quality but also in emotional projection. One particularly pitiful example is "Supercali" etc. from Mary Poppins. Those who are even remotely cognizant of Julie Andrews' performance must surely wince at the thin, feeble rendering that we are confronted with here. Just singing the right notes at the right pitch is NOT making music. The same goes for the tone and expressive qualities of Meneer Rieu on his fabulously expensive Stradivarius. Surely, Antoni Stradivari did not intend a precious and priceless instrument like that to be manhandled by a former-concert-master-in-a-provincial-(in every sense of the word)-symphonic-orchestra-turned-businessman? The band as a whole sounds top-heavy (where are the basses?), the engineering being so lacking in finesse that only with difficulty can separate instruments in the ensemble be discerned; no transparency, no clarity (except when there's a solo). Have they ever listened to Bis, Chandos, Decca, CPO and other state-of-the-art recording companies' productions I wonder? Live it may be okay, as an audio experience it is sadly obvious that to Rieu music is not an end in itself but a means to a different end: running a company. Hats off then that time and again he succeeds in peddling something so decidedly lacklustre and pedestrian to a gullible and ever increasing sea of undiscerning lemmings who just parrot each other in saying how wonderful it all is.

reviewText:
It is rare that I will write a review of an album on Amazon because I tend to have pretty decent luck when making music purchases.  So when I found out that Judas Priest was putting out another new album that was a concept album, although skeptical, I was very excited none the less.  So much so, that I coughed up the money and got it the week that it came out instead of hemming and hawing and waiting to save money for it.

It took me almost a week an a half to get through this dribble.  The first disc is so unbearably boring and tiresome, that I would only recommend this as a "Having trouble sleeping?  Take a listen to this." album.  The music is repetitive and droning, and Rob Halford's "singing" is atrocious.  The majority of the time he is grunting out one word at a time in a monotone single syllable reading.  The lyrics are good and there is so much promise if only he would pick up ANY sense of pace.  I know that this is a concept album, but is it still supposed to be a rock and roll album.  A song that should only be about three and a half minutes if it was sang instead of read to me like I was a two year old learning Dick and Jane, is drug out to an eight minute snore fest.

Disc two is slightly better, only because of the first three songs.  They are decent (not fantastic), but at least have some sense of rhythm and flow.  They had a great opportunity here because there are concept albums that work.  Take Queensryche's Operation Mindcrime (The first one, not the god-awful volume 2) or Gamma Ray's No World Order for examples.  Those are both fantastic albums because they work as an entire concept or as individual songs.  You can sing with them, you can listen to just one song and enjoy it by itself, and even better - you can stay awake while you listen to it!  Heck, even KISS' Music From The Elder is a masterpiece compared to this slop.

If you want good Judas Priest start with Sin After Sin or Defenders Of The Faith.  Both are different eras of Priest, but both work.  This does not.
label: negative

reviewText: RCA/BMG have taken yet another potentially great idea for a new release and screwed it up again! Will it never end?! The title "Complete '68 Comeback Special" is a LIE in itself. This set is NOT COMPLETE! The big blunder is the fact that disc 1 is called "The Original Album", which is the LAST thing they should have included here! I enjoyed it when it was first released, but I think that most serious Elvis fans have learned since then that there were MANY things wrong with this LP! A lot of what should be in true stereo were only included in flat mono sound, including "Memories" and "If I Can Dream"  and the opening of the Gospel Medley ("Sometimes I Feel Like A Motherless Child") was completely cut from the album. The instrumental breaks on this medley were shortened as well. A few years back, RCA released the 2-disc set "Memories-The'68 Comeback Special", and although this was far from complete, it DID include the entire Gospel Medley completely un-cut! Why then did they go back to releasing the cut version on this set which claims to be complete?! You would think a set like this would by now be the definitive version, but it's not! I really believe the label does these things purposely to get as much money out of the poor Elvis fan as they can! Even the huge DVD set of this show had a mistake in it. The "It Hurts Me" sequence was only included in separate pieces (the way it was filmed) and not in its' entirety! A 4-disc set!...and I also had to go out and buy the single disc version, which came out later, just to have this entire song sequence, which is one of my favorites! If you're a casual Elvis fan, then these things probably won't mean anything to you...but if you're a die-hard fan like me, then you'll still be longing for RCA/BMG to get something right so we won't have to keep buying it over and over!

reviewText:
Who's making these marketing decisions at the Magic Kingdom, deaf monkies in the dark?

Aside from John William's original Star Wars orchestral scores, how often do people buy albums JUST for the background music (which is what a good film score does; if you find yourself noticing the score more than you're paying attention to the plot/dialogue/action, then the movie is either lame or the sound engineering was done drunken interns).

Forcing us to buy 12 pieces of instrumental music just to get to the ballads/anthems/etc that we REALLY want is just plain dumb.  It also denies artists like Regina Spektor and Switchfoot (et al) cash in the form of royalties never paid because of songs never bought.

I'm not knocking Gregson-Williams, his heroic, Romantic score does the job of the Heroic Fantasy we watched.  But without it's cinematic context, it's just so many bits and pieces.

I first checked for the Spektor/Switchfoot songs on iTunes and got hit with the "Album Only" non-sense.  I wasn't surprised, iTunes does this sort of thing all the time.  Amazon, typically doesn't.  Hence Disney's clearly the one at fault here, dictating the terms.

How about a little corporate courage?  Disney needs the Amazon outlet (portal?) much more than Amazon needs Disney soundtrack CDs.  Use your customer base to get us what we want how we want it.

reviewText:
"Never Say Die" is the very worst Sabbath album.  Black Sabbath is the very best heavy metal band, and also the fist, but this was their worst hour.

Checkout "Master of Reality" or "Paranoid" or "Volume 4" or "Black Sabbath" (self-titled) or "Sabbatage" or "Sabbath Bloody Sabbath".  Those are the very best heavy metal albums of all time.

After "Never Say Die", the next worst Sabbath album is "Tehnical Ecstacy", but its really a cut above this fart.

Albums from the non-Ozzy eras (Dio, Gillan, Hughes, Martin) have very solid and innovative guitar playing and the absolute "most" signature riffs from the original inventor of the heavy metal guitar riff, Tony Iommi.  Tony Iommi really makes quality music, apart from "Never Say Die" and "Technical Ecstacy".

I've listened to every Sabbath album from 1970 to 1999.  On "Never Say Die", the guitar player, Tony Iommi seems to have stopped practicing altogether.

The guitar playing on ANY other album by Sabbath is really good.  Really, you can't go wrong with any Sabbath album from any era, except for this one.  Apparently, Tony thought they could make it as a pop/glam band with no guitar riffing.

A good lesson for all of us, Do What You Do Best, and only then expand from there!  I am glad Ozzy left the band!  The albums from the next two vocalists (Dio, and Gillan) were some of the the heaviest innovative albums for the genre!

Look at it like this:

1978 - Black Sabbath is making glam-rock that isn't even catchy.

1979 - Ozzy quits

1983 - Black Sabbath is making music so heavy that Death Metal bands are still covering it twenty years later.

See what I mean?
label: negative

reviewText:
Creed are the ultimate statement on the watering down of the "grunge" aesthetic that swept the world roughly 10 years back. Nirvana actually had some "cred" and were a breath of fresh air for those in the mainstream (and perhaps a different matter for those in the independent scene), but then came Pearl Jam...then Bush... then Live... then along comes Creed. And to make matters worse, now there's a whole slew of "post-Creed" bands like Nickelback and Default. Someone get me a gun!
An intelligent fellow remarked that Creed are today's answer to '70s Journey. Whilst you're at it, you might as well add in the likes of Foreigner, Boston, Kansas and all that other turgid pap that ruled the airwaves back in the day. Creed and their ilk are safe, cliched, formulaic, humourless drivel that sap the life out of music as we know it. If you seriously think this is what rock'n'roll is all about, then you just ain't looking hard enough.

In particular, sections of "A Night on Bald Mountain" get louder and softer a few notes apart when the music should play at the same volume. In an era when you can purchase individual pieces of music, this soundtrack can easily be stitched together from more modern recordings. The one star refers to the quality of the recording. With good sound quality, Fantasia would be a five star compact disc.

reviewText: First of all, I hear what this guy is trying to do....I really do. I have a deep love of acoustic guitar music in addition to electronic music. I've seen some of the greats live in concert--Bruce Cockburn, Leo Kottke, Steve Howe, et al. I even liked the overcast cloudy day scenery on the cover of his CD...gave me the impression I was going to hear some very atmospheric acoustic and/or electric guitar journeys. What I got instead was music so amateurly-performed that it would have been laughable had it not been so shocking. He knows how to pick a guitar, but it's astounding how out-of-synch his playing is with his back-up musicians--for all intents & purposes, this sounds like it was recorded at someone's house during very preliminary rehearsals. And I do mean VERY preliminary. This CD should have never seen the light of day...it should have been kept in Jerry's possession and not released, as it shows an utterly unbelievable lack of polish or professionalism in the way it was executed. Shameful.

I bought this album that day it came out, listened to it twice and put it on my cd rack severely disappointed.  Every two years since, I grab the CD thinking, "Hey, it's the Crowes, it can't be -that- bad".  And every time, I put it back on the shelf.

It come down to this, if you like the Black Crowes and don't have this album, don't buy it.  I read all the press when this came out.  The album was supposed to be a return to their early days (ala Shake Your Moneymaker).  In my opinion, Moneymaker is good, but not nearly as good as Southern Harmony and Amorica.  Although By Your Side has the Shake vibe, it is at best secondhand rehash of that album.

In reading the positive reviews about this album, I have to think the authors aren't normally Crowes fans.  This album sounded like a hollow attempt to reclaim radio glory.  If you like radio rock, it might be for you.  If you think the Crowes are best when they are experimenting and grooving (ala Amorica) stay away from this one.

reviewText:
Another failed attempt:
- Kick drum click, click, clicks in your ear on every song. So obnoxious and detracts from the music.
- The snare is choked, without that great, loud crack on the original, and the toms are even muddier than before. The cymbals are so faint.
- The guitars have lost their bite and sound incredibly thin and are further down (quieter) in the mix.
- Geddy's vocals, which are so key to delivering the raw, powerful emotion on this album, shouldn't have been touched. So many critical inflections and subtle layers that were removed or made so faint that they lose their intended impact.
- The mixer (Dave Bottrill) took several liberties with the vocal tracks that completely shift the mood and emotion of every song.

Over a decade of putting up with the horrible sounding original mix when all the fans wanted was a remastering to correct the damage caused during the original mastering. Instead, we we get this hacked up, over-processed, emotion killing, oh, and click, click, clicking down beat sold to us. Hard to believe Rush would hire someone to take such liberties with their most personal work and then approve this horrible remix. Even harder to believe Dave has worked with a band like Tool, who have incredibly well-produced albums.

With sentiments like "See only what you want to see" and "Congratulate yourself", it champions self-deception and self-centeredness.

The pieces for barrel organ and player piano are played at incredible speeds-but to no purpose whatsoever. This is one of those experimental music albums that you listen to once and then put away forever.

reviewText:
Words cannot describe how breathtaking this CD is. It is easy to understand why this hot new collection has already sold millions of copies the world over. The fabulous Britney Spears {along with her fellow top 40 and rap contemporaries} have blessed our generation with three vital things sorely missing from all music that came before her....ORIGINALITY, ARTISTRY, and most of all, TALENT!

Indeed, few musicians in recent decades can compare with the overwhelming musical ability that Spears injects into every fiber of every song on this incredible album! When it comes to sheer vocal talent, Brit has no equal. When she dips into her lower registers, there's a haunting and soulful feel that would make Karen Carpenter proud. And her upper registers RIPS with operatic ruptures that would intimidate inferior singers like Celine Dion into an early retirement!

However, outstanding vocals can only get you so far, and Spears has always had much more to offer than that. Her groundbreaking guitar solos are so jaw-droppingly inventive that Eric Clapton, Jimi Hendrix, or Chet Atkins sound like total idiots in comparison. Her drumming is rock steady, her complex bass lines flow like water, and her piano playing is also of the calibre that classically trained musicians like Ronnie Milsap or Billy Joel could never compete with. While most stars can only play one or two instruments, Spears is responsible for every note played on this amazing collection of songs!

Then, of course, there is songwriting ability, which is something that Britney has taken to a level beyond anything Beethoven or Mozart ever dreamed of! Britney's lush compositions are so incredibly sophisticated in both lyrics and melody that they more than deserve their place at the top of the charts. Every song here stands on it's own as a timeless masterpiece of American music, and each one makes a truly unique musical statement that is only enhanced by the radiant musical prowess that IS Britney Spears! For both musicians and songwriters the world over, her unmistakable talent is undeniably inspiring and refreshing...

Thank God that after sixty plus years of horrible music with no redeeming qualities whatsoever, we have been blessed with the true artistry that Miss Spears has given to our culture. The 20th century was a terribly bleak time for American music in terms of sheer talent and originality, but here in the 21st century Brit has elevated an art form to standards we may never be priviledged to witness again.

And how do I know that everything I've said here is true??? Because unlike many people, I turn to the right sources to help me decide what music I should be listening to. I allow MTV, Simon Cowell, and my local DJ to do my thinking for me because these people are the experts who understand what REAL TALENT and GREAT MUSIC is all about!!!

Enough said. If you don't own this CD, you were born without a brain.....

reviewText:
In short, Gould's Bach may be technically impressive but stylistically it's all wrong.  His approach dates back to that of Tureck and E. Robert Schmitz when these pieces were played like technical studies, with strict metronomic tempos, total lack of embellishment and overlong phrases more suited to the romantic period.  As far as I can tell, he completely ignored the musicological research that was going throughout his career.  He certainly was an intelligent man but I've long felt that his eccentric behavior (sitting so low at the keyboard, the incessant humming along with the music, baggy clothing...) was most responsible for his popularity (see album cover).  I've long felt that he's best represented by his performances of twentieth century music (especially Prokofief...his much admired Schoenberg recordings are too loud and four square rhymically...he plays it like a lot like he plays Bach...listen to George Li playing these on youtube!!) and his Wagner transcriptions.

Furthermore, Bach keyboard music simply doesn't work on the piano.  Despite the advantage of being able to control dynamics, the tonal color is virtually identical throughout the range of notes spanned by the pieces whereas on the harpsichord the timbres from the bottom to top vary greatly and add much needed variety to the overall sound.

Listen to Ton Koopman's performance of the Goldberg on Erato if you want to get an idea of what can be done with this music.  Koopman has been the greatest harpsichordist and improviser for the last thirty years or so.  You can't go wrong with anything he does.  When it comes to baroque and classical repertoire, his recordings are still the standard.  His continuo playing in his Messiah is more exciting and musically interesting than solo playing by most others.  Simply put, this man truly IS a first rate musical genius.  His recordings and performances speak for themselves.  No hype is necessary.

reviewText:
Bonjour Crimheads,

Around 2007, Robert Fripp and Steven Wilson embarked on a long and fascinating journey in the rehabilitation of "older KC patients". They were to use the original analog master tape of each album (ITCOTCK's master tape only reappeared in 2004), extract their "soul" out (digital multi-track flat transfer), rejuvenate them, and finally assemble a new stereo mix and a modern 5.1 surround version. They resuscitated all the old albums and are now moving into the 1980's catalog and up.

Like most old Crimhead, I purchased all of the 7 older albums in their 40th anniversary box set which includes one regular audio CD (with a NEW stereo mix by Wilson) and one DVD-A (with an original 5.1 surround mix, also by Wilson, and other stuff). Originally priced at around 29.99 $, that was fine with me... but I probably forgot to mention these purchases to my wife!

First on their working list, for 2009 releases, where "ITCOTCK" (as it was released in 1969 and was indeed 40 years old!) and "Red". It took me a while to realise that the audio CD in the "Red" box set did not contain a NEW 2009 stereo mix by Wilson but the "good old" original album (30th anniversary?) stereo mix and two bonus tracks (6-7) which were curiously remixed by Wilson, in 2009. The box's cover (and booklet) do mention this fact, so there is no false advertising but...

How is it possible that they did the whole "Red" album in 5.1 and only 2 tracks in stereo as you probably have to go through the stereo mix to get to the 5.1 mix? They had the original tape in their hands so what happened... time constraints?

4 years later (in 2013), comes out this 2 CD edition of "Red" (with exactly the same liner notes as the 40th anniversary booklet!) which features: a 30th anniversary stereo mix (on CD 1) and, finally, a NEW 2013 (44th anniversary?) Wilson's stereo mix that should have been in the 2009 box set! Confusing... indeed... and this is kind of an "Epitaph" joke!

So, this is a bit of a rip-off and this 2013 edition should be sold for 4.99 $ max., as an apology to all KC customers! Mr Fripp is well (that's an understatement!) known for denouncing the music industry malpractices (with good reason) but this time, he is guilty of one himself!

Moral of this story: don't pay more than 15 $ for this "new" 2013 set!

And yes (not the group!), "Red" (not the color!) is a 4 stars album for me!

CG (Montreal)

reviewText:
Arguing about the merits of this band is like debating whether it is better to shove your nail or a pencil into your eye.  Both are equally bad choices and should be avoided--just as this junk needs to be given a very wide body-swerve.

The Raconteurs are nothing more than a tired blast of everything you've heard before played badly by some morons who should be serving you burgers.  This CD is utter, total and banal horse manure.  Without question it is a temperature reading of just how dire things have become when used toilet paper is sold as a valuable commodity, while good albums (imaginative, incisive and creative) don't win any prizes.  For Christ's sake, I beseech you to buy Scott Walker's The Drift rather than this!  If appalling music is a cancer, then is a cancer stewed twice and brought back to give it another run.

Just like The White Stripes, who are the equivalent of listening to The Cramps and Captain Beefheart on mind-pummelling, taste-neutralising tranquillisers (yes - I wish I had no talent, Jack - then we could all die braindead and happy!), then this utter detritus is a tour through all the things you never cared about enough to save before you last switched them off.  I sincerely hope that all the `musicians' concerned who made this vomit die really horrible deaths, as they can never pay me back for the minutes they stole from me while I wasted my time listening to their output.

I actually took my copy of this album and threw it with all my might into the bin in my study.  Pleasingly it shattered on impact and I actually hoped--via some contagious occult link ala Frazer--that it might have resulted in the band shattering as well.  No such luck, as I checked the entertainment news and there wasn't one headline saying "over-hyped idiots explode into hundreds of pieces".  Instead I will have to content myself with watching them suck on the world stage until the cynically marketed void they are exploiting swallows them whole and causes them to vanish from musical history without a trace.

Final Score:  you should only buy this album if you've never heard any other music, don't know anything about music and think music is a waste of everyone's time.  This is bilge and it could stink out an entire room in Kane's mansion.

THE X-FACTOR is the best example (Along with VIRTUAL ELEVEN and NO PRAYER FOR THE DYING), how Maiden suddenly and tragically totally run out of ideas in the 90's. Be it coincidence or not, that began to happen when guitarrist Adrian SMith was replaced by axeman Jannick Gers. THis guy Gers is famous for playing live at stage with immense energey and non-stopping action, but he simply does not have any finesse, any style to his playing. In the solos, it's a real tragedy: he simply can't play a solo, be it from his own mind or from Maiden's past hits.
I keep laughing at some things people say about this album: "the best Maiden album of the nineties"" ... big deal... all Maiden albums of the nineties are completely waste of time, including FEAR OF THE DARK. The first MAiden albuns had absolutely none, or at maximum one, fillers. In the nineties, the contrary was true: all the songs were fillers, with one or two great tunes.
The only (and important) merit they had was to stick to metal formula, however outdated and formulatic it can be, and didn't sell out their music to stay alive.
What they did was hire Dickinson and Smith back, a clever business decision for both parts.
THE X-FACTOR has only one extremely interessant song: SIGN OF THE CROSS. THe rest......you know the answer.

Unfortunately, Kaufmann is not cut from the same cloth.  With some effort, he could become a useful baritone.  But his premature and unjustified desire to enter the tenor range is quite ridiculous, producing a strained, constipated and thoroughly unpleasant sound.  And he should learn to shave.

reviewText:
Someone had a tape recorder rolling one night at the Star Club in Hamburg, Germany and as a result we now have a document of the Beatles' lineup including Pete Best as they worked to perfect their sound.

HIGHLIGHTS:
If there is one, it's probably the chance to hear them do "I Saw Her Standing There" in an early version. Oddly enough, there's a version of the Olympics' hit "Hully Gully" with a honking sax at the intro. As the Beatles didn't play sax, I assume this was someone from the club? Or another band's member doing a sit-in?

LOWS:
Again, nothing really in particular except perhaps "Mr. Moonlight" which I've never liked as a song (It's the lowpoint of "Beatles for Sale" for me.) The sound is VERY "iffy" for repeat listening...it's exactly what you'd expect for a reel-to-reel placed haphazardly without any effort given as to left-right balance...etc. There are obvious dropouts at times.

BOTTOM LINE:
Only for completists. Most people who want to know how they sounded in the Hamburg days will be happy with the track or two on the "Anthology 1" disc. Skip this one...

reviewText:
I will be the dissenting voice amid all the kudos thrown at this album.  Make no mistake - I am a BoDeans fan, and I know they can crank out catchy, heartland rock like no one else.
Unfortunately, this album only has flashes of future brightness.  While the music is "good", it's not great. When you consider that this album came out in the late 80s, it is a miracle that it was released - the influence of simple, catchy songs from the late 50s and early 60s is unmistakable, and really went against the grain of overproduced, synth-based music of the release year.
While the music is fun and solid, it fails to rise above that - never enters the "great" zone, that leaves you humming a riff or intro for the next few days, nor do you want to crank you car volume to 11.
However, what ruins the album for me - and yes, "ruins" is correct - are the vocals. For whatever reason, Sam Llanas sings lead on most of the songs. I'd compare listening to his voice akin to scraping the inside of my skull with a fork, only less pleasant.  Sam's voice is extremely limited in range, as well as being quite nasal.  Kurt Neuman's voice - when it can be heard - is in fine form, and I wish he had sung lead on more of the songs.
The siezure-inducing quality of Sam's voice is curious, because with later BoDeans albums, it's much better.  Either his voice become stronger, or their budget for production effects got bigger, or both.
My recommendation:  skip it unless you find it cheap somewhere. Start with "Go Slow Down," "Black and White" or "Blend."  Those albums feature Sam and Kurt at the height of their writing and singing powers.

reviewText:
There are a few things that you just have to consider when evaluating this score. Originally, Gabriel Yared was hired to write the score for Wolfgang Petersen's "Troy". He worked on the score for a year and everyone seemed to be pleased with the result. Even more, some considered Yared's Troy score as the best he's ever written (and after listening to some sound clips of his score, I agree with that). However, one foul test screening seemed to be enough for the producers to kick Yared and reject his music. One month before the movie's premiere, they turned to James Horner.
I don't know what Warner or Petersen expected from Horner; to pull off a (two hours long) score in three weeks that is superior to a score another composer worked on for over a year?
Now, instead of an inspired, refreshing and unusual musical score by Gabriel Yared, we get 75 minutes of Horner's bare essentials. I have to agree with the other reviewers that the "theme" for Troy is truly annoying. What's even worse is that Horner used his danger motiv ad nauseam; this score is littered with it. It takes bits and pieces from Horner's previous efforts without developing an own character.
And I don't blame James Horner; he certainly couldn't have written something better in the time available and his "Troy" is better than other last minute scores,like Mission Impossible or The Hulk. The producers alone are to blame for this lowblow.
I could give the Soundtrack four stars for Horner's work ethics, but I won't because Warner's and Petersen's behaviour are just inacceptable.

reviewText:
The critics favorite whipping boy is back with another album. Judging from the lackluster sales of "Lenny"--no one seems to care and for good reason. Mariah Carey will be relieved to have some of the pressure taken off of "Glitter" by her Virgin lablemate for sure.
On his new album, Lenny Kravitz has attempted to trade in his 70s affectations to channel Bon Jovi circa 1984. He wrote all the songs and, in a move that is surely a testament to his own self-absorbtion, Lenny played all of the instruments. What the listener is left with is a soul-less, hollow album with few, if any, bright spots.
Kravitz has always been reviled for his "image-is-everything" posturing and his habit of graverobbing musical icons in an efforts to invoke their talent. "Lenny" was supposed to be the album that showcased the real Lenny Kravitz. Unfortunately, there is nothing much there. No social commentary ("Bank Robber" is a hook free failure), no driving rythms, no catchy romatic odes, no nothing --except for bland preachiness.
On tracks like "Dig In," "If I Could Fall In Love," and "Battlefield of Love," Lenny goes out of his way to bore the listener to tears. Only a die hard Kravitz apologist or a supermodel could appreciate this dreck.
Taking his cue from the wildly successful single "Again," Kravitz tries and fails to recreate the sound on "Lenny"--an album full of hairband power ballads that go nowhere with airy lyrics that say nothing. No much has improved since Kravitz penned "We've got to love/and rub-a-dub/We've got to dance and be in love."
Was he singing to Seasame Street's Ernie?

reviewText:
Let me get things straight: I never really liked Kerslake drumming and Daisley bass playing on this record. Several times, I said to my friends, in confidence "I wish some else would have played those songs... they would have been so much better, like they are on Tribute..." That, is one thing. But re-record? You cannot re-write history, Ozz! You should know better than that!

Please, don't get me wrong, I think both Robert Trujillo and Puffy are great musicians, but re-recording is a tricky, all but impossible thing to do, at least to do it right, and it is painful to say, but that is the case here: Ozzy DOES NOT PULL IT OFF! Yes, I would have sold my soul to have Tommy Aldridge on drums and Rudy Sarzo on bass from the start, but the fact is, THEY WEREN'T THERE! Replace the original recordings? Technically, it is close to impossible to do that. Why? Because technology changes! You can't have brand new drums and bass (or vocals, or guitar, or anything for that matter...) put together with the original instruments, it just doesn't sound right!  The mixing of such a re-record is a complicated matter, and it is fairly easy to screw up the album... such is the case here.

Not to mention the fact that different players play differently, and therefore, try as they might, Robert and Puffy could never hope to adequately replace the original playing. But even in the case of having the same players, you cannot play something exactly the same twice! IT IS IMPOSSIBLE! Technology has changed the way records are made, and god knows technology has given several giant leaps since 1980.

You cannot reproduce the sound of a classic record using different instruments(bass,drums, amps,strings, etc), different producers and different players, and even if you had all the same elements, you cannot play the exact same thing twice, and I know what i'm talking about, cause im a musician, and playing is so much more than the actual contact with the instrument: it implies your mood, the atmosphere, the place you're working at, the people you're working with, etc.

The excuse of not wanting to pay royalties to both estranged musicians is quite lame, since they both contributed to the writing of the songs, they will both keep receiving those royalties. That is something you cannot erase, Ozz.

Also,and most important of all,it sets a dangerous precedent: Ozzy can now remove whatever musician that sues him, in order to prevent having to pay him. If you think that is irrelevant, bear in mind that Phil Soussan has also sued Ozzy, that Ozzy never really got along with Jake E Lee, and that Bob Dailey plays bass on the vast majority of Ozzy's records. Can you imagine "Bark at the moon" with re-recorded bass and guitar? I don't think so!!!

I was curious to hear the bonus track "You looking at me looking at you"(being a huge Randy fan, i keep looking for every single piece of music he ever recorded), but I think I will pass for the time being. It is pretty safe to expect the re-release of the rest of Ozzy's catalog (with deleted musicians?) in the coming months, so i'll probably wait for the reissue of "The Ozzman Cometh" to have those horrible re-recorded versions of "Over the Mountain", "Crazy Train", etc. Bottom line: go get the 95 remasters while you can. And don't walk, RUN! I know i will...
