reviewText:
I'll admit it, I was a fan of Khia's only hit "My Neck, My Back (Lick It)". It's a fun song.. sure it's hard to ignore redundant, Lil' Kim wannabe swagger of the song, but it was catchy. The album it was from, "Thug Misses", however, wasn't a good album by any stretch of the imagination. Despite having amazing song titles like "F*** Dem F*** N*****" and "F*** Dem Other H***" it prove to be a plodding and uninteresting listen. Khia simply doesn't have the personality, or flow or lyrics to support an entire album's worth of material. Her delivery is an interesting as someone listing pizza toppings to you over the phone and her beats sound cheap and hollow. In fact, the interludes were more captivating than any of the songs on the album.

"Gangstress", Khia's second album suffers from all the same problems as her first album, but for some odd reason the result is ten times worse than before. The interludes are not funny and there are 11 of them. That's right... 11 interludes/skits, and not one is funny or interesting. Not to mention that sound quality of most these is so bad that you can barely make out what's being said.

From the 12 remaining songs, there are some listenable tracks ("I've Been High", "Ah Ha" and "Snatch The Cat Back") but the rest of the songs are interchangeable, deep bass, minimalist beats that go on for upwards of 5 minutes. "Respect Me", a song that clocks over 5 minutes of Khia misspelling Respect ("You have to R E S P C respect me") and giving eye-rolling reasons as to why she deserves respect. Sure, she does her beats and lyrics herself, but they are awful... so who cares? "Thug Misses" and "Gangstress" are NOTHING to brag about, and neither is being a One Hit Wonder. First time I heard "Respect Me", I seriously said aloud to myself: "Does this song... end??" The chorus must be repeated somewhere close to 50 times.

Once you've heard "Respect Me" you can turn off your stereo, because this is what the entire album sounds like. Khia produced "Gangstress" herself and you can tell.

The concert footage on the bonus DVD packaged with "Gangtress" basically sums Khia up. Boring (she stands in one spot and raps), bizarre (does every one of her shirts have to be sheer??) and cheap (the audio is distorted and the camera work is shaky, at best).

Skip "Gangstress", unlike "Thug Misses", it doesn't even have a guilty pleasure hit on it. "Snatch The Cat Back" is the closest thing, but is far from the smile-and-sing-along quality that "My Neck, My Back" had.

I'm not saying they don't deserve one...hell they're my favorite band ...but often a greatest hits album signals the end of a band's career. Not always ...but often. Axl is apparently refusing to release the forever forthcoming album of new GNR material Chinese Democracy beacuse he doesn't want two GNR albums out in the same year. Hell Axl you released two at the same time with the Use Your Illusions albums.

But anyway ...the album is balanced out fairly equally. Three cuts from Appetite For Destruction ("Welcome To The Jungle", "Paradise City" and ofcourse "Sweet Child O' Mine"). Their acoustic hit "Patience" from Lies (there was only four new tunes on the album after all ...and needless to say "One In A Million" wasn't going to be included). Three tracks from Use Your Illusion 1 ("November Rain", "Don't Cry (original)" and "Live And Let Die"). reviewText:
I'm sorry.  I had waited so long for this reassembled group's return to recording (unfortunately minus Christine McVie)...and wanted so much to love "Say You Will."  I think I would have bent over backwards and overlooked a great deal to call this new project a success...but I just cannot.
The magnetic energy and infectious melodies of Fleetwood Mac's earlier works like the self-titled white album, "Rumours" and even the often experimental "Tusk" are sadly absent here.  Truth be told, with few exceptions ("Bleed to Love Her", for example) there just aren't any great and lasting melodies here.  When you recall old Mac tracks like "Storms", "Don't Stop", "Never Going Back Again" and "Landslide" you realize that none of the new tracks from "Say You Will" elevate one's soul into the stratosphere or necessarily carry the listener on any unique musical or lyrical journey.
There is a great deal of focus and attention spent here on technique and virtuosity (namely Lindsey Buckingham's often amazing guitar playing), and an equal amount of time spent on overproduction and unnecessary electronic tampering with the mixes.  I realize that the group may have felt that in order to successfully step into the new musical millennium they needed to electronically update their already uniquely contemporary sound, but it comes off sounding like a gimmick....artifical and unnatural for them.
Sadly, the bottom line is that the songs are just not that musically memorable.  After 15 or 16 tracks they all begin to sound the same as there is limited musical variation.  Beware...there is also a great deal of noise here...such as on the last few minutes of track two.  Very unpleasant and just plain noise!

Okay, what on earth happened here?
I personally thought that "Millenium" was a very good album and showcased much greater maturity, talent, and emotions and was a vast improvement over their debut, which I thought was almost unlistenable in some places save for "Everybody" which was suprisingly backed up by an awesome Halloween-oriented video. Most of the rest of that album is so forgettable with awful songs like "Hey Mr. DJ", "If You Want It To Be Good Girl". "Millenium" was a marvelous leap forward for BSB and I, to a degree, still enjoy that album even today.
However, this third offering from the group was a HUGE, disappointment and is IMO a grave mistake for BSB, by sinking low enough to resort to that unlistenable Swedish-pop Britney Spears oriented sound that made Britney's albums so awful.
Every song on here is so predictable, and far less intriguing than most of "Millennium". The music is so bland, unvaried, with the songs sounding so similar and with the same-old-same-old breakup, love songs but without any sense of emotion present. "Shape Of My Heart" sounds almost exactly like "I Want It That Way" but without the edge, "The Call" is virtually unlistenable with too much of that awful Swedish-pop production that made me hate a lot of music from 1999 through 2000.
Already, this album and it's style of music is aging rapidly and I already find a lot of teen pop from this era to sound dated. Even a lot of 80s music has aged better than this.
This album might as well be remembered as the album that probably closed BSB's career and also would be blown potential for this group. Their hits collection proves this.
My best bet is to get their "Millennium" album as it's pretty much the only BSB album that you'll ever really need.

reviewText:
I went back and re-listened to this album recently -- inspired by the release of the excellent Progeny box set. I recalled not liking it when it was released, but I thought maybe I'd judged it too harshly the first time around.

Boy, was I wrong.

Upon reflection, this CD is even more ill-conceived and awful than I remember it. On paper, it sounded like a neat idea -- Jon Anderson, breaking away from the more pop-oriented eighties version of Yes (of 90215 and Big Generator fame) to team up with former Yes members, including the much-missed Bill Bruford. Talk about promise... which makes the end result that much more mystifying. There is nothing here -- nothing -- that recalls Yes's early 70s heyday (when all these players were still active in the band).

The overall sound is the worst kind of 80s synth-pop -- all drum machines, new wave-style keyboards and jangly guitars -- the 80s-era yes and Asia albums sound much better in comparison. And Jon Anderson's lyrics are some of the most ridiculous and puerile he ever committed to tape -- think dumbed-down versions of "Circus of Heaven" and you'll get the picture.

To be fair, I don't think that -- aside from a few moments on the first Asia album and maybe four songs on 90215 -- any of the Yes members besides Bill Bruford did anything truly noteworthy after 1980 (the 80s version of King Crimson was pretty astounding). This album, though, really marked the beginning of the end -- none of the studio product that came out under the Yes banner after this (Union, the Ladder, etc.) was worth the time it took to listen to. The exceptions, I think, were the live albums -- the live portions of Key to Ascension were terrific and proved that these guys can certainly still play like no one else.

I know that if you're a diehard Yes fan like me, there's very little I can say to convince you not buy this album. Just curiosity alone will be too much to resist. But, still, all I can say is -- really, I listened to this so you wouldn't have to. It's awful, don't waste your time.

You were warned.

The lyrics are incessant whining and sound contrived -  it is Kid Rock's cry for sympathy though he doesn't need it, nor does he  deserve it.  Many of the songs on this album sound like a ill-conceived  cross between Vanilla Ice and Poison, with the only remotely good song  being "I Am The Bullgod", which rocks harder and has some  engaging lyrics.  The only reason why it's popular is because everyone is  buying it since Carson Daly and MTV told them to.  Without merits of its  own, it's safe to assume that "Devil Without A Cause" would be  languishing in obscurity if not for MTV's support.

reviewText:
As many people may know by now, Sony was recently caught with egg on their face when a security specialist found out that a recently purchased CD (Van Zant: Get Right With The Man) from Sony music not only installed DRM software (digital rights management, to limit and outright prevent copying music to certain devices), but it did so in such a sneaky way that it hid itself entirely from Windows, and opened the system up to security issues such as viruses.

This CD has the same copyright protection, called XCP. When installed, Sony hijacks your computer and installs custom software which:

1) Hides itself entirely from Windows by installing as a rootkit

2) Hides itself in such a manner that any files begining with $sys$ are also hidden. For example, if you install the XCP copy protection software on your machine, and rename "document.doc" to "$sys$document.doc" it then becomes invivisble to you forever.

3) Installs its own custom CD-Rom drivers to hijack your system. It also sneakily names these drivers "Plug and Play Device Manager" to seem as if it's a part of Windows. Trying to delete these drivers manually will disable your CD-Rom drive entirely.

4) Offers no uninstall option until you manually contact Sony

As of my writing this review, Sony has "apologized" for this incident, and claims they will "re-evaluate" this copyright protection software on their CDs in the future.

In the meantime, a virus is currently running wild, which names itself begining with $sys$ in an attempt to hide from the user and virus scanners.

Several class action lawsuits are also pending against Sony right now.

In summary, as you can tell from above, Sony's actions here are absolutely horrible. This is your music. You purchased it, and they should not have any right to dictate how you can use it, let alone install software which compromises your system security.

This is one of the CDs with Sony's XCP copyright protection software on it, and as a result, you should not buy it to send a message to Sony that this will NOT be tolerated in the future.

reviewText:
I don't understand how these remixes are getting such good reviews. Nick Davis used to do such amazing recordings. What happened? When did he become such a fan of over EQing everything? Can't everyone hear how overly EQ'd these mixes are? They simply aren't enjoyable to listen to. They're harsh and thin with a boomy low end and hollowed out midrange and clearly have inferior musical balances than the originals. I guess it's a case where people buy into believing remastered always means better even without volume matched comparisons. Remember, louder doesn't mean better.

I can take about ten minutes of these discs before my ears just start ringing and I have to shut it off. They've lost a lot of the punch and power the original mixes had. The sound of the SSL console EQ Nick used has a distinct tone. They will ring when overused. You can hear it all over this set. It should be annoying even to those whose ears haven't been trained.  There's a lot of poorly chosen EQ that adds a nasal quality to the instruments. The cymbals are harsh and Phil's vocals are nasally and sound like a they're coming through a megaphone. Things sound small and jammed together.

I won't even go into detail about how much better Hugh Padgham's mixes are. Hugh is obviously a better engineer as he made Genesis sound powerful and important. Nick Davis has made them sound like a small transistor radio, albeit a very loud transistor radio.

And what's with all the compression? These heavy mixes are ridiculously inappropriate for this beautiful, emotionally dynamic music. These songs used to have dynamics, loud and soft orchestrations that built the music. Now everything is LOUD! The LOUD! parts are LOUD! and the soft parts are LOUD! That's not detail you're hearing, it's just compression.

It makes me sick to my stomach that these loud, overly EQd, overly compressed remixes are going to replace the dynamic, fuller and more artful original mixes.

Welcome to the MP3 generation where sound quality just doesn't matter as long as it's loud. I guess I should get a cheap stereo that makes everything sound bad. That way these Genesis remixes won't upset me so much.

Genesis... the George Lucas of the music world. ICK!
label: negative

reviewText:
Metallica fans, before you get too excited at the prospect of a follow-up to 2008's "Death Magnetic," please know that this is in no way a Metallica album.  Lou Reed fans, before you begin to think your favorite member of The Velvet Underground has finally gotten off of his concept album kick following his four track ambient meditational album, "Hudson River Wind Meditations," please know that he has not.

When Lou Reed and Metallica first announced they would be collaborating for a full album, imaginations of fans ran wild.  Metallica is easily one of the most successful and influential metal acts of all time and Lou Reed's work with The Velvet Underground created his legacy as both a songwriter and musical innovator.  Their combined efforts had to result in something extraordinary, right?

Wrong.

Even in his prime, Lou Reed was never much of a vocalist.  As a songwriter, he ranks among the best, but his voice is not the reason his albums sell.  At 69 years of age, his voice has only gotten worse and it shows on "Lulu."  For 87 minutes, what Lou Reed does on "Lulu" could rarely be classified as singing.  In fact, most of the time "Lulu" sounds like a cross between a drunken rant and the mumbles of a crazy person talking to himself.  To be honest, I'm not convinced it isn't literally a combination of those two things.

The concept of "Lulu" is basically Lou Reed taking on the persona of a young woman who has had terrible experiences with men and decides to give a drawn out monologue.  The creepiness of a 69 year old man playing the part of a young woman aside, Metallica's backdrop feels terribly out of place.  Their trademark guitars still create a staggering wall of sound, but the energy of each chord quickly dies as they're sustained through Reed's banter.

It's obvious neither Lou Reed nor Metallica truly care what people think of this record.  "Lulu" is a musical experiment by a group of artists that can afford to do it, nothing more.  The unfortunate side-effect is that it punishes the most loyal of fans who blindly purchase the album expecting greatness.

For those of you who pre-ordered "Lulu" as soon as you heard about it, I'm sorry to say it isn't even worth listening to once.  Take the album, stick it in your blender and press the liquefy button; you'll be doing your ears a favor.  At least the dreadful noise created by that should only last twenty seconds or so.

Okay, it's not that I hate it, but these music reviews - to be utilitarian - must evidence some measure of comparative merit.  Except for a handful of DiPs and 2 RTs, I've got the entire commercially released catalogue (incl. box sets) - I am not referring to studio albums - and I can honestly say that this show along with RT 2.4 (Cal Expo '93) have been played less (maybe twice?) than any other show I possess (I didn't say "own" b/c I've got a number of downloaded, commercially unreleased shows).

While this show has a number of things going for it - a varied setlist for one, opening with Dancing and including Spoonful, She Belongs..., Gloria, and staples from Workingman's and AB - it simply doesn't have the inspired or exploratory play evidenced in proximate performances at the Kaiser (9/11 and 11/21-22), let alone the bulk of superior releases from the late 60s and 70s.

So, if each star represents a 20-percentile range from zero-to-100, then I can confidently assert that DiP 21 ranks in the lower 20% of all shows that I've heard./K

reviewText:
Just insert any word that's commonly associated with producing quality music, such as, brains, creativity, originality, skill, etc. Essentially anything that is good in any sense of the word was clearly not required to make this album.

An astute reviewer, a few pages down, makes the observation that Collins released "boy band music without the boy band." This is a point no doubt lost on that particularly strange and perplexed species called his audience. The point of boy band music, such as N'Sync or NKOTB before them is simply to appeal to the lowest common denominator of a target audience. Naturally, their's was a teenaged group and that is the only way they differ markedly from Collins. All of the elements that are necessary to appeal to the lowest common denominator of your particular target group are found in each. You must of course lack all originality and any semblance of uniqueness for that cannot be counted on to hit the target. You must have a sound that is an unmistakeable product of its time period and not so much as a millisecond ahead. It works well at the time, but it has the unfortunate side effect of driving the point home of just how stagnant and stuck they were in their narrow little time frame a few years later, which is abundantly clear with No Originality Required. You must compose lyrics that address the most common and trite concerns of your audience. Interestingly, you'll find that this doesn't differ much between the two. If there's one thing boy bands excel at, it's in performing emotionally shallow, intellectually vacuous offerings about the trials, tribulations, and occasional triumphs of the heart that are guaranteed to appeal to anyone who are themselves, emotionally shallow and intellectually vacuous. The NKOTB classic, "The Right Stuff" found the lads singing the anthemic chorus of "You got the right stuff, baby. Love the way you turn me on!" Mr. Phillip Collins smash hit of the 1980's, "Sussudio" finds our beloved baldster chanting emphatically "is she coming? I'll be there, I'll come running, anywhere. She's all I need, just say the word.", and of course, "sussudio!"  What we have here are two examples of smitten men who lack both the intelligence or emotional depth to convey their feelings in either a mature or meaningful way. The only essential difference is one of them has an excuse because he was at the time a snot nosed little runt (and I know that sounds an awful lot like Phil Collins, but I meant the kid from NKOTB). In this respect, the minions have usurped the master. I'll grant that it isn't easy to write a genuinely good and powerful love song, but I've seen more inspired stuff hastily scrawled on bathroom walls.

Insufferable tripe like "Sussudio" helped pave the way for the dance pop of more recent times, from Justin Timberlake to Britney Spears. The only critical difference is that the common rule of thumb is that if you're going to produce muck like this to appeal to the lowest common denominator of the dregs of society, it's usually ideal for the mouthpiece to be young and attractive. The diminutive pudgster Collins, hardly fits this bill. It's obvious that he was being marketed almost exclusively to sad middle-aged housewives and idiots on No Sack Required, but it is truly noteworthy that the record company had such faith in the commercial potential of this record that they would package the songs with that face on the cover. I take it back, there's definitely some sack required for that.

 Anyone who adores American Idol is personally indebted to Phil Collins. Anyone that loathes the continuing and rapid decline of anything even remotely approaching quality music can merely stand in the long line of those of us that wish some court would impose a gag order on this little troll.
label: negative

reviewText:
Another rip-off reissue!  How many more times can they repackage this classic? : (1.) original off-pitch LP with miss-titled tracks (All Blues/Flamenco Sketches) , (2.) off-pitch LP with miss-titles corrected (except in Europe!), (3.) off-pitch CD issue, (4.) correct pitch CD reissue, (5.) CD digital remaster with bonus out-take, (6.) Davis/Coltrane box set, (7.) SACD, (8.) HQ LP.

Now a reissue which includes (5.) & (8.) plus a (9.) CD in session order including breakdowns and studio chat.  This latest CD has been available as a bootleg for years - it is really only for obsessives (like me) and is not particularly interesting except that it shows how quickly they created this masterpiece.  But why an LP and CD? Any music listener with a quality sound system and good ears will always prefer CDs despite the variable remastering.  LPs are for retro listeners who prefer the sound of vinyl.  The markets do not overlap!  Every time I put on an LP to transfer to digital I wince at the noise - clunk-shoop-shoop-shoop-crackle-shoop-click- music-click-music-crackle etc etc.

Do not buy this - get the boot of the full session from the net and listen for interest.  Issue (5.) has great sound and if you have a SACD player and surround sound sound system get the SACD to listen to a transfer of the 3 channel master recording (turn off the rear channels).

The DVD has also been around for many years in much less expensive issues and only includes 'So What'! Hardly 'Kind of Blue Live'

reviewText: Going for a more rock sound, the band is about a decade too late to the party.  While they were able to maintain their cutting edge status through about mid-80's, by early 90's they were directionless and kept stabbing in the dark.  Rockoon is a fine example of this, this time going for the edgier, hard rock sound.  What results is another bland album, but this time it's more upbeat than any of its predecessors.  There are a few OK pieces here, most notably Rockoon and Big City Dwarves, but they sound as tiresomely uninspired as the rest of the album.  Linda Spa and her alto sax in a few pieces not only fail to make things interesting, but rather they create a rather laughable smooth jazz effect more at home on one of Kenny G's offerings.  All the while we're treated to Zlatko Perica's guitar riffs that would have been better off backing for Yngwie Malmsteen.  Both of them bring a sound that is as incompatible with the TD sound, as it is jarring in its context.  The resulting dissonance ends up scattered through pieces that bore as much with their geographically-derived names as with their Casio-keyboard sound. Sadly, all this from once undisputed masters of the synthesizer.  Skip this one, nothing new here, and go for their pre-'87 works.

reviewText:
I must admit I get really cheesed off when I see great DVDs of Queen, Elton John, etc cropping up year after year, and Yes fans get these crummy lousy quality drink coasters for themselves.
I thought Keys to Ascension was bad, but it's streets ahead of this lumbering piece of junk. The only redeeming quality is the lineup but you quickly forget that after about 5 mins as the appalling sound and video quality begins to sink in and you wonder why you spent 30c on this rubbish.
There's this awful metallic squeal from one of Rick's keyboards, Chris Squire is almost inaudible and Jon sounds like the cat's being strangled (this is not his fault - it's just that the EQ is horrendous and really, why didn't they just put this out in 2.0 instead of 5.1 which is totally wasted?) There is some nice stuff from the players such as Rick and Steve but as you can't really hear them above the hiss and distortion it's a bit of a waste of time. Even seeing The Ancient performed live is not really a saving grace - the mysticism and wonder of this piece is completely ruined, like watching Lord of the Rings on those tiny aircraft TV screens. . .
The producers have tried to cover up the abysmal sound quality by having lots of hysterical fans screaming at the start and end of each song - maybe an attempt to add atmosphere as well, but as I was completely disgusted by this time the effect was lost.
I skipped over to see what Chris Welch had to say, but he's bored and boring and it's nothing new anyway - it's almost as if he'd seen the video and figured it wasn't worth putting any effort into the commentary.
And that stage just keeps going round and round - The Roundabout Revolving Restaurant, I bet the band wished they could have got off before this stinker came out.
Only worth buying if you find it in a car boot sale, (which you probably will!) Buy another Yes DVD instead. ANY other Yes DVD.

You put out one halfway-decent album before turning into (oh God) a "jazz fusion" rap jam-band, biting Digable Planets, Stetsasonic, Eric B and the Brand Nubes. And then you called it your own, to a round of stifled, embarassing laughter.
But now the joke is on you. You'll profit mightily from this slab of recessed bad meat, roll your bank accounts one more time for posterity, help soundtrack a cadre of graying 40-somethings (like yourselves) reliving their cannabis-hazy youth as they shuffle their children from their suburban hellhole homes to soccer practice, kids listening to Modest Mouse or The Kills on their MP3 players to drown out mom's choice of music in the mini-van, finally yelling "mom, turn this wack stuff off!", or simply laughing at each other, knowing their mother is equally as wack as the old farts who made the CD in question.
There is no further evidence necessary of how low and sad the state of American music is in today than this awful, awful album you've made. Its program reeks of insipidity and trite lyrics. The cover, obviously intended as a tribute, veers on tastelessness and offensiveness. Your personalities have become mere cartoon characters in a world you created, no longer offering anything original or important to say, now taking cover behind a wall of pseudointellectual political posturing that you know nothing about except that it's "hip". The production and sound of this album is rock-bottom garbage when placed alongside the revolution in sound available in this genre (if you can even call this "hip-hop" at all). Basically, you've committed career suicide, and 19 years too late, I say.
There is no need for anyone with a shred of interest in hearing anything with intrigue, originality, creativity, and integrity to be bothered by this crap. Goodbye, Beastie Boys.

reviewText:
For 40 years now, Phil Collins has a waged a one man war on the Western world by unleashing a barrage of some the absolute worst music that ever had the misfortune to see the light of day. This album is where the masterplan seems to have originated. A glimpse of the cover art, which looks like fairly uninspired scribbling of random shapes by a slow-witted child, is the first indication. Here for the first time, Collins assaults us visually as well aurally.

This album requires a bit of a history lesson on the boys, a tedious prospect I know, but unfortunately necessary to place this steaming pile of garbage in its proper perspective. A couple of years before, Collins had opened up a second front in his personal war on mankind by unleashing what is indisputably the muscial equivalent of getting a root canal. I'm talking about his solo career. Free from the chains that bind him to the muscial excesses of his bandmates in Genesis, Collins was able to focus single-mindedly on composing adult-oriented (provided said adults aren't very intelligent), made for top 40 radio and MTV, soft pop. His early solo success in addition to Genesis' moderate commercial success with the early 80's "Duke" and ghastly "Abacab" albums had provided the dim, narrow path of which Phil would trudge along dully like a war weary soldier in 1960's Saigon forever more.

I suspect that his handlers at the time had encouraged Phil to make an album that would sound more like his solo material than the long-winded and exceedingly dull prog-rock that Genesis was more commonly associated with. This would prove to be the approach, albeit with the violent exception of "Home By The Sea".

Well, why waste any time? The first track gets right to the point and leaves no one in doubt of just how bad this album is going to be.
"Mama", this is Phil doing his weirdo routine, which he enjoyed from time to time. Seven minutes long and believe me, the listener is aware of every sluggish ticking of the second hand that passes while this pseudo-shock rock plays its tired self out. Collins plays a stalker-esque, severely unhinged individual that is lamenting his failures to acquire the woman of his dreams. Needless to say, it wasn't much of a stretch. Live performances of this found the balding, petite Collins sticking his tongue out while making weird faces in a semi-crouch position and moaning idiotically (apparently feigning constipation) in the middle of the song. Frightening? Well, perhaps to Genesis fans who were probably still regarding Duran Duran as pushing the boundaries of what's acceptable in pop music at the time.

 "Illegal Alien" was to be one of the earlier examples in a string of increasingly embarrassing videos the band would release. The track finds Collins singing in a ridiculous and poorly conveyed Mexican accent as he laments with all the fiery histrionics of a teenage queen, "it's no fun, being an illegal alien." The aforementioned video would also find him dressing up in quite a tasteless and stereotypical version of what in Collins' myopic mind , must have been the spitting image of an illegal alien. Clearly, Mexican immigrants are something that an American audience knows about and of course does not resonate in the UK. I'm of the opinion that Collins' handlers cautioned him to direct this album towards a US audience, not simply for the usual reason that it's a larger market, but also in view of the fact that by 1983 people in the UK were probably beginning to realize just how big a joke Phil Collins was. I'm not sure whether the track generated any backlash at the time, but that was perhaps another machination of his handlers. On the one hand, the track could rightfully be accused of being stereotypical, possibly even outright racist, but on the other it could provide some of that classic rock and roll rebellion Genesis never really had because their music was boring and their singer looked like a lonely school teacher whose sole companions were probably a small herd of live-in cats.

"Home By The Sea". Well this would be yet another in a very long list of the boy's unconvincing attempts to lend some credibility to the proceedings. A two part epic meditation on nothing much at all, totalling in excess of 12 minutes. Fans will probably insist that this track was the band maintaining their principles in the face of record company pressures to create ever more commercial flop-pop for mass consumption of a musically undernourished and dietarily uninformed record buying public. For my money, it was just another  effort to appear serious in an album chalked full of songs that blatantly declare the opposite. No one told the lads that just because you play a dismal song for what feels like an eon, does not increase the chances that it will lend one iota of respectability to your sad record. The track inspires only one thought in the serious listener and that is that he finds himself harboring the wish that Phil and the boys would make their home in the sea instead and spare us all from any further bile-inducing banalities.

The album closes with Phil assuring us that "if it's gonna get better, it's gonna take time." 25+ plus years on and that statement has never been more untrue.

I first heard this piece in when I was in high school. I heard it  live at Mann Auditorium in Tel Aviv, the Israel Phliharmonic was conducted by Gennady Rozhdestvensky, I went to every performance during  the week it was played (I had a friend that allowed me to sneak in).

Needless to say this is one of my favorite pieces.

I own the following recordings of this piece:

Bernstein with Chicago Symphony, Haitink with the London Philharmonic, Masur with New York Philharmonic and my favorite  Ashkenazi with St Petersbug Phliharmonic. All of those recordings are excellent. There is an authorative feel of drama, pain, struggle. The context of these pieces is apparent, and the conductors in those recordings made sure to offer this piece as a complete work. The orchestras are also engaged and inspired by these Maestros. I highly recommend those recordings.

Words cannot describe the disappointment I had from this 2-Orchestras-for-the-price-of-one recording.

It is shallow, out of context, detached. An insult to the listener's intellegince, the only struggle Gergiev has through this piece is probably how to make more money with his grandiose, bloated productions.

There was only one good thing in this piece: the timpany first drum roll in the first movement. But thats it. Even the wind solos were unimpressive and unengaged. This is the sloppiest recording of this piece I have ever heard, the fact that it is a 200 people orchestra is no excuse (I heard double orchestra concerts, live, with no hick-ups what so ever), on the other hand this behemoth of ensemble surprisingly lacked punch at the orchestral climaxes.

Just stay away.

reviewText: I've been waiting a long time for Robert Palmer's early albums to be remastered so I was excited when I learned about these new Culture Factory versions, which boast vinyl replica packaging and "96K/24-bit" mastering.  The vinyl replica sleeve packaging is fine, perhaps not quite up to the standards of the Japanese mini-LPs I have but very good.  The problem is the mastering of the CD.  I compared it to my old Island CD and my original vinyl pressing.  This new CD is incredibly bass-shy compared to both the LP and Isand CD.  It's also much brighter and sounds boosted in the treble frequencies as compared to both the Island CD and the original vinyl LP.  The only good news is that it is not brickwalled or way too loud.  But it nevertheless does not sound good at all.  I bought all of the Robert Palmer vinyl replica CDs from Culture Factory and I am not going to keep any of them.  Do not waste your money unless you're a collector and packaging is a big deal for you.  If improved sound is what you're looking for, it's not here.  I think it is shameful for a company to market a CD as audiophile with "96K, 24-bit" mastering and then deliver this kind of poor quality.  I guess we'll have to keep waiting for decent Robert Palmer remasters.  What a missed opportunity!

reviewText:
I have to admit, the controversy of Milli Vanilli got me interested in listening to their debut album - "Girl You Know It's True".  My objective was to listen from a musical standpoint to hear what the album had to offer.  Milli Vanilli is famous for having their Grammy award for "Best New Artist" stripped from them following a notorious lip-syncing scandal.  What people might forget is that Milli Vanilli was a huge phenomenon in 1989.  However I subscribe to the thought that if there was no scandal to begin with that this would be an overrated album.  Separating the music from the lip syncing, I still found this album from a musical standpoint to be very disappointing.

Milli Vanilli was brainchild of producer Frank Farian.  Fabian had formed a group consisting of Charles Shaw, Johnny Davis, and Brad Howell.  At the time, Fabian's band had a unique combination of Synth Pop and an early form of Hip Hop.  While Fabian knew he had what a marketable sound, he felt that he couldn't market the musicians he had.  Enter the duo of Rob Pilatus and Fabrice Morvan.  Fabian basically would use the duo of Rob and Fab to front the Milli Vanilli band - even though from a musical standpoint, they had nothing to do with the album.  With Music Video, this would serve as the primary mechanism for Rob and Fab to front the band.  Rob and Fab would lip sync their way through the videos - combining this with what was considered some innovative dance moves.

While Milli Vanilli were given the "Best New Artist" Grammy in 1990 based on their album "Girl You Know It's True", in reality this was their second album (so I find it confusing how they were even eligible for this category).  The momentum with Mill Vanilli would grow as each single was released from "Girl You Know It's True".  The album's title song would score a Top 10 hit.  Then the next three songs would go #1: "Baby Don't Forget My Number", "Girl I'm Gonna Miss You", and "Blame it on the Rain".  As the songs and associated videos were released, there was nothing really unusual about it.  The nature of most music videos involves lip syncing - and if you are going to subscribe to the concept of a music video, then you are going to have to accept lip syncing.  The videos done for the "Girl You Know It's True" were entertaining.  The "Milli Vanilli" dance even caught on.  However, things would fall apart when Milli Vanilli would start to tour.  As they toured, they were forced to lip sync.  Whle many artists lip sync to their own music - even in concert, it soon became apparent that Rob and Fab were not the vocalists for the music.  Fabian would confess.  There would soon be a big backlash.  The Grammy was Rescinded and even the record company lost a judgement suit that would rule that those who purchased the album would be entitled to a refund.

While I can't defend what Farian did, part of me has the attitude - "what do you expect?".  I've never been a big fan of music videos because the do endorse lip syncing and I am not a big fan of lip syncing.  Music videos often spoil my own "vision" of the song.  Suppose that there were no music videos or MTV, then perhaps there wouldn't have been a need to front the band with the likes of a Rob or Fab.  However, if I listen to the music and ignore the video aspcts, I still did not care for the sound.  I found many of the songs to be boring.  There is no real strong drum presence on this collection - and I found the percussions to be weak synthetic percussions.  I also found that many of these songs were heavily remixed.  These aren't the kind of songs I would want to play over and over again.

There are two songs that did catch my interest.  The album's best song is a lesser-known track called "Dreams to Remember".  This song has some merit from a musical standpoint.  This song features a soft synth pop sound with an R&B flare to it.  I like the use of the horns in the song - it gives it a jazzy feel.  This is a very mellow song and not one fits the image was portrayed in the music videos.  The other song I liked was one of the more popular songs - "Baby Don't Forget My Number".  This is a more traditional style Milli Vanilli song.  It has a Synth Pop beat and combines some of the prototype Hip Hop sounds with some intricate harmonies.  This song also has a very chorus....."ba ba ba ba - ba ba ba ba Baby...Don't Forget My Number" .  This song is arranged well and "switches gears" at several points nicely.  I think this song has a lot to do with launching the Milli Vanilli phenomenon.  It was a good song to begin with - and then a very catchy music video was attached to it.  By attaching that catchy video, it catapulted the band to stardom.

I always felt the title track "Girl You Know It's True"  was weak.  The album actually contains two versions of the title track.  It is worth noting that this an early example of sampling.  You will hear parts of Bobby Brown's "Don't Be Cruel" sampled in the remix.  I'm not the biggest fan of sampling, so I don't feel this is adds to the song.

Overall - if Rob and Fab weren't associated with this album and I were reviewing the work of Charles Shaw, Johnny Davis, and Brad Howell - I'd still be very disappointed with this from a music collection.  While "Dreams to Remember" and "Baby Don't Forget My Number" are good songs, I still would not recommend getting this album for the music.

reviewText:
This could be the final nail in the coffin of Janet Jackson's career.
After the impossibly weak "Damita Jo", forgettable "20 Y.O." and now the simply embarrassing "Discipline", it is safe to say that she's done. Out. Finished.

Now this comes from one of her biggest fans. At one point in time, I would have gladly set myself in front of a moving train for her. I have committed most of her albums to memory. But THAT Janet is gone, and THIS one is plain awful.

I perused some of the "five-star" reviews, and many of them are clearly misguided. For example, one remarks that her "harmonizing" is terrific. I think even her boyfriend Jermaine Dupri would laugh to that comment. The easiest explanation for that review is that the writer really doesn't know what "harmony" is.

Janet's vocals have always been thin, but she's always used her limited range to maximum effect. Her previous producers knew how to wring the best performances from an admittedly average instrument. Here I envision her handlers simply nodding and telling her that everything she does is "amazing" or "terrific"...there is no editing, no one telling her to tone it down,  no one sitting her down and saying, "Janet...this is just not good."
For at least THREE albums now...
The 5 star reviews need to be taken with a grain of salt. They judge the artist, not the art.

Compare any vocals from her last three records to ANYTHING from the rest of her career. Notice how they are losing character, depth...soul? They're flat, expressionless. It's not even a subtle change. It's obvious.

Need more evidence? If she were to put out a greatest hits album off the last three albums, it would be a single. "Just A Little While." That's it. To compare, her first greatest hits album was filled with songs off pretty much just two records. Since then, she's had hits like "All For You", 'Someone To Call My Lover", "Together Again"... but those were a long, long time ago.

Back to the record...

Those "interludes" just have to go. They're juvenile and self-indulgent. And stupid.

You know how someone who tries really really hard to be "sexy" usually falls flat on their face? Like it's the most "unsexy" thing ever? For the last few records, Janet trying to be sexy feels like a little girl putting on her mom's makeup. It's not just fake...it's just child-like and dumb. Her attempts are feeble, and no one is telling her otherwise.

Using text-language for words..."Luv", "2Nite", "Never Letchu Go"...was old back when Prince did it 30 years ago. Incidentally that was before text messaging. It was before the Internet. It was before cell phones. Here it's just infantile. So last year.

Another thing: there are no songs on this album. There are beats. A groove...often the same one over several tracks...or two. Noise. Special effects. Non-sensical lyrics. Those irritating pointless interludes. Not a single song, let alone a "good" song.

You will continually need to remind yourself that she can sing. Remember "When I Think of You", "Because of Love", even "Whoops Now"? There is not one single real sung note here. It's all breathy, mechanical, monotonous.

She could be a smokin' hot, over-40 dynamic performer...but here she is a faux-coquettish, wannabe sub-Britney Spears.

How embarrassing is THAT?

Anyone who has seen the movie will know how exciting the score was during the luggage room battle, the Annex Skywalk gunfight, the ejector seat escape, and the fight on the wing. reviewText:
After attempting to return to their sound and style of yore with the okay-but-not-great "Euphoria," (1999) Def Leppard released their most commercial outing yet with their tenth album, "X" which was released in the summer of 2002 to a generally apathetic public.

While Def Leppard is undoubtedly one of the best rock bands of the 1980s, they have been rendered toothless ever since the death of guitarist and founding member Steve Clarke. Clarke was undoubtedly the most creative and talented member of the band. As the clich goes, when Clarke died, the band died with him. Throughout the 1990s the band has struggled on, a ghost of its former glory. First was the candy-ass lightweight, "Adrenalize," (1992) followed by the excellent, updated sounding "Slang" (1996) which unfortunately and unfairly met with sound of crickets chirping, then came the overrated-but-bombed anyway throwback album "Euphoria."

Which leads us to the ultra-commercial "X." To be fair, for an album of its type, "X" is not a bad album. It's just not a rock album. It's an album of the Rod Stewart, Bryan Adams, Sting, Matchbox 20 variety. It's an album not aimed for rock fans, but fans of soft-rock and adult-contemporary fare. Much like the more recent offerings from Aerosmith, there really isn't all that much difference between the sound of "X" and the boy-bands that were popular at the time.

I'm all for bands breaching out and experimenting and reinventing themselves, but why the hell would Def Leppard want to make an album like "X"? Why would they want to make an album that sooooo doesn't rock? Except for the die-hards, their base isn't going to dig it. Fans of "Pyromania" (1983) and "Hysteria" (1987) are going to listen to it once in disgust and proceed to sell it to the nearest used CD shop. The teens of 2002 weren't going to buy this album as they had their own candy-ass crap to buy...so I'm not sure what target audience Def Leppard had in mind when they created "X."

As previously stated, for an album of its type "X" isn't bad. But then again, this sort of music sucks. It's like saying for a fast-food restaurant, Burger King is pretty good, but then again, fast-food restaurants aren't good compared to gourmet French cuisine.

When I listen to Def Leppard's first four albums "On through the Night," (1980) "High and Dry," (1982) "Pyromania" and "Hysteria" and then compare it with "X," it's hard to fathom that I'm listening to the same band. With the exception of "Slang" and "Retro-Active," (1993) listening to any post-Clarke Def Leppard album leaves a bad taste in my mouth and diminishes the bands legacy in my eyes. It's hard to believe that what was once such a great band has fallen so hard. The irony is that the more commercial and pop the band becomes, the less albums they sell.

Clarke's replacement, Vivian Campbell was great in Dio. Guitarist Phil Collen is also a good player. While the Campbell/Collen duo can't be expected to mach to stellar Willis/Clarke, or Willis/Collen combo of Def Leppard's prime, they should be able to churn out better songs than what's here. And what happened to Joe Elliot? He was once a great singer and frontman, with the pipes of Bon Scott, and now he sounds like Bryan Adams...what's up with that?

If you're a fan of Def Leppard's classic 80s albums, don't even bother with this. A fan of old-school Def Leppard listening to "X" would be like a fan of "Rambo" watching Sylvester Stallone star in "The Vagina Monologues." Only completeists need buy "X."

reviewText: Wow. WOW. I was one of the first people around my area to praise King's X when their debut 'Out of the Silent Planet' was released, followed by the INCREDIBLE 'Gretchen Goes To Nebraska'...I was so happy to discover this amazing band, with their unique sound and positive spiritual message--and they ROCKED HARD while still being melodic, with spacey and somber interludes thrown in for good measure! Then they regained some of that edge on the self-titled 'King's X'. But after that, I just sort of tuned out on the band. They never quite seemed to match their former greatness. I remember hearing the song 'Dogman' once and being impressed with it's heaviness, but never heard it in it's entirety until recently. Recently, I began listening to the first 2 albums again, and missing the band and out of curiosity, I decided to give 'Ear Candy' a shot. The used copies were cheap--and I'm glad. This album STINKS. Really guys--shame on you! Firstly, we have a 'grunge' opening track (thanks I'm sure to the apparently stoned Pearl Jam bassist Jeff Ament's proclamation in interviews that "King's X invented Grunge!"...really Jeff? I thought you guys said it was Neil Young who did that? And even THAT was far-fetched B.S.! So Jeff, let me get this straight. It was in fact King's X that started 'Grunge'? And what planet was that on? Or what was it you were smoking in the wooded areas of Seattle that weekend camping? Kings X are about as 'grunge' as SLAYER! It was a ludicrous comment that apparently the guys in KINGS X ran with.  After the muscular (and MUCH better)'Dogman', the band wimped out, and 'un-learned' how to rock with style. I think in an attempt to cash in on Pearl Jam's (and their profoundly "Errrlll" vocalist Eddie 'Don't Watch Me Sing I'm Too Cool' Vedder) success. Grunge killed MANY talented bands. And I HATE it for that fact. And where is 'Grunge' now? Where ever that may be--leave it there PLEASE! Poor old truly talented King's X were most likely frustrated that their much deserved success always just seemed to be dangling in front of them...slightly out of reach. reviewText:
The fact that nobody has bothered to review this until now speaks volumes about this particular release. This is the fifth commercial release of Mahler 1 for the Chicago Symphony (Giulini; Solti; Tennstedt; Boulez; Haitink). For Haitink, this must easily be his fifth or sixth M1 too. Sadly, from a purely audio standpoint, this CSO Resound job is the best one of the lot from Chicago. But I greatly prefer the somewhat more congenial acoustics of Medinah Temple, captured on Giulini's lovely EMI recording from the early '70s. The story with Haitink is a simple one: he's simply getting slower and slower with pretty much everything that he's been re-re-re-re - recording. The playing from the CSO is pefectly fine - as you might expect - but this is still possibly THE snooziest Mahler 1st ever to have come down the pike. End of story - there's no point in going on further.

If it's Haitink you want, stick with his second one from the Concertgebouw; the one with the exposition repeat included (I think it's from the middle '70s). For the Chicago Symphony, any of other ones will do fine. If you happen to like it slow (can't imagine why), stick to the Tennstedt. It's vastly more "weird" and interesting.

reviewText:
It's always close by, like the threat of nuclear war. In the frozen food section of your supermarket, in the elevator of your office building, wafting through the lobbies of hotels and corridors of conference centers. It bears an eerie resemblance to music, as wax fruit resembles something nourishing, as paintings of sad clowns with large liquid eyes and dogs playing poker resemble Guernica and Crows On A Wheatfield, as a lightning bug resembles lightning.

In a way, this is perhaps forgivable. Everything Henry Miller ever said about American bread is true, it's really unfit for anything except perhaps blotting up spilled ink. But there are those people who like bologna on Wonderbread, and why shouldn't they have their fun - or more properly - lack of fun? Perhaps Wonderbread is the only appropriate delivery mechanism for peanut butter and jelly. So be it.

In this context one can attempt to excuse the chain of albums churned out by Mr. G, like so many spiceless sausages. But one cannot forgive this. Here he approaches those who are far beyond being his betters, they're from a different dimension. To listen as KG addresses 'Round Midnight is to question the existence of God. A smooth jazz draft of Ipanema is rather like painting a polar bear in a snowstorm. But the height of impertinence and grandiosity is playing a duet with Satchmo. It was a tawdry bit of grandstanding when Natalie Cole did it with her dead father, but at least that was all in the family. Here it is a hideous attempt at bridging the gap that will forever separate the real from the really, really awful.

reviewText:
This album's reputation is legendary, no doubt.  But is it really as good as everyone says it is?  Not really.  The songs are, for the most part, mediocre, especially in light of Young's first four solo albums, "Deja Vu" and Buffalo Springfield.  The playing is inept and lifeless and the singing is abysmal.  Young's voice is strained and off-key for most of the album which does nothing to enhance material that isn't very good to start with.

You don't even get very many original songs...."Tonight's the Night" is played twice for no apparent reason and "Borrowed Tune" is the Rolling Stones "Lady Jane" with new lyrics--bad ones.  The Stones, bizarrely, aren't credited as co-composers.

Some of the material was not even intended for this project.  The best track, "Come on Baby Let's go Downtown" was recorded years earlier at a Crazy Horse concert....This track has taken it's rightful place now on the excellent "Live at Fillmore" record.  The second best track, "New Mama" was intended for CSNY's "Human Highway" album.  I'm grateful that this song found a home somehere--too bad it had to be here!

The rest of the album, 9 tracks in all, are wretched.

reviewText:
This is one *weird* CD.
First of all, do not believe the other reviewers here who tell you that, for the most part, you get the original versions of the S&G songs.  For the MOST part what you get are NOT the original versions of the songs.  You get a lot of live versions but, what is worse, you get a whole lot (perhaps 80%) of "new" versions of the classic songs.
This isn't a bad thing if you already own the S&G classics -- but if you own them, why in the heck do you want this CD?  Yes, the sound quality is superb, but the two CDs here by and large sound like some sort of S&G "cover" band: a very good cover band, but nowhere near the original music.
This is not the first time someone has put together a "collection" of what is supposedly their greatest hits, but it's the first time I've ever heard one with such odd reorchestrations.  "Cecilia" is done at half speed, "Baby Driver" with such over orchestration it goes from being cute to pretentious, "The Only Living Boy In New York" goes from intimate to overblown.  And so on.
Anyone who grew up with S&G (or anyone who wants the best) needs to own "Bridge Over Troubled Water" and "Parsley, Sage, Rosemary & Thyme".  These two essential S&G CDs will give you both nearly every song in this "essential" collection, but give them to you in their pristine, S&G classic sound versions.  Then if you want to hear new versions of these classics by all means go ahead and buy this collection.  But don't buy it thinking you're getting the essentials -- this, as Robin Williams once said, is not essence, it's pee-pee-ca-ca.

reviewText:
This could be the final nail in the coffin of Janet Jackson's career.
After the impossibly weak "Damita Jo", forgettable "20 Y.O." and now the simply embarrassing "Discipline", it is safe to say that she's done. Out. Finished.

Now this comes from one of her biggest fans. At one point in time, I would have gladly set myself in front of a moving train for her. I have committed most of her albums to memory. But THAT Janet is gone, and THIS one is plain awful.

I perused some of the "five-star" reviews, and many of them are clearly misguided. For example, one remarks that her "harmonizing" is terrific. I think even her boyfriend Jermaine Dupri would laugh to that comment. The easiest explanation for that review is that the writer really doesn't know what "harmony" is.

Janet's vocals have always been thin, but she's always used her limited range to maximum effect. Her previous producers knew how to wring the best performances from an admittedly average instrument. Here I envision her handlers simply nodding and telling her that everything she does is "amazing" or "terrific"...there is no editing, no one telling her to tone it down,  no one sitting her down and saying, "Janet...this is just not good."
For at least THREE albums now...
The 5 star reviews need to be taken with a grain of salt. They judge the artist, not the art.

Compare any vocals from her last three records to ANYTHING from the rest of her career. Notice how they are losing character, depth...soul? They're flat, expressionless. It's not even a subtle change. It's obvious.

Need more evidence? If she were to put out a greatest hits album off the last three albums, it would be a single. "Just A Little While." That's it. To compare, her first greatest hits album was filled with songs off pretty much just two records. Since then, she's had hits like "All For You", 'Someone To Call My Lover", "Together Again"... but those were a long, long time ago.

Back to the record...

Those "interludes" just have to go. They're juvenile and self-indulgent. And stupid.

You know how someone who tries really really hard to be "sexy" usually falls flat on their face? Like it's the most "unsexy" thing ever? For the last few records, Janet trying to be sexy feels like a little girl putting on her mom's makeup. It's not just fake...it's just child-like and dumb. Her attempts are feeble, and no one is telling her otherwise.

Using text-language for words..."Luv", "2Nite", "Never Letchu Go"...was old back when Prince did it 30 years ago. Incidentally that was before text messaging. It was before the Internet. It was before cell phones. Here it's just infantile. So last year.

Another thing: there are no songs on this album. There are beats. A groove...often the same one over several tracks...or two. Noise. Special effects. Non-sensical lyrics. Those irritating pointless interludes. Not a single song, let alone a "good" song.

You will continually need to remind yourself that she can sing. Remember "When I Think of You", "Because of Love", even "Whoops Now"? There is not one single real sung note here. It's all breathy, mechanical, monotonous.

She could be a smokin' hot, over-40 dynamic performer...but here she is a faux-coquettish, wannabe sub-Britney Spears.

How embarrassing is THAT?

reviewText: I had always known this LP was "iffy", but I only recently listened to it all the way through. Turns out to be a bigger disaster than I expected. Following the epic "Odessa" and Robin's exit, Barry & Maurice continued as The Bee Gees. These sessions produced an odd combination of country-pop tunes and meandering MOR offerings, with little of the inspiration of previous Bee Gees music. The opener, "If I only had my mind on something else" is probably the highlight, and "Then You Left Me" isn't half bad either, but the remaining tracks are just plain dull. "Don't Forget to Remember Me" has a memorable chorus, but you must suffer through Barry's hillbilly-inflected vocals to get to it, and it's barely worth the bother. Even so, this went to No. 2 in the UK charts, the best chart showing of any of the tracks. The Carribean-flavored "IOIO" is downright annoying right off the bat, and the insipidity continues elsewhere, with "My Thing" being a real time waster. Where are the big choruses, the gorgeous melodies, the drama of past work? It must be said that this is one of the weakest LPs by a major group I can think of. "Cucumber Castle" is squarely situated in Blandsville.

reviewText: Jay-Z, probably the most pretentious rapper ever, has returned with another appallingly dreadful album that shows us yet again that every one of Jay-Z songs are essentially the same melodic backgrounds, with variations on the so-called lyrics. With the opening track "The Rulers Back", we can already see we're headed for danger. An enjoyable trumpet background, that could've worked extremely well as a 70's retro tune, is spoiled by Jay-Z's overuse of offensive words as well as his repetitive swearing and various moans grunts, that are obviously included just to show how much of a `bad-mofo' he is. Something we found amusingly interesting was the background vocals on "All I need", being extremely impressive and melodic at the same time, but it wasn't sung by Jay-Z (obviously). In our opinion, we would've enjoyed the song a lot more if the backing tune was included without Jay-Z's front lyrics, thus making the song a lot more endurable and perhaps even pleasant. The tune is followed by "Renegade" featuring Eminem, the whitest rapper on the planet, making the CD even more intolerable. As well as this, their combined `feuding' on the track is so questionably far-fetched, you'll feel cheated out of a so-called `rapper duet' that could've been an unintentionally funny song. In the end we never actually though that there'd be a rapper worse than `Emin', but yet again Jay-Z has amazed us. A note to those of you offended by cursing: there's a clean version of this CD as well but it won't be much different really, just less interesting.

reviewText:
So there I am, cycling down Mira Mesa Boulevard on what promises to be a long, music-induced session.  Passing The Wherehouse I suddenly get the bright idea of stopping to get the new Annie Lennox CD.  What new Annie Lennox CD, you may ask?  Well, there's the trouble.
So I go up to the counter.  Two female employees.  One is on the phone, turned away from the counter, the other is, I discern as I approach her, in tears.  I say, "Did I come at a bad time?"  The young lady is too discombobulated to render any service, or to notice my ironic tone, so her friend grudgingly tears herself away from the phone to find out what this provoking intrusion on her private time is all about.  I tell her to just point me in the Annie Lennox direction and she does and I go over to check out the CDs.  As I am walking away, the girl returns to her phone conversation and it becomes clear that she is acting as an intermediary in some teenage heartbreak of which the tearful girl is the tragic heroine.  I hear her say, "No, I don't think she should talk to him right now.  Did you know he pushed her down on her throat?"  As I'm walking away I bemusedly think to myself that I can see where this guy is coming from.
But anyway, like I say, there is no new Annie Lennox album and so as plan B I decide to get the EBTG mix album, having heard "good things."  Don't ask me where because I don't remember.
So I take it to the counter and manage to buy it while the soap opera is raging to fever pitch.  The tearful girl decides she just can't hold it together out here anymore and so she flounces off like something out of a French Novel.
"Bad breakup," her friend tells me.
I say, "Well, when you get to be my age you'll look back and realize it was all utterly meaningless."  The girl looks at me with sullen incomprehension as I take my change and leave.
So I put the CD in the player and cycle off down the road and there I am cycling in a state of spiraling demoralization, hitting the forward button again and again as I hit one unbelievably wack track after the other.  And then it begins to dawn on me that I've just wasted [good money] and music that I really do get something out of is apparently the work of two people whose taste in music is absolute drek.  Never having been a big fan of house, I find myself cycling as if in syrup or making my way through a dense fog.  Each track takes the groove to lamer and lamer levels.  This compilation should have been titled, "Fuddled music for nowhere people."  Finally I give up in disgust and put on John Digweed.
label: negative

reviewText: [This is a reaction of a very traditional folk musician to Dylan's first electric album, which was somehow mislaid for years. I'm an anthropologist: THESE ARE NOT MY OPINIONS!] Can you imagine my shock when, getting Dylan's newest LP, I slipped it onto the turntable and set down to prepare myself. Dylan's LP from last year, The Times They Are a-Changin', was a rather intense album, full of protest and venom, and so I was preparing this album to be just as radical as that was. And do you know what I heard??? Electric guitar. Terrible, I know. Dylan, who might have been the next Woody Guthrie, has turned his back on the people that made him big. His skill's phenomenal, and while the first album, BOB DYLAN, is a nice little folk record, it's the latter efforts that are consistently stunning. Freewheelin Bob Dylan (Reis) has so many anthems it makes your head twirl, and "The Times THey Are A-Changin'" is an album full of protest at this world. That's what Dylan does best - protest songs. He squanders his talents when he invests them in this pop drivel. "Another Side of Bob Dylan" , although tremendous in its own way, should have been taken as a warning. Here we find Dylan moving away from the protest songs that our generation so needs. While, as folk music, it does have its qualities, Dylan is abandoning his strengths when people need him the most. Yet, sadly, nothing else equals in talent or conviction of writing. That illustrates what a shame Dylan has become. But while "Another Side" does have the already cited faults, it stands as a worthy addition to Dylan's catalogue. Now we have this ramble-shack of an album. After finally making it through the first three songs, I had to take a break because of the whole shock. Yes, I must confess, for this review I did listen to the entire album. The first side's that damned electric rock. Dylan's become the epitome of the crossover. He's a traitor. The two worst compositions are the opening track and a song called "Maggie's Farm". "Subterranean Homesick Blues" starts this album off, and as soon as you hear that you know this album has serious problems. Its fast-spoken lyrics that go by in a blur, leaving you in a daze. This type of material (fast beat, fast lyric recitation) will never become a significant part of this culture, or if it does it shows the deterioration that we have allowed instead of standing up to the problems, just like Dylan himself urged us just two albums ago. The rest of Side 1 is just more of this drivel, but the most troubling is "Maggie's Farm". Here, he essentially argues for the demolition of the music that he once stood for. He essentially states he won't sing folk. Instead, he'll become a turncoat. This is a grievous blow to our side, for, regardless of what this album may indicate, he does have tremendous talent. For those of you who liked his absurd sense of humour, evidenced on "Freewheelin'" and "Another Side", there is one track called "Bob Dylan's 115th Dream", which is funny, but beware because it still has that electric guitar. Side 2, opening with "Mr. Tambourine Man", just keeps the pace of this abysmal album. Side 2 is acoustic music, but don't get your hopes up. This is not the Dylan that we hoped. This is Dylan doing what the "high culture" deems as poetry. He basically uses random imagery strung together for senseless effects. "Mr. Tambourine Man", although bad, cannot equal the absurdity of the following Dylan composition called "Gates of Eden". To quote some portions of the song (please don't cringe to bad), I will show you what I mean. "The motorcycle black madonna -- Two-wheeled gypsy queen -- And her silver-studded phantom cause -- The gray flannel dwarf to scream -- As he weeps to wicked birds of prey -- Who pick up on his bread crumb sins -- And there are no sins inside the Gates of Eden". Remember, these terrible lyrics are coming from the same man who wrote this: "Come gather 'round people -- Wherever you roam -- And admit that the waters -- Around you have grown -- And accept it that soon -- You'll be drenched to the bone. -- If your time to Is worth savin' -- Then you better start swimmin' -- Or you'll sink like a stone -- For the times they are a-changin'." As you can tell, the later is obviously superiour. We have clear cut meaning, well within the confines of traditional folk. "It's Alright Ma, (I'm Only Bleeding)" shows promise of us getting the old Dylan back, but then these hopes are crushed with "It's All Over Now, Baby Blue". Some may interpret that it just means he got this out of his system, but I fear that is not the case. We should have realised what was happening when "Another Side of Bob Dylan" was released. Dylan deliberately abused his talent, and while "Another Side" in and of itself is not as troubling, it has planted the seed. I urge you all to not buy this LP. Tell your friends to stay as far away from it as possible. If there is enough of a public reaction, Dylan will come to his senses and become the good little folky he's supposed to be. He has so much talent he must not abuse it like he has done on this. Its just a misstep (a terrible one, granted), and the results are this mess of an album. With enough of a public reaction, his next album will be a gentle folk album. He daren't cross us again so defiantly. You know what to do. If he doesn't straighten up this LP will be the end of his career. Let's pray and hope he comes back into the fold.

reviewText:
Ladies and Gentlemen,
The Rolling Stones.
Seriously, U2 has filled another diaper.
I think that in the five intervening years between this album and the last,  our favorite Irishmen since Joyce and Wilde looked around the musical landscape, and pushing fifty, starting wondering how they were going to grow old gracefully. and profitably.
Who did they have as examples to follow?
The Who? Really only one guy anyway, Pete Townsend and the man he used his hate for to motivate him, Roger Daltrey. They did their best work at their most antagonist. But the last fifteen years with the Who have been strictly cash and carry.
Can you name a single Who song from the last fifteen, even twenty years?
and then of course, everybodys' favorites, The Rolling Stones.
They havent' released a great song or a good album in twenty years. and guess what ? they don't care. and I guess, neither do their fans, judging by the hundreds of millions they rake in on every world tour. They release an album, whatever it sounds like,with the regularity of a bowel movement and then hit the road  to collect the bullion. As long as they play Jumpin' Jack Flash, it doesn't really matter what the last album (or five) sounded like. and don't get me wrong, I love the Rolling Stones.
But I digress.........
I guess U2 could've begun this  path three albums ago but instead played a dirty little trick on us by releasing  a truly  brilliant album, 2000's All That You Can't Leave Behind. they remined the old shafts and amazingly, found gold.
Joshua Tree, Achtung  Baby, Zoorapa, Passengers, Pop and ATYCLB: how many masterpieces could we expect from one band? and that was the problem with ATYCLB: its greatest made us think they could do it , and do it again.
Wrong.

reviewText:
Let's face it: if "Vapor trails" had been recorded by any of those interchangeable 90's hardore/rock bands, there wouldn't be all this hype. Claiming that this album is a masterpiece is admitting one's lack of musical culture. Some readers may think I am provocative, and I am sincerely sorry for them. I've heard too many good records in my life (including Rush's albums) to kneel at that one.
OK, Peart's lyrics are good. But it's not enough to make a good record. When I want to read good lyrics, I take a book.
Some reviewers seem to deem that when a record sounds hard, it is inevitably good. They think with their guts, not with their brain. Rush used to be both a brainy and a gutsy band. That was the band's trademark, from "Fly by night" to, let's say, "Roll the bones". What the hell happened to them? Taxes to pay?
Now, each time that a "golden age" prog-rock band, whether it is Yes, Saga or Rush, releases a new record, I'm anxious. Anxious at discovering that its only message will be: "Hey, we're still there!". Great. Tom Jones is till there too.
What's the use of making records at all costs if it doesn't bring anything to the Legend?
Last thing: to those who think that I am just an old grumbler - too bad, I'm 28. And, too bad - that doesn't make me a mug.

reviewText:
Usually when bands implode it is done through the dreaded phone call to a band member(s) who is getting sacked from the former friends & business agent, the musician showing up to a "scheduled" recording session and nobody is around or the final mix for a CD somehow dropping the (now former) band member.

For The Clash, though, it was taken to a new level with - for a time - two bands with the name and this final studio release for the group - session musicians and a drum machine - being fronted by Joe Strummer, with songwriting and production "assistance" from manager Bernie Rhodes.

It is a mess, as the songs - besides This Is England - would not have made the final cut in previous albums and the instruments buried in a muddy mix. Arguably the best musician throughout is the drum machine, but rumors remain that it even wanted to flee the studio.

The rift between Strummer and Mick Jones had been growing for years and this final product was the acrimony still being played out after Jones was sacked. In its glory years, the band wrote songs that oftentimes took aim at the bloated greed of the music industry. But in the end, the band could not survive the gluttonous egos that seemed more fitting for any number of generic stadium-rock ensembles.

In what world does Blues Traveler need to bring other musicians onto an album, much less this group of talentless nitwits? Hanson...Really? And what the hell is rap doing on a Blues Traveler album. Blues Traveler is what you put on to escape from that awful crap. The songs are outright unlistenable. I just don't get it. The lessons the band members themselves have admitted learning when working with Steve Thompson and Michael Barbiero on Save His Soul and Four have become a distant memory. I truly have to question if they can even produce music without Thompson and Barbiero, as without them...Look what we wind up with!

To the band and to all others who read this, I have a challenge for you. Please sit down and listen to the ALBUM, "Save His Soul," and indeed, I mean the ALBUM. Not a collection of who-knows-what, with no discernible connection from song to song. The songs flow on SHS, the lyrics have meaning, their is a strong sense of feeling and emotion in the group's playing; the songs clearly mattered to them. Chan's distortion, Brendan's rhythm and ride cymbal, Bobby's runs matching note for note with Chan on songs such as NY Prophesie, these songs demonstrated passion and amazing skill. The album finishes with an amazing and brilliant suite- going from the BS Lament through to Fledgling.

Take a listen to, "Four." Runaround is awesome but forget that...Listen to Crash Burn. Can Popper even play that anymore? Just LISTEN to that track and listen to it loud! Travelers & Thieves - Listen to Chan on "What's For Breakfast"- Such a tight groove. There is ZERO groove on this album.

I love this band and don't want to insult them but how can they get tired of a sound...they created? And at the same time, I want to give them a kick in the butt, every one of them and just ask a simple question, "Why? What is this new record supposed to be? Why are you distancing yourself from the sound that got you to where you are today?"

If by some off chance the band reads this and even more to the point, cares about what their fans think...do not play this crap live. And further, please get back to New Orleans, with Thompson and Barbiero, return to your roots and mother f'ing rock! Go visit Nightingales when you're in NYC...play a show there!

Get Popper to quit smoking and drinking. He's not 20 anymore and why a person would jeopardize their livelihood for nicotine and alcohol is dumbfounding. His lungs are his life. I get it...he's a rock star. But I still picture him as that kid, playing in the park in Princeton NJ with his buddies and I don't want to see him die young. He's had enough health problems.

One thing is for sure- If you care at all about your fans, those who have spent countless dollars on your music and  have traveled to your shows, who support you unyieldingly, and appreciate your sound during a time when everything on the radio is garbage, you must get in a room with Steve Thompson and Michael Barbiero again. And if they are not the antidote to whatever disease this recording is, please find some sort of cure...Because after your last few efforts, I'm running out of hope.

Bands develop their sound over time. Blues Traveler is going beyond backwards to a scary place, no true fan wants them to be. Popper confirmed in Rolling Stone that this was their manager, Lani's idea. Lani should be fired and banned from the music industry. Popper also stated that the band wants to continue with this nonsense and my hope is that he is kidding.

I love Tori Amos and I was never disappointed with any CD of hers I purchased...until now. This single contains three musical selections: two versions of "a sorta fairytale" and a non-album track called "Operation Peter Pan." The non-album song (which is an okay song and the only reason to buy this single) runs about a minute and a half--so it's not really worth the money.
The versions of "a sorta fairytale" on this CD are both subpar. Both songs are trimmed down versions of the album version of the song, with the 101 mix varying only slightly in instrumentation from the regular single version. The worst part of these edited versions is that important lyrics and moods are altered or completely eliminated, therefore undercutting the beautiful meaning of the song. To boot, the edit is so bad that the listener can actually tell where the song was sliced and diced...it's so painfully obvious that there is more to the song than was is delivered on this CD. I have my doubts that Tori Amos ever approved of these versions of "a sorta fairytale." She is such a perfectionist, and this single just stinks. It's tough to imagine Tori lowering her standards to this level.
The CD "Scarlet's Walk" is a wonderful CD and I recommend that whole-heartedly. But you can skip this CD altogether. You are not missing a thing.
