reviewText: DO NOT BUY this or any other insidiously copy-protected CD.  This is not the same digital audio disc you have been buying for 20 years, but rather, a non-conforming good.  Phillips has forced manufacturers to remove the "CD-Audio" label from discs containing copy protection.  This practice is in violation of the court-upheld doctrine of "Fair Use", i.e., making copies of the music you have purchased for YOUR OWN PERSONAL USE.  This technology does NOTHING to stop the illegal copying and distribution of CDs, as it can be easily defeated by a determined individual, and thereafter distributed ad infinitum.  This technology only serves to hinder the enjoyment of the LEGAL purchaser, by preventing the creation of back-up copies or digitized copies for a PC or portable player. reviewText:
What was once unique and incredible about the Dave Matthews Band has been replaced with commercial monotony and mediocre music. Whereas "Everyday" was just plain awful, "Busted Stuff" boarders on sacrilege.
The mp3 versions leaked to the internet, also known as "The Lillywhite Sessions," that were once slated to appear on "The Summer So Far," now comprise most of the album for "Busted Stuff." At one time, "The Lillywhite Sessions" recordings were a relief to the true fans of the Dave Matthews Band not fooled by the multi-format radio friendly Glen Ballard pop tunes featured on "Everyday." But now, the Lillywhite tunes suffer much the same fate. When at one time Dave Matthews Band might have had an incredible album to add to the likes of "Under The Table And Dreaming," "Crash," and "Before These Crowded Streets," they instead repeat the mistakes of the recent past and end up heading down the path to pop music boredom.
"The Lillywhite Sessions/The Summer So Far" might not have been perfect to release, but the versions found on the internet far surpass those now found on "Busted Stuff." Tracks such as "Busted Stuff," "Grace Is Gone," and "Digging A Ditch" are now not what they were; bittersweet ballads, almost minimalist, but complex and soulful. "Grey Street," when performed live finishes off with one of the tightest orchestrations that all five members of the band have ever created; instead, it now ends with a studio fade-out. Lyrics to "Big Eyed Fish" and "Captain" have been changed, not for the better. And missing from this rendition of "The Lillywhite Sessions" are "Sweet Up And Down" and "John The Revelator." Songs that can easily be compared to the upbeat classics of albums past such as "Rapunzel" and "Tripping Billies." These two songs are left off the album, leaving a void in their place. Where every Dave Matthews Band album, even "Everyday," has included songs ranging from the most downbeat to the most upbeat, "Busted Stuff" lacks any such differentiation.
Overall, the album is incomplete and the last studio album from the band that I will purchase. Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me.
Perhaps they should stick to releasing only live albums from now on. And everyone should get their hands on "The Lillywhite Sessions" rather than "Busted Stuff."

reviewText:
"In the Zone" may be the most under-the-radar thing that Britney Spears has done all year. And since it's all about clubbing, partying, and gettin' some, that's a pretty frightening statement. Graduating from vapid teen pop to vapid adult pop, Britney aims for early Madonna's style... and misses.
Her songs tend to be either wispy but passable ballads (the self-pleasure ode "Touch of My Hand" or the piano-led "Everytime") or vapid dance pop, like a collection of Kylie Minogue's rejects. Her duets are particularly embarrassing: "Me Against The Music" is mainly Spears muttering fast against an electronic backdrop, and the Ying Yang Twins make a forgettable appearance in the deeply embarrassing "(I Got That) Boom Boom."
Things go rapidly downhill as the album progresses, with the faux-sexy "Breathe On Me" and "Hook-Up." The lowest point is the leaden "Outrageous," which may be the worst-written song of last year ("Outrageous... when I move my body/Outrageous... when I'm at a party/Outrageous... in my sexy jeans"). There's a slight upturn with the weird but catchy "Toxic" and the wispy "Everytime," but those few listenable tracks are bogged down by all the empty dancepop.
There's little that's new about "In the Zone." Madonna did the poppy electronic beats long ago. But then, she never made an album quite like this -- the electronic synthesizing is so heavy and thick that it feels like muddy water. Spears's voice is the most synthetic part of the album, especially when laced with moans and gasps.
Partying sure hasn't done wonders or Britney's voice. She never could sing well to start with, but there's a strain and crack to her vocals that shows up despite the heavy electronic coverups. It's not written anywhere that good vocals are necessary for dancepop, but Spears is only passable (never good) in a few of the songs. She also cowrote several songs, which don't appear to have improved for her contribution. At best, they're mediocre. At worst, they're embarrassingly bad.

reviewText:
This is one of the few times I bought an album based on buzz instead of the album cover. I had to, because there was nothing on the album cover, anyway. I kept hearing about the Faces and finally broke down and bought this album just to check them out. Until 2010, I had never played the entire album. A few years after I bought it (early 70's), I read a review of this album where the reviewer said they were a great live band that had trouble translating that energy in the studio. I have to agree. To give them a second chance, I listened to the samples here on Amazon and my opinion had not changed from what it was twenty some years ago. I remember their song Itchycoo Park (as the Small Faces) and remember liking it, especially when they used that phasing technique (tape delay). That song was a far cry from this later album. The only way I can describe this style of music is sloppy. I like things loose and not sanitary (as a few bands like to do on record) but this is a little too sloppy for my taste.

As of February, 2010, I burned this to CD so I could listen to it in detail, maybe for a bit of self-torture. I wanted to make sure I listened to every track at least twice, so I could see if my review was unfair.

Nope, I still don't like the album. I have now listened to the whole thing multiple times and came away with the same impressions. It is not as sloppy as I remember it, but only by a little. Part of my problem now is that there are no good songs on the album. There is a bit too much of a country vibe, too much of a party vibe, and way too much cheesy organ. I love keyboards, but the style here just does not do a thing for me.

The musicians are competent, but I don't see any of them stretching themselves here. I appreciate Ron Wood's style, but he does much better with the Stones. I also don't feel too bad about my one star review. I've read that some of their other albums are liked much better.

Their live version of Baby I'm Amazed shows that they had the crowd going, but I just don't like that song, no matter who plays it. Their other live cut, On The Beach (I think) is even worse. It sounds like a drunken party which should be cool, but the music is nothing special and it could have been any bar band playing.

I know they can and have done better than this.

I'll take Ogden's Nut Gone Flake anytime over this, even though it isn't exactly the same band.

reviewText:
There are two things wrong with this album that are completely unacceptable, the primary one being this:

The final track is not Lewis Black. That's not his voice. I've listened to almost everything he's ever done on both audio CD, DVD, even Comedy Central specials and some cameos in other media. I think I can recognize his voice by now.

No, there is no conclusion. It ends with someone trying to sound like him giving the audience a fake--literally, fake--goodbye. It's not him, go listen to it.

Now, as for the material itself, half of it is recycled. All of it is of absurdly poor audio quality. You have to really hear it to believe it, because it truly is horrific.

The half of the material I haven't heard before is actually good, even if it's old. The Dan Quayle skit is a riot, as is all the stuff about the stealth bomber and a myriad of other political issues from about 25 years ago, easily.

But the age doesn't bother me, because I still think The White Album and The End of the Universe are, without question, his best works. As time went on, he was still good, but his prime was when he first was starting out. Nothing, absolutely nothing, beats the second-half of The White Album. From the Heaven's Gate cult skit onward, even my other favorite comedians, like Dave Attell, Mitch Hedberg, Jerry Seinfeld, and Jimmy Carr, that's the best of the best of any of them.

Really, I can't recommend this due to the recycled and ultra-poor-quality audio, and the astonishing final track that is someone imitating him because, I don't know, they didn't record the end of the thing?

Stay away, even if you're a Lewis Black fan. I'm listening to it on Sony Music Unlimited, so I listened to it through that subscription service on my Nexus 7. But I wouldn't buy this on CD for the terrible carelessness of the production, as well as the outright deception that this is new material, or even professionally-recorded material.

I was really so happy to see that The Motels SHOCK album, finally re-issued after way too long.  even though I do like their earlier efforts better, Shock is a decent 1985 ready album with good catchy material, albeit dressed up in the typical mid 80s fake drums and super gloss. The important thing with albums of this particular era is that the artist in question can rise  above the cheesy production style and still write and perform good songs.  The Motels are a good example of that. Title track is especially catchy and engaging

But the main reason i was compelled to write a review is because the other reviewer here--cool first name btw--is apparently the only one with "ears" or maybe just not dumbed down by loud MP3 downloads and harsh overly loud mastering of the past 5-7 years. the review does come off annoyed but i don't blame him. he's dead on with this.  I mean, you can listen to this CD on possibly a car stereo and be okay with it, but on most players and stereos, it only causes nervousness and fatigue.  Moreover, it's too loud to turn up and enjoy.  When they do albums like this, it's like they're already too loud when you're listening at low levels.  And right, it's like they've just maimed the original recording. And for me, it's rendered this release annoying at best.

Really like the packaging. Shame.  Good packaging is important to me and they've done a nice job here. But please, for the sake of honest music oriented people, stop the over compressing and red level EQs on these good albums.  Simply start with the original master and let the damn thing breathe a little. There IS something called "Dynamic Range"  Good numbers for this important quality in music (which allows music to surprise and wash over the senses nicely) are normally around 10-14.  CDs like this have a dynamic range around 5 or 6. And there lies the main issue with why it comes off so loud, off putting and after a few minutes , grating to the human ear. When you look at a wave file for a "mastering" job like this, there are no peaks...it's just a giant square block of loudness. is that what music is supposed to be?

I read that this label screwed up the Little Robbers album and possibly All Four One.  I'll tell you this, if this one here is considered "good" and THOSE are "screwed up"??  I hate to hear them.

Again, you can listen to this CD, but that doesn't make it enjoyable. I think the reviewers calling this spectacular remastering are just conditioned to these recent brutally loud albums.

To each ear his own, I fully appreciate that.  But mastering like this is just wrong and insulting to the original music. Like the -one- reviewer said, i also like the remasters from the 90s because even though they were louder they still allowed the music to be music.  They incorporated "useful" compression which simply bumped up the overall to give a more full impressive feel.  But the stuff that's going on these days isn't like that.  It's just harmful and ignorant to the original vibe and tonality of the music.

But go ahead, buy it and enjoy it if you can.  but trust me, if someone could give these compression conditioned people an example of quality mastering and dynamic range, there;'s no way they would come out saying something like this really sounds good.  But that's how it goes; people's ears get used to things...even if it's a near distorted wall of harsh sound like this.

reviewText: OK, maybe it's actually worth two stars, but I'm just trying to do my part to add some balance/objectivity/sanity to the reviews of this third-rate fake-psych dreck. I haven't read all the reviews here, but I bet most of them are from people who remember hearing the album in the era it was released in. Approaching this music free of nostalgia, and in context with all the music of the time and since, it's clear this band is barely holding it together, struggling for identity between "heavy" rock that makes Iron Butterfly sound graceful by comparison, and awkward folk-rock, like "Black Roses" -- not a terrible song, but marred by a vocal by a dude who sounds like he's gargling glue. Really, the most ham-fisted and brain-dead garage band of this era would be preferable to this, because at least bands like that knew how stoopid they were. This music, by contrast, reeks of pretension. These guys are only known today because they were Elektra's third rock band, after Love and the Doors, and their bassist played on the latter's sessions. Drummer Dallas Taylor later joined CSN and, eventually, Y. But those connections to music whose quality these hapless rockers could only dream of is no reason to subject yourself to, or waste your money on, this album. Look elsewhere, young jedi! Like here, for instance...Da Capo

reviewText:
OCTOBER 17, 2009
I originally reviewed this album back in June 2008 (the review is below) and I shredded this album pretty good.  Now, nearly a year and a half later, I felt compelled to "re-rate" this album.  Per my review below, make no mistake, this album is recorded and produced WAAAAAAAAAY too hot for my liking.  The volume is annoyingly loud, and I still wouldn't say the songwriting is top-notch.  But the hooks are still there, and inevitably, most of this album is fairly catchy.  The melodies stay with you, even if the lyrics don't.  I gave this album 1 star in my initial review, but I wanted to go on record here and say this album isn't THAT bad.  If I could change my review, I'd change it to two-and-a-half stars.  It isn't a bad album to buy used for $5.  I can't say I would buy it new at full retail price, because it just isn't that good.  In the scope of the Def Leppard catalog, I think it's one of their weaker albums, but it's still got enough of the classic Def Leppard sound that I can reasonably say it's "okay".

JUNE 5, 2008 REVIEW
I really can't believe how much I disliked this album.  I loved their previous album "Yeah" (and I have never been a fan of 70s glam).  I even liked "Euphoria" and "X".  I'm not one of these people who think, "they HAVE to have Mutt Lange" or "they haven't been the same since Steve Clarke died".  They've made good music without Mutt, and since Clarke's death.  But this album sounds like a disjointed, choppy mishmash of generic, bland rock music, with the volume turned up to 11 in an attempt to cover up the fact that the music is just unimaginative and uncreative.  If this album had been put out by a lesser band, it might not be so shocking to me.  But this is one of the all-time greats in my book, and I think this album is just a loud bore.
label: negative

reviewText:
It's ironic that Gardiner -- one of the conductors responsible for establishing "correct" performance style for Baroque music -- especially the use of flexible and imaginative (rather than  "metronomic") phrasing -- has presented us with a set of  Beethoven symphonies done in the worst-possible metronomic, overly fast  "Baroque" style.
Simply put, his tempos are breathlessly fast,  and _always_ inflexible. Unlike the classic Leibowitz and Harnoncourt  cycles, which provide fresh and sometimes profound insights, Gardiner's  "performances" are utterly mechanical. It's impossible to tell  whether these works are being played by human beings or a computer. If they  _are_ being played by people, it sounds as if they're trying to get home as  quickly as possible. (The Mackerras traversal of the Mozart symphonies is  similarly shallow, joyless, humorless, charmless, and overwrought.)
Don't  get me wrong -- I'm no fan of Furtwangler or Klemperer. "Slow" is  not "profound," nor does it automatically reveal musical  subtleties. It's how the conductor paces and phrases the music that opens  it to the listener's understanding. Gardiner's Beethoven is devoid of any  sort of intelligent or insightful interpretation.
Ideally, music should  "unfold" -- it shouldn't sound as if a human mind is  "interpreting" it. Listen, for example, to any of Fritz Reiner  performance's of Romantic music. There's no dragging or rushing, no obvious  imposition of the conductor's personality on the music -- but you are  unlikely to hear better interpretations. And these _are_ interpretations --  not bland traversals of the notes.
It's nice to see that reviewers in  Fanfare and The Abso! ute Sound are finally starting to talk about  "correct" performance practice for Classical and Romantic music,  and what a vast gulf there is between just playing the notes correctly and  bringing true insight, imagination, panache, and taste to  performances.
Gardiner's Beethoven cycle is one of the worst recordings  of all time. Had he applied the flair and insight he's shown for Baroque  music to Beethoven, we might have had a cycle that would have eclipsed all  others. Alas...
Get the Harnoncourt set if you want to experience  profound thinking about how Beethoven should be performed. And pick up  Gardiner's "Messiah," too (arguably the best recorded performance  this work has ever received), so you can hear what an incredibly clever and  insightful conductor he can be when he wants to.
PS: I wanted to give  this recording a negative rating, because it's beneath contempt. But I'm  forced to give it one star. It isn't worth even zero.

The performances on the songs are not very good or emotional.  Gillan's voice is really in bad form, like he has permanently damaged it (which is not the case since he sounds better on later albums).  Blackmore's guitar playing is the most uninspired I have ever heard from him.  When I got this, I had to check the credits because I didn't think Blackmore was even on it.

I've been a Deep Purple fan since In Rock came out (their 4th studio album).  I think the first three albums by group (with the original Mach I line up) are the best.  You can get these in a nice remastered boxset with all kinds of great bonus tracks.  However, it is probably not for those who think Battle Rages On is a great album.  Then, I really like the jam albums Live and Rare (it is also known as Scandanavian Nights and not to be confused with the other Live and Rare) and In Concert, with the 20 to 35 minutes jams.

reviewText:
I've been an avid Donald Fagen and Steely Dan fan ever since I discovered both upon the release of "The Nightfly" back in the early 1980s. I started listening to the Steely Dan albums in reverse order from that point on, then kept up with them as they released their albums in the new century. I've liked just about everything, although Becker's solo albums never were to my taste, and the Dan album "Everything Must Go" was a bit too by-the-numbers for my liking. I really like "Morph The Cat," Fagen's previous solo outing, and even have a warm spot for "Kamakiriad" which many others are now not fond of.

Having said that, I cannot exactly put my finger on why this album did not warm to me. The sound is as you'd expect it--clean and clear. Meticulous, even. Yet, the production feels as though it is lacking energy. The songs just don't fall into a groove or have the rhythmic drive like they did with The Nightfly or his other albums. The only song I found here that stands out and reminds me of his past recordings is "Memorabilia". Other than that, I don't find the songs to be memorable as they were in the past. There is nothing in this set that really reaches out and grabs me like all of the other solo albums. "Out Of The Ghetto" is the most embarassing production of Fagen's that I've ever heard committed to a recording: not only are the lyrics misplaced from his point of view, the production reeks of cheap nightclub jazz, like a band of washed-up jazzers trying to sound hip and cool.

The whole album sounds like aging hipster Muzak to my ears...and it hurts me to say it. The weak production does the music no favors either. Maybe bring Becker back on board to produce the next one.

As for sonics, I have both the high-resolution 24/96 download and the vinyl edition. I must say that the vinyl is also a disappointment. I have never been a fan of clear and/or colored vinyl, and this pressing is a prime example: clear or colored vinyl is noisier and scratches easier. I haven't scratched this one at all, but there is a very faint background noise which I hear on none of my other 180g vinyl pressings. The vinyl just doesn't sound like it is clean. It is like a combination of hiss and very fine crackle. A cleaning on the record vacuum might help it, but I doubt it--this just sounds like inferior vinyl to me. The digital version is in the typical antiseptic Steely Dan flavor as of late.

If you're a die hard fan or completist, the vinyl edition might be of interest. Otherwise, I'd pass on it and find a cheap CD. Musically I also found it to be a disappointment, and I find myself going back to the other three DF albums to get my fix. There really isn't anything I can say to recommend this album, except to fill a spot in your collection. "Memorabilia," as the song says. Give this one a pass. There are far better recordings of his out there.
label: negative

reviewText: Ray Wilson??? Genesis would have been better off signing Ray Walston for lead singer. At least there'd be some character and identity to the singing. Wilson was the Ted McGinley touch for Genesis- a last ditch effort to bail out a sinking ship. A lifesaver on something that should be euthenized. Wilson will go down to Genesis what Oliver was to the Brady Bunch. The absence of Collins was never more apparent than with this bomb of a CD, which I bought out of habit of buying anything with the "Genesis" brand name. I can say this for the CD: it makes an outstanding coaster for jumbo size travel mugs. "The Congo" was the band's big push to get radio play and some respectibility. The song did neither. Never were Genesis songs more mundane, pointless, uninspired and lacking the soul that was Genesis. It's true that the band had long grown away from it's original recipe. And you can always get an argument as to which era was the best. I personally liked the latter Gabriel- early Collins era the best. "Invisible Touch" was the last CD before my interest began to dwindle. But there's a reason that this version of Genesis had to cancel their tour to promote this CD: it stunk, and the public wasn't buying, CDs nor tickets to their shows. That had to be humbling to Tony Banks and Mike Rutheford, but not surprising, as any long time Genesis fan will tell you from the sales of CDs each made on solo efforts. Time and again I wipe the beverage stains off this CD and throw it on, juuuuust to make sure I didn't judge it to hastily. I didn't. Save your money. Buy a Steve and Edie, Robert Goulet, Starland Vocal Band, Partridge Family, or Donny Osmond recording. Any of them are more worth a liisten than this smear to the once cherished name of Genesis.

reviewText: Dreck, schlock, cheese... What an embarrassment it must be for Cohen -- if he actually does have a sense of shame -- that this recording exists still... what an, um, exercise in humility. Back when I was a younger man, more inclined to overconceptualize things, I thought that maybe the impossibly syrupy and trite arrangements were some sort of vast self-parody on Cohen's part, that he was deliberately mocking himself, achieving some sort of perverse self-transcendence by allowing himself to be contextualized in such an asinine way... I kind of got off on it, actually. "Memories," in particular, seemed more like a flagelletory orgy of self-contempt and a bad joke at the author's own expense than a sincere attempt to craft song. Maybe it was... I've briefly picked up this album to give it a spin after many years and just keep WINCING (and grinning). Poor Lenny. "Don't go home with your hard-on" IS a funny little keeper, among the wreckage -- with inaudible background vocals, so the liner notes claim, by Bob Dylan and Allen Ginsberg... But this album -- for Cohen's sake, leave it ALONE.

reviewText:
This is a copy-protected cd.  Why is this a problem?
a) It can't be copied, even for legally accepted personal use.
b) It *will not* play on computer cdrom drives, playstation, dvd players, or many portable car cd players.
Basically, it's useless.  I received a promo copy that won't even play on my *regular* stereo, which is gathering dust in the spare bedroom.  Hm.  So, in addition to everything else, it doesn't play on *old* cd players either.  As it turns out, Universal will be manufacturing all copies of this title this way, and will be moving "most" of its catalog to this format in 2002.
This cd *does not* conform to the Red Book Compact Disc audio requirements, and therefore qualifies as a defective product, not even as a cd per se.
I have no real interest in "ripping" this, as there are only a couple of songs that seem like they might be interesting, but as I listen to all my cds on one of two computers or the PS2, I can't even listen to the thing.
Consumer beware.

reviewText:
Motley Crue faced a difficult period in the 1990's and to certain extends the early 2000's. As a famous 80's act it was though for them to even manage to survive the 90's. Lead singer Vince Neil was out of the band in 1992 and the Crue had to adapt to the changing times and music scene and face a future without Neil. The 1994 self-titled album with replacement singer John Corabi was an excellent album but it didn't sound anything like Motley Crue and a lot of fans couldn't accept someone other than Neil fronting the band, and some people who liked it couldn't accept it because it has the words Motley Crue written on it. 1997's Generation Swine was the band's reunion album with Vince Neil back on board although it was clearly written with Corabi's voice and style in mind and Vince had to fit his voice into a mold that had already been made. Tommy Lee left the band after the Greatest Hits tour in 1999 an a year later we have New Tattoo, an album that aims to capture the band's sound of old whereas their previous two albums were products of their times. New Tattoo was written with Neil's voice in mind which should have been a step in the right direction and Randy Castillo replaces Tommy Lee on drums.

There aren't many high points on New Tattoo, the opening track "Hell On High Heels" is one song that I still play and I think it fits well along other Motley classics and somewhat succeeded at recapturing their 1980's heyday sound. The album starts out well with what is probably its best song but doesn't go far.  "Treat Me Like The Dog I am" is a tad too much on the repetitive and generic side. "New Tattoo" the title track is the second highlight for this fan, it's a slower song almost ballad-like and is one of the more enjoyable tracks of the album. The band's cover of "White Punks on Dope" is just a pain to listen to. Even the better songs like "Fake" and "Porno" stars are nothing special. The truth is New Tattoo sounds uninspired, unoriginal and tired and it's easily one of the worst Crue albums, a contender for sure.

It's not that Randy Castillo doesn't do a good job here but obviously Tommy Lee's drumming had elements that were crucial to the core of the Crue's sound. The drums here just sound dull and boring as if they're just going through the motions instead of playing a big part of the music like they used to. Even Mick Mars, who usually provides great riffs, flamboyant solos, dirty near bluesy on steroids and distortion-stuff fails to shine here. The version of New Tattoo I own has a bonus live disc consisting of six songs with Samantha Maloney (Hole) on drums but even that can't redeem this album. Interestingly future Sixx A.M. (Nikki Sixx's side project) collaborator James Michael gets co-writing credit on six of the songs.

Supposedly New Tattoo was made with the intention of being the album that could have been a follow up to Dr. Feelgood, honestly it simply doesn't work and falls far of achieving what it set out to do. The fact that Motley doesn't even play any songs from this album live is telling. I don't want to sound like the bad guy here but the last time I checked it's ok to have an opinion and this is mine, New Tattoo is a BAD album.  I think the follow up; Saints of Los Angeles (2008) fared much better and was much more honest and Motley-like album. 1 star for "Hell In High Heels" and the title track. Quite forgettable. Hardcore fans only.

reviewText: I honestly can't believe the ratings that are being given to this performance.  It seems to me that DG would almost be too embarrassed to actually publish this cd.  Practically everything that could have gone wrong musically, did.  But Karajan should carry most of the blame.  He obviously had no vision of the piece, had no idea how Bruckner composes, or knew what to do when very poor ensemble playing is happening right in front of him.  The Vienna Philharmonic might as well be playing without a conductor.  Karajan BARELY got away with glossing over Beethoven and Brahms.  Bruckner, however, is not a composer you just gloss over and have your poor intellect be covered up by the notes and harmonies.  When you have grotesque sentimentality coming from the strings,  immature playing on part of the brass players, and a conductor who is completely lost, you do not get a very performance.  There is really only one man who actually knew Bruckner's music and that is Sergiu Celibidache.  When you have audience members openly crying in a performance of a Bruckner symphony and a crowd that is so stricken with awe that they almost forget to clap, THEN you know you have a real performance. reviewText:
I realize you will never personally read this.  You undoubtedly now employ a legion of sycophants to perform such tasks for you.  Not so long ago, you were without doubt the most fastidious rock 'n roll performer around.  And your millions of adoring fans loved you for it.  Whether it was a recording session, a concert, a warm up gig in Asbury Park, you were meticulous in your preparation and presentation.  Now comes Magic, your latest CD release.  My, how times have changed.

I must say, I cannot have been listening to the same CD others have reviewed here and awarded 4 or 5 stars.  Maybe the CD I bought was defective.  But probably not, because others have noted the same deficincies I did.  Notably the sound quality. Half the songs are nearly unintelligible.  It sounds as though all instrument tracks and vocals were recorded simultaneously on a cheap cassette recorder you bought at the flea market.  What's that about?  How could you ever allow such a travesty to reach the market?  I read the lyrics in the booklet that accompanied the CD and it appeared you had lots of interesting things to say (as usual).  The problem is, there is no way I could (or anybody else could) possibly decipher your words on half the recordings.

The sound quality on your earliest recordings was vastly superior to this latest effort.  Phil Spector had his "wall  of sound."  I guess we can call this your "sinkhole of sound."  I literally checked all the connections on my CD player, amp, and speakers to see why the sound was so bad.  Then Magic played, and it sounded fine.  So I guess someone intentionally produced your music in this manner.  Why?!?!?  Is this some kind of a cruel joke?  Did you aim to turn out as poor a product as possible, and see if you could still make $10 million off of it?  Is this some jab at Sony over some contractural issue?

I realize you have had your problems in the past with the legal and business side of the music industry.  In the CD credits you list more lawyers and business people than musicians!  Is that what this is about?  Has it just become all about the Benjamins?  Well, if that's anywhere near the truth, you've lost the edge, buddy.  If that's what's going on, you need to hang it up, and pass the baton on to somebody else.

I grew up a couple towns away from you.  We're the same age, and lived through many of the same things.  When you sang about Keasby and Highway 9, I was right there with you.  I followed your career with interest since the early '70s.  My cousin and I even met you, and had a beer with you in a little bar in Asbury Park way back when.  You have certainly earned every success you enjoy, and I wish you many more.  But don't let this latest CD be the final chapter in your storied career.  Fix this horrible recording.  Insist it be re-engineered in accordance with current state of the art standards.  Your work deserves nothing less.  Let your fans trade their current CDs for a properly recorded version of your music.  But please,..., don't allow this CD to stand as is and become part of your legacy.  Unless it has become just about the Benjamins.  That will be too bad.  And a big loss to lots of fans.  But we'll get over it.  But I don't think that's how you want to go out.

Well, best wishes to you and yours.  Read back through some of your old lyrics and listen to some of your old recordings, and see which way you're gonna go with this.  I hope you'll do the right thing.

--A Big Fan

reviewText:
I am a huge fan of Oingo Boingo and I am not from the west coast.  I discovered the band in 1983 and listened to them at least once a week for about a decade.  I own everything they've ever released, in addition to some unreleased demos.  They are my favorite band of all time and I am grateful every day for their music.  So I am a geek for this band.  I hope I've made that clear.

I have a theory about Amazon reviews, which is that most people don't review albums they don't like.  It's unfortunate, because it puts the reviews and ratings completely out of balance.  Basically, you'd be hard pressed to find an album that has received a large number of negative reviews (I challenge you to find an album with 10+ reviews, where at least 6 of them are not positive).

My advice:  Unless you are a Boingo geek, like me, and must own it all, there is no reason to own this album.  It is by far the worst in their catalog.  When I bought it the week it was originally released, I was so excited to see the cool artwork on the cover (especially after the 80s paint-streaked cover of the preceding release,"BOI-NGO").  I was a bit disappointed with their previous album's sound - a bit too tame.  There were some great songs on it, though.  And the artwork of "Dark. . ." tricked me into believing this one would find the band back to their unique, weird sound I'd loved on their earlier releases.

Well, upon hearing the disk for the first time I was blown away by how awful it sounded.  Oingo Boingo always had a heavily produced sound.  And for me they were brilliant at walking the fine line between brilliant and cheesy (although most of my friends in North Carolina only heard cheese).  But "Dark. . ." just sucked.  Maybe they were feeling label pressure for another hit record like, "Dead Man's Party," or possibly they were trying to make a transition into the '90s.  Whatever the reason, this album sounded the least like Oingo Boingo to me.  I finally understood why my friends laughed at me for liking this band.  This album was awful.

The promotional photos on the inside of the CD jacket showed the band dressed in cowboy shirts - Danny had a bolo - and they did not look cool at all.  They looked like sales associates at Circuit City.  What the hell happened?

Steer clear of this release.  Get Nothing to Fear or Good For Your Soul or any other Oingo Boingo release than this one.

I think the folks who are giving positive reviews to this disk are either too young to know what Oingo Boingo is about and they're into really mainstream pop stuff like old Paula Abdul or they had a bad trip at one of the legendary Boingo Halloween Christmas shows in LA and have lost their sense of musical taste.  Regardless, this is a bad album.

But, with all of that said, a bad Oingo Boingo disk is still not the worst musical purchase you could make (assuming you have the rest of their amazing catalog).

Enter this "tunnel" at your own risk.

Terrible recorded sound and a soloist who has no grasp of the overall structure of the work and cannot convey the broad melodies that form the basis of this concerto puts this version at the BOTTOM of the shopping list.

Even Rubenstein, from 1959, in somewhat dated dry recorded sound is preferable to this: Rubenstein may offer a bland old fashioned approach but at least he conveys the magic of Chopin's music and the orchestral playing is clearly recorded with good overall balance.

Weissenberg/Skrowaczeski offer great recorded sound and an approach that is beyond this timid offering. If you want something DIFFERENT go for this 1968 recording which happened to be Glenn Gould's favourite version. It sounds far more daring, modern and interesting than Pogorelich in the 1980s. The Paris orchestra beats the pants off Chicago for sensitivity and sonority.

reviewText:
In the mighty history of rock music and all its joys and glories, there has never been any-one as completely out of touch and hapless as Gary Numan.
Fat and futile, Numan represents in a single human form, everything that's wrong, and ever has been wrong with popular music. Clunk-headed and entirely cretinous (whether crashing his plane in India and getting arrested for spying, or marrying his stalker), he is a career loser. Lacking soul, warmth or even - God help us - humanity, his miserable drones reveal better than any review the true depths of defeat and hopelessness he plumbs.

His contemporaries thrashed him outta sight: OMD, Eyeless in Gaza, Trio, even gimpy cruds like Blancmange kicked his rump effortlessly - but then they all had tunes, a modicum of self-effacement and weren't solemnly and indignantly pretending they were 'futuristic'.
Futuristic!? This stuff set music back 20 years - it was as if punk had never happened. Dressed in what looked like a DS9 leisure suit and with a voice so nasal it made Kenneth Williams sound like James Earl Jones, Gazza went on and on and on.... croaking incessantly about sub-Arthur C Clarke themes like alienation in (gulp!) the 'modern' world; dehumanising mechanization; space (the final frontier etc.. not the stuff between his ears!); bio-chemistry and the like - you get the picture.
Write down the most boring, nerdy topics you can think of and within an hour you'll have a pretty comprehensive and astute summation of 'The Pleasure Principle'.

Ever the space-cadet with the intellectual capacity of a weather-balloon, Gazza would have us believe he's some kind of proto-new wave Mr Spock, but in reality, he's more aligned with Kowalski out of 'Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea'; bashed with a spanner every week but relentlessly returning to stupidly get bashed again.

You can be too serious about this electro stuff. It had a bad rep as cloying and un-emotive, but others managed it ok. It was only Gazza who made himself a Holy Show with his Billy Idol snarl and short-circuited robo-dancing.

Begrudgingly; 'Complex' has the foetus of a good tune, soon lasered away by the unnecessarily brutal 'Metal'; smothered to death by Gazza's parachute in the guise of the hideous 'Random' and wait 'til you hear the live version of 'Me, I Disconnect From You' - a fun-packed extravaganza of doom and horror guaranteed to forever shift your aunt (y'know, the rich one, the one leaving all her money to the Battersea Dogs Home and none to you!) when she decides to descend on your parlour, tea, and scones.

Get those samples going, you don't need to hear the full album to experience the despondency and it's saying something when your brave-heart reviewer had to physically stop his ears oscillating, such was the feeling of discomfort and unease brought about by a cover version of 'On Broadway' - the final cankerous catastrophe.

This review could apply to any of Gary Numan's albums as they're all as bad as each other.

reviewText: For me the immediate musical connection I make with the film Philadelphia is that it features (in the party scene at the 74 minute mark) a genuine live performance by the gay male acapella group The Flirtations - starring the remarkably gifted singer/songwriter/composer Michael Callen. They sang their very camp arrangement of "Mr Sandman", which I'm happy to own on their truly brilliant CD album which was recorded in 1992 (and released in 1994): "The Flirtations Live: Out on the Road" The Flirtations Live: Out on the Road. I believe that it is simply and blatantly a massive wrongdoing for the soundtrack album of Hollywood's first major gay-themed film to have excluded this openly gay group, who were not only supremely talented musicians, but also vital gay community activists. Michael Callen died in 1993 (the year of the film's release) from AIDS related illness. He was open and honest about being HIV positive and maintained a high profile among ACTUP (AIDS Coalition To Unleash Power) activists who demanded government action on drug research and hastened availability. Michael was also a pioneer proponent of the concept of "safe sex" through condom use in order to limit the spread of HIV. There's a 4th February 1994 Entertainment Weekly article by Melina Gerosa (in their issue #208)in which she writes: "If you enjoyed the 30 seconds of a cappella singing during the party scene in Jonathan Demme's Philadelphia, don't rush out and buy the soundtrack album. The group seen in the film is the Flirtations, and their campy, customized cover of ''Mister Sandman'' -- with revised lyrics that include ''Give him two legs like Greg Louganis/But make him public about his gayness'' -- is available only on their album Live: Out on the Road (Flirt Records). While the all-gay vocal group may not share space on the Philadelphia CD with Bruce Springsteen and Neil Young, head Flirt Jon Arterton says the group is getting mainstream attention. ''We're attracting more and more straight and & 'homosexually challenged' people every day,'' Arterton, 48, says. That includes director Demme, who saw one of the Flirtations' posters while filming in Philly. ''I thought, 'A gay a cappella group?''' recalls Demme. '''We gotta have 'em.''' The fivesome -- Arterton, Cliff Townsend, Aurelio Font, Jimmy Rutland, and Michael Callen (author of 1990's best-selling Surviving AIDS) -- formed in New York in 1988, but their big break didn't come until 1991, when National Public Radio began playing their first album, The Flirtations. The network was swamped with would-be fans, who were directed to the only places you can find their albums: progressive and gay bookstores (and select Tower outlets). Later that year, on Donahue, the group serenaded the first televised gay wedding. Being excluded from the soundtrack album was a disappointment (''We kept waiting, but they never asked,'' says Arterton), but the Flirts have since faced a much graver loss: the AIDS-related death last December 27 of Callen. ''I wish he could have seen the film,'' says Arterton, who notes that the group has no plans to replace its beloved soprano. ''He was such a media whore -- it would have been very like him to dish it.'' Today, 16th October 2013, 20 years since the release of the film and the death of Michael Callen, I've just viewed the newly arrived Blu-Ray edition of Philadelphia and I'm happy to report that it looks and sounds magnificent - but I won't be bothering with the drastically incomplete and inadequate soundtrack CD.

reviewText: I did a 3 part review of this on a music board, that I'm going to attempt to port over here edited in a way that makes sense & doesn't violate any of Amazon's policies. This first part was written before I received the set. It ended up being pretty accurate, so........ Part 1: I did a bunch of comparisons with other releases. Here's what I've found: Disc 1: Otherwise unidentified 1967-68 versions of Dino's Song, Gold & Silver, I Hear You Knockin', Stand By Me & Calvary are also on the studio out takes disc 2 of the out of print Unreleased Quicksilver: Lost Gold and Silver. That would seem to leave at minimum 4-5 songs exclusive here. Unfortunately LG&S while a 100% official release doesn't give specific recording dates for either disc, so all I can do is guess. Disc 2: Voiceprint has 2 1966 Avalon shows, but no Fillmores. WGV also does not show anything from 5/66. There are both early & late shows circulating from Fillmore 2/4, 2/5 & 2/6 including on Wolfgang's Vault; 2/4/67 is one of the Voiceprint releases (as is 2/6/67). However the tracks here attributed to 2/4/67 are different than either of the Voiceprints & while all tracks show up on the WGV 6 show run, they're not even close to all being on 1 show. My GUESS is what they're calling 2/4/67 here is a "best of" the 6 shows. Disc 3: I have seen the 3 Fillmore tracks on boots, there is an 11 song 'leg circulating from 6/7/68 & 6/8/68 combined. WGV also has a 5 song 6/7/68; all three of these are on there. These same 3 titles (without month/day) are also on the live 1968 disc1 of the oop Lost Gold & Silver. The Winterland '70 seems to be 6 of the 10 tracks that WGV offers as 4/5/70. The Fool is not on the WGV show, in it's place is something called "Subway"; might they be the same song? If so these would be the first 6 of the WGV 10. If not this version of The Fool might be a rarity. I have not seen the Old Mill tracks elsewhere & I THINK most of the video on the dvd is new to me. So as far as the 3 cd's go, it APPEARS that 18 of the 42 tracks have a reasonable chance of being exclusive to this set; more if you don't consider legal WGV downloads as official releases due to there not being a physical disc involved. Part 2: I'll write more after I've played the entire set, but quick question: Did anyone else buy this? The last song on disc 2, "Who Do You Love", has got pretty loud digital static in the last 2 minutes or so. There are no scratches on the disc, so I am ASSUMING it's a mastering issue. I also scanned the cd with Nero CD/DVD speed. While the score of 98 / 745 C1 Errors/ Max 14 would cause me to throw out a burned disc (& there's no horrid error peaks at the end of the disc) , that does not account for the issue with Who Do You Love. I assume it is in the mastering. If you bought this, does your copy have the same issue? Quicky review of discs 1 & 2: Sound quality & performances vary wildly. It is pretty loud/compressed. Live stuff on D2 has problems with wow & flutter on the master tape, which makes the band sound a little out of tune. The reason I've never opened/bought any of the Voiceprints is I guessed they would be similar to the WGV's & the boots. Disc 1 has at least 5 tracks not on the out of print CCM. I did not compare every song, so no idea if the others are the same. The CCM studio disc (equivalent to disc 1 here) has better sound. Another interesting note is nothing is mentioned here about licensing . The CCM states everything was licensed from Capitol, though since all this stuff is also showing up on Voiceprint UK & Wolfgang's Vault USA, who knows who owns it? I just scanned the dvd. Very disappointing, it is bootleg quality. The first 3 tracks are watchable, though they should be better as they are from legit films; the rest is poor bootleg quality, though the audio on the 6 Winterland tracks is better than the video, on fact as far as wow & flutter the audio on the Winterland part of the dvd is better than anything on disc 2, though the tone is a bit muffled. Packaging is pretty nice except for the cardboard sleeves with no inner sleeves. The booklet is long on photos (a good thing) & short on information about the tracks. One interesting note; the included "poster" is cloth! While I haven't played D3 yet, my suggestion is unless you're a hardcore fan, save your $'s. Wish I would have. Part 3: Fillmore East 6/7/68 on disc 3 is by far the best of this set. Great stuff. WGV also shows this date, they add Codine (one of my fav QS songs), but omit Back Door Man; which they have from 6/8/68; probably the same source as for this one. Winterland 1970 has mediocre sound (though better than disc 2), but is ruined by Dino Valenti's vocals. 3/29/70 is just a sloppy jam with no audible bass guitar on much of it; the bass fades in & out on "Rain". Pluses: 6/7/68 & a few tracks here & there; attractive booklet Negatives: Crap bootleg sound (& video) quality on most of it, no info in the booklet (I had to look up band members for each show on Wolfgang's Vault), & many weak performances. My advice to QMS fans: If you'd like rarities buy the out of print CCM set on Amazon Unreleased Quicksilver: Lost Gold and Silver & 6/7/68 (& possibly 6/8/68). The CCM set also doesn't give specific dates, so I am wondering if disc 1 on LG&S is a compilation of 3/4 of 6/7/68 & 6/8/68. Unfortunately, even if it is the sound quality on the live disc of LG&S isn't very good; lots of wow & flutter. I'm also really curious about the licensing issues, as WGV has a ton of QMS & my understanding is they are licensing everything they sell, & Voiceprint has also really numerous QMS live 2 cd sets from these same shows, & they are also known for acquiring licenses.

reviewText:
Dear Robert Smith,

Hello. How are you today? Let me just tell you that your early work, everything from 1978 to 1992, was great and thanks. But this record here sir, this is strike three, your third crappy record in a row, and I'm afraid to say that I've about had it. We all remember how "Wild Mood Swings" was one of the most unlistenable piece of garbage ever, and its followup, "Bloodflowers" was a feeble and uninspired attempt to stay relevant in the face of nu-metal.

But somehow fortune has shined its good graces on you and you are now an elderstatesman of alternative rock, and why not celebrate with a new record? One that shows your position is justified. One that shows the world the Cure still have it and can still write amazing tunes. But it seems that while your weist line has expanded to monolithic proportions, your work ethic has greatly declined, being that there is not one decent, memorable moment on this whole record.

Let's take your lead off track, "Lost" for example. Built around the ugliest, most redundant riff ever, you wail off key while this version of the Cure tries desperatly to keep up. This track sounds as though you are ripping off a Cure cover band. As the record progresses over the next eleven tracks, this didn't seem to be a throwaway track either. It was a mission statement. A mission statement of sucking.

Through the entire course of the record the lyrics are border line retarded, the guitars sound out of tune, and that ungodly wail that you proclaim to be your singing voice now is so hideously off key that I needed an asprin to finish the remainder of the record(somthing simiular to my "Wild Mood Swings" experince).

Sure, all right, "Anniversary" is all right, but for the life of me I remember absolutley nothing about it now. There are no memorable melodies over the course of this sad excuse of a record.

The guitars and vocals are too high in the mix, the keyboards almost non-existant. And, a question I have to ask: where is Simon "Elvis" Gallup? His melodic bass lines where the driving parts of many of your best songs, but here he seems sadly M.I.A. Was he at the pub trying to numb himself after hearing this schlock replayed over the studio moniters?

It reads in the booklet that this record was recorded in the Spring of 2004 and released a mere two to three months later. And that's exactly how it feels. It feels as though this record was written and recorded in a weekend to capatilize on your new hipness. But I don't buy it. I recomend to you that you take a listen to your back catalog to remember what made the Cure a great band in the first place: atmosphere, melody, heart, emotional vocals that never over took the songs. You know, just all around good songs.

Something that "The Cure" lacks in abundance.

Please write good music again. There is a Ho-Ho in it for you my friend.

THANKS

---CURE FAN

Pop Kulcher Review: According to Amazon. Com, people who bought this cd also bought greatest hits collections from Boston, Journey, Foreigner, and Styx. What I'd like to know is, where ARE these people? Is there any way we  can round them up? Our safety is in jeopardy as long as they live among  us.
Now, personally, I know some people who own one of these albums,  maybe even two. They're good people -- culturally famished, obviously;  lacking in taste, unquestionably -- but not necessarily people you'd cross  the street to avoid. But people who own ALL FIVE of these albums? I must  admit, it's difficult to visualize the sort of person whose record  collection includes Styx, Foreigner, Boston, Kansas, and Journey. I suppose  they would have a bit of Bad Company, Survivor, REO Speedwagon, and  Meatloaf thrown in for the sake of variety. The walls would no doubt be  adorned by posters of Molly Hatchet and black velvet unicorns. X-Men comics  would litter the closet floor; a few faded photos of Heather Locklear would  be tucked beneath the mattress.
While it is tempting to gather these sad  misfits and lock them away from civilized society, we must -- MUST -- hold  out some hope for their redemption. Find these people, my friends, find  them SOON. Buy them a Clash album, some early R.E.M., some Replacements.  Offer them moderate doses of the Velvet Underground and Sonic Youth and  Pavement. With care and nurturing, we CAN redeem them. Onward!

reviewText:
MJXM hit the nail on the head.  Geffen records (the label that swallowed up Rawkus) is simply trying to cash in on Rawkus' great past.  The problem is this album is nothing more than a glorified Mos Def's Greatest Hits album.  Are the songs on this album great?  No question about it.  But Rawkus' history is way deeper than Mos Def, Talib Kweli, & Common -- these are the artists being headlined on this album if you read the sticker on the front(and Common was never even on Rawkus).  Where's Shabaam Sahdeeq or Company Flow?  How about some cuts from Soundbombing I & II as well as Lyricists Lounge I & II?  Do they mean to tell me that Pharoahe Monche's "Simon Says" wasn't worthy of an appearance?  Hi Teknology had some bangers on it as well.  And then the the few songs they have from the albums I mentioned aren't even the best songs from their respective albums.  There are so many great songs in Rawkus' catalogue and this is just lazy and pitiful.  This album should be viewed as an insult to a great legacy and a testament to the greed of major labels.  No one wants to make good music (or at least a decent compilation), they just want to make money.

I do understand that this is the first installment, but this album simply lacks variety.  There shouldn't be any problem mixing things up with the catalogue that Rawkus has.  A good 80% of these songs feature Mos Def.  I love Mos as much as the next Joe, but this is simply overkill.  If you were a fan that bought the albums and singles when they were coming out then there's no need to pick this one up.  If you don't have these songs, you're probably not a big Rawkus fan anyway.  Let's just hope they even things up with the second installment instead of throwing their most popular astists on the album in hopes of moving units.

reviewText: I continue to be amazed at the mostly very positive reviews "Aloha" gets here and elsewhere.  While I am an enormous fan of 70's Elvis, this famous recording for me is the King at his nadir.  I have to be honest about this even though it may be painful: he clearly is out of it throughout the concert, sounding weak and disinterested.  I didn't expect explosive performances on the rockers, but at this point in his career he could at least perform ballads with real soul and emotion; don't expect that here.  Listening to the Beatles' "Something" makes me want to cringe; his vibrato out of control, no power or authority in his voice... what are people hearing in this depressing, dispiriting recording?  The arrangements are lackluster, and at least on the original LP, the packaging is a disgrace (as per RCA usual): among the graphic design embarassments is a shot of some Hawaiian lovelies posing with a cardboard cutout Elvis... couldn't he even make it to the photo shoot?  I know the many many die-hard fans refuse to accept that Elvis may have been capable of sub-par material, but unfortunately he was, and "Aloha From Hawaii" is surely a prime example.

With a discography as large as the Stones, it's inevitable you will hit a speed bump or two. Unfortunately, this vile creation is quite a stain on the band's earlier history. Some of the worst possible songs are selected for covers, and while the original material still outshines this material, it's of a lesser quality than on the previous 2 outings.

'Heart Of Stone' is one of the originals, and is by far the best on the album. It foreshadows the darker, rougher edge that would surface on later albums, but it is nowhere near the quality of those later efforts. The rest of the album is an absolute waste. I cannot, in any way, understand how 'Little Red Rooster' topped the British charts. Granted, it was 1965 and the song is mostly famous for showcasing Brian Jones talents, but the song is just embarassing lyrically, and as with most of the blues the Stones covered, it's musically a drag. Other songs like 'Mona (I Need You Baby' and 'Baby (We Got A Good Thing Goin' suffer the same problem. Honestly it's torturous having to sit through such quagmires of sound.

This is undoubtably one of the worst albums I've managed to sit through, and should be avoided by all under any circumstance.

reviewText:
Slayer really dropped the ball after Seasons in the Abyss -which even then wasn't a great album but certainly was decent. Divine had maybe 3 or 4 good songs on it and everything after was a joke. Now I've been into Slayer back before anybody knew who they were, when they were playing small venues in L.A. and back when they wore the ridiculous make-up and armor.

In short, God Hates Us ALL is an exhausting album. Yawn here Yawn there. Bloodline is the only song that even remotely flirts with melody. Paul Bostaph's (of Forbidden) drumming is pretty good, but since they can't seem to write a half decent song his efforts are wasted.

Slayer definitely had one of the greatest outputs of any bands in metal genre. Show No Mercy, Haunting the Chapel, Hell Awaits, Reign in Blood and South of Heaven are all still really good and stood the test of time. But this? Here is a band that is actually afraid of trying something new. The last time they did that (for South of Heaven) I remember everyone trashed them for it. reviewText:
Aerosmith rolls out of bed for a snore-fest, just as they do every ten years or so.  Only this time, they forgot to change their man-diapers.  I'm a devoted fan from Boston, and remember when they walked on water at WBCN, in the Fens, at the Rat and Paradise, etc.  So, I go way back.  I want to like their new stuff.  I long to like their stuff.  It's "me".

I felt as flat as warm beer in a lip-stick rimmed Solo cup from last night's Allston rave when I played this lousy CD.

The songs on this CD are as lifeless as a blow-up doll after a Boston College frat party.  They reek like the hairless armpits of a neurotic Harvard undergrad during finals week.

Honestly, if you just listen to the samples on Amazon and iTunes, you get a sense of how spiritless these tunes really are. Smells like teen spirit?  Try: smells like Rico Petrocelli's bedside commode.

No sense wasting your dollars on what will be -- along with "Just Push Play", "Nine Lives", "Night In The Ruts", to name a few of their Pepe LePew albums -- nothing more than recycled insulation blown into the walls of your crazy Auntie Jean's Hampton Beach rental bungalow.

It's a shame, because the brilliance of this band --"Pump", "Rocks", "Toys", hell, even the sloppy "Draw The Line" -- is truly awesome, memorable and "crankable".  An aural eargasm.  Those are "stand and beat your chest like a great baboon" CDs.  Even the snot-nosed, AM radio friendly molasses that is "Get A Grip" is better than "Dimension".  And "Get a Grip" stinks!

The "Dimension" CD is like a whoopie cushion with a hole in it.  Full of promise for a good time, laughs and fun, but ultimately a deflated mess.
label: negative

reviewText: After a lifetime supply of movies and two wildly successful albums, Jennifer Lopez aka J. Lo-or, now, 'Jenny'-decides to crank out a third attempt at making a big name for herself in the music world: 'This Is Me...Then,' whose tragic missteps are far more drastic than anything her previous work can make up for. Filled to the brim with uninteresting, uninspired ballads that Jennifer's weak voice can't handle, this is easily the worst album to her name. Its lone standout track, the guiltily infectious "Jenny From The Block," is hardly enough to redeem J. Lo's reputation as a worthwhile artist. And even that song feels blameworthy, because her desperate attempt to prove to the world that she's just your ordinary neighborhood diva falls embarrassingly flat when she starts quoting other songs of hers ('I'm real, I thought I told ya') and glorifying her other misadventures experienced throughout the road of stardom ('I've really been on Oprah, that's just me/From In Living Color and movie scripts To On the 6 to J. Lo to this headline clips I stayed grounded as the amounts roll in). "I'm Glad," is another track that stands out, I suppose, because though its lyrics are typical, it does have a catchy rhythm and is one of the few tracks here with a mid-tempo beat. But the rest is pure, mindless filler, to the bitter end, complete with the Ashanti-esque ballad, "The One." And no matter how much of an Affleck fan you are, "Dear Ben" is conspicuously mawkish-and heh-I guess you regret that one today, don't you, Jen? Anyway, J. Lo needs to lay off the dreary R&B and hip-hop and reuse the formula that made her millions in the music world-if she's not willing to do that, then she needs to leave and take this miserable excuse for an album and her self-proclaimed realness with her.

reviewText:
Chances are this review is going to make you mildly irritated if you're the kind of person who becomes defensive over music that is not your own. Don't take this the wrong way if you're unfamiliar with what I'm talking about. I probably can't avoid appearing dismissive of the artist as opposed to just this album so I'll just say right now that it's not my intention. Rather, I'd like to extend a recommendation and explain why: do yourself a favor: pick up a copy of Geogaddi or Music Has the Right to Children by Boards of Canada - the band which provided literally everything that Tycho launched his entire career with. There is a stupidly high count of musicians attempting to emulate their signature sound, many of which have signed to labels and attained various degrees of commercial success, but Tycho is the only one I've seen that seems to have no dignity, literally going far beyond imitation and straight into ripping them off in so many aspects while bringing absolutely nothing new to the table on this release. It is approximately an hour and ten minutes of what I can't quite call plagiarism and yet "generic" isn't quite heavy enough. I don't hand out a 1/5 rating lightly. I've nothing against the guy personally and he's since shifted in style, but the method employed to get him anywhere in the first place was nothing but honing the skill of emulation. From all the music to the nature theme to track titles like "Sunrise Projector", he dishes out an extremely watered down third rate version of something you could be hearing done far better and earlier. To no surprise, Tycho tends to either indirectly target or just incidentally has garnered a different audience as well, and of course, they never seem to be familiar with even well-known early innovators associated with ambient techno/downtempo/et al such as Aphex Twin, let alone anyone else that I hear very clearly and abundantly borrowed from here.

In short, it's "IDM" for the "chillout" niche of the "EDM" crowd. On this album, Tycho is to BoC as Owl City is to The Postal Service. People who have never heard anything like this before will find some ear candy here and they may enjoy it, but anyone not as naive will find this lackluster. Generally speaking, I wouldn't give it such a low rating for this reason alone as there are plenty of albums that are essentially the exact same thing. The key difference here is that the artists behind these albums didn't have the shamelessness to take their bandcamp releases without any sort of innovation and charge this much money for them. Tycho had no problem with this. Therefore, at the risk of sounding overly contentious (and I don't really care to be honest how this comes off), this spade deserves to be called a spade and nothing more. There is so much music on par or greater than this in the realm of "sounds like Boards" that is completely free and if you're going to pay for it, get the real thing.

b) the whoa ho ho ho ho's
c)the riff ad nauseam's.
d)Harris being present

Shadows of the Valley too had some potential but was spoiled by some of the same old ...

The other tracks are awful, but out of respect and also weariness I won't get into them.

I've got to be kind, they seem to be trying something, despite the cliches which they or Harris seem to be beyond controlling ...

This is a collection of mostly somber yet mild ballads that lack musical substance as well as meaningful lyrics. The songs all follow a pattern that are trying to say something, but I am having a hard time understanding exactly what. It sounds more like Savage Garden meets Jars of Clay with a rock track thrown in here and there. Sure, they toss in the F-word a couple of times to remind us they're still trying to be edgy, but it comes off as pretentious. This really is an embarrassing attempt from a band that successfully bridged the gap between nu-metal and hip-hop with their previous two albums. Make no mistake, I think Hybrid are the finest breakbeat production team around. Their album from 1999-2000 WIDE ANGLE (released in the U.S. as WIDER ANGLE) is a masterpiece of dance music, enhanced by the Russian Federal Orchestra conducted by Sacha Puttman. However, REMIX AND ADDITIONAL PRODUCTION BY..., a mixed compilation of several of their remixes for other producers, is ultimately a disappointment.
REMIX AND ADDITIONAL PRODUCTION BY... lacks some of their most amazing remixes, such as that of BT - "Godspeed" or Moby - "South Side." Instead, much of this compilation consists of lackluster remixes (Moby - "Bodyrock") or shamelessly commericial radio-friendly efforts (Filter - "Take a Picture"). I was very pleased by FSOL - "Papua New Guinea", which took an early trance classic and updated it for a comeback in today's progressive scene, but one shouldn't buy the whole CD for that single track.
REMIX AND ADDITIONAL PRODUCTION BY... isn't really a misstep by Hybrid. After all, it seems to be marketed to a commercial audience and not to underground fans of progressive breakbeat, but in my opinion fans of Hybrid's work will not be happy with purchase of this compilation.

reviewText:
Being the President of the Australian Knappertsbusch Association, I knew beforehand I was going to loathe this convergence of Mackerras and the Scottish Iceberg Chamber Orchestra: so it proved to be. The laudatory snippets from the Gramophone - nowadays, it's the Inner Station of the Last Man - razzed me up further. Worse still, an old English nursery-rhyme came to mind as the torture began:

Jack Sprat (Mackerras) could eat no fat.
His wife (Lenny) could eat no lean.
And so between them both, you see,
They licked the platter clean

Whatever the implications of this might be, it befouled me further. Before we deal summarily with the performances in question, chastisement is required:

IRR: "...a performance of absolute mastery." International Record Review. Response: that Fifty Shades of Grey stuff is more invasive than what I realised. On the basis of this claim, the Gimp is alive and well and enchained at the organisation in question.

Recommended: "there's so much to enjoy on these discs...and vivacity aplenty" Gramophone. Response: why thank you, Martha Stewart!

Classical CD of the Week: "Those who bought the last instalment will not want to miss this outstandingly well-engineered sequel." (four stars) Sunday Times. Response: this comment was directed at the coprophiliacs in our midst.

"Mackerras is the man, with rhythm and vigour to the fore." (four and a half stars) BBC Music Magazine. Response: geez, this makes the mild-mannered Australian conductor sound like Austin Powers, the International Man of Mystery, does it not? Did he drive a Shaguar?

"...it's hard to imagine the final climax of the Linz more conclusively or majestically presented." (four stars) The Guardian. Response: as the words `Majestic' and `Mackerras' are antonyms, this claim left me in a Sonny Liston state of mind, staring up at the ceiling from the canvas.

"This is some of the best Mozart I have ever heard..." (five stars) Audiophile Audition. Response: this guy must have just seen Amadeus for the first time.

"Some of the best Mozart symphony recordings ever?" (five stars) Classic FM Magazine. Response: do you really want an answer to this question? Praise the Lord and pass the mesh-lined sick-bags.

"Mackerras has an unparalleled feeling for Mozart style..." (five stars) Financial Times. Response: tell that to the shade of Bruno Walter. Verily, the Day of the Locust is upon us.

"Each of the disc's five symphonies is a gem in its own right...The glorious results are self-recommending." BBC Online. Response: champ, those gemstones are more vitreous than what you suspect!

"Everything comes stamped with character, intelligence and beauty." (four stars) The Times. Response: King Lear just sent through an invitation to join him on the heath. The prospect is enticing.

If you're attuned to diet-Marriner where the chamber-orchestra in question is the usual two-stroke engine job with no tonal allure to its name, clover awaits you. This is a small-scale Mozart who ain't dangerous or transfigurative in the least. Its rectitude - keep those repeats a'comin' Sir Charles - is in inverse proportion to its visionary reach. Play it to your old maid of an Aunty: she will swoon. Play it to your pooch: it will yap. Play it at bingo: to the last, the old buggers will rise as one. Luxuriate in geniality and rollicking good tunes!

reviewText:
Chingy - Powerballin' (2004, 2nd album)
Explicitness:  4/5
Lyrics:  1/5
Production:  2/5
Overall Rating:  1.5/5

*sigh* I didn't want to dislike this CD but...

Chingy was on top of his game when he released his debut album, Jackpot, but this CD is a different story.  His new album flopped because he didn't spend enough time in the studio thinking it up.  Plus, the last time he was heard of was only from the fairly recent (at the time) hit, "I Like That", which he was featured in, and people thus were getting tired of him.  In case you haven't noticed, this CD's overall rating is below three stars, and many of the helpful reviews have only one star.  In fact, the only hit off this album was "Balla Baby", and that was only minor.  "Don't Worry" never got anywhere.

This album's terrible, and the only songs really worth listening to are "Give Em Some Mo", "Balla Baby", and "All The Way to St. Lou".  Everything else is unlistenable.  Filler infests nearly ever track on Powerballin', like on "Wurr Da Git It Gurlz At" and "I Do".

Production from the Trak Starz is nothing to be impressed about, especially in tracks like "Fall-N" and the "Lil Jonish" "Balla Baby Remix".  They seem to be created in a way that would get tiring once combined with the inferior lyrics.  This is especially true in "We Do", where in the chorus, the music holds and then soon bangs on the percussion on every syllable of, "We Do!", which the big Bun B yells out.

Wack guest stars that mostly no one knows about also pollute the album, like in "Make That [Thing] Talk" (which features Ziggy, and no, it's not Bob's son) and the absolutely hideous "We Do" (which features Bun B), and too many of the songs feature a fake group called G.I.B. (B.I.G. spelled backwards?) or its members.  G.I.B. makes five appearances on Powerballin', which makes me wonder if Chingy should really be called Chingy & G.I.B. instead.

Lyrics are also terrible.  By listening to this CD, you'll think that Chingy wasn't even trying to write them carefully, especially in "Fall-N", where the intro constantly repeats, "Fall-N (pushin' n*****)", and "We Clubbin'" doesn't even have a point.  If you want interesting lyrics, you don't need to make them so annoying - just make them innovative - and Chingy seems to lack this skill.  The only possibility for an advantage in the lines (the limited usage of the f-word) was completely negated once "Bring Da Beef" ruined that with a chorus replete with the expletive.

As mentioned earlier, the only good (if even acceptable) tracks are "Give Em So Mo", thanks to its catchy beats and Chingy-feel; "Balla Baby", because of its dope lyrics; and the catchy "All The Way To St. Lou", which features David Banner and a nice-but-weak chorus from Nate Dogg (he's featured in everything, but doesn't do well when he releases his own album).  Other people seem to be okay with "26's" and "Don't Worry", but 26's annoying point of big wheels plagues it while it suffers from mediocre production, and "Don't Worry", the only slow track on the album, sounds marginal with Janet Jackson's cheesy chorus and the Trak Starz' boring music.

One other stupid thing is that the outro comes before three other mediocre tunes (including the "Balla Baby Remix") that are supposed to be bonus tracks but are just regular songs that are even listed on the back of the CD case.

Once this CD has reached its end, you're bound to be completely exhausted by all that horrible music without any break.  It seems as if Chingy is going in another direction - the direction of being repetitive and drunk-sounding - and that's why this album flopped.  Chingy is no longer what he used to be; Jackpot might be a much better album than this.  It certainly won't be long before Chingy retires.

I recommend music from Snoop Doog or Jadakiss if you want rap, but if you need a St. Louis rapper, at least buy from J-Kwon, since the beats produced by Jermaine Dupri that he raps over are dope.

reviewText:
Everyone's favorite burlesque troupe and leather corset supporters return to the pop spotlight with second album, the rather cockily titled Doll Domination. It's not clear what arena of the pop world they are trying to dominate, as few can claim to be as overtly skanky since Christina Aguilera's "dirrty" days and none are as completely and totally manufactured as the Dolls (although Danity Kane comes to mind), who branched out from stripping in a series of calculated moves to become famous that included a reality program, a Vegas show, and some classy clothing.

Doll Domination immediately plays its best hand off the bat with lead single "When I Grow Up," an electro-pop song about vapidity that signifies everything that is wrong with the Dolls' music and sounds eerily similar to Basement Jaxx's far superior 2003 track "Plug It In.". Bouncy synth lines and thudding bass provided by A-list producer? Check. Voices Auto-Tuned to perfection? Check. Lyrics about being famous and rich that include such Hilton-esque lines as "you can talk about me / `cause I'm a hot topic"? Check. Sure, it's catchy, but if you're looking for any sort of depth or anything more than a guilty pleasure, you're not going to get it here.

Unbelievably, the album continues for fifteen (!) more songs, all of them marking a low point in the 2008 music year and none of them approaching the single marketability of "When I Grow Up." Snoop Dogg's entirely appropriate guest spot on "Bottle Pop" (after all, he did host a few Girls Gone Wild) is one of the weaker ones of his career to say the least, and the track's lackluster chorus deflate any energy he might have afforded them. Although the Dolls didn't hold back on production, which benefits from help by Timbaland and Darkchild, or guest spots from R. Kelly, Ne-Yo, and Missy Elliot, no amount of help is able to give the Dolls any sort of identity separate from the obvious "models playing as singers."  Main singer Nicole Scherzinger's vocals come off as vanilla diva pop, and while the beats are definitely club-ready, there is nothing mind-blowing enough here to qualify the Pussycat Dolls as anything more than artificial pop stars propped up by an industry desperate to make a buck.
label: negative

reviewText:
Of course, the reason we loved Suede was that they were different from all the rest, a glitter of artifice in a smog of earnest, 'normal', indie rock.  Their influences were limited, but impeccable - the arch gallows humour and literate sensitivity of The Smiths; the sonic adventurousness of Bowie; the rawk assault of The Stones - situated in Brett's mental map of London, with its ephemeral joys and tatty lows, grounded in a very real, detailed, grimy London, as suggested by the title of their masterpiece, 'Dog Man Star', the old Oscar Wilde gutter/stars aesthetic, that wrenching pull between physical excitement and spiritual abandon best expressed in those huge, excessive, reckless ballads.
That Suede is no more.  Suede have become a conventional rock band, glorying in the cliches - black T-shirts; serious 'acoustic' solo numbers; talk about clear, taut, classic rock, without the embarrassing frills, all ambiguity and idiosyncracy ironed out.  In one interview, Brett used the damning phrase 'You can't make an omelette without breaking eggs'.  That's about the level of imagination that went into the making of this album, all colourless retreads of former glories, and tired tales of the nuclear city.  No thanks.
