reviewText: This is a 5 stars album no doubt about it, BUT!... The 45th Anniversary Super Deluxe Edition contains three mixes, of the original album. Plus new/original mixes of the songs from "VU" and "Another View" The last two discs are live recordings from 1969, taken from "The Matrix Tapes". The performances on "1969: The Velvet Underground Live" comes from those tapes too, and some of the songs are dublicated here. Some of the song like "Sister Ray" are also dublicated (but as inferior audience recordings) on The Quine Tapes. So there is barely anything new on the 45th Anniversary Super Deluxe Edition. Polydor chose to release half the songs from "The Matrix Tapes" on this expensive 6 disc set, and only 1 year later "The Complete Matrix Tapes" on another new 4 disc box set. A lot of fans were cheated. They were mainly interested the 6 disc, because they wanted the Matrix live recordings, and would never bought it if they knew, that the complete Matrix recording would be released in just a year. A very deliberate way for Polydor to milk the fans, and a dirty trick even for record label.

At first I tried not to hold this album against the band.  They'd release good albums from Queensryche through HITNF and while Q2k was a really bad album, they rebounded with a couple of eh ok releases in Tribe and Mindcrime 2.  Key words there being ok releases, not exactly stellar, but at least they had hope of being good again.

Well this is the first albu since Q2k for me to like less than 5 songs, and it wouldn't be the last.  Course I didn't know that at the time.  I figured it's a covers album, so I can't be too harsh on them for it.  And I'll try not to be.  Overall a lot of the aspects of the band since Degammo left are here, the bad production, Tate's overly produced voice which sounds like crap, mostly.  Overall I just really didn't like much on here.  Welcome To The Machine and Neon Nights were ok, but I'd rather listen to the originals, Tate these days can't hold a candle to David Gilmour or Dio, and Dio was always better anyways, but they play these songs well enough.  Most of the others I care nothing for either way.  Sure I don't like them, but I haven't listened to them in years, so I won't even bother with them.  I do have to ask..  For What It's worth?  Really?  Another cover of this song?  How many bands have done this song?  Just ouf of bands I like, recently at this point, think back to 07, and Rush had just released a version of it on their covers album in 04 or 03, don't remember, and Ozzy Osbourne did a covers album, and put this song on it in 05.  If Queensryche had done it first, I'd have given it a chance.  As it was, I never had a desire to listen to it.  I know of at least 2 other covers of this song too, not even including the original.

Now the little good.

I actually found Innuendo to be the best albeit only an ok song, on here, and Red Rain was decent.  Red Rain actually features Tate's best vocal performance, largely due to the fact they didn't ruin his voice with crappy production, and actually allowed it some room to breathe.  he sounds fairly good on this song, and it's the other song I like off of this otherwise useless album.

This sadly would not be their low point as they'd release their 2 worst albums yet, as of 2011 in subsequent years, American sldier and Dedicated to chaos, just awful.

Still some will enjoy this album for what it is, but I personally did not.

reviewText:
Let us return to the days of bedtime stories. I quote tid bit from wikapedia:

"An Emperor who cares for nothing but his appearance and attire hires two tailors who promise him the finest suit of clothes from a fabric invisible to anyone who is unfit for his position or "just hopelessly stupid". The Emperor cannot see the cloth himself, but pretends that he can for fear of appearing unfit for his position; his ministers do the same. When the swindlers report that the suit is finished, they mime dressing him and the Emperor then marches in procession before his subjects, who play along with the pretense. Suddenly, a child in the crowd, too young to understand the desirability of keeping up the pretense, blurts out that the Emperor is wearing nothing at all and the cry is taken up by others. The Emperor cringes, suspecting the assertion is true, but holds himself up proudly and continues the procession."

In a nutshell what we have here is an amateur who:

1- Can't play very well (all tracks are the most basic of basic, no high musicianship whatsoever on this collection)
2- Can't write very well (Lots of "speech singing" here, someone writes our words and forces them into ill competent backing tracks)
3- Can't sing very well (falsetto meaning false, one who can't really sing so to mask the poor voice the falsetto is used as a cover)

So little musical effort was put into the creation of this CD. It's the most basic of basic. The most lazy of lazy. The most droning on of droning on. In all honesty, this is the ultimate of dull & boring.

Don't believe all the hype from those who say this is the greatest thing to ever emerge from a music maker. It's not. Once again critical praise for something like this is one of the reasons releases like this give the current music realm a bad rap. As far as musical substance it's simply NOT THERE.

reviewText:
I caught the Goodman Theatre production in Chicago and enjoyed it immensely, although it was obviously greatly flawed. I was fairly sure that several of the numbers were going to have to be cut before it reached Broadway--and I assumed they'd be cut before it reached the Kennedy Center--and that the name would have to be changed. The book was actually much stronger than the score, which is unusual in a Sondheim production, but the book was entertaining, the staging was effective, and Richard Kind, although he can't sing at all, was great.

Well, here is the score in its likely final form. The show is still called "Bounce!" (joining the not-so-proud tradition of hyperbolic exclamation-point musicals). All the numbers are intact (with the addition of a very lame "bonus track" number that never even made it to Chicago). I've listened to the cast record many times now, and on the whole I can't stand it. I know all of Sondheim's scores, and there's no question in my mind that this is the worst.

The packaging is disproportionately lavish (disproportionate to the lack of content on the disc itself), which to my mind makes the thing even sadder.

reviewText:
Songs like Superman, Empty Box, Invert, Teddy Bear and the like are engraved in my mind forever! Simply put, they're classics that made Blindside's previous releases some of the most amazing and more importantly, memorable, rapcore/hard rock albums I've ever heard. Unfortunately, with "Silence" the group decided to get a new producer for the 2nd straight album, and as much as I hate to admit it, the quality of music has been greatly affected.
What we are left with is a sound we hear all too often from Mr. Benson. Remember the not-so-recently released "Satellite" by P.O.D.? Who was the producer? Anyone remember? None other than Howard Benson. What did we see there? Yet another drastic change in the style of P.O.D.'s music to become more appealing to a larger audience. I mean, seriously. Who could have imagined songs like Alive, Youth Of The Nation, Satellite, Anything Right, Ghetto, and Thinking About Forever on any previous P.O.D. release? I didn't think so either.
Look, guys. I don't mean to be the bad guy, but please either get rid of Benson, or make sure your sound isn't affected as much by his influence in the studio. And Mr. Benson. Please, for the sake of all the hard rock fans out there, please keep a little distance from the underground groups we all luv, and stop turning them into mainstream funk rockers with little or no difference in musical styles from every other pop-rock group.

reviewText:
Oh well, here I find myself at the mighty, towering altar of yet another washed up, brigade of ex-junkie geriatric relics of the 70's. 2009 marks a momentous year in the long, long history of this band from across the pond. For starters, it is the 40th anniversary of their debut album. 40 years old and believe me, it sounds it as well. There is certain music and certain musicians who simply have neither the brains, creativity, or originality to offer something that can't instantaneously be pinned down to an exact time period. This band is one of them. They are such a staple of classic rock radio in any city in any state merely because, like the Who, they exemplify what it means to be 70's rock. Given that this record was made in 1969, we can I suppose say they were ahead of their time by a year. That only means of course that they foreshadowed the absolute worst aspects of 70's rock. Long, masturbatory, exceedingly dull guitar solos, unimaginative lyrics about women (and usually little else), and on one fine moment on a live album, a 12 minute drum solo called "Moby Dick" or something inane like that.

2009 has also made for a busy year in the world of classic rock radio DJ's and virtually every balding, tubby, beer swiggin' 50+ year old man engaged in the emotive, soap operatic, tug of war of the "will they or won't they" reunion gossip. I haven't followed the developments closely because unlike Jimmy Page and the average Led Zeppelin fan, I actually have things to do that are relevant to the future, but from what I can surmise this sad attempt to bring the boys (I use the term loosely obviously) back together for the money has been sabotaged time and again by Robert Plant who refuses to accept a tour performing songs that are 35 years or more old for millions of dollars. Why? Well, unlike 1994 when he reunited with Jimmy Page for an uninspired acoustic performance on MTV (of mostly very old songs of course), his career isn't in the toliet. Apparently his latest effort with Alison Krause was nominated for a Grammy, not that that actually means it has any merit, but that it did well commercially. I'm afraid a reunion will have to wait until Plant is scraping the bottom of the barrel again commercially (not in artistic terms because he is of course already a more than competent bottom feeder in that department) for a Zeppelin reuinon. That's the bad news. The good news is that that probably won't take very long. There's more bad news though and that's that Plant's voice which was horrible in 1994, is even worse today. Still more bad news, of course the ticket prices if and when the reunion takes place, will be exorbitant. This is an especially harsh fact given that most of Zep's fan base is probably approaching pensionable age and may well be on  fixed incomes.

There are a number of really solid, impressive debuts that signal the beginning of something very unique and significant. This isn't one of them. There has really never been anything sadder in the world of rock music than a group of white musicians mimicking the sounds of African-American blues music. They didn't just mimick it, they parroted it. Imagine Jimmy Page is a parrot and instead of repeating vocal expressions verbatim, he repeats blue riffs. I doubt any Zep fan will want to own up to this, but one of their "classics" was just ripped off from an old blues player named Willie Dixon. This was a fact that took years to properly address and only in the last ten years or so has Dixon been credited along with the members of the band in the composition. That's a song on another album, but it highlights what these lads are lacking. I don't know if I really need to fill in the blank here, but here goes. Talent, orginality, creativity, intelligence, and last but not least, basic scruples. But then again if any of the above is of interest to you as a music fan and consumer, you probably aren't listening to Led Zeppelin anyway.

I find the prospect of a track by track review as tedious as I found listening to the album so I think we can sum it all up with a few words about the last song (which incidentally provides a great punchline for many occasions). How many more times must we listen to some overweight, musical ignoramous on any given classic rock radio station crank out songs that were already dated in 1969? This was the modus operandi of this band. They found their muse looking backwards. Way backwards. "How Many More Times", aside from being self-indulgent, excessively long, and just plain dull, is a perfect and pitiful exemplar of everything that is wrong with this sad foursome of blues riffs hijacking wanna-be's. The sound that is on display is nothing short of coma-inducing. If you want to hear the blues, let's listen to the originators of this style of music. All black, all American, all blacklisted on radio because they were black (this is 1969 remember). So what you get in their stead is a group of white youths from England who, despite doing their best impersonation of real blues musicians, are an inferior, frankly piss poor substitiute. I don't like the blues much at all. I hate imitatory little scumbags who bring nothing more to the table than a carbon copy of a music whose heritage lies elsewhere. The band wails and screeches on, Page unleashing one frightful solo after another, whilst Plant moans like a pig in heat. Plant's lyrics, as per usual, are pre-occupied with the pre-pubesecent concerns of life. Girls and  all the things that they do to him. How could this go on for 9 minutes? It does and the liner notes to the album should have contained an apology. In lieu of that, I'll do you one better and say that I do indeed, without any equivocation whatsoever, feel sorry for anyone who ever listened to this album and thought it was decent.
label: negative

Nothing ventured equates consistent stagnancy in my book, which is simplistic and disinteresting.

The third Foo Fighters album proved that he was more into slick production and radio play than deep content (the latter tends to traditionally polarize the bulk of audiences, unfortunately; Choruses of "I don't get it."/"It's... weird." abound.)

This is just another of his Probot-esque mash-up projects that, while having immense potential if not tethered to his pop-flavored shackles, falls flat due to a lack of true chemistry and innovation. When will these high profile artists realize that you can't simply dump other high profile names into a melting-pot project, stir for five minutes, and expect greatness? Maybe it was all done just for fun and not meant to be anything but an experiment for them all, but it just sounds far too pasteurized for me to take seriously.

Dave should ease up on the endless celeb-stew albums and stick to his own thing; With his track record I predict (with dismay) that he will likely push a Nirvana "reunion" within the next decade, with himself as vocalist of course. reviewText:
It's amazing how hype can carry someone so far when they have delivered so little.
After the massive hype when the album launched, you would think Leona had done the unthinkable for a talent show winner and come up with a distinctive debut that really established them and set them apart from the crowd.

Sadly, it's just another classic example of PR and label execs hyping up something not up to scratch.

I don't mean to be scathing and I'm not having a go at Leona... She deserved her victory on the X factor.. You can't argue with her voice, it's a mega find. But winning the x factor was really the easy bit and you'd think Simon Cowell would have learned this by now with how many young kid's dreams he's built up, profited from and then shattered. Her 10 months spent away really gave me hope that only the best songs would have been chosen for her to record. I had foolishly believed that the length she had spent making this was a good sign. I was sure nothing bland and derivative would pop up.

This album is nothing better than the rubbish Westlife churn out every year in time for Christmas sales. Leona sang other people's songs on the X Factor but made them sound great and her own. Here she's given the sort of pap Westlife call exciting original music in between their covers when their writers "creative spells" dry up. It's bland ballad after bland ballad. This really could have been a Westlife album. On the X factor, she sang songs and really made you feel them. Here she's been given a load of bellow par songs. Honestly, I defy Simon Cowell to argue that any other artist could release any track off this album other than the cracking Bleeding Love and have a hit. The reality is it's not Leona's fault. Her voice is excellent, Simon Cowell has failed her. He didn't find anything exciting other than Bleeding Love that was worth the wait.
Honestly, most of the tracks here don't and won't stand up over time. Bleeding Love is an instant classic and has carried Leona this far but what does the next few months hold... I fear a bit of a media backlash because she won't sell much more albums anyway, this has sold over a million to date, the media will have a field day knocking down what they helped to build up only months before, the label will cleverly blame huge album sales for poorly performing singles and Leona's dreams will be slipping fast away.

 I really can't see her having any other hits off this album. After a while they all start to sound the same, start with a piano refrain and build up to a modern beat that carries them to their conclusion. Take a Bow is an attempt to break this cycle and try modern RnB. Beyonce and co won't be having sleepless nights anyway. It's painfully bad. There's really nothing else that stands out. Whatever it takes is okay, catchy maybe but nothing to get excited about.

At the end of the day, Leona's voice is great but the material is bland and unoriginal. As for cracking America, Bleeding Love might deceive some into buying this lacklustre album, but she runs the risk of being a one hit wonder there and elsewhere in the world because she simply doesn't have the material to back her up or the same hype. In the uk/ Ireland , I'm sure we won't see more than three singles max because they simply aren't here. Maybe, they'll repackage the album with some new tracks but that would be just cynical and greedy.. so they probably will do it! It's a shame Leona's debut hasn't lived up to the hype.  I wanted her to do well and have a long career.. she deserves it but based on this , the jury's definitely out still.

reviewText:
What happened to Genesis is truely heartbreaking. They started off with Peter Gabriel and his strange vision that culminated in 1974 with the masterpiece The Lamb Lies Down On Broadway. When Gabriel left, a not-to-confident Phil Collins took over as singer. They continued to progress until about 1982 (when Phil Collins became a superstar with his version of You Can't Hurry Love). Since then, the other members of the group have tried desperately to write the Big Hit.

I Can't Dance, Jesus He Knows Me, and No Son Of Mind were all failed attempts at this. Most of the other songs are washed-out, slow-moving exercises in futility. reviewText:
This is an altogether uninspired album, meandering along in a pleasant countrified mid-tempo (even when it desperately, and unsuccessfully, tries to convey excitement), doing nothing, being wallpaper. It would be an acceptable first stab at a vague country pop genre by an artist still seeking his/her path and honing the songwriting skills, but considering this is the product of a once-brilliant musician, it's depressingly sub-par.
I had never heard it upon original release, just picked it up a few days ago at my local library, out of curiosity. Perhaps it could fall under the rubric "Why you shouldn't mess with serious drugs unless you think you're Keith Richards," but perhaps that had nothing to do with John's sudden loss of his muse. Many artists simply run out of steam, but few do in such a short time. The lyrics, apparently, are full of personal and often gripping messages, but I find it hard to care because the music is so prettily bland and uninvolving. All songs rely on melody, but the melodies are so unimaginative that they're hard even to perceive, let alone remember. The sporadic harmonies are seldom rich, the conventions of rock (echo, driving beat) are sacrificed for the sake of amiable trucking along as you fall asleep. Presumably, that was precisely the point - John wanted to divorce himself from what he'd done with the Mamas and the other Papa, and express himself in a new way. Honorable effort, but meager results.

Not everything is bad. The liner notes tell me that "Mississippi" was the only song to chart, albeit not very high, and I find that incomprehensible - I mean, that it would chart at all, no matter how low on the charts. A less memorable song you could hardly imagine, and its effort at a catchy little refrain is pathetic. To my ear, the best song here is "Captain (The Mermaid)," which may not be too surprising, since it sounds just like the Mamas and the Papas, and "Down the Beach" has a lot of charm with its funny jazzy air. Of course, this works if you were a Mamas & Papas fan to begin with; if you weren't, perhaps you have a less jaundiced view of the album than I do, because you're not comparing it to what I considered to be the epitome of excellence and originality.

Now consider that this is a beautifully produced album, with stellar players and surely no penny spared to make it sound its absolute best, because John was still a big, and financially solvent, star. I can't imagine how it would have sounded in its bare-bones incarnation. What did John hear in his head, when he first sat on his sofa and clunked out one of these songs on his acoustic guitar? Did he not hear that it needed work, plenty of work? I guess not. Even the demos among the bonus tracks are not telling, since they, too, are pretty fully produced for demos, especially for that time of non-digital equipment.

Perhaps it was the drugs, which eventually (and relatively quickly) killed him, perhaps it was being a star and having no one to tell you the truth. Any way you look at it, this collection of non-tunes does not stand on its own, does not stand as a testimony to John's enormous talent, and as for trying to find in here a "Monday, Monday," "California Dreaming," "Look through my Window," or even the quiet, simple, beautifully executed lesson in sophisticated songcraft called "Got a Feeling", we're miles and miles away.

reviewText:
No one can deny that Clark had a good voice on American Idol.  He still has a good voice, with its flaws, which show on this album.  That is the positive aspect of of his self titled album COREY CLARK.

COREY CLARK is an uninspired album anyway that you look at it.  The first flaw that you notice from the very first track is that it way overproduced.  The production is too slick and it just grates on you.  Everything is synth based, which is alright if you work synth-based production the right way, but in this case, you would hope that an acoustic track might appear. True, it is a dance/teen pop album, but it is tiring because the synths are too "draining".

The next flaw is the fact that Clark does drabble in many influences.  Normally that is a positive thing, but in this case, it doesn't always work or sound unified.  On "Paulatics", Clark sounds like Michael Jackson singing on an N'Sync or Backstreet Boys song. There's nothing wrong with sounding like Michael, but teen pop is already in a dying breed and an album like COREY CLARK sets it back further because it isn't anything that hasn't already been done or already heard.  It is so undistinguished that it could never stand out among much better modern dance-pop/teen acts (Ciara, Jo Jo, etc...).  Against Michael Jackson or any of the boy bands for the most part it doesn't stand a chance.  Furthermore, against his main competition Justin Timberlake, Usher, even Mario, Omarion, Marques Houston, etc... it doesn't even compare.

As I stated earlier, Corey Clark has a good voice, yet it has flaws.  It grows annoying in general over the overabundance of dance-pop, synth-based tunes.  His upper register (as noted on American Idol) grows sometimes a bit overdramatic and over powered, sometimes where it sounds like he overshoots or screams.  As a musician myself, you have to learn not to "power" everything and not to overdo singing, which is incredibly easy to do.

The most listenable tunes are "Out of Control" and "Paulatics".  Otherwise, Clark drabbles too much in uninspired teen pop tunes that just have no substance and prove too repetitive and too based upon the production rather than the vocalist. reviewText:
When it comes to electronica and house, it's not that hard for an album to strike a chord with some segment of the population.  There are more than a few different species of rave music, and although it means critics can sometimes get bogged down in semantics (do we call this hard house? progressive? deep? industrial? techno? trance? digital box pop? blah blah blah), it also means, on the plus side, that there's usually something out there for all kinds of HouseHeads.

Ignoring the touchy subject of definitions, there's one thing that can definitively be said about this album: it's not very good.  In fact, it's pretty bad.

So-called "newbies," seeking an introduction into or an argument for club music, will not be seduced or persuaded by this hasty conglomeration of petty and pretentious songs.  The album labels itself as "Progressive House," which is a smug enough title as it is; then you have songs that, in deep bass, urge you to "Shhh...be quiet.  Listen!" or that holler, self-righteously, "In the beginning, there was house music ... and from this groove came the groove of all grooves ... and then one day some DJs declared, 'Let this house be progressive!'"  Give me a break.

There are some old standards on this record (emphasis on the "old"), so an argument could be made for it as some sort of record of house antiquity (if such a thing is even necessary).  Darude's "Sandstorm" was once a club staple (and still calls up nostalgia among older ravers), Da Hool's "Meet Her At The Love Parade" is a song that will probably sound familiar to almost anyone -- it was once "progressive," I guess, but it's now the formula a DJ follows when s/he's run out of ideas.  The same could be said for the Vengaboys and their "Up And Down," a song that plays like it was bought from a vending machine.

Any one of these songs might survive in a club, played alone, and sandwiched between songs of higher skill.  They have their place just as much as, say, the B-52's "Love Shack" or Ace of Bass's "Don't Turn Around."  They are novelties, once popular, good now as something to snicker at and even nod your head, too.  But an entire album of them only makes you realize how incredibly trite and grating they really are, and shows you just how far the genre has come in such a short amount of time.  House, this music may be, the Best, it most certainly is not.

reviewText:
You can find at least four other reviews of this CD here on amazon, all of which give it five stars. Am I intimidated by being the odd person out? Not in this case. This recording is the best evidence in the world of the superiority of 'historically informed performance' on original-period instruments, sung in an appropriate style.

Listen to the samples! Don't waste your money on buying the CD for comparative purposes. You'll hear that both singers - soprano Marshall and contralto Valentini-Terrani - employ steady, wide, unrelenting vibratos. The result is that lugubrious warble associated with "fat lady" jokes. Aside from the preposterous ugliness of such a vocal technique, when used for Baroque music, the vibrato completely obscures the tuning of the relatively 'open' chords of which this music is composed. It's worse when the two singers attempt the duet movements; the whole effect of the organum-like harmonies, chiefly parallel thirds, is destroyed by the interference patterns of two rippling vibratos over lapping each other. However, to be utterly blunt, even with the aid of vibrato, neither singer is even close to consistently in tune with her own intervals, let alone with the orchestra.

And an orchestra it is! NOT a basso continuo, with obbligato instruments! In fact, the organ basso continuo only occasionally penetrates the congestion of the orchestra, giving me "where did that come from" shock. It's muddy, it's turgid, it's 'in tune' only by committee consensus.

Claudio Abbado, perhaps to give his singers acoustic space for their vocal wobbling, takes the most sluggish tempi in most of the movements of any recording I've heard. He also lurches melodramatically into his frequent chorale-like fermatas. It's clear that he 'hears' the Stabat Mater only as a dirge, and not as a prayer for empathy and intercession, which it should be, and a paean of love for the Mother of Sorrows. His is a stodgy Sunday concert hall interpretation, without of flicker of stained-glass illumination.

I actually enjoyed nearly ever song off the previous album because each one was different and unique. The one thing that ETF kept reminding me of in this album is Avenged Sevenfold, a band whom I think blows. Again, this is just my opinion. I literally can't tell any of the songs apart.

This War Is Ours had more punk-rockish songs that had fast beats. The bass stuck out in a lot of songs, the drums were unique and the guitar was very catchy. Self titled ETF feels a lot more studio produced, the drums are generic metal, the breakdowns are bland, the singing isn't anything special at all. The lyrics are also very generic. There is absolutely nothing that stands out on this album at all. If it were by any other band I would never listen to them again. I hope ETF will not continue to make music like this, otherwise I will no longer be a fan and I'm sure I'm not the only one either.

reviewText: I am not a musicologist, music historian, musician, music major, nor do I read music, much less music scores, annotations, or orchestral arrangements,. I cannot tell you that a conductor separated the first and second violins, nor discern the violas from the cellos in the mix [see  the Skorwaczeski review - I found unlistenable].  I listen with a SUBJECTIVE ear. I repeat,the basis of my Beethoven Symphony evaluation is BIASED -- I heard/watched Disney's FASTASIA at an EARLY age! That imprint, aural memory has held fast, like a mussel on a rock, since!  Therefore, I am BIASED toward the 6th Symphony, the Pastoral, as the ROCK!  Cut to the chase = there are lots of GOOD, EXCELLENT renditions of the COMPLETE cycle.  I have listened to most all of them, from Furtwanger,  [impossibly S-L-O-W] to Zinman, [3 movements average/Good],  MOST COMPLETE collections are fine, and have their merits, including the latest, Barenboim, and the standbys, like Karajan. All well and good. For me =buy the individual Essential Classic cd's for George Szell, and the Cleveland Orchestra, or the NY Philharmonic, with the incomparable Leonard Bernstein.. When an orchestra, and a Conductor meld it is magic!  With the NY Phil, you have Lenny, the Hand and the Orchestra, the Glove. If the 1st movement is a tad FAST, the pure musicality. instrument isolation, clarity of sound doubles in Spades.  Szell gets it 3 Bears right, and the recording is almost there = Lenny 98/100, Szell 100/98 . I listened to Harnoncourt,  [unlistenable!],and thought it was another [bad] Symphony,  Ormandy,[ the recording  was muddy], and the rest were either OK, or the Orchestra was LIGHTWEIGHT!  Forget Lenny with the Germans= MARGINA!  Josef Krips, weird orchestration, in 3 movements? Very GOOD, lightweight orchestra ,Roger Norrington, a fine conductor. produces a middling, average good result, OK/good orchestra,  Well, then Jochum,  is no Wunderkind, but is OK,  These are VERY SUBJECTIVE evaluations, but I believe Beethoven is about MUSICALITY.  Lenny, and Szell, and Karajan will set you back @$75 - $100, and you will be glad of it. Do not buy the Complete Szell, because it is oddly cut, divided, rather buy the individual CD's.  And if your "yardstick", is another Symphony, have at it!. BUT, Szell, and Lenny/NY, an von Karajan, will not disappoint! Anon, and alas.

reviewText: Count me in as one of the people that have been not only gravely disappointed, but downright revolted by this album. Since the rather mediocre Heretic, we would hope that after an anticipated eight year wait that we would get an album that showed us that it was still the band we held in high regard. Of course, I didn't expect it to be at the same level as their masterpieces, but I sure didn't expect it to be at this level. The band has officially made the aforementioned Heretic look masterful in comparison. While tracks like "Blades of Baal", "Existo Vulgor" and "Nevermore" are by far the better material on here (despite them being rather average), it still doesn't make up for the remainder one bit. Throughout this album, we are left with haphazardly constructed songs that mindlessly throw in electronic and 10th rate industrial metal to try to make it sound like they're experimenting. That's not going to fly this time. To go from highly complex, well-written songs with classical undertones to repetitive, dance hall rhythm based trash like "Too Extreme!" and "Destructos vs. the Earth" shows that over this waiting period, primary songwriter Trey Azagthoth has lost his mind. Out of all the songwriters in death metal, why him? Let's not forget that David Vincent's vocals have taken a turn for the far worse, sounding like he recorded them straight after a 24 hour chain smoking session. This isn't Morbid Angel. This is the result of what happens when death metal veterans feel the need to betray their fan base by using the trademark name to pass off their insipid wankery. Maybe this is all a sick joke, but whether they're playing games with us or not, this should be boycotted by all means necessary.

reviewText: If you know me I listen to a vast spectrum of music-from some classical and (yes) even a few tunes now and then from Soundgarden ("Black Hole Sun" anybody?) and I LOVE some classic punk (The Clash are one of my favorite bands)but THIS!!!!!Okay for starters I remember when this record came out-I was still in the days of acid wash jeans,perms and U2 and stuff and along comes 'Nevermind'.What do I LIKE about this album?Well I LOVE the album cover-it's one of my favorites and it makes a great anti  establishment statement. But the music?????O-H M-Y G-O-O-D-N-E-S-S!!!!!!!Who.....made this stuff,since I could hardly call written. Sometimes I wonder what goes through rock critics (of all ages) minds when they reviewed albums and put the moniker 'classic' on it. Okay first off Kurt Cobain is a rather pittiable figure-depressed and a drug addict he wrote songs and sung in a way that would get him locked into the mental hospital where I come from-I feel sorry for him. And his band (sorry) are so ametaurish it isn't even fresh or funny. Bands like U2 or The Clash were inexperienced at first but still made great,lively and powerful music from the beginning. But all this ends up is as an aural heroin 'daze'-the guitars are cloudy,Cobain's already ruined voice is barely audible and the only recognizable pop song here "Something In The Way" still has no vital spark. To me it makes me angry that an obviously sad and suisidal man such as Cobain wasted his talented (which may in fact exist) on forcing us to endure his inaudible,drug crazed 'wailing' of rants like "Terrestrail Pissings".And the acoustic "Polly"?Sounds like the worst garage band in the world. So why is 'Nevermind' called a masterpiece?Simple-Nirvana,despite fancying themselves anti establishment were (and still are)the recipiants of one of the most wide spread and carefully crafted PR campaign since the days of The Beatles. But there (again despite critics) is where the comparasin between Nirvana and The Beatles ends-for one "Smells Like Teen Spirit" is NOT a modern day "More Then A Feeling" and nothing Grohl,Cobain or the others do is anywhere close to Beatle-esque. Not only that (even if it's not Cobains fault) his music set a new record for rock n' roll underachievment unpresidented in all these years and from which the music world has barely recovered from-to this day alternative rock radio tends to be more or less grunge in disguise and ALL of these records sound like 'Nevermind'.Also Cobains cynical and sad outlook,although baught on my his mental problems inadverantly caused a whole generation of youth to simply.....stop caring and deny and even mock the more positive elements of their past. So this began the 'grunge generation' in earnest and even if it was all spin doctored is this a lousy record?Technically very much?Should it be stripped from the market?NEVER,and that's the only reason why this should exist. Every artist has the right to express themselves however they want as long as no one is getting hurt-it's in the constitution. But also everyone has the right to their opinion so I felt compelled to get one. So if you subscribe to the grunge culture and don't have this you probably should,you'll love it. But if you like me are one of those people who are looking for something more then drugged out babble,lack of melody and nothing but minor chords then you like me should probably steer clear. But I had to hear it to have an opinion. My main point is not every rock critic should hail this as a masterpiece because they want to go along with joneses-I know others feel as I do. If Nirvana could make a recording like this and become geniouses for it then everyone has the right to a different opinion and like mine it doesn't always have to be a picture perfect one.

The chorus offers the worst kind of neutered, wimpy singing that gets featured in the very worst of HIP performances and recordings. The shoe never drops with this group, which seems to treat singing as a "Ready, Aim...Aim...Aim" affair.

But the real problem with this recording lies with the vocal soloists, whose singing doesn't rise to the level of accomplishment one will often encounter at high school variety shows. The singing here barrels over into embarrassing when the soloists attempt to get artsy and ornament their singing, hilariously so in the bass recitative "Thus saith the Lord," where our musically challenged soloist decides to add a shake to his voice every time he sings the word "shake." Are you kidding me? Hey, why not also spit every time you sing the word "sea" and fake a dry voice when singing the words "dry land?" This is amateur hour writ large.

Good points? The recorded sound is excellent! But what good is that when the recording itself can't be taken seriously?

reviewText:
...as others have mentioned, this CD is copy-protected, meaning once bought, you can't exercise your right as the owner of the CD to do as you please with its content (i.e., rip it to your hard drive, put it on your iPod).

I encourage all prospective buyers to boycott this CD on principle.  Like all major industries (some with more egregious agendas than others), the music industry is rife with avarice and scum.  Regardless of what the band or their label contends, this stuff is public domain once released, and they have NO RIGHT to limit the accessibility or manipulation of the material once purchased by the consumer.

Being legally blind, I missed the copy-protection denotation on the back of the CD ("the big print giveth, the small print taketh away").  I only discovered this when I attempted to rip it to my iPod.

Feeling bullied and victimized, I went back to Virgin Megastore and DEMANDED they give me an exchange.  The glib cashier initially gave me a problem.  But I was livid, and I refused to accept "no" as an answer.  I debated adamantly with the store manager until she caved and granted me an exchange (I got "Hemispheres" by Rush, which not only contains much better music, it's also NOT copy-protected).

The moral of the story: even if you've already purchased this disc and are bummed you can't put it on your iPod, don't accept the fate of having wasted your money.  Go back to the store from where you bought it and, as the consumer who works hard for his/her money, DEMAND they either give you a credit or an exchange.  As the CONSUMER, you have rights, so FIGHT for them!

Lastly, if the retail rep gives you BS and attempts to place the blame on you instead of the record label for "assuming the risk of buying the copy-protected CD," don't budge.  It's the RETAILER who assumes the burden/risk of carrying the label's junk product, thereby likely incurring the wrath of angry consumers who feel jipped (sp?).  They (the retailers) should know better, and they undoubtedly do.

I'd truly like to review "A Beautiful Lie" for its music, which is neither great nor bad.  It's decent.  But it's the UGLY LIE on the part of the band's label which gives this a crappy rating.  And if the band has any integrity, they'll address the copy-protection issue and do their best to make the fans happy.

'Nuff said.

reviewText: I recently streamed this release out of sheer perverse curiosity since I would never listen to anything with Bocelli in it. His inclusion alone disqualifies it for further consideration. But it must also be said that the singing of Renée Fleming is, to put it mildly, distasteful and grotesque. Listen to her 'Libera me' where her blues-jazz-informed phrasing makes her sound as if she is seeking a different kind of liberation, of which kind I don't know. I'll leave it to your imaginations. But musically, her interpretation (and an interpretation it is) is unacceptable, for she has removed all manner of piety from or even respect for the music. It is imperative that the willfully ignorant and the naive and unknowing be properly guided and directed to recordings of the work that truly matter and that do justice to the music and its context. There are of course a good number of exceptional Requiems that have been released over time. One of them is the historical Tullio Serafin from Rome, recorded in the 1930s. I will skip many commendable others but not before naming the two recordings of the work with soprano Cheryl Studer: with Riccardo Muti/La Scala and with Claudio Abbado/Vienna. In my opinion, she is even better for Abbado. Listen to her 'Libera me' and then tell me if anything more heart-rending, sublime or beautiful exists. But please don't just skip to the 'Libera me'. To summarize: There is a time and place for everything, I suppose. But there is no place for slumming in this most venerable of Requiems. It is airtight. In 'Summertime', maybe, but not here.

reviewText: When I was a youngster just getting my indie wings with albums like Lonesome Crowded West and Doolittle, I saw this album and thought it looked interesting. With two supposed classics under my belt, I listened to this album late at night while I was by myself in my room one time (that's when I always listen to music I've been anticipating, just for the amazing atmosphere it provides, or used to) and I couldn't finish the album. I felt disappointed, like I was missing something, or there was something I wasn't getting. So, I tried again, and finally managed to finish all of it. I came out feeling pretty much the same as I did going in. Tired, a little agitated, and somewhat bored. In a few days, I bought the Mountain Goats album "Tallahassee", which is now my favorite album. Also, I later tried to get into the nitty-gritty indie albums shortly after giving up on Spiderland, and enjoyed a lot of what I heard very much and came back to it, but this is one classic I just couldn't appreciate, I guess. The lyrics are good I suppose, and I like chaotic and minimalistic music as much as the next indie fan, but this seemed to over do it a bit. I don't care for slacker music, but just flat-out lazy and droning riffs that seem almost purposely made to sound boring and flat is a little different. Also, the whole spoken word thing seems to be the same thing. Maybe they just did everything in a way that was so weird and non-technical or traditional that it would instantly appeal to fans of weird music, reguardless of whether they actually liked it or not? Or maybe it's just me. To each his own, but this just isn't for me.

reviewText:
Too many times one can get lured into spinning miester. I bought this CDs upon 5 star rating by several Amazon listeners. Now having heard all five available reportoirs : this one, Solti/VPO, Bohm/DPO, Sinopoli/VPO, and RCG/Dohnanyi, I can say that Solti's Sofiensaal-recorded version is the one to get. There, Decca has cleaned up the sound using Cedar/SNS 96KHz/24 bit technology, but more so on the drama, tension, superb noise-making by VPO, and overall feel of getting the value from the money well spent.

Here is the analysis of this CD: The sound quality here is mono, muffled, and with lots of hiss, if you are trying to listen to the soprano. It sounds more like recording from Bayreuth (esteemed venue of worst recordings), but actually from a live performance from Salzburg Festival on 17th August 1964 at the Groes Festspielhaus.(see [...])

It just mars the experience of real / royal bitching by Elektra and Klytamnestra. The dogs - I mean Aegisths and Orest are even worse.

Upon further exploring the music, I checked the quality of ADD conversion. What I found is that Orfeo did not do even the least work on restoration of this work, especially if it is of such monumental nature. The WAV stream depicts the problem. The most rancorous sound is set at max volume, thus causing all subsequent amplitudes to be so drastically reduced that this is the criminal act on part of record producing. Most of the WAV is @ 15-22% of max amplitude (i.e volume). If you were to use a decent wave editor/ cleaner (like GoldWave, WavePad, Audacity, Nero, SoundForge, SonicFoundry, Sonar, etc..) you could know that the problem ....Orfeo did not do the job correctly.

In contrast, I think Karajan/VPO/Decca&EMI monoaural version of Der Rosenkavalier  is far superior to later recording in stereo. It not that Orfeo cannot do it, they chose not to do it for this CDs. And that is the qualms for spending full price money for third-class record.

If you really need to hear a covers record where the lead singer mumbles, stumbles and otherwise mostly talks his way through the vocals, where the normally gifted musicians just sort of phone it in and play incorrect notes (down-tuning to accommodate the very pronounced vocal dropoff of the singer at fault here, perhaps) and where otherwise the songs are not even second-ran, but more like fortieth-ran versions of the power, glory, majesty and overall, if you heard either a covers band in a bar or someone performing karaoke at this level, you'd probably (rightfully) leave in disgust. This would have made a bit more sense 10 years ago, but now, unless he's trying to end his career full circle from where he started and document his deterioration, this seems a silly, silly travesty. In interviews, he can talk about his Lake Tahoe house and how much everyone who hates the album is living in a basement and stealing their mother's broadband (whatever that means), but looking around and seeing various Whitesnake albums, including the bleach-the-hair-and-take-over-America years, the stellar "Live In The Heart Of The City", the actual Purple albums he was on, I'm one of those who made him able to afford whatever houses he lives in and whatever fast cars he has parked in the garage for chippies to be draped across the hoods of. He seems stuck in that bleach phase, both with his insults for whoever dislikes this ridiculous near-parody of an album as well as the idea that his word will be taken for anything other than PR. In this age, every one of these songs is on YouTube, including the awful soulless rendition of Soldier Of Fortune and the incredibly awful puking of Mistreated. My suggestion is to go there and try before you buy. Most irreplaceable on the songs is Blackmore (sorry Reb Beach, but you're still an excellent musician) himself, who incidentally sprinkles various Purple covers in his current band. If you want to hear the songs done in a different manner, but skillfully and actually on key, best to check into those.

reviewText:
When will people realize that Arrau used rubato in order to hide his kindergarten level technique. I have played the fantasy impromptu for a decade already and what Arrau does here is against the basic tenets of classical music. He slows the passage every few bars and blurs his slips with pedal so people will call it "romantic". Fantasy Impromptu is a flowing piece with active passages in both hands ....... Arrau turns this into some type of cocktail lounge/cabaret fest music.

He does this over and over again, in the etudes, in Liszt.... whenever a passage is difficult.

There is no concensus involving Arrau's playing that can forever be substantiated by 30 Amazon reviews (taking into account that some times people who are passionate about a certain product put multiple postings... not that I am saying this is the case here). This is deceptive in the sense that many pianists, including the great Horowitz (and another review here if that matters), have been very critical of his playing. Now to be fair, he was one of the more popular pianists, especially in South America, but this fact in and of itself has little relevance.

I established the fact that I am intimately familiar with the piece as a basis for my contention that Arrau does not play Chopin, but rather Arrau. I could of course lay out pages of specific reasons for this - primarily bizzare, indulgent use of rubato, not playing what Chopin writes, etc. The fact that he is one of the greatest Liszt interpreters (which I wholeheartedly disagree with) does not address this particular Chopin CD.

The only way you could justify this playing is by validating the reciprocal - namely - that unlimited rubato, slower than conventional tempi, quirky reservations on numerous passages, superficial romanticism, is fine. Until that is established as legitimate playing, I will continue to criticize this type of playing, especially since there are so many pianists that have treated these pieces with more care (loosely, Ashkenazy, Horowitz, Richter, Rubinstein, Moravec, Pollini, and many more).

Of course the Kissin review that claims he plays 4 times faster is hyperbole - but it fits the picture in sofar as it pertains to illustrating the ludicrous and entirely infantile level of technique ( and again I can't accept the fallacious correlation between lack of technique and emotion).

No piece of classical music should condescendingly be called minor, and to a larger extent, a wonderful piece by Chopin. Finally, I don't comprehend the contention that Arrau has some type of technical (supernatural) superiority that he hides from the public lest it be deemed superificial. The only way one could know this is if people close to Arrau secretly revealed his hidden abilities. Regardless, in some pieces technical aptitude is an unambiguous requirement. If Chopin writes Presto, he means presto. It is just impossible to take Chopin Etudes seriously without the necessary or close to necessary level of technique. The other weird assertment is that there is a correlation between Arrau's reluctance to display technique as being a trigger to his increased emotion. This argument doesn't hold water since there are pianists that have both technique and other attributes.

For more authoritative versions please turn to Moravec, Rubinstein, Ashkenazy.

reviewText:
Over the years, I have heard so many Floyd phoenatics flaunt this album and Syd as a masterpiece.  So many consider "Piper at the Gates of Dawn" to be Floyd's magnum opus as well as a work of genious.  Huh?!?  I am a Floyd fan.  Had all theirs on vinyl up until 1986, have their solo works.  Having said that, Barrett's departure (although unfortunately due to personal problems on his behalf of which I feel bad about) from Pink Floyd and his replacement (David Gilmour) are the best things to happen to Floyd and it saved Floyd from dying as a band in 1968/1969.  Those who say Barrett is the icon and the legendary figure of the band don't fool me.  His goofey lyrics and corny pop melodies sound rediculous at best.  For me, Floyd started as a band with "Saucerful of Secrets".  I had this on vinyl and tried to listen to this quite a few times.  It just got worse and worse with every listen and it finally made its way on a garage sale display.  Nobody bought it so I ended up getting 35 cents for it (and it was in mint shape) from a record exchange store that buys used vinyl.  35 cents is about all it's worth.  There was nothing redeeming about it.  The best part of the album is when it ends or when you stop it.

Syd Barrett may have had some mental problems (and I feel bad for it) and a tragic life.  I sympathize with him.  Musically though, he was a disaster and so is this album.  If you want early Floyd, skip "Piper" and get "Ummagumma".

Also, on many occassions, Floyd fans tell me I don't like Barrett because I can't understand him and am not capable of understanding what Syd was trying to portray (as if Syd is only for sophisticated folks).  When I say "No, I don't understand, please try and explain", I usually get no reply back from them.

I used to be a downright Tori Amos fan. Except for Suzanne Vega and Kate Bush, she's the only solo female-artist I'm into. Or better said: WAS into.
She made three amazingly good albums, amongst them my absolute favorite: Boys For Pele; often misunderstood, but undoubtedly a masterpiece of crafty, original songwriting, great instrumentation (using even harpsichords) and melodies that can still deeply touch me. Even the B-sides to these three albums were great; listen to Flying Dutchman, Cooling or Humpty Dumpty, and you'll find yourself amazed. You can better spend your energy on looking for these tracks than buying this..album.
Her decay started with the heavily uninteresting From The Choirgirl Hotel; was I dissapointed when I heard the bad, mediocre songs on that one! Was she only flirting with awful, inappropiate 4-to-the-floor beats and synths on that one; the even more bad follow-up To Venus And Back was loaded with it. I'm into a lot of beat- and synth-heavy music, but Tori really should stick to her Bosendorfer.
Now, there's Strange Little Girls. I lost my interest in her since Venus, but now it's even worse; what a total, total failure is this.
I gave it a few listens but couldn't discover one interesting note on here, except for her nice cover of Real Men, which proves she still has something of her covering-qualities in her (mind her beautiful cover of Billie Holiday's Strange Fruit). I won't be interested in the next Tori album, as it seems to be the tradition to get worse by every record. What a loss, and what a total waste of CD's that could have been used for new talent.

reviewText:
(Before you click you hated my review based on the title, please give my review a read - thanks.)

I'm not a vindictive man by any means, but when I was handed this to review and smelled the obviousness of it, my blood ran hot. I took a long look at this very compact import box set and wondered "how can I review this?"

If there is one thing about the six album six year long output of this incredible quartet from Long Beach, California, it's the music - it's both old and new, and with every play you always find a new gem to explore. I've been a fan of them since the late 1980's when I found original cassette copies of all of their albums. I knew that I had tapped into something wonderful and special, but I was just too young enough to remember their music when it first charted and it was played on my old AM radio of mine...

But now it's 2011, sadly Jim Morrison has been dead 40 years this month, and this is The Doors' 8th (EIGHTH!) incarnation of "greatest hits/total album packaging." I'm not gonna lie, I really had to step back before I wrote this review. Here's what I got, and I'm being as brief as possible.

The sound quality is okay, it sits compact on the shelf, and that's well and good, but I've heard better (more on that later) - and all you really get here is the same CD's packaged in paper sleeves with the feel of vinyl covers for all six albums. No new music, no outtakes, no new surprises, which to some might be wonderful. It's a straightforward collection of their original albums, that's it.

But this is all I can say about it.

So why put another collection again, I asked myself? I gave you the reason a few seconds ago - Jim Morrison has been dead 40 years ago this month. Why else would the three remaining members (or their lawyers) agree to put out the same albums? Here's where I got upset, but I stepped back and gave this a good reasoning:

Back in 2006 the remaining members put out the ultimate collection of all things Doors with "Perception," which was supposed to be the end-all-be-all definitive complete album set by The Doors, with sound quality on the 6 CDs (and 6 DVD-A's on the more expensive version of the set), surpassing the older 1997, 1999, 2000 and 2003 box sets and greatest hits albums by light years! They included some newer outtakes of songs never heard before, extended cuts of songs and more, with interviews and videos and hours of watching (and listening) with sound quality from the original masters so cleaned up, remastered and crystal clear in my opinion is unsurpassed by anyone since this release.

It was amazing, and I listened to it for hours, and it really took me back and it was wonderful. It's in my top twenty of what I'd bring if I was deserted on a desert island music albums...

But then I came back to earth and once again I asked "why this little no-frills set? Why put out a set 5 years after their Mount Everest, with okay quality sound at best?"

Then that nagging thought came back to me again -  Jim Morrison has been dead 40 years ago this month in 1971.

Sadly, I had thought of yet another reason this was released...

Greed. Plain and simple. How much money can they extract from their fans? Only Aerosmith and Bon Jovi are more obvious, blatant and greedy to retread their hits and sell you four, five (or in this case eight) different versions of greatest hits/album collections. Their lawyers must have looked at the calendar and thought "hmm, we can make a buck or two with this... All hail the almighty cash..."

So that's it, and that's all I want to say about it without being any meaner. PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE take a pass on this, because as a basic collection of The Doors albums it's nice, but they've done far far better in the past. Do yourself a massive favor and search out and find the "Perception" box set, and then drink a glass of wine (or whatever gets you to that higher plane) and relax with that.

This set is obvious, cold and really has nothing new worth picking it up for, as any real Doors fan could see the obviousness of it a mile away as well and say "no thanks."

I gave this back. You should too.

(Thanks for reading my review, and please leave any comments or votes you've got.)

There is something inherently prosaic in this dead dull "music of der future".  Fortunately, man has still some sense of individualism, but barely, and Kraftwerk's fascist goal for music has not rendered vocals obsolete.  Listening to this, it harkens back to the techno geek 1970's when Germans laden in neo-fascist uniforms with thin ties and a pound of grease on their hair, showed no emotion on stage, acting like machines.  Most of them wore leather pants so tight that they froze while playing, hence the dumb and inarticulate Krautbot look.  They copied architecture chic from the 1930's, added some 70's porn montage and called it "modern"  1970's and praised the revolution of robots and computers.  Not only is that very idea horrifying, but it is also silly.  "Kraftwerk" means "cheese plant" in German and they are very cheesy.

The CD is probably one of the most horrible things I've listened to.  If you can get to the end of it, you'll find all sorts of unwanted electronic noise, Krautbot voice dubs, electro fuzz, beeps, computer konks, repugnant computer-generated vocals, static, repulsive synthesizers, and extremely unpleasant clamor that goes on forever, that you'll soon be reaching for a hammer to crush the CD.  In my estimation, all crap.  A few American bands at the time tried the stale trend with deadly results, Gary Numan The Pleasure Principle (1979), Styx Kilroy Was Here (1983) , both tossed their careers away because of it.

You'll be reminded of foolish telephone companies, lumbering computer screens, electronic wires and moronic techno cabarets in dark German cellars.

Missing is the strong live playing of his regular band (a programmed beat is provided by the cheap sounding keyboard) and there are none of the gorgeous harmonies of Willie P. Bennett. A few, or maybe more than a few, of the cuts might actually be good songs. I can hear I-75 and Wichita, for example, being great if they had been recorded on any of Fred's other CDs.

Because this is Fred Eaglesmith, I have listened to DUSTY four times hoping I'd grow to like it. I haven't and will probably never listen to it again. Fortunately, his other CDs are nothing like DUSTY and we can hope that this was a one time mistake.

reviewText:
10-2-2014  This recording of  the Chopin 2nd Piano Concerto in f-minor, was acquired in late June of 1987 and also bears as fillers, "The Grand Fantasy on Polish Airs," the "Grand Polonaise brilliante and the preceding "Andante Spinato, Op. 22.  Mr. Ax plays a modern replica of a Chopin instrument he used at that time of composing these popular works, and along with the Orch. of the age of the Enlightenment," under Sir Charles Mackkeras.  This combination of "authentic" sounds goes far in suggesting to the listener just what this music of the earlier 19th Century may have sounded like, in detail.  A splendid and charming idea as the music of the Polish Master of the keyboard has left us two wonderfully melodic and tuneful concerti, the First of which I may review soon.
Burt, as for this f-minor it runs an adequate 31:45 and with the added pieces, the total playing duration is a generous 59:31, and nicely priced to boot.
  ARTISTIC IMPRESSIONS

  The sound is very crisp, clear and clean, indicative of anything Mackkeras touches.  this lovely remake of the "Chopinesque" instrument is a pure pleasure to hear.  The true heart of  this beautiful 2nd Concerto is the rapturous "Larghetto" of only 9:15 and I could of easily stood for more, lots more.  but, for Chopin, often brevity is his forte as he doesn't , as I earlier felt, he does not drag out the sentimentality, but gets right to the heart strings with a personal and direct style.  Despite the highly ornamental nature of his writing, as I often debated with my wife, as she absolutely loves this composer.  I felt it frivolous and too ornate, almost "Baroquish" in tone.  I guess I've mellowed in my advancing years, and that is, surprisingly, a matter of contentment for me.  I actually now look forward to his language and mannerisms as being some of the most eloquent expressions in all of music.  I must admit that as a conservative in just about everything of any real importance, I rarely change my opinions but, somehow, Chopin has managed to do just that, L.O.L.
  The 8:11 "Allegro vivace" draws the work to a fitting close. Composed back to back, 1830 (#1 ) and also 1830 (#2) the second one is less fiery than #1 and seems more reflective as well.  I was, am still a bit puzzled as to why this sounds like the case, at least to my hearing and meditation on this apparent difference.
  I also admit the 2nd track, the "Grand Fantasy" didn't hold my interest that much as I moved ahead to the "Grand Polonaise Brilliante" and it's two part construction, unique in the Concertante literature.  The genius of this "Molto Allegro," is comfortably rendered by Mr. Ax in a more "moderato" tempo I found very good and a fine fit.  In fact, I had to stop typing and just sit back and listen to draw it all in, then resume with this modest review.
  If you love Chopin, as I am beginning to,  this is a vital addition to your shelves as it was to mine, so do not hesitate, go out and get a copy soon and simply enjoy this 4.5 rating and solid recommendation.  Best wishes and God bless each and every one of you, my friends, Tony.

I suspect that folks who buy this stuff are unfamiliar with the "Great American Songbook" and when they hear one of these timeless songs they enjoy it so much they rush out to buy Rod's version. He has chosen some beautiful classics to record. Really though, you should look for these songs as performed by great Jazz artists like Diana Krall, Frank Sinatra, Chet Baker, Eileen Farrell, Bill Charlap, Stan Getz, Tony Bennett, Ben Webster or Billie Holiday. You would be amazed at how great these songs are when performed by someone with the musical ability to provide a valid interpretation. Rod must be laughing all the way to the bank! His rock and roll material is awesome-no question. But he has neither the talent nor the skill to successfully interpret this material. His croaking efforts make me cringe!!!! Perhaps Kermit should consider recording some romantic songbook material?

I just hope other aging rockers don't decide to cash in and emulate Rod. Can you imagine Robert Plant warbling "Stairway to the Stars"? Or Mick Jagger growling "You'd Be So Nice To Come Home To"? If Jim Morrison were still around, I guess I wouldn't mind hearing his version of "Sleep Warm". After all, he was a serious fan of Frank Sinatra and had the chops to successfully mimic some elements of Frank's style in some of his better love songs!

One rock artist who can turn in credible interpretations of this type of music is Brian Ferry. Check out his "As Time Goes By" CD. As Time Goes By

reviewText:
It's unique, but it seemed like they were trying to do way too much with this album and there's nothing really exciting here.  In fact, the album remains mid-tempo or slower almost the whole time and seems to meander into bland nothingness because of this quite a bit.  I find myself reaching for the "next track" button quite a bit too.  I'm all for mid-tempo rock songs, but something is missing here.  I can't put my finger on it.

Now, as an avid Wilco fan, I'm all about creating an ambience to surround the song, but this album didn't really interest me in any way.  The ambience doesn't add anything and, infact, the songs seem to drag on past the point of relevance quite a bit.

Now, that's not to say the album is a complete bust.  I do enjoy some of the tracks ("Hoodwink" in particular), but it's not enough to save the whole album.  Also, there are some really cool percussion items (stomping feet come to mind), but a beat alone is not enough to care an entire album and, frankly, I've seen/heard the "unique" percussion thing done in indie rock in the past year by The Arcade Fire already.

Maybe this band's live show has something to offer me, but you'd have to buy my ticket for me.  The album doesn't convince me it's worth the price of admission.

reviewText: I love Donna Lewis.  I have all her albums, and I think she has an amazing ear for pop music and pop sensibilities in her song writing.  That said, this album is an incredible misstep for her.  It's primarily cover versions, done in what attempts to be a casual, jazzy-inflected atmosphere.  In trying very hard to not turn in slavish versions of the originals, Lewis offers drawn-out, winded, phrasings that consistently fall off-beat and seem lazy and lost.  Billie Holiday was the consummate master of the syncopated vocal--her ability to deliberately fall off rhythm and then land back on it expertly was one of her trademarks.  Lewis is not Holiday, and her performances on this disc lack any sense of passion or intensity.  They just seem limp.  Even her cover of her own biggest hit "I Love You Always Forever" seems to lack any connection to the heart of the original.  The entire album just feels like an exercise in pseudo jazz without any of the heart and passion that would ignite it.  As much as it pains me to write a review this negative about any Lewis album, this is just terrible.

reviewText:
Starting in 2001, Toshiba and Sony Japan successively released 18 Pink Floyd titles in LP-mini-sleeve replica format.  With only 5000 copies of each title manufactured for worldwide distribution, they quickly sold out, then soared in aftermarket resale value, as supply never even began to approach demand.  A full set, new (if you could find a genuine Japan set, not a bunch of Russian fakes), would probably now be somewhere north of a thousand bucks on eBay.

From a collectable standpoint, those Japan mini-sleeves are held by all fans as THE Pink Floyd catalog to own, and it is EXACTLY that pent-up demand and desire that EMI is attempting to exploit with this "Oh By The Way" box.

This box set is nothing more than Capitol/EMI's wretched attempt to wring as much final revenue out of the old remasters as possible.  Put quite simply: THERE'S NOTHING NEW HERE IN THIS BOX but a poster and two coasters.  If you buy it, you're allowing EMI marketing vermin to wretchedly devour the contents of your wallet, snickering at you as they drag your hard-earned cash back to their dank coffers, all the while leaving a slug-like trail of slime in their wake.  If all 10,000 box sets sell thru, multiplied by the set's wholesale price, even after production costs, EMI stands to net a cool million plus.

At the very least: DON'T fall for the marketing gag of the faux "LP album sleeves", as their quality is far less than the Japan `sleeves, DON'T be fooled by the "limited edition" marketing, as this set will depreciate in value from the day you open it, and DON'T fork over big bucks for the same masters you either already own, or can find new or used in standard jewel-case editions, and for far less money, than this expensive, redundant, worthless box set.

WHAT IS A JAPAN "MINI-LP-SLEEVE" CD?

Have you ever lamented the loss of one of the 20th Century's great art forms, the 12" vinyl LP jacket? Then "mini-LP-sleeve" CD's may be for you.

Mini-sleeve CDs are manufactured in Japan under license. The disc is packaged inside a 135MM X 135MM cardboard precision-miniature replica of the original classic vinyl-LP album. Also, anything contained in the original LP, such as gatefolds, booklets, lyric sheets, posters, printed LP sleeves, stickers, embosses, special LP cover paper/inks/textures and/or die cuts, are precisely replicated and included. An English-language lyric sheet is always included, even if the original LP did not have printed lyrics.

Then, there's the sonic quality: Often (but not always), mini-sleeves have dedicated remastering (20-Bit, 24-Bit, DSD, K2/K2HD, and/or HDCD), and can often (but not always) be superior to the audio on the same title anywhere else in the world. There also may be bonus tracks unavailable elsewhere.

Each Japan mini-sleeve has an "obi" ("oh-bee"), a removable Japan-language promotional strip. The obi lists the Japan street date of that particular release, the catalog number, the mastering info, and often the original album's release date. Bonus tracks are only listed on the obi, maintaining the integrity of the original LP artwork. The obi's are collectable, and should not be discarded.

All mini-sleeve releases are limited edition, but re-pressings/re-issues are becoming more common (again, not always). The enthusiasm of mini-sleeve collecting must be tempered, however, with avoiding fake mini-sleeves manufactured in Russia and distributed throughout the world, primarily on eBay. They are inferior in quality, worthless in collectable value, a total waste of money, and should be avoided at all costs.

reviewText: First of all, I love Elvis' music and have collected it for years and I have to admit if this is your first Elvis CD you probably will be satisfied. My problem with this CD is that Fool Such As I and The Wonder Of You are not the original hit versions that played on the radio way back when and helped build the King's legend. Fool is an alternate take and Wonder is a different live performance. These takes were never #1 anywhere and when you compare the original hits with these alternates you realise that RCA picked the right masters to originally release. In my opinion this is obscuring the King's legacy and in a way changing history for the new listener and not giving them all the goodness that was Elvis. Why would BMG do this? I suspect it is to coax the serious Elvis collector to buy yet again another rehash of hits that they have already bought many times over, just to get these two "special" tracks, and the novice Elvis collector wouldn't notice the difference. I would much rather have preferred a new two CD set of all the correct recordings remastered with today's technology (like the The Top Ten Hits did in 1988) and then have a seperate collection of nothing but unreleased alternates. However, these alternates always get sprinkled very sparingly in these endless Greatest Hits rehashes. But then again, I'm not a BMG marketing director, just another one of the millions of Elvis fans with money in my pocket.

reviewText:
I liked Gnarls better back when he used to sell me copies of "Grit" magazine and cut my hoop nets when I was looking toward the fire he'd set in my wastebasket. Now, he's whooping it up like a sitcom diversion, jibberjabbing like a simian slutdive bellhop. I like mockingbirds in a guilty way when they don't know I'm awake, spying on their mating chatter. But this, this by nature is grandiose, cellular, predisposed, grating. And I'm having a major case of deja vu. Does it even matter anymore? We're an expendable society, so why not embrace polymers? Why not kill all the fish?

But I plodded on, wondering what this "soup of the day" really was. Were those bits of carrot or flesh wounds? And it didn't matter because we had techmologicalized. We were pushing buttons now and DNA-approved to gain access to pay-per-view oxygen. We evolved through hope and memory loss. By the time I reached "Whatever," I really didn't care, which provided perhaps the finest moment of this failed experiment -- a time-transcendent conversation with Gnarls truly, wrapped in tusks of irony. But I still didn't know the way out of this cardboard box jungle -- the bird, strangled by glory-trolling, decaying in uncaptured sunshine.
label: negative

reviewText:
Everybody knows or should know that Killing Heidi are nothing more than a poor man's Mavis's, or rather, a watered-down, mass-market-acceptable, cynical record company executive's version of the Mavis's.
The Mavis's were a band led by a kooky-looking brother and sister from rural Victoria who combined insanely catchy pop hooks with noisy guitar. Unfortunately they were a bit edgy and challenging for the mainstream pop audience. What has clearly happened is some record company genius has said "What we need is a band like the Mavis's, but one that is a bit safer, and will do what it is told." Hence Killing Heidi. I couldn't and still can't believe the amount of record company hype they had behind them - even before they had a record out they were in Melbourne's best selling newspaper virtually every day - their publicist must be the hardest working man (or woman) in show business.
Killing Heidi are a perfect example of the cynicism of the music business which has inflicted on us such lame acts as Bush, Creed and all the other god-awful acts we have to put up with on a daily basis.
I'd say more, but it's time for my lunch break... (likes the Smashing Pumpkins, fer pete's sake!!)
What's the record like?  Lousy, obviously.

What's even worse about this collection is that Cre 2 Cre, the band's hilarious yet maligned early nineties rap collaboration, was ignored and left out. reviewText:
Britney Spears insipid and uninspired cover version of Bobby Browns seminal R'n'B anthem "My Perogative" amounts to musical high treason.  Browns original, a precursor to new jack swing, was a sexy, sassy funk number with a chugging bassline, captivating hook and addictive swagger.  Speers is tuneless, crass, over-produced, devoid of soul, unimaginative and characteristically hollow.

Where Browns original captivated dancefloors with its groundbreaking blend of staunch hip hop beats and harmonious vocals (and indeed, still does to this day), Speers is a throw-a-way record company cash-in, designed to increase sales for an equally uninspiring Greatest Hits package.

Unfortunately, the travesty that such an enduring and famous funk anthem has been desecrated will be lost on much of Speers fanbase, the majority of whom would not be old enough to remember Browns original version and therefore continue to believe in their baseless "superior cover version" nonsense.

reviewText:
With apologies to all those Minneapolis slackers still picking their feet in their parents' wood-paneled basements, this disc isn't fit to carry "Tim"'s gym bag. Sure, the Replacements had a major obstacle to  overcome with the departure of lead guitarist/nutjob Bob Stinson, but the  great bands meet these challenges head on by breaking up.
For starters,  the production on this album is hideous. Each and every electric guitar  tone has all the menace of a Rockman loaded with some seriously cheap-***  batteries; it's like a Marshall stack that Nigel Tufnel's  "Stonehenge" dwarf could stomp into oblivion. The drums feature  the same super deep reverb left over from "Tim" (it didn't work  there, either), making them sound like they were recorded in an abandoned  tool shed.
As for the genius of Paul Westerberg's writing, to me this  batch of songs heralds his plummet from once-great to hopelessly average.  "Alex Chilton" and "The Ledge" show some traces of the  old spark, but the whole thing seems so formulaic, as though the  inspiration went with Stinson. (Westerberg's ability has since dropped even  further, to the point where he could probably join the likes of Bowie and  Paul McCartney in a has-been consulting agency.)
Mind you, I saw the  Replacements perform much of this material during the "Pleased to Meet  Me" tour, and let me tell you: THEY ROCKED!--despite the colossal gall  of Slim Dunlap rendering note-for-note replicas of Stinson's solos. I went  out after that show and picked up this disc, and was frankly horrified by  what I heard. Every once in a blue moon I slap it on, still hoping to be  proven wrong. Forget about it. Go pick your feet.
