And forget ANYTHING about creativity - Santana's classic blues/rock/Latin/jazz guitar tone is dispensed of completely for the most part.

Speaking of selling out, how else could somebody explain the awful disco epic One Chain (Don't Make No Prison)? Seriously, disco and arena-rock ain't Santana's thing. The cover of Traffic's Dealer is awful, stripped of even remote energy or excitement - same goes for his cover of Buddy Holly's Well All Right (via Blind Faith), which is at least better than Invitation, One Chain, or Stormy, so stupid it'll make your IQ lower while you listen to it. Okay, not really, but I don't like the song regardless. You'd expect the two instrumentals to save the day here, right? Well, one of them does: the exciting Wham!, which is even then a more commercial Soul Sacrifice - the other, Life is a Lady/Holiday, is a Europa ripoff so blatant Carlos should've sued himself for writing it. I'm gonna be the early Santana purist here - the debut, Abraxas, III, Love Devotion Surrender, Caravanesari and even Festival blow this out of the water.

reviewText:
Toby Keith's 35 BIGGEST hits? My God, the only thing bigger than this guy's cowboy hat is his ego. Granted, he's had a few hits since 2001, when a national tragedy lurched him into the spotlight with "The Angry American." I'll also admit that since I live north of the Mason-Dixon line and east of the Hudson River, I don't have cause to hear his stuff with regularity, but saying that Toby Keith had 35 hits (and according to the title, that's only the `biggest' ones) is like saying that Bucky Dent (a `Yankee') hit 35 home runs a year - It just ain't so. Who does this guy think he is? Elvis? Hank? George? Hell, even the estates of Lefty and Jimmie had the good taste to restrain themselves from such pomposity.
 I guess I don't need to tell you that contemporary country music is certainly not about restraint, and Toby Keith is the perfect representative for the state of contemporary country music. As the old joke goes, `everything's big in Texas,' and these days, everything's big in country music, from the size of the hat to the size of the production. Problem is, that production is so bland that it's generic. Synthesized keyboards and processed echo dominate most of these tracks. You could erase Keith's voice and replace it with some Celine Dion drivel, and you'd end up with a perfectly serviceable (and perfectly awful) pop album. About the only thing that defines this as `country music' is the subject matter (cowboys, drinking, divorce, trucks...) and Keith's big ol' hat. I thought that songwriting style and instrumentation were the main factors in determining whether or not something was `country', but I guess I'm just too old-school.
 If Toby Keith is writing for the `contemporary' country audience, though, then he must think they're a bunch of dumb-%$es. He overstates the obvious on virtually every song and leaves nothing for the listener to discern. A good example is his jingoistic rally cry for American revenge (Courtesy of the Red, White and Blue"). Another example of a guy who simply can't imply anything that can be overtly spewed  is "I Wanna Talk about Me." He just doesn't know how to be subtle, does he? It's telling when the best song on disk one is a duet with Sting ("I'm So Happy I Can't Stop Crying"), and the best song on disk two is a duet with Willie (Beer for My Horses"). I know a lot of country fans will figure that I'm the dumb-a%#, but if this is Country, then I'll let Celine Dion eat my hat.  D  Tom Ryan

reviewText:
West Side Story came out the year I graduated prep school.  I saw it on Broadway at the Winter Garden in August 1960, which was an experience that still resonates within me.  I love the show and I love the music, and it struck me as a bit unusual that there is such a diversity of opinion in the reviews here at Amazon.

Not wanting the whole CD particularly, I downloaded two songs, Tonight and One Hand, One Heart, in an attempt to evaluate the leads, and I have to concur with the critics that find fault.  Scaglione's voice does not have the quality I would expect in a lead of a show of this magnitude.  Not only does it thin as the pitch goes higher, she seems to have trouble hitting notes right, and her vibrato comes when it detracts from the song.  I assume she must be miked for the production as I can't see that voice filling a theater.  When I saw the show, Lawrence and Rivera had departed, but the woman doing Maria had a fine voice, and once I accepted that she wasn't Carol Lawrence, I was totally engrossed in the show.

Cavenaugh comes across better, but his voice is nasal and he sings tentatively as if he was not comfortable with the part.  There is a sense of urgency, a tension, in many of the WSS songs and this was particularly lacking in Tonight.

It seemed to me, particularly in Tonight, that there was much more orchestra than was needed.  The OCR sounds as if they used the pit band and this track sounds like they have the whole symphony and it dominates when the singers should be front and center.  Perhaps this is just poor engineering and mixing.  I wonder also about the tempi.  It seems to me they are slow.

A reviewer mentioned that instead of using the cast to snap their fingers, an electronic device is used.  That probably says more about current performers than needs to be said and the use of Spanish is a bad idea.  If it ain't broke, don't fix it, but it seems to me, in trying to make it better, they broke it.  There apparently isn't a Jerome Robbins to get it done right.

One question:  I would love to see the original production, if only to see the dances, even if it wasn't the whole show.  Is any of it available on DVD?

reviewText:
(Warning--This review only covers the orignal CD Reissue of 12 songs.  For a different view see Richard Luhrs review.)

I have repeatedly listened to this album in order to find something nice to say about it.  The best I can say is that it is not offensive.  The original 12 song reissue checks in at 26 minutes.  While I don't believe in measuring music based on length of time, a certain measure of value has to be considered.  If the music is good, we don't care so much about the time length.

But here the music is sweet, almost sickly sweet.  Elvis appears to have lost all direction and inspiration. Not a single song does he claim as his own, and given the weakness of the material, he would not want to.  His performance is so below what he is capable of that one wonders if he wanted to do this session.  The arrangements and the performances lack any kick.

I just can't bring myself to describe what a flat, letdown this set is.  There is not a single song that I want to hear again.  There are many, many great Elvis CD's out there.  Invest your money (and time and ears) in those sets.

reviewText:
There are very few heavy bands that back up what they're trying to say. Modern day 'metal' bands have gone so commercial that it's hard to find the difference between them and, say, Britney Spears. Beneath the hate and anger, Trent Reznor has a feeling for music. That feeling has no better showcase than The Downward Spiral.
It's very clever. It works as a whole. A mixture of loud guitars, intoxicating electronics and putrid lyrics, it comes across like a splash of vomit. And, of course, it comes across perfectly when you're feeling angry.
Reznor's music doesn't depend on his vocals, but he gets away with it most of the time. Unlike someone like Billy Corgan, Reznor's voice is flat, undemanding and plain stating. It all comes with the whole industrial thing. Modern day machines tugging along at the beat of a factory. Music must be behind in ideas, because this kind of thing was exploited by the Futurists in the 1910s.
As I said, it's really an album rather than individual songs. There are techno works (Heresy), groundbreaking songs (Closer), and instrumental reflections (A Warm Place). Without doubt it is one of the true originals of the 90s and one of the best. The Downward Spiral doesn't make for comfortable listens. It makes for a decent brain cell battering.
label: negative

You know, I'm not very fond of the state of the world right now, but I don't throw trite little temper tantrums like Slipknot does. I mean really, there are people out there that suck and yes, we've all felt depressed, but I've never once felt the desire to write a bad diary entry about killing everyone. And that's what this album is. A dismal, inane, angsty mess wrapped-up in a blanket of fake death metal.
I mean, I'm all for songs about emotional strife, but I prefer something a little more mature or challenging. Serious, powerful music this is not. Come on, if you want extreme metal, you may as well buy a Napalm Death record. Want noise? Listen to The Boredoms, early Sonic Youth, or Lightning Bolt. Slipknot is one of those bands that might be appealing in those angsty teenage years (I don't really see how though), but really, it's quite ridiculous. Trust me, this is stuff you'll grow out of. If gimmicky, "please look at how shocking we are" nonsense if your cup of tea, dive right in.

reviewText:
Mike Patton is an exciting spectacle. He amuses well. Sings well. He composes well. And more importantly, he gets into trouble all the time.
Despite such traits, my 1*'yfication is forthcoming.
To begin on an obscure note; The artistic value of the pathway affront my home is in question. The Local Council would be adamant in delegating the workmanship of it to 1*, unless they could get out of giving it any* at all. Because... it has my dog's footprints in it. Yes, 'in'.But despite the pathway art's lack of dogly forethought, it recieves 5* from me. And just as my unwavering love of dogs is a requirement for my appreciating this cemently handywork, being unalterably intrigued by Mike Patton is a requirement for liking this cd. This is the nature of accidental art. So, I appreciate the fact of its existence (hence, no moral objection to such abrasive projects), but I didn't respond to it any.
You won't find Patton's 'higher brain function' on show here. Instead, you will get to experience "a day in the life of..." his mind, in a solitary low-concentration setting. Even though I'm aware that this is no sophisticated pursuit, my enjoyment needed there to be some variation in the sounds produced. If you close-mic. everything, even different sources tend to sound relatively indistinguishable from one another. Distinctivity is even less likely if you bark and spit into the recording device. But, sameness does have it's very own lure. For example, with meditative cd's containing rainforests and thunderstorms, sameness throughout the cd is a pre-requisite. But you must like the first sounds, if you're to even concieve of wanting it to continue. So if you like aggressive and vulgar vocalization, it's not inconcievable that a whole cd worth of it would be within your pleasure. But here, being just 'mildly' receptive to this sort of thing, just won't cut custard (as the saying surely doesn't go).You must be a "Gold-Card Member" of this sort of expressiveness. Me? I haven't even recieved the application form.
I've heard that this material was done mainly after concert performances. If this is true, his creative energy would've been sapped by the time he engaged this activity.(Beware! A theory approaching). -He may have engaged this activity merely to help himself down off of the highs of a performance (a difficult transition, undoubtedly), gradually calming himself so he could sleep.(?)
None of this explains why he decided to share it with the public. But I guess if you are interested in him enough to journey his personality (through thick and thin), you may find this oddly intriguing. I know myself the pleasure of low-concentration activities when I'm feeling sedate. But I doubt if I'd show it to anyone, sometimes not even to myself for a reliving.
Hence my 1*'yfication (That is a word, isn't it?).
label: negative

So first she made her fans excited with the news of releasing something really interesting (something she hasn't done in years) only to take it away from them.

So Joan doesn't like to look back huh? Okay, both the Hits & Misses compilations, released in 1996, were probably recordlabel driven, but what about the three compilations she released in 2004/2005? So called concept compilations that offered nothing but Joni's egoism and now this boxset of already excisting material. How much more collections of her work will she offer us? No way in hell will this fan spent his hard earned dollars on another boring Joni Mitchell collection.

reviewText: My wife likes this guy so, unfortunately, I felt compelled to listen to the CD since she insisted on buying it (even though I have a wall of Verdi operas from the true masters past and present).  What a depressing experience.  I kept thinking about all the struggling singers out there who could really pull this off and will never get the chance to sing these roles on the stage, much less be recorded, because they don't have a Marketing machine backing them.  There is too much that is horrific about the singing on this CD that to enumerate them would be time-consuming and ultimately pointless since it is clear that his fans are hopelessly numb to any kind of critical thought.  I would just urge anyone toying with the idea of buying this CD to do themselves a favor.  Buy it if you must, but then also seek out a compilation of Verdi arias by Domingo (there are a couple of them extant) and compare.  The differences are not just technical.  You will find far more passion, heart, and intellect in a great Verdi performance than this meager disc offers.  Don't settle for mediocrity.  Sure, this is better singing than Michael Bolton, but let's set the bar a little higher, shall we?

reviewText:
If this rating seems lower than it should be, try to listen to it first before buying as I was able to.  Whatever made CT great isn't here. Some albums are quickly cut out for a reason.

I worked at a record store when this came out in summer of 1986. My boss had an advance cassette, and he lent it to me to take home. I listened once, gave the album my undivided attention, and took it back the next day. I could have probably paid him a few dollars for it and kept it, but I did not like it at all. At the time I had seen CT live 4 or 5 times, and owned every CBS/Epic (now Sony) album. I was a diehard CT fan.

The songs on "The Doctor" are all either juvenile subject matter, or based on sex or love. No clever, interesting, or irreverent lyrics, as I was used to hearing from CT. No melodies made an impression. Instrumentation was nothing special. None of the trademark "hooks." This probably sold fewer than 20,000 copies. I feel badly for those 20,000 people except for the ones who posted here and unexplicably like it.

The album sounds as if it was made to fulfill a contract. The 80's certainly weren't CT's prime, but any CT album preceding this one is much more worthy of your time and money. I don't know about the music post-"Doctor."  Although they have since recorded much stronger material, this is last CT album I heard all the way through. (Adapted from my review of January 13, 2000.)

reviewText:
This is a remarkable achievement. With his 13th Symphony, Allan Pettersson succeeded in writing a piece of music that is about as pleasurable as oral surgery. How did he do it? Well, he wrote a continuous 67-minute span of music with no sense of structure or shape at all. There's no contrast between sections, no memorable themes, no sense that the music is going anywhere. The whole thing is smothered in dense, mushy orchestration; occasionally you hear some jackhammer-like busy stretches, but no development to speak of, and no real climaxes. It's relentless, but after a few minutes it gets aggravating, then painful, then just plain dull.
I actually rather like Pettersson's 7th and 8th symphonies, where he keeps his self-pity somewhat in check; but 13 was definitely an unlucky number for me. If you're a masochist though, or if you want to *experience* misery rather than just have it depicted for you, you might like it.

reviewText:
First things first, this is not for vinyl freaks because listening to these releases you will start lo laugh immediately (just check out Atom Heart Mother poor transcription from a wasted master).  So please stop here.

A person, who likes PF and wants to complete his CD collection with a top quality release, must get the Japanese mini sleeve replica (the original ones not the Russian fakes) since these are THE definitive releases. So this set Oh By the Way is not for you.

If you want to be the first boy in your block with the lastest Pink Floyd release then this one is for you, if you have $ 200 plus left.

Hard core fan - collectors of the band will buy this item sooner or later to complete their collection.  There's nothing we can do about it.

From my point of view, the main thing with this release is that there is nothing new in it.  The same albums we have loved for years (and still we do) are here once again as regular editions but packaged in a thin cardboard cube box.  I was waiting for special mixes like the quadraphonic Wish You Were Here, an alternate take of the classic tracks, unreleased tracks, an unreleased live show from the BBC, or even a booklet with rare photos of the band.

I am very disappointed with this box set, not for the music, but for the price and mostly because this is the easiest way for EMI to earn money from all the fans of the band at the minimum cost.  It's easy, they put the same music they have in their catalogues inside a cheap mini LP replica, add an attractive package with of course limited edition tag and then put it in the market at $ 200 plus; the result is a great deal for the record company.  It's a real shame.

This is the reason why devoted hard core fans release CD's like Pink Floyd BBC Sessions 67 - 69 getting the best source to produce a custom made product to satisfy anxious fans all over the world that for years have demanded a proper release of these legendary shows with the great late John Peel at the helm.

reviewText:
Let's cut right to the chase: the piano on this recording is so badly out of tune, this CD is unlistenable. Worse, the quartet is tuned sharp to the piano, presumably because the piano itself is so badly out of tune what could they actually tune to? Every time the quartet rests or takes an accompaniment role, what you hear is an excruciatingly flat, badly out of tune piano taking up the tune. It literally sounds like a honky-tonk upright in a southern bar, but without any of the fun! Not only that, Cristina Ortiz sounds like she's sight reading this music; she fluffs and fakes her way through several passages. And the Fine Arts Quartet sound like a student group, at best. I am completely baffled this passed muster to any of those involved. It is unbelievable that the Producer/Editor/Engineer, Steven Epstein, could not hear what was going on while he was in charge at the controls. Even more amazing that the performers themselves could not hear they were not tuned to the piano, and that Ortiz was having a very bad day, playing badly on a very bad piano!

This recording is an absolute disgrace. Naxos needs to cut their losses right here and now, pull this back from availablility and look for a competent group of performers and start again. This is glorious Saint-Saens and it deserves a great recording. It certainly does not receive it here."

reviewText: This really makes you want to cry. What's even more disturbing is the people that defend this album under the explanation of "Glenn trying something different". Give me a break, he was trying for a paycheck. This is Glenn Danzig we're talking about here, Glenn Danzig!! One of the best singers and songwriters of all time! This guy has written some of the most haunting songs we've ever heard! If you have a voice like his, would you want to distort it? That's one of the biggest reasons we listen to Danzig! On this album it sounds as though he's shouting through a pair of blown speakers. I don't know what happened to the original band, but they were so much a part of his sound, though he would never admit that. Maybe he got rid of them because they were starting to get their own identities. People came to like the other members, and Glenn probably caught wind of the fact that people realized there were other members in the band besides himself(probably why he changes lineups so often now, to confuse us). I don't know what's up with Danzig these last few years. He should donate his ego to science after he dies, maybe we'll find some answers. I'm sure this is probably why he left The Misfits, people started associating the group with Jerry Only as well(and we can't have that!). Hell, I'm siding with the new Misfits anymore! At least they're sticking to their guns, and not putting out a NIN or Korn album. Please people, get one of the first four Danzig albums if you're new or curious, and really see the genius at work. Those albums are classic and hold the test of time. Even if you're not in the Danzig mood, putting on one of the old albums will put you in the mood. It's four great musicians at their best. Where the hell did John Christ take off to anyway? He was a very underrated guitarist, and Glenn never let him truly shine. Hopefully, Glenn will come to terms with his blunder, track John down, apologize, buy him ice cream, whatever it takes. He needs to get off his high horse and get that band back!!!!

reviewText:
First of all, there's a reason this so-called "best of" compilation doesn't contain most of Judas Priest's signature tunes:  it was actually first released back in 1978, by a small independent label called Gull Records which put out JP's first two proper albums "Rocka Rolla" and "Sad Wings of Destiny."  And indeed, it is just a sampler of songs from those two albums.  Gull released it shortly after Judas Priest moved on to sign with CBS Records and released their first major-label album "Sin After Sin."

If you like the songs on this album (and they are pretty good, and an interesting document on Judas Priest's early formative years), you might as well just dish out the extra money and buy "Rocka Rolla" and "Sad Wings of Destiny" in their entirety.  The only thing that "Best of" has that those first two albums don't have is the interviews with old Judas Priest drummer John Hinch.  According to the band's official web site, those interviews are misleading and full of lies, and Hinch was let go because they found him musically inadequate.  What's more, the band does not encourage their fans to buy this so-called "best of" album.

I really did not know what to make of this piece when I first listened to it. I mean it is a track by track re-recording of the AC/DC Classic "Back In Black", and then when the vocals come in it goes downhill. Knowing this happens a short minute after the original begins you know there is a lot of hill to roll down. Musically the CD is tight as it is an almost complete copy of the original record. It shows that the group is capable of playing more than their usual style of music which is indeed very heavy. It might have been a smart idea for the vocalist Chris Barnes to also try to use a different voice. It would serve better as an homage to the band in doing so.

I don't know what the relevance of re-recording such a classic album in the way it was done will hold for this did not appeal to anyone I played it for. I did not want to be the sole opinion on this, and said maybe I was missing the boat somewhere. Everyone who heard it agreed the music was well done and then ruined when the singing kicked in. Steve Swanson, Greg Gall and Terry Butler do however a fine job of the playing of the tunes.

It is difficult to determine who will enjoy this CD. I think the only people who "might" like it are the die-hard fans of Six Feet Under (and these fans need to own everything the group releases). Classic rock fans of AC/DC will be insulted by this, as there is no need for a redo of an album that broke hard rock ground on its release. Death metal fans themselves might not enjoy it for it is not speeding fast or even relevant to their musical interests. I strongly suggest you play MP3 samples of it before you purchase it, you might thank me.

I do not understand the cult behind the Shaggs.  There is deliciously bad music out there to enjoy, but even such music (as released on the "Incredibly Strange Music" CDs) is listenable and enjoyable.  I cannot say the same for this album.
Why did a major label like RCA re-release this?  Unknown.  They must certainly be disappointed that this re-release has only generated about 1,000 sales since last year.  The answer for low sales is simple - listen to the samples and see if you don't agree that the answer is that it is unlistenable.
Order the "Golden Throats" and "Incredibly Strange Music" CDs for a hoot.  Avoid this one.

reviewText: Well, the packaging IS cool, with reproductions not only of the LP sleeve and disc label, but also the inner paper sleeve. However, the sound is a disaster. The entire disc has been given an extreme treble boost, which creates distortion and completely changes its character. On many songs the percussion (especially cymbals and snare) dominates the mix, making a song such as "Tamp 'Em Up Solid" sound almost like cocktail jazz. The old CD sounds muffled in comparison, but it - like the rest of Reprise's domestic CD reissues - was true to the original LP sound. Warner Brothers engineers (and Ry) had wonderful ears, and I'm sure the mix we heard in 1974 was close to the one they wanted. This is like listening to a band from inside the snare drum. I don't know how someone listening to this album for the first time would react to the new mix, but I can't handle it. Painful and disappointing.

reviewText: It's interesting how styles change in classical music. Today, everything is played at a fast tempo. The faster the better. In the 1940s and '50s, conductors such as Bruno Walter and Otto Klemperer played everything at a lethargic pace. I tend to favor the more sedate tempi, but this recording is insane. One awaits the next note to sound with the same dread as when your car has a dying battery. It's no longer music, but it resembles that experiment -- Nine Beet Stretch, by Leif Inge -- where Beethoven's Ninth Symphony is digitally stretched out to 24 hours in duration (with no pitch change). That actually sounds more musical than this mess, because the musicians here don't seem to know how to play the Maestoso tempo at Largissississississimo without inducing many awkward moments. I'm flabbergasted at the number of positive reviews here. No doubt the fans are all devoted votaries of Gould, and he could've played it backwards, and they'd hail it as a masterpiece. For me, Bernstein's disclaimer says it all. Glen Gould is said to have admired the tune Downtown by Petula Clark, too. What's that? You already have several recordings of it? Of course you do.

When Nirvana released their second album Nevermind in September of 1991, thankfully it was ignored in its first few months as heavy metal bands like Guns and Roses and Metallica ruled the rock and roll mainstream with their Use Your Illusion 1 and 2 and Black Albums respectively plus Anthrax, Judas Priest and Megadeth released great albums amidst the hair metal trash.

In 1994 (almost three years after this album was released), my prophecy came true as he offed himself like a yellow dog.
Cobain, unlike Hendrix, was a deplorable guitarist and un-revolutionary IMHO!

It irks me to see people compare this album to real classics like Dark Side of the Moon, Who's Next, Sticky Fingers, Hotel California and Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band. Nevermind is overrated.
Aside Teen Spirit, other lousy songs were "In Bloom", "Come As You Are" (should have been titled "Don't Have a Gun") and "Lithium" (who would write a song about a sedative to combat hyperactivity). "Territorial P*ssings" sounds like he was writing about a pack of wolves marking their territory. "Endless Nameless" was annoying. "Drain You" was silly.
Whom in the blue Hell came up with naming a generation "X", last time I checked Generation X was a punk band that Billy Idol was in back in the late 1970s. I get down on my knees and seriously thank God I dove heavily into Queen's music when Nirvana were at their peak. Also, people comparing a real rock legend like John Lennon to, what "The Motor City Madman" Ted Nugent aptly called a "weenie", Kurt Cobain was like comparing solid gold to tin foil. Lennon was about happiness and wanting peace in the face of all negativity and horror in the world we live in whilst Cobain just whined, complained, p*ssed and moaned and cried about how bad his life was and wanting to die and sounded like a three year old who had his toy taken from him.

While having been a Cohen fan for many years now, I had avoided this record precisely because of its reputation (and the fact that Cohen has mostly disowned). I understand now. This is, frankly, gawdawful, perhaps the single worst production job I have ever heard. If these songs were recorded outside, on a busy street corner, on a rainy day, using a a 1970's Sears portable cassette player it likely would have been vastly better. One need look no further for proof that Spector is insane.

Where to begin... Not sure I can, so let me put it this way - Leonard Cohen is one of the great songwriters of the last 75 years. The production on this record is so bad that I honestly cannot tell even if any of the songs are any good AS songs. I am giving serious thought to grabbing a guitar and playing them in my living room to try and see if they are decent songs under all that bilgewater. Of course, I'll have to hunt up the tabs and lyrics becuase it is nearly impossible to make out either listening to this. Really - this is virtually unlistenable: a tinny, haphazzard mess.

I love Leonard Cohen's music. I hate this record.

reviewText: When in high school I almost destroyed my treasured "Yes" LPs, because I listened for these albums for hours and hours - as thousands of other suckers did, searching for some secret knowledge and hidden message. Bugger it - there is none. Centuries later I suspected already the existence of Internet, but I didn't know anything about Amazon - otherwise I would have bought them from Amazon and save the trouble of a trip to "Tower Records" in London. Well, I bought them on CDs and kept listening to until I came to a painful conclusion: we are dealing with musical Maoists who are in the dark room searching for a black cat, and they don't even want to admit that it's not there. Somehow the music reminds an elaborated and over-decorated facade which hides an ugly naked truth - a simple concrete pavillion of a public WC. "Yes" are exceptional musicians who go on and on into lengthy improvisations, showcasing of instrumental prowess and complicated construction of songs, while tin falsetto of Anderson wandering above - looking to which part to stick to. It became a music for self-appointed cognoscenti and illuminati - not literate enough to know classical music, but wishing to be above "art crowd". All these virtuoso ventures to my most humble opinion cover one simple thing - "Yes" plays instruments, not music. Meditating with the candles was a good try, but the inspiration obviously got lost in the darkness, while the candles should have been used for better purposes. Composing is not their forte, all these artificial complexities cover a sheer misery of melody. It was a good show, I really loved it - time to face the truth. I got rid of my "Yes", and listen mainly to "Rare Bird", "Frumpy Live" and - if you want progressive - Czeslaw Niemen. Until now I keep some LPs - because of Roger Dean. P.S. By the way, Touch - most humbly, but strongly recommended - did it all in 1969. Actually, pre-dated and blew away (if given a chance) many of British prog-rock peers.

But there's nothing here but the sense that the band is tuning up for something that never begins.  I read they got four hours of tape out of this session, and these 33 minutes represent the finest moments.  This is not, as other customers have opined, an under-appreciated "gem", or "territory John McLaughlin would later explore," or powerful fusion.  It's just a half hour of sad noodling from a guy who used to be an intense, churning guitarist who always drove the music hard. They remind me a lot of The Darkness gone completely wrong, (who, lucky for us, got it all right). Pray For The Soul Of Betty seems to be at their best musically when they attempt the (very) occasional ballad, but their lead singer's voice just isn't up to the task. In all, this seems to be a hodge podge of different sorts of musical talents, - yes, there is a glimmer of talent here - all forcing themselves to hopelessly mesh together into a band that can't decide which path to take. And the lifting of riffs from "older" songs, (possibly because listeners will have have forgotten them?!) is ridiculously obvious. Unfortunately, for example, they chose to lift riffs out of songs from the likes of Black Sabbath. Older, yes, forgettable, uhmmm...I don't think so. They seem to pull a lot from the eighties, also, which, let's face it, certainly isn't the best decade of songwriting to aspire to, and only leaves me thinking, "What are they thinking?!" The lyrics, while genuinely their own, are uninspiring and even boring - they're the type that can be heard at local rock clubs by house bands who travel 20 to 25 miles at most for a gig, yet dream of stardom. My advice to Pray For The Soul Of Betty: Split up, each of you find a band with a genre more suited to your style, and beside sounding better, I think you'll be much more satisfied with your ability to showcase your talent (this only applies to the few that do have talent) - sorry, but the rest/most of you just need to find a new line of work.

reviewText:
*1.5 Stars*

In case you didn't know, this is Katy Hudson's (I mean Perry's), second album. Her debut was all the way back in 2001 when she was a Christian good girl. But since the US mainstream doesn't accept anything less than the debauchery so present in pop culture, Katy was going to have to undergo a major overhaul in order to get the attention she so desperately craves. After a long string of failed starts and tearing through record label after record label, she finally found Glen Ballard and the Matrix. With their help, and the assistance of countless pop crafters (Max Martin, Dr. Luke to start the lengthy list) they Katy was able to rework herself into a bona-fide attention whore (emphasis on the whore). That is what she wants after all, attention. And nothing personifies it any better than "One of the Boys".

If the lead single "I Kissed a Girl" doesn't clue you in to the carnality this album, then don't worry, it will become so obvious it flies in the face of Katy's old Christian image. As catchy and irresistible as "I Kissed a Girl" is, and "Hot n Cold" is also another exceptional pop song, the rest of this album plays like one tired and repulsive stereotype and clich after another. Indeed, `Kissed a Girl' only plays into the bi-curiosity of the teen culture in 2008, but at least it still has a strong vocal performance and a pure pop production to match. But the quality stops there. "Waking Up in Vegas" is another tune with a good beat and confident vocals, but it only promotes the `throwing away your money' mishap that so often happens in Vegas. "Ur So Gay" uses an offensive slur to only widen the gap between heterosexuals and the LGBT community. And the added `penis' at the end really shoots down any respectable aspect of Perry. Basically, "One of the Boys" is homage to all of the gross, risqu, repugnant, and utter trash of the 2000s decade. Between the tales of Katy `laying face down in porcelain' to her juvenile attempt to bash her lover by calling him a `mannequin' instead of a man (really creative insult Katy), what you are getting is what the mainstream wants to hear. But what makes this album an utter joke is the closing track "Fingerprints". It claims that Katy wants to break the mold, but if she were to examine her behavior: singing whatever messy rock-pop is thrown in front of her and sinking down to the crass image of the pop machine is not breaking the mold, it IS the mold. Katy is a lot of things, but so far, being original isn't one of them.

She can either make her long-fought-for breakout into pop music, or she can try to show off her talent, but unfortunately she cannot have both. Even more unfortunate is the path that Katy decided to take. But rest assured, she is not completely un-talented, and even in "Thinking of You", it's obvious that even she's disgusted with the image she's been forced to adapt to. If you take this at face value, not a millimeter more, then this is just enjoyable pop music. So congrats to Katy, she's managed to finally put herself on the map, but has also tarnished the name of pop music (among other things) in the process.

reviewText:
Wow, this album is one of the most divisive I've ever heard. Nobody thinks that Captain Beefheart's Trout Mask Replica is simply "okay." Most of the reviews on this page either dismiss it as contrived, deliberately atonal, pretentious trash, or think it's a work of genius, and naturally both crowds are antagonistic towards each other.

So let me clear this up: You are not necessarily an MTV-watching mainstream drone for hating this album. By the same token, enjoying Trout Mask Replica hardly makes you a Mensa member (that said, you probably are more interested in "out-there," non-conformist music if you are in the latter camp). This album is strictly an acquired taste, and that's how the Captain intended, I think. I enjoy plenty of weird stuff--Zappa, The Boredoms, some RIO prog, Mr. Bungle, Fantomas, Zorn, etc. along with quite a bit of abstract jazz and fusionized metal; and after multiple listens I still find this album to be pretty exhausting, especially in one sitting where 2 LPs of this material tends to become obnoxious after a while. It probably would've been better as a single record.

I don't hate the Captain for making this album. For better or worse, it's interesting, and both a product of its era (in that it seems to be psychedelic in a rather odd sort of way) and yet exploits musical idioms that were unheard of in rock during its time. The free-jazz-meets-Delta-blues-at-a-postmodern-poetry-slam sound of Trout Mask Replica is rather unique. There's plenty of abstract rhythmic ideas going on--it all sounds rather stupid at first, but Beefheart actually intended it to sound this way, and the Magic Band practiced for nearly a year trying to hammer these compositions out. So, you can't call it "amateurish" or "incompetent." These guys knew what they were doing. As for Beefheart himself, I rather like his great bluesy growl at times. It's like Howling Wolf if he read a lot of Burroughs and did plenty of acid.

Trout Mask Replica is definitely innovative. So, why do I persist on giving it only one star? Actually, if I could change the rating I'd give it two, as there are a few decent (not outstanding, merely decent) tracks on here that are listenable--Ella Guru, My Human Gets Me Blues, China Pig, Moonlight On Vermont, and Veteran's Day Poppy. And then there are the straight poetry tracks and other bits that are amusingly weird, though not musical in any real sense.

The rest of Trout Mask Replica is not my bag, frequently bordering on unbearable in its pursuit of the abstract. It goes off on tangents that make bags of cats thrown in a dryer seem downright musical. Case in point: Either of the Hair Pie Bake tracks. I can't imagine many people listening to this album without hitting the skip button at least once.

So, what we have here is a bold, unconventional, and influential recording...that does not compel me to listen with any sort of frequency. It's just not worth the effort, and believe me I have tried.

Those interested in checking Beefheart out probably shouldn't start here anyway. The bluesier Safe As Milk is more accessible and musical, while still being quite avant-garde. If you like that album and want to dive deeper, go right ahead and try your hand at Trout Mask Replica. You may love it; you may hate it; but you should definitely *listen* to it.

reviewText:
If I had to sum up the record in one word I would say it was "forced". Rubin has admitted to challenging them to recapture the sound of the first couple of Sabbath records but he didn't seem to understand that wasn't available to them.

Iommi hasn't written in that style in years and Ozzy's solo stuff took him into an entirely different direction which ultimately led to mediocrity. As such, neither of them were prepared or able to recapture the old sound. So, they basically came up with a slate of uninspired stuff that sounds like a crude forgery of what they once were.

There are plenty of copycat songs based on earlier tunes that were far superior. This technique has been employed by Maiden, Priest and many other metal bands whose best songs are behind them. The playing is perfunctory, it offers no excitement. The music is boring because it sounds like they were bored recording it.

I don't know why people think Rick Rubin is a great producer. His mixes are generally second rate at best and his musical direction is often misguided. He should have let the band do whatever they were feeling NOW, not tried to force them back into a mindset they have long since abandoned.

I am sure the fact Tony was feeling under the weather didn't help. How do you tell a legend who is fighting for his life his ideas sound uninspired? Well, they fulfilled their contractual obligations. They put out some songs and will now do the tour. Sadly this is not the way a great band should end their career but it seems like most of them do end this way nonetheless.

reviewText:
The 60's gave us the young Beatles.  The 70's gave us the Bee-Gees.  The 80's gave us the Go-Go's.  The 90's didn't give us much to be happy about.  Today, we have Creed to make us feel good about ourselves and our situation.
That said, we can place "Weathered" on par with the rest of those artists--somewhere between "bury them alive" and "hang 'em from the highest limb."  Knowing why radio stations used to play and still continue to play music from such happy-go-lucky bands (because people like to feel GOOD!), you can see why Creed is such a hit.
The music is just as soulless and juvenile as anything by Nirvana, and just as empty and lifeless as anything by Type O Negative.  Bass?  What bass?  There is no bass.  Guitars?  Yeah, right.  I've heard better guitar work from Spinal Tap!  Vocals?  Sure, if you think ol' Marble Mouth can carry a tune, more power to you.
Anything significant to say?  Hardly.  How significant is "Let us put aside our differences and unite as one great body of humanity!"?  We're bombarded by that message from the news media and other forms of mass communication every day.  After the zillionth time, it begins to lose its punch.
Anyway, back to the music.  What we have is a collection of songs that have been studio processed more heavily than Cheez-Whiz to be more easily digestible by anyone unfortunate enough to listen to it.  Listen to a live Creed concert sometime and you'll find out that they're almost as incapable of playing instruments as the Monkees were.

reviewText: With all due respect to Mr. Anderson, who has still has one of the most distictive voices in rock history, this album, the more urban-sounding 'The More You Know', is a ridiculous attempt at a more modern '90's ethno-pop  sound which fails on most accounts. The main problem is a lot of these  sappy lyrics, which are so uninspiring and sickingly sweet as to induce  terminal nausea. It is hard for even the most open-minded of listeners(Yes  fans or otherwise) to even get through this album. Jon's collaborators, the  Jocky brothers(who would be better off without Jon or his Linda McCartney  wife hovering around) are running the whole show here, with Jon adding  little more than his lyrics and vocals and Jane Anderson doing little more  than hovering around. I'm not against this sort of direction, all these  urban grooves, rap-pop chanting and sequencers/samplers, but here it just  doesn't sound interesting and again these sappy lovey-dovey lyrics about  his wife aren't uplifting, they're annoying. This album has to be heard to  be believed about how ridiculous it sounds, but don't bother. Anderson's  more soul-influenced side worked to better results on his 1988 'In The City  Of Angels' album. For more pop/r&b sounds from the amazing voice of Jon  Anderson, get that instead. Other than the first two decent songs, which  you can't help but tap to, there isn't really much here.

reviewText:
Geez, what has been with Maiden recently. They are my favorite band and all but it seems like they can't release a new album without releasing a best of album right after. It started in 1995 with the X-Factor, with Best of the Beast. OK, so that was good, because enough time had passed sinced the self-titled debut. Then Virtual XI, with Ed Hunter, then Brave New World and Dance of Death with Edward The Great, then The Essential Iron Maiden in 2005, then A Matter of Life and Death and Somewhere Back in Time. Now, we have The Final Frontier and this pointless release?!?!?!

I'd be lying, though, if I said I wasn't impressed with the fact that they are releasing compilation based solely on the 1990-2010 stuff, because both Fear and No Prayer, X and Virtual, and BNW-TFF have some of Maiden's most important stuff yet. In particular, the Reunion albums are important- Bruce and H are back for good this time and they're continuing to make music. I'm one of the few who prefers the new albums, as they are more thoughtful and meaningful, as well as reflective.

But honestly, don't waste your money on this- BUY THE ALBUMS!!!!!! The new Maiden's albums are like symphonies. They require to be listened from first track to last (OK, skip The Assassin on NPFTD). Sure the selection on this is great, but they're only fragments of amazing albums. You WON'T be left satisfied. Furthermore, the live versions of the Blaze tracks have already been released on a 2 CD set entitled "Best of the B'Sides". As anal of a fan as I am of Iron Maiden, I worry they may become the next Aerosmith with how many compilations they are releasing. If you want a compilation, I suggest you get The Essential Iron Maiden as it pans most of Maiden's career.

Like I said, buy the albums. The new material isn't just "listen to one song and you're full", the entire albums must be heard from the first track to last.

reviewText: One can't argue the fact that Pearl Jam are not a dynamically sound band that overflows with confidence.  When Pearl Jam departed from its grunge sound, the band promised a new and better music layout.  I have yet to see those words made into action.  Binaural is yet another god-awful attempt to salvage Eddie Vedder's reputation for evocative silliness.  I can credit this record for its occasionally bright concoctions, such as Insignificant, Evacuation, and Of the Girl, but that's about as far as the CD goes, in terms of good direction.  Light Years, Typing, and Rival are almost as terrible as the earlier horribly stingy single Yellowledbetter.  Eddie Vedder can sing, and that's good to know, but Binaural's unoriginal, tasteless alternative rock material insures that won't ever matter.  When Pearl Jam graduate to the aptly wonderful sound that they promised fans years ago, knock on my door and I'll give it a listen.  Until then, hit and miss LP's like Binural will continue to flourish in their own scavely scattered rock messes, and will definitely stay out of my CD collection.  It's clear in songs like Nothing As It Seems that the group have an ego to follow and that they believe in their music, which is something great that I couldn't say for some bands nowadays.  However, Vedder and his group need to check the quality of the irritating music that they're so blindly believing in.

reviewText:
Could this recording title have been a clever inside joke? They're laughing all the way to the bank.
Back in the 60s, visionary musicians like Hendrix, Davis and Santana transcended the established musical boundaries of their time to courageously explore new directions for jazz and rock. They ignored the business side of the recording industry to focus their energies on the music.
Today, Santana seems to have completely reversed his goals. I don't hear an ounce of creative breakthrough in his new work. I hear the recording business money makers calling the shots, marketing Santana like a new pair of Nikes. And it works, he's more popular than ever, playing the least inspired work of his long career. What a sham, and a shame. Could Carlos, the guy who brought us Abraxas, Love Devotion and Surrender, and Caravanserai actually like this stuff?

Artistically, Fumbling Towards Ecstasy was the beginning of the end for Sarah McLauchlan. The songs are mostly weak; the muddied, unsympathetic production by Pierre Marchand is simply dreadful. Save your hard earned money and buy the Cowboy Junkies great new album Demons or just about anything by Kate Bush or Margot Smith.

reviewText:
The Good

"One Way Ticket" is lead by one of those simple riffs that tend to get caught in your head for days, similar to an AC/DC one. The chorus is quite catchy and vocalist Justin Hawkins doesn't sound as irritating as it has in the past (don't get used to it). "Knockers" may or may be about what you're dirty mind is thinking about, but I highly doubt it. The lyrics are quite cryptic, but the bluesy rhythms and guitar licks are what make the track enjoyable. "Dinner Lady Arms" recalls classic AOR arena rockers sonically. Hawkins throws in plenty of his trademark falsettos and lays down one fiery solo. This, my friends, is when our trip into hell begins...

The Bad

Take everything you remember about The Darkness and throw it out the window. On their first album the group tried to bring back the glitz and glam of eighties power pop and glam metal, on this album that take a few steps back; creating more of a seventies pop rock/eighties AOR sound (remember when KISS went disco?). The music itself sounds great, but the main problem remains to be vocalist Justin Hawkins. He just can't sing. He has his moments here and there, but with each passing track he becomes more and more annoying. Maybe if he focused more on singing in key, the songs would be a lot better. It also seems like there was not a lot of effort put into writing the material.

The Verdict

They ain't kidding; this is a trip into hell. The only way back is to hit the eject button.

reviewText:
This band would be funny if it wasn't serious. This is musical devolution.

It's quite true that either you like Mortician or you hate them. This is mostly because Chainsaw Dismemberment is the same song over and over again. If you liked the first "song" then you'll like the album unless you have a tendency to like albums with variety. If you hated that song then you'll hate Mortician's music.

This band sounds like a muddy gurgle with horror movie samples. The guitars play the same two chord riffs over and over again. The drums,..I mean drum machine is fast. The "vocals" are gutteral and grunted. Fortunately, there are enough points when I can't hear them because they don't sound too much different from the drum machine. I also heard there was a bassist but maybe I was mistaken. False advertising indeed. There are lyrics, but I feel no need to discuss them. Bands like Deicide get a bad rap for their repetitive and often unintelligent lyrics. But this is ridiculous. On the plus side, it's hard to beat Mortician for consistency.

To sum up, some people apparently like this band. That is completely fine. I happen not to. I don't find monotonous riffs over even more monotonous drum riffs and monotonous vocals particularly appealing. Yes, that sentence was redundant. Still it has more variety than this album, at least is uses different words. This is a compilation of brutal nosie for the sake of brutal noise. If you want good death metal, then try Death. You might find a hint of musicianship, meaningful lyrics and real songs. Try Cannibal Corpse if you want brutal, less than technical death metal.

reviewText: After buying and listening to And Then There Was X, I quickly decided to  never buy another DMX album again!! This release is a slap in the face to  the entire culture of Hip Hop. The only reason I was able to rate  this album with one star is because of the only two good songs contained on  it, What's My Name and What These B**ches Want. Other than those two songs,  the listener will be in for a disappointing journey over X's preaching and  singing. His best work came clearly on his initial release, It's Dark and  Hell Is Hot. Swizz Beats is displaying that his work is  also declining in substance. The best track, as far as production is  concerned, is What These B**ches Want, which was produced by Nokio from the  R&B group Dru Hill. With the release of And Then There Was X and The  Opposite of H2O by Drag-On, the Ruff Ryder camp is proving that it can not  live up to it's early-life hype. Is anyone else sick and tired of this sub-genre of bands who parlay an unfortunate broken home experience into a career? Like Everclear before them and Good Charlotte, Nickelback makes strident, one subject music that serves as the soundtrack for the younger people working in support collection units nationwide. Nickelback is the more militant of the bunch because they seemingly know of no other subject to write about and somehow, when you listen to this and watch the videos, there's a creepy sense of this whole stance being a targeted demographic than anything truly cathartic and that's despicable.
"Never Again" is about the best of the lot here, which isn't saying too much since it can easily be mistaken as a Bush outtake. The hits are there for people who buy into the notion that Chad Kroeger's the new spokesman of the generation and that his Jesus-like look is hot. For everyone else though, a little of this stuff goes a very long way and if you can sit through an entire listening of this CD without wanting to scream "get over it" at the stereo, then you should be commended for having a very high pain threshold.

reviewText: There is a certain sadism to this box set. Care was taken with every step of production until pressing. So what should have been the greatest case ever for the superiority of vinyl over every other sound medium fails to be made. Don't get me wrong. Where pressings are as quiet and centered as they should be, vinyl wins over CD hands-down. I know because I A/B'd them both at my hi-fi store on state-of-the-art equipment. But where they are marred with noise (which is far too often the case), the records remind you how much we have been spoiled by the quiet of digital sound. These recordings should have been flawless pressings, arguing for the greater density, detail and texture of vinyl sound. But every "tic" and "rumble" just makes you tense with angry disappointment. Don't buy this box. Make EMI apologize to the world for this quality control disaster and reissue the set with every pressing perfect. I'd be willing to pay $30 per pressing ("wholesale") to hear the Beatles as they must have sounded during original mixing at Abbey Road.

reviewText:
I have always felt that the Pet Shop Boys are guilty of making just good albums. Whether the album is a commercial success or not the actual material has always been consistently good and in many cases sadly overlooked by the general public. Then PSB released "Elysium"  - an album that was in my  opinion filled with incomplete songs, trite lyrics and lazy production. The album was a commercial failure and for the first time for me a musical dud also. Less than a year later PSB stunned their fans with the announcement of  "Electric" -an album promised to be filled with heavy rhythms, electronic soundscapes over surging dance tracks. Almost a year after "electric" being released this album is still for me PSB's worst album. It is at best a lazy effort and at worst uninspired, pandering music.

Electric includes 9 tracks. The songs here range from tuneless retro 80's italo house ("axis") catchy but repetitive pop ("shouting in the evening") to the absolute awful ("Thursday")). Pet shop Boys have always been intelligent songwriters who happened to use dance music as their genre of choice. What is sad about Electric is that the album is devoid of substantial lyrics or songs. What is presented is an album that lacks any vision or focus and offers bland,  generic club music that sounds dated. "Vocal" is quite possibly the most forgettable single in the PSB discography with its almost banal description of pop singers. "Fluorescent" is a cool track but is probably longer than it should be and never really does more than pulsate for 7 minutes while Neil talk/sings his way through some jibberish.

Elysium may have disappointed however Electric is an embarrassment when held up against PSB's previous work. Nightlife was also a "club" inspired PSB album that still managed to feature strong songs, memorable melodies all while being dancefloor ready. Electric should have been  disco 5. This isn't a real album in my opinion and definitely forgettable.

reviewText:
The name Lifehouse would hint at perhaps a Who influence, as it was lifted from a shelved Pete Townshend rock opera.  However, the music that Lifehouse produces doesn't even approach that legendary band's lesser period toward the tail end of their careers.

Lifehouse's first album was essentially Creed-lite, which is pretty sad considering how lightweight Creed were themselves.  Frontman Jason Wade does his best to bellow and snarl Eddie Vedder-style, but the background music is so docile and toothless that it renders whatever he has to say meaningless.  Ditto for the slightly more aggressive follow-up, Stanley Climbfall.

That brings us to the third album, for which they went the self-titled route.  That hints at a possible change in direction - however, it definitely wasn't one for the better.  Somehow Lifehouse found a way to become even more bland, as this type of music fits seamlessly between Phil Collins and Celine Dion on your local "soft rock" station.  The lyrics are the typical treacly love pablum, the songs have the most generic, lifeless arrangements, and the singing provides the perfect bland accompaniment.  The single "You And Me" is basically a perfect example about how trite and painful this album is, as it sets the tone for everything else you hear.

In summary: Lifehouse's self-titled album epitomizes everything that is wrong with the music of today.  This is the kind of band that wouldn't have even been signed about ten years ago, yet now not only is it getting released (and likely preventing us from actually hearing some decent music), but it flies off the shelves at record stores and people proclaim Lifehouse to be the greatest thing since sliced bread.  I recommend that those people look away from the "soft rock" stations that shove this tripe down their throats to find the more challenging music with substance that will definitely have a longer shelf life than this.  Expect to find a proliferation of copies of this album going for bargain price within a year or two.

There is now an unfortunate trend of bands way past their prime releasing a collection of cover songs. I suppose the intention is to give their fans something to listen to between official studio releases. Sometimes these ideas work, most of the time they don't. "Take Cover" by Queensryche is one of the ones that doesn't work.

The obvious problem here is that every single song is better than anything Queensryche, a talented band that has lost it's ability to write great songs over the years, has produced since 1990. "Neon Knights", "Welcome To The Machine" and "Synchronicity II" are great songs and are much better in their original form.

One other complaint is that "For What It's Worth", a wonderful song by Buffalo Springfield, has been covered by Rush and Ozzy Osbourne (his version is an abomination) over the last three years. I am sure they know these other artists have covered this song. Why not do something that hasn't been covered yet.

There really is no reason to buy this unless you are a die hard Queensryche fan who must have everything the band releases.

reviewText:
This San Fernando quartet sometimes gets lumped with the likes of Korn and Limp Bizkit, mostly because they used to rock and rap, but Incubus also has a lot in common with the SoCal hardcore scene they live 200 miles north of.  This time around, Incubus delivers non-rap tracks, perhaps in an attempt to prove that they can indeed write "songs."  Sometimes sounding like the Offspring or Sublime, and sometimes sounding like harder edged acts Linkin Park or System of a Down, Incubus tries to create a musical bridge between X-Games-inspired surfer-slacker-skater punk and flat-out metal.  The results usually don't work, but they sometimes do, as on "Megalomaniac," the album's opener.  Other songs clearly meant to rock out strangely lose power; "Priceless" and "Leech" might create a rush live, but they sure feel like filler here.  Guitarist Mike Einziger tries to keep the tunes fresh, and the overall sound of A Crow Left of the Murder is solid, mixing in mechanical droning and distortion.  Sadly, Singer Brandon Boyd's schizophrenic vocal style is pure metal through and through, and this takes its toll over an entire CD.  Boyd, refusing to stay in a single vocal register for more than a nanosecond, might start out crooning in a gravelly bass (and sounding oddly like Brad Roberts of Crash Test Dummies) and then shift into, well, yodeling.  Plus, you sort of have to hate a guy who writes an interstellar, party-dude twist on Merrick's "To the Virgins."  Boyd first lures party gal out of the room ("Participants all in black and white / You enter in full blown Technicolor"), then in bed assures her that everything's okay because he's a wounded soul, too ("If only the lights would dim out / I'm weary about eyes upon my scars"), and finally delivers his c**k to the doorstep ("Pink tractor beam into your incision").  And just when you want to smack Boyd around for chauvinism, he beats you to it ("I came here expecting next to nothing / So thank you for being that kind of girl.")  Creep!

reviewText:
I love Death Magnetic. I won't waste my words on praising it - many of the others have done it. It's new and fresh - there are some great ideas and dynamics in there, and I am not getting bored with it.

However, my ears are going to explode at some point. The sound quality is simply bad, and frankly, embarrassing. As some others have experienced, when I played it in my car on a bad stereo and with all the background noise, I did not even notice. When I played it using my headphones, dear lord, all the crackling was a bit too much. How did this get out?

I played it back-to-back with Porcupine Tree's Fear of the Blank Planet, and boy, what a difference in production. If the Metallica boys haven't heard of the frontman/producer/composer/multi-instrumentalist Steven Wilson, they might consider getting his services to re-master and save this album (although it would appear that an amateur can do a better job).

I normally wouldn't rate this album a 1 (it's really a 4 or a 5), but I am joining the "protest" vote in order to see if something can be done about this.

Sony's copy protection scheme installs harmful rootkit software on Windows machines. This software can crash your machine, and make it easier for viruses to infect you. It also causes a small but constant drain on your processing power - even when you're not listening to music.  By design, it is impossible to uninstall without advanced technical skills.

Sony recently released a patch to mitigate these concerns. However, the patch only addresses the issue of potential virus infection. Uninstalling the software is still nearly impossible, and if attempted incorrectly can render your CD drive unusable.

For more information, search for "sony rootkit" on the sysinternals web site.

reviewText: Produced by Prefab Sprout mastermind Thomas Dolby, I bought "Dog Eat Dog" in the hope it might give a picture of a singer/songwriter whose earlier (primary!) work I did not then believe I could appreciate. However, regardless of the beauty and delicacy he could bring to such hyper-literate masterpieces as Steve McQueen and Jordan: The Comeback, here Dolby just appeared to be copying the tricks of his awful-sounding solo albums like Astronauts & Heretics. Whilst Joni's voice at first listen undoubtedly sounded palatable, after a while on such songs as "Good Friends" and "Shiny Toys" the production seems as mechanical as if Joni were making a generic techno(!) album. The chorus of the acclaimed "Impossible Dreamer" sounds honestly no better today. Indeed, the amazing melodies of "Song For Sharon" and "Shadows And Light" that I have recently discovered are totally absent here, to be replaced by political ranting that really does place this album in the 1980s - and not really a time capsule when one considers the album only reached #63 on Billboard. Rather, it is a once-great artist failing altogether to stick to her own game in a serious way. By this time, Joni Mitchell clearly had given way to such artists as Kate Bush, Mark Hollis (of Talk Talk) and Mary Margaret O'Hara. This album really is not required even if you're an established fan. Go with Hissing Of Summer Lawns and Hejira instead.

I am not a retrograde who listens solely to Medieval chants or Mozart piano sonatas.  I enjoy Barber, Ives, Delius, a little Glass and even the [insane] Scriabin.  But this is...something so utterly "unmusical" that I have trouble keeping a straight face.
Is the whole thing performed tongue-in-cheek or, worse, is the composer (quote unquote) actually serious with all of this screeching and noise?  Is it so wrong to ask that music deliver even a tiny tiny bit discernible melody or that something approaching Western music be granted to the paying audience?
I am not asking for Chopin or Elgar but a minimum of musical worth and sound.

As a classical pianist, I have yet to understand why the need or importance for a "prepared" piano except as a show.  I've heard this recording while playing games on the computer, reading a book, sitting in the dark, eating a snack...in other words, I have tried to enjoy this recording in almost every possible setting with no success.
There is a trend in the art world that is deeply disturbing:  Namely, that "anything" is art and anyone who declares himself an artist becomes one.  As someone else stated, this may be good for movie backgrounds but not for an audience.  Chances are that none of the good reviewers will be humming these melodies in the car on the way to the store.

reviewText:
Oh, where to begin to describe this heaping mash of aural garbage? Who would have thought that the humble, but earnest beginnings of emo would, almost two decades later,  be spun off to bear this as its illegitimate, disfigured offspring. I keep listening to this record, desperately trying to come up with a single redeeming feature, only to be slapped in the face once again with how abjectly awful everything about it remains.

The instrumentation is designed so that a 9-year-old with cerebral palsy could play it by ear in about 15 minutes. I've never heard so many power cords in a single disc before (and yes, I've heard all of blink-182, the reigning kings of simple songs). It really is quite incredible how moronically simple these songs are. There is no originality, no musicianship, and no SOUL to this music. It exists simply to exist, it serves absolutely no purpose.

And then...sweet lord...then there are the lyrics. I'm still somewhat in a state of shock at how idiotic these songs are. I could ALMOST look past the asinine song titles if there was any lyrical substance in the songs themselves. I assure you that this is absolutely not the case. Its almost commendable, if it were parody. If they had come out and said "We did everything we could to make this as stupid as possible," there would at least be some wit behind the album. As it stands, it seems as if these Las Vegas rejects are actually thinking they're making legitimate music. I think I'm going to be sick. If you don't believe me, go actually read a lyrics sheet to the inanely titled "The Only Difference Between Martyrdom And Suicide Is Press Coverage." If there is a single person who can make any kind of sense to these lyrical feces, please, for the love, let me know.

I'll be the first to say I'm a pretty big detractor of the whole emo movement. The "heart-on-your-sleeves/love me because I'm more sensitive than the other guy" thing is just a pretty dang stupid musical device. But at least up until the turn of the century it was a legitimate musical movement. Now all we have are the idiots looking to eat of the scraps of a table almost completely picked clean.

I'd recommend better music, but anyone listening to this trash doesn't really deserve to hear it. As it stands, the growing popularity of bands such as Panic! At the Disco has me not only saddened by the state of the record industry, but humanity as a whole. I'm not sure I want to live in a world populated by the kind of people who like this music.

reviewText: First here is what gives the star to this album (and it is a big star, sorry there aren't more): the epic synthesizer odyessy "Funeral for a Friend."  I think without this song the time I spent alone in this world would be so much harder than it was.  as it is this song will move you.  I was so touched the first time I heard the full album-length version (they play a short one on the radio--don't listen to it!).  It is a true synthesizer symphony for the 1970's, a heart-wrenching string of emotions and feelings.  This is truly the music of the soul.  Search yours and you will find pain here, but also something uplifting.  Now the problem is the rest of this record: it is too much of a brainless party anthem record.  After such a deep beginning, songs like "Saturday Night Fighting" seem pointless and make me angry.  "Candle in the Wind" would be more meaningful if I could understand the lyrics (what does "lend me dairy case" mean?) and if he had made up his mind if the song was about Marilyn Monroe or Princess Diana.  Were they both really like candles in the wind?  Did Princess Di never know who to cling to when the rain came in?  I know he changed the words but it still confuses me.  "Bennie and the Jets" is a horrible screeching car-wreck that hurts my ears after the sublime beauty of "Funeral for a Friend."  Several songs are morally distressing to me, as in "Jamaica J-Off" and "All The Girls Love Alice."  I know that people were different in that decade but in the case of a pop record that is obviously geared toward children I think it is a bad thing.  I guess maybe I'm being harsh but this is how I feel and I wanted to share that with you all.

reviewText:
Cetera groused for years about the artistic restraints placed on him in Chicago, and then groused for several more about Warner Bros. pigeonholing him as a balladeer. He bolted WB for the indies only to record more ballads. More annoying is the fact that he rarely bothers to write his own material anymore. What happened to one of the most prolific songwriters of the '70s and '80s? Judging from his reluctance to even pick up an instrument throughout his solo career, the most likely explanation is just plain laziness.
"Another Perfect World" reinforces this--Cetera ekes out only three cowrites here, doesn't play any bass, and overall sounds like a shadow of the artist he once was. The terrific "Perfect World" notwithstanding, there isn't a single outstanding performance or memorable hook from start to finish. reviewText: Mr Rieu is quite a nice fellow with a pleasant, if at times slightly insipid, sense of humour and a keen business acumen. He got bored as the leader of a provincial Dutch symphony orchestra (no great wonder, what with their programming of the perennial favourites over and over again and pedestrian standard of musicianship, Rieu included; they have in the mean time mended their ways though), started a small string band which led an only marginally successful existence and every once in a while toured with a pick-up band recreating the music of the Strauss family and like composers. Since his chance hit "The Second Waltz", a watered down version of a Shostakovitch composition, he has seen the light and has since that time carefully edited, truncated and simplified the lighter classics and "classified" all kinds of overly familiar music. He dressed-up the lady musicians as fairy princesses, made his male musicians smirk, and have them all gaily wave their instruments and display publicly what a good time they all seem to be having (all carefully rehearsed, as are Rieu's carefully edited jokes; very little happens spontaneously). This eclectic mixture seems to hold an enormous appeal for millions of CD and DVD buyers and concert goers. No problem there. I do however have a problem with the fact that many "fans" seem to think that what Rieu presents is classical music, the real stuff. Actually, no, it's not. They also seem to think that Rieu is the world's greatest violinist; well, he plays a Stradivarius, so he should be, shouldn't he?. Well, no, he's not. Why do these "fans", without knowing Mozart from Wagner and a symphony from a concerto, so vociferously state that Rieu is the greatest, without ever having taken the trouble to listen to classical music (other than perhaps a Strauss waltz or a Puccini aria by Paul Potts or that Scottish hag whose name escapes me right now), and that all who say otherwise are snobs, elitist, intellectual, arrogant and grumpy old men, who sit in cheerless concert halls listening to penguins playing music that no one understands? It's that ill-informed, lazy, overawed and reveling-in-an-underdog-position what irks me about the hype around Mr Rieu (for which he himself can hardly be blamed) and is reason for me to counterbalance the silly raving reviews ("me mum likes it, so it must be good") with one star.
