reviewText:
Mariah Carey is arguably the best selling female artist in the world (a title that's hotly contested by her equally legendary peers, Madonna and Celine Dion), and the sheer depth of Ms. Carey's catalogue speaks to that. Since her debut in the spring of 1990, she has overtaken Elvis Presley's record of #1 hits on Billboard's Hot 100; the first fifteen of these chart-toppers released during her time at Sony BMG's imprint Columbia Records, and the latest #1 being the Island Def Jam single "Touch My Body".

It's at best a headscratcher, then, that her post-Sony output has been completely ignored by Columbia in favour of a retread of her Nineties back catalogue.

To add insult to injury, however, this 2CD collection also doubles as an inferior re-release of her 2001 collection, Greatest Hits. At least Greatest Hits had the excuse of trying to stem the tide of a dark period in Mariah's career -- a year plagued by anti-Glitter sentiments and the tabloid fodder of Mariah's alleged breakdown -- by reminding the public of her hitmaking past.

The Essential Mariah Carey has no such rationale. With her biggest misstep now more than a decade behind her, and her since having returned to form as an artist, it makes no sense to ignore her more recent releases.

And when I said that Essential is a double-dip of Greatest Hits, I wasn't exaggerating. The hits "Someday," "Forever" and "Sweetheart" were swapped for three non-commercial tracks ("Vanishing" from her 1990 self-titled debut, "Close My Eyes" from 1997's Butterfly and "Bliss" from 1999's Rainbow), the album versions of "Anytime You Need A Friend" and "Emotions" were replaced by their club mixes, and the cute bonus remix of "All I Want For Christmas Is You" was jettisoned for Ms. Carey's collaboration with Mobb Deep ("The Roof").

And.... well, that's it, really. The Mobb Deep track is the only item that hasn't been on a physical album proper, and was previously only available on the digital edition of The Ballads (also a second-rate collection, given the sheer volume of ballads and downtempo songs Mariah has churned out).

It's rather insulting that such a collection has been released. The existence of both Greatest Hits and 2003's The Remixes in Mariah's catalogue render The Essential Mariah Carey moot. And, as I said, her post-Sony catalogue has also been ignored.

You want to know how egregious that particular oversight is? Well then, here's a list of Mariah's US hits (major and minor) from 2001 to the present day:

1. Loverboy (#2 Hot 100, #1 R&B, - from 2001's Glitter)
2. Never Too Far (#17 AC - from 2001's Glitter)
3. Through The Rain (#1 Dance, #17 AC - from 2002's Charmbracelet)
4. I Know What You Want (#3 Hot 100 & Rap, #2 R&B - from 2003's The Remixes)
5. Bringin' On The Heartbreak (#5 Dance - from 2002's Charmbracelet)
6. U Make Me Wanna (#8 R&B, #9 Rap - from Jadakiss' 2004 album Kiss of Death)
7. It's Like That (#1 Dance, #16 Hot 100, #17 R&B - from 2005's The Emancipation of Mimi)
8. We Belong Together (#1 Hot 100, R&B, Dance, Pop, #3 AC - from 2005's The Emancipation of Mimi)
9. Shake It Off (#1 Pop, #2 Hot 100 & R&B - from 2005's The Emancipation of Mimi)
10. Don't Forget About Us (#1 Hot 100, Dance & R&B - from 2005's The Emancipation of Mimi)
11. Fly Like A Bird (#19 R&B - from 2005's The Emancipation of Mimi)
12. Say Somethin' (#1 Dance - from 2005's The Emancipation of Mimi)
13. Touch My Body (#1 Hot 100 & Dance, #2 R&B, #7 Pop - from 2008's E=MC2)
14. Bye Bye (#18 Pop, #19 Hot 100 - from 2008's E=MC2)
15. I Stay In Love (#1 Dance - from 2008's E=MC2)
16. Obsessed (#7 Hot 100, #1 Dance, #8 Pop, #12 R&B - from 2009's Memoirs of an Imperfect Angel)
17. I Want To Know What Love Is (#2 Dance, #10 AC - from 2009's Memoirs of an Imperfect Angel)
18. Oh Santa! (#1 AC, Holiday - from 2010's Merry Christmas II You)

True, there's not as many Top Tens as in her heyday, but they do exist, after all. At the very least, the three Hot 100 #1's ("We Belong Together," "Don't Forget About Us" and "Touch My Body") should have been included to round out the collection. At least The Remixes had the decency to include remixes of "Loverboy", "Through The Rain" and "The One," the radio edit of "I Know What You Want" and the track "Miss You."

But The Essential Mariah Carey extends no such courtesies, and thus fails to live up to its name.

This two-disc set could have been a far stronger retrospective of Mariah's chart-topping career but, as it stands, its narrow scope (and the fact that the discs are nowhere near their full capacity) merely makes it a weak echo of her more superior compilations. So, if you can, just find a copy of her Greatest Hits and, if you're into both her club music and her hip-hop collaborations, pick up The Remixes while you're at it. Both together will set you back about the same as (or perhaps even less than) The Essential Mariah Carey... but you'll have twice as much music.

P.S. If you also want an example of a double-disc anthology done right, give a listen to the late Donna Summer's Gold collection, released in 2005 and containing 34 of her greatest hits (a remarkable achievement in updating her previous Anthology, as Donna's catalogue is stretched out over more than 30 years and half a dozen different labels!).

reviewText:
This album should be titled "Compression".
To start with, the sound is so compressed it sounds as if it was recorded inside a Tequila bottle, and then squeezed out. It's a far cry from that rough "Tres Hombres" sound, or from the disco-boogie era that followed, or even from the crunchy "Antenna". For twenty years ZZ sounded raucous, but clean. On "Mescalero", everything - but specialy guitars and vocals - is mudded out amidst merciless compression. Of course it is just a matter of taste. Some will like it, some will not. Count me on the latter. Perhaps so much compression will fit a heavy metal outfit, but, to my ears, not a blues-rock band. ZZ is now sounding artificial to me, or, in other words: they are outfocusing the true Texan sound.
I also did not appreciate the material. I couldn't find a catchy tune, a moving riff or a memorable solo. Either they ran out of ideas (and "Que lastima" is evidence to that), or I was in a bad listening mood; or the thundering compression led me, or them, astray.
I'm not saying they should rework "La Grange" for every release, but the songs herein are so indistinctive they just won't linger.
Although with "Mescalero" the band zzbottomed entirely, I'm a fan and won't give up on them.
Next...

You cannot load this to your IPOD or Media Player. I think it's time the buying public just boycotted CDs that do this. In addition, this product puts spyware and malware on your PC. The license agreement, written by slick corporate lawyers of course, does not actually tell you what is being loaded on your PC. When I returned the CD, I called Columbia Records to have the spyware removed from my PC. This is a rootkit - it is delivered uninvited and hidden. Plain and simple - check the news.

First I went to the Sony site. I filled a form out to have it removed. No word back in half a day. I decided to call Columbia in NY (if you read reports - the form response leads you to another form apparently - it's in the news reports).

They gave me a website, the wrong website. This one.

(...)

I left the people here an email. To their credit, they replied and mentioned that the copy protection and malware (you cannot unload it using the control panel) was not theirs. Tongue in cheek I believe (because Sony/Columbia now has lawsuits in NY and CA filed against them because of this software), they wished me luck.

I called again, and was transferred by phone to another group. I was disconnected. I called yet again (long distance mind you, they are in NYC) and was routed to an IT person. Hey gave me yet another website:

(...)

Now, the question really is, is it worth it to you to listen to a decent (not great) album at the cost of having your PC invaded by malware you cannot easily remove which reports who knows (your music habits? what's on your PC? who knows?) back to this corporation? But after loading it without telling you, then backtracking and posting that fix AND considering the class action suits and fraud suits brought against them - are you going to believe what they say?

It may or may not have an effect on your computer.

But it shouldn't be there.

It IS a security risk and some smart hacker will figure out how to manipulate that for their gain and your loss.

Sony/Columbia now uses multiple copy protection companies. Who knows what they will load on  your computer next?

Finally, with products like this, a simple CD is no longer a universal standard. You can rip this CD on a MAC. You cannot on a Windows PC. I imagine it works ok on a regular stereo, but didn't take the time to find out. Sony already got enough of my time.

To those bemoaning the criticism of Sony here and/or IPOD use: This is about the music yes, I don't disagree at all - BUT -  it's also about the entire PRODUCT. And the spyware/malware/virus enhancer, time and money spent are all part of this product experience - just as the music, liner notes and other packaging materials are.

Finally - for those of you who don't think this software is a big deal:

Antivirus firms are reporting that masses of emails containing a Trojan that exploits Sony's digital rights management (DRM) program are circulating on the internet.

The Trojan, dubbed Stinx, has been mass-mailed to UK email addresses but is able to hide itself if a computer has Sony's controversial anti-piracy root kit program installed, which is embedded on some CDs.

Graham Cluley, senior technology consultant for security firm Sophos, said: "By installing Sony's software it opens a vulnerability that hackers can exploit and in this case they have. From that point of view it is a bad thing regardless of the fact that it stops people stealing music."

reviewText:
You might remember a story from a few years back that found Bob Dylan picked up by the Long Branch NJ police department for checking out several available properties around town - the only problems being the absense of a realtor and the fact that he was dressed in a trenchcoat and double hoodie that obscured his features - making several residents uncomfortable and suspicious. Upon intervening in his pre-concert stroll, the 24 y/o responding officer radioed her superiors with the immortal line - "This guy says he's Bob Dylan, have any of you ever heard of Bob Dylan?" After they finished rolling over in laughter, Dylan was cleared and released.

I just have to wonder if the officer's best friend was somehow involved in picking the talent for the new 50th anniversary Dylan tribute, Chimes of Freedom - The Songs of Bob Dylan. My interest and appreciation of Dylan is to the point where I will routinely pick up anything he issues (many times regretting the habit.) The concept behind Chimes sounds great, new and old artists taking a shot at reinterpreting his immense and immortal canon of music - how bad could it be?

Other reviewers have pointedly said - "It Sucks!" I probably wouldn't go that far but I can certainly see their point. Of course there are some highlights, Jackson Brown, Sting, Adele, Jeff Beck, Mark Knopfler, Johnny Cash to name a few. However, when you have to fill four discs please stop when you arrive at a talent pool that has shown little capacity to harness their own material much less Dylan's. Evan Rachel Wood, Ke$ha, Maroon 5, Miley Cyrus.... Really? Seriously?

There's nothing wrong with drawing outside the lines and taking five decades of music for an unscripted spin. I get it. It's just that too many of these artists sound like they just returned from an archeological dig (perhaps in Long Branch) and are clueless to the fact that the fossil they're using as a beverage coaster is actually priceless.

It's regrettable that precious and eclectic for the sake of being precious and eclectic doesn't guarantee five stars. Here's looking forward to Dylan's 100th year tribute.

I consider myself a huge Kid Rock fan.  I have his early albums, the ones before Devil Without a Cause, have seen him perfom three times, and generally revere the man.  With that established, I must say I am sorely dissapointed with this album.

Simply put, I miss the old Kid Rock.  Even at his most cocky, with arrogant, self-praising lyrics, I always felt Kid Rock was poking a little fun at himself.  Yes, he was brash, but you knew he did not take himself too seriously.  I always felt his songs were good at pointing out hypocrisy in a sly manner.

On this album, the lyrics are very simple, inane even.  The songs just say the same words over and over again, and I am sick of every song when it has about 30 seconds left.  I find myself skipping forward just to end the monotony.  Kid Rock's previous songs had clever lyrics that made me want to listen closely, and they often told a story.  The songs on this album all sound like a good time beer commercial.  I know Kid has his own brand of beer.  They will not have to look far for background songs for the commercials showing the people of different races and professions having a great time together.  The whole album is just too Brady Bunch, goody-two-shoes.

I miss the old Kid Rock that stuck it to the man, made me look at myself in a different light, and mostly made me laugh.

reviewText: I was under the impression that I would like every album Kanye put out. I even liked 808s & Heartbreak [+video] [+digital booklet]. This album, though, is nothing like his previous albums and that is not a good thing. Gone are the clever lyrics and, more importantly, quality production. Almost every song has a gratingly irritating beat accompanied by Kanye delivering asinine line after asinine line. I would definitely not recommend this album or even any individual song on it. Here's the blow by blow: 1. On Sight - Starts off with what sounds like feedback from an amplifier before transitioning to a still irritating industrial video game sound at :15 (heard in the sample). Kanye starts at :34, but he's almost irrelevant because all I can focus on is the awful beat. Between 1:17 and 1:30, the song abruptly drops everything it's doing and cuts to what sounds like a children's choir. While it sounds better than the rest of the song, it doesn't fit at all. 1/10 2. Black Skinhead - This is the fastest pace song on the album and is probably the second best song. Unfortunately, the beat sounds like noise more than part of a cohesive song to me. 3/10 3. I Am a God - Starts with some singing from Capleton that was apparently recorded to another beat (heard in sample). What follows is predictable narcissism from Kanye rapping over a halting beat punctuated by a sci-fi sound. Oh, and you get some irritating screaming towards the end. 2/10 4. New Slaves - The electronic-sounding beat changes so often in this song that Kanye might as well have recorded the lyrics without it. He only fleetingly catches the beat because there isn't much to catch. Unfortunately, that detracts from Kanye's attempt to address racism throughout the song. The outro is well done, though. 2/10 5. Hold My Liquor - Best song on the album. The song is really good before :30 and after 2:20, in which vocals and the beat work great together. In between is a brief lull of nonsense uttered through the autoune (heard in the sample) before, at 1:05, Kanye's greatness is obscured by what sounds kind of like a pneumatic tool releasing air. 5/10 6. I'm In It - Kanye, apparently impersonating a demon, starts the song with semi-misogyny interrupted tastelessly by an MLK quote (heard in the sample). What follows is a largely unintelligible reggaeton verse from Assassin and then Kanye starting almost every line with "Uh." The beat includes the sounds of a car alarm beginning at 1:00 with occasional dog barking, both of which are irritating. 1/10 7. Blood on the Leaves - If you can stand the nasally Nina Simone syllable that gets interspersed every three seconds through much of the song (heard in the sample), then this one might work for you. I couldn't stand it. Kanye uses autotune through the whole song and the beat gets industrial from 1:05-1:45 and 2:03-4:28, which are the best parts of the song. Too bad the other parts are so irritating. 3/10 8. Guilt Trip - The beat is punctuated by what sounds like Nintendo-era video game sound effects, which work against the rest of the beat and in some places are louder than Kanye's voice. The best parts are the chorus (heard in the sample), which is screwed and lacks the video game effects, but is lyrical nonsense. 2/10 9. Sent It Up - It sounds like this song was recorded in a tire shop with a rhythmic pneumatic impact wrench (heard in the sample). You get a brief break from the wrench between :57-1:17 and the last 46 seconds, but it otherwise dominates and ruins the song. 1/10 10. Bound 2 - The nasally wailing you hear in the sample is a constant throughout the song. I can't think of anything to redeem the song, which is probably the worst song on the album. 0/10

reviewText:
I've always had a soft spot for Bush despite the fact that their sound is a complete rip-off of Nirvana.  Despite the fact that Gavin has some of the most inane nonsensical lyrics around, and even when coherent he's whiny and self-pitying.  Despite the fact that he's dating the antichrist, Gwen Stefani.
-Sixteen Stone (was bad), but Everything Zen wasn't half bad, and the rest of the singles were fun for the first 10 listens.
-Razorblade Suitcase was more of the same, but it had cool Steve Albini production and was actually a halfway decent record despite the lack of any real hit singles other than Swallowed.  Bush at least deserved credit for using Nirvana's producer, mocking everyone who called them what they were, a Nirvana rip-off band.
-The remix record Deconstructed was good, largely because Bush didn't really have anything to do with it other than doing a great remix of Mouth.
-The Science of Things saw Bush giving more of the same yet again, and except for the hit single it was kind of dumb.
So what the point is Golden State supposed to be?  Bush seems intent on setting some sort of record for repeating themselves.  One has to wonder how they can even stand writing songs anymore.  Going into the studio probably seems like doing hard labor at a concentration camp by now.  Plus, the new record probably has the worst cover art I've ever seem, with the exception of perhaps the latest No Doubt record.  Maybe that's why Gavin and Gwen seem to get along so well; they probably just sit in their mansions all day dreaming up what sort of horrible music, videos, and artwork they can force down the public's throat.
To be honest, I've only heard parts of the new record, and it may even be better than Sixteen Stone, which is basically a worthless slopped-together mess of a record.  I don't know who on earth could get sincere enjoyment out of Golden State.  Gavin keeps repeating his earlier work, which is hard to comprehend this because all that stuff was so horrible.
If you still have any thought of buying this record, even for the curiosity factor of knowing what happens to early nineties grunge rip-off bands when they start growing older, put them down right now.  Even the most off-key local garage band can write more interesting/honest music than Bush, and that's saying something.

reviewText:
I really don't understand by bands such as Uriah Heep continue to make albums. This is bland, standard-fare rock. Bands such as Heep, Scorps, and countless others (Def Leppard, UFO, etc.) deserve their due... they were great...innovators...pioneers... when they were 20 years old and "the scene" was in full swing.

It's 2015 now. Uriah Heep, Deep Purple.... all of them are finished. They just keep making CDs that a computer could make if it analyzed their prior output.

The only two bands that have any business making new records anymore are Metallica and Iron Maiden. Maiden I gather makes decent records because they still have some spark, and because they were always able to churn out reasonably decent, interesting HIGHLY ORIGINAL output. Metallica is WEALTHY and can throw money at all the cutting edge producers, writers, and talent-shapers. They're in a different class altogether...

Everyone else is just releasing material for the sake of doing it. I can't blame them... I'd say it's BETTER that they do, than that they quit. Don't get me wrong - Scorpions and Judas Priest at their lot are LEGENDS and once they're dead, there will be no more output. So even if the output is lackluster, they might as well release it while they're still around.

Still, that output is almost not worth actually listening to for enjoyment, and in fact has only archival, historical value. Buy it, put it on a shelf next to their old CDs, and spend your time listening to new, fresh, cutting-edge output from younger men riding the wave of modernity.

First off, Obituary was one of my favirote death metal bands when I first started getting into metal in my teens. Death, Obituary, and Carcass were all the best back then. Cause of Death was, and still is, the pinnacle of their career and pretty much all of the mid-paced junk that followed isn't even worth mentioning.

Having said all of that, this album is stuck in time. Reforming and creating a new album after 10 years or more usually entails some pretty drastic changes. Peopel mature, musician's grow, and tastes change. Apparently, none of this is true for Obituary. Everyone here seems to want to love this cd because it sounds like they did in '89(which is totally wrong anyways, this stuff doesn't even come close to Cause of Death). Making muddy distortion, adding way too much reverb to a drumkit, or using mundane drumbeats and palm-muted child-like guitar riffs in 2008 doesn't cut it. Many things are timeless, especially in music and there are some bands I would love to do what Obituary has done by recreating their best sound, but this cd is such total mediocrity at its worst. This band is simply an embarassment to bands like Death or Carcass who actually DID evolve.

I'm sorry, but if you want to live in the past and prefer your music to sound like something a garage band full of pre-teens recorded on their Tascam 4-track, then get this cd. If your into anything sicne 1995 that has pushed metal beyond the bounds of midnight radio such as Death, Opeth, or Dark Tranquillity, then by god stay away!

reviewText:
Many forms of life exist on this planet, including insects. And insects deserve music. Philip Glass, music's foremost combiner of triads and triplets, has made a career of supplying it for them.
Of course, like most insects, this listener took one look at the title of this CD and said, "Koya... what??" Luckily, the first track, "Koyaanisqatsi," features a bunch of low-voiced males chanting the word over and over for our benefit. Word has it that the chorus featured here had been looking for work since the "Omen" movie series ran out.
Musically, this work features influences that move, for once, beyond that of Viennese master Carl Czerny ("40 Daily Exercises;" "The Art of Finger Dexterity"), Glass' mentor. We hear Gustav Holst's "Saturn" in "Cloudscape"--so much so, that concerned listeners have to assume that the original work is one that is open to such borrowing, i.e. in the public domain. And we hear the influence of the alleged score to "Grease" in track five ("Vessels"). While this music is not as blatantly referenced as Holst's "Saturn," the source is obvious, though the plodding beat, in context, is pure dragsville. A version of "Grease" populated by zombies might use such an extended jukebox jingle, but otherwise, this movement is half-speed "Happy Days." Obviously, this is some kind of comment on Ron Howard.
Remember--as moronic as this music may sound, it isn't. It's really very brilliant. Unfortunately, I listened to this CD without the benefit of the liner notes, so I can't tell you why.

reviewText: Normally, a new Dream Theater album is an experience worth waiting for. This was certainly the case with every one of DT's previous albums, including their 3 live albums. Unfortunately, this is not one of those instances. This album lacks focus, sounds too pop-pish, doesn't have enough heavy music, tries to be too many things for too many people, etc etc, you get the drift. Every song is a disappointment. After suffering through the first seven tracks, I had high hopes for the closing, 24-minute title track. I should have known better. The intro is a shameless rip-off of Pink Floyd's "Shine On You Crazy Diamond'', right from the gentle atmospheric keyboards to the distant, chiming guitar riff. The rest of the track rips off Yes and Genesis, even down to a reference to a ""machine messiah'' which is a Yes song on their Drama album. If I had to use a single word to sum up this CD, it would be ""insipid''. Petrucci's guitar sound is weak and buried in the background, even for the few solos he plays. As a guitar player myself, this is sacrilege. Rudess' keyboard sound is fine, but the melodies are nothing great. Portnoy and Myung do their part to hold it together and adding an orchestra was a nice touch but it isn't enough to save this bloated, over-indulgent waste of money. I own all DT's records and DVDs and all have been played at least 10-20 times. This won't follow suit.

reviewText:
Hmmm, when Joss Stone starts imitating an Amy Winehouse, it means that 'soul' music from Britain is officially dead.

Don't get me wrong. I loved Joss Stone on her debut when she first came out. I mean, at the time, everyone wanted to love the anorexically beautiful white girl who sounded SO much like a talented black soulwoman. She was a novelty piece, lets face it, but at least she had some semblance of a voice, and the production on that CD was tight.

Now, amidst allegations that Joss Stone is an immoral harlet who will 'do anything' for 'good tracks' (and these aren't my words, mind you, its her producers) comes this controversial new album with a really nice cover.

I did sit with this for a good while today and listen to it. Hmmm. First impression wasn't very memorable so I went back to a few tracks a second time. Again, not much to report, except that this album sounds very much like she took the producers took the concept of her debut album and reverse-engineered it on the premise of "how badly could we do it". Well, the album sounds like it could have been recorded by Cassie or Monica, which is a REALLY nice way to kick that concept off. Then, the added instrumentation really get in the way of her sometimes smoky and lovely voice (not as lovely as Corinne Bailey Rae or Melissa Etheridge, but still..... anyway, I digress)

"Music" sung with Lauryn Hill is average. So is "Arms of My Baby". Is it just me or do female vocalists who want to show emotion sort of "scream out" their lyrics these days?  I had a similar problem digesting Amy Winehouse's new album.

However Amy has in spades what Joss does not, and this new CD is testament to the fact that producer Saadiq has totally lost it, or just did not have much in the first place. I mean, listen to the 'Intro' and 'Outro' here. It makes Janet Jackson's pathetic interludes from "Damita Jo" sound like masterpieces. If you don't remember those interludes, you aren't missing anything!

To sum up, this was a nonsensical waste of time. But I'll say it again, the album cover was artistic. Too bad that if you open it up, you'l find a more civilized form of horse manure (seriously).

Do yourself a favor and stay away from this overproduced British mess. I'll take some of Simon Cowells' insipid boybands anyday over this trainwreck.

reviewText:
When I think of classic true metal, I think of Dio-era Black Sabbath, Judas Priest, Iron Maiden, Saxon, Savatage, Megadeth, Crimson Glory, etc.  I think of great musicianship, soaring and expressive vocals (both clean and aggressive), epic melodies, moving and powerful lyrics, and a sense of triumph.  What I do not think of is monotonous clanging and smashing, rough, unintelligible lyrics barked in a voice that has almost no range of emotion or pitch,  and an ambiance of defeat and morbidity that makes the listener feel like hope is something you see at work only in Disney movies.  I've been hearing praise for Reign in Blood for years, and it's on many top ten lists of metal listeners, but what I have discovered lately is that to really enjoy this album, you must chiefly value the sounds of aggression and noise over any other musical element.  I had briefly thought, as a devout metal fan, that I was missing something, but then I realized my perception of this record was off.  This is not a metal classic that I need to learn to enjoy; It simply isn't metal. It Is 100% thrash, and that is a poor derivative of true metal that no metal head should feel guilty about avoiding.

I think a food analogy is now helpful:

 I will concede that certain elements of thrash are desirable, but it is a matter of degree.  Just like you wouldn't want a burrito that is comprised 98% of habenero sauce, a "metal" album that is 98% thrash is unpalatable.  Thrash is a seasoning-- a condiment, not a meal.

reviewText:
Yes, we got the "library" book and all (which is mostly pictures).
First off, this sounds nothing like Boards of Canada, Autechre, Aphex Twin.  I am familiar with all of them.  I often feel that many have difficulty differentiating the sounds of electronic artists perhaps because it is so "new" ...  many seem to hear the electrons bursting but can't hear the structural signatures yet.  If you want to know how Amnesiac sounds, read the review in (publication) (not to be mistaken with the article/hype).
  I have explored electronica, trance, concept work, minimalism, atonal stuff, avant garde (inclu fripp, calix, etc), love impressionism, Bjork is my mainstream ...  I am not a radio junky ... and I can enjoy 5-piece rock bands and ethereal machine music equally.  One more bit:  I enjoyed Kid A right from the start.  And now for my theory.
  In the video called "Meeting People is Easy", Radiohead was featured in all the realm and glory of OK Computer success.  Thom Yorke was MOST perturbed about how unnatural it was for them to be hailed and treated like gods.  The idolatry stunned and bewildered them all and really stabbed Thom at a the deepest level.  We know the band's familiar themes of pinpointing negative patterns of modern culture/society...  then they unwillingly "became" gods within that very society they loathe and ache inside of.  OUCH!!  Think about it.
  The material from Kid A and Amnesiac were recorded at the same time soon after that.  In Kid A, I believe Radiohead took the opportunity to play around with those "exciting new" electronic sounds now that they felt the full freedom to do so, knowing that they will lose listeners who cannot appreciate music of this nature which has a more ethereal beauty since it resonates at a higher frequency than many operate on.  In short, if you can't hear past a 5-piece rock band (and maybe some hackneyed Mozart piece), Kid A was obviously not for you.
  The rumors began that a "real" rock album was coming out soon after. Then comes Amnesiac.  After being let down a few releases in the last year, I truly began listening to Amnesiac with NO expectations.  After a minute into track two my theory came together.  (I have this "silly belief" that I can hear intentions behind music -call it intent,sincerity, whatever.)  Amnesiac is overall quite painful.  Radiohead is trying to lose their HUGE fan following.  I believe that to blindly praise their every release as brilliant is causing them even more duress.  They are testing the intelligence of their listeners -- will ANYTHING they put out be hailed?  Did they really hear the quality in Kid A or is our name synonymous with some gross concept of perfection!?!?  When I hear this CD and read articles and reactions, everything up through the closing verse of Glass House seems to validates my theory, -- "is somebody listening?"  Does Amnesiac = "FORGET US"?!?
  Sure, a FEW tracks are semi-decent compared to the norm, but not by Radiohead standards.  Truly, you wait for them to really take off --like the loungey Knives Out that never spins out, for example.  To paraphrase a friend of mine, "they never throw you the bone."  These are the scraps from Kid A they could've easily melded to titanium -but didn't.
  Thom Yorke's voice is gorgeous and sure, they know how to play. Amnesiac is a collection of sounds alternating from potentially gorgeous ballads DELIBERATELY CAPPED to numb listener satisfaction ... to sonic tracks with (in my opinion) NO musical value.  THIS IS DELIBERATE.  I truly believe it.  Not a single blip on here even compares in quality to any previous b-side of theirs (post-Pablo Honey).  Unlike the aesthetic relativists, I still see distinctions between art-music and free-for-all-ism.
  Read the(publication) review (can't believe I'm recommending them!) and it will even further enforce my theory about the band's psychological intentions with this release.  For the rest of the tracks that aren't total junk, it is a dark purge directed at the fans for their overzealous glorification of a band comprised of a few fellow human beings.
--could be wrong, (doubt it!!)
label: negative

reviewText: I try not to bother too much with negativity, but since I'm running low on music to praise at the moment, I've decided to devote some time to the ample store of music that I find utterly loathsome.  And Lenny Kravitz ranks right at the top of that list (well, right next to Limp Bizkit, anyway).  Many, probably including Lenny himself, seem to want to fancy him some sort of Jimi Hendrix for the modern day.  However, while Lenny has pinched substantial elements of Hendrix's look and sound, there are some important differences between the two.  First of all, Jimi Hendrix had things like creativity, ambition, and a fully-functioning soul.  Mr. Kravitz's music, meanwhile, is about as original and exciting as vanilla ice cream in a plain cone, probably because he makes sure not to do anything that might alienate adolescent girls or collegiate preppies.  Hendrix, while far the most technically skilled singer, had a voice that was often deep, soulful, and evocative.  Lenny, meanwhile, tries way too often to hit high notes and winds up sounding like an eight-year-old boy who's just been repeatedly kicked in the crotch.  Jimi's solos were searing, technical, and often epic and experimental.  Can anyone name me one Lenny Kravitz song with a memorable guitar solo?  Jimi's best-known ballad was probably the the moving, bluesy, and lyrically profound "The Wind Cries Mary."  Lenny's best known, ballad, conversely, is probably the repulsive "It ain't over till it's over," which features cliched lyrics, bland pop musicianship, and Kravitz's hilariously inept attempts to hit high notes with his voice.  I could go on and on, but here's the point to my semi-coherent rambling:  Lenny Kravitz is a boring and ultra-derivative hack who has little or nothing in common with the men who made classic rock great.  I mean, if you really need an "old-school" rock fix, here are some much better places to look, from a wide variety of time periods: Jimi Hendrix, Stevie Ray Vaughan, Creedence Clearwater Revival, Queens of the Stone Age, Rush, Yes, Black Sabbath, The Clash, on and on into infinity.  Really, though, pretty much anything is preferable to this clown.

reviewText:
It's pretty hard to write objectively when the subject is one of the most infamous figures in modern pop culture. Then again, sometimes you need a little nastiness to be really truthful.

And in this case, the subject is one of the most justifiably mocked albums of 2006 this far has been Paris Hilton's "Paris," a light-as-air album full of lightweight club beats and processed vocals. Given that all she ever sings about is how hot she is, it's kind of like listening to a sex robot.

The most prominent single is "Stars Are Blind," which probably has the best melody on the album. Of course, that's because it also blatantly imitates the reggae beats of "The Tide is High," the pop song by the quintessential blonde pop star. Although it's nearly impossible to imagine Hilton singing that "I'm not the kinda girl."

The album hits its nadir early on, with the appalling hip-hop song "Fighting Over Me." Jadakiss does most of the vocals. Hilton only sings the bridge -- and a narcissistic one it is too: "Everytime I step out the house they want to fight over me/Maybe cause I'm hot to death and I'm so so so SEX-EE!" she squeals, sounding delighted.

Things only get worse with the wispy club beats of songs like "Turn It Up," the meandering "I Want You" and the lackluster heavy beats of "Nothing in This World." There's a dabble in guitar pop, still heavily synthesized, before the style switches back to lightweight club pop. Unsurprisingly, it wraps up with a breathy cover of "Do Ya Think I'm Sexy."

Basically, there's not much to recommend this album, except to people who will listen to anything with a techno beat. It's generic musically, not really memorable in any way -- but its quality is brought even lower by appallingly narcissistic lyrics and terrible vocals.

And it's undeniable that Hilton's voice is a terrible one. She sings in a Betty Boop voice, which has been processed until it sounds robotic. But no amount of computer tweaking can hide the fact that she has zero vocal range, and even gets a little off-key. When she's coos "other half of my heartbeat," you can hear that she's straining to hold the note.

Don't expect the "music" to cover up the multitude of sins in Paris's voice or the songs written for her. The lightweight techno is just a predictable series of electrobeats; I doubt this took more than ten minutes to whip up. It's fairly pleasant in terms of catchiness, but it's also completely forgettable and gets annoying if you listen to it more than once.

Listening to "Paris" is like listening to a self-important sex robot rhapsodizing about her wares. Even as bubblegum music, this is appallingly empty and derivative.

reviewText:
Both the band and several reviewers have noted that "Heaven and Earth" doesn't sound like anything that Yes has ever put out.  This has been their major defense of the album.  I, for one, agree completely.  It doesn't resemble anything from the Yes catalog.  And it's also really bad.  REALLY bad.  The band sounds like they are either hungover, lazy, old, or recovering from major surgery.  Whatever the cause, there is simply no energy or drive to their playing on this latest album.  Geoff Downes consistently plays as if he's nervous about hitting a wrong note on the keyboards.  If you're that scared, practice more (and then get the harpsichord riff on Siberian Khatru right when you're on tour!).  Good news for progressive rock fans: Alan White seems to have mastered the polka-shuffle beat.  As a member of a band, Steve Howe should really reconsider the benefits of playing rhythm guitar, at least on occasion.  I admire the job that Jon Davidson is doing on tour, but his songwriting is pretty pedestrian.  In the end, what a disappointment.  And, if you think I'm overstating things, go on Youtube and check out their playing from the Talk tour from 20 years ago; it's like watching a different, much better band.  How sad.

P.S. It pains me to write a review like this.  I'm a huge Yes fan, but this is simply unacceptable.

reviewText:
This album is more or less major crap, especially when it's coming from the last good rock band. If you want to get into Guns N' Roses, go get Appetite For Destruction, don't get this. Don't get me wrong, I love most of the album, but it's not really great for a greatest hits. First of all, why are there only 3 songs from AFD on here? The inclusion of Nightrain, Out Ta Get Me, It's So Easy, Mr. Brownstone and Rocket Queen are all essential songs by GN'R. Now, more songs from Lies would have been nice too. I Used To Love Her is a great song, and also one of their most famous hits. And to give it something from all the albums, Mama Kin or Reckless Life should have been included. Now onto the Use Your Illusions. The songs picked from Use Your Ullusion's I and II was much better than you could expect on an album like this. There were really only 2 problems with the stuff from these albums. First, 7 songs from UYI I and II is WAY too much if they can only put on 3 songs from AFD. Second, Civil War and Yesterdays should have been cut and replaced with Estranged, quite possibly the best song between the 2 albums. Finally, "The Spaghetti Incedent?" songs. For an album that recieves as little praise as this, 2 songs seems like a bit much. Both great songs, especially Since I Don't Have You.

Although it's tough to make a compilation for a band of such magnitude, this list would serve damn well:

Welcome To The Jungle (AFD)

It's So Easy (AFD)

Nightrain (AFD)

Out Ta Get Me (AFD)

Mr. Brownstone (AFD)

Paradise City (AFD)

Sweet Child O' Mine (AFD)

Rocket Queen (AFD)

Mama Kin (LLAS)

Patience (Lies)

I Used To Love Her (Lies)

Live And Let Die (UYI I)

Don't Cry (UYI I)

November Rain (UYI I)

Knockin' On Heaven's Door (UYI II)

Get In The Ring (UYI II)

Estranged (UYI II)

You Could Be Mine (UYI II)

Since I Don't Have You ("TSI?")

Hair Of The Dog ("TSI?")

Oh My God (End Of Days soundtrack/Chinese Democracy)

One last thing, the most important reason not to buy it...the band wouldn't want you to. When Axl and former Gunners Slash, Duff and Matt heard about Geffen's idea to release a greatest hits to "tide people over until Chinese Democracy", they protested. Obviously, they lost in the end, but would GN'R really want you to buy an album that they never wanted released? And if you want it just so you can get Sympathy For The Devil, download it on iTunes, it'll save you $12 bucks.

reviewText:
I'm a moderate fan of Kylie Mingogue - her 2000 release Light Years still stands as one of the best pop releases of the decade - but this attempt at going R'n'B is, frankly, bloody awful, and since the release of the career review "Ultimate Kylie" the album stands as completely pointless.

Why it turned out so bad is a bit of a puzzle, because it begins so well. Slow is one of the most groovy and funky tracks she's ever did, and accompagned by a mighty sexy video (one of the best she ever did!) the album could not get have a better launch. However, from here, it turns into one long nightmarish ride through poorly written and poorly produced slick R'n'B tracks with heavy beats and no hooks.

Well, with one notable example. As surprising as the decline in quality after Slow, Red Blooded Woman lies as a diamond in a pile of junk, sparkling, glittering, and having everything the rest of the album seems to lack: Charm, hook, melody, quality. Not surprisingly, this track was picked as second single and faired excellent (in spite of an awfully boring video).

Chocolate, third single from the album, has all the potential to shine on the dull backdrop that the rest of this album forms, but never really takes off for me. It's quite plain and mediocre, which, however, still makes it better than the rest of the album. I guess Loving Days is the only other none-single track which bears singular mention, as it has actualyl a nice melody. In fact, this is a better track than Chocolate for me, albeit marred by poor vocal production. Apart from this track, I'd say all tracks worth having on this album is also on "Ultimate Kylie".

If you want to look into Kylie's album catalogue beyond collections like "Ultimate Kylie", for God's sake don't start here. Go pick up the sparkling Light Years that contains only keeper tracks (and about a handful of obvious singles that were never released!). 1997's Impossible Princess (later retitled: Kylie Minogue) is another interesting place to start, and even the recent 'X' actually is a good (albeit uneven) listen.

If you must get an impression of what this album's about, I advice you instead to pick up the DVD from the Album Launch at the Apollo Theatre. At least this DVD will offer you the live version of Breathe / Je T'aime, which although not exactly amazing, does form a marginally interesting listen.

reviewText:
First the good:

-Awesome album by Pat Travers (5 stars)

-Incredible packaging on this first ever available on CD (8 page booklet with nice period piece interviews, photos, and new commentary from David Ling -albeit with a few glaring typos) -4 stars

Now the bad:

-these are obviously vinyl transfers (source being taken from an actual record album instead of the original master tapes), although the best vinyl transfers I've heard yet.  You will not hear any scratches, pops, or clicks.  But there are some sonic shortcomings that are inherent in vinyl that is still present.  Low frequency rumble for one (at the beginning and during some quiet passages, you can actually hear the needle riding the record groove) and the ever increasing distortion that record albums have as the needle progresses towards the end of each side (there was a reason that they didn't cut the record groove any farther towards the center than they did).  Each revolution that the record makes keeps getting shorter and shorter in length, but the speed of 33 1/3 rpm remains a constant.  So with each revolution of the record, the same amount of time & music (approx 7 seconds) is given less and less space or distance.  Thereby reducing sound quality gradually with each turn of the record.  Think of it in the tape world where slower speeds mean less sound & picture quality (VHS in the SLP or EP mode anyone).

One would think that vinyl transfers to digital CDs to not even remotely be a legitimate source (as far a legal licensing from the original record label -in this case it is now Universal).  It's something that the high class bootleggers have been doing and now it's gone legitimate mainstream.  The linear notes of this CD clearly have all their legal bases covered, with full licensing approval from Universal.

In closing, I will say this:

-in light of anything better (real digital transfers from the original master tapes), I am happy to see these available.  Pat Travers is a true legend and deserves to have his entire catalog available.  I understand that it was too expensive for Lemon/Cherry Records to go the better route.  So for that I say thank you for releasing them.

On an ironic note:  the CDs themselves are adorned to look like a record album, which may be more telling then my review above...

The songs are whiney and pretentious, and it amazes me how many people think that based on these songs this woman is an "angel" of sorts. reviewText:
Pierre Boulez is one of the world's last "icon" conductors. After the death of Karajan, Bernstein, Kubelik, Vegh and Celibidache, I can only think of one other conductor of Boulez' caliber: Carlos  Kleiber.
Boulez is indeed very good with Bartok, Ravel, Debussy, and  Stravinskij. His recent recordings on DG are all an outstanding proof of  his "feeling" for this music. The recordings are even better than  those excellent ones he made on CBS (Sony). No wonder that Klemperer saw  him as his natural (and only!) successor.
But where his mentor was a  natural Mahler conductor, this cannot be said about the apprentice. Why  not? Boulez' Mahler is crystal clear, every note is played and explained in  details. And yet Boulez seems to forget that this music is a living  organism. This music cannot be played "putting one brick on top of the  other", you need very much "Fernhr" ie. having the very  last note in mind the moment you play the first.
After one of Boulez'  concerts with Mahler's music (with the LSO) Benjamin Britten noted that he  never understood why Boulez conducted so much music that he (Boulez) did  not like. When Britten was asked how he knew that Boulez did not like  Mahler, Britten answered: "Well, that is something you can hear, isn't  it?"

reviewText:
This scrappy performance was given on the occasion of the reopening of the Bayreuth Festival after the war in 1951. Perhaps Herr F. was dragooned into the event to add stature or perhaps it was a way of implicitly announcing it's time to lay to rest concerns re: his past conducting of official concerts during the Third Reich. Whatever the connection, it's a scrappy and uncentered rendition, with the choir and orchestra of the Bayreuther Festspiel barging around and contributing nothing worth caring about. The soloists, also big name, do not redeem.

Does anyone know HOW MANY different Furtwangler performances of the Ninth are on the market? 20? 30? I thought the emotionally charged occasion of reopening the Bayreuth Festival would take away the roulette aspect of choosing blind, but it was no help. My fate was to pick this dud. And woe is me --- there are dozens more Furtwangler 9s to roll the dice & risk the pocketbook on. It's probably best to wise up and act only after FM shows the way.

reviewText:
Whenever most audiophiles refer to Moby's crowning career achievement, most will mention his 1999 breakout album, Play. The creativity and originality of Play was a shining moment in the electronica genre, but unfortunately, Moby's creative light has fizzled in his latest offering, Last Night.

With his last album (Hotel) being less than stellar, Moby fans were forced to wait three years to see if he could musically reconcile with his loyal following. However, much to the chagrin of this reviewer, Last Night was a deplorable effort from an artist who was once electronica royalty. When a musician feels inclined to explicitly describe the concept of an album instead of letting the music speak for itself, something is amiss. In the album's liner notes, Moby states, "It's me trying to take 25 years of going out in NYC and condensing it into a 65-minute record. It's also trying to condense an eight-hour night into just over an hour of music." Although many of Moby's listeners haven't experienced a true "clubber's night" out in New York City during it's heyday, Last Night takes you on a flashback through the DJ's hazed eyes.

This album showcases Moby's keen production prowess, though at most times it seems to be brutally uninspired. A "clubber's night" parallels the plot structure followed in a screenplay or a novel. As the exposition of the album unfolds, Moby paints a musical picture of the anticipated good night out in "Ooh Yeah." Starting with a chilled out track to signal the quiet before the storm is an accurate depiction of the beginning of a stereotypical clubgoer's night out. Nevertheless, if Last Night is a purported concept album of a condensed "eight-hour night," Moby must not have had a very thrilling 25 years out in the NYC scene.

Intermittently, there are flashes of classic Moby energy. Grandmaster Caz, responsible for co-writing one of rap's all-time anthems, Rapper's Delight, was recruited to deliver a few bars over a Latin vibe during "I Love to Move In Here," where he repeats that "old school's takin' you back." This is another instance where Moby feels inclined to unambiguously tell the listeners the direction which the album is headed, certainly not a positive quality in writing or music. During the rising action of Last Night, "Alice" is a rare flash of brilliance on an otherwise lackluster album. Grabbing a strong energy from 419 Squad's hip hop vocal delivery, the album catches a bit of groove until the pills kick in during the next track. "Hyenas" is sexy, dreamy track which creates an ecstasy-fueled alternate state of consciousness with French vocals.

As the album reaches the climax of it's "roll," Moby pumps out some tracks which are obvious nods to 90's rave culture. "I'm in Love" sounds as if it was pulled off of a Paul Oakenfold album. Ironically, both artists have strayed to a more apathetic mode of production as they have gotten older. "Disco Lies" comes off as a flamboyantly gay club anthem... Not that there's anything wrong with that. With the falling action taking place during "Degenerates," Last Night has a very abrupt change in pace. If by this time, the album hasn't degenerated enough to lull you to sleep, this song will do the trick.

During the album's denouement, Moby kicks into serious late night NYC chillout afterparty mode as the pills start to wear off and the night's energy comes to an end. It seems unusual that Moby dedicates such a large portion of the album to the final moments of the night, as nearly a quarter of the album slips into a musical coma. Closing out the album with the title track, the diva swoons, "If this be my last night on Earth, let me remember this for all that it's worth." If this is Moby's last album on Earth, hopefully he will not be remembered by it's disheartening worth, for Last Night is truly forgettable.
label: negative

reviewText:
Look, it's been what, three years since the Met-boys released their latest album of all-original material (Lulu is a collaboration and not strictly speaking a Metallica project, per se). I am a HUGE fan of the old stuff -"Puppets" was my FIRST real metal album (I was 13 & got it in '87) -then subsequently went out and got "Kill...", "Ride..." and "Justice" plus a few of the EPs floating around at the time -all on vinyl. I didn't really care for the infamous "Black" album or any of their 90's crap including "St. Anger" -it mostly sucked.

When I heard they were FINALLY getting around to recording something new, i.e. original material, I admit I was stoked and a bit skeptical. We all know the 90's sucked for thrash, and when death metal stagnated around 94/95 -real metal was in trouble and the Met-boys showed us the road they were travelling by paving the way for commercially acceptable "metal". Well I decided not to purchase "Death Magnetic" for awhile but finally found a used copy in Zia Records here in Vegas in '09.

First off: the absolutely over-compressed/overly loud production. I have the 2011 re-issue of Death's "Human" -obviously being a complete re-mix AND re-master the volume has also increased. I listened to a tune off "Human" and then one off "Death Magnetic" -same volume and the Metallica song was hella loud! Realizing this is a newer recording I tried comparisons to other new recordings -same result. The Met-boys win in this arena -the clipping is so bad I never listen to the album. I actually got rid of the CD it was so bad. I don't play Guitar Hero, so I don't know how those versions sound but as far as the album release -terrible, utterly terrible.

The songs themselves aren't terrible. They are a throwback to "Justice" and the "Black" album era -with a different bassist. I actually like a few tunes -the issue is none of them are memorable. Even the "Black" album has a ton of memorable songs, like'em or not -and any metal fan worth his/her salt knows the intro to "Puppets" and the classics of the band. Songs on the album aren't bad, they just don't stick -like someone sprayed'em with Pam cooking oil. They actually sound uninspired and contrived -i.e. forced. It's like Metallica recorded this because they had to or something because they failed to release any real metal for almost 20 years to that point.

Metallica is a band who does only one thing right: they tour constantly -which keeps them in the public eye (ear) and they play all the "hits" -people go to party and hear loud music. The Met-boys only real talent is touring (anymore) and they have capitalized and cashed in on this. How many tours did they do in the 90's? How many during and after "St. Anger" -the "Getting out of the studio because we have no ideas & we're bored" Tour...?! They are a business, pure and simple. They haven't been in it to make music, metal or faux metal, for a long time. Their strength and security is in touring and keeping the name alive.

To prove my point: they have released two albums with original, Metallica inspired compositions between 2000 and now -they record an album with Lou Reed -a collaboration project and they continue to tour non-stop (The Big Four Tour, anyone) to keep up their credibility. Look at the "free" downloads of their live shows available on their site and you'll see almost the same songs over and over (every band has live staples, I get that) but they have no variety anymore. They are a tired band that keeps rehashing the same tired "metal" music over and over and over. Hell, I would even get sick of "Puppets" if I had to play it all the time.

Metallica are done, from what I can see at this point. Unless they get a new drummer and inject some fresh ideas to create real metal, they're just a "metal" version of the Grateful Dead, a band that just keeps touring. Musically speaking, this album is a decent step but the horrible production makes it unlistenable; whatever good songs are present were irreparably ruined by the over compressed mix and production. At least "Justice" had memorable songs -sterile, dry production notwithstanding. Glad I didn't waste my money and buy this new...
label: negative

reviewText:
Many reviewers will tell you that "Kid A" is the sound of a band challenging their audience with experimental new sounds, radical new approaches to arranging songs and a fresh take on what it means to make "pop" music.
I - on the other hand - will tell you that "Kid A" is the sound of a band totally out of sync with the rest of the world, with an inflated idea of what their role as "pop" musicians are, and with absolutely no clue as to what an experimental rock album should sound like.
(An experimental Rock album, well, that's your "Sgt. Pepper", your "Pet Sounds", your "Dark Side of the Moon", your "Achtung Baby"... )
I can't decide if Radiohead should take MORE drugs or less drugs, but I do know that they ought to stay away from music until they start falling in love with songs again. Because this is the sound of a band that at the moment hates music.
label: negative

reviewText:
And they did it again... It seems that Sony/BMG/Universal Music, through their many labels (like Hip-O, under which this album was released), are becoming the leaders of the infamous "loudness war" (Google the expression for more info). Basically, that means mastering the CD with the audio normalized beyond the CD format dynamic range limits. That way, on many of the songs, louder parts are simply clipped, that is, those audio frequencies are simply not present anymore, because the audio was mastered so loud that the audio was clipped (cut off) when it reached the limit the CD format allows, and those frequencies are irreparably lost in the process. The idea is to deceive the average consumer into thinking that he is getting a better sounding recording, when it's the exact opposite - it's just louder, and worse - with parts of the audio actually missing.

I've just received the CD set and ran a full audio analysis of the "On And On" track. There are at least 446 clipped samples on the left channel and at least 264 on the right channel. To see the sound carnage for yourself, just extract the track and open it with an audio editor like Cool Edit, zoom in on the clipped sections, and see the poor sound wave cut off into a flat line, with the sound it was meant to reproduce completely LOST.

reviewText:
I kind of have to agree with M. Chapman on some of what he says here. I decided to give three of these original album classics a shot (Patti Smith, Byrds and Mahavishnu Orchestra). I am a collector of the japanese mini LP box sets. However the economy being what it is I have had to pass up a few of the one's I would have like to have gotten. In the case of the Patti Smith box, for example, we're talking about around $200 for the Japanese mini LP box vs a hair under $30 for the Original Album Classics box. I just got all three of the boxes I ordered in the mail today and all I can say is you will very definately notice every last one of those $170 dollars difference between the US vs the Japanese sets. And I do not mean that in a good way.

Now I don't know what M Chapman is talking about with regards to any liner notes being out of date as these boxes include absolutely nothing beyond whatever the front and back cover artwork of the original albums were (and NO gatefolds by the way!). In the case of the Mahavishnu Orchestra discs that means you get the songs and line up's more or less and the occasional "I worship at the feet of the golden smurf" poetry. What you do NOT get are ANY sort of protective innersleeves - . I am not talking about the Japanese detail to the first pressings like the original CBS advertising inners. I am talking about anything at all that would have prevented 2 of the discs to fall right out of the covers when I removed them from the box and fall onto the pavement! For that alone I will dock this set 1 point - that is just unbelievably cheap and stingy on the part of whoever made these. Secondly you won't get the 1 sheet inserts that came with a few of the original albums: again: something that would have been SO inexpensive for the label to duplicate and inclue that the ommision of these is just stingy. There goes another point for that. Finally: Visions Of The Emerald Beyond... one of my all time favorite LP covers. One of my all time favorite GATEFOLD LP covers. And Columbia reproduces it as a cheap looking non gatefol issue here. In a box that purports to includes replicas of the original LP sleeves. In the case of the Mahavishnu box that means one less point. Would it have killed Columbia to make that ONE sleeve a gatefold?

Finally the covers themselves are made of really cheap cradstock. This means they have minor scuffs on them from the moment you remove the shrinkwrap. This might not mean anything to the casual buyer who just wants to get 5 cd's cheap (and I WILL credit the US recod companies for that one small favour: at least these sets ARE cheap - because they certainly are NOT worth a penny over let's say $30, if that) but for a collector or for future resale value that kind of means that the packaging could never be called "Mint" or even a true "Mint Minus": and THAT pisses me off big time as a collector. Yet one more point. Leaving this particular Mahavishnu box as a 1 star rated box in my opinion. On the Byrds and Patti Smith's they were all single sleeved covers to begin with. In the case of the Patti's every single one of the original albums had lyric sheets - not one of these do. In the case of the Byrds set... well I have to give that point back because none of them were gatefolds and none of them came with inserts...

And here's my main problem with the entire series: When I was a kid growing up in the 60's and 70's I remember the phrase "Made In Japan" as something that was a catch all phrase for when something would be an inferior and extremely flimsy and cheap knockoff of a US made product. Here the US record companies are taking an idea for boxsets that the Japanese pretty much invented and make so lovingly and caringly. And the US record companies make an EXTREMELY low budget flimsy and cruddy looking knock off. I won't be purchasing any further volumes of this series. You get what you pay for and as a collector it IS worth the extra $100+ dollars to get the well made Japanese mini LP box with the incredible attention to detail etc. Those are gorgeous to look at and they hold their value and they are worth every expensive penny they cost to buy. These one's here? They'll never escalate in value and they all but scream "Cheap Cheap Cheap!". The best thing I can say about them is that unlike 5 jewel box cd's they take up a lot less space. But at least in the jewel box versions you got nice booklets with all the artwork and great liner notes. You just do NOT win with these original Album Classics box sets. Which is really sad: for once the US record industry COULD HAVE gotten things right and created an inexpensive collectable that would have been something very cool to own at a great price. But once again they got just about every single aspect of the whole thing wrong and utterly fail to understand what makes the collector buy these sorts of sets in the first place. Yeah: you have the music and the music still sounds great. But you can get that music - and have been able to get that music - for years now in jewel box format with superior packaging. If these boxsets are geared towards collectors like me who were looking forward to replacing their jewel box versions of these cd's and hoping to save some money by not buying the expensive Japanese boxset equivalents then once again the US record industry did not even come close. It's true that you cannot play the packaging, but when you create a series geared towards the collector then to the true collector packaging is every bit as important as the music...

Let me start by saying that I have been kind in the past to lead singers who have with much drama changed out their entire band (see my reviews of Evanescence's Evanescence and Guns `N Rose Chinese Democracy for the proof).  My review has nothing to do with all of the drama in how "Queensryche" got to the point of releasing Frequency Unknown.  It is just about the music.

Oh, and Frequency Unknown is a stinker of the highest order.  Geoff Tate and his new crew produced ten songs that lack any sort of unifying thought.  At times they try (emphasis on the try) to sound hard.  Both "Cold" and "Slave" see to channel Ozzy's band from 20 years ago.  Then you have "Everything" which sounds like Tate took a page from Axl Rose on Chinese Democracy with the addition of electronics.  I could go on, but what would be the point?  Just in these three songs you get the lack of unity, and they just aren't well done.

With what I have written so far, I would give this two stars.  I don't like it, and I wouldn't recommend it.  However, I have also heard worse.  What makes this a bottom of the barrel offering is the final four re-recorded songs from Operation Mindcrime and Empire.  I can't imagine that there is any way that Tate can listen to these and say, "Yep.  I'm proud of that fine work."  His vocals show the wear and tear of 20 plus years, but the instrumentals are just awful.  It is an insult to the original musicians to release these counterfeit versions.  If you are not familiar with the originals, do yourself a favor and check them out.  They are some of the great songs from that time in music.

In the end, the difference between the Queensryche reboot and those of Evanescence and Guns `N Roses is that Frequency Unknown just doesn't measure up to Queensryche's history.  It doesn't have to be the same style.  Chinese Democracy couldn't be more of a departure from Appetite for Destruction, but it is musically brilliant in its own right.  What Geoff Tate and company produced here is an atrocity to the recording industry at large.  When it is original, it is subpar.  When it revisits the past, it isn't even a faint shadow.  You can find something better to spend your money on than this.  You'd even better burning it than buying this.

reviewText:
...there are few artists out there that have received as much unwarranted hype and mass hysteria as James Blunt.

This guy has blown up around the world - even in the U.S., where most British bands and artists are unjustly ignored.  But Blunt actually cracked the Top Ten and already sold 500,000 copies - you want to know how he did it?  By recording a safe, syrupy, and shallow collection of maudlin soft rock ballads designed for "power rotation" on all the Adult Contemporary stations in the country.  He basically took the Coldplay formula and simplified it even more - is this what music has come to, where we are exalting ordinary pop pablum such as this?

On his debut album Back To Bedlam, Blunt doesn't so much sing as he does bawl his way throughout the entire album.  Sad and depressing music can be both powerful and moving in the right hands, but in the case of a hack like Blunt, every single song is a long, drawn-out weepfest.  This guy can make winning the lottery and falling in love sound as if they were the most miserable, depressing experiences a person could ever have.  Here's an idea of what Blunt's unintelligible caterwauling sounds like:

"WAAAAAAHHHHHH - my girlfriend is leaving me!  WAAAAAAHHHHHH - the school bully took my football away!  WAAAAAAHHHHHH - my parents sent me to bed without my milk and cookies!  LIFE ... IS NOT WORTH LIVING ANYMORE!!!"  Awwwwwww, what's poor little Jimmy gonna do?  Don't you worry, you poor baby - all that money coming your way will help you buy a house, some milk and cookies, a football ... and a new girlfriend.

There's easily enough hand-wringing, tearjerking, cry-yourself-to-sleep themes on this album to make this a chick flick lover's dream come true.  But everything here is delivered in such a simplistic, trite and inarticulate manner, that you have to ask yourself what people see in this guy.  Look at the guy, he's got so much going for him between his having the good looks of an actor and a label willing to make him a big star at any cost - what does he have to be all sad and despondent about anyway?  He's nothing special at all - get over it.

In summary: Bland, mundane and completely irrelevant, the best use for James Blunt's debut album would be either as a frisbee, a beverage coaster, or a substitute for a box of tissues.  Instead of buying the album, why not donate the money to the owner of the studio that Back To Bedlam was recorded in - I'll bet Blunt cried so much that it flooded the building and caused equipment damage to the tune of thousands of pounds.  Why embrace bland fluff like this when there's much better music coming out of the UK - check out Kasabian, The Music, Gomez, Arctic Monkeys, Art Brut, Nine Black Alps, Elbow, Embrace, Hard-Fi, Bloc Party, etc.  None of these bands have broken the U.S. mainstream yet, but these bands have put out albums that are far more intelligent and interesting than what you'll hear on Back To Bedlam.

reviewText:
My, this isn't very good, is it?  Not that expectations were particularly high, but sometimes one can be surprised.

Here, it's yet another case of what happens when famous people are surrounded by sycophants sharing not a cahone amongst them to offer honest feedback. With hundreds of real, talented musicians literally starving for a shot, angel investors instead bankroll a "name", hoping to cash in. But success has proven elusive for most of these ventures, as well it should. Musicians devote entire lives to honing their skills and it's a never-ending process.

Actors in fact "can" sing  - sometimes - and with time and effort, pretty much anyone can improve their voice. But whether due to the fact she's concentrated most of her past efforts on a completely different genre of entertainment, or as is the case with so many others, simply has mediocre talent, Scarlett's not yet ready for prime time.

Conversely, many musicians who've tried acting have experienced success:  Cher, David Bowie,  Olivia Newton-John, Debbie Harry, Gene Simmons, Roger Daltrey, Sting, Meat Loaf, Jon Bon Jovi, Will Smith, Ice-T, Ice Cube, Mark Wahlberg, and Donnie Wahlberg (Band of Brothers - WOW is all I can say about his stunning performance,)  - to name just a few.

Still, one cannot deny the guilty, rubbernecking pleasure of a small train wreck. And Scarlett's in good company with William Shatner (so-bad-it's-almost- good camp), Leonard Nimoy, Clint Eastwood, David Soul, Eddie Murphy (please God, help me to finally forget "I Just Want to Party All the Time"), Billy Bob Thornton....the list is large.

Of course, there are some notable exceptions, such as  John Travolta who may not be a technically great singer, can do it with style AND dance.

Wielding a voice with all the dynamic range of A to B and mercifully buried in tweedly arrangements, Scarlett's is a foray into the pointless and forgettable.

Lost in translation, indeed.

reviewText:
Rarely has someone been so famous for so little, and that fact shines through in "Greatest Hits: My Prerogative." While much-publicized pop star Britney Spears has produced four albums thus far, all that becomes clear in her "greatest hits" is that her music has never been that good, and it's only getting worse.

This contains several of her hit singles, arranged in no particular order -- expect to bounce madly between slinky technopop and bouncy bubblegum with no logic in mind -- the obvious hits like "I'm A Slave 4 U" (future bondage-porn soundtrack?), "... Baby One More Time" and "Oops!... I Did It Again" are set alongside much lesser pop hits like "Toxic," the flaccid Madonna duet, and several others that were more or less forgotten.

Like virtually any other greatest hits album, it has some bonus materials. There are from several remixes, none of which are too good -- for example, the Darkchild Remix of "Overprotected" is a clattery, feedback-laced affair. Spears also releases several previously unheard songs, such as the generic "I've Just Begun (Having My Fun)" and equally dull "Do Somethin'."The most hyped song is "My Prerogative," an electropop cover of a Bobby Brown song -- with lyrics like "I don't need permission/I make my own decisions," it sounds like an immature, defiant finger-flip at the world. Good luck with that.

Usually "Greatest Hits" albums are put out for one of two reasons. Either a band/singer has been around for eons and has enough glorious songs to fill an entire album, or the label they are/were signed to is trying to cash in. For the latter, think "Best of Mandy Moore," which Ms. Moore had nothing to do with. Sadly, Spears' "Greatest Hits" album is neither -- instead, it feels like an effort to keep her at the forefront of music store displays.

Her music is pretty standard for whatever kind of pop is attempted -- polished and overproduced. And, I might add, very predictable -- virtually every blip and note can be detected before it's heard. While "Toxic" has a halfway decent beat and some electric violins, Spears strikes out with her newer pop melodies, especially the ones that sound a lot like No Doubt covers.

Her image also veers wildly through the various songs, starting off with the sound of a giggly teen who has done something naughty. Then she's launching into the more sexual stuff, especially in the horribly-written "Outrageous" ("Outrageous!/My sex drive/Outrageous!/My shopping sprees...."). But it doesn't feel genuinely sexy -- rather it feels like a little girl dressing up in mommy's lingerie.

And Spears' vocals have never been too good -- her early material displays a voice that is pretty typical for a teenage girl. It has little range, and it's a sort of breathy, thin voice. That doesn't last -- her voice deteriorates over the more recent tracks from her fourth album, becoming drier and more computerized. The sound peaks in "My Prerogative," where Spears sounds like a congested robot.

Everyone has an opinion on Spears' much-publicized love life, but the quality of her pop music is pretty clear. While her early material was innocuous in a teen pop sort of way, her pop ditties have only deteriorated with time.
label: negative

reviewText: Note to Chris Rea: when you make a sequel album (and anything called "Part 2" definitely counts), what you provide is either a) more of the same, or b) the same concepts covered in a novel way. Road to Hell was high quality, well executed rock album covering social themes. I have no idea what Part II is. Yes, there are some social comments here and there, but largely (and I'm sorry to say this), this is a steaming pile of electro-crud. I bought this album after hearing Part I. Thank goodness I didn't stop my Chris Rea exploration here, or I would have missed out. The Road to Hell (pt I) was great - a real tour de force, and the moment when Chris Rea finally and deservedly crossed over into wide popularity. He followed with the equally good (or better) Auberge and other good work. He seemed to have finally found a way to make his own music, with integrity, and in a highly popular way. That's why it's so confounding that the excellent Blue Cafe was followed by the garbage on this album. I agree with JDogg - this album is virtually unlistenable. It's full of annoying backing vocals (generally saying the same "yeah, yeah, yeah" in each song), electronic beeps that belong in the early '80s (at best), and virtually no distinguishing melodies. It's hard to understand what Rea was thinking with this album. It's different from his usual, but not in a good way. And it doesn't seem like an album that was rushed out the door - there's little here that could have made a good song without considerable work. The one exception is "Keep on Dancing", where the backing vocals are made acceptable by a moderately strong sequel to Part I's "Let's Dance". "Marvin" and "Firefly" are not bad, but I mean that literally. They would be unobjectionable filler on a better album; here, they're two of the few songs that don't grate. I tried to think of whom this album would appeal to, and only came up with this: if you enjoy the song "Oh no, not you again" from Dave Stewart's Greetings From the Gutter - not the main song, but the part at the end, where Stewart and Carly Simon have a whiny argument for several minutes, then this is for you. In short, and just to hammer this point into the ground: this is a BAD album. If you want GOOD music, try any of the albums mentioned above.

This is pastiche. The adult swim kids who just got into metal will gobble it up and talk about "open-mindedness" and experimentalism, but their dads were listening to more adventurous music than this before they were born.
