I was really looking forward to this comp. I knew a lot of bands on it, and it sounded like it would be really cool. Punk bands covering mainstream pop songs, what could go wrong? Well, In a nutshell, everything! This is the most disapointing, and most likely the worst comp. I own.
First of all, I have a problem with the title. Its called "Punk goes Pop". About 80% of the bands on here aren't exactly punk, they are more pop/punk. Therefore, the sound is not exactly "punk", and instead, it sounds like the original songs, only with some guitaring mixed in. Two, 90% of the songs here are grindingly slow. Punk is supposed to be fast and hard. Here, most of the tempos are exactly the same as the original song, leading to not much of a difference between the original and the cover. Three, its as if these bands on here didn't even try. I really liked Dynamite Boy coming into this, and their cover is slow, and extremely uninspired, as with almost all the other covers on here. Even if the tempo is slightly faster, the songs still come out terrible, just listen to the Nicotine and Reach the Sky covers.
There are two exceptions however. One, the Thrice cover is awesome, they do not disapoint. Two, the Knockout cover isn't bad, I've never heard of them going into this comp., but they do a very good job. With those two out of the way, the rest are just... uninspired mid tempo pop/punk junk.
This really could have turned out cool, instead, it turned out very disapointing. This is not what I hoped for at all. Avoid this comp. at all costs, or just buy it for the Thrice cover.

reviewText:
This is Adams at his worst. He can be flash(as in Faast Ride,loopalooza etc) but at least those pieces sound like good film music at best.

The Violin concerto to me actually doesn't sound at all like Adams!! I am really surprised people who like Harmonium(his best piece by far) like this. It is actually very unpleasant to listen to.

 It is relentless(why doesn't Adams like rests?!!), tedious and actually plain dull and uninspired. There appears to be NO direction in the first movement,just like a boring inmprovisation. And yes I have tried to hear it quite a few times.

The second movement is the best but sounds a bit like bad Frank Martin(a wonderful Swiss composer who  mixed atonality and tonlity with much success)I advise readers to listen to Martin;s 'Petite Concertante'.Adams is just not good at trying to incoprporate atonal elements with tonal ones-he also just sounds like bad Ives here.

The last movement is typical  of Adams-very flash technically but no substance. It is again relentless but just plain tedious,empty and machine music. It is reminiscent of the Barber but that at least DOES have depth even though I am not a big fan of that (though Adams could learn from Barber's first movement which is lovely,breathes and has rests!!).

This is all a shame as Adams in Harmonium showed he could write music that breathed and was really musical.
label: negative

reviewText: And that isn't what we have here.  Patti Lupone, a forceful actress with a unique voice (you either love it or hate it) doesnt do well by this score; she is content too often to shout emphatically rather than sing, and she  doesnt bring enough vulnerability in the few places where Mr. Lloyd  Webber's screeching score will allow for it.  Mandy Patinkin, another  singer with an odd voice, is far to weak to match up to the anger and drive  of his songs.  All of this discussion, however, implies that there is  something in Evita worth performing.  This is truly one of the worst scores  ever to be called great.  The music is all loud, forceful, grating, and  numbing, a strange hybrid of opera, showbiz-glitz, and Europop (Lloyd  Webber's favorite idiom.)  The occasional passages in which the composer  deigns to give us a fully-realized melody and not just a barrage of rock  chords cant be enjoyed, however, because they are the only times we can  hear the lyrics, which are amateurish at best.  At worst, they are  laugh-out-loud stupid.  All in all, this record does capture the true  essence of a show that has been called, quite correctly, "as colorful  as a trash heap."

reviewText:
Fallen was a masterpiece!  It  stayed on the charts forever and sold 7 million copies in the US alone.  Every song was wonderfully crafted, catchy, and terrific!  Musical perfection it was with that goth/metal/sweet voice!  The Open Door the second CD paled in comparison and sold a couple million copies mainly because of the success and anticipation after the first CD!  Now 5 years later comes even a worse effort than The Open Door. I'm sorry Amy Lee can't hardly write good songs musical at all anymore.  They all rely on basic hooks repeated throughout the song, they are generic sounding tunes that sound like Evanescence, but not great Evanescence!  After I heard most of them 5-6 times, I don't want to hear them again!  Is this the best she could come up with after 5 years?  I'm sorry there is NO WAY this is going to be a hit.  Maybe Gold?  It would be surprising if Evanescence (2011) even goes Platinum. I seriously doubt it!  All the die hard fans raving about this CD, how many of you are there actually?  I bet there won't be 100 of you to come here and rave about this CD!  There was 2,000 that came here and raved Fallen including myself.  That's what makes a hit album, a GREAT CD, great songs, great production, songs that long to be played on the radio (one after the other), great word of mouth, and next thing you know millions have bought the CD!  Not 50 people who would say anything they come out with is a 5 star masterpiece.  Your WAYYYYYYY to easy to please!  Now that said, there are a few good songs on this CD!  I do like "Sick", "Never Going Back", "End Of The Dream", "Swimming Home", Disappear, and "Secret Door" is an AWESOME song.  WHY IS THERE NOT MORE SONGS LIKE THAT??????????  The last two songs I listed are from the bonus CD.  But we're talking 4 out of 12 or 6 out of 16 (on the Deluxe version).  10 songs on this album aren't even worthy of release.  Somehow I doubt Amy has really been working on this CD for 5 years, considering all the strife and firing most of the band members, this is part of her problem.  She thinks she alone is Evanescence!  Evanescence was a band where more than one person had an input and contributed to the songwriting and production.  This is Amy Lee trying her best to recapture what they made during Fallen. It doesnt even come close!  And give me all the thumbs down you want, let the success of the album tell the real story!  I believe it won't even last 4 weeks in the top 10!  And it will never come back into the top 10 again!  And 4 or 5 years from now, Amy will be trying again but the interest is going to keep fading as time and MORE bad albums are released.  I will not take her seriously again, she has to prove me wrong next time!

UPDATE 11/12/2011  Well it fell off after 4 weeks alright, down to #28 (from #13 in week 3).  This album is not even going to go Gold.  It's a terrible album like I said all the people that love this CD there aren't that many of you (only 170,000 people even bought this CD in the entire US).  Definitely for die hard fans only!  Coldplay is suffering the same fate after 1 good sales week, Mylo Xyloto is taking a huge dive.  It's the same reason as Evanescence, their new CD stinks!  Two huge disappointments from two bands I really like.  In Evanescence case (like Coldplay), it's not because they aren't popular.  Evanescence is still VERY popular! People want to hear great new material, and pass the word, hear singles on the radio, and acquire BRAND new fans who are getting into the new music.  But an album like Evanescence 2011 is NEVER going to produce any hits, or turn anyone new on to this band.  Amy Lee needs to collaborate with someone new and come up with some killer tunes, better production, better songs musically, and make something catchy.  Not just generic songs that resemble old Evanescence songs, but unique, great compositions that will put them back on top.  I'll be waiting and hoping for that day to come in a few years or so.

reviewText:
Indubitably, David Zinman is the Toyota Prius of his profession. He offers transportation, not journey. Indeed, he presages Googles driverless car. Feel the timbre of the steering wheel: its plastic. Open the bonnet and ponder the dimensions of his two-stroke engine. Unlike those big German diesels, theres no need for exhaust pipes. Hes so damned efficient as to negate aerodynamics. A squeak-o-meter measures his torque. Zinman zips up mountains (well, the base of them at least). He zips around corners. He zips over bridges. With safety ever in mind, he artfully skirts the abyss. However snootily, Jeggy commends his brisk efficiency. Provided Zinman never has to stop and think about what hes doing (his default modus operandi) nothing is beyond him. A bit like those Dancing Elvis-es on the dashboard, he offers novelty in the way of perky, HIPster inspired brass and timpani. In the scheme of things, that doesnt amount to much but some might enjoy the gyrations.

And here is his standard fare: perky, superficial, church-mouse Schumann that is devoid of grandeur, mystery and passion. The Ozone Layer can relax: there are no pollutants here. With éclat, Zinnman prius-ifies the opening movement of the Rhenish and the bridge into the finale of the Fourth: they're mere dots on the map. Purged of anachronistic mysticism, the slow movements of the Second and Third revert to being glorified intermezzos. Im not going to waste any more words on it. For once, Im going to abjure my maxim Subjectivity is King and laugh at those reviewers who laud this wannabe flyweight.

One should not under-estimate Mister Prius. Hes painted an exit door on a solid wall of concrete and how many of his colleagues are tempted, in lieu of anything else in their kit-bag, to reach for it. In his advocacy of energy over interpretation, Zinman is a lodestar to the likes of Abbado, Rattle, Dudamel, Paavo Järvi, Ivan Fischer, Nézet-Séquin and Ticciati . Brace yourself: its the Charge of the Light Brigade. Cup your ears: the air is aswarm with the hum of hybrid engines.

reviewText: Guster is a huge breath of fresh air for me. I discovered them on a van ride on my way to backpack in Wyoming, and loved every single song on the album Parachute. This music is never played on the radio stations and has that enchanting accoustic and vocal harmony mix with bongos and congas and a bunch of other cool percussion that makes me delight in awe of their musicianship. Their first two albums seem to be about something and have very thoughtfull lyrics. They didn't make that music for anybody but themselves. Their third release, however, has left me in a bad mood. The word "sellouts" comes to mind after listening to this contrived radio-friendly garbage. "Fa Fa" happens to be one of the best songs on the album and it is listenable, but I had expected there to be some songs that are similar to their previous stuff. There weren't any songs worth buying this CD for. The only reason I could think to buy this album is because I want to support the band and let them get enough money in order to not have to make another good-selling album. If you liked Guster's old stuff, don't buy this, but if you are one of those crustacians who cling to "the new cool band", and liked their radio hit "Fa Fa", then by all means support this overhyped Sample.

reviewText:
After Kelly Clarkson won my unofficial guilty pleasure of the year award and I enjoyed Carrie Underwood's debut album guilt free I could be warming up to the whole American Karaoke thing. So I decided to check the dude Carrie beat in the latest installment, Bo Bice.

After my first listen through his debut, The Real Thing, I thought, "How horribly bland." It is really hard to write a review of an album that constantly puts you to sleep out of boredom. The songs are very familiar to his sup-par outing on Santana's album except Bice Bice Baby doesn't have Carlos' guitar to bail him out here. Instead Bice brought in members of Bon Jovi, Chad Kroeger of Nickelback, Ben Moody fresh of his work with Lindsey Lohan and Ashlee Simpson, and John Shanks who is also best know for working with females who try to rock. That's not necessarily a Murderer's Row of rock music. At least with pre-for mentioned Lohan and Simpson, their music strikes an emotion, even if that emotion is hatred, which is still better than the uninspiring music that Bice has made here. I would much rather have people hate me than to have no opinion at all.

But the music isn't even the worst part of the album, the writing here makes Lohan's confessionals on her latest album look like Keats compared to the lyrics on The Real Thing. You'd think someone who doesn't write their own lyrics (Bice only have co-writing credits on two tracks) would at least pick out songs that didn't sound like a middle schooler who relies way too much on trying to rhyme like, "I'll open every car door, I won't go out anymore, I'll even eat off the floor" (You're Everything). It's not too surprising that Kroeger didn't save that gem for his band.

So with The Real Thing, American Karaoke's miraculous streak of good music has ended and hopefully Bice Bice Baby will say hello to Justin (whatever his name is) on his inevitable trip to obscurity, or even worse, The Surreal Life house.

Nor does the blame fall on Matthew Katz.  After all, he managed Jefferson Airplane also and they did quite well despite his "bad" management.  Columbia Records is hardly at fault. One of the greatest labels of all time, Columbia broke Dylan, the Byrds and Big Brother.  The "label" certainly didn't stand in their way.

Moby Grape didn't make it big because they really weren't very good.  Let's face it.  Plenty of groups had flop singles (see The Kinks).  It didn't stop them from having an extremely successful musical career.  Renaissance or Fairport Convention NEVER had a hit single--nor did they have hit albums.  That didn't stop them from making great music for decades.

Airplane had SIX singles released in their first YEAR!  Four were flops.  Two were hits.  Why? Because the hits ("Somebody to Love" and "White Rabbit") were actually GOOD.

So stop blaming everyone else for the Grape's failure.  The Grape failed because they weren't that good.  Bad management and label problems didn't stop Buffalo Springfield from acheiving legendary statuure.  Nor did it deep-six the lengthy careers of its individual members.

It might actually be possible to listen and appreciate this group if the undeserved hype would die down!  It's so overblown.  And flat out untrue.

The Beatles sound like incompetent amateurs compared to the "Grape".  Sheesh!  Enough already.

reviewText: I really wanted to like this album, being a big fan, but . . . too much Amy.  Now, I love Amy Lee's voice which is one of the all time rock voices which made the first album ground breaking! She's great at the 'tortured' style and at this stage of her career, I was hoping for more variety.  I listened to this album 4 times before I rated it at one star (I started with 3 out of 5).  Here's why:  Most of the songs are mid tempo with the same torture lyrics and voice (again, a GREAT voice), but Amy's singing throughout the entire songs.  One guitar solo on the album which lasts about 10 seconds.  Yes, the staccato guitar bursts are there, but is this rock or opera?  I wanted this album to be a great rock album, but the lack of guitar solos makes it redundant because I need a break from the vocals.  Even, some percussive breaks or the orchestration which they piled on these songs would have worked.  No orchestra solos, just a lone piano break here and there.  Somebody down there at Blackbird studios (one of the best in the country) should have put the reins on the vocals. The orchestration is way overdone.  The album is 'over produced' and loses it rock edge.  Maybe, this was the intention.  Maybe, the guitar guys were afraid to solo thinking that it's all cliche?  Not in rock. baby.  I would have loved to hear some male vocals harmonizing with Amy.  Who knows, maybe her backing band are good singers?  It's a stretch, but live, this band would rock.  Live, all you're gonna get is Amy singing with no guitar solos or breaks.  The constant vocals get boring but, with more balanced arrangments, having solos, breaks, etc. - when that voice returns in the songs - what better impact it would make.  Also, the album art is boring.  The front title should have been bigger.  The back CD artwork is plain and it's hard to read the titles - please, next time, number the tracks.  The fonts inside are way to small (a trend on all CDs).  The few good things I hear are:  great vocals, good production, intersting lyrics.  Again, it's the same 'mood' throughout the CD and I would have loved better songwriting with more variety:  some thrash, maybe a blues based song, some rock and roll (remember that), some metal, something upbeat and positive.  I listen to music to escape, but don't want to escape into a depressing world - one in which I already live in.

reviewText:
Throughout the years Opeth has gained lots of fans, but they have also lost lots of fans.  The main argument from the new wave of Opeth fans is that the old school "metal heads" are dumb, unsophisticated, close minded, and ignorant for not liking the new stylistic approach created by Mikael Akerfeldt.  I think there are some metal heads that don't like the new album specifically for the lack of growls, but most of the Opeth fans I know lost interest in the band directly after the "Ghost Reveries" album.  While still a solid album, it lacked on some songs.  Then came "Watershed" which I found redundant and mediocre, yet I stuck with the band.

I was excited and glad to hear that "Heritage" would have no death vocals because it was all too evident that his ability to growl was gone; it could be heard at live Opeth shows and especially on the latest Bloodbath album, "The Fathomless Mastery."  Also it was exciting to think about my favorite band expanding their musical horizon.

Unfortunately both "Heritage" and the new album "Pale Communion" fail to evoke any kind of emotional connection with the musicians and the listener.  Pale Communion features Mikael Akerfedlt's worst vocal appearance ever.  His inability to sing a simple vocal melody is confounding.  Akerfeldt stretches out every syllable in every word and then cuts off the words by breaking his vocals.  The song "Eternal Rains Will Come" is the only song in which he actually starts out singing beautifully (somewhat reminiscent of the "Damnation" album), but then during the chorus he does the vocal key breaks.

Musically the album is bland.; it is nothing more thank cookie cutter prog filled with dry drums and horrible hammond organ rolls.  Guitar wise there is nothing stimulating going on to hold my attention.  The same Opeth fans who claim to love the new style, somehow think that Frederik's shredding metal solo style fits into Opeth's music.  Frederik's solo's are the most forgettable guitar solo's since hippy jam bands like Phish and Widespread Panic.  Any of Frederick's solos could be placed over any metal riff and be perfectly at home, yet somehow they are here in these "PROG" songs.  And since when did prog become the be all end all of music genre's.  Opeth used to be a band that didn't fit into any genre (even though Mike proudly declared the band as "death metal" - they were beyond death).

In the end "Pale Communion" is an imitator, not an originator album.  I think Mike is trying to hard to mimic his prog idols of the 70's instead of doing something original.  I like some prog, King Crimson, Yes, Camel, Pink Floyd, and some others, but prog isn't a music genre that is incapable of producing horrible records.  I hear a lot blame from the metal old school guys that he's trying to hard to be like Steven Wilson, but I don't think that's even close to it, if anything after listening to their Storm Corrosion project I was very hopefully for this album.  Storm Corrosion was beautiful and haunting, I was hoping for something epic from Mike after listening to Storm Corrosion.  I thought something new and exciting was coming after the train wreck that was "Heritage" - which  was nothing but a bunch of disjointed song ideas thrown together.

Maybe it is a good think that some fans like "Pale Communion".  I do have hope that by their 14th album or so Mike will come up with something inspirational, but trust me in saying this, most Opeth fans left the band during the "Watershed" era and now most haven't even bothered with buying these last two records.
label: negative

reviewText:
For anyone wanting to read a multitude of honest reviews of this product, rather than all of this nonsensical blind praise listed here, please read the reviews at Amazon's UK site.

The "remastering" on the two latest DD releases is terrible! The remastering engineer turned the volume WAY TOO LOUD, creating heavy compression and severe distortion. It's resulted in an all around unpleasant listening experience. This has become too common place among CD reissues, especially over the past several years. The "Loudness War", as it is termed, is the result of the iPod generation. The labels, and sometimes the artists (who may not necessarily know the downfalls of their request), want their songs to POP from the speakers when in shuffle mode or added to a playlist, so the result is the volume on CD's gets louder and louder. Of course, this is at the sacrifice of the dynamics and definition of the original music. EMI are already in financial turmoil, and the negative reviews of their products are not going to do anything to help their sinking ship stay afloat.

Some artists go out of their way to ensure their CD's do not suffer from the pitfalls of the loudness war. Thomas Dolby posted a message during the remastering of his first two albums to inform concerned fans that he was going to ensure the dynamics of his music remained. The result was two stunning remasters of his classic albums.

Alan Wilder oversaw the remastering of the Depeche Mode back catalog, and as a result none of those albums were compressed, and most were completely satisfying to fans. If these labels are blasting their music for the sake of standing out on an iPod, then release a CD with proper dynamics, then turn up the music another 100 decibels for the MP3's that you make available on iTunes or other download sites. That way everyone wins. This overblown volume and distortion/destruction of music has got to stop.

UPDATE: EMI have recently responded to the loads of negative comments regarding these two reissues. The only thing they admit fault on was the damaged intro to 'Girls on Film'. They blame a damaged tape, but anyone with an ounce of simple home PC audio software experience can tell you a glitch like this can be fixed in seconds. What's worse is EMI mention nothing about the overblown volume, distortion, and generally terrible sound quality, and state they do not intend to rectify any of the problems. Funny, but I don't recall a single negative review about the sound quality of the original DD CD's from the 80's. It's pretty bad when a CD mastered 20 years ago sounds worlds better than a CD done today. Great job EMI. Just another hole in your already sinking ship.

reviewText:
A Tedious, Tiresome and Disappointing Continuation of Frisell's  Exploration of American Traditional / Public Radio / Folk / Sleep Music.
Enough Already Bill!! How About Some Interesting Music For a Change, Like you Made 10-20 Years Ago.

Bill Frisell was (note the past tense WAS) the most innovative jazz guitarist of the 1980's-90's.
He created his own trademark sound: a twangy, bending, echoey wash of color, making his own distinct wall of sound
on every recording of his and every recording that he guested on.

I was such a huge fan of Bill that I would seek out and purchase every album that he appeared on to hear his performance.

There were dozens of albums which he contributed to, putting his signature wall of sound on.
Seek out the albums "Power Tools," or Marc Johnson's "Bass Deisres" (1987) or the 1991 Live album
with Kermit Driscoll and Joey Baron to hear Frisell in a powerhouse performance.
The 1996 piece "Faith In You," from Marc Johnson's "The Sound of Summer Running" has a duo
between Frisell and Pat Metheny which is one of the most beautiful compositions I've ever heard.

Then around 1998 he decided he was going to move away from that eclectic fusion of sound.
His 1998 album "Gone Like a Train" opens with an exlposive fusion composition, then turns into a mush of uninspired improv.
That was the point he left the exciting guitar sounds and changed his career into experimental ad-lib American Folk Soundscapes.

Those of us like myself who purchased his next album "Good Dog Happy Man" were disappointed beyond belief
when the entire album was an uninspired, lifeless recording of Meditational Sleep Music, from beginning to end.

Most of us fans hoped that this was just a temporary venture for him. Instead, for 10 years now he increased his popularity
on National Public Radio and has released one album after another, sometimes 2 albums a year of this meandering slop.

The bottom line is folks, with "History Mystery,"  the MYSTERY is: What happened to this once admirable musical prodigy?
This release is 2 discs, 90 minutes of what I've described above. Incorporating some fine musicians for sure,
but frankly, wasting their time just sitting around playing a few notes throughout this dullness.
Despite the efforts that went into it, and the fact that this album was part of an NPR special & part of his concert tour,
Frisell's music in the last 10 years is so boring and dull that even those suffering sleep apnea and insomnia would need

reviewText:
(In regard to a certain someone else's comment, this review is not a "joke".  What IS a joke though is this album.  As much as I love Mike Rutherford for his brilliant contributions to Genesis, I'm not just going to hand him a 4 or 5 star review for any old thing he puts out.  And unfortunately, there's simply no getting around the fact that this album is terrible.)

Aside from Mike Rutherford's first solo album, 1980's "Smallcreep's Day" (which is very much resemblant of Genesis' "Duke"), he comes across as an almost completely different and nearly unrecognizable artist with his solo/ Mechanics projects compared to his contributions to the legendary Genesis. The main familiar element has tended to be Mike's rhythmically precise, looping guitar technique (I don't know how else to describe it). Mike & the Mechanics' music over the years has been relentlessly ultra-slick, ultra-contemporary pop-rock--with barely any detours at all, let alone interesting ones. Their albums generally have occasional bright spots, but are often exhausting, loaded with pedestrian songwriting, both musically & lyrically, & overproduction a-plenty. Anyone who thinks Phil Collins is a sellout who lead Genesis down the wrong path, or that his 2002 "Testify" album was lacking "real instruments" should get a good, ahem, "wake up call" from listening to "Rewired", a sad disaster of an album. "Rewired" was previously released in 2004, and now Rhino has given it a US release in September of 2005.  To put it a certain way, this is an album that makes the first Mike & the Mechanics album sound like "Abacab". Even on Phil's "Testify", he was clearly staying true to himself, making music that was homegrown, sincere, & largely satisfying. True, not every song on that album is a masterpiece, but there's solid songwriting, hooks, & TASTEFUL PRODUCTION to be found. The soulless ultra-'modern' production values that Mike embraces on this piece of dreck make him sound desperate. It doesn't make a lick of sense to me how any long-term Genesis fan can trash Phil's "Testify" (or any of his other solo albums for that matter) & proceed to shower praise on this album.

I don't know who's particularly to blame. The album was produced by Mike & Peter Van Hooke, but certainly Paul Carrack is no innocent bystander, even though this album sounds joltingly different from Carrack's solo work from the 2000s. Opposed to the first couple Mechanics albums where Carrack played the role of an outsider brought in to sing some leads, he's subsequently become a fully integrated member of the group. Here, they go as far as to deem this as a Mike + the Mechanics + Paul Carrack album on the cover, and he & Mike co-wrote every track on here (with others chipping in on certain tracks).

Listening to this album, I'm not sure what Mike is thinking... Is he desperately trying to strike it big commercially? Is he drinking some wine & having some fun with modern production stylings? Is he thinking that he's being innovative? Is he so burnt out that he doesn't know/ care what the hell he's doing? Based on the combination of songwriting & production, it sounds to me like an artist/ band, desparately trying to remain hip & contemporary, no matter how much it flaws the end product. In terms of songwriting, the album is quite familiar--songs that are supposed to be uplifting, yet are melodically limp & lyrically shallow (and on "The Perfect Child", gratingly lame-brained). The things that really make the album such an utter headache... First, not only are the tracks weak to start with, they're so bloated & go on way too long as if there was a law that they have to run at least 4 & 1/2 minutes long each (often, they're over 5). Second, they ran rampant here with techno/ electronica/ whatever "influences", filling up the album with grating sound textures & synthetic percussion that further suck the life out of the songs. It isn't simply because it sounds "modern" that I hate it--they did some respectable "updating" of their sound on the previous album, "M6"--it's because it sounds terrible; it's displeasing to listen to. You can just sense you're in trouble as soon as you hear that robot-style vocal effect on Carrack's voice on the opening song, "One Left Standing". It's not true that there isn't a single moment on the album with some promise--on another day, on another album, IN ANOTHER TIME, Mike could have perhaps put them to decent use, which is damning with faint praise indeed. This is Mike Rutherford here, a key member in one of the greatest bands of all time, Genesis.

It's rather scary to even think of where Mike & the Mechanics might head from here after this massively headache-inducing and disastrous attempt at staying contemporary and "hip". Don't even think about buying this album--it's a sad washout for Mike & The Mechanics.

reviewText:
"Fade", "It's Been a While", "Change", "Epiphany", "Suffer", "For You", "Outside", "Waste", and "Take It"...  These songs (9 out of the 13 on "Break the Cycle") all contain the word "feel" (and/or "felt" or "feeling").
DAY ONE:
I'm at a friend's house right now, and he's playing "Break the Cycle" by Staind.  That singer feels a lot.  So I infer that he is pretty complex.  If he "feels" on 9 out of 13 songs on this CD, and each one of these songs have a different premise (speak of different feelings), then there's a really good chance that at least one of those songs will relate closely to how I feel about certain things going on in my life.
DAY TWO:
A friend played some Creed for me today in his car; I had never really listened to it.  When this song "One" came on, my friend cranked up the volume.  That guy -my friend informed me that his last name is Stapp- "felt" something at least eight times in that one song.  Man, and I thought Staind were feelers.  This Stapp dude feels "angry" and feels "helpless" and feels "violent" and feels "alone" because he can't unify the world; I've felt all of those feelings at some time or another, but for all sorts of different reasons, so I guess I can relate to Stapp, too.
DAY THREE:
So I'm at a party, and notice that the first three bands -none of whom I have yet been introduced to (Linkin Park, Nickelback, and especially Puddle of Mudd [who "feels" on "Control", it sounds, to be "feeling" for no coherent reason])- blaring from the speakers all "felt" like crazy...  Just like Staind and Creed did.
After fleeing the drunken revelry, I started to wonder why all of these bands that pretty much sounded the same (singers with a hybrid voice of Eddie Vedder and Scott Weiland, and 4/4-beat, riffy music) all incorporated the word "feel" into their lyrics.  I started to think of these bands' motive.  When I arrived home, a dollar fell from my pocket as I was rummaging through my pockets for my house key.
It was at that point when everything culminated:
NOW:
When the word "feel" is mentioned in a song, people listen...  ESPECIALLY when that word is associated with turmoil.  Thus, the song has a greater chance to persuade a listener to buy the CD.  What will NEVER be heard from beloved Staind is any attempt of resolve.  'The world is a horrible place, that's just how it is, and I'm gonna vent my frustration and whine in my overused (but profitable) fake voice until the day I die.'  Why is this standpoint abused by modern rockers?  Because it sells like hotcakes, baby.  If a singer says, "I feel violent", it triggers a natural response mechanism; it's unavoidable -innate-, and the record conglomerates KNOW it.
Question Staind's integrity, folks.  I regret to inform you that you wouldn't hear this monotonous babble (musically, lyrically, and vocally) if the bands wouldn't have caught the record conglomerates' attention in the first place by selling their "product" to them.  These bands do not write lyrics and concoct their purposely-simplistic garage music to satisfy themselves emotionally; they do it because they want to live the American Dream: to be rock stars, and make a lot of money.

reviewText:
There is not one sound, one spark, one vocal turn of phrase on all of "Live It Up" that in any way distinguishes Lee DeWyze from the crowds of coffeehouse-ready, guitar-toting male musicians who have risen up and dominated the airwaves, for better or worse, this side of 2001.

This album is like a vending machine in any given office building. It has an assortment of quick-fix snacks that, while temporarily pleasing, are processed, unwholesome and leave you hungry - hungry for something better.

 Whether it is lead single "Sweet Serendipity" or the romance of "Brooklyn Bridge" or the title track, DeWyze's personality - if he has one - is absent from this recording. All the songs blend into a single, steady sound that at best provides background noise and at worst fogs the mind. It is a new, freshly released recording, yet it is already appropriate for bargain bins and grocery store intercoms.

The problem is not that DeWyze has no talent. In fact, the album might be more interesting if he didn't, but that's not his fault. It's simply that everything here is smoothed out and utterly seamless - faceless, powdered vanilla. That the direction of his sound was influenced by a bevy of hitmakers unleashed upon him following the conclusion of his "American Idol" duties is obvious.

There is still more, though. He sounds shockingly like someone else - perhaps John Mayer, perhaps Jack Johnson, perhaps Ray LaMontagne - but whoever it might be is not as important as the fact that his very essence - his voice and how he has been encouraged to use it - is inherently lacking in individuality. It certainly sounds as though he is deliberately invoking a pseudo-soulful, blue-eyed growl at some points and that requisite cool-as-cucumber slacker vibe at others. Not only does it sound contrived, but it doesn't sound good.

If the essence of 50 other young troubadours was boiled down to a sparkling spotlessness and then amalgamated into an eerie sheen, removing all idiosyncracies, the results would sound like "Live It Up." He checks all the boxes and hits all the right notes with the passion and personality of a flight attendant passing out peanuts to passengers. It is all business, and can be seen coming long in advance. That is not exciting. It is boring.

Listeners deserve better.

reviewText:
No no no no no no no.  This is a really offensive release- the epitome of the self-congratulating bloated rock star going through a mid-life crisis.  First of all, rather than a tribute to his new love interest, Laurie  Anderson, it comes off as a horribly insensitive kiss-off to his ex-wife  Sylvia (anyone remember "Heavenly Arms" off The Blue Mask?).  His  epitaph for Sterling Morrison, "Finish Line," seems really unfelt  and possibly irrelevant...you don't get any sense of pain or loss, nor does  it seem like a celebration of the life of a loved one.  He obviously spent  about as much time thinking up this song as he spent thinking about  Sterling in real life.
"Riptide," "Trade In," and  "Set the Twilight Reeling" are the evil triumvirate here, lacking  any kind of musical pleasure and consisting solely of lyrics that are meant  to puff up Lou's ego and put everyone else's down.  "Riptide" has  gotten better in concert, and it is about the only place on the album where  Lou does anything interesting with his guitar, but the whole "she's  out of her mind" and "what you gonna do with your emotions"  chorus just stink.  The histrionics at the end of the title track are  embarrassing.
"Hookywooky" was supposed to be some sort of  hit single, but nobody knows what the hell it's about.  "Egg  Cream" sort of succeeds on this level, but doesn't rock nearly enough  for a man who said this was supposed to be a "fun guitar album"  (he said this on MTV to Matt Pinfield, of all people).  Plus the album is  riddled with really boring, standard rock ballads and midtempo numbers that  never really go anywhere.
"The Adventurer" kind of picks things  up a bit (although it suffers from Lou's rythmic retardation: that  knee-clamped sort of farting sound also seen on "Mystic Child"),  and "The Proposition" is the only tune here that I actually like,  kind of slow and groovy and looking forward to the better follow up  "Ecstasy."  The Laurie influence is clearly visible.  "Sex  With Your Parents," while a bit obvious, is actually pretty funny and  entertaining, with Lou showing off his newly learned fingerpicking  technique.
Man, you're really best off skipping this one.  At least when  he was making bad records in the 70's they had a sort of  man-falling-apart-at-the-seams charm to them...this is just inexcusable.  And for someone who is supposedly renowned for his gearhead sensibilities,  the rock guitar just doesn't rock hard enough.  There's little variety to  the sounds and he's usually just overdubbing way to many rythm guitar  tracks.  The tour for this album consisted of just cranking everything up  so loud that the audience was pounded into a captive submission.  The  drummer was really kind of a second rate rock-star wannabe who ruined every  song with an unneccesary "big finish" that meant less everytime  he did it.  IF you must, get it for the only good recording of "Sex  with your parents," otherwise: keep away.

The album never really gets off the ground.
If anything, this is like one of those "rarities, B-sides" albums made up of rejected tracks that didn't even qualify for album fillers.
Having heard their previous release "Heaven or Last Vegas", I expected more.
I didn't even get "similar", just "much worse".
I bought this album when it came out, and try as I did to like it, to get into it, to find maybe 1 track that would somehow justify its existence in my collection, but none shone. None stood out. Just a long ride of gray upon gray with no light or color in sight.
The album ended up sold or traded in a used CD shop back in 1995.
I recently played the album again from a very popular webpage thinking that maybe I was too harsh, unfair, didn't really appreciate the album...
I have changed my mind about a few albums that I previously passed by or rejected.
Sadly, my impression from 22 years ago remains intact. A pity. I really wanted to like this album.
... and being a vinyl collector, the ridiculous price of $229- for this "rarity" is a big disappointment to anyone, even to Martin Shkreli, who would well deserve it.
If they ever remaster this album on vinyl - unlikely seeing how mediocre it is, but regardless - they'd have to price it very attractively for completists to shell out the bucks. Probably for a listen or two, then to be shelved.

reviewText:
I can still remember buying this album a few years ago, and then throwing it away about a few months later. I tried and I tried and I TRIED to be able to appreciate this album, but it was just getting too boring, too fast. More importantly, I am completely fed up with those people who call this music "metal" whereas it is really metalCORE, which, in essentials, is just hardcore punk with metal influence. That being said, I have now finally considered it a priority to throw in my two cents.

As I see it, Phil Labonte fails to convey an adequate amount of edge or angst, especially for music that some may consider to be "heavy" by any standards. When he is not merely screaming his lungs out like a toddler having a tantrum, he just sounds like nothing more than a boy-band singer. I would describe him as a louder version of Chester Bennington from Linkin Park. On top of that, the drumming and guitar work may be somewhat okay, but as much as others may be able to appreciate it, I myself cannot help but feel as though it does not carry the emotion of the songs nearly as much as it could. Simply put, I just find the music on this album, as well as the band themselves to be much too simplistic for my liking, but someone has to love it, and I have no problem with that.

Do not get me wrong, I am not criticizing this band for the fact that they are "not real metal," but for the sole fact that I bought this album, gave it a try, and decided that it does not do anything for me. Heck, there are bands that I enjoy that are not metal, despite being called "metal" by a number of their fans, i.e. Godsmack, Disturbed or Mushroomhead. ATR are what they are, and if you like them, then who am I to tell you not to like them, or the metalcore genre in general? Heck, I bet anything that this band is not even trying to be an actual metal band. Do I have a problem with that? No! I just find that their style does nothing for me. Simple as that. Personally, I much prefer bands like Dark Tranquillity, Insomnium, Firewind, Sonata Arctica or Mindwarp Chamber to give but a few of so many examples.

To the fans of this band - I think it is awesome that you like this band and enjoy their music, but DO NOT proclaim that they are actual metal, because they are not. For those of you who enjoy ATR, but already know enough to know what is metal and what is not, you have my fullest respect. Thank you all for your understanding. PEACE! \m/\m/

reviewText:
The "herd mentality" of the human race (especially the American music-buyer) never ceases to amaze me. I find it very difficult to believe the number of people who bought this CD and actually like it. (Of course, I think the truth of the matter is that Madonna KNOWS she has established such a strong fan base, that "whatever" she happens to put out will still go multi-platinum because her fan base is made up of mindless lambs who will flock to the record stores, no matter what [garbage] she releases.) There is no way this CD can be considered excellent, good--or even mediocre. If this CD had been released by anyone else in the music industry, it would have never even broke the Top 100. Yes, it looks like Madonna's fans have been afflicted with the same disease as Mariah's fans--they will buy anything and everything she records--no matter how good or bad it is.
People, people.... There is so much REAL music out there--most of which never even approaches the Top 100 or Top 40. It is a shame that good quality music continually gets overshadowed by the mindless mentality of the "human herd" who rely on their radio to define what is "good music".  I truly believe that Madonna could record the blandest version of "Three Blind Mice", and her fan base would make it a #1 hit. Wake up, people. There IS good music out there, if you would only take the time and initiative to find it.
One reviewer wrote if this album was as bad as people claim it to be, Madonna would never have released it, since she has millions.  Are you for real?  I think Madonna has gone way beyond the point of having to do ANYTHING (singing, touring, acting, etc.) for money.  Madonna released this CD (whose only listenable song is "Music") as an attempt to remain mainstream.
Do any of her fans ever wonder why Madonna continually hop-scotches from producer to producer with each new CD?  It is simple: she hears the "sound du joir", usually on European radio, and then hires the "producer du jour" to produce her CD.  Hence, her sound always sounds "mainstream" because of the PRODUCERS--not because of anything SHE has done.  As for her songwriting, another question: Why do each of her songs list 5-7 writers--and oh, by the way, one of the writers always happens to be "Madonna"?
Wouldn't the TRUE test of Madonna's "genius" be if she were to write and produce every song on just ONE of her CDs?  When Madonna finally does that, THEN maybe I will be impressed with her.  Until then, let's all acknowledge reality: Madonna's true genius lies in her ability to MARKET herself--and not in her ability to "create" music.

This review is NOT about the music itself, but of the quality of the vinyl pressing that it came on. I enjoy this album, however, this pressing is near unlistenable. The amount of distortion is horrendous. This is nearly all throughout the entire album and not just in the 'inner grooves'. One channel is louder than the other the entire time. This is not an issue of cartridge alignment, as I do not experience this with any other records. Nor is it an issue of static build-up or a dirty record. I cleaned this record multiple times and used an anti-static brush and an anti-static turntable mat and played this record through enough times to the point where all of the static that the record came with was dissipated.

Bottom line: if you're looking for a good vinyl press for this album, think twice before buying this. I've had very bad luck with mine in terms of sound quality. It's NOT warped at all. it's a beautiful, 180 gram black vinyl. However, the sound quality is abominable.

reviewText:
Yes, they have a new album!
I was absolutely thrilled when I found out from this wonderful website that S Club 7 is BACK! Day by day, I waited for the release of the album in Singapore. Great hits like "Never had a dream come true", "Two in a million" and the ever so irritatingly uplifting song "Reach" were all in this album. Then, one day it was released in Singapore... Zooom, I made a beeline for my local cd-store and previewed the album... You may call me capricious, but a general malaise befall on me. I was overwhelmed with chagrin!
Here's some salient and egregious points that one shouldn't ignore:
Track 2: Natural
This song really puts me off. The inter-weaving melodies clashes into a turbid imbroglio especially in the chorus, mellifluous is definitely not the word to describe it. And if you didn't realise, there is a tune in the melody that sounds exactly like Gabriel Faure's Pavanne...
Track 5: Best Friend
One song that really don't fit into the album. The rap is simply plebeian and uncatchy, in my opinion, it's a paragon of charlatan.
The ballads in the album:
Featuring Track 3, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 ,13
After a while, the unison singing supported by a lead singer starts to get really monotonous. I'm sure anyone with a tinge of sagacity will suffer from ennui after hearing it for some time. These are songs that will never mollify you to a reverie. And not to forgetting to comment, the mid-range voices reminds me of Britney Spears...
The Upbeat Songs:
Featuring Track 1, 4, 7,
Unison singing again... They can be pretty galling to one's ears especially with asinine and peurile lyrics.
If you really think S Club 7 is good, you should really consider the group, Steps. They sing in parts and all three girls have the vocal power to become solo singers! Well, unless you don't give a damn, and just think their unison singing (like it requires much effort!) is great and prefer to live in oblivion, then be my guest, buy this album, and maybe write a fulsome review.
Oh, by the way, I didn't walk out of the store empty-handed... I had another CD in my hands:
Buzz by Steps

reviewText: What the..... Kreator, what happened here guys?  I've always loved this band but from 1992-1999 they seemed to be struggling to find an audience.  Renewal (1992) was a huge step in a new direction and I actually loved this album, then they followed that up in 1995 with Cause For Conflict, a return to their thrashier style but still retaining some of the industrial elements from Renewal.  In 1997 they released Outcast - a more straightforward metal effort but still a solid album.  Then in 1999 - still apparently confused as to which direction they should go, they unleashed this travesty of a record.  I don't know who they were trying to appeal to with this one, the goth/vampire/emo-boy crowd?  I didn't understand this album and that doesn't bother me one bit.  Thank goodness they got their act together in 2001 with Violent Revolution and have seemed to stay on track ever since.  Endorama is better off forgotten.

reviewText:
The original Black Aria is the best album of its type ever recorded, a true epic, symphonic, atmospheric masterpiece loaded with interesting motifs and original sounds. That album is priceless; it is a religious experience to any with the spirit to hear its wonders.

Black Aria II is nothing like it. I knew it probably was going to be pretty bad when I saw the wretched cover art, but I never could have expected anything this pitiful. This record is simply a travesty that should never have been released. It is impossible that an artist of Glenn Danzig's greatness could feel proud of such an effort as this. Honestly, this isn't even music. An intelligent child with a Casio could beat this. That's not an exaggeration. There are no musical ideas on this album at all. Every track just repeats the same absurdly simple sequence of notes or noises over and over and over for a few minutes, and the sound is nothing but third-rate synth darkwave of the kind Mortiis or Dargaard do, only they do it much, much better. This isn't just bad or boring, it is non-music. It wouldn't even do as the background music for a low-budget computer game. However bad you can imagine this being, it is even worse when you actually hear it.

Those who respect (and in my case adore) his former works, please don't pollute your ears and ruin your good memories by listening to this thing...

Looking at Nevermind on a musical level, it still doesn't hold up. Nevermind is hyped for how "revolutionary" it is, but is it anything special? No. I'm now reading about how Cobain is supposedly Generation X's equivalent of John Lennon. I am lumped into the generation branded "X", and Kurt Cobain is not my John Lennon. Lennon is my Lennon. He is truly a legend because he left a legacy of love and freedom; Kurt Cobain is the polar opposite of him, so there is no room for comparison. Cobain professed his hatred for those not like him (he despised all athletes just because he had a few bad experiences with some in school). Cobain was also not for love and freedom, because he was bound by the selfishness and shackles of heroin addiction.
Look at these "profound" lyrics, and have a good laugh (yes, they are the actual words straight from Cobain's pen: "I'm on a plane/I can't complain" (from On a Plain), "I got my diddly spayed" (Beeswax), "You give, you give, you get/You get to me" (Pen Cap Chew), and "Little men eat and run/Poke your ass for the fun" (from Pay to Play). Now that you're done rolling on the floor, now how many of you can honestly claim Cobain is Lennon-esque? I recommend anything by Lennon and the Beatles instead of Nirvana. But if you're looking for straight out-and-out rock mastery, I will say with high regard to go for Jimi Hendrix, the god of the guitar. I'm sure Jimi is up in heaven rocking out, having a good old time in a psychedelic haze, while Cobain is stuck in the bowels of hell... with Smells like Teen Spirit blaring and mocking him for eternity.

reviewText:
Both the music on the four discs in this collection and the excellent hardback book about the 60s San Francisco music scene that the discs come with deserve five stars, no question.  The music is everything from early cuts and big hits by well-known Bay-area artists (the Airplane, the Dead, Janis Joplin, Santana) to little-known but real gems by bands who didn't have long careers (Johnny Was A Good Boy by The Mystery Trend, Foolish Woman by The Oxford Circle).  The book is very well written, with commentary on each of the songs and outstanding photography.  A lot of thought went into compiling this collection.

But how could the Rhino label, usually a supplier of great music, have been foolish enough to think it was a good idea to put the CDs in bare cardboard slots at the back of the book?

I'm now on my second copy of this collection.  With the first one, two of the four discs had such bad abrasions from the cardboard slots that they didn't play properly.  I returned that set to a local retailer for a refund.

Then, I decided to try buying the collection from Amazon, even though the price was higher, thinking that I might have better luck.  No dice.  Again, the same two discs (1 and 3, because of the way the carboard slots are constructed) have bad abrasions.  I'll try listening to them to see if they play, but if they don't, I'll be returning the set to Amazon for a refund and give up on this collection altogether.  If they do play, I'll be storing the discs in jewel cases to protect them properly, rather than returning them to Rhino's poorly designed holders.

For people like me (and other reviewers here) who are stuck with damaged discs, Rhino should make replacements available -- it would probably be cheaper for them than having all of us simply return the whole set for a refund.

I hate the prospect of not having this collection, because it does contain a lot of great music and the book is really interesting.  So I hope the discs will play properly this second time.

But if the discs are again messed up -- and the visible abrasions suggest that possibility -- this set is going back to Amazon, and I'll be staying away from future Rhino sets unless the discs are packaged to protect them from damage.

Shape up, Rhino!!  Your "clever" packaging is undermining the outstanding content of your collections.

As many people may know by now, [...] when a security specialist found out that a recently purchased CD (Van Zant: Get Right With The Man) from Sony music not only installed DRM software (digital rights management, to limit and outright prevent copying music to certain devices), but it did so in such a sneaky way that it hid itself entirely from Windows, and opened the system up to security issues such as viruses.

This CD has the same copyright protection, called XCP. When installed, Sony hijacks your computer and installs custom software which:

1) Hides itself entirely from Windows by installing as a rootkit
2) Hides itself in such a manner that any files begining with $sys$ are also hidden. For example, if you install the XCP copy protection software on your machine, and rename "document.doc" to "$sys$document.doc" it then becomes invivisble to you forever.
3) Installs its own custom CD-Rom drivers to hijack your system. It also sneakily names these drivers "Plug and Play Device Manager" to seem as if it's a part of Windows. Trying to delete these drivers manually will disable your CD-Rom drive entirely.
4) Offers no uninstall option until you manually contact Sony

As of my writing this review,[...] claims they will "re-evaluate" this copyright protection software on their CDs in the future.

In the meantime, a virus is currently running wild, which names itself begining with $sys$ in an attempt to hide from the user and virus scanners.

[...]
This is your music. You purchased it, and they should not have any right to dictate how you can use it, let alone install software which compromises your system security.

This is one of the CDs with Sony's XCP copyright protection software on it, and as a result, you should not buy it to send a message to Sony that this will NOT be tolerated in the future.

reviewText: Here's a test for anyone Bruckner-wise: what do you think of this performance? The Berlin Philharmonic is superlative. The Teldec sound is excellent. There is no impatience from the podium. All well and good - yes? This is a stinker. There are merits to Barenboim's second Bruckner cycle (9, 5, & 1) but this ain't one of them. There's no greater demonstration in discography that mere animation is not synonymous with life, or to quote the maxim from Mahler: the most important thing about music is not the notes. Who knows whether Barenboim was trying to ape Furtwangler on the night. I hope not: the latter's good name should not be associated with this vacuity. For all the surface excellence, it's a genuine `swing and miss'. The opening movement makes all the right gestures but fails to connect with anything (the coda is as mystical as a bucket of fried chicken from Colonel Sanders). The adagio is the ground-zero of this performance: twenty five minutes or so of empty rhetoric. The final two movements are bouncy enough - I suppose. I would love to organise a `Dr Frankenstein Bake-Off' between Barenboim and Maazel in the Bruckner 7th. Each of them would be provided with an Igor (the Berlin Philharmonic or the Bavarian Radio Symphony Orchestra - though LM has called upon both in his necrophillic traversals  &Bruckner: Symphony No. 7). Assume that the sound engineers step up to the plate in both instances. I expect Maazel would prevail on the day as his rival can at least convey mere energy if nothing else. Whatever. Any of the three recordings should come with bolts on the sides of the cases to forewarn the public. Avaunt - thou unholy cadaver!

reviewText:
I could have weeded or painted the downpipes. The bathroom needed to be cleaned but it was serenely ignored. Prodigally, I sat down with this set and trifled away a few hours.

One could almost indict Sir Simon on a charge of plagiarism. He has clearly set out to imitate the likes of Zinman and Harnoncourt - such as they are - with no ideas of his own. After all, he has never displayed any sort of affinity with Beethoven, as evidenced by his ho-hum survey of the piano concertos. And this cycle is indubitably the VPO's blandest excursion in Beethoven - how they must have slunk away afterwards.

Here, the sleek, homogenised, emasculated performances of Symphonies One to Four could almost be labeled a 'Salute to Maestro Zinman', albeit with less inner conviction or insight. Five is devoid of genuine grunt for all the blare of the brass. The Sixth is the most cadaverous rendition in the market; it is actually the set's claim to fame: what other Pastoral brings to mind Death Valley? Seven and Eight are the equivalent of low-fat yoghurt and equally as memorable. Nine is less worse - at least it has a sense of occasion - but it does not trouble the front-runners in this domain. Sir Simon's incessant point-making is ruinous.

This endeavour begs a wider question: what was EMI trying to achieve here in squandering its resources, meagre as they are nowadays, on an endeavour of this scale? It was never going to challenge the frontrunners. At best it was a cynical marketing exercise. And now Warner, in its wisdom. has re-released it . . . .

Sir Simon should cloister his tendancies to record Beethoven for a decade or so; he should ruminate, reflect and perhaps fall to his knees. Self-flagellations and pious ejaculations might be in order. Perhaps then, and only then, will he have something worthwhile to say, Beethoven-wise, to the world.

Until then, behold the Flight of the Uber-Turkeys.

reviewText:
Others have smashed this travesty of interpretation (and failure of nerve) and I'd like to get in on the beat down. The Chamber Orchestra of Europe is crisp and professional as expected. But YNS brings nothing to the table but the usual HIP mannerisms, and so the result is a set of Schumann symphonies that will leave you cold.

With Schumann, it's go big or go home. The best readings reach for the cosmos. This is not salon music, but don't tell that to the doyens of the Gramophone, who loved this weak stuff. The canard that Schumann's symphonies need to be slimmed down is obviously a driving factor here - YNS has a string section of 9,9,6,5,4 - so no wonder there is no impact in the tuttis, and RS's gorgeous string textures are reduced to colorless scratchings. All color and emotion is gone.

Brass and timpani overpower everything - although the timpani manage to sound both too intrusive and too punchy and - there is no resonance. The opening bars of the Spring Symphony are almost comic in their miniaturization of this epic music. It's enough to make you set yourself on fire.

This is not to say that Schumann can only be played one way - artists as different as Karajan, Szell, Sawallisch, Levine, Kubelik, and Bernstein have much to say in these symphonies. But all of these greats understood that with RS, you have to dig deep. Mere technical proficiency is near worthless without some soul.

Don't waste your time with these weak, earthbound readings when the catalogue is otherwise overflowing with great interpretations.

reviewText:
Everyone's favorite burlesque troupe and leather corset supporters return to the pop spotlight with second album, the rather cockily titled Doll Domination. It's not clear what arena of the pop world they are trying to dominate, as few can claim to be as overtly skanky since Christina Aguilera's "dirrty" days and none are as completely and totally manufactured as the Dolls (although Danity Kane comes to mind), who branched out from stripping in a series of calculated moves to become famous that included a reality show, a Vegas show, and some classy clothing.

Doll Domination immediately plays its best hand off the bat with lead single "When I Grow Up," an electro-pop song about vapidity that signifies everything that is wrong with the Dolls' music and sounds eerily similar to Basement Jaxx's far superior 2003 track "Plug It In.". Bouncy synth lines and thudding bass provided by A-list producer? Check. Voices Auto-Tuned to perfection? Check. Lyrics about being famous and rich that include such Hilton-esque lines as "you can talk about me / `cause I'm a hot topic"? Check. Sure, it's catchy, but if you're looking for any sort of depth or anything more than a guilty pleasure, you're not going to get it here.

Unbelievably, the album continues for fifteen (!) more songs, all of them marking a low point in the 2008 music year and none of them approaching the single marketability of "When I Grow Up." Snoop Dogg's entirely appropriate guest spot on "Bottle Pop" (after all, he did host a few Girls Gone Wild) is one of the weaker ones of his career to say the least, and the track's lackluster chorus deflate any energy he might have afforded them. Although the Dolls didn't hold back on production, which benefits from help by Timbaland and Darkchild, or guest spots from R. Kelly, Ne-Yo, and Missy Elliot, no amount of help is able to give the Dolls any sort of identity separate from the obvious "models playing as singers."  Main singer Nicole Scherzinger's vocals come off as vanilla diva pop, and while the beats are definitely club-ready, there is nothing mind-blowing enough here to qualify the Pussycat Dolls as anything more than artificial pop stars propped up by an industry desperate to make a buck.

While "The Fame Monster" was a breath of fresh air to a pop/rock field which had become stagnant, "Born This Way" is stagnant.  It is over-produced, each track actually sounds identical to the next and the imaginative edge which Ms. GaGa experienced and defined in her first recording is seriously lacking in this attempt. It seems that her message, while being blunt as always (which is fine) is so in your face that it touches no one. The album is dull, unimaginative and boring. GaGa is a talent, there is no doubt about that.  What she needed to do is pour more of her talent into this album and less into her social causes and her meat dress.  A sad second release.

reviewText:
I'm reviewing the 2016 180g remaster of this great, great album.

This review was a tough call.  I'd give the content five stars in a heartbeat.  One of the greatest rock albums of all time -- challenging in scope, but endlessly rewarding to those who choose to pay attention.  But a Joe Reagoso-remastered version rushed out just before a competitor is about to release what could be adefinitive version?  It's lucky to get one star.

Here's my big issue:  The timing of this release seems like a cynical attempt to cash in on Atlantic's back catalog before Panegyric's Steven-Wilson remastered Blu-ray Audio / SACD / CD packages ship in October. If that final release in Panegyric's Yes series is as jaw-dropping as the previous four, anybody who buys this new 180g LP may find themselves wishing they had held out just a few months longer for the real deal.

I understand that vinyl aficionados may prefer a 180g LP over any new-fangled hirez digital disc, and as a long-time audiophile and vinyl evangelist, I respect that.  But even I had to shake my head at the incredible sonics offered by Wilson's first four Yes remixes, even in comparison to the superb Steven Hoffman remasterings.  The Panegyric packages also provide generous helpings of truly listenable bonus features, including needledrops of the original vinyl LPs and related singles and extra audio CDs of the remixed material.

But what may be the biggest dealbreaker for me is that this 180g vinyl (if info at other sites is correct) was remastered by the infamous Joe Reagoso of Friday Records, a guy notorious for releasing 180g vinyl created from digital "masters" and refusing to reply to questions from the press about his mastering methods or sources.  Buying a Friday Records release is always a crap shoot, but if you want somebody with a track record, Wilson and Hoffman are known quantities who consistently produce stunning work.

According to the Amazon page, the Panegyric version will ship in October & is available for pre-order.  Details are sparse but IMO, that may be the last copy of TFTO that any of us will ever need.

... or 45 minutes, anyway. What happens when the LEAST talented band member becomes the primary creative force? In this case, 50-year-old Mike Love tries to trade off of the band's stereotypical image of teenage summer hedonists to come up with the band's last, and worst, studio album. It's an obvious attempt to create an album-length "Kokomo" - the same mechanical production (courtesy of Terry Melcher, substituting for the totally absent Brian Wilson) and cheesy "fun in the sun" lyrics (thanks, Mike). Even the vocal harmonies sound sterile.

The album is such a lame, immature and phony affair, with zero artistic merit. The new Love/Melcher songs have a little bit of everything, from bad social commentary and egotism (title track) to the worst rapping from a white man that's ever been recorded ("Summer of Love"). The oldies remakes (including two Beach Boys oldies, one featuring touring drummer/"Full House" star John Stamos -- ugh!) are pretty appalling, for the most part. Most dismaying is the great Carl Wilson reduced to a clumsy "Walking in the Sand". Depressing.

The single, a cover of Sly Stone's "Hot Fun in the Summertime", actually works as a pleasant, low-key affair. And Al Jardine's strong chorus vocal on "Strange Things Happen" raises the song to tolerable levels. But that's about it. A pathetic end to the group's recording career.

The album was so bad that Brother Records couldn't find a major label to distribute it in the U.S.A. It didn't stay in print long as a result, so any copies left now fetch hefty collector's prices. Don't be fooled, though! In this case, collectability value is inversely proportional to musical value. Beach Boys completists need only apply,and even they will be saddened by this mess.

reviewText:
I'd love to buy Neil Diamond's "12 Songs," but I can't.

It's not because I don't have the cash or lack access to a record shop. Surely, I can go to any store and, under different circumstances, pick up a copy if I want to.

The problem is that the CD is loaded with copy-protection software. Over the last year, I've bitten my tongue in my reviews about Sony/BMG CDs loaded with a program that prevents the listener from ripping the music directly onto iTunes. But when I saw that "content protected" logo on Neil's CD, I said enough is enough. The last straw finally broke this camel's back. Sure, I could download a digital copy off iTunes, but, as a music collector, I like to own physical CDs which contain liner notes, production credits, and lyrics. You can't effectively review the music unless you have these three important elements. What's more, recent reports have revealed that these CDs contain a form of spyware that relays to Sony via the internet what music you're listening to, when, and how often. This is a serious privacy concern that should worry all music listeners. I had the misfortune of loading this trojan on my PC, and after scanning my system numerous times, I still can't remove it.

Sony/BMG should be ashamed of itself for alienating and inconveniencing its consumers. Technology should be embraced to attract consumers, not discourage them. Copy protection is a self-defeating practice that spooks the very market the music industry wants to grow. There has to be a more sensible alternative for fighting piracy.

"12 Songs" has been getting stellar reviews. Too bad I can't write one of them.

reviewText:
What a tub of lard! I don't see how anyone could listen to this record with pleasure. It is an assault on all which faithful musicians and composers hold dear to them. Just take a look at the score while you're listening to this music, and you'll see my point. For starters, this is one of the longest performances of Beethoven's 9th on record. The first movement is 18 minutes long, and the 2nd almost 11 with a repeat omitted. The third movement is an astounding 20 minutes long. Bernstein takes this literally at half tempo, as he always does with important adagio movements that have "much to exploit." And then comes the big finale - 28 and a half minutes. All told - a 78 minute long symphony. Average performances clock in at about 70 minutes; faster performances which follow Beethoven's metronome markings are about 60 minutes long. So, Bernstein was "just a little slow", eh? Sure. Two minutes longer and Deutsche Grammophon would've had to market this performance using two CDs. (And what a pity for them. They would have made a killing off of it for sure.)
  That's just the tip of the iceburg. Rhythmic intensity and accuracy are thrown completely out of the window. Everything is blunted to a fault. Bernstein's pickup orchestra, some of the best musicians from the best orchestras in the world, lose their footing because they are not used to beating Beethoven about the head as Bernstein has them do here. There are numerous mistakes - some are noticeable, some are more hidden. These folks do not play as an ensemble, and who would expect them to, with all the different styles present? One might expect that Bernstein, faced with this dilemma, might be sensible enough to give them some direction as to how to articulate similarly - or at all for that matter. Not the case here. He just trusts that everyone will understand how things go, attempting to hammer out something resembling a phrase through sheer force of will. The orchestra responds with careless and sloppy playing. Harmonic progressions are lost amidst a sea of angry robotic ostinatos. There is no shape or balance to the music. The poetry is gone. Bernstein gesticulates and says, "Here you go, be inspired," but they don't know how. On the rare occasion that a bit of unique and interesting music is made, it is completely out of context and of a character not suited to this symphony.
  Another side effect of lousy direction is one of the most complete structural collapses in the history of the 9th (how fitting, considering what is being commemorated here). Bernstein's failure to acknowledge this symphony as more than just a bunch of spliced 2-measure character pieces wreaks havoc on the musicality. There is no forward drive, no anticipation of the next musical idea that blooms from the previous one. There is no continuity. The fire dies. "Oh, but wait!" the other reviewers would say. "There is much fire in these performances! Just listen to the climaxes! Heavens, what energy!" Well, Bernstein inciting his musicians to play extremely loudly does not equate with a real energetic performance. A string quartet could play with more intensity than this lost group. Bernstein doesn't stoke up the fire, but instead sears us in the back with a hot branding iron.
  This recording can be summed up as being retrograde. Instead of setting free emotions and thoughts of joy and freedom, this performance inhibits them. I'm not sure how the Berlin audience could get through the concert without crying from sheer boredom and irritation. I see no joy here, only a languid, aggravating and oppressive mish-mash of bad execution and bad interpretation. You may certainly buy this because of the occasion, but what is the point of celebrating if the music itself won't even let you do that? Don't waste your time on this.

reviewText:
Before you hit the 'no' button on "was this review helpful ?", let me say up front that my review is based entirely on the *sound quality* of this set. It does not reflect the actual music itself, which has been described in detail in many other reviews here.

If you care about the sound of these songs, please be warned that the remastering job was horrendous. These songs have been remastered using a progam called No-Noise (or a similarly-like program) which basically acts as a Dolby system like we used to find on analog casettes. The life has been sucked out these recordings and they sound very compressed and quite "digital". If you want to hear this for yourself, please compare any song (try "In My Room" for example) from this set to the older 'Endles Summer' compilation disc. When the vocals enter on the older set, they sound rich, full, warm, etc. The same vocals on this set have zero impact - they are flat, cold, sterile, and lacking any sense of dynamics whatsoever. There is no comparison. The dynamics that are found on the older and frankly superior-sounding set are gone. There is no more warmth or excitement left in this newer set. It is a shame, since there is wonderful music here. The problem with noise reduction programs such as No-Noise is that when engineers try to remove the hiss from these older recordings, this hiss or "line noise" cannot effectively removed without affecting the entire signal. Some engineers DO take caution not to overdo this process, but on this recording it has been way overused - and consequently ruining this collection sonically.

I post this because I work hard for my $$$ and when the recording industry charges this amount of money for a set of music that they want us to believe is SUPERIOR sounding due to the fact that it is newly remastered, it is a crime. This is a poor remastering job and the public ought to be aware of it.

If sound quality does not interest you, then by all means go ahead and enjoy this set. But if you are a bit hesitant, please try to hear a friends copy to decide for yourself if 'Good Vibrations' is worth the $$$.

I hope this helps. I will never sell my 'Endless Summer' disc as it is sonically superior to this set in every musical aspect.

Not much then, even less now.  Bach's bellowing, tuneless howl still screeching to a blood-curdling degree, he softens up on insipid ballads (e.g.  `By Your Side', whose chorus is a near-note-for-note melodic rip-off of his own `I Remember You') and laughably attempts a hardcore hierarchy he'll never live to see (`American Metalhead', `Negative Light').  His inherent theatre queen is still prevalent in his more cowed vocals; it was the stage, after all (surrounded by those `faqs' he thought would end up dead) where Bach lingered for most of the past decade after his band mates fired him. Some might call this The Return Of Axl, but Rose's wheezing vocal hiccups on the few cuts he's featured on are barely recognizable amidst the cacophonous muck `n mire - it's astonishing how Rose's voice was once the force of nature it was.  Hmm, it makes me think what Bach has over Rose to blackmail him to this extent.  My grade: C-

She's physically attractive, she's related to someone with lots of money and fame (although I've never heard of the guy), and she plays music that won't offend anyone.  A load of Grammys for that?  Wow, our music industry is really desperate!
Now granted, Norah has more to offer than Britney Spears or Eminem, but that's basically saying she actually has an electron worth of talent. This is music for elevators, fancy restaurants, dentist's offices, and maybe even massage parlors, but if you try to play this in your car, you're going to create a traffic hazard because there is nothing that will put you to sleep faster.  This genre of music (not sure what it is exactly) is boring and bland by nature, and there's not a whole lot you can do with it, so Norah doesn't stand out in it.  She got her voice heard on MTV, and they patronized her, so everyone in America wants to own a Norah Jones CD now.
I hate to go all-out to bash an artist who has good intentions, but I really have a problem with all the positive attention Norah gets while countless talented artists get left in the dust. But there are ignorant people out there who say that Norah Jones is the only respectable artist in the entirety of the music industry.
