Okay, first of all, let me start by stating that I am not a Korn fan, at least not since the first album which was good.  I am a music fan, collector, and historian and this is one of the worst ideas in music that was ever conceived, and not only that, but the fact that a musician the likes of Robert Smith would even think about appearing on this makes me lose what little respect that I had left for him.
For those that are unaware, Korn is the band that gave birth to the mid to late 90's aggro rock craze, brought us the fad of whining about our parents to distorted guitars, a rocker wearing a jogging suit, and down-tuned so far that all you hear is deep rumbles of guitars and a clicking sound out of the bass.
Someone thought it would be a great idea to rip away all of the distortion so we can really hear what they sound like.  Now we, the haters of this band, have real evidence to the fact that their riffs are weak at best, they wrote a total of two drum beats that appear on all of their albums, and Jonathan Davis cannot sing or write a good lyrics for the life of him.
I did get this album (Though I did not Korn my money) just because someone had to preserve this for history's sake.
I know Mtv has been horrible for a long time, but the Unplugged concerts were usually pretty good.  This is the worst exception and quite possibly the lowest point for Mtv (which is saying a lot).
DO NOT BUY THIS ALBUM.  DO NOT MAKE PEOPLE THINK THAT THIS IS A GOOD IDEA!
If you do, the next thing that Mtv will be trying to force feed us will be Slipknot unplugged or Limp Bizkit unplugged or any of the horrible musicians they play on their station in this stripped-down fashion.

reviewText: Ever since Reed took to talking instead of singing to music back in the early eighties, his work has been inconsistent at best.  The style works well on some material, particularly the songs that were intended for that  style.  On this album Reed applies his new method indiscriminately,  including a selection of 70's tunes on the songlist. I suppose the point  was to reinvent both his past work and to make it more 'contemporary.'  The  result is enough to leave you aghast.  "Coney Island Baby,"  "Vicious," "The Kids" and other oldies are cruelly  betrayed in spirit and form. Listening to these versions, you would have a  hard time persuading the uninitiated that they were once good songs.  Without inflections of melody, Reed simply chatters flatly and drowningly  while the music jangles pointlessly along in the background.  Whatever  vestige of beauty might be left after this butchering job is left  completely to the listener's imagination.  Upon listening to this album I  was forced to pull out the old versions and confirm I wasn't having a bad  dream. If Reed dislikes his past and  his old material so much, he should  refrain from bringing it up altogether -- it makes him look worse than his  past ever did.

reviewText:
A complete snoozefest of an album that doesn't have it's own voice or anything interesting to offer, it's sorely lacking those classic Tears For Fears vibes. The song Sowing The Seeds of Love (from the album The Seeds Of Love) was an interesting diversion but it should've been a one off. With this album it's like Beatles overload, it's just too much and I don't care for it at all. It's a shame that this shoddy project was the album that would bring the duo back together again, because despite the hype there's not really anything worthwhile going on here. I'm not seeing how people can rate this 5 stars, it's very generic, safe, and doesn't approach the greatness of their first three albums.

Even Secret World (which everyone says is a great song) isn't that good, trust me. It's missing that originality and uniqueness that made me fall in love with this group in the first place. The mix of the album is poor as well, there's no depth or richness to it. The album sounds like you're listening to it under a pillow, it's muffled and dull. Take the album The Seeds Of Love (which has amazing production) up against this and this record gets smoked, it's not even close. Now obviously I never expected this to reach the heights of their classics but this is really a pretty poor album even by modest standards, both musically and lyrically. I think it's fair to judge it as a Tears For Fears album, and as such it's a big failure and letdown, very disappointed. Maybe you'll dig it if you're a big Beatles fan or want something to fall asleep to because everything about this album is so pretend and non engaging that the only way to enjoy it would be to view it as an oddity and hear how to make a boring, pretentious album masquerading as "art." I don't know, not for me. Easily takes the top spot for the worst Tears For Fears has ever done.

reviewText:
Folks, the TERRIBLE cheap looking cover art tells you everything you need to know about the wretched Ashlee Simpson and her pathetic third album, Bittersweet World.

The merits of the album are best graded on the skills of the artist to whom it is credited.  Ashlee Simpson is essentially a singer and lyricist, and one who wouldn't have a recording deal if it hadn't been brokered by her Svengali father, former minister Joseph Simpson.  If one talent-deficient daughter can manage a career in entertainent, why can't another one?  But let's try to focus on the content of the album.

Is Simpson a good singer?  One look at her "performance" on Saturday Night Live a few years back, where she displayed her remarkable lip-syncing ability, and her ill-advised attempt at actually singing at the following year's Orange Bowl which was met by catcalls, would indicate that she is not.

You're probably thinking that she must compensate in the lyrics department, right?  Well, song titles like "Boys", "Little Miss Obsessive", "Ragdoll" and "Hot Stuff" should indicate otherwise.  Here's some lyrics from "Outta My Head (Ay Ya Ya)": "And all I hear is ay ya ya ya ya / You're talking way to much / I can't even hear me now / All this noise is messin' with my head".  And how about this brilliance from "Rule Breaker": "Got Tattoos / We gonna smash things / And we like to scream things / Ahhhhhhhh / You don't want no problems / You ain't got no beef / Ahhhhhhhh ... I don't wanna fight, tonight (Hey hey!) / But I ain't goin' home for no one".

The producers do the best they could working under these circumstances, but they can't put the Midas touch on the audio manure that is Bittersweet World.  Songs like "Outta My Head" serve little purpose other than reminding the listener that Missing Persons and Berlin were far superior to Ashlee Simpson's pale imitation of that sound.

And how about the way Ashlee Simpson CONVENIENTLY announced in the past week that she is now engaged AND pregnant?  That didn't have ANYTHING to do with the fact that she had an album coming out, right?  Couple that with the decrease in airplay she has received as of late and it becomes pretty obvious that her announcement was nothing more than a cry for publicity.  Awwww, no one's paying attention to Daddy's spoiled little girl anymore, so she has to resort to blowing her own horn.  Go figure - I wouldn't expect anything less from a talentless hack.

In summary: It's a dark period for music when people think that Ashlee Simpson is a brilliant artist.  Someone who writes banal lyrics and cannot sing in tune without the use of studio equipment has no place in this industry - PERIOD.  The point I'm trying to make is that Ashlee Simpson is no better than hordes of karaoke singers all around the world - she just was blessed by having connections and money behind her.  Promoting Ashlee Simpson is a drop in the bucket for Geffen - it's all Papa Joe's time and money at play here.  This album is just a waste of both.
label: negative

I own the original cassette of this "Patti Austin" album from 1984 - it is one of my all-time favorites. So when I saw it was re-released on CD I bought it here on Amazon. To my surprise, I found that while this disc would play in my living room stereo - it would NOT play on the laptop I use when I travel. It doesn't even show up as a CD in there. Nor will it play on any computer, actually.

This is some more copy protection nonsense the record company is pulling - while charging us money for something they claim is a "CD".

Well this disc is NOT a CD according to the definition of it and should not be allowed to be marketed as such. I will be returning the one I purchased to Amazon and asking them to refund my money immediately. I am NOT paying twice for this album and I cant even play it on my laptop. That is insane.

Should these guys actually release a real CD version of this album, I will be happy to buy it and give it a full rating, but as is, I recommend people do not buy this phoney version - it is a desecration of a classic album. The record company is showing zero respect to the music lovers who are buying this thing, most of whom I would bet, like me, have already paid them for it on LP and on CD - and are buying it again.

This is a disgrace - and you wonder why consumers are cynical about the record industry? I am getting my money back from Amazon - they can take it up with whomever sold them this nonsense.

Once again, there are four discs in the set, but only two full albums.  The other discs consist of remixes, remixes, remixes and a few choice rarities, most of which are available on the "Supersonic & Demonic Relics" CD.  In all fairness, I should point out that as a general rule, remixes do nothing for me.  Do we really need FOUR versions of "Hooligan's Holiday" in one box set???  Seems to me if you have the album version, that's pretty much all you'd need.
When I heard another four-disc set was coming out, I assumed that the remaining four studio albums would be included along with their attendant rarities, like the first set.  But it appears that since Motley Crue is pretty much over, they're milking the catalog for all its worth.  The next box will be built around the two weakest albums in their catalog, the so-so "New Tattoo" and the atrocious, what-were-they-thinking-when-they-recorded-this "Generation Swine."  Now, THAT'S milking it...!

reviewText:
As probably Barbra's biggest fan I can hardly find the words to say what a crushing let-down this CD is. My boyfriend gifted me, knowing what a fan I am, and I was so pleased that he chose such a personal gift. But when he played it my jaw dropped. I thought they had put the wrong CD in the package at the factory. The voice that came through singing "Windmills Of Your Mind" was deep and throaty, husky almost, and the degree of technical enhancement was just plain absurd. We examined the CD and, sure enough, it was the right one. But on all the songs she sings in a register lower than Tony Bennett's. All the songs, without exception, are slow and plodding and dreary, and can be likened to a collection of funeral dirges, if you ask me.

After listening two or three more times to what amounts to just a lot of congested yowling and strained attempts at the former vocal theatrics at which she was once so adept, we decided he could give this CD to his grandmother instead since she also loves Barbra Streisand and her hearing isn't so good.

I guess that's it for Barbra, then. I mean, I'll still cherish all my old releases. But if this is what it's come down to then I really can't see throwing money away on what is essentially a mere shadow of a voice that once was truly glorious.

Maybe she could start writing children's books instead of singing. It worked for Julie Andrews. Or better yet- cookbooks! She always says the thing she loves most is food.

A word to the wise, added later:

Those of you who sense a hollow ring to a lot of the glowing 5-star reviews you see for this product and others, no- you're not crazy. As someone who has worked for a major media corporation's marketing department for the last twelve and a half years, I can tell you directly that many of these reviews are "plants" by people who have a financial stake in the product and need it to do well. These people don't care that many who purchase the product will end up being disappointed. This is irrelevant to them. They care about one thing: taking your money. These same people will pile their comments on to the end of an unfavourable review like football players in a game of tackle. Their aim is to intimidate the reviewer into deleting his contribution to the discussion. Some of the comments posted in response to this review have been so foul that Amazon has apparently found it necessary to delete them.

As the old saying goes: "A fool and his money are soon parted." When considering what you read, ask yourself:

Honest opinion?

Or Sales Pitch?

reviewText:
I know this recent Abbado cycle with the Berlin Philharmonic looks like a tempting proposition, but don't make the mistake of buying this thing! I bought part of it separately and I listened to the rest of the symphonies I didn't buy and I must tell everyone to beware the very poor recording quality that this set offers. You would think that such an expensive set would have great sound, right? Well, you would be severely wrong to think that the imbeciles at Deutsche Grammophon could actually provide a decent digital recording!

The sound as you will instantly notice is recorded at a very low level. It is very distant, like the equivalent of listening to your neighbor play music through their apartment wall and you strain to hear the details. Ok, so it's not that bad, but it is still awful! I turn up the sound really loud and still get a very rounded, small, constricted experience. I know I'm not deaf, I just put on Karajan or Bernstein or Gardiner or damn near anyone and hear the full impact of this music so much more clearly. I recently reviewed Simon Rattle's Vienna Philharmonic Beethoven cycle, ( see my review ), I thought Rattle's cycle was very poorly recorded but Abbado's is just as lousy.

Do not be confused that because the BPO play in a chamber-scaled ensemble for several of the symphonies that the recorded sound should be so low. Gardiner and Harnoncourt play with small orchestras and sound much more powerful.

Ok, so you're saying, the sound is awful, but are the interpretations worth persevering for? Quite simply put, NO!
Claudio Abbado has been studying Beethoven for many years, he recorded the symphonies in the 1980's and since then he's been conserving his energy for something new and radical?! I wish. The only new thing Abbado brings to this cycle is lighter textures, crisper ensemble and faster tempos. That's it, no revelations. The period instrument movement was way ahead of him. The performances are shockingly polite, sedate and boring.

I applaud the Berlin Philharmonic for their wonderful playing but isn't there something more about Beethoven than wonderful playing? How about drama, power, passion, a sense of adventure? You don't find that in this Abbado cycle, but you will find a polite and delicate ensemble. It's true that Abbado once in a while struts his stuff, like the finale of the 7th symphony for instance is taken at a very hectic tempo but the effect is muted by the distant sound.

I listened to the Eroica and felt absolutely nothing! Listening to Abbado's vapid Ninth might make you hate classical music. John Elliot Gardiner is quite vapid too for instance, but at least he's gutsy and fun.

Do you enjoy dinner parties with friends and need some inoffensive background music for the occasion? This Abbado cycle will be perfect for that.

Do you actually want to hear the rage, the power, the beauty, the passion of Beethoven, one of the greatest musical minds that ever lived?

Try the following performances. Karajan in Symphonies 1 and 2 from the 1960's cycle on Hybrid SACD. The digital Karajan Gold performance for the Eroica or Harnoncourt's Eroica with the COE if you want a smaller yet still kinetic sound. Furtwangler's insane Symphony 4 on Music and Arts. Karajan's massive 5th from 1962, on Hybrid SACD. For the Pastoral, try Karl Bohm or Bruno Walter. For a truly devastating 7th, Furtwangler on Music and Arts. Karajan Gold again for a thrilling 8th, and last but not least, listen to the magnificent Solti Ninth with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra from 1972 if you like slow speeds, available in the Solti Collection or the hair-raising Gunther Wand record on RCA if you like fast intensity. For a historical Ninth Symphony, Furtwangler is the man to go to, in 1942 or 1951.

Any one of those recordings is an 'event', an experience to cherish. I will not however be cherishing Claudio Abbado's Beethoven cycle, it's disposable. If you want to hear Abbado and the BPO in full glory and great sound, try out their great Brahms symphonies, recorded more than a decade and a half ago. At least you'll know they can be great together in something!

P.S. JUNE 2009 UPDATE!

Abbado and DG have admitted the artistic and engineering failure of this cycle. They have consequently released a new boxed set of Abbado conducting the complete Beethoven symphonies. Do a search and it comes up easily. It is much better recorded and was made live during concerts in Rome. They kept one performance from this set, the 9th. But symphonies 1-8 are new versions by Abbado and are much better performances than what you have here. If you're an Abbado fan, I strongly urge you to buy the newer box and skip this one which will soon be discontinued.

reviewText: You'd figure that for an Ozzy box set, there would be a vault raid containing all the rare and unreleased material one would expect.  Then again, with all the cash in attempts that Ozzy's wife Sharon has made on her husband's name (The Osbournes MTV reality show and soundtrack, "Essential Ozzy Osbourne", "Live at Budukon", etc.), what is contained on "Prince of Darkness" is hardly a surprise.  Just about everything featured here, minus the disc of covers and a few demos and such, can be found on Ozzy's albums which any and every Ozzy fan already own.  Not to mention that you'd think Ozzy's hit duet with Lita Ford ("Close My Eyes Forever") would be on here, but instead we get a duet with Miss Piggy (yes, you read that right).  A few of the covers, including "Mississippi Queen" and John Lennon's "Working Class Hero", are solid and rocking covers, but his interpretation of "Sympathy for the Devil" is undoubtadly headache inducing.  "Prince of Darkness" is hardly worth laying down your hard earned cash for, no matter how much of an Ozzy fan you are.  It's sad that Ozzy's career has gone to these depths, but then again, the blame can't entirely be put on him.

reviewText:
With a slew of mix-tapes and a couple of albums with the Coke Boys out and the release date for Excuse My French pushed back multiple times, one would think Moroccan born rapper French Montana's plan would be to build up to something grand in the form of a debut solo album, but the reality is different. Although he probably planned for something uniquely special with Excuse My French, the album comes off sounding like what we have heard time and time again from Rick Ross, Lil Wayne, Ace Hood, Birdman, and 2 Chainz, who all make appearances on the album, and who all may arguably have a greater stake in the rap game than Montana himself.

Backed by Diddy's Bad Boy Records and Rozay's Maybach Music Group labels, Excuse My French certainly gets mass promotion and recognition but falls short in the originality arena. Most of the album is consumed with Montana rapping about his money, material possessions, and sexy lady friends not to mention drugs and violence too. Montana is a competent rapper but settling with formulaic subject matter pulls the album down several ranks.

In other words his writing forays are a little too recognizable. Some (not all) of Montana's verses lack the type of lyricism that is meant to make the listener think really hard, leaving only rhymes that serve the purpose of connecting one line to the next. While the engineering and sound quality may be nice and professional sounding, the beats rely too often on garish synthetic flourishes instead of harmonious, melodic instruments. The only facets that will garner noteworthy attention are star power and the adequate portrayal of the high life only a successful mob boss would enjoy.
label: negative

reviewText:
I'd be more forgiving to yet another compilation of Pete Townshend solo work if there wasn't this supposed magnum opus (called "Floss") still sitting around that he's been working on for years.

If you are a seasoned fan, you can name the albums by heart and off the top of your head. Who Came First, Rough Mix, Empty Glass, ....Chinese Eyes, White City, Iron Man, Psychoderelict, Lifehouse boxed set, Scoop comps and Live material both only from his site and more commonly released. That's it.

Is there anything here a completest needs? Then buy the last two tracks as an MP3. The, in my opinion, too little and far too late protest song,Guantanamo and a forgettable rocker, How Can I Help You. If these songs were surrounded by even 6 other new songs, then I'd like them more and probably would like the album. Instead, you are stuck rethinking the same tired old material in a different context AGAIN with two new songs tacked on behind them. I am so thankful for digital technology. Now musicians and greedy record companies need to find another method of marketing these "The Very Best of" compilations because people can just pay for each song and flip off the rest of this album. I hate it when they offer a fig leaf of new material to rope in fans to buy the same other songs twice or even more if you bought other best ofs before buying the original albums. It's the same with that Who compilation, Then and Now from a few years ago.

As for the material, it's not what most people would associate as Townshend's "Very Best". Three from his debut album, three from the Ronnie Lane collaboration, only two from Empty Glass, two from Chinese Eyes et al. Sure, it covers all of them but what's the point? Soon people will be writing reviews for different best ofs and completely forget the sources.

Here's a suggestion to Townshend and the record company, Why not reissue the Eelpie live matieral on a more commercial level? Varied settings, varied set lists, interesting NEW material for most people who never bothered buying directly from the Eelpie site???

Compilations, unless they genuinely fill more of a purpose than a couple new songs jammed in at the end are good. The Who Hits 50 compilation is excellent. It includes single versions of songs, extended tracks, different edits of material alot of which you couldn't get on the albums and a new song thrown in for good measure. This is at least the fourth repackaging of Townshend's solo material that I know of off the top of my head. The Gold collection, the Definitive Collection, a best of from the mid 90's with the long title coolwalking.....something, now this, Too much.
label: negative

reviewText:
While Boston's Tom Scholz was battling CBS's withholding of royalties, a tactic to pressure the engineer to finish the tapes for the third Boston album, former Boston guitarist Barry Goudreau and singer Fran Cosmo formed Orion The Hunter.  These two worked together previously on Goudreau's 1980 solo project and in Orion they were joined by former Heart drummer Michael De Rosier, bassist Bruce Smith, and on tour by keyboardist Brian Maes, who later appeared in Goudreau and Boston singer Brad Delp's early 90's project, RTZ.

The eponymous Orion the Hunter features five songs co-written by Brad Delp, who also provided back-up vocals.  Orion relies heavily on the synthesizer sound popular in the 1980s, including electronic drum pads and sound effects like swishes.  The production is terribly dated but great for a chuckle if you grew up during the period when these sounds were considered fresh.

Perhaps it's needless to say, but Orion sounds nothing like Boston, except perhaps for Fran Cosmo's voice, reminiscent of Delp's but stuck in high register on most of these songs, uninspired and forgettable 3-4 minute pop-rock compositions.  The album's hit, So You Ran, shamelessly borrows the guitar riff from I'll Be Watching You (released only a year previously in 1983 on the Police's final album, Synchronicity).  The band gained some media exposure with a video on the new MTV network and in an opening slot on a summer tour for Aerosmith, but one listen to this album and it's no surprise Orion quickly faded into obscurity.
label: negative

reviewText: I haven't heard the whole collection, but I've heard enough to know that it's not worth getting.  Gould simply did not understand (or like) Mozart, and he certainly did not know how to play him either.  For example, in the first movement of the Sonata in A (K331), he rushes through it and pounds away on the keys.  Gould's version of that movement is only about eight minutes long, but it's a piece that needs to enjoyed like fine wine, not gulped like cheap beer.  Lest anyone think that I am being too harsh on Gould, let me say that I am actually a big fan of his Bach recordings, and I even like his recording of Mozart's 24th Piano Concerto (K491).  The quality of that recording might be due to the moderating influence of a conductor and orchestra, but there is no moderation in these sonatas, which is critically important to playing Mozart.  Anyone who wants to hear Mozart's piano works as they should be played might want to listen to Ingrid Haebler.  But Gould's set should be avoided like an ebola-infected monkey.
label: negative

reviewText: Reviewing an album like Pop Muzik by M is a tricky affair. On the one end of the spectrum there are hardcore fans who will attest to the albums greatness. But I, for one, do not hear what they talk so highly about. I do like a lot of music, many of which would be considered rubbish by many and some in line with those who are hardcore. I was familiar with the title track "Pop Muzik" which I really liked back in the days. Unfortunately, it is the only good track along with the remix version that is included. I really liked this song and still find it to be a good danceable track. Unfortunately, one track does not make an album. The rest of the songs are simply rubbish in my opinion. These tracks would not make the cut if they were written by other artists. It does kind of remind me of classic David Bowie music but it stops there. Don't get me wrong I do love David Bowie's material. It's just that even from that standpoint I did not enjoy the rest of the album. If you are purchasing this album for "Pop Muzik", you are better off just downloading that track. Listen to the other tracks before you make your mind because we all have different tastes in music. Even those who share similar interests in music have differing tastes within those genres.

reviewText:
Really, a dud...this thing is THE most disappointing album of 2011 by far...and I wanted to like it, as I've liked/loved their past records, and I'm an Adam Schlesinger fan.

Tinted Windows this ain't.  To paraphrase what I wrote about this record on the Velvet Rope on a thread about this, er, long-awaited opus, by FOW, here goes:

Don't hate me, but I am REALLY disappointed with the new FOW "Sky Full Of Holes"...if anything, take the title and replace the word "Sky" with "This Album Is" instead and you have a true statement.

Sorry.

If anything, some songs start really promising like "Someone's Gonna Break Your Heart" and the song does not live up to its promise or really stick like a good powerpop song should. "Radio Bar" is another, but it comes off like a cheesy hybrid tribute to Billy Joel and Bruce Springsteen. "A Road Song" sounds like a bad America parody...the fact that America is covering it reminds me of a worse take on when Motorhead did their Ramones tribute "R.A.M.O.N.E.S." and the Ramones covered it...

A coupla songs venture into alt-country territory, just not nearly as good...Chris Collingwood is no Gram Parsons, sorry. Plus, one thing I never truly liked from the beginning with "Radiation Vibe" was Chris' ultra-nasally voice...like a bad hybrid of Gordon Gano, John from TMBG, and Weird Al Yankovic, that on top of their ultrastiff, ultraBORING, deer-in-the-headlights, live shows...and I've seen em twice (thinking they'd redeeem themselves after their 1st snorefest) or get less boring...NOPE)...BUT FOW had some really undeniable really good powerpop songs on their records, like "Radiation Vibe", "Red Dragon Tattoo", "Stacey's Mom", which countradicted their boring and nerdy (not nerd-CHIC, but nerdy-AWKWARD), tendencies...

BUT this new album does not contradict these bad elements at all...with the acoustic-rooted arrangements (not so much loud hooky tuneful, powerpop), it unfortunately renders these faults a lot more distinctly and brings them into focus a lot more glaringly. Plus, the album feels lost and all over the place, throwing stuff against the wall to see what sticks, with zero logic whatsoever. It really does not work for me AT ALL...just being honest here...I wanted to like it but I really don't.

I hate to say this, but this record made me more than a little uncomfortable listening and the album as a whole is a contender for most disappointing of 2011...plus it's a case in point about why, for me, hooky, catchy music is more important than lyrics...the lyrics might be like well-written short stories and all about "lovable losers" as people call it, but if it's not matched with exciting, tuneful, captivating music, the effort might as well be lost and out the window.

B- for the effort...but a D overall...D for dud...

Sorry, "Sky Full Of Holes" is a royal flat dud, and I tried to get through it twice...it felt like a chore, even worse 2nd time around. Tinted Windows are a better band and more my thing, real powerpop and Taylor Hanson is a much better singer than Chris Collingwood...if "Sky" matched "Tinted", I'd be in powerpop heaven...I'm sure Ivy is better too...I'm very disappointed because I'm an Adam Schlesinger fan and he deserved better than this FOW record. I had a hunch it wasn't going to be good.

Sorry for being harsh, but I felt LISTENING to "Sky" was harsh...on my ears!!

reviewText: I never would have thought about giving a Smashing Pumpkins album a low rating as one star.  I've been a fan of Smashing Pumpkins for over 20 years and this album fails.  The first single released "Being Beige" isn't bad even though it felt more like a Zwan song.  However, when "One and All" was released I grew anticipation.  That song harkens back to the earlier Pumpkins that many of us remember from their magnum opus Mellon Collie & the Infinite Sadness and their classics Siamese Dream and Gish.  The anticipation grew after hearing that track.  However...this came out to be the biggest fail of an album for Smashing Pumpkins.  Don't be fooled by "One and All" because this album is not anything like that song.  Billy Corgan has dumbed down not only making anything musically amusing but dumbed down the lyrics so far that it is unlistenable.  The song "Run2Me" is by far the worst Smashing Pumpkins song I have ever heard and stands right beside the Teargarden crap "Owata" and "Widow Wake My Mind".  How many times does he have to repeat the title of the song?  Other songs that are garbage are the repetitive "Dorian" and the awful "Anti-Hero".  Sure there may be songs that give a bit of guitar but you need to have good lyrics to go with the music.  This album is uninspired.  I cannot believe all of the 5 star reviews.  Give Mellon Collie, Siamese Dream, Gish, and well I'll throw in their mellow Adore and experimental bliss of Machina a listen.  Also, check out the worthy rocking (although somewhat flawed) Zeitgeist.  I even thought Oceania was average but had great tracks on it even though it was not as good as earlier records.  This is by far the most uncreative, lazy, most poppy record Corgan has ever come up with musically and more importantly...lyrically.  I was happy to download the single "One and All" because it is by far the best song on the album.  The other decent tracks are the Zwan-ish "Being Beige" and the Faith No More funk sounding "Anaise".  Other than that leave this album alone and pop in both Mellon Collie disks or any of their disks for that matter because those albums are what Smashing Pumpkins really are.

reviewText: DRG is a CD company obviously devoted to completists. With their current release of Happy Hunting, you can now have a complete collection of Ethel Merman's Broadway shows. Merman herself referred to the show as a jeep among limos--- the trip was bumpy, but it got you there. Based loosely on the Grace Kelly Monaco marriage, it's quite similar to the Merm's previous Broadway outing, Call Me Madam, except that Hunting is not very good. Merman was lucky and smart enough to surround herself, usually, with talented creators, but the score is awful. Composed by Harold Karr, the man parodied as the composer-cum-dentist in Bells Are Ringing, there is neither a hit nor a memorable song in the show. The male lead, Fernando Lamas, is wooden and unmusical, and caused endless trouble for Merman on and offstage. History reminds us that this was Lamas' only Broadway show, but his antics such as wiping his mouth after an on stage kiss, and then telling a TV talk show host that kissing Merman was like kissing a cross between your uncle and a Sherman tank could not have endeared him to his female lead. Only a solo and a duet with the Merm have been embarrassingly immortalized here. All in all, this is the ultimate CD to play at the end of the night when you want all of your guests to go home. Few if any would survive the first few cuts, and fewer would find an unkinder cut anywhere.
label: negative

Problem is, he and the band are playing World music...not Blues, not Blues/Jazz, but World. "Joyous Noise" has chants, Indian influences, citars instead of guitars. It's not what I thought I was buying based on his first 2 CDs, and certainly not something I'd have expected from the guitarist from The Allman Brothers Band. If I'd have known he had decided to change genres entirely I would not have bought this CD. It sure doesn't belong in my Blues collection! Sorry Derek...let me know when you decide to return to the Blues!

reviewText:
Recordings like this make one wonder if Munch seriously lost touch with some of the German repertoire when he changed his nationality? His recordings of Schubert, Schumann, Brahms and several other composers who form a major part of the central 19th century repertoire are all distinguished by a cold, heartless glitter; they resemble executions more than performances; they are loud and aggressive; and machine-like in their instrumental perfection. It is what (rightly or wrongly) Europeans associate with an American style, except that Munch was not an American. But it is exactly what you get on this recording, of which I am at a loss what to say except "stay away from it". Don't be taken in by the ridiculous trumpeting about the sound. The sound of WHAT? Maybe for its own sake? Because this music making hardly deserves the name, let alone brilliant encomia about how it sounds. Unless of course you just collect records of the Boston Symphony, good or bad indifferently!
Unfortunately I can't answer the question I have raised about Munch. The short biography I have read leaves us in the dark about his motivations, whether they were cultural, musical or political, except that his migration occurred long before Hitler assumed power. However, whatever the explanation might be, it will not serve as an excuse for this unmusical disc. If he did hate the music, why perform it? Unless he saw it merely as his professional duty and that's the end of it. And yet this is the man who studied with Hans Pfitzner and Carl Flesh and led the violins of the Gewandhaus Orchestra (1923)! Whatever the case, we record buyers are the losers; because for every such disc you buy, you miss out on a more deserving, more spirit enhancing version!

reviewText:
Even though I'm the wrong generation, she died 5 years before I was born, I love Judy Garland and have listened to her since I was a kid. I was very excited to see the show on Broadway and wasn't too surprised to see Tracie Bennett do the usual Judy-Shakes performance. You know the one, where some funny queen at a party camps it up and dramatically asks for a cocktail while wringing their hands and jerking their body like a rag doll. Ms. Bennett gave the same performance, only she took herself WAY TOO SERIOUSLY. With out modulating the good with the bad, the antic with the sublime, you watched a controlled car wreck punctuated by classic songs.

This collection takes the worst of that show and gives you more! Ms. Bennett is an actress, not a singer. She 'channels' Judy as well as any psychic relays messages from your dearly departed granny. Her attempts at intentionally missed high notes, her chest shaking bravado are all impressive; now if only there was something besides grotesque parody behind it. I'm sure this was created lovingly, but it would appear the goal was Ms. Bennett's success as an actress, not to Judy's memory, and certainly not her talent.

It's not that she is so bad, it's the context and the archness that makes this album absolutely untenable. In the end, the product offered is a collection of songs. Purchasing it assumes you would want to keep it to listen to, correct? If so, why would you buy THIS 'artful' collection and not an actual Judy album?

You know, Pat Metheny -- who I similarly think is as close to the muse as Jarrett -- does this stuff occasionally too.  Maybe it's me.  I'm not an accomplished musician. reviewText:
Does anybody miss the eighties this much?? If you long for the days of Duran Duran videos, Billy Idol remixes, and new albums by Erasure, then you must be in heaven. I, however, am in retro-hell. As far as I'm concerned, the only thing worse than eighties electro-pop were the haircuts worn by the people who played it. In all honesty, the `80s stand as the least musically relevant decade in the past 100 years, and yet it refuses to go away. Vince Clarke is a founding member of Depeche Mode and the instrumental half of Yazoo (or Yaz). Both bands had a significant influence on `80s pop - not much of it particularly good (despite Alison Moyet's awesome vocal abilities), and Erasure was his post-Yazoo stab at retaining relevance. He hired singer Andy Bell as his new vocal foil, but nothing they recorded was particularly memorable, except perhaps for the way that Bell's baritone bore a spooky faux- (and fey) resemblance to Moyet's.

Well, in spite of every law of nature and every element of common sense, they're back, and apparently, this duo spent the past twenty years cryogenically frozen. Nightbird sounds as though Clarke found the complete CD buried in his closet after losing it twenty-some-odd years ago. There is not a single sound, not an iota of an idea suggesting that Erasure has experienced anything since 1985. Most `80s productions have aged about as well as yesterday's sashimi, but Erasure serves it up anyway. Even their equipment sounds identical to their work from twenty years ago - couldn't the guy at least buy a new synthesizer? "Let's Take One More Rocket to the Moon" sounds like it was retrieved from a satellite that fell in the Atlantic Ocean twenty-two years ago. "I Broke It All in Two" "borrows" generously from "Only You", while "All This Time Still Falling Out of Love" should have been called "All This Time and I Still Re-Write `Don't Go'. Why buy this CD when you can get the original hits on Yaz's "Upstairs At Eric's" in a 99-cent bargain bin?

Is there anything topical on this CD? No. Is there anything that suggests the culture we now live in? No. Is there anything socially relevant to our times? No. Is every whiny self-centered song about a bad relationship? Why, yes! There is no new audience for this CD, only saddened ex-club hoppers now cruising through their forties, taking one last forlorn look over their shoulders.

Perhaps somewhere in the world, a manager for a gay disco is celebrating the return of Erasure. I, however, feel that this is one CD that should have remained in the closet.  C-  Tom Ryan
label: negative

reviewText:
I was going to write a review of this album, but everybody else has pretty much said it all. Most of it has been released. I understand that "Sucking in the 70's" was out of print for a long time and therefore many cuts on it were elusive, but "70's" was (inexplicably) remastered and re-released earlier this year.

The two stand-outs here are the official CD releases of "Let it Rock" and "Through the Lonely Nights." The overall sound of the CD is less than stellar, however -- as if the songs were over-compressed.

I do admire the packaging, though; there are current photos of the band and the liner notes are fairly extensive. But whoever wrote the liner notes made a few mistakes; for instance, the notes say that "I Just Wanna Make Love to You" was off "No Security." It wasn't. It's actually a B-side to the "Highwire" CD-single. Also, the writer states that "Mixed Emotions" "wasn't a massive hit upon release." Well, I was there -- they played that song on the radio all the time and it was impossible to turn on MTV without seeing the video. The song reached #5 on Billboard's Top 40. That's a fairly big hit in my opinion, considering the Stones staple "It's Only Rock n' Roll" only reached #16 and "Wild Horses" only went to #28. (Charts are funny: technically, "She's So Cold" was a bigger hit than "Wild Horses" and "Mixed Emotions" was a bigger hit than "Beast of Burden"***)

Most of the songs here that aren't on "70's" are on the "Collectibles" CD (released in '91, it contained the entire "Flashpoint" CD as well as a second CD full of great B-sides and remixes), "No Security" and "Stripped" -- all official releases.

The bottom line here is: If you're just getting into the Stones--wait before buying this. If you're a casual Stones fan, these songs are okay, may indeed be "rare" to you, and are worth getting. If you're a super-huge fan, you've heard all this before but you're probably a big enough fan to be a completist, which obligates you to buy it anyway.

***Source: "Billboard Book of Top 40 Hits, 7th Edition"

... "Blind" by Korn?

A suck of breath, someone shouts "GO!" and the song is off.

No. It's supposed to be "ARE YOU READY?!". Jonathan doesn't say "GO!" until the third album, they got it all wrong.

This is the start of "Loco", the first act of musical purgery by nu metal sideshow Coal Chamber. And it's the best one on the album too. From here your patience will only wear ever more thin as Dez and company play redundant song after song, each one based on a single idea stolen straight from Korn's self-titled. For example, as I write this I am listening (perhaps for the last time ever) to "Faget" er I mean "Clown" er I mean "Big Truck" s*** lemme try again.

The same lack of original content permeates the entire record. The best argument for listening to this record is the 45 second "Amir of the Desert" - partly for its saintly length and partly for its mildly entertaining middle school humor. Here Coal Chamber are either the least creative band in nu metal history, or the most dishonest cover band in music history.

reviewText:
I'm gonna get slammed for writing this review, but I don't care.  These Amazon reviews are idiotic.  Everybody just reviews their favorite stuff, so you end up with every single CD, (from Creed to the Insane Clown Posse) with a 4.5 or 5 star rating.  I consider myself a pretty open minded guy when it comes to music.  I'm a huge music fan and I listen to anything I get my hands on: electronica, jazz, indie rock, hip hop, etc.  And once upon a time, I even dug prog rock and heavy metal.  I still spin my old Genesis albums every once in a while.  Anyway, when I first heard about DT a few years ago, I tried my best to enjoy them, but I found it to be a difficult task.
No matter how hard I try, I can't get into them.  My main complaint is that they sound incredibly cold and mechanical.  If you program a bunch of robots to play instruments flawlessly I imagine this is what you'll get.  Sure, they have amazing technical skill, but unless you're a 15 year old teenage boy, that won't be enough to hold your attention.  Queensryche and Rush might not have had as much technique, but atleast they could write some good songs.  And anybody that says this James guy can sing like Geoff Tate is kidding themselves.  His operatic wailing is grotesque.  Also, I'm not all that impressed by John Petrucci.  To me, he sounds like he just plays a bunch of fast scale runs.  I'd rather hear a lyrical guitarist like Marc Ribot than a guy who sounds like he's practicing his scales.  (I've seen John Petrucci's guitar video and it was VERY revealing)  I think a great guitarist is one like Wes Montgomery... a guitarist that might practice all day, but can leave his practicing where it belongs... at home, and not on stage.
To be honest, I'm being a bit harsh.  I would probably give it a 2.5, but I'm giving it a 1 instead to offset all of the raving 5 star reviews.  The band is certainly ambitious, which is commendable.  Also, there are certain times when DT can trancend their flaws and actually make moving music (like in the pretty good "Images and Words" and the okay "A Change of Seasons").  But those moments are few and far in between on this album.  On a side note, you prog rock guys should listen to Ween's "The Mollusk".  Absolutely hillarious prog rock parody.  (a lot of it sounds exactly like vintage ELP)  In conclusion:  Bring on the unhelpful votes!

reviewText:
After listening to their previous albums, it became clear that these dear sweet young adults are wasting their talents.  This CD is bright to be sure, but only in color.  The lyrics are insipid and hardly resonate with coherent themes.  Not only that, but the annoying production values undermine the vocal aspect of the music, quite simply, I do not like the fact that they sound like they are screaming over a microphone.  Their first album "Jump5" is a favorite of mine.  Yes, it sounds like it is cheesy pop music, and it is, but the lyrics are far more adult than those presented in "Dreaming In Color".

For a group that based a name on dancing (Jump5-hello!?), I find it odd that this is the least dance friendly album.  "Jump5" was full of dance floor anthems, "All The Time In The World" was less enjoyable but possessed a few gems, "Accelerate" had some rather meaningful and exciting songs.  Now, that was a great blend of the today sound and dance attributes.  "Mix It Up" was rather disappointing, but it too had some great moments.  I do not count their Christmas CD (I never count specialty albums as such).  Do not get me wrong, they have great potential, and for few moments, some of the songs on "Dreaming In Color" gave me promise, but then they turned into horrid fast/slow "rock" songs.

I do like the remixes, however.  They destroy the harsher sounds of the original sounds and replace them with much more ear friendly synths.  Course, all the rage at the moment is making mock-rock, but once people grow up and realize that the words mean nothing, the sound is grating and childish, and the singers are no longer singing, well then maybe Jump5 can go back to making good music.  Then again, I do have my memories of the younger, yet seemingly older Jump5 and that will last with me.  Ahh...the days of listening to "All I Want", "The Meaning Of Life", and "When I Say Your Name"...

In the words of Pete Burns, "Isn't it a pity."

reviewText:
Jon Anderson fans have been waiting quite a long time for this album to have its first CD release and when it was announced on Jon's website we were all excited the wait was finally over.

Unfortunately, instead of putting forth the proper effort and use the original analog master tapes like a normal CD remaster they decided to source this CD from a worn LP played on a turntable that was out of alignment.  You can hear crackles and pops throughout and the sibilance of the vocals sound more like "shh" than "sss" due to tracking error of the phono cartridge.  The pitch has also been noticeably lowered for some reason.  It's not at true pitch which is a bit odd.

On top of that they incompetently compressed, limited and EQ'd it into a distorted mess.  It sounds hollow and has the classic U-curve sound that many inexperienced engineers turn out, you know all bass and treble with a heavily recessed midrange.  Also, the digital levels are run so hot they are in constant digital "over" which causes audible clipping and the whole album to sound even more distorted.  It's a total mess that was approved by Opio Media!

It seems those who released this Animation CD have conceded their efforts were lackluster.  I'm told they now know where the tapes are but I still can't believe the amount of people who argued this CD was acceptable and sounded fine.  I'd wait for them to finish the re-worked CD they will be announcing soon.  Even if you love this album this CD is certainly NOT worth your money.  Save your money for now and wait for a new version.

Why would they ruin such an opportunity like this?  Hopefully they decide to start caring about Jon's music, spend some money, use the correct master tapes and do a quality mastering job this time!  Just give us a proper CD release.  I would think they would instate an exchange policy for those of us they conned into buying this first abortion.  This is what starts class action suits.

Jon Anderson deserves better than to have these people be in charge of his catalog.

reviewText:
Just because you can doesn't mean you should. Case in point is "Sir Lucious and I Refuse to Type the Rest of the Stupid Title."

We're out West riding in stagecoaches, decked out in tracksuits, caps, platform sneakers and shades. Nothing more complex going on around here than, "I want my baby back, baby back ribs."

Joined by what sounds like The Fixx on vocals and synthesizers, "Follow Us" is a tough guy at the chocolate factory, a self-conscious monstrosity built out of reconstituted new wave and halitosis. "Turns Me On" sounds like a sexed-up, pan-fried "The Little Drummer Boy." Later, beer and ashes turn a gray paste on the counter, slags of gnats a halo under the fluorescence, buzzing and sparking. Ghosts on my shoulders, footsteps in the hallway. The sky resting above my brow, threatening to descend and spin me adrift.

Later, I awake, naked and glistening in petroleum layers, sticking to the Twister mat in my happy place. I feel sore, woozy and slightly creepy, like I've been squeezing maple syrup up the lower end of my alimentary canal for a good spell. I take a spot under the sun, spread out my sugar wings, face-down, swelling into crystal form, smiling into a million-me.

reviewText: After the hopeful signs in Lily on the Beach, I was eagerly awaiting the follow-up.  It was stunning to realize just what an awful dreck this was on the first listen.  Although I tried giving it a fair chance and gave it a go multiple times, each time I walked away with the sense that zero imagination and effort was put into this album.  It's as if Froese & son grabbed all the cast off pieces from the work on the already awful Optical Race, repackaged them and released them under a guise of a new album.  This is a rudderless boat, and it ends up drifting aimlessly from one uninspired piece to another.  The title track, Melrose, is a perfect example: it opens unpromisingly, seems to find a bit of an interesting territory for about a minute, but then the synthesized piano and sax kick in, dragging the whole effort firmly into the elevator music territory.  Similarly, The Art of Vision seems to hold out some promise, straying into some sequenced passages, but the sounds used and the overall direction south of boredom sink this piece quickly.  Everything here is just vapid adult-contemporary pieces suitable solely for background shopping music at Walmart.  This whole album screams mediocrity.  From the overuse of California location names for the pieces, to the maudlin compositions of the bulk of the pieces here.  The choice of the cheesiest synth sounds, the sequenced drum machines, the sax, and the tom-toms as annoying as they may have been in the past two albums, really smother this one in its entirety.

reviewText: What's changed since Bon Hoki sped up his voice to hit the high notes on Livin' On a Prayer in 1986? Well, the lad and his band are using new haircare products, all posey like Reservoir Dogs with hundred dollar bouffants and holstered water pistols. Pinch yourself if you expected Crush would be anything other than Slippery When Wet, Version 8.1 - underachieving teeny-bop pop metal with heavy investments in dream date posturing and a bit of moldered bread crust for lyrical and musical development. Rife with simpleton observations (It's My Life, Just Older) and grade school rhyme schemes scotch-taped with a hamfist, this is negligent evolution at it's most patronizingly ignorable. The harmonies are a study in gobbledy vocal tricks, a wad of gimped and fussed-over enthusiasm for a textbook of unabashed chintz sentiments nicked arrantly from a Barbie colouring book (Thank You For Loving Me, I Got the Girl, She's a Mystery). The rest is just-add-water puff rock; imagineless chungling boom bam for everyone but dreamy-eyed, teddy bear-hugging Teen Beat girlies and beer-blitzed white boys cruising in Billy Joe Jim Bob's bondo'ed Trans Am on Main Street, Popcorntown, U.S.A. Give the trophy though to Captain Crash and the Beauty Queen From Mars, now officially the stupidest song title in the history of rock.

reviewText:
This recording exists for one reason and one reason only: as a vanity project for Placido Domingo.

That vanity means a whole lot of splicing and dicing of Domingo's contribution to the recording. This is, after all, a role that is simply TOO DIFFICULT FOR HIM to essay live on stage in an opera house. And that's why this is a vanity project - it allows Domingo to fake that he could actually sing this role. He can't. He has never sung the role on stage, because he would have never made it through the entire role in an evening, and it shows.

How do we know that? Well, for one thing, anyone who has had the chance to hear Mr Domingo in any of the hundreds of roles he has sung onstage (and having sung them anywhere from competently to very well) will have a reaction similar to mine: ie: I've never heard him sound like that in the theater. By that, I mean that the engineers have spliced together snippets from this take or that take into what they think sounds like a cohesive whole for Mr Domingo. Well, it isn't. It sounds faked, the same way you would know a video tape was a fake if it looped a 100-yard-dash video for an hour without break. You would look at that and say, "sorry, but no human being can run that fast for that long a period of time."

And that's the thing about Domingo's fake Tristan - it is obviously faked for this recording. And you can say that based not only on the way Domingo actually sings in a theater, but by the way any tenor who has ever sung Tristan in the theater approaches the vocal challenges of this role. In fact, that's the biggest giveaway that this recording is a fake ie: the fact that Domingo does not have the kind of understanding of the role that comes from essaying it on stage to know where the singing should rise and fall, where the energy should be turned on or lessened, and where one needs to find a way of singing that keeps the voice varied and interesting. It's telling that in Domingo's case on this recording, the application of extra energy serves to make the voice SMALLER, when it should be expanding and soaring (check out the "O diesse Sonne" section in Act 3), a sure sign that a singer is pushing, rather than singing, the same way that a young pitcher is "throwing," rather than pitching.

I guess it comes down to how much fakery you are willing to abide in a musical performance. Would you, for instance, find a recording of Beethoven's Hammerklavier Sonata satisfying if you were told that the pianist playing it didn't have the chops to actually sit down and play the thing, but that they COULD play the right hand and left hand separately with no problems, and so the engineers went ahead and recorded the hands separately and spliced them together into a recording that appeared to be "normal" otherwise? No, I think you'd think, "hell, even I could do that."

Once we're past Domingo's fakery, the obvious question is: would you buy this recording with this cast, this orchestra and this conductor if the Tristan were someone other than Domingo? And, the answer there is most likely, "are you crazy?"

So there you have it. Perhaps we can look forward to Andrea Bocelli's Tristan in due course as well.

Will the actual physical copy cd suffer this same fate? Time will tell...but more than likely.

It's time to end this ignorance in the studio. I'm not going to get into how weak and sterile music mastered like this sounds...or how tiring/fatiguing a listen it is after a song and a half. It's all been covered and the info is out there for the taking.

Many reviews mention how the music all sounds the same. The style of mastering this digital release suffers from will most certainly contribute to a sterile, "samey" sounding experience. I laugh when I hear statements about how "awesome" this sounds. WOW! Really?!?

Many out there don't realize what is going on. They just know it sounds off somehow. I don't fault them...at least they are noticing something. I'm getting the word out there...the painful truth. Actually this release is very surprising because I haven't seen this much clipping on much of anything released lately. This is a major step backwards. I thought by now (with the awareness) that the issue of clipping, at the very least, would have been addressed across the board...but apparently not.

Clipping is when you chop off the top of the audio waveform because the levels are pushed beyond what the medium (cd, etc.) can handle. Essentially you then have "damaged" music.

If when released and analyzed, the physical product cd has a better waveform and dynamics, I will adjust this review accordingly.

At what point is the majority/listening public going to wake up, get educated on this matter, and demand better audio quality? (they certainly would be drowning in their own tears if video quality was this pathetic). Reiterating, I have read a couple reviews claiming this release has "awesome sound". I can only shake my head at the level of conditioning that has been administered by the record labels to form such opinions on what "awesome" sound is. What can one expect when the benchmark for top-notch audio quality is a $2 set of ear buds providing a lossy format.

reviewText:
then I think that ScarJo should stick to her posing and preening on screen and keeping my interest piqued in her when she's not in a movie by taking even more near-nude photos for men's magazines. Wow, this reminded me immediately of so many other throwaway CD's I've listened to this year.

The album consists of 11 tracks, and if the first instrumental track "Fawn," is any indication of what lay ahead, then you would be well advised to turn back NOW.

The rest of the 10 tracks bleed together by the connective tissue of wind chimes, feedbacking synthisizers and sometimes, the handy dandy noise of wind. When I listen to this, why do I keep envisioning a little rich girl in clean clothes visiting an abandoned urine-soaked crack house and putting up pink "Girl Power" and unicorn stickers everywhere while throwing glitter?

She's going out of her way to try and imitate the vocal straining of Tom Waits, which for him works, but... Scarlett - please - this is not for you. I can almost see her as she "prepared" for this - smoking cigarettes to get her voice to purposely sound "husky" and in a lower register, and then warble lightly just enough out of tune to get the desired effect, her vocal lightly sprinkled over the clanging clashing of possibly more out of tune instruments.

It smacks of the typical celebrity self-indulgences: overwrought noisy ambience, and to be honest, it's TOO goddamn noisy. There's wind chimes (and I mean a lot of them), music boxes, the occasional strain of a violin, and wait - is that a Hammond organ moaning in almost EVERY track, to give it some sort of "depth"?

I've heard women over the years sing Tom Waits songs, and they don't go overboard like this. There is some kind of strange lonely sadness in his music, and if she had simply approached these wonderful works of musical art and sang the song accompanied only by a single piano, she would have had my interest.

Her voice is very very soft, which means she either meant to do this on purpose or she can't actually sing, but does what everyone who listens to the lite-rock stations in their town does - kinda sing along, a little bit, and then forget the song completely.

But as it is, does Scarlett J. feel as if she has suffered enough in her well-documented life and is a fan enough of this particular kind of pain to let us know she likes Tom enough to put THIS out?

Well, sorry to say, she's made me suffer. It's as if Bjork, The Shags and Gloria Balsam (of "Fluffy" fame) all decided to put out a compilation album. And I'm sorry, but this is just too distant and too convoluted to understand the words. I know they're covers, but in the end, I think I'll stick to Tom Waits, thank you very much.

I'll give you 2 stars for the effort, because not very many 25 year olds know of him, but this was not the way to pay tribute to someone who has was or is an influence of any sort in your life.

Next time, write a thank you card.

(p.s. - I wrote this on the Amazon discussion board a few days before this was released. I had to put this up here because, well... it sucks.)

As I listened  to this weak and pathetic album, I wondered if the aliens that Steve Vai  refers to in "Alien Love Secrets" had abducted the great Joe Satch and  replaced him with a changeling.
The Joe on this album has nothing in  common with the Joe on previous albums. This CD has no energy, emotion or  warmth whatsoever. Gone are the lush guitar tones, riffs and creative  writing. Instead, the listener is subjected to techno that has no place  backing up Joe's guitar. You think Joe would have listened to Zappa's "Jazz  From Hell," and learned that techno has no place in a guitar virtuoso's  world.
The only song that keeps this album from being a total wash out  is the fourth song, which is very telling because I can't ever remember the  title of the track!
If you are one of the unlucky that has paid money for  this vapid effort, get your money's worth and use it as a coaster.

reviewText:
This CD is a sad lesson in what can result when even a Legend such as Dionne allows nepotism to take a front seat to common sense. Her son may have meant well, but he's done more damage than good to dear ol' mom. No seasoned producer worth his salt would have allowed Dionne to go through with this project, not if they were honest and cared. It was just a rotten idea from the start. Can any of us imagine, for example, Quincy Jones hearing the poor production values on this CD and giving it his blessing? David Foster? Clive Davis?

Dionne had been shopping this project around for more than 2 years to various major record Labels and none of them were interested in her "Trio of duet CDs of my old hits" concept. For a moment, many fans feared the worst--that she'd never get signed to a major label again, that the prevailing sentiment in the industry was that Dionne's once beautiful, raspy voice that could do no wrong had finally lost its power and ability to enthrall music listeners.(Let me state for the record, that was not the case for me, having seen her live as late as November of last year and witnessing Dionne in fine voice as she brought the house to its feet with stirring renditions of her classics).

Finally, Concord decided to take a chance, signing her to a 3 CD deal. Fans were elated and hopeful that the powers that be would at least encourage her to go in a more creative direction, or at best, choose an experienced producer who would breathe new life into the songs she selected, using REAL INSTRUMENTS instead of synthesizers and drum machines. Unfortunately, they gave her carte blanche to do as she pleased, hence, this pitiable result, which will no doubt add another stain to the twilight years of her discography.

Why Dionne insists on re-recording her old hits is beyond anyone's comprehension. There isn't a single fan I've spoken to who is happy about her obcession with this idea. Quite frankly, we all consider it a mystery. She sings these songs over and over every night in concerts around the world. Now, never getting bored of singing them in a live setting,(as she's said in many an interview) may be one thing, but re-recording them for a fanbase that has NO DESIRE WHATSOEVER to hear them in recorded form is another. There are so many NEW songs out there that would better suit her deeper, more reserved alto. Where is the artistic creative musician that was once Dionne Warwick?  Is re-recording her past hits many times over the best she can offer to the world at this stage of her life? This is beginning to border on musical psychosis....No, you say? Let's take a look at the history of this musical malaise.

In 1997 there was "Dionne sings Dionne" which covered several of her big hits. Then, at the turn of the century there was the "Dionne sings Dionne 2", consisting of more covers, issued as a Japanese import(and much to her chagrin, as these were basically demos left over from her '97 River North release. Not owning the Masters, she had no control over its release). And then----we have this 3rd installment, which, if Dionne has her way, will actually be the 3rd IN AN INSTALLMENT OF 5 CDs(!!) whereby she's re-recording her hits(don't forget folks, she has 2 more in the can for release after this one!).

Wasn't Dionne the girl singer from New Jersey who defiantly hollered to the world "Don't Make Me Over!" back in 1962? It's high time she took her own words of advice. This latter-day butchering of her near perfect earlier recordings, which she will never be able to top, and which quite honestly, true fans realistically don't expect her to- has got to stop. For the love of God, Dionne, please! We beg of you. Enough is enough! You're breaking our hearts.
label: negative

reviewText: As one of the many who have fallen under the spell of Leroy Anderson's ingratiating orchestral miniatures, I looked with much anticipation toward this new Slatkin survey. Unfortunately, I found the pieces have received rather flat performances with little of the bounce and verve that gave them so much life in earlier editions. Can't say for sure whether it's the fault of Slatkin himself or that the members of the BBC Concert Orchestra just miss Anderson's particularly American blend of jazz-twinged light pop. Take not my word for it. Seek out the performances by the composer  himself, available on a budget MCA multi-disc set on Amazon, or the equally fine performances by Arthur Fiedler and the Boston Pops. There, pieces like Fiddle Faddle, Sandpaper Ballet, Bugler's Holiday, Plink Plank Plunk, and the rest, have an effervescent bounce that brings out all of their lyrical charms. There's an earnest quality that comes across, a vitality and direct involvement that is totally lacking in Saltkin's merely dutiful renditions. If you haven't heard those earlier versions, and are relying only on the current set, a whole different world of Leroy Anderson delight awaits you. As far as the Slatkin set  is concerned, I frankly wouldn't waste my time with them.

reviewText:
On his first recording in over 5 years, our beloved Ozzy sounds a little sour. Indeed, this record has more to do with '95 Ozzmosis than any other previous record, with a more modern, contemporary sound. However, what the record gains in punch (the songs definitely slam harder)it looses on the songwriting front, and therefore the record never really strikes a chord for me: Opener "It gets me through" is slamming, but lacks a really good hook; ballad "Dreamer" sounds suspiciously similar to earlier Ozz slow numbers like "Goodbye to romance", "So tired" or "Tonight", but never hits the mark of any of those songs.

And where are Zakk Wylde's guitar heroics of yore? Sure, he plays on the record (or at least he's credited to do so), but by listening to this record, you could never tell. I don't understand why Ozz fired Joe Holmes and brought Zakk back for this... want proof? Listen to "Junkie", "That I never had" or any other song, and then play any song on '91 No more Tears, or even Ozzmosis... there is only noise. Bottom line: Ozzy has given us a record equivalent to Aerosmith "Just Push Play": yes, they sound new, and yes, they may get somewhat more radio airplay... but by doing so, they have forsaken their unique sound and identity... Ozzy and Aerosmith have actually been sharing the same list of songwriting collaborators for the better part of a decade now: Jim Vallance, Steve Dudas, Mark Hudson, Marty Frederiksen... no wonder why they're starting to sound similar...

Bottom Line: this is a mediocre album (as of March 2007, Ozzy himself has PUBLICLY admitted as much...): I've been listening to it for 6 years now, and the damned thing never grew on me, no matter how much I'd listen to it... it is not his worst, but definitely far from his best...if you're a latter day Ozzy fan, you'll want to pick this one up, but if you (like me) are a long time fan, this release will leave you feeling more than a tad disappointed...plain and simple...

reviewText:
When I first heard that Judas Priest was doing a 2 disc concept album I was intrigued, but I had my doubts.  I then heard there would be symphonic elaments.  I thought that could be cool.  Usually when rock and symphonic music mix it can have varying results, but the concept is a good idea.  Unfortunately the album doesn't deliver, for me anyway.

I'll say that I'm not the biggest Priest fan.  I like a few songs off of each album, but there isn't really a whole album that I love.  That being said I was willing to give this a shot.  The first thing that struck me was the lyrics.  I was enjoying the first intro track that blended into the first actual song, but then the chorus of "I am Nostradamus," came in and just threw me off.  I know I like some songs with bad lyrics, but that just didn't fit.  Still I pressed on.  The lyrics didn't improve much, I got sick of every two lines rhyming.  I know it hapens in music, but it got to the point where I was predicting, insert bad nostradamus joke of your choice here, the which words he'd use to rhyme, ask pass and so on.  I would have liked some variation, maybe instead of every two lines rhyming, maybe have two out of four rhyme, in some songs.  When I finnished the first disc, I felt the same as when I'd heard Angel of whatever their previous album's called.  There were some good moments, but nothing really grabbed me.  Also having so many intros became predictable.  Speaking of which why were those seperate tracks anyway?  The last track on this disc kinda did something for me, but there was no chorus, which wouldn't necessarily make it a bad song if it was something progressive that built towards something, but it didn't.  That is one thing this album both discs misses is that song with the great chorus that sticks in your head, it doesn't have to be overly poppy, but memorable.

The second disc was a much more nausiating experience, but it did produce the only two tracks that did anything for me on first listen, Alone and Visions.  On this one they lost what variety they had on disc 1.  Pretty much everything was rediculously slow and boring.  Then there was the title track.  It moved, but again with the Nostradamus over and over again.  I know the album's entitled Nostradamus, but come on at least try to be poetic, rather than beating us over the head with it.

After it was all over, I couldn't help but feel empty.  I gave it more time, and a few songs kinda did something for me.  I like revalation, but Halford's singing in the chorus sounds like he's bored.  That brings me to another thing on this one.  Halford's vocals lack the passion of previous albums, with and without Priest.  This is the same man who gave us Resurrection, a great album.

My last complaint is that the guitars were too far in the background, and I didn't really hear many memorable riffs.  I could elaberate, but I'm tired of typing.

Bands grow and change, sometimes for the better and sometimes not.  I'm not opposed to that, but they have to remember their fans and give them at least a few songs of an older style.  I will say this for them, at least they didn't go alternative pop.  Why people call that growth when a band does that is beyond me.  Songs I like are Visions, Alone, Future of mankind, Revelation, Death, and Pestilence And Plague.  I wanted to wait a while to let this grow on me, but it just didn't.  If you're looking for a metal concept album I'd recomend Iced Earth's Crucible of man.  Actually I'd recomend Iced Earth in general.  They're a great band.

reviewText: I remember hearing this album back when it debuted in the mid-70s. My first reaction was no reaction. After experiencing truly remarkable groups like The Who, Cream, Hendrix and of course, The Beatles, I found Bad Company to be, at best, a decent-sounding garage band. reviewText:
A Public Affair is Jessica Simpson's fourth album, coming a few years after the surprisingly popular In This Skin.  That album basically proved what little worth she has as a recording artist, as every song featured weak, breathy singing about how deeply in love she was her then-husband, boy band refugee Nick Lachey, over incredibly synthetic arrangements.  To coincide with the show Newlyweds on MTV, a new version of the album was released to capitalize on the show's popularity, with a couple of horrid covers thrown into the mix.  Simpson & Lachey have Newlyweds to thank for all of their success, because at best they were third-tier bubblegum pop stars that were likely rescued from having to work the deep fryer at Mickey D's by doing that show.  In This Skin became a huge smash despite being a very weak album - just goes to show you how easily the media can manipulate some people.

After some time off and the dissolution of her marriage, Simpson returns with the release of her fourth album, A Public Affair.  Coming off her last album and her sugary-sweet rendition of "These Boots Are Made For Walkin'", it may surprise some to know that Simpson still seems to be in a state of arrested development.  I'll give her this much - at least she seems to be taking the divorce better than her crybaby ex Lachey, whose album What's Left Of Me is going head to head with Paris Hilton's album for the dubious distinction of Worst Album of 2006.  The title track is a lame ripoff of an unspectacular song (Madonna's "Holiday"), and Simpson's voice is so breathy (and likely computer enhanced as well) that it sounds like she's singing "All the camels coming out for a public affair".  Well, that would be an interesting image to say the least.

Simpson's biggest flaw, besides the weak lyrics and synthetic arrangements, is the fact that her voice still lacks polish.  Not only does she sound like a 12 year old when she sings, but she sounds about as professional as one as well.  Did I mention that the lyrics on this album are awful? For further proof, look to songs like "B.O.Y." and "Push Your Tush" for moments as cringe-inducing as the titles suggest.  The other songs have titles based around simple pronouns - "me", "I, "mine", etc. I guess having your pimp ... er, I mean father boost your ego every day will make you feel like the center of the universe. In addition, thumbs down to the pitiful version of "You Spin Me Round (Like A Record), originally performed by Dead Or Alive.  Simpson has certainly shown a knack for ruining other people's songs over the years - give her that much.  Check out Dope's version to hear a far better cover of that song.

In summary: Move past her heavily made up appearance and ample bosoms (that's the only reason she has any male fans), and you'll see that Jessica Simpson is about as worthless a performer as you'll find.  She has people with clout backing her up that can turn garbage into solid gold, but it's not going to work this time.  Not only does this album lack creativity and depth of any kind, but Simpson as a singer is in the company of hacks like Hilary Duff, Lindsay Lohan, Britney Spears, and yes, her dreadful sister Ashlee.  Anyone could become a recording star if they had a tireless manager like Papa Joe hyping them up.  I think it's safe to say that without the publicity afforded to her by a popular show, this album has a one way ticket to the bargain bin.  Jessica Simpson is nothing but a talentless hot to trot publicity hound - look, she's hooking up with the equally talent-lacking corporate pop star John Mayer ... like anyone that has a life cares.  Pass on A Public Affair unless you enjoy forgettable corporate fluff.
