reviewText:
First, I agree with other reviewers who state a true best of PF would have to be a multi-disc set...
Including masterpieces like Echoes, Shine On, and Atom Heart Mother would require it!

As a longtime fan of the band, I can and will include my "Best Of" compiled from the Discovery Box Set...
Sadly, The Early Singles/Relics were not included in Discovery so I eliminated them from my selections for a single 80min Disc.
A disc of Barrett Floyd & another of Gilmour Floyd would make the best retrospective IMHO...

Discovery Box "Best Of" 79min

01) Astronomy Domine (an epic Syd driven Psych Floyd track that must be included)
02) The Gnome (any Guitar player can appreciate these changes! Syd's Bridge Vocals Rule the tune!)
03) Remember A Day (this one is signature Floyd - incredible flow and emotion)
04) Cymbaline (Gilmour shines on the vocals - nice changes - Live versions EXPLODE)
05) The Narrow Way: Part III (Pt1&2 build up to this fantastic audio assault)
06) Summer '68 (This song simply blows me away and any true Floyd fan would say the same - Wright at his best)
07) A Pillow Of Winds (Lots going in on this multi-layered groove - Gilmour swoons)
08) Wots...Uh The Deal (An acoustic melody and lyrics that completely mesmerize the listener)
09) Childhood's End (The most in your face Rock & Roll Floyd tune ever - Gilmour rips it big time!)
10) Stay (Obscured By Clouds is my favorite PF album & the Wah-Wah work here is so beautiful)
11) Have a Cigar (Hey! This one is on the compilation...lol... It is a really solid tune :o)~
12) Sheep (No big solos here but the gallop of the tune and the chord progression at the end are amazing)
13) Young Lust (The funkiest/disco PF song ever... tops anything else on The Wall for me by far)
14) The Heroes Return (Fletcher Memorial? Really? - The Hero Returns and chops that tune to bits! ROCK!)
15) On The Turning Away (PF struggled in it's 1st post-waters release but they tapped into the magic here)
16) Lost For Words (Sweet Acoustic Riffs and Heartfelt Vocals from Gilmour - Wipe The Slate Clean!)

There it is folks.... My Best Of...
No Dark Side Tracks? Nope... Impossible to break up the immortal album...
I simply can't do it.... It's a single statement!

Hopefully, some of you will use this list to "Discover" some hidden gems in the PF catalog...

reviewText: I mean back in the early-to-mid 'Sixties when they first came out on vinyl? When Capitol got hold of the masters from EMI Parlophone, they saw 14 tracks on these early pre-Pepper albums and said; "Not so fast. American kids don't deserve that much music". Don't forget, rock-oriented youth in those days were seen as potential candidates for juvie. Rock was still being proclaimed from pulpits as Satanic. Capitol was like any other business--run by an older generation who hated and feared their own children. So they decided to trim a couple or three tracks off each and make some extra albums. Bleed off a little more of that paper route and babysitting money. Kind of an audio version of the way they water down beers from that part of the world when they hit this side of the pond. They wound up just saying the h/e/l/l with it and retitled all Beatle albums previous to "Rubber Soul". Remember when CDs first came out? Us Yank brats finally were liberated from the tyranny and venomous age-ism of the Generation Gap (now that we were thirtysomething and too old to be victimized by it anymore) and were offered the original Parlophone releases as the Fab Four and Brian Epstein intended them. I promptly bought ALL of 'em, despite what I'd heard about clumsy editing on the first Rolling Stones CDs. These "American Releases" are NOT--repeat--NOT real Beatle albums. I'd say the so-called "nostalgic value" of these releases is more than countered by them being bitter reminders of ripoffs past.

reviewText:
Dream Theater remains the best progressive rock band of all time, but Octavarium falls flat on so many levels it's embarrassing. Why did this album ever see the light of day?
Sure, it has hints of what it could have been. Some of the music is fantastic and has a great hook. Octavarium goes in places no other Dream Theater record has.
Unfortunately, these moments are few and far between.
This is a monotonous album, almost agonizing to listen to. Just when you think a song is going to really kick in, it instead drops heavy. No song ever really draws you in. And quite frankly, I had to force myself to listen to the 20-some minute epic song "Octavarium," which had only a brief splash of interest at the end.
On top of that, the lyrics are almost painful to listen to. Dream Theater is much more talented than this. There are so many cliches in these lyrics and really, such a level of cheese, I felt embarrassed listening to them.
Dream Theater had a lot to build off of after "Train of Thought." It's always exciting to see which direction they'll go in next. I didn't realize they'd go the direction of boring.
The band has said they recorded this album to sound like "Images and Words." Nice to say, but far from true. This album has no appeal like I&W, or Metropolis II, or Six Degrees. It has nothing in common with any previous DT album except the equally subpar "Falling Into Infinity."
Perhaps James LaBrie saved all the best material for his excellent solo record. But this is one Dream Theater fan who is extremely disappointed with this disaster.

reviewText:
It hurts me to say every word of this, but the new Dave Matthews Band album is a complete let down. As a dedicated fan since 1994, it hurts me in so many ways to write here that this album should not be purchased, let alone listened to.
I looked forward to this band's next release with great anticipation for well over a year. With every little piece of information that leaked out about the up-coming release of a new DMB album in 2000 I grew more excited. However, the more time it took to create the album and the more times its release date was pushed back, the more doubtful I became. But then I found taped material from the summer tour last year and caught them live toward the end of their tour. The new material was fantastic and listening to its progress from shows at the beginning of the tour to the very last show proved how well they developed their new material. I was hyped and excited about what they could then do with it in the studio.
But when they scraped the entire work they had done with producer Steve Lillywhite and the studio recordings from Virginia and decided to head out to Los Angeles to work with Glen Ballard, I began to worry. And now, several months later, after having listened to "Everyday" several times, I know for sure that my worries were, in fact, grounded. "Everyday" is terrible. All of the songs are written by Dave Matthews alone and were written over the course of 12 days; they definitely feel that way. None of the songs grab me in a way that would cause me to wear out the CD like all of their previous releases have. The lyrics are uninspired and the music feels completely rushed with no feeling in them. "When The World Ends" and "Everyday" are the only decent tracks, but still pale in comparison to all of their other work. These two tracks are both ended much too soon, but can possibly be salvaged in concert. The rest of the CD isn't worth mentioning.
In just the few days that I've owned it, I can no longer bring myself to listen to "Everyday." Not when I know that there are studio recordings in the world of such great new songs as "Grey Street," "Grace Is Gone," "Bartender," "Sweet Up And Down," "Busted Stuff," "Raven," "Digging A Ditch," and "JTR."
"Everyday" is the Dave Matthews Band equivalent to Van Halen's "III;" it just shouldn't exist, because they are capable of so much more.

I remember my brother reviewing R. Kelly's latest album TP.3 Reloaded and giving it a one-and-a-half-star rating, and I asked him, "R. Kelly's album is really that bad?" He said yes, but I still listened to the album for myself and, well, he was right.

Not only is this album too long (75 minutes), but you can tell that there is only one thing on Kelly's mind: sex. This album gets so sexual that even the guys in Silk would say, "Okay, we get the point, man!" But the bad thing isn't merely the sexuality of the songs; it's how stupid the songs are. This is obvious when Kells shoots for sexual metaphors like "Sex Weed" and what is probably the worst song of his career, "Remote Control". Here, I guess since Ron Isley wasn't available, Rrah does his best Mr. Biggs impression himself, and he kicks the entire song in falsetto, making the song painful on the ears. In fact, that song is so bad that I had to stop in the middle of it.

Things aren't any better when Kells makes songs for the club, because they all sound like reheated "Fiesta" remixes. Not only that, but he's RAPPING again on "Girls Go Crazy" (featuring Baby). "Burn It Up" kind of sounds like Akon's "Bananza" (which is a bad song in itself), and "Hit It Til the Mornin'" is a bad song made worse by a guest spot by Do Or Die, of all people.

Other travesties include "In the Kitchen" and "Put My T-Shirt On". And I can't even say that the five-part epic "Trapped In the Closet" saves the album because I never even liked Chapter 1; plus the chapters get stupider as they go on. The only song out of this whole disc that I can even stand is "Touchin'". Although I have no idea how Nivea got on this album, she and R. have good chemistry on the song.

There's another song, the confessional "Kickin' It With Your Girlfriend", where the first verse begins with: "Go on and slap me again." And that's exactly what I want to do to Kells for even letting this album see the light of day. If you were unfortunate enough to buy this, just bury it somewhere and forget it ever happened.

Anthony Rupert

P.S. In response to another reviewer, Pretty Ricky is a group, not one person.

reviewText:
Let me first state that I have been a die-hard Queensryche fan since I first heard "Take Hold Of The Flame" on the old Metal Shop radio show way back when The Warning was a new release, and I have bought everything they've released since - up until now. Fortunately I was able to listen to this sonic turd before making what would've easily become the most disappointing record purchase of my life, a record mercifully (and ironically) still held by Geoff Tate's (first) solo album. Listening to this all the way through was a very painful experience.

It saddens me to see the band I once considered to be the Pink Floyd of heavy metal reduced to this: The Geoff Tate Experience. This is NOT a "Queensryche" record, but is instead part 2 of GT's aforementioned abyssmal solo record ego-stroke. Clearly, this man desperately needs an equal, a Chris DeGarmo-like, STRONG musical foil to contribute heavily in the songwriting department; left to his (and his cronies') own devices, he's just not a very good songwriter, and Kelly Gray just makes matters worse. That guy never fit in with this band, and is no better fit as a producer/engineer. The same goes for Slater. Wilt couldn't have had anything to do with these songs, could he? Was he sick during the songwriting process or something?!

Anyway, suffice to say this is one EXTREMELY ill-conceived, poorly-executed and just plain miserable effort by a "band" that used to be one of the very best the genre has ever seen and has no business being released as anything other than a Geoff Tate solo record, it's THAT bad.

Sad... truly, sad. Seriously, time to pull the plug, guys, and you have no idea how much it pains me to say that!

reviewText:
Ex- Guns N Roses & Velvet Revolver bassist Duff McKagan serves up another offering from his self named "Loaded" project, which if you go by the reviews posted on-line is a very good album.  McKagan's punk influences have always shone through in his music right back from early GNR days, and now that he is able to steer his own ship those influences have come to the fore even more.  This album has quite a degree of punk overtone and as such it sounds quite raw and full of attitude, the latter for which McKagan has become renowned.  The result of making such an album though is that the production sounds quite noisy and chaotic.  I actually quite like a certain degree of "rawness" which I believe is severely lacking in a lot of music produced in today's digital age and McKagan should be commended for bringing this quality through, but the overall sound here is just not appealing to me at all because it's just too noisy.  I also think that part of the problem with the sound is that generally speaking the songs just aren't that good either.  Maybe I could have handled the sound better if the songs themselves were better, but with production like this and bad song writing it makes for a pretty poor album overall in my opinion, and not one that should be a contender for my top five 2011 albums in the slightest.

It doesn't help when the man really hasn't been blessed with a decent voice, and certainly what McKagan lacks in vocal ability he makes up for in attitude and effort, but that alone isn't enough for me when this album also has the previously mentioned detriments.  As far as the songs themselves go the whole album in my opinion consists of pretty poor stuff that doesn't really rate a repeated listen, with a few exceptions in the songs Executioner's Song, Dead Skin, We Win, and Indian Summer.  However these four songs are by no means anything special, in fact they're just pretty average really.  And as for the last song Follow Me To Hell ...well we really do with that one, it's just awful.

So with Velvet Revolver on indefinite hiatus and apparently no likelihood of a GNR originals reunion on the horizon at all, McKagan is highly unlikely to get any sort of mainstream success anywhere near the level he has achieved previously by releasing this kind of stuff.  (He probably doesn't need to or even care to now though, he's been there and done that so now he can release what he wants so good luck to him in that respect).  This album does have its fans and the on-line reviews are testament to this, but I suspect the majority of fans will generally either be fans of punk music (or those who don't mind a good dose of it), or those who themselves are "loaded" when they listen to it.  For someone like me who grew up on NWOBHM & hair metal, then later became a fan of power metal, Euro-metal, symphonic metal and other sub-genres, the hard rock/punk genre has little appeal at all, and this album does nothing to change that.  (Plus the cover is a rip-off of Accept's Objection Overruled album, McKagan has just used 2 of the same hand).  So my advice is listen to it before you buy it.
label: negative

reviewText:
I'm glad to see that ninjas aren't buying into this garbage album.  Just because it's a Psychopathic Records release, doesn't mean it is any good, and it is alright to reject it.  This album is a perfect example.

The production is garbage.  The beats are weak, none of them give a gangster rap vibe that Blaze is known for.  When you think of Blaze, you expect a powerful and ruthless gangster sound.  These beats sound like b-sides from Violent J's solo album.  Speaking of Violent J, most of the songs were written by him, and sound as if they were inteded for him.

The rapping is soft, weak, and unorthodox for Blaze.  It sounds like Blaze's version of Violent J's rap style.

The guest spots are a massive letdown, especially the KMK track "Ride the Whip".  On paper, that sounds like a hype, slamming, street pounding track, but it's quiet, the raps are soft....another letdown.

Overall, the album is a failure and a step in the wrong direction for Blaze.  1 Less G in Da Hood and Clockwork Gray are what Blaze is about and I hope he returns to that style for future projects.

**UPDATE** 3-May-2011

After the release of the Gang Rags Extended version, that puts the final nail in the coffin for this album.  The bonus disc contains WAY BETTER songs.  Blaze's initial title for this album was "The Last House on Dead Street", it looks like all those songs were scrapped for Gang Rags.  The bonus disc's songs should have been released as the album instead of this pile of crap.  Songs like S**t's F**ked up, Napalm, Give'em What They Want, Simply Fresh, and Zombie King are way better than anything on Gang Rags.  If you have the means, get the bonus disc instead and pretend this album never happened.

reviewText: The 5.1 suround sound mix of this great classic hard rock album is horrible. I can't believe that Rush put so much time and money into the new cover art, great packaging and the very cool comic strip that goes along with the story line of this great concept album but when it came to the 5.1 surround mix they gave up. There's only a horrible reverb effect through the rear speakers. The 2 front speakers and the center speaker sound alot like the original stereo version. No effort to the rear. The 2112 Overture is one of greatest hard rock instrumentals of all time. There was no effort put into the 5.1 mix to have different guitar, bass or drum sections move around or behind you which is what a 5.1 surround sound mix is all about.  The packaging is awesome. The new cover art is awesome. The remastered stereo CD is better than the DVD as far as the over all sound is concerned. I took the Remastered CD and played it through Dolby Prologic (fake 5.1 surround sound) through my surround sound system and it sounds better than the DVD 5.1 surround mix does. The Fly By Night DVD that comes with the Sector 1 Rush box set that was released before this sounds alot better. At least By-Tor And The Snow Dog from the Fly By Night DVD audio 5.1 mix offers Geddy Lee's bass and Alex Lifeson's guitar moving back and forth in the rear speakers behind you during the battle section of the song. The whole Fly By Night DVD audio has a great 5.1 mix. I can't believe I waited so long to hear 2112 in 5.1 surround and this is what Rush released.  Buy Rush Sector 1,2 and 3 for the DVD surround versions of Fly By Night, A Farewell To Kings and Signals. They sound alot better mixed in 5.1 surround than 2112 does. Sorry to say. 2112 is too great of an album to have been mixed in 5.1 surround sound this poorly.
label: negative

reviewText:
Bryan Adams has been around for 28 years, sold millions of albums, and is now 48 years of age. He's managed to stay around for almost 30 years while others have faded away. He's managed to remain a celebrity enigma as well, since I can't think in all of these years too many interviews with him, nor interviews revealing much about himself.

"11" is his eleventh studio album in 28 years, but I have many issues to take Mr. Adams to task about.

Does "11" have any memorable melodies? No. Does "11" have interesting lyrics? No. Does "11" have anything to offer in terms of entertainment value? No. Could you, in effect, play "11" in the background of some party and no one would remember it? Yes.

There are no melodies like "Cuts Like A Knife", "This Time", "Straight From The Heart", "Summer Of '69", "Somebody", "Run To You", "One Night Love Affair", "It's Only Love", "Heaven", "In The Heat Of The Night", "Victim Of Love", "Hearts On Fire", "Everything I Do, I Do It For You", "All For One", "Please Forgive Me", "Have You Ever Really Loved A Woman", "On A Day Like Today" etc., etc.

Let's be frank. Bryan Adams has never been a brilliant lyricist, and "11" is no food for thought. Just look at the titles..."Broken Wings"--isn't that a Mr. Mister song? "She's Got A Way"--isn't that a Billy Joel song? "Mysterious Ways"--isn't that a U2 song? "The Way Of The World"--isn't that a Genesis song? "I Thought I'd Seen Everything"--wait a minute isn't  that a Bryan Adams song? Oh right, "Thought I'd Died And Gone To Heaven", that's it.

What is so annoying about Bryan Adams is that he has never taken a musical risk in 28 years. It's always the same. It's like a fast food. You think it might taste good, so you buy it. Only to find that it was truly unsatisfying and you wish you could take back your money. There's nothing nutritious, and a day later you've forgotten you even ate it.

This might sound like harsh criticism, but come on! You Bryan Adams fans are really going to get behind "11"? You're going to give it five stars? It's better than "Reckless"? Or better than "Waking Up The Neigbours". Are you really going to say that "11" is the best thing Adams has done? At 48, is Adams really writing great songs like he used to? Some of the lyrics are downright childish and adolescent.

Let's go to the numbers. After "Waking Up The Neighbours" in 1991, every album Adams has released in the states has been diminishing financial returns. I mean "18 'Til I Die" (1996), "On A Day Like Today" (1998) and "Room Service" (2004) combined haven't sold as much as "Reckless" sold in 1984/1985. Yet, he still manages to woo the Europeans for some reason, and THEY think WE have bad taste in music?

"18 'Til I Die" was the last Adams album that had an American hit on it, and it was tacked on from a movie soundtrack, meaning it wasn't originally intended for the album. "On A Day Like Today" didn't have a hit, and "Room Service" didn't have a hit. Why is this? Could it be, that like "11", they don't have that old Bryan Adams magic?

Believe it or not, I have stuck with Adams for the past 25 years, but I'm not going to gush about the atrophied state of his musical career. I dare Bryan Adams to do something unexpected and interesting. I dare him after 28 years to come up with something so unique and original that he wins back the millions of fans who have fallen asleep and forgotten about him in America. Even my wife can't remember the last time she heard something from him, and she has trouble remembering a song from Bryan Adams because it has been so long since he made good music.

So there you have it. Give me the negative votes for being honest, but "11" is the worst. I listened to it every day this week, and I couldn't wait to get it out of my player, which is not how I felt about "Reckless".
label: negative

reviewText: Its simply mind boggling how many people rate this release as quality material. This CD simply is ill suited to Eric's guitar based bluesy style. Eric's guitar has no power and many times it is barely even heard from. Don't get me wrong, Eric Clapton has recorded many soft sounding gems such as Let It Grow, Wonderful Tonight, Lay Down Sally, and Believe In Life from his latest release. However none of the songs on Pilgrim even come close to his best work.  The major problem with this album is the over-reliance on drum machines and synthesizers. Do you realize that eleven of the fourteen tracks have no live drums? Also eight of the fourteen tracks rely on a stringed orchestra background. I do not think Eric Clapton recorded eight tracks with strings in a studio on all his other recordings combined. Combine all this with a hip hop beat from track to track and the result is just plain bad! Almost to the point of taking a Sirloin Steak and covering it with Chocolate Yogurt! I could understand if Eric Clapton wanted to recorded a couple of hip-hop/dance oriented tracks on a record. That would be tolerable as long as Eric's signature guitar sound was still front and center. However, Eric's blues roots are mostly smothered here. Eric's style sounds best in a raw environment with a few mellow tracks mixed in for stylistic diversity. Circus and the cover of Born In Time are pretty good songs and River of Tears and She's Gone have decent structures, but the rest just represents Eric so poorly. Gosh, the version of Going Down Slow is butchered beyond the imagination. I did see Eric Clapton in concert and in a live setting with live instruments, the Pilgrim songs are soooo much better. Heck River of Tears was even a concert highlight with some scorching guitar solos and strong drumming. However, the music quality of this release is still substandard. Please Eric....you do not have to resort to appeasing the masses of this artificial style of music. Be your own man and record the music that comes from your soul.

reviewText:
... and then you're rotten.
Okay, it pains me to write such a negative review of "Ripe."  After the wonderful "Awake is the New Sleep" I felt Ben might finally deliver on the tremendous potential he demonstrated on "Grandpaw Would" and to a lesser degree on "Something to Remember Me By" and in his Noise Addict days.  Alas, 'twas not to be.
"Ripe" sounds like a demo tape for a new Brady Bunch movie (you know, a bad remake, like the "Bewitched" movie a couple years ago).  What decade is it, Ben?  The drum machine, the facile lyrics, the formulaic tempo transitions ... <sigh>
Let's look at the tracks:
1. Love Me Like The World Is Ending - okay, the album starts with arguably its strongest pop track, but hasn't Ben sung this song -- like four or five times already -- under a different title?
2. American Television - Play this and then listen to Kim Wilde's "Kids in America" ... at least she sang "Kids" in the 1980s -- which is where this song belongs.
3. Birds And Bees - I was wondering if Ben Lee weren't perhaps mocking Mandy Moore with this song.  It is ... awful.  The spoken lines only make the song more embarrassing.  This song should have never been allowed to be recorded.  It is a song where listening to it once, all the way through, is more than enough.  The fifth time?  It is like fingernails on a blackboard ....
4. Is This How Love Is Supposed To Feel - a nasal whining track with the droning beat of the drum machine.
5. Blush - probably the best track of the disc.  Nice sound, clever lyrics.  Reminiscent of Traveling Wilburys at their best.
6. Numb - I've wondered what Ben is trying to say with this song.  Perhaps this awful album is because he is angry at his label and is simply fulfilling his contract with a bunch of half-baked songs?  In any case this song is McCartneyesque, but certainly a post-Beatles McCartney.
7. What Would Jay-Z Do? - C'mon - the "What would ______ do?" joke became annoying about 15 years ago.  Is this the spiritual awakening you've been boasting about, Ben?
8. Sex Without Love - A dreadful tune.  Perhaps if this were released in the 80s it would've gotten some airplay at middle school dances after Frankie Goes to Hollywood's "Relax."
9. Home - "I'm tired of being alooone, I want to take you hoooome" ... with lyrics like this and contrived bridges this song is nearly unlistenable.  Reminds me of songs on demo tracks of bands that *don't* get contracts.
10. So Hungry - A forgettable track.  Nothing there.
11. Just Say Yes - Another anthem.  Why is Ben writing arena rock when his concerts are in bars (where he generally makes for a delightful evening of entertainment)?
12. Ripe - Not bad.  If you can make it this far.
If you like saccharin, over-produced, droning music that insults your intelligence, go ahead and buy "Ripe."  If you like Ben Lee, do yourself a favor ... keep it that way by not buying this disc.  Get "Awake" or "Grandpaw" if you don't already have them.

reviewText: It's very interesting to scroll through the reviews of Russell Watson's debut CD, because they basically fall into two categories; 1) people who are "in the know" when it comes to music and performing, (in other words, they've had some type of music training themselves), or 2) people who have no idea what's going on on this CD, but they "know what they like when they hear it", and get bitterly resentful when people tell them that something is afoul in Watson's performance.  Well, add me to the growing list of Type One.  When it comes to musical performances, there are things that you do and don't do.  If you are singing in a foreign language, you do research and find out the CORRECT pronunciations of the words.  You try and find pieces that are within your realm of capability, and you DON'T try and sing things that are out of your league, too early in the game.  And you also do not adapt a "look at me" attitude by calling your first project "The Voice", especially when you do NOT have the skills to back it up.  Just because you can sing high A's and B flats, does NOT mean you automatically have the chops to perform a piece like "Nessun Dorma" or "La Donna e Mobile".  (Case in point; listen to the recording of "La Donna e Mobile" on the "Three Mo' Tenors" debut album, and you'll hear how the cadenza-like section at the end of the song is SUPPOSED to sound; EVERY note can be heard clearly on their version.  When Russell Watson sings this same section, the scale passage becomes a sloppy slur of notes, which is not acceptable for this piece at all.)  To put it in a different context, just because you can jump high enough to touch the rim of the basketball net, doesn't mean you can go out and join the NBA!  I fully expect to get razzed for criticizing poor Mr. Watson, but I hope some of you will actually stop and think about WHY those of us who are musicians in our own right are upset with this release. I feel it's absurd that an untrained musician should be able to waltz into Decca Records and get a contract, when there are so many others in the world who have worked hard at their craft, and are much better at it, yet they go unnoticed.  Yes, Mr Watson has a potentially powerful voice, but it certainly cannot be referred to as THE voice; it is untrained and it shows.  Maybe not to the casual listener, as some of these other reviews attest, but regardless, the problems are there.  You can hear the tension in his voice when he goes for the high notes; if he keeps this kind of thing up, he won't HAVE a voice in a few years.  It simply will not hold up to the kind of abuse he's inflicting on it.  I would challenge customers to listen to this CD alongside some of the great voices of our time, or for that matter, of other eras as well. Browse through classical or vocal sections of music stores, and take the time to seek out artists who KNOW their craft and have actually spent time shaping it. Maybe you'll start to hear what the rest of us are hearing.....or NOT hearing, as the case may be.
label: negative

reviewText:
This is the debut from Eamon, a guy who can be described as a cross between Eminem and someone from one of those faceless pseudo R&B boy groups from the early '90s (like Color Me Badd or All 4 One).  If your idea of entertainment is melodramatic singing and the vocabulary of a fifth-grader over synthetic music and beats, then I Don't Want You Back might be your new favorite album!
The album's obvious centerpiece is the title track - this is the reason why it's selling like hotcakes.  Here's a little piece of information you might want to think about if you take this song to heart - you noticed that just shortly after this song hit the radio, the guy's "ex-girlfriend" Frankee recorded a response song that's even more dopey and contrived than this track.  Don't even tell me that these two didn't have something brewing - I get the feeling that this "couple" (assuming they ever were one - heck, they might still be together!) came up with a marketing scheme to sell albums, which they needed considering their lack of talent.  Rather than trying to address what went wrong in an intelligent light, the song (and the response song) is filled with an endless stream of obscenities - no wonder why kids are eating this stuff up.
The rest of the album is as pointless as Los Del Rio's album was - it's basically just one song surrounded by sound-alike songs which are ready made should the album's centerpiece become a smash hit.  Therefore, if you fell for the stunt and actually enjoy the hit single, you'll like the rest of the album provided you don't mind a bunch of inferior retreads.
In summary: An overrated new artist that needed to cook up a publicity stunt in order to generate sales for himself.  Don't buy into the hype - there's far better stuff out there regardless of your genre of choice.

You know what "deja vu" refers to, but what about the meaning of "vu deja"? Vu deja can occur when you go to a new place for the first time and you know, that you have never been there before.

This is a very weak, boring and extremely short CD. John may have hit the wall and the glory days are behind him now.  Other reviewers claim that he is now relaxed and doing the family thing, etc.  This may be true but with a high price and a determent to the previous edgy and unhappy Fogerty.  The drive, desire, passion and hunger for perfection has now resulted to a thing of the past.  Before you know it, John will be another lounge singer, just like Rod Stewart.  I can't believe that it took him seven(7) years to record ten(10) songs.  To me, this was the most disappointing part of Deja Vu.  You be your own judge and see if you agree with me that he could have put this together in seven (7) weeks or less!

Mr. CCR must take a hard look at himself and realize that he needs someone else to produce and have new material written for him.  If his ego is too great to accept this then I can only pray that next CD will be less than 30 minutes long and will take John 8 years to put it together.

I wish he would duplicate his Blue Ridge Rangers theme.  I have played this CD more than any other piece of music that I own.  Whenever I play it and someone near by has not heard it before, they will immediately buy their own copy.

Jake

reviewText:
Reviewer "R. Diaz" of Seattle has posted three Humble Pie reviews.  As he posted on this page, one assumes he purchased this Fillmore Japan edition.

This release is an older, jewel case CD that has been re-pressed for years in Japan.  As the Japan CD market is far smaller than the U.S.'s, Japan companies constantly re-press CD's in far smaller quantities.  Yes, it is the same master that is used for the U.S. domestic version, and yes, it sucks... but it's NOT the 2007 remaster, which I assure you, is phenomenal.

Unfortunately, the 2007 remaster, which was only released in mini-sleeve format, was sold out when it originally streeted in Japan and never made it into Amazon inventory.  As of this writing, it has not been re-pressed.  However, many people, including myself, have posted reviews on the 2007 remasters, quite rightly raving about them.

So, "R" just picked the only other Japan release he could find on Amazon without matching the release date.  Then he compounded the problem by mistakenly posting an erroneous review, which, unfortunately by the vote count, is now also erroneously influencing other readers.  Hopefully, "R" will read this, and correct his mistake, by removing his review.

I have loaded the image for the 2007 Japan mini-sleeve remaster above, and as you can see, the OBI is completely different.

WHAT IS A JAPAN "MINI-LP-SLEEVE" CD?

Have you ever lamented the loss of one of the 20th Century's great art forms, the 12" vinyl LP jacket? Then "mini-LP-sleeve" CD's may be for you.

Mini-sleeve CDs are manufactured in Japan under license. The disc is packaged inside a 135MM X 135MM cardboard precision-miniature replica of the original classic vinyl-LP album. Also, anything contained in the original LP, such as gatefolds, booklets, lyric sheets, posters, printed LP sleeves, stickers, embosses, special LP cover paper/inks/textures and/or die cuts, are precisely replicated and included. An English-language lyric sheet is always included, even if the original LP did not have printed lyrics.

Then, there's the sonic quality: Often (but not always), mini-sleeves have dedicated remastering (20-Bit, 24-Bit, DSD, K2/K2HD, and/or HDCD), and can often (but not always) be superior to the audio on the same title anywhere else in the world. There also may be bonus tracks unavailable elsewhere.

Each Japan mini-sleeve has an "obi" ("oh-bee"), a removable Japan-language promotional strip. The obi lists the Japan street date of that particular release, the catalog number, the mastering info, and often the original album's release date. Bonus tracks are only listed on the obi, maintaining the integrity of the original LP artwork. The obi's are collectable, and should not be discarded.

All mini-sleeve releases are limited edition, but re-pressings/re-issues are becoming more common (again, not always). The enthusiasm of mini-sleeve collecting must be tempered, however, with avoiding fake mini-sleeves manufactured in Russia and distributed throughout the world, primarily on eBay. They are inferior in quality, worthless in collectable value, a total waste of money, and should be avoided at all costs.

reviewText:
I went to see Dream Theater last night. Overall, I can easily say that Dream Theater is comprised of 5 of the best musicians living on planet Earth today. Jordan Rudess is equal parts Jon Lord (of the almighty Deep Purple for those of nu-metal breeding), Beethoven and a carnival organist. His sense of timing and rhythm is unparrelled and he outshines even Dream Theater's prior keyboard wizards. Jon Myung plays bass as if he was learning scales in the womb. His fingers move effortlessly up and down the neck of his six string low-end instrument and he fails to make even a minor mistake. John Pettrucci is comfortably one of music's greatest axemen. His sense of melody and catchy hooks are combined flawlessly with his astute technical mastery. Mike Portnoy...one cannot watch his octapus arms flail about a dum kit in anything other than complete awe. In short, Mike Portnoy doesn't make mistakes and he is probably the best drummer of our generation. Finally, James LaBrie is, according to Dream Theater's website, a classically trained vocalist who still takes lessons when not touring or recording. His range ability is on par and even more defined than some of music's most famous vocalists.
What is the point of talking about Dream Theater in a review like this? Take a look at the bands on this CD. Generally, they have all been categorized by the media as "metal" and I've read countless articles and interviews with various members of the bands listed who complain about their loack of exposure is comparison to mainstream pop, despite being all over radio and video all the time. Unloco I've never heard before so I'll leave it at that, though I've heard that they are nu-metal through and through. Taproot is color-by-numbers rap rock and members of that band have even expressed their uninterest in most rock and metal altogether. Chevelle is probably the brightest spot on this CD. That being said, they still bear most traits that I despise in modern rock music and comparing them to Quicksand and Helmet insults those that they liken themselves after. Disturbed is obviously the main headliner here. Admittedly, I do admire the persistance that they displayed in getting to where they are but at what expense to "metal". They fashion themselves as the next evolutionary step in the genre while concurrently pounding out three note songs with little or no tempo changes, improvisation or leads. The songs that Disturbed are championed for are bland, unoriginal and rely mostly on guitar sound than pushing the envelope.
I've seen Chevelle and Disturbed live. I've seen what they do time and time again on TV and on heard it on radio and so on. I've also been a fan of the metal genre for over 15 years and grew up with Iron Maiden, Anthrax, Slayer and King Diamond and never do I hear the aforementioned nu-bands play anything remotely close to as intersting or technically-challenging as the metal greats that I have mentioned. As metal has progressed from the Iron Maiden's and Slayer's to the Dream Theater's and Cynic's of the genre, the band's that comprise this compilation seem to take the most simplistic and unoriginal parts of rock's more mainstream acts and formulate their own take on the matter and in the process make fans hand over fist that seemingly will move on to the next trend as the masses never fail in doing. If you want to experience some truly challenging and exciting new music, give bands like Soilwork, Dream Theater, Iced Earth, Clutch, Meshuggah or Lamb Of God a listen.

reviewText: After listening to their last album, I wrote Midtown off as another whiny pop-punk band that was just barely ahead of Simple Plan in terms of maturity.  Then someone told me on their new album, Midtown was going to be trying things a little harder and with a little more social consciousness.  Sadly I somehow believed this could be true.  On Forget What You Know, Midtown has apparently aimed for a Bad Religion level of self-rightousness(especially the song God is Dead), but they still come off with the same vapidness that their mall punk peers are chock full of. The lyrics obviously had a point behind them somewhere, but they're mild and sometimes meaningless. "Don't You Know..." is a good example of this.  The title hints at substance, but the song opens with the line "Baby spare me your pretension, I know you can't spread an infection," and the rest of the song is pretty much the same senseless crap. But how much can you expect from a band that avidly supports PETA, one of the most ridiculous fringe groups in America?  There are so many more important things to worry about in this country than whether or not poultry and dairy farmers are exploiting their animals. War, terrorism, invasion of privacy, our rapid loss of free speech. There's plenty of good subject matter out there, but they avoided anything too specific. Musically, this album isn't a great departure from their old sound. Yeah, they're trying to sound a little harder, but it's really the same old Midtown.  I'd suggest you buy the new Bad Religion (or any old Bad Religion for that matter) or wait and get the new Sparta album.  I could've given three stars, but I know there will be plenty of 12-16 year olds who'll give it five stars, and hardly any album deserves five stars, especially not Midtown.  And for the reviewer who suggested I compared this band to Simple Plan, please grow up and look at what I said.  I said they were barely ahead of Simple Plan in terms of maturity. I never said they sounded alike. That was in reference to their last album anyway, not this one.

reviewText:
I listen through every CD I buy at least once to verify that it isn't defective, no matter how bad it is.  I broke with tradition on this collection of Pink Floyd dropout Syd Barrett's "Best."  I didn't miss Syd Barrett's songs.

I give this 1 Star instead of Zero Stars.  Only because for some strange reason, Barrett decided to write a real song--Bob Dylan Blues--and though it remained unreleased until this compilation, it's the best tune here. It has an actual chord progression, sardonic lyrics, and should be covered by somebody with more than a $5.00 studio budget.  Is it real or is it Memorex?  I think it's Memorex--or somebody's cassette recorder.

The rest of this alleged cream of the Barrett corpus is Barrett's one BB ricocheting around in his head.  He knew (more or less) how to fit in lyrics, and there's an occasional bar or two of interesting music (undoubtedly played by someone else).  This isn't experimental music--these are songs by someone whose aesthetic is so wrapped up in his own mind that he doesn't know or care that he can't communicate anything to other human beings.

This can't be the worst music ever recorded--given the mountain of recorded music, there has to be material even worse.  Had Barrett been a struggling musician who showed up at a studio with these songs, he'd never get near a fried tube.  But his early membership in Pink Floyd gave him some credibility and enough fans to support releasing his creations.  I'd rather listen to Alvin and the Chipmunks cover The Archies.

I'm sure this review is heresy to those who regard Barrett as a genius, but anyone expecting to hear how Pink Floyd would have sounded if Barrett had remained on board is in for disappointment.
label: negative

reviewText:
I couldn't agree more with Dan Davis' review of this terrible disc.  Thank goodness I didn't buy it, and only had a chance to the 2nd concerto on the radio.  What a frustrating experience it was.  Just as I felt when I heard his anemic account of the Tchaikovsky 1st on radio, I was so angry when the last note sounded and I heard it was Lang Lang. I was enraged. Like my professor used to tell me, I really don't have time for mediocrity.  It pains me to see that every time I go to the classical section or a concert hall, there are fewer and fewer young people.  It pains me to see how terrible of a shape classical music is in now, and it just seems to get worse and worse.  This recording is a symptom of this viscious downward spiral.  Large record companies continue to record the same warhorses and continue to promote mediocre "stars."  Seriously, do we really need another Rach 2nd concerto (or the Rhapsody) when we have such wonderful recordings by (in no particular order) Kissin, Ashkenazy, Jando, Cliburn, etc.?  We need more recordings of Alkan, Busoni piano concerto, Sorabji, Roslavets, Medtner, and all those worderful composers in the Naxos American Classics and Milken Archive series, to name a few.  We don't need another new Beethoven Symphony cycle or Vivaldi 4 Seasons or Bach Branderburg Concertos or, in this case, another Rachmaninov 2nd concerto.  Although Hough's recent Rachmaninov cycle for Hyperion was a tremendous effort, perhaps the greatest cycle ever produced and in complete agreement with David Hurwitz in his ClassicsToday.com review, I'm not so sure the recording did much to classical music.

In order to tap the world's largest market, Deutche Grammaphone is aggressively promoting Yundi Li and Lang Lang.  While progressive record companies like Naxos and Hyperion try to move the field forward by continuing to produce exciting new music and projects (while promoting first-rate pianists like Hamelin, Howard, Hough, Demidenko, Lane, Biret, Jando, Sherbakov--all whom are better than the two mentioned), large traditional companies continue to promote mediocre artists and record the same, over-played, warhorses.  How pitiful!

Going back to this CD.  It adds nothing to what has already been done countless of times before.  Mediocre sound + mediocre orchestral accompaniment + solidly mediocre piano playing = a terrible disc and a complete waste of time.  Please stay away from this disc and save your money!

reviewText: When this album came out I was thrilled. I love the dancehall style and Buju is a master. Let me also say that slackness in the genre didn't bother me too much in the past since we can go back decades in reggae to Iroy and Max Romeo and find it there too. I also gave Buju a pass on Boom Bye Bye because, like lots of fans, figured that conscious lyrics were all that we were going to get from now on. But here, on what I believe is otherwise his best album since Til Shiloh in terms of style and content, homophobia reappears.  You'll find it in the song "Nothing": "Nothing in a underpants and nothing in a brief, nothing in a single it must can repeat, gal pickney alone can make me feel sweet." First line, what we find in underpants and briefs is obvious, second line is in thinly veiled code, what can do in a single or repeat, a little critical listening makes it clear he is talking about a gun, and in case the audience missed the meaning of those first two lines Buju gives us the context we need: "Gal pickney alone can make me feel sweet".  I can't abide anymore homophobia in the dancehall and once I deciphered the lyric I was really crushed.  I hate that dancehall is dying but it's dying because of hate towards gays and lesbians and I can't support it.  This is a real blow, I can't listen to "Complaint", "Murderer", "Close one yesterday" or any of his other  excellent songs that touched my heart now without it breaking.  We need reggae artists to stand up and make clear unequivocal statements against murder lyrics or the genre is going to continue to decline outernationally.

reviewText:
Record label/artist problem: It's 1977, and Columbia's Leonard Cohen is ten years worth of famous in folk circles for singing his own lyrics, mostly with a minimum of adornment. The songs are poetic, novelistic, sometimes strange but compelling. His voice, imperfect for sure, is however quite believable. Even his songs which are obviously pure fiction sound like autobiography...not altogether a bad thing in a singer/songwriter. The perceived trouble is: How to expand his audience, and offer something fresh to the public in his next LP?

Solution arrived at: Get hot rock/R&B producer and arranger Phil Spector to bring his "Wall of Sound" style to Cohen songs.

Result: Total failure. The profuse instruments and background vocals overwhelm Leonard's distinctive voice and verse, making him a "background" on most of his own record.

Having been a Cohen fan since before his first  release, I have heard a lot of his subsequent albums, but not all. I have loved some of his releases, but not all. Of those I have owned or heard over the decades, this one is the least satisfying. Even if one of the songs is pretty good, the production ruins the performance for me. I found this in a "bargain bin" (new) for four bucks recently, but it was no bargain.

Question: If one becomes famous as a songwriter/singer, does it not stand to reason that one's fans like the person's voice and lyrics, and want to hear both well on any record? And also that to win new fans, hurting the two things existing fans buy your products to experience is not a smart move?

Finally: Now, 33 years later, the world knows that Mr. Spector, in spite of having made a lot of cash for himself and various artists and labels in the '70's, is one really evil guy. How ironic that his collaboration with Leonard was titled (after one of the songs) "Death of a Ladies' Man" when Phil now is in prison for causing the death of a lady. And more irony: One of the songs is titled "Don't Leave With Your Hard On" when Mr. Spector apparently pulled the trigger on a woman who refused to STAY when HE had a hard-on. It makes one wonder if Phil ever got over making this record. Meanwhile, Leonard, even around the age of 70, is singing his heart out in concerts and selling records, but avoiding doing any of the songs on this turkey. Of course, he could not recreate the "wall of sound" on the concert stage even if he wanted to...but I trust he is smart enough to know that the lyrics he issued behind Phil's production really were not good enough to be resurrected with even the simple accompaniment that best suits his strongest work. Skip this one, at any price.

reviewText: Having performed all the Beethoven symphonies countless of times with some of the greatest 20th and 21st Centuries' conductors as a first chair musician in a major orchestra, I intimately know their every single note, and am compelled to say that the performance of these two works, albeit excellently recorded by Telarc, is what results when a great orchestra is handed over to the mercy of a conductor, who is no more than a time beater!!! He races through the music as if he is trying to beat the clock, glossing over some of the most exciting and dramatic moments, with complete disregard for rounding out a phrase and/or awareness of the grand architecture of these works. In my opinion, he may have never heard Furtwangler's and Otto Klemperer's interpretations of these works, and if he had, he either was unmoved, or ignorantly chose the more straightforward, pedestrian (or shall I say equestrian) approach of racing through everything, as if he is trying to get all this over with, and get to the next gig! The interesting thing to also observe is that even a fine orchestra such as the Cleveland Orchestra, in the hands of this time beater is allowed to sound out of tune in many sections, as evident in the sharpness of pitch in the cellos, basses, and at times bassoons! A great conductor once said: "THERE ARE NO BAD ORCHESTRAS, ONLY BAD CONDUCTORS!" This very much applies here! Do not waste your money on this!!! Beethoven: Symphonies No. 5 & No. 7

Innumerable listeners, (especially the unwilling ones), cite sampling - violent, moronic, and misogynistic lyrics - mind-numbing repetition - pseudo-gangster posing - pretensions of significance - cretinous anti-musicality - and the complete absence of anything remotely pleasing or nourishing to the spirit - as evidence that rap represents the lowest point in the history of music. Frankly, it's hard to take issue with this perspective. But every bottom has a cellar below it and the Insane Clown Posse actually found a way to make rap even worse.

When ICP poured out of their little circus car and onto the scene, they brought a whole new level of degradation to the rubble. The clown make-up is probably there for the same reason Kiss has used freakish make-up all these years, to disguise hideous ugliness. That's one thing. But ICP also borrowed heavily from the world of professional wrestling, that twisted landscape combining pretensions of machismo, thinly veiled homosexuality of the muscle-man variety, bombast, and Cro-Magnon, uni-brow sensibility into an unctuous goo of theatricality appealing to the basest human and sub-human emotions. The ICP's pointless yelling, rants, challenges, and threats of bodily injury almost provide ample distraction from their complete lack of anything that might pass as talent.

With the imprimatur of the Stern show, (the absolute baseline of all sludge, the gold standard of bad taste), they were on their way. Seltzer water in the faces of their fans was only the coup de grace, the last touch. Maybe that's the good news of ICP. Perhaps they will help people finally see rap for what it is - hideous clatter produced by clowns with no musical aptitude and nothing to say.

reviewText:
Does a self-inflicted hole in the head make one a better musician? I thought not, so let's drop the charade that Kurt Cobain is a legend. If Nirvana and Kurt Cobain were the be-all, end-all of the music scene, it wouldn't have continued to evolve much less thrive after Cobain took the cowardly way out of life ten years ago. This proves that Cobain was unimportant to the music world. Look for yourself and try to find any contribution he brought to music. When you see it in its totality, his mark on the rock music scene was minimal, and his mark the music scene as a whole was detrimental. Most music in general is stagnant because it continues to include Kurt Cobain as an essential influence, but rock is regressing because Cobain is the man who allowed Nu-Metal and Hate-Rock to be bore from Nirvana. Nirvana had none of the passion, drive, and true grit that makes honest musicians stand out. Nirvana fans confuse laziness and sloppy musicianship with pure honesty just because Kurt says that's what it is. That's how easily-duped they are. When I see Kurt Cobain compared alongside Jimi Hendrix, Bob Dylan, and John Lennon, I find it sickening because Cobain, as he's been anointed by his fans and critics alike, is King of the Slackers. He was a lazy opportunist who fed off his legend status to finance his "heroine" habit. A modern musician and artist I've stumbled upon recently is Tracey Chapman. Unlike Cobain, she truly could lend her voice for the persecuted because she herself has been persecuted. She spoke of all the desolation Kurt Cobain never faced but claimed he had. She spoke of inciting a revolution for the poor to rise and gain what they had been denied; Kurt Cobain just wanted to incite a revolution for spoiled middle-class kids from divorced parents to gain what they never were entitled to. Tracey's wails could both move people to tears and prove injustices of the downtrodden all at once. Could Kurt Cobain HONESTY do any of those things? No.
When getting into music, I suggest anything besides whiny nasal bands, Nirvana, pop-punk, and any form of Metal, especially for younger people getting into the music scene. If you read that and ask, what else is there to choose from, I think the you've given in to the media already. Once teens discover Kurt Cobain, they think that just because the media and stuffy critics say so, that there's nothing beyond him, which is a lie. I saw bypass him and Nirvana altogether.
I recommend: Tracey Chapman, The Cranberries, The B-52s, The Beatles, John Lennon, Bob Dylan, The Moody Blues, and anything else experimental or strange. Nirvana was just lazy.

reviewText:
There is no question about that when you sometimes are overexposed as a artist, you can definitely be too much to handle. That unfortunately is the case when there is too much of you, where music lovers might want to just go somewhere else. That sadly is the case with Rihanna, who has been overexposed the past couple of years. The wannabe artist who just has been overplayed with Umbrella back in 2007. Since then, her album A Good Girl Gone Bad has been overplayed on radio and on stations like MTV Hits, and others across the country. t has been so much where she has lost a lot of credibility, and just became too much of an it girl. Not only that, but the album was re-released and expanded last year as Good Girl Gone Bad: Reloaded by adding more songs into the mix, and sadly those songs felt more like they have lackluster appeal. Now, yet another push of getting Rihanna's voice out there yet again, in just a mix if the studio.

Rihanna's 2009 remix album Good Girl Gone Bad: The Remixes, again is Def Jam's way of trying to cash in on Rihanna as a singer. Deeply and with no regret, the album shows absolutely less appeal than it did before. The songs here are all remixed, but it isn't just that on the album alone, where you get the songs from the original version of the album remixed like Umbrella, Don't Stop The Music, and a lesser-than appealing remixed duet of Hate That I Love You with Hip Hop singer Ne-Yo, that doesn't show much chemistry as it did before. Not only that, but the album dissapoints those who just purchased the expanded version, Good Girl Gone Bad: Reloaded, by not including remixes of her added tracks like Disturbia, her made-up duet with Maroon 5 on If I Never See Your Face Again and Rehab to a be as a part of the album.

All in all, many rexmixed albums feel like they are less the heart, and more about cashing in with dance rhythms. As for Rihanna, I really wasn't interested in A Good Girl Gone Bad before, and I am definitely not someone who recommend the Good Girl Gone Bad: The Remixes. There are times that there can be too much of an artist, and this is one of those times. I'd really recommend listening to other acts like Leona Lewis instead.

reviewText: "The Funky Headhunter" was one of the worst ideas that Hammer (nee' MC Hammer) could have come up with.  It proved that he was not completely committed to dance-drive, entertaining brand of rap, and was influenced by the criticisms of others of his earlier efforts.  While it is true that his two mega-hit albums "Please Hammer Don't Hurt 'Em" and "Too Legit 2 Quit" don't quite qualify as 'hardcore' rap (Heck they aren't even in the same zip code), they did earn Hammer a legion of fans who loved his style of music.  Unfortunately, he caved to the criticism and came out with this 'hardcore' album.  His reputation with the tougher elements of the hip-hop industry was already cemented.  So, there was no way this album could change their views.  The effect it did have was that it alienated all of fans who enjoyed his earlier work.  Raunchy bump-and-grind tracks like "pumps and a bump" and lackluster anthems like "It's all good" are just embarrassing attempts to obtain some sort of 'credibility'.  Hammer should never had made this album.  It is hardly surprising that his career imploded after this.

reviewText:
I'm really sorry, but this album is Sia's worst ever. It's just her, a drum machine and a keyboard. There are NO real instruments whatsoever.  She did an excellent job with the vocals since it is just her doing ALL of the backing vocals, harmonies, and other types of vocal layering, but no real instruments? Really, Sia? Sia has more money than ever and her shoe string budget album "Some People Have Real Problems" (truly one of the greatest albums EVER) has real drums, real guitars and real strings and is a beautiful recording.  She also recycled lyrics from her 2008 song "Lullaby" (on "Some People Have Real Problems") to make a chorus for 1000's "Burn the Pages" and the chorus for 1000's "Free the Animal" sounds a lot like Rhianna's "Shine Bright Like a Diamond."

1000 Forms of Fear was also engineered for the pop market. It's got a harsh EQ on it that juices up the bass and treble and sucks out the midrange. It's also a somewhat fuzzy recording. I was so excited to buy it since "Chandelier" is a great song, but the overall album is disappointing. There are a few clever hooks and some good lyrics, but I don't see myself listening to it often.  What upsets me the most about this album is that Sia didn't do her best with it.  It was slapped together just to make a quick buck.

I'm also upset that Sia is claiming to be recovering from depression, but she is selling a perfume called "Wet Dog" as well as blond bob wigs (just like the one that's on the cover to this album) on her website. I think the image of a meek and emotionally fragile person who sings on stage with her back turned to the audience and wears a paper bag on her head is nothing more than a lame marketing stunt. I'm sorry she made a few bucks off me on this album.

If you read my review of her DVD concert "TV is my Parent" you'll see that I once adored her work. I'll keep listening to "Some People Have Real Problems" and "We Are Born." Those albums are brilliant.

***UPDATE 20 JULY 2014***
I just sold my CD copy of this album for $1 at a used CD store.  I feel a little better.

reviewText:
It is about 90% of the time that when the lead vocalist leaves a band, their career is going to go downhill. It happened to bands like Sepultura and Cannibal Corpse. Now it has tragically happened to Norma Jean. This is nothing like "Bless The Martyr and Kiss The Child". "Bless The Martyr" was a landmark noisecore (not hardcore) album that showed the band's progress from being Luti-Kriss in 2001. However, Josh Scrogin left the band shortly after BTM&KTC. New vocalist Jake Schultz is absolutely inferior compared to Josh.

The music also tends to be too reminscence of the groundbreaking Seattle math-core band Botch. I read in an article of Alternative Press that one of the Norma Jean members bought Botch's "We Are The Romans" the time it came out while traveling in Europe. Now we have our direct source.

The album also sounds like it was poorly put together. The chord changes and Jake's mediocre vocals tend to ruin the album, which is sad, because the band had plenty of time between BTM&KTC and OGTA to make a quality album, which they failed to do in this case.

The band really sunk into mediocrity with this album. I recommend that you check out Botch, Converge, Torn Apart, Psyopus, The Number Twelve Looks Like You, and Circle Takes The Square instead of this.

reviewText: If you are looking for a classic interpretation of Tchaikovsky's 6th, this is not your product.  Check out Mariss Jansons' version with the Oslo Philharmonic on Chandos.  Why is this one so bad?  Every single movement is elongated; the fourth and last movement is almost doubled in length.  Ask yourself, was Tchaikovsky torpid and turgid? No.  Do people associate those qualities with him (meaning Tchiakovsky and not Bernstein)? No.  Do people expect torpor in listening to Tchaikovsky? No. Exactly my point.  I expect some tragedy and pathos in the 6th, not torpor and turgidity. To me, this wallowing performance is terrible.  It dishonors Tchaikovsky and Tchaikovsky's abilities.

reviewText: After picking up 'OK Computer' and really enjoying it, I came on here to see which album I should buy next, and 'Kid A' was the only album in the 'Key Albums' list. That should not be the case. This album made me want to shoot myself or something, the whole thing is paranoid, depressing, and downright scary. Listening to this will make you feel like a mental patient. I got the special edition 2x10" vinyl edition for my turntable... I doubt I'll be playing it very much anymore. I really tried to like this album, I really did, but I just can't listen to this anymore or I'll go insane. It's nothing at all like OK Computer, and it's very electronic and experimental, which I don't mind since I'm a fan of a few experimental techno bands, but this whole album had an aura of fear and paranoia surrounding it that I don't want to touch it again. It starts out with 'Everything In It's Right Place' which sounds so scary and closed in or something, and right then you know this is nothing like the previous album. The title track 'Kid A' contains some seriously distorted vocals, and is not a track I'd like to listen to by myself, it's just scary. 'The National Anthem' is more upbeat, but it's just plain annoying and has some very loud and out of tune horn sections on it that really bother me. The only songs that I sort of like on here are 'How To Disappear Completely' and 'Optimistic', both of which are very depressing songs despite the name of the second one, the former of which has a chilling section at the end with Thom humming along with the music. The latter is just a decent pop song. The last side of the album, which contains 'Idioteque' and 'Motion Picture Soundtrack' just finish off the whole paranoid suicidal feeling of the whole album. Finishing this album was like finishing a suicide note. "I will see you in the next world" are the last lyrics to the album. I pretended to like this. I really tried to like it. But I just can't stomach it anymore. I don't know what kind of masochist would want to listen to such an album, and I can't believe it's listed as the key album here. That one should be 'OK Computer', not this awful thing. 'OK Computer' was a 'down' album, but this one, I don't even know what the hell to call it. Not recommended at all. :(

reviewText:
I am so sorry that this is considered an STP album. I mean, I am not exactly surprised given that Shangri-La was a disaster (this album is better, I will say that much), but I am annoyed. Actually -- I am not even peeved, as STP stopped making great music so long ago now, that I do not expect much anymore. ... this is coming from a very old fan, a former fan page webmistress that used to be linked from their site. I was a fan, and I am still a fan, but the new stuff just sucks.

This album is not really that inspiring. It is not lasting and there aren't any songs on it that really stick out in my memory. Going through the album, it was hard trying to find songs that I liked... then I rated them in comparison to other songs on the album vs. what I actually could stand listening to. Of the 4 songs that I liked, it was hard to give it such a good rating.

-Scott's vocals managed to screw up songs that may have been otherwise memorable, which I've never said about him before.
-Album felt like it was trying to be something that it's not.
-STP seems to have forgotten its hard/er sound that made them so exciting.
-Tiny Music... seemed to have more craft in its sounds, lyrics, and overall presentation. The album as an entity flowed together well, the sound was really ... different, and I really enjoyed how unique it was. The softer/experimental side of STP is fine with me, so long as they pull it off. This album here just seems like they sat together and just recorded what came to mind. I don't think this would've been released if it weren't coming from STP; it probably was released because they are already established and are trading on their old name. It's not marketable, fresh, pushing any lines.
-Lyrics seem contrived

I am so bummed. STP was a favorite of mine growing up, I expected more.

reviewText: I'm a lawyer in Miami. This is a review. I wrote it because I wanted to share my experience of watching this movie. My wife made me watch it. I just gave you a scooch of the experience of watching New Year's Eve, a movie overstuffed with characters who exposite who they are, what they are doing, and their motivations. The result is a sad spectacle of A and B list actors almost painfully going through the motions with stilted dialogue, explaining to the audience at every turn exactly the implications of the plot developments. "We're not sure if we'll be able to fix it." "But we must fix it before midnight!" "We want to have the baby right after midnight so we can get the prize money!" I mean, are you kidding me with this dialogue? To sum up, I really hated this boring and pointless movie and didn't care about what happened to any of the characters at all. There was one short scene in which a woman was mean to an aspiring actress server that was well done. Right after that there's a speech with a woman holding a dog with no less than three continuity errors involving the position of the dog. (My wife pointed this out. I was proud of her. It's the kind of movie where you notice these kinds of things, as they are the most interesting aspects of the movie.) As a sidenote, earlier in the day I watched We're the Millers (Blu-ray+DVD+UltraViolet Combo Pack), which was incredibly hilarious and well done. Watch that instead. Another note: whoever was able to assemble this cast deserves some kind of award. A shame they were all squandered. (Caveat: Sofia Vergara is amazing as usual.) It's kind of like one of those yogurt places where you can get all kinds of toppings. Amazing toppings, but the yogurt is actually dog poo. (Spoiler alert: the dog poo is the movie.)

reviewText:
I need to quantify my review up front. In my dictionary, you look up the words 'music', 'class brass',' professional', and you'll see CHICAGO. Anyone who knows me, knows that CHICAGO is, and has been, my favourite group since dirt, hands down. The only other band closer is the Beatles. I own every 331/3 album, and every cd, twice. My key chain says "CHICAGO". My refrigerator and front door has CHICAGO magnets inside and out. Anything with the CHICAGO logo on it gets saved. Need more proof of my loyalty ?

This cd saddens this loyal fan to the point of heartache. I didn't say anything when this group started re-issuing albums and continuing to count them as progressive Roman numeral issues, I figured they earned the right, plus they had to eat. Despite the sad death of guitarist Terry Kath, the loss of drummer Danny Seraphine and bassist-singer Peter Cetera, this group really worked hard, both in the studio and at the concert venues to remain a vibrant part of the music scene. It is not easy to stay current for 40 years and please everyone.

When the new guys came on the scene, you didn't hear me speak ill of Jason Scheff for sounding like Cetera. Cetera was gone, Jeff was in and that's that. I didn't ever expect any one of Chicago's subsequent guitarists to sound like Terry Kath, and frankly, I didn't want them to. Even the drummer, Tris Imboden, was musically right for the fit of this band, all of them bringing their own piece of continuing Chicago talent into the fold.

But folks, this is not right. Chicago has more talent than this.

Part of me wants very hard to salute them for being there for 40 years, the other part says that I will not pay high ticket prices to stand in a cold Seattle rain to hear them play this music in concert. I can hear the same stuff on" Night and Day",

"Chicago 21" and all the Christmas songs that I have already bought years ago. I don't know, maybe I am just getting to old, but I think my sixteen year old is going to akin XXX to elevator music as well.

If you have to have it, then buy it. If you are hard up for money, save it for food or something worthwhile. I know my mom said that if I didn't have anything nice to say then I shouldn't say anything, but I am not getting a warm fuzzy feeling hearing this one. Usually I am stoked and can't wait to tell a friend. I may have to pull the shades and bolt the door and turn off the telephone. Thank goodness I have 29 other Chicago albums to listen to. Better luck next time fellas.

Maybe there was just too many cooks in the kitchen?

reviewText:
I`ve been a long fan of this album and I have been listening to it since 1991. My CD was starting to get old, so I decided it was time to substitute it for a new one. So I bought the remastered version, thinking that it would sound better than my old album from 1990.
It definitely doesn`t.
The sound of this new remaster is compressed and if you give it a try for 15 minutes your ears will start to ask you to stop it. The quality is ok if you listen to it in low volume. If you turn the volume up you will notice that the sound will suffer from some distortion. The drums will sound flat, the bass won`t have any kick and so on.
I`m very disappointed.
If this is a remaster, it should sound better, not worse than the original version from 1990.
The original version was already perfect. It had dynamic sound, the bass was great, the drums felt like you were in front of Richard Bailey, the guitar was astounding and the keyboards were a show apart, specially in the last track of the album.
These things are not present in the remastered version.
These remasters today are all a hit or miss. Pink Floyd, Genesis, Frank Zappa have good remasters. Iron Maiden, AC/DC, Supertramp are not so good. I don`t know what happens, but it seems that every remaster is made for the sound to be louder, but that doesn`t mean it will have better quality, which is the case of Blow by Blow.
I`ll stick to my old cd, which allows me to listen to it in loud volume without ringing my ears.
If you`ve never heard this album, buy the 1990 version, that is great. This new edition sounds terrible and you`ll do yourself a favor not to get near it.

reviewText:
Sigh, It seems so long since Tori put out a truly great album.  I'd go back to as far as Scarlet's Walk.  She's made some really good songs since Scarlet's Walk, but it seems that each album is padded with alot of fluff, annoying or rehashed sounding material.

The first bad part about this album, is it's really hit or miss on her song choices.  The second bad part about this album is the orchestra really doesn't enhance or change the dynamic of the original song so much.  When it does change the dynamic its not always in a good way.  For the most part I'm happy or happier with the original versions of all these songs.

Since Scarlet's Walk, Tori Amos has slowed down.  I'm guessing that as she ages she can't play the piano as fast as she used to be able to.  However, on this album she manages to keep the tempo up of the original songs, so I'm not knocking that.  However, she doesn't seem have the vocal chops to pull off "Silent All these Years", "Flying Dutchman," "Precious Things" and "Winter" anymore.  These songs don't sound right with a "grandmotherly" voice.  For that matter, "Jackie's Strength" doesn't come across very well vocally either, and I don't understand why she couldn't pull that song off very well.  (She's not hitting that octave and conveying the emotion/angst of her youth in these songs).

If you thought "Yes Anastasia" was too long, then you might like this version.  She shortened it to her recent concert length performances.  Personally, I prefer the original, long verison that slowly builds up to the dramatic sounding ending.  The orchestra is front and center on this song, but it's also out of place.  I could've enjoyed it more if Tori hit all the high notes of the original, but once again vocally she under performed.

I enjoyed Cloud on My Tongue, Gold Dust, Star of Wonder, Snow Cherries from France and Girl Disappearing.  Marianne was okay, but the original version is better.  Flavor and Programable Soda are not songs I enjoyed in either format.

Overall this album would've worked better if Tori stuck to more recent material, or performed older material she still had the vocal range/emotion necessary to perform the songs properly.  In concert, nobody really notices when your vocal range diminishes or if you're off a bit emotionally.  On this album, it's all too apparent.

reviewText:
Digging through RCA vaults in search of unreleased Elvis "treasures" recorded in the studio has its merits.  Elvis was one of a handful of recording artists whose alternate takes could be as  compelling as the master takes.  Much of the artistic success of the  _Essential Elvis_ series is based on this fact.
Enter the next phase in  the process of scraping through the vaults in the BMG's relentless quest to  release every note, giggle, joke and body function Elvis ever committed to  tape:  _The Home Recordings_.
There is absolutely no reason in the world  for these tapes to have been issued.  The sound quality is uniformly shoddy  and the performances are, at best, afterthoughts.  Indeed, many of the  performances on this CD are incomplete.
There are those who will argue,  "But, Strangebird, you fool!  These recordings give the listener an  educational insight into Elvis' musical roots!  These are  essential!"
To this I say "Nonsense!"  Those listeners  (and anybody who's reading this for that matter) can gain an insight into  Elvis' musical roots by listening to his early Sun recordings.
As for the  songs themselves, "When the Saints Go Marching In" is already  available on _The King of Rock and Roll: Complete 50's Masters_ box set  (which you either already have or need to get) while "I'm Beginning to  Forget You" and "After Loving You" are available on  _Platinum: A Life in Music_ (again, which many of you probably have).  These are the highlights.
"Tumblin' Tumbleweeds", "San  Antonio Rose", and "Tennessee Waltz" are simply horrible,  with Elvis and his partners in crime stumbling and laughing through these  performances.
The absolute nadir of this collection is a perplexing take  of "Indescribably Blue" in which Elvis sings over a barely  audible studio backing track, presumably as a rehearsal for his later  studio take.  Awful!
If this is any indication of the quality of the  Elvis material remaining in the vault, perhaps the time has come to put an  end to this never-ending stream of "unreleased treasures".  Maybe  it's even time to reissue _Having Fun with Elvis Onstage_ on CD!  Just  kidding, BMG!  Just kidding!
