reviewText: I don't know what the inspiration behind a big-band Monk record was. Commercial greed? Nah. This came out in 1968, remember? If Monk was in it for the money, he would've jumped on with the fusion bandwagon, which would just be creepy. Need to try something new? Well, Monk had already pioneered jazz beforehand. His producer being a moron? Yeah, sure, sounds good. As I alluded to before, this is Monk with a big-band. Arranged by Oliver Nelson, who was best remembered for arranging TV themes. Do you see where this is going? To bad-idea hell, that's where! Probably just to prove he was the one in charge, Teo "I'm the boss and you're my mindless minions! Bwahaha..." Marceo wrote and contributed a couple of the worst tracks ("Just a Glance at Love"; "Consecutive Seconds"), though Monk can be blamed for a couple of the originals as well (overcooked pastrami like "Reflections" and "Little Rootie Tootie"; "Monk's Point", which has none). And what's up with these rerecordings of Monk's old classics? "Straight, No Chaser" may have started off promising, but it ends up as a bunch of clichd, lifeless horn blasts; "Let's Cool One" sounds like it could have been performed by a crooner, like Bing Crosby or whatever; "Trinkle Tinkle" is an idiotic, disgraceful mutation. The one song I enjoy is "Brilliant Corners", which is given a swinging, enjoyable rendition: elsewhere, this is easily Monk's worst. You may get it by accident because you have it confused with Monk's Dream or Monk's Music. Try not to.

reviewText:
So it's 1986, the band Slayer has just released "Reign in Blood," an album that redefined thrash metal by raising the bar of speed and agression in metal. The album was a huge success, and ensured that Slayer would end up as one of the Gods of metal. It was a good year for Slayer.

 What happened to this band? Since 1986, the band has gone downhill steadily, and in some cases, rapidly. In 1988 they released "South of Heaven" which was a focused effort, if anything, but was a complete change of style from their Reign in Blood material. It was noticeably slower, less aggressive, and toned down. At the time, fans feared the band was going soft to attract a more mainstream audience, but those suspicions were refuted 2 years later.

 "Seasons in the Abyss" came out in 1990, which was basically a faster, heavier version of "South of Heaven", but was arguably much better in quality. Some songs retained the "Reign..." energy, with the focused direction of "South..." Not a bad album in any regard, but in my opinion, it wasn't even close to their first 3 albums in terms of quality. Anyway, the band felt a renewed sense of self-confidence, and with the fans behind them once again, they were ready to continue.

 Four years pass with only a live album released in between. "Divine Intervention" was released in 1994, and is the first huge crack in Slayer's armor, as the album was a lackluster shell of an effort. It attempted to recreate the success of "Seasons..." but ultimately fell flat on its face. It was a dud, pure and simple. The band at the time was in danger of becoming stale, and began searching for new methods of selling their albums. Personally, I feel the band feared becoming stale as well, which is why they infused much more "punk" into Divine then in previous albums. Not a smart move, in my opinion, which is an opinion justified by their next blunder.

 "Undisputed Attitude" is an album almost universally despised by old school Slayer fans. Slayer decided it would freshen up their credibility a bit if they wrote a few punk songs to put on an album, and then fill the rest of the album with cover songs from other punk bands. What a desecration. Not only were Slayer's songs the worst of all the punk songs on there, proving they could not do punk any better than they were doing metal at the time, but the entire album was just a laughable joke. Judging by the album's poor results, I'd imagine it didn't win Slayer any punk fans, just like it didn't convert any metalheads into punk fans. It failed, miserably.

 Two more years pass, and Slayer releases their newest album, entitled "Diabolus in Musica." Let's take a minute and recap. Their weak thrash album "Divine Intervention" didn't work, their punk album "Undisputed Attitude" didn't work, so what should they try next? Nu-metal? Why not? It's very popular with the kids these days. And that is exactly what Slayer did. They down-tuned their guitars, turned up the angst and turned off the intelligence in their lyrics, and introduced new vocal stylings similar to those found in Korn, Coal Chamber, and other Nu-metal bands of the time. They needed a younger, dumber fan-base to buy their albums, and it shows with this piece of garbage. They succeeded in their effort and obtained a fresh new breed of trend-seeking, cash hemorrhaging, pimple-popping disposable fans to sell their albums to, however the "metal" fans were just about done with one of their ex-favorite bands. Diabolus was to many at the time, the official end of Slayer.

 Then, 3 years later, on September 11th, 2001, a day when the worst act of terror was committed in the world, Slayer released "God Hates Us All." Without getting into the coincidence that the album was released on that day, I will talk about the album only. With the failed attempt at nu-metal still fresh in their mind, the band once again changes style, towards the aggressive "hardcore" style of their touring buddies Hatebreed. This new style would allow them to continue playing simple music, but would also enable them to build a "true, angry" image for themselves. "Hardcore" punk has never been a music style based on complexity or musical ability, it has survived all these years on its "f*** you" attitude and "tough" image. That, coupled with its "scene" of teenagers, it made for a sweet feeding ground for Slayer to get their profits from the young and the easily influenced. No worthwhile riffing, no solos, annoyingly distorted non-stop shouting, poorly written angst/aggression lyrics, hardcore type moshpit beats... not really what I would consider good things for a former thrash legend. With this album, Slayer has proven that they will change into anything if they can catch the wave of cash the current trend will bring.

 Slayer will soon be releasing another album, and claims it will be the best album since Reign in Blood. The original lineup has reformed, which hasn't happened since "Seasons..." Don't be fooled, people. Slayer hasn't been Slayer since 1990, and has been a shadow ever since. Even with the reformed lineup, they will be nothing like they were back in their glory days, and no amount of hype will ever change that. The bands roots have run dry long ago, and they will not be getting any of my money with their up and coming abomination.

 To any new fans of Slayer, get their first 3 albums and see what made them so great in the 1980's. After that, just be aware, you're in for one hell of a downhill ride.

reviewText:
This is like seeing Emo as a fetus in its fetid mother's womb, you just wish you could kill it and stomp it out before it gets strong and explodes out with its deranged fists and sharp claws. If I could go back in time I would erase the master of this album. Of course perhaps someone else would have dropped this A-bomb of awfulness eventually, so maybe it's good we got emo out of the way early.

This album tricks you, the first listen is fantastic. But on the second listen there are no more illusions, this is the true spawn of satan, coming out of one of the best genres that always sang about satan, a gross disfigured being that has nothing left to do with the humanity that spawned it. Every song is the same. Just a lot of screaming about how they hurt so much and their hearts, oh their hearts. I can hear them castrating the genre I love, going way emotional for their last hurrah. The sound is brittle, without any moodiness, without an ounce of atmosphere. It's so sonically thin you will wonder, after the album has played, if it was even there. All you'll get out of it is a guy screaming at the top of his lungs over the most turgid, uninspired playing you've ever heard out of Sweden.

What's really sad is these guys were at one time good players who constructed technical, brilliant songs on their album TRITSIO. Yet on their album Slaughter of the Soul, you hear a band who's so compositionally frigid, it's impossible to compare them to their former selves. They're practically a different band by this point, they've lost their passion for being interesting. I wouldn't hesitate to call sots boring. The drums are recorded in the most asinine way, like the drummer was literally pounding on a dull pile of chicken skins. He's so repetitive it's ridiculous, mechanical and barely there but merely to collect a check. The guitars do a good job of blending into all the other merciless muck, creating a distorted gummy sound that doesn't break out. A lot of bands would go on to copy this automatic recording technique, as it fills in for laziness. No longer do you have focus on all the different players and their exceptional or unexceptional talents, but rather a band in a tin can who can be sold for a quarter on a shiny disc. So many southern California punk and ska bands fall into the tin can trope. To me the way this album was recorded is a de-evolution in music, a dumbing down for the masses.

What this band spawned, as they say on the interwebs, cannot be the fault of atg, but I can be really mad about it and blame them anyways since Lord knows the ones who ripped them off don't have any conscience about the horrible music they make.

After all, there's now much, much worse music these days which we can attribute entirely to computers and digitization. I don't hate digitization any more than tin can hardcore, but my seething hatred for bad, misdirected music burns on, and blame must be meted out.
label: negative

reviewText:
One-star reviews are something I rarely give out. I don't like reviewing a product if I have nothing remotely positive to remark about it, but I simply feel obligated to on Bow Wow's latest release, Price of Fame. Front and forward, I've gotta comment on the title of this release; Price of Fame. Bow Wow tricks unsuspecting buyers into thinking this could possibly be a mature, and introspective effort from the nineteen year old who dropped the "Lil'" in his name two LP's ago. Bow Wow's at a good age to offer wisdom from a youthful perspective, as Mobb Deep dropped The Infamous at the very same age.. however, while Mobb Deep were dropping knowledge over hardcore hip-hop backdrops aiming for classic status, Bow Wow's dropping club track after club track over poor, and overproduced beats hoping to rake in some cream with an album that, simply put, is well below subpar.

Firstly, Bow Wow's flow is horrendous. His breath control, or lack thereof, is abysmal. The beats he's chosen for his album are commercial rejects; much like everything Bow Wow's mentor, Jermaine Dupree, produces. Bow Wow doesn't even write his only songs, so I'm simply wondering, who the hell is ghostwriting this kid's lyrics, and why on earth does he still have a job? One reviewed quipped that the 'haters' who give this album negative reviews are jealous of Bow Wow's swagger; what swagger? Bow Wow doesn't sound comfortable on the microphone, despite having over half a decade in the game under his belt.

Bow Wow does offer a surpisingly insightful track in Outta My System, but even that one bit of insight can't save this abortion of an album. I didn't come into this release expecting anything more than a more mature, refined Bow Wow, and I came out seeing the same artist, and person he's been for the last six years; there's been no progress, and Bow Wow feels like little more than a persona created by JD, and his horrible entourage of ghostwriters. Even the likes of Nick Cannon could become a respectable artist in the hip-hop community, but Bow Wow isn't dropping any Can I Live?'s on Price of Fame. It's more of the same exact product you've been listening to since Bow Wow was telling you to "Bounce With Me." When Bow Wow says he's going to move all the 'old rappers out of the way' on Don't Know About That, you can't help but laugh at the sheer stupidity of that statement, and cringe at the disrespect. Bow Wow maybe young, but he's more washed-up than legends like KRS-1 or De La Soul, or even mainstream darlings like Snoop and Ice Cube; which is horrible, considering he was far below-average at his peak. If Bow Wow could dramatically, and quite frankly, miracuously, mature between this and his next release, then he maybe able to survive in the game, but if Bow Wow keeps going like this, it's time for this kid to hang up his hoodie.

reviewText: I have most of Little Feat on vinyl records and enjoy the group tremendously.  I went shopping for a representative "Best of" CD and the other collections available, I feel, have poor selections and don't represent the group's best tunes at all.  This disk has many of the selections I wanted, so I ordered it.  Unfortunately, the sound quality of the remastered CD is so bad that I don't find it enjoyable at all, in fact it's distracting and unpleasant because I know what the songs SHOULD sound like.  Digital recordings are generally regarded as higher fidelity than vinyl but on this particular one, the original vinyl recordings are much more detailed and rewarding.  The sound quality is muddy and what's more, the mixing is very poor, with instruments overwhelming the vocals and not at all comparable to the original recordings.  In the final word, unfortunately there are no collections of Little Feat that properly represent the group; the only alternative is to purchase two or three separate CDs which include the songs you like most--for me these are "Feats Don't Fail Me Now," "Time Loves a Hero" and probably "Dixie Chicken."  My money was wasted on this "Best of."  When purchasing 70's-vintage analog to digital recordings I expect some loss of fidelity and have no problem living with it.  However this one is so bad that the tunes are barely recognizable.

Hey!  Another incompetent garage band featuring a raspy-voiced baby who whines incessantly about his parents and senselessly opines his uneducated stance on war and parties to get away from all the inflictions of society and...

Folks, Smile Empty Soul makes everyday turmoil look like an inescapable black hole. Smile Empty Soul offers not one attempt of resolve.  They are culprits of The "Feel" Conspiracy, and yet another reason why I, for one, continue to have such a cynical outlook on modern rock.
But if you want to be perpetually ridden with despair and hopelessness, then by all means, get this CD.  Your eardrums will be --once <yawn> again-- infiltrated by sloppy, writhing electric guitars; low-end basslines that my dog could have concocted; and drumming of Hootie and the Blowfish-caliber: all of which are quite fashionable --moreover, profitable-- devices used to express one's petulance.  Please, buy this CD, and keep that immature, bratty attitude alive on the airwaves; please, keep on begging garage band scouts to find more junk like this so that the record companies can continue to shamelessly profit from the MYTH of society's downward spiral.

reviewText:
I'm not sure which is more of a crime:  Kenny G's successful career in music, or Tammy La Gorce's review of this album.  The word "genius" has really come to be thrown around more and more in recent history than I can stand.  It seems to be misused particularly when people who have either zero or minimal understanding of the arts are speaking of the arts.  For Tammy La Gorce to call virtually any album she reviews "genius" is just blatantly uninformed and unintelligent (particularly in Kenny G's case).

In the event that one is unaware of the jazz community's utter hatred for Kenny G, he or she should search the Internet for Pat Metheny's highly-praised (and thorough) article on why Kenny G is utter blasphemy to music.  Another option would be talk to students and/or professors from some of the country's leading schools for saxophone performance (including Northwestern University, Indiana University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, University of Minnesota, Louisiana State University, and the Eastman School of Music).  They will all tell you the same thing:  Kenny G has a very elementary understanding of jazz, which is demonstrated through his immature phrasing, sound quality, "improvisational skills", vibrato, and ability to play in-tune.  He has managed to become a household name simply because most people in this country are uninformed when it comes to musical artistry.  In an ideal world only the people would know better, and Kenny G wouldn't even be capable of getting a record deal.  Unfortunately, this is not the case, and there are many jazz artists in the world who are far more developed, far more musically educated, and, in short, far more deserving of the fame and fortune Kenny G has acquired.  Some of these people end up having to quit music (which, at one point, was the absolute center of their entire being) and taking on jobs they despise because they respect the performing arts, their previous mentors, and their predecessors too much to sell out like Kenny G.

As if La Gorce's completely idiotic praising of this album weren't enough, she put the nail in her credibility coffin by finishing off her review stating that, based on her preference for Chaka Khan's interpretation of "Beautiful", Khan should have been the original artist behind the song.  If she and Christina Aguilera both find it to be a moving song they believe in, both of them have the right to perform it.  Besides, Linda Perry (not Tammy La Gorce) is the one who wrote the song, and she gladly allowed Aguilera to use it and interpret it for her album.  Perhaps La Gorce is to be trusted as a music critic even less than Kenny G is to be trusted as a true musician--and that's saying something.

This one here focus' not on the "best" of Alice Cooper, but the best of the "Trash" (1989), "Hey Stoopid" (1991) & "Last Temptation" (1994) albums. This really puzzles me as to why the heck this one has been released at all seeing as how ALL THREE of those albums was released in 2009 under the title "Triple Feature" which had all three of those albums on 3 disks, all for the price of 1... yet here comes this one in 2011, another release, this time cut down into 2 discs, and not including a whole CD worth of songs, then I just have to shake my head in wonder and wish I could put the persons idea to release yet another badly done random selections from these 3 albums and call it a best of... again. This has been done plenty of times before, there are many other useless Alice so called "best of" or similar releases... man, I wish Alice would take the person responsible and force him/her/them into one of his guillotines or hang him/her/them for the stoopidist ideas in history to keep releasing these things one after the other... especially when they finally got it right with the Triple Feature! That one was perfect, it did not say "best of" or "definitive" or "Best of the 1989 to 1994 era... no, just "Triple Feature" and had 3 great albums that don't contain fillers, the albums are all great from start to finish... so WHY, i repeat, WHY, do they keep on doing this to Alice???

Throw in the fact that Higgenson has the line 'this songs for you' (a blatant rip-off from "Mrs. Robinson) and you have people falling all over themselves to proclaim Plain White T's a new Simon and Garfunkel. reviewText: Whoever compiled this disc should be imprisoned for crimes against music!  When it was released I was elated that I could finally have my favorite Marillion track, "Cinderella Search," on CD.  Imagine my horror when I discovered that it was some chopped-down version that FADES OUT just as the crescendo begins.  Yeah, THAT'S brilliant!  Who wants a passage of climbing intensity that leads into a satisfying slam-bang of an ending when you can just fade out?  I actually jumped up out of my chair and headed for the stereo, thinking there was something wrong with it!  (No kidding!) Then the horrors continued: I listened to the rest of the disc (I had skipped right to "Cinderella Search," as I wanted to hear it right off the bat), and discovered that "Lady Nina" was also missing its slam-bang finish, as well as "Market Square Heroes," which had the extra indignity of missing its final verse.  It's the most frustrating thing to have to sit through.  If I wanted these songs to fade out I could turn down the volume knob myself!  And it's amazing with some of them: if they had just let the songs play for another 10 seconds, the ending would have come.  The fade-outs don't exactly save us any time.  If you want the good versions get the double-disc reissues of the albums, or, better yet, the box of singles.

And please Fred Durst, STOP TRYING TO RAP!! You're horrible at it!!  If I wanted to hear rap, I'd put on Ja Rule's album.  I'm so glad I didn't succumb to the hype surrounding this album by purchasing it. reviewText:
Judas Priest not only introduced me to Heavy Metal, they taught me how to play guitar, and how to write my own songs and not sound like every other band from the NWOBHM and onward into Thrash/Speed metal. They were a Juggernaut that with every release pushed themselves and myself to greater abilities of writing/playing and live shows that I will NEVER forget. Black Sabbath introduced dark lyrical themes and both Blues leanings and off-kilter time signatures to a heavier style of music. But in my opinion, Judas Priest invented HEAVY METAL, without question, and for that I am eternally grateful.

However, the Priest that I've seen live (even on the unrecognizable "Turbo" tour) is no longer around it would seem. 'Nostradamus' is unfortunately the release from the Priest that exists today, and it shows that whatever magic Halford/Tipton/Downing had for writing some of the most killer metal songs of all time such as "Screaming For Vengeance", "The Sentinel" and "Painkiller", is now lost, probably forever. And I hang my head down and light a candle for the death of it. The mighty Priest has fallen.......

p.s. And to save time on some rebuttal questions, no I do not expect them to repeat themselves over and over. I've played guitar for long enough to know that is idiotic and talentless. In my opinion though, this release is nothing like Judas Priest as I've known them over the years, and they HAVE changed over those years. Just not into....whatever it is that "Nostradamus" is.

reviewText: Diary of an unfulfilled pop star or sympathy card to his generation? Does it matter? Bowie's 23rd album spares us another round of trend-hopping, opting for a more believable adult-contemporary groove, but his pathological ironic detachment makes him hard to take seriously as Love's Survivor. Even so, this album didn't have to be so weak -- the emotional heft in Bowie's songs has never come from him but his guitarists, from Mick Ronson to Stevie Ray Vaughan. A pity that Reeves Gabrels is such a cipher. His latest collaboration with Bowie is typically stagnant; bloodless guitars and synths substitute half-baked "moods" for genuine emotions. As for lyrics, take your pick from obtuse, half-finished or banal. "Sometimes I cry my heart to sleep ... Sometimes my courage fell to my feet," the auteur laments in "Thursday's Child." That would be drippy even if it didn't come from a billionaire married to a supermodel.

Perhaps there's some bits that could have become fairly good songs. The song Ectasy comes closest to being something interesting. For an artist that could write such great songs, this is definitely a low point in his career.

From "Paranoia in the key of E":

"Sometimes you're like an eagle strong like a rock" - And this coming from a great rock n roll poet???

And from the song "Mad":

I know I shouldn't had someone else in our bed

reviewText:
This is definitely my least favorite Kiss album. The mid to late 80's was a weird time for Kiss, as they tried to sound like all of the other hair metal bands that were popular at that time, like Cinderella, Bon Jovi, etc. Their albums continued to sell very well...all of them went either Gold or Platinum, but they didn't deserve to, seeing how bad the music was.

Gene Simmons was still in the band, but only physically...his mind seemed to be everywhere else. His songs on most of the Kiss albums after "Creatures of the Night" were amongst his worst ever. I can't recommend or even remember the songs that Gene contributed to "Crazy Nights". That left Paul Stanley to pick up the slack and unfortunately, most of his songs weren't that memorable this time around either. Or, if they were memorable, like the horrible title track, one wishes they weren't! This was Kiss doing Eighties pop hair metal and if I didn't jump ship with Asylum( though I wanted to!), I definitely did this time. I mean, when the best song on a Kiss album is a BALLAD( "Reason To Live"), you know you're in trouble.

When listening to this album again sometime last year, the thing that bothered me the most was Eric Carr's boring, unadventurous 4/4 metal drumming. Carr( may he rest in peace) was easily my least favorite Kiss drummer. Guitarist Bruce Kulick was technically very proficient, but he was all about flash and notes, not feel. He was also not much of a songwriter.

"Crazy Nights" is very much a Kiss album in terms of lyrics, which deal with partying, hanging out with lots of naked women when you're not breaking up with them, etc... It's a very happy album, I guess, though it doesn't cheer me up at all.

I can't recommend it!

reviewText:
It shocks me that alot of people who have listened to this album are respecting it and claming it to be something reminiscent of "Pinkerton" or "Blue Album". No.

This album, quite putting it in a blunt manner, bores me. While in Pinkerton you heard lyrics that were screamed and not coming from a guy who took voice lessons, It was something more pure and had more of a core. It was something that tore into your heart and comparable to everyone else's lives. Make Believe has about as much emotion as any kind of music you could find in "Tiger Beat".

Almost every song starts with some kind of annoying guitar whine. On top of that I cringe when I hear a "clap along". I expect it more from a band like "The Darkness", which is a band I respect in a jokingly manner.

On top of that, a comparison to the "Blue Album" is truley a upper cut to the face that is my musical taste. If you want to talk about something that was raw and catchy...and immortal in the minds of every "rock geek" that likes a good sweater and thick glasses, then that album was it. Maybe the band is missing some sort of flavor since bassist Matt Sharp left the band is questionable. Maybe the reason is that the lead singer is a lunatic and doesn't know what music to stick to. If you don't agree with that last comment, read the latest Rolling Stone Magazine article and try to argue it. That is if you can bear to read anything out of that over political, self justified, liberal piece of trash.

I'm only passionate about putting this album down because I feel that Blue Album and Pinkerton were such masterpieces, that it is uncomparable. I won't mention the green album, since it was the worst to date....Maladriot was something close to good rock music, but still pretty bad. If you are buying this c.d., do not buy it based on their past music. The weezer we grew up with in the early 90's is now dead to the world. If you are into a more flock of seagulls sound, then hey, this album is all for you.

This album will be forgot within 5 years like every other album that was begging for more of a paycheck then anything else. I don't have a problem with a artist being a sell out...but have something worth selling.

Hope my review helped. Thanks for reading.

reviewText:
In the 1990s, the Country Music began to go through some transitions. Country music which had for the most part stayed in a vacuum began to go mainstream and embrace other genres of music. As a result, the sound started to change. By the end of the 90s, Country Music had full blown established music superstars in Shania Twain and Faith Hill. But back in 1992, this metamorphosis was still in the early stages. I personally, have been intrigued by country music - but I would admit I am not a purist. I enjoy the fusion of different genres of music with country that would eventually lead to these new superstars.. Thus we come to Mary-Chapin Carpenter's (MCC) 1992 smash "Come On Come On". This album doesn't quite mesh with the mainstream - it is more pure country and has much more of a folk-ish twist to it. The bottom line is I don't think this is a very good album.

 Perhaps I bought this album for the wrong reasons. I had been pleasantly surprised when I heard the remake of Lucinda Williams' Passionate Kisses on Don Imus' radio program. Yes it was different than the original, but MCC's version did something to interest me. She has a very good voice. As a result, I felt it was an investment in the collection that contained this song would be worthwhile. I had also heard that this album had some of the "fusion" elements - particularly with the folk sound. I immediately discovered two problems with this album: 1) The "fusion" element I felt was very lacking. Many of the songs of this album still have a traditional country sound. I did mention, I am not a country purist and I wouldn't rip an album for that reason alone- so the next reason; 2) The Songs are just not that good. There is little on this album that helps lift it to the next level. Despite MCC's great voice I heard on "Passionate Kisses", the remainder of the songs don't do as much to put MCC in the category of a great female vocalist.

 There are a couple of interesting things that I discovered as this album has sat in my CD rack for the better part of a decade. Country Star - Roseanne Cash (Johnny's daughter) does background vocals on opening tack "The Hard Way". On this very country-ish track, you really don't get a good much of Roseanne's voice and it almost is a complete waste of a good talent. Another background vocalist is Shawn Colvin (who would eventually become a mainstream star in the late 90s). Colvin uses a folk-sy style in her works, so looking back in hindsight she might have been influenced on this album. Colvin actually does the background vocals on "Passionate Kisses" - which isn't a very folksy song. Again, you aren't going to get a lot of Shawn Colvin - this was very early in her career so you won't hear her distinctive sound on this track. Country artist Joe Diffie does a decent duet on "Not Too Much to Ask", but the song is pretty dry and doesn't do much for me. Finally, Amy Ray and Emily Sallers - pop artists from the Indigo Girls appear on the track "Walking Through Fire" - this is a pretty decent track and actually one of the better cuts, but this isn't a song that is going to make me do handstands.

 Another song which is worth mentioning is "The Bug". This is a country version of a Dire Straits song. It was written by Mark Knopfler who has always had somewhat of a country/folk element in parts of his music. Dire Straits actually released this song around the same time as MCC's version. MCC does a very nice job with her rendition of this. I still think the Dire Straits version is superior - but this version definitely holds its own and is one of the better cuts.

 For fans of MCC and this style, there are some nice liner notes included with the collection. All of the lyrics - with all of the appropriate credits are included with the collection. The version I have of this CD does have this in a fold-out format as opposed to a booklet (which is annoying, but not terrible). The back of the foldout includes a big picture of MCC.

 I think if you are a MCC fan, my review probably isn't going to influence you. But if you are more of a genre-neutral music fan and are going to invest in this album - think twice. This album isn't going to do much to capture your imagination and will most likely sit in your CD rack like it sits in mine. You probably will find more luck elsewhere.

reviewText:
This may be Callas's very first Traviata, but it is one to avoid like the plague, NOT because of her, but because it sounds like not a single rehearsal took place prior to performance.
After a merely adequate performance of the Act 1 Prelude with de Fabritiis in the pit, the listener is then treated to some of the most embarrassingly bad ensemble playing ever committed to disc.  The chorus, orchestra and solo singers are so "out of sync" at times, that it is difficult at times not to laugh out loud!  Callas is in fine voice, however.  Valletti, in lyrical roles a wonderful singer, is here out of his element as Alfredo.  A more vigorous impetuous heroic style is really demanded in this role.
I must admit that I couldn't stomach listening to enough to actually hear Taddei as Germont pere, so I can't comment on his performance here.
To add insult to injury, the slipshod ensemble playing that runs ramshod over this wonderful piece is not assisted by an even more constricted choppy recorded sound than usual for these Mexico City live Callas opera performances.
So unless you are a die-hard masochistic Callas completist, who relishes poor recorded sound, and doesn't mind wallowing in musical chaos, I would NOT recommend this set under any circumstances, especially when you have the Lisbon live and Santini RAI Callas versions both available on CD.

reviewText:
What the....4 and 5 star ratings everywhere, I don't get it. How can you be that disillusioned or naive. This is an embarrassing album for Neil, I am sorry. If this were released by ANY new artist it would be a career ender for sure. I am in a Neil "phase" right now , happens about once a year, where I listen to his first 10 albums over and over and over, up until around Rust Never Sleeps. This stuff is the bomb, classic, timeless and untouchable. I will even tolerate his 80's Geffen catalogue , Trans, Reactor, Blue Notes etc. What was once regarded as also embarrassing I find quite interesting now.

With the exception of Greendale, I consider his last 4-5 albums to be really bad and getting worse and worse. Living with War was worth 1-2 listens for its immediacy but after repeated listenings I couldn't stand listening to that "Drums 101" track on every song, Are you Passionate has that same damn track, I know its not a machine but it might have darn well been. The same wanky leads on every song. Neil has options to play with anyone of his previous brilliant band members but he is wasting their talents on these brainless rhythms.

More of the same on Chrome Dreams II, totally dumbed down music and lyrics that are almost laughable. How can you associate this album with the former Chrome Dreams from the mid-70s that had Powderfinger, Like a Hurricane and even Homegrown on it. Some people in these reviews are comparing song by song from each of the 2 albums "Like a Hurricane" vs "you name the crappy track", come on people ...can we take some reality pills here? If "Ordinary People" is the standout track on this album and a song that ranks in the top 20 of Neil's catelogue, like many are claiming here, then we are all in more trouble than we think. The best reviews are the ones calling Chrome Dreams II "Album of the Year". I suppose yes if you are only buying one album a year and it happens to be a Neil Young album.

Sorry I'm grumpy but I bought this album based on all the 5 Stars and was completely in disbelief when I listened to it for the first time.

I am not calling for Neil's head here, I want everyone on the planet to go out and buy every single album he has ever made....but, based on quality and merit, not because he is "Neil" brilliant and flawless. Buy it all , Trans, Shocking Pinks, Prairie Wind etc, like it, don't like it, I don't care but don't try and convince the masses that every new piece of poop that gets passed is more glorious than the last one. Please don't stack these records track for track, pound for pound agaist Harvest, Comes a Time nor Freedom. Its like you are trying to rationalize the existance of these songs using history to back up your arguments. New songs are really supposed to stand tall on there own are they not?

Neil, sorry man, I will always be one of the faithful, til the day I die but PLEASE slow it down, instead of a bad album a year, try doing a good one every 2 years or so. Age gracefully, I still believe you have what it takes to do some amazing work in the future. I don't want your legacy to be ruined by sub-standard material, you have rebounded before, you can do it again.

reviewText: As if the customer service of PonoMusic wasn't non-existent enough, as if the accusations about the credibility of Pono's marketing and sheer purpose weren't profoundly in question, what is PonoMusic CEO Neil Young's apparent solution? Ignore it and just crank out yet another album. It seems fair to say that Neil Young is obsessed with quantity over quality. As if Neil Young didn't turn enough of a profit from his tossed-off audiophile atrocity "A Letter Home", now he's supposedly fulfilling a lifelong dream by recording live in front of an orchestra as if he's Frank Sinatra. Neil evidently decided that a good way for him to line his already rich pockets even further would be to jack this new album up to a 2 CD set by including "full band" versions of all the songs on one disc, and solo acoustic (guitar, piano, ukelele, whatever) versions on the other. So, in effect, you get a double opportunity to witness how weak his songwriting is here. YES, I AM CONCERNED ABOUT THE ENVIRONMENT, but Neil is settling for cheap attempts to pull the heartstrings in place of any real depth, which is characteristic of him nowadays, including his dimwitted and deceptive attempts to try and con you into buying a Pono. And musically speaking, "Who's Gonna Stand Up?" feels like a rewrite of "Slowpoke" from the 1999 CSNY "Looking Forward" album, and the orchestration is flowery schlock that would have done Mitch Miller proud. Anyone who's impressed by Neil supposedly being so prolific needs a reality check. Subsequent songs follow suit. "Glimmer" and "I'm Glad I Found You" are so sappy and cheaply sentimental, you'd think they were originally intended for Josh Groban. "I Want To Drive My Car" has a "swinging big band" arrangement, with Neil repeating the title over and over again. I can't help but thinking, "Neil, if you want to drive your car so bad, then just go drive it already and stop churning out disposable music." Plus, at Neil's level of wealth, maybe a more sincere title would have been "I Want To Drive My CARS". Song after song is such an embarrassment that, if you're a veteran fan of rock and pop music, you can hardly help but sit there slack-jawed at how in the hell Neil Young ever became such a supposed legend. To reiterate as I have stated in the past, you should reward Neil Young for when he does QUALITY music, not just ANY music. That said, here's something for people who are apologists of all things Neil Young to consider--did you ever think that, despite the fact that he keeps cranking out album after album, that NEIL YOUNG IS ACTUALLY OUT OF IDEAS AND SCRAPING THE BOTTOM OF THE BARREL? But, fear not. Neil Young may be out of ideas, BUT WE ARE NOT. Instead of pointlessly listening over and over again to both discs of "Storytone" thinking that it might "grow on you" (anything can grow on you, including fungus--that doesn't make it good), STOP, TURN OFF Neil Young, and TURN ON Total Bull Crap--Do Not Rebuy Your Old Favorites Yet Again. At Total Bull Crap, we, ahem, STAND UP against proverbial bull crap. You want a rock band that tells it like it is, and AIMS to bring self-respect back to regular everyday people just like you? Check out the raging rocker "Boycott the Po-No", where we very justifiably take Neil Young to task for his deceptive marketing tactics. Want a band that encourages you to continue your education, including the acquisition of another "Foreign Language [Explicit]"? Listen to the uptempo country-pop of "Break Out of My Shell [Explicit]". Want a band that champions women instead of treating them like mere sex objects a la Jason Aldean? We do that too, with the country-rock riff-fest "Sexy Lady [Explicit]". Want a band that looks to the future, to the days when you will possibly be able to download your food? Check out "Downloadin' My Food [Explicit]". Want a band that acknowledges the past and contextualizes it for the present as opposed to mentioning it for the sake of sheer nostalgia? The wistful "Defunct Retail Store [Explicit]" is the answer. Want a head-banging rock song for the whole family? "I'd-a-Ho (Oh) Potatoes [feat. The Rock & Roll Advocates for Optimal Wellness]" is your ticket. Or, do you just plain need a quick pick-me-up? How about getting a little taste of "Redd Bull Donuts (feat. The Rock & Roll Advocates for Optimal Wellness)"? To diehard Neil Young apologists everywhere... FREE YOURSELF FROM THE VICE OF WHICH NEIL YOUNG HAS YOUR PROVERBIAL BALLS TRAPPED WITHIN. STAND UP, and realize that Neil Young is fleecing you for all you're worth. "Storytone"? Forget it. Kick some excitement into your life. GET REAL, and check out "Do Not Rebuy Your Old Favorites yet Again [Explicit]". Neil Young has had two albums in 2014, but they both suck--what the hell use is that? We have had ONE and ONLY ONE, and it rules. Now THAT's efficiency.

reviewText: Being a John Denver fan since the mid-'60's, I have a lot of history with the man's music, as well as having had a friendship with him over the years.  I was truthfully looking forward to this release for as long as I can remember hearing of it coming out, and having heard every track on line, I can tell you that, by and large, it is an overwhelming disappointment.  I can't expect the majority of the artists on this album, most of whom weren't even alive during most of John's career, to duplicate his work note for note.  However, to rearrange the songs into something that wasn't intended, specifically the Dave Matthews' treatment of "Take Me To Tomorrow", is as much of an insult as you could possibly have, nor can the man do little else but mumble the lyrics on key.  Matthews is the executive producer on the project, and it's his label that released it, and I wish that someone else had taken that role.  The best recordings on the project are Kathleen Edwards stellar rendition of "All Of My Memories", and Emmylou Harris' and Brandi Carlisle's read of "Take Me Home Country Roads".  Mary Chapin Carpenter does an admirable job with "I Guess He'd Rather Be In Colorado", a song that became identified with John, but written by Bill and Taffy Danoff before they ever met him.  Other than those, I found no redeeming qualities to this album.  Lucinda Williams sounds like she's ready to breathe her last on "This Old Guitar".  The other artists, not of my normal listening material, do adequate jobs with what they perform, but nothing to satisfy me, let alone knock me out.  If someone were to give me a copy of this recording, I might...MAYBE...keep it as part of my Denver collection, but I can almost guarantee you that the likelihood of my listening to it would be slim.  Save your money.

Don't get me wrong, a lot of this stuff is among his best work, but how many repackagings of his years at Mercury need to be released? Isn't the "Reason To Believe" boxed set enough? Plus, for every great track on here, there is a ton of filler to augment it.

Bottom line: Stick with the "Storyteller" boxed set, which includes most of the songs on here plus all his best work up to 1990, and then download all his stuff from "Vagabond Heart" onward. This collection is unneccessary.

reviewText: ...and N*Sync doesn't deserve ANY! Before I go on I will say this: as I write this, I am listening to my sister's copy of Celebrity so that I can't be accused of being biased. In the end, instead of evolving, it simply makes the "music" even more laughable. Justin's "beat boxing" at the end of "Pop" is nonsense. The song "Pop" itself is ridiculous. Do N*sync seriously think they aren't a trend and won't fade out simply because they don't want to? If they think they're here to stay, why write such a defensive song? They said rock 'n roll was a fad years ago, but neither the Beatles, Rolling Stones, or Jimi Hendrix wrote anything directed at the critics, they just kept writing good music. And speaking of writing, where did Justin come up with these lyrics? Who is he kidding? No, Justin, the sad truth is we wouldn't know you if you weren't a celebrity. Now you see why the writing is left up to hit makers like Diane Warren and Max Martin. N*sync are trying their best to quiet the critics, but just like last year when they tried to become more popular than BSB, they try way too hard. If its edgy hip-hop you want, check out Dr Dre, Snoop Dogg, and 2Pac instead. If you want some real music, check out Led Zeppelin, Jimi Hendrix, Metallica, and Pearl Jam instead. 5 years ago Hanson and the Spice Girls were popular, and now I can't even return their CDs to any used CD dealer. There is no doubt in my mind that the same fate will come for this album and this group.

reviewText:
There have always been two competing, conflicting trends pervading Paul McCartney's musical career. One, he undeniably is a great musical talent. He can rock when he wants to and at one time was a superb tune smith. Another trend, a contradictory one, is that he is a rank sentimentalist.

He was careful to balance the two trends in the beginning. This trend surfaced early in Paul's career with the song, "Yesterday." Lennon was incensed by this song, and considered Paul a traitor to rock and roll with the release of this song. But Paul rocked on with other Beatles songs like "I'm Down" and "She's a Woman." That last one was actually by all accounts a true collaborative effort. No matter, the point is that if he put out a sentimental song, he would balance it afterwards with a rocker.

This is not to say that sentiment is wrong. Far from it. When PM was at the zenith of his solo musical talents, shortly after he left the Beatles, the results were magnificent. The mistake that many music lovers made when listening to "Silly Love Songs," is that they were confusing Paul the rocker and Paul the rank sentimentalist, and wanting him to rock instead of waxing sentiment.

There were two other trends which at times worked against each other. Paul has always been willing to experiment. This is a good thing, and can yield good reasons. McCartney II, for example, was Paul's experiment into electronics which was one of John Lennon's personal favorite albums Paul released. It showed a lot of courage, it rocks and was a good, if underrated, album. He has since released efforts with the Firemen, which is respectable ambient music.

 But there is another trend which is problematic. He has an almost maniacal impulse to churn out product, no matter how good or bad it may be. This rarely produces good results; in fact, more likely than not, it produces garbage. Much of his efforts at classical music fits into this category. The music is forgettable -- it really isn't his music at all. Paul McCartney, like many rock musicians, cannot read or write musical notation. Consequently, when PM releases a classical release, it is usually a collaboration with a recognized musician, who has written down PM's musical ideas, much like dictation. This irrational desire to release albums and songs is a hit and miss thing. It is usually a "miss," however, and produces garbage. Like this album.

Words really cannot convey how bad this album truly is. The crooning I don't mind, but McCartney doesn't croon very well. He falters, he hesitates, his voice cracks -- not an inflected, intentional, crack, but a crack of a seventy-year old washed-up rocker. This album is an embarrassment; it is an outrage; it is just a poor rendition of lounge singing. Paul is a complex, complicated musical talent, much more than John ever was, but this album is surprisingly simple. It is simply BAD.

While listening to this album my thoughts were with the old Saturday Night Live. In the early shows the troupe would do skits called "Bad Theatre," Bad Poetry," and the like, portraying, well, a play or poetry poorly done, usually hosted by Dan Akroyd. While listening to this album I thought, "If the old SNL were around they would call this  "Bad Music.'"

I also thought of that Bill Murray character -- I couldn't concentrate on the music, it was so terrible -- of the cheesy lounge singer in the glitter tux and slicked back hair, who, of course, thought he was good and cool, but was, of course, terrible.

Then I thought, well, maybe Paul is releasing this album for the sake of irony, as a kitsch experiement, a parody on lounge singing and lounge singers. No, he really thinks this stuff is good and he's doing a good job. Well, it is not and he doesn't.

 The only parody is the title of the album, Kisses on the Bottom. What's up with the title of the album anyway? This is apparently Paul's attitude for anyone foolish enough to buy this album. If you don't like my album, well, you can just,  ....

 This is not to say that all interpretation of standards are all bad. Far from it. Rod Stewart is a good example of an ex-rocker who is successful in his interpretation of song standards. But Rod Stewart makes no pretensions of being a rock and roll star anymore. He left that persona, sadly, years ago. But he is good at what he does. Stewart's voice is perfectly matched to sing these classics; he is a befitting successor to Tony Bennett.

 But Paul McCartney singing lounge songs?  Paleeez. Other reviews have noted that his voice is creepy. There is some truth to this. His voice lacks the intimacy that is must be present whenever engaging in this type of singing. So Paul is deliberately softening his voice to give it that soft intimacy, to make it more personal. What he has done, of course, is exposed the natural weaknesses of advancing old age, making his voice sound foreign and, yes, a little creepy. All those years of yelping like Little Richard have taken a toll on his voice. To me, though, his singing is just plain bad. Bad, bad, bad.

 And this is not to say that the album is totally irredeemable. As in all CDs, if you inadvertently buy this album, it will make an excellent coaster, and can be used as a reflector, or a car ornament. Or you might do the Green thing and simply recycle this CD to your local recycle center. This is probably the best use of this CD. It is not fit for listening, so do something contructive and good for the environment. It's no good as music. It is a joke, sadly on anyone who buys this CD.
label: negative

reviewText:
These recordings, and this conductor, have acquired a kind of halo over time that makes it hard for music lovers to retain a bit of common sense, and indeed to judge these performances on what they actually deliver. In part this happens because the words "great conductor" are pronounced without the ancillary issue being considered - is he also a "great interpreter"? Let's not beat about the bush now: If total professionalism was the sole criterion of importance, then how could anyone deny that Ormandy, 50 years at the helm of the Philadelphia Orchestra, must be one of the two or three greatest conductors in history!?
I put this rhetorical question to you for the sake of perspective. Mravinsky was certainly a superb conductor, perhaps better said drillmaster - of his orchestra. But although I've auditioned a fair swag of his recordings (of which most are public performances anyway), I cannot discern a great Interpreter. He has a habit of sacrificing meaning to "objective" criteria, sometimes to the point of fanaticism. It may be what the regime demanded as a virtue of social realism, but that's not an excuse for his stone-cold execution of a score. Sometimes outstanding performances result quasi as a "collateral effect" of his hard driving. But this is exceptional. Mostly I feel dismay at the end of one of his concerts, because the excitement he conveys is visceral, and this one gets used and then it subsides. But of depth, authentic feeling, let alone caressing music that demands it, there is not a trace.
These Tchaikovsky recordings are accurate mirrors of his predilections. They are raw, the orchestra is pushed to extremes, the rhythms remind one more of Le Sacre than Tchaikovsky, the trumpets blare like denizens of hell. And now the point is that the "great conducting" cannot actually be heard, you hear an orchestra, and it does not reflect what you might mean by "great conducting". Moreover this ain't no Chicago Symphony or Berlin Philharmonic! It sounds more as if time and again they're in a panic.
So I question the appellation "great performances". I know a great performance when I hear it, and if I were to put the question in all earnestness to you, I suspect you would say the same. So this is not a great performance; it is an occasion of great visceral excitement, and that's the end of it. If you are at all in tune with Tchaikovsky, you'll enjoy it maybe 3-4 times, then enough! Better turn to a more modern recording, and there are plenty. So as not to evince prejudice for the West, let me point to Svetlanov, Kondrashin, Gergiev, Pletnev - all Russians, all passionately involved with Tchaikovsky, and their orchestras sound infinitely better.
But if the lure of dubious fame attracts you, by all means try it out. But don't complain when you get sick of this exaggerated and out of character wildness. Tchaikovsky was far too sophisticated for this kind of interpretation to be "right". So this is occasion to thank heaven for the many other versions available which convey a love for the composer's music, rather than draw total attention to the performers alone!

reviewText:
Yawn.  Snooze.  Here's yet another boring, double (!) album from a guy who just isn't trying anymore.  Witness the 'vigor' with which Buffett sings something like "Fins".  Virtually talking your way through a song and emphasizing the word at the end of every phrase does not make you Reed or Dylan but let's face it, this guy was never in the running for that kind of prestige anyway.  It does clearly demonstrate, however, someone well past his prime continually cashing in on his former glory.  Even his band sounds bored.  And well they should, as they're about to play "Margaritaville" for the 1000th time.  What a thrill.  I actually pity Buffett that he has to play this heap of a song every day of his life.  If he had known it would become his signature song, I'm sure he would have buried it at the bottom of the ocean.  Granted, his new music is lame but his so-called fans will never let him move on.

To Buffett's credit, he hasn't had to try very hard since the '70s.  Trendy yups pay to see him everytime he comes around, no matter how bad his latest album just so they have an excuse to get drunk, vomit in the car on the way home, and go into work late the next day.  (Personally, I need no excuse for that type of behavior ;) )  But even the hardest of the hardcore partiers from the golden age of Buffett have given up on this guy, myself included.  Buffett and his music used to be the reason for the party, the crowd merely participants.  Maybe he's simply gotten so bored with his own music, these days he'd rather the crowd be the party.  That's a fine money-making strategy but it makes for a painfully tedious album.

While not a perfect live document, if you're truly interested in what Jimmy Buffett was all about and could accomplish at the peak of his creativity in the '70s, pick up "You Had to Be There" instead and leave this dog of an album and its brethren where they belong - in the cut-out bin.
label: negative

There's only so much you can say; large percentage of cover versions, a few naff originals, big production trying to disguise the formulaic, almost deliberately insidious awfulness.. And on and on it goes...

Rhydian's a bore. Just because he's from Wales means nothing, only that he's a Welsh bore. There are no words to competently describe the mundanity of this selection of songs, no phrases or expressions to adequately convey the feelings of abjection and inevitability about 'I Believe' (Bachelors, Robson and Jerome) or 'Bridge Over Troubled Water'.(No, please not that..)
A year in Stockholm and L.A. (Wales not good enough obviously) to come up with something as miserable as this is just plain, economic waste.

Rhydian's hysterical video for his wan single: 'An Impossible Dream' (It WAS Rhydian - you lost!) had him wandering an atmospheric coast-line, flapping his arms about like a big, mad, bouffant gull. People in the shipping lanes were thinking he was one of those mythical Sirens - compelling sailors onto the rocks with ghastly wailing.

One thing 'Rhydian' does have in it's favour is - it's reassuring. You expect it to lose and when it duly obliges, you get a nice warm feeling. Replaces some of the energy you lost laughing as Rhydian slumped to defeat against that charismatic entertainment colossus- Leon Jackson.

I would have left this alone had there been an iota of bite or storm, one note of spontaneity or intuitiveness - but there isn't. It floats about rudderless, stuffed to the gills with it's own worth and grandeur, but under the glitz and ersatz shimmer, it's the same old acre of greedy, venal economics.
About as far away from real and true 'talent' as you can get.

reviewText:
Culture Club emerged at a time when the pop charts had become stale as moldy bread, and most of the more interesting of the new music coming out of England (and other places where aspiring young musicians picked up synthesizers instead of guitars) had a distinct gothic gloom that the average member of the record-buying public found to be  cold at best (and alien at worst).

In such an atmosphere, Culture Club came across as sunny rather than cold, human rather than mechanistic, colorful rather than monochromatic, and emotional rather than distant. Even the moody "Do you really want to hurt me", which was most of the world's first real exposure to the band, came across as smooth and engaging.

Culture Club's emergence also coincided with a resurgence of interest in Motown, whose influences on Culture Club's music were quite obvious ("Church of the poison mind" blatantly lifts from Stevie Wonder's "Uptight", for example). And, similar to Motown, Culture Club's music appealed to a variety of people as it blurred some of the rigidly defined categories the music industry had thrown up around everything.

This box set reflects very little of that appeal. Half of the first disc consists of demos that, for the most part, aren't that interesting (though they are surprisingly polished for demos); half the second disc jumps several years ahead to Boy George solo material; and the remaining two disc are a horrid mishmash of solo material, reunion tracks, unlistenable remixes, and more demos.

The packaging is similarly awful. The track listings make no distinction between Culture Club tracks and Boy George tracks, so you're likely to be very confused about what is what on the later discs unless you have followed Boy George's solo and DJ careers very closely. And there is little in the way of liner notes to speak of; what little there is tells only Boy George's side of the story.

In any event, it seems clear that this is not really a Culture Club set, but a Boy George set. In that respect, this collection is clearly mislabeled. I'm surprised that Virgin were even willing to release the thing.

If you want an overview of Culture Club's brief career, I'd suggest sticking with either the Greatest Moments/VH-1 Storytellers disc, or the more recently released Greatest Hits collection. Just avoid this.
label: negative

reviewText:
If you are hoping to hear the next "Let's Dance", "'Heroes'", "Space Oddity", or "Ashes to Ashes" types of hits, you'd be better off looking elsewhere.
David Bowie knew he was dying, and he completed this album which came out on his birthday this year (2016). A week later he died of cancer.
Many fans will rate this swan song album 5 stars and fill the internet with praises, but the truth is that this is really a depressing album, with no potential singles (no matter what "The Fans" say), and essentially, if you like this type of hard to reach music and poetry because it makes you feel superior to the apes that still listen to Billy Joel and Bruce Springsteen, then this is the snobbish album for you.
It is listenable, but you won't be singling along, or taking it to the car to play while you drive. You will probably play it a second time to try to "get it" like all those cappuccino hipsters that claim they "do" but you won't like it and you will feel like a failure for not loving it. You will not play this album a 3rd time and will either put it in a pile appropriately named "Yogi's Pile of Myerda" to take it to your local CD and vinyl shop to exchange it for store credit before people stop liking it and begin to dump it on Amazon.
I can't even call it a "concept" album, as at least one track came off some play that he wrote or was involved in.
But as a whole, it is a collection of tracks recorded in secret and in a hurry as the clock was ticking, and his body was writhing is convulsive pain as the cancer riddled his innards mercilessly. The album goes nowhere, despite what stories are stringed up in desperation.
Your best bet if you are still curious but won't commit the money, is to borrow it from a sucker friend or from the library.
This is only "interesting" because he died soon after its release, otherwise, Rolling Stone and even the rest of the brainless snobs would give  this no more than 2 stars, but I'm not a liar like anyone rating this myerda 4 or 5. This is David Bowie's "Bronx Salute" to the world - his "Metal Machine Music" as a final farewell .

reviewText:
A few confessions up front:

1) I've never been a huge Yo-Yo Ma fan.  I've heard a number of his recordings, which have struck me as competently played, small-scale, and unimaginative.

2) I think that Maazel is an underrated conductor, and not deserving of the brickbats often tossed in his direction.  He can be prosaic, but he's usually competent.

3) The Dvorak concerto was the first piece of "real" music I heard when I was ten years old, and after 45 years, it's still among my favorites.  Over the years, I've collected dozens of recordings, many of them superb.

This recording, however, is probably the worst.  In my opinion, should never have seen the light of day, and I'm shocked that Sony ever issued it, much less reissued it.  Ma is no more than competent - as previously, I find his tone small, unattractive, and utterly faceless.  Worse still, Maazel seems to be asleep on the podium.  The music simply plods along without much variety or interest.  Moments that virtually every other conductor gets right go right by Maazel and his orchestra (is this really the same band that recorded this work with Karajan?).  Listen, if you dare, to the first movement coda, which plods along mercilessly. This is followed by an Adagio that nearly falls apart, losing any sense of momentum, and the finale is no better. The timings look a *little* slow, but don't begin to tell the story of this recording.

In short, avoid this one.  If you want the Dvorak concerto, virtually any other recording will make a better case for this marvelous work.  Any of Rostropovich's (I prefer the Boult, but Karajan and Talich are also excellent), Fournier, Gendron, Casals, May...well, pretty much any other recording.  I haven't yet heard Ma with Masur, but surely it has to be better than *this*.

ADDENDUM: I had the chance to hear Ma's remake with Masur and the NYPO, and it's better than the above in every possible way.  It's still not a great recording of the Dvorak concerto, but it's certainly enjoyable.  Ma's playing isn't much more imaginative or impassioned, but the engineers did a better job of capturing the beauty of his sound.  Masur isn't dramatic enough for my taste, either, but at least he doesn't plod a la Maazel.

Seeing this production in Toronto a few years ago proved to be one of my worst experiences in the theatre.
The movie should have made a fantastic musical.  And the opening theme gives the proper film noir feeling... But Andrew Lloyd Webber cheated and instead of writing a new score for this show, he chose to recycle cut-out songs from previous failed musicals.  The result is an uneven patchwork that never effectively settles on tone.  The title song, for example, sounds too contempoary for a story set in 1950.  The lyrics are bland and filled with all too obvious rhymes and slang expressions that are often out of synch with the characters. Why does Mr lloyd-Webber refuse to collaborate with a good lyricist who could make his music come across more with more effect.  (He did once, with Tim Rice... but that partnership ended.)
SUNSET angers me.  A good source was turned into an inferior musical.  Yet, simply because it was the only new book musical to open on Broadway in the 94/95 season it was awarded the Tonys for Best Musical, Best Book and Best Score.  It did not deserve any of those awards.  However, audiences were not fooled.  It closed on Broadway after a short run and lost millions.  The London production had a longer run and still lost millions.  The Toronto production lasted less than a year and lost millions.  And the national tour folded almost before it started...and again lost millions.  Maybe people are finally catching onto Webber's endless recycling!

reviewText:
With her second album "The Boy is Mine" Monica has outdone even the Spice Girls when it comes to proving that there is indeed such a thing as "girl power."  Not to mention that like the Spice Girls, she writes all of her songs by herself, with no interfering songwriters like Rodney Jerkins or exective producers like Clive Davis interfering with her artistic freedom.
At first glance, you might think the title "The Boy is Mine" and the picture on the cover of the album mean that Monica is one of those girls who only exists to chase men and claim them for herself.  In fact, you might think this album sends kids the message that it is important for girls to base their entire lives around boys.  Think again.  This album is the most powerful feminist statement of our time.  Monica is saying that she is a girl, she will do what she want, and boys are only hers to be used as she feels like.  And the cover shot of her putting her hands strategically over a certain unmentionable part of her body is not meant to attract guys, oh no.  It is instead merely an example of Monica saying that a woman's body is her own and she is completely comfortable with it.
What abou the songs?  Well, "Right Here Waiting" features one of the most innovate and soulful artists of our time, the excellent 112.  The title track isn't a song about two girls fighting over a boy, as the video might have led you to believe, but instead a statement of female power and solidarity.  And "The First Night" finds Monica saying that she won't sleep with guys on the first night that she meets them.  Instead she will wait all the way until the second night.  Wow.  She is such a role model for saying that, she deserves major props.
Also, you might think that songs like Inside and Take Him Back find Monica with nothing but a headful of boys.  Think again.  If you pay attention, Inside is really probably a song about just one of her many platonic male friendships of hers, certainly not about a boyfriend of hers.  And Take Him Back is a song about a puppy that she gave up but is thinking of getting it back because she misses it so much.  Its definately not just another song that finds her pining over a boy.
***In all seriousness, she does have a great voice and is still a heck of a lot better than Brandy.  In fact, some of the songs on this album are actually quite good.  But this commercialism and lack of artistic freedom in music just needs to be stopped, NOW.  Its ridiculous and demeaning to women, even to Monica herself, who I'm sure is actually a very nice, talented person.  She just made the all-too-common decision to trade her artistic freedom for money and fame.

reviewText:
With six platinum certifications under its belt, Metal Health turned Quiet Riot into one of the biggest acts in rock almost overnight. As I stated on my review of that album, the biggest problem for this band was its utter lack of songwriting talent in a genre that was driven by catchy singles. Knowing this, the boys just tried to replicate Metal Health's sound to a tee, even re recording a second Slade cover, Mama, Weer All Crazee Now, and making it the flagship single of the record. With Party All Night they tried really hard on delivering a memorable raucous metal anthem like Metal Health for the second time, but sadly it fell kind of short, and again, the rest of the songs are just mediocre filler.
Despite its major shortcomings, Condition Critical managed to reach platinum level sales, but considering its predecessor's success it was declared an utter failure by the band, the label and everyone in the music business. Sadly, since the band had signed a record contract that handed the band's first two albums royalties to the record label's owner, its members weren't really enjoying the success they deserved. This situation created a lot of resentment, especially on vocalist Kevin Du Brow, who spent most of the mid eighties badmouthing everyone in the industry, from label executives to record producers to other bands he considered were unjustly riding on his coattails. Eventually, this attitude would make him the most hated man in heavy metal (predating Lars Ulrich for more than a decade and a half!) causing a press backlash that brought a lot of band tensions which resulted in Rudy Sarzo's exit from the group in 1985. Another consequence of Kevin Du Brow's constant badmouthing of other metal bands was the loss of a sizable portion of Quiet Riot's fan base that also supported those groups. By the end of this album's support tour, the band's condition was indeed critical, and only a miracle would stop its downward spiral. Since this album has only two good songs, I strongly recommend buying any Quiet Riot compilation instead.

Read some books, look at some instruments in a museum, then try to re-create ancient performances. Great idea! Now, go ahead and claim that this is the way it actually sounded back then. How much of that kind of drivel would YOU believe? I think not!
For a period perfomance of this seminal opus, try Sir Neville Mariner's version. It's got what this one is missing- excitement!
Two times I've heard Hogwood conduct this masterpiece all the way through. Two times I wondered why I ever thought I liked it... the Messiah, that is.
And that is not right! There is a malais settling into modern classical performing styles- note perfect (Render unto me a break, PLEASE! Note perfect does not mean playing lifelessly! Fritz Reiner was famous, as was Toscanini, for wanting it done as the composer wrote it. Neither man, to my knowledge, let his forces turn in dead performances.) dead from the neck up, emotionless, colorless, distilled water tasting dreary monstrosities often seem to pass for great performances. Classical music is not bloodless, people. It's about and for real human beings, with wants and hatreds and loves and desires. Let's not continue with this trend, which renders so many works into bloodless cadavers. Does the spirit of Dracula roam freely now throughout the great venues? Is Hogwood a creative vampire of the soul? I hope not!

reviewText:
My dad is out of control.  I can't stand it anymore.  All the dude plays is Pearl Jam.
Pearl Jam in the car.  At home.  Pearl Jam T-Shirts.  (He used to make me wear them...uggg.)
Pearl Jam discussions.  Pearl Jam coffee.  Pearl Jam license plate. (PJ10Vedr)

I can't stand it.  I love him and stuff, but he's really hard to be around.
I embarrassed to have him drive me and my friends places.
He always pops in Pearl Jam or puts it on the stupid Pearl Jam station.
Like anyone needs Pearl Jam 24/7.  But people do...like my dad.

He thinks he's getting music cred by playing it.  My friends are polite, but it's very embarrassing.
They are all like, "Dude, your dad's music sucks.  What's up with that lead singer?  He's always Yaaarling and Groaning...and the songs have no melody.  Your dad's music sucks."

"I know," I say.  "But your dad listens to Phish...so...."

It's bad, and a lot of my friends have similar problems with their dads being mad wack.

I have one whose dad just plays Dave Matthews all the time.  Or the one who plays Phish.  That really sucks.  That guitar dudes solos grate on my ears.  Makes me wanna vomit.  They go nowhere fast.  I guess people are into dudes who play fast???  Can't forget the Rush dad....wow...horrible.

I'm not alone, but sometimes I feel like I am.

This new album came in the mail.  (My dad still buys music.)
And he is reenergized with Pearl Jam love.
It's almost unbearable.  He had a listening party at his house with all of his friends.
They think they know a lot about music because they are into Pearl Jam.
Try to pass it off on me...it's pathetic.

They all got drunk and I went upstairs to surf the net.
They all started playing their favorite Pearl Jam songs.
"Daughter" came on and they all sang it at the top of their lungs.
So pathetic....It's a horrible song.  Who writes songs about people with learning disabilities?
Yo.  I got this sweet song.  It's about a girl with LD.  Cool.  Not.
And here are these grown men singing about this...
Why?  I can't even fathom.  The song is so wack.  It must give them something missing in their lives.

They partied all night.  It was their Wild Hogs moment.  I hope they had fun.

When I woke up in the morning, I head music coming from the bathroom downstairs.  I walked by and saw my father standing in front of the mirror with a radio on singing "Nothing Man" as he stared at himself.  WTF?

It's just been absolutely terrible.  And my dad started liking Pearl Jam in 1993.  For 20 years they have been his favorite band.  He really doesn't listen to anything else.  He may listen to some U2, Tom Petty, Led Zeppelin, or Black Crows...but 95% of the time it's Pearl Jam.  I usually get bored of band after a couple of months.  I like to explore and taste the world.  Not my dad.  Pearl Jam forever.

When I was a baby, I didn't even like music.  I would cry when the teacher started to play the piano for sing alongs in kindergarten.  I thought she would start Yarllling and Grunting and Growiling.  It took years of reconditioning for my ears to accept music.  All because my dad wouldn't stop listing to dumb Pearl Jam.

So.  If you like Pearl Jam, buy this album.  It will fulfill you delusion.  Have fun with it.  Run with it.  Pearl Jam for life.  I don't care.
I love my dad.  He's been pretty cool to me and my mom and sister.  I'm pretty lucky.
I wish he would give Pearl Jam a rest tough because, inadvertently I end up listening to way more Pearl Jam then is ever needed.  And their bland, faux rock and roll dulls my world.  And makes me seasick.

I just wish he were into cooler music.

Maybe someday I'll be the same.

But I doubt it.

and datta-datta-datta-datta...
and bwaaaaaaa.....bwaaaaaaa....
and thunder noise....
and creepy escalating orchestral noise/scraping noise/thunder noise, etc

"Harvey Two Face"  has  some potential, but briefly.  Is that a theme trying to make it's way out?  Well, sortof,  I think.  Is that a piano struggling to find a melody?  three notes?  It  takes about 6 minutes but we do get to a beautiful, albeit brief, swell of strings and surge of horns, but  over sadly too soon.  I would have moved more of that.
