reviewText:
These comments will not be enjoyed by the deathless legions of Domingo fans who have chimed in with their 5-star rating of this fiasco but I feel compelled to swim against the raging tide of almost universal raves.  I found this recording nauseating on many levels.

EMI, in a desperate move to keep itself afloat as a viable classical music company, has come up with the most shameless Hollywood style public relations campaign imaginable for any recording made in my 58 years on this planet.  The Rhett and Scarlett style cover art says it all.

There is much talent on display here and they all are in fine voice, so why did this recording leave me frothing in frustration? Perhaps it is the blatant attempt to suborn my complicity into thinking this is a great, an immortal recording.  It isn't.  Far from it.  It is glitzy, shallow and patched together like a finely woven quilt; very colorful and, like a quilt, two-dimensional.  Unfortunately the second dimension in this fabric, the depth, is entirely missing.

Nina Stemme is widely considered to be the great Isolde of the 21st century.  I remember her debut at Bayreuth as Freia in the first season of Levine's Ring there, 1994.  She was nothing special sounding but that is not a role upon which to judge a soprano's gift.  This Isolde was recorded very early in her international career as a Star.  I always wondered at the speed of the rise of her reputation based upon so little.  But she definitely has the Goods, big voice, solid technique and intelligence.  Her diction is sometimes wanting but that is not uncommon in big voiced sopranos.
And at this time the wobble that has become more prominent of late was only intermittently hinted at.  Hers performance, along with Pape's Markes and Br's Kurwenal are almost worth the price of purchase.

Ren Pape is an excellent Marke, younger than the norm which I think is apropos.  In those days he was probably considered a wizened old man at 40, it's all relative.  What is wonderful with Pape is that he keeps his very long, potentially boring, scene in Act 2 interesting for the listener.  An outstanding King on record!  Olaf Br was a great baritone in his prime and it is great to have him singing Wagner.  I wish he'd undertaken Wolfram von Eschenbach in Tannhuser as well!

Pappano is a highly capable operatic conductor, more successful in the Italian repertoire than Wagner but still a formidable in that repertory.  The Orchestra of the Royal Opera House Covent Garden has been honed, by Haitink before him, into a top-notch recording orchestra, something it hasn't been since the Colin Davis years of the 1960s.  So far so good.

Here come the onions.  Domingo is all wrong for the role of Tristan, especially at this late stage of his long and illustrious career.  He's a great Verdian but his Wagner performances, though sung very well, do not convince as characterizations, but rather come off as circus stunts to show off how versatile and 'amazing' he is that he can 'do so much' that well.  Fine, but I have to draw the line at the role of Tristan.  He bleats too much for one thing.  I guess that's supposed to be his plangent tone and all that, but that aspect of his singing is gone now in his mid 60s (the time of this recording) and he comes off as a very artificial vocal fakir.  It's a beautiful sound, no doubt, but that's all it is.  There is no connection to Tristan's dilemma, the reactions are frozen in aspic and do not move the heart at all. The agonizing emoting in Act 3 convince on the surface but upon repeated listening holds no emotional wallop of any substantial kind.  It's almost glib, as if he were assuming his audience were already won-over to his performance just because it's Him singing it.  I confess to an undying distaste for singers who take on recorded roles they have never, and never COULD, sing on stage.  I had this problem with Studer's Salome too.  Those kinds of recordings I categorize as publicity stunts simply to make money.  And there was all that baloney about EMI never making another opera recording and how the recording industry would die if we didn't rush out and buy this gold-plated turkey.

This Tristan recording is not helped by the relentless cutting and pasting that has gone on inside the editing booth.  Nothing connects, there is no tissue, just a smooth, though not seamless, creation made available by the miracle of computer technology.  The sound is not so great either.  The English horn solos in Act 3 sound as if the player were sitting in an echoey toilet stall just off stage left.

I don't understand the popularity of Mihoko Fujimura.  She possesses a lovely voice with the ability to fill a hall, that's all to the good, but she has no temperament at all, at least on recording.  Her Brangne is smooth as pudding, like the recording itself, and leaves this listener cold as stone when her calls from the tower should have reduced me to a chocolatey mess on the floor (listen to Christa Ludwig for Bhm or Yvonne Minton for Kleiber and you'll hear what I mean).

This recording is a perfect example of how vanity is destroying the recording industry.  And if you think Pandora is going to run opera 24/7 think again.  I just hope we can still buy compact disc players when I'm in The Home!

I have only given away 5 Wagner recordings in my lifetime;  Barenboim's and Levine's wretched Hollnders, Barenboim's Tannhuser, Thielemans's awful Tristan (not his fault, terrible cast) and this set of Tristan.  It was a packet down the drain but I knew I would never want to hear it again.

Open your ears, listening public, and stop swallowing all the b.s coming from the publicity departments of creatively moribund companies like EMI.  If you want a fine Tristan recording there are several out there, and 2 or 3 truly great ones (Bhm, Karajan-Bayreuth 1951, Kleiber, Bayreuth 1975).  If you want Flagstad you have a choice between Reiner at Covent Garden (Flagstad in her pre-world fame prime), and the famous Furtwngler with his transcendental, wizardly conducting.

This expensive, all-star recording from EMI plummets to the bottom of the pile.

reviewText:
"Goes to Hell" is the follow-up to the excellent "Welcome to My Nightmare".  Indeed the storyline of "Hell" is very similar to "Nightmare".  Because of the success of "Nightmare", someone (was it Alice or Ezrin?) thought that a repeat with weaker material would be equally successful.  I tend to think that it was Ezrin as Alice was "not all there" during this period.  Or maybe Alice decided that he could do anything and it would be great?  I can imagine the conversations in the studio went like this -- picture Alice being followed around the studio by a bunch of "Yes Men".  Alice: "Hmmm...maybe we should do a disco song?" Yes Men: "Brilliant, Alice. What a great idea! You're a genius!" Alice: "You know, I've always admired Barry Manilow.  Perhaps I could BE the next Barry Manilow?  How 'bout we do a Barry Manilow-like ballad about crying and self-pity?"  Yes Men: "Absolutely brilliant!  You're a God, Alice, I tell ya -- A GOD!!"
Incidentally, these Barry Manilow-like songs were the only hits from the period of "Goes to Hell", "Lace & Whiskey", and "From the Inside".  But (not that I care for Barry Manilow) if I want to hear a Barry Manilow like ballad, I don't want to hear it from a self-deluded former hard rock performer.  Gimme Barry Manilow.
On the positive side, there is some fine guitar work by Steve Hunter on "Wish You Were Here" and the song "Go To Hell" has its' moments.
Overall, not one of Alice's better efforts during an admittedly difficult period in his life.  Only for the true die hard Alice fan.

reviewText:
Dream Theater remains the best progressive rock band of all time, but Octavarium falls flat on so many levels it's embarrassing. Why did this album ever see the light of day?
Sure, it has hints of what it could have been. Some of the music is fantastic and has a great hook. Octavarium goes in places no other Dream Theater record has.
Unfortunately, these moments are few and far between.
This is a monotonous album, almost agonizing to listen to. Just when you think a song is going to really kick in, it instead drops heavy. No song ever really draws you in. And quite frankly, I had to force myself to listen to the 20-some minute epic song "Octavarium," which had only a brief splash of interest at the end.
On top of that, the lyrics are almost painful to listen to. Dream Theater is much more talented than this. There are so many cliches in these lyrics and really, such a level of cheese, I felt embarrassed listening to them.
Dream Theater had a lot to build off of after "Train of Thought." It's always exciting to see which direction they'll go in next. I didn't realize they'd go the direction of boring.
The band has said they recorded this album to sound like "Images and Words." Nice to say, but far from true. This album has no appeal like I&W, or Metropolis II, or Six Degrees. It has nothing in common with any previous DT album except the equally subpar "Falling Into Infinity."
Perhaps James LaBrie saved all the best material for his excellent solo record. But this is one Dream Theater fan who is extremely disappointed with this disaster.

reviewText:
From a band that I used to consider my favorite current artists, this is about as dull as they get!  "Being There", "Summerteeth"(especially), and "Yankee Hotel Foxtrot" are 3 of my all time favorite albums.  The cream of the crop!  But this album puts me to sleep and not in a good way like the Velvet Underground's 3rd album or Big Star's "Sister Lovers", but in a "Why did I waste my money on this!" sort of way.

I chalk it up to the sacking of Jay Bennett.  The tension between Bennett and leader Jeff Tweedy worked in a way like Lennon balancing McCartney or David Gilmore and Roger Waters created tension in each other's lives to help them create wonderful works of art.  Before Bennett, Wilco was mildly interesting, then with Bennett, one of the greatest bands, and now without him, Wilco is duller than ever.  No one, prior to this album, regardless of personal opinion of Wilco, would have called this band dull, EVER!  But that is exactly the case here.

The noisy outros of white noise, the swirling keyboard arrangements, and the ultra catchiness with extremely dark lyrics of the songs from the previous trilogy are all missing here.  Everything that made them Wilco in my eyes is gone. Evolving is one thing, going from being the most extraordinarily innovative band to this snoozefest is another story ...Oh well.  At least they made 3 of my favorite albums, that is more than most bands will ever have achieved!  Please buy THOSE 3, you will be challenged with every listen, this one should be skipped over.

Buy those three albums and skip this one!!!

reviewText: Eagles fans, beware. This two-disc set is horrible. The Eagles went into decline after "Hotel California," even though they kept charting with lesser material for a few years afterward. Then, while their position on the creativity scale had secured itself at the "Mediocrity" mark, they retired, thankfully, before descending further toward "Painfully Bad." Well, now they've re-emerged, only to reveal that their downward spiral had continued, inaudibly, all those years, and they've now fallen below "Painfully Bad" and into the category of "Unlistenable." With the exception of one cut -- "How Long," which was written by non-Eagle (but frequent song contributor) J.D. Souther -- "Long Road Out of Eden" proves the creative songwriting well of the Eagles has gone dry. Bone dry. Death Valley dry. Had any songs (apart from "How Long") on this set been offered up to a record label by an unknown songwriter, they'd have been summarily rejected. The melodies are comprehensively unengaging, and the lyrics are amatuerishly trite and cloying. Take my word for it, fans (and I count myself in that group), this reunion was an artistic waste of time -- don't waste your money on it.

reviewText:
Ok, I'll be blunt with what what I'm about to say in this sentence - Bow Wow's fifth studio album, "The Price Of Fame", SUCKS! You'd think an album with such a title would provide music that dug deeper, both musically and lyrically, than the short-lived Pop-(c)rap he's made a living on for the majority of his career, but it doesn't. Actually, let me ask you this - how many of you really expected this album to be great? How many of you really set your expectations high enough to the point of expecting this album to be some kind of "Illmatic", "Doggystyle", "Reasonable Doubt" and all the rest of those critically acclaimed Hip-Hop album classics?

Seriously, Bow Wow has little to no brains. Yes, he's a decent rapper, he's got a natural sense of laid-back cool, he's a millionaire, his affiliation with Hip-Hop legends like Snoop Dogg gives him street credibility, ladies and little female kiddies love him, guys envy his success and the dude managed to hook up with one of today's most successful R&B artists of this decade, Ciara. Unfortunately, none of it amounts up to anything when it comes to his lyrical ability, which is -to (once again) be blunt - awful. The unconvincing "Intro" jacks the beat from his previous mini-hit/Lil' Romeo "diss" "Fresh Azimiz", while the bland wannabe club banger "How You Move It" sounds like an actual rip-off of "Fresh Azimiz", and that track was already bad in the first place. The smooth vocals Chris Brown & Johnta Austin provide on lead single "Shorty Like Mine" can't hide the fact that Bow Wow is a horrible lyricist. For crying out loud, half of the album's tracks feature guest artists, all of whom chew Bow Wow up and spit him back out like the moronic hack he really is.

Even when he tries digging deeper in songs like "Outta My System", where the evidently talented songster Johnta Austin's soulful vocals are forced to play second-best to T-Pain's reedy squeak, he still sounds bland and emotionless. He even ends the aforementioned ode to ex-girlfriend Ciara with this mushy conclusion - "If I could, I would turns back the hands of time / And correct all the mistakes I ever did / But now I guess I gotta move on, right? / It's still hard / And I stick love you to this day / Peace". Really, Bow Wow? If you truly loved Ciara like you said you did, why did you two really break up? Why are you more concerned with tryna pick up dime-a-dozen h*es with radio-bound garbage like "Bet That", "Damn Thing" (feat. long-forgotten rapper Da Brat), "I'm A Flirt" (feat. R. Kelly) & the raunchy "Give It To You"?

If there's one thing that truly shocked me about this album, it's not that Bow Wow co-produced some of these album's tracks, but the fact that he does a GOOD job doing so alongside other producers like Jermaine Dupri. I'm not sure who produced what, but whoever laid down the hard-hitting, synth-heavy beats of the Bow Wow / Cocaine J. / Young Capone collaboration "Don't Know About That" or the Bow Wow / Lil' Wayne / Lil' Scrappy / Short Dawg / Pimp C collaboration "4 Corners" deserves some serious recognition for making the listening experience of "The Price Of Fame" a little less painful.

Altogether, a terrible album that teaches you nothing you don't already know, nor does it provide you with the entertainment you might've been hoping for. 1 STAR!

N.B.:
To Bow Wow,
 For the love of love of whatever it is you love most, cut down on the boasting, keep your clothes on and act like the man you continually claim to be. I respect the fact that you have -to some degree- worked for years to get to where you are, there's no denying that your music essentially remains unchanged after all these long years. Where's the ambition, hunger, thought-provoking substance and introspective material that made greatness out of Hip-Hop legends like Nas? Where's the quality music and unexpected surprises you promised to your fans, haters and readers?

On another note, get your facts straight. You evidently can't create a hit song of some kind without the help of someone else, your acting skills are weak, you're not as "gangsta" as you think, you're not the hottest thing to hit the block and you clearly do not possess the talent, dedication, time, talent or focus to find talented musical individuals, nonetheless push them into the mainstream or fund them with the necessary materials or experience required for artistic growth.

Assuming that you're reading this, you're probably thinking that I'm just another babbling hater with nothing better to do, but I'm just speaking what I truly feel - something that I was hoping from you on "The Price Of Fame". If you think I'm wrong, then prove me wrong and do something more worthwhile than shaving your head and flashing your ugly flesh across global TV screens.

From,

Had I have purchased 'My own prison' first before 'Human Clay' my initial thoughts would definitely have been "`One' hit wonders!'"  Even with the millions of copies sold of "Human Clay" and the huge success, would I have even risked the effort of plummeting into my pockets to buy their next album?  Hey, in the music business, surely you only have "one" chance to put your stamp on the market...it better be a good one.
Tip:  If you already own 'Human Clay' and never heard 'My own prison' then avoid it at all costs and maintain your propitious opinion of Creed!

* The Long Lost Godzilla Review has finally arrived!

This review was written in late 1998 or early 1999.  I posted the review back when it was originally written but the review never appeared.  This should have been one of the oldest, if not the oldest, review of this product on Amazon.  It was issued on Amazon.co.uk on January 21, 2001. I remember "Undercover" being a somewhat funny, rather ridiculous song.  I still stand by what I said in the original review though, even after over a decade of not having heard the album, that this was a soundtrack caculated slowly at reaching as many different type of markets as possible, and the record feels disjointed and does not flow. Godzilla: The Album Review
[There's a lot of great music out there with high integrity]...and this ain't it.  Good album ... from the commercial standpoint.  This album is pure product, nothing more.  (Which, by the way, is what is ruined about Beatles for Sale).  A few people have praised it for the variety of music contained therein.  Sorry, on this record, not a strong point.  It was just a blatant cash-in.  Wallflower's cover of Heros costed $500,000.  That is how much they paid the band.  This was widely criticized in the recording industry.  There was not a track put on here that the producers did not think would help them sell more of these LPs (still think in record terms).  And they were right.

Actually, in terms of what they were trying to do (make pure product) this album is 5 stars because they succeed so well.  In terms of artistic quality, like how the album will stand the test of time, - 5 stars. ; 0 )  It won't last at all.

Truthfully, I do like all of the music on this album.  But the thing I don't like is everything on this has such a commercial feel.  The movie (which I haven't seen...never appealed to me, although I am a big fan of SF/Fantasy movies) I have not seen, but have been told its just a special effects flick.  It was supposed to be the big hit of the year.  It did not go over as well as expected, though it did decently.  That's how Godzilla: the album did.

Cine Come With Me, being (besides Heros) the most talked about track, is perhaps also one of the most disgusting.  When you try to combine such different genres as rap and classic rock, it is bound to be hard to do successfully.  Being a huge Zep fan, I couldn't believe they did that.  And in the liner notes of the Zep Box Set, Page talks about how you have to be careful with tampering with music because it means so much to people.  Here he was just rearranging the song sequences.  Can we say...hypocrite?  Although it is interesting, granted, it is truly a crime that they did that to Kashmir, one of the ultimate rock songs!  That would be like taking the orchestra crescendos out of A Day in the Life.  If Puff Daddy has to depend on established rock classics to sell his records, he is in very sad shape.  Especially considering he did such a poor job.  Page should be shot for allowing him to do that...even played on the damn track.  Had I been Plant (who like the version) or JPJ, I would have torn into them.  For Jones...he's been getting treated so crappy by his former bandmates.

(Interesting Factoid: John Paul Jones did the string arrangements for R.E.M.'s classic Automatic for the People.  Now there's a real 90's album for ya!)

Bottom Line: If you want good rock, go get the real stuff.  If you want commercialized tracks with no consideration for art; you've hit the mother lode.

There has to be a balance...everyone has to make a living.  But there has to be some art to it too.  This is entirely out of balance

The Ultimate Soundtrack of the 90s: Singles.  Although it does not have Nirvana, it defines the grunge movement.  That has art.  It's the best sound track of the 90's I've heard.  Don't waste yr money on this commercial crap!  Go with Singles!  Damn good album!

reviewText:
Bob Dylan has a new album, Tempest, an event that would normally not interest me so much had it not been for the large portions of praise the songs and performances have drawn from smart rock and pop critics. There are some pioneers, some esteemed geniuses that a generation of record reviewers (and a generation of critics after them) don't want to let go of, let alone admit that the later work isn't as interesting as the  material that drew you to the artist to begin with. There is a problem with reaching one's zenith so early, in that everything you do afterwards is compared with the singular work you'd done years before. It's not fair to the particular artist, whether great or mediocre.

 For Dylan, though, the generally solid reviews that he receives for his stream of albums seems an irrational response from someone who  hasn't demonstrated more than the capacity to be mysterious and inscrutable . Mystery and inscrutability are qualities that in themselves that do not make for something that will turn my head ahead and cause me to cogitate beyond reasonable length when the disc is done playing. I don't know what the fuss is all about other than it seems to be a recurring outbreak of Everything- Dylan -Does-is -Genius fever. Musically it is solid, well produced, and the musicians have a disciplined grittiness that has more polish than the cluttered and slapdash quality of much of Dylan's recent work and yet avoids sounding slick and corporate. It is obvious that sometime was spent over the sound board adjusting the mix. The pity is that Dylan is far from his best form here; for all his striving to write with an idiomatic tone his bucolic phrase making has nearly always seemed practiced, rehearsed too much in a mirror. What is obvious to me is that Dylan continues to traffic in cliches ; he is , as Lester Bangs remarked, selling off what is left of his charisma with under-constructed songs and ideas.

 Much of the lyrics for this album seem like a parody of an aging musician long past his brilliant work doubling down on bad version of himself; there is an art to sounding as though your lyrics are from a vernacular , but the magic happens when the listener, the witness, forgets the contrivances and believes , for a moment at least, that the voices are from an era and place forgotten . This is what Robbie Robertson did with the Band; lyrics giving elliptical tales a plain-speaking, direct address from within the narrative line, not from without. There is something genuinely conversational and intimate in the best of the Band's rustic workings, no large message or grotesque  rumbles of  philosophical swell. Life is too short and interesting to try to makes sense of it and the characters Robertson and his band mates are rather too busy telling everyone what just happened, what happened before, what things were like  before any catastrophe, cataclysmic event or history altering debacle made the tides rise and the price of gas to go up.

 Dylan wears his age as if it allows him to say what he wants because he has wrinkles you can hid your money in--he  stands apart, saging about, the voice that is too busy documenting feats and folly:  it fits neatly into the covert self-mythologizing Dylan has turned into his secondary art. His principle art, his music and his lyrics, are what Andy Warhol foretold decades ago--art is anything he can get away with. What I hear, though, is a slovenly , lazy, uninteresting filter of the creaky, eyebrow raising cliches and obvious transitions ; there are no amazing associational leaps of fancy here,no "Desolation Row", no "Memphis Blues Again", nothing as truly brilliant as the succinct parables in "John Wesley Harding";  the man who gets the credit and the blame for expanding the pop lyricist vocabulary  is now involved in convincing his audience that the contrived, the hackneyed, the severely corny and portentous are ,in his hands, masterful reworkings and reinventions of old forms. I think it more apt to say that he makes me think of a bankrupt interior designer who is constantly rearranging the same old broken, tattered, torn furniture in a wan hope that few will notice how tacky the whole thing actuall

reviewText:
Briefly put, this is by a wide margin the worst recording of this opera ever made.  The singers do a solid, but not especially revealing job with the text and music, but Georg Solti conducting this opera is like a barber attempting brain surgery.

At every bar Solti's ineptitude is clear and obvious.  His mind could no more comprehend what's going on in this score then my pet cat can comprehend quantum mechanics.

PLEASE...get another recording.  The new Naxos recording is quite good, but, to me, the Kegel, Boulez (the old one on Sony) and Rosbaud recordings lead the pack.  Out of these three, Kegel is my personal favorite, but Boulez is pretty much a tie.  The Rosbaud recording, pretty much an equal to the previous two, was also the world premiere of the work.  Rosbaud accomplished the feat in only eight days!  Although recorded in the mid 50's the sound is surprisingly clear and noise free. Rosbaud's conducting and understanding of the score is beyond dispute and a strong case could be made for the superiority of Fiedler, Krebs and Steingruber compsred to their counterparts in the other recordings.  The only really weak voice in the Rosbaud recording is that of the Ephraimite.  However, that character has only a few lines so it's not a major concern.  I guess you can pretend he's a very old and winded Ephraimite.

In closing, the only reason for this recording to remain in available is to illustrate Solti's pathetically superficial grasp of this music.  I still keep it for that purpose only.

There is a great performance with Scherchen conducting from a mid 60's Maggio Musicale but the sound is mediocre.

reviewText: Jeff Carney's review hits the nail on the head. The music of Genesis golden era has been compressed down to appease the iPod generation. A signal can still be compressed without it's makeup gain being cranked up. There are no peaks and valleys left in the waveforms. It's all basically the same volume! That's why you hear all those little nuances you couldn't hear before. But you know what....that is nothing like real, live music! It's fake. It's processed. It's fast food. Without dynamics, it's unexciting, unmusical and just plain boring. If you like these simply because they're *louder*...try finding the original versions Jeff speaks of and turning your stereo UP. There's a concept. Once you hear what excitement and realism, dynamics in music brings...you'll be using these as coasters.

reviewText:
This album was released in 1979.  It is 44 minutes long and there are no liner notes.  It was Santana's worst selling album of all time (it did worse than Santana's forays into jazz).

There are only 2 tracks on this CD that are any good, and they are both instrumentals.  Aqua Marine may be the prettiest composition that Santana has ever done.  Runnin' is a short, driving instrumental tacked on to Stand Up.

The rest of the CD is soul/pop.  I like pop.  I like soul.  I like Santana playing pop and soul.  This CD is just bad pop/soul.

Part of the problem is the new lead singer, Alex Ligertwood, who sings all the vocals.  He has a bad, in your face, over the top style.  He will be a bane for Santana for years to come.

After 3 smash Latin-rock albums, Santana migrated to jazz fusion.  In the later seventies, he started moving back to his Latin-rock roots.  But then he overshot and started doing pop with a Latin tinge.  And tried moving into soul.  From the late seventies and all through the eighties, Santana had a stripped down pop sound.  He started getting it back together in the nineties.  However, no matter what he was into, Santana always put on a great concert.

reviewText:
In the song, "The Fly," from their 1991 release "Achtung Baby," U2's Bono sang, "Every artist is a cannibal/every poet is a thief./All kill their inspiration/and sing about the grief."

Thanks for the warning.

U2 are fond of making grand statements that fall short of their expectations, but this is ridiculous.  "Pop," is not only uninspired and lifeless, it is probably the most deplorable album of the 1990's.  What's worse is that it was deliberate.  These are not compositions.  These are jumbled, disassociated words set to the same maniacal hum.  How is it possible that these tracks ever got selected for the album?  It must have been torture deciding which song would do the least amount of damage to their career.

Produced almost exclusively by Flood, "Pop" is packaged with a glitzy obsession that the material never justifies.  The goal, it would seem, was to mix this recording into a muddled confusion so that we never actually hear just how awful it is.  I suppose the half-baked theme of this mess is that pop music can no longer survive under the weight of its own expectations.  But, so it seems, neither can U2.  It is really not at all surprising that they would record an album like "Pop."  What is surprising, however, is that no one had the presence of mind to erase the master tapes after they finished.  The only semi-acceptable track, "The Playboy Mansion," derives its rhythm from a sampling of The Turtles' classic, "You Showed Me."  Unfortunately for U2 this exercise only proves that the Clark/McGuinn tune has such staying power that even U2 can't screw it up.  "Staring At The Sun" is a pleasant little ballad, but basically it is just a re-working of "Like A Song" from the "War" album.

Ironically, U2 sound disconnected from the music as if they themselves have grown tired of the nonsense.  They are saying nothing new here and the results are painfully obvious.  Bono is even more directionless than usual.  His vocal styling is so flat and insipid that it makes me want to get my hearing checked.  Somewhere through the years he has developed a slow toneless lackluster approach that makes every song sound identical to each other.  This monotone renders him incapable of making us excited.  But this band never was comprised of trained musicians.  The Edge (why the hell is he still going by that nickname?) and Adam Clayton stopped playing their guitars three albums ago.  Perhaps they have run out of ways to manipulate the same five chords.  Lately they spew a noise equal to that of someone jumping up and down on their instruments while smashing saltines against a microphone.  Larry Mullen (he dropped the Jr. after "Rattle and Hum") was the only member of the group that had any obvious talent, but even he has slipped into relying on tape loops and kits to supplement his floundering imagination.

The main problem with U2 is that they don't know when to shut up.  Not since The Rolling Stones has there been a rock band without enough common sense to stop recording.  Gone are the raw edge and power of their earlier works, like "War" and "The Unforgettable Fire."  These albums had vision, originality and thought-provoking lyrics.  Admittedly, "October" may have been rushed and unfocused, but it had guts.  Even the over-slick production of "The Joshua Tree," the album that launched U2 into the spotlight, was capable of yielding enough angst to defend its reputation.

Most amazing are the uninspired, yet, overabundant photo collages by the usually inventive Anton Corbijn weighing down the lyric booklet.  One look and it becomes apparent that these faces have forgotten how to smile.  Sporting shaved heads and the occasional goatee, they look more like a pompous sulking street gang than rock and roll's reigning kings of anxiety.  Indeed, this is a band that takes itself way too seriously.  The grunge-thing just doesn't work for them because we all know it's an act.  They don't look intelligent; they look arrogant.  Personally, think the world could use one less sourpuss on an album cover.

U2 have become victims of their own over-publicized reputation.  They have waxed themselves into a creative corner from which they haven't the slightest idea how to escape.  Their attitude is that they have a social axe to grind, but they traded in that axe years ago for the dull security of conformity.  They no longer confront their sociopolitical ideals with fervor.  Instead, they have chosen cynicism as their method of communication.  Basically, they are no longer a fun band to listen to.  They are moody, defensive and pretty much a bore.

By the time the final track, "Wake Up Dead Man," rolls around the conclusion is definite:  By creating a wall of sound to hide in, U2 have devised a self-serving image into which they themselves have been devoured.  It may be their own unique wall of sound, but it's still a wall.  And walls separate.  Perhaps, a more appropriate name for the song would have been "Wake Up Dead Group."

But probably the worst thing about "Pop" is the overall hypocrisy of its argument.  By using tape loops to sample other artists U2 have failed to take their own advice which they extolled so honestly in "God Part II," from 1988's "Rattle and Hum" album, in which Bono lectures, "I don't believe in the 60's/in the golden age of pop/You glorify the past/when the future dries up."

Amen, to that, brother.

U2 is clearly a band that has outlived its usefulness.  They have lost their ambition, their imagination and their drive.  To paraphrase John Cage, a pioneer of the avant-garde, they have nothing interesting to say with this album and they are saying it.  The music industry would be far better off if they would just face reality, and break up.

reviewText:
Simple Plan are one of those bands that genuinely want you to feel their pain, maaaaaan - to tap into their anguish, as artificial as it may seem (at least, to those of us over the age of, say, 13).  I don't buy it for a second - their pain is about as contrived as their "punk" classification.  And let's face it, the only connection they have to punk is extraneous - because they wear spiked bracelets and probably run around knocking over clothing racks and getting into food fights at shopping malls, that somehow warrants their musical categorization.

This is what it comes down to: If you think Simple Plan are punk rock, just listen to this CD.  If you still insist on labeling them as punk rockers, you either:

a) Think Avril Lavigne is, as she proclaims, "like, a hardcore punk!"
b) Probably own an 'N Sync or Britney Spears CD
c) Have never listened to classic punk acts like The Clash or Sex Pistols, or contemporary acts like Bad Religion or Pennywise
d) Believe that someone must appear on TRL in order to establish their "punk credentials"
e) All of the above

The music on Simple Plan's sophomore release Still Not Getting Any is so tame and streamlined, it's impossible to believe that some members of the band actually have roots in punk rock (going back to a band called Reset, who were actually decent).  Comparisons to Avril Lavigne and Good Charlotte are not without merit (heck, even Good Charlotte rocks harder than this), or I would even go so far as to compare it to the sound of a boy band picking up instruments and playing what they considered "edgy rock music".  Yeah, edgy - most of these songs make John Mayer look like Cradle Of Filth.

What makes this album even worse are the lyrics.  It's basically the same "My life is so miserable despite the fact that I'm a millionaire with many luxury cars and a girlfriend who loves me" themes that we've come to expect from Simple Plan in the past.  The funniest part of all is that the members of this band are pushing 30, yet the songs appear to be written from the perspective of a whiny teenager.  Witness these brilliant lyrics from "Welcome To My Life": "Do you ever wanna run away? / Do you lock yourself in your room? / With the radio on turned up so loud / That no one hears you screaming ... You don't know what it's like to be like me".  Yes Pierre, you're right - I don't know what it's like ... to have nothing to overcome, to have no adversities, to have millions of dollars, multiple luxury cars and maids and butlers to wait on me hand and foot ... so yeah, I guess you're right.  Or how about "Me Against The World": "I'm a nightmare, a disaster ... But I'll make it on my own ... Me against the world" - all over the same glossy, overproduced pop/rock that they've always put out.  These guys are millionaire rock stars with millions of fans around the world - do they actually think that any of us are dumb enough to fall for this "woe is me, I'm all alone in this world" charade?  Well, this album did go to # 3 on the charts, so apparently there are some people who fell for it.  Further proof that the buying public has become increasingly naive - and increasingly favors image over substance.

In summary: It's another slick, commercial, and incredibly bland album from Simple Plan - just as I expected.  And these pretty boys are using a sales pitch as old as time: Pretend you've been abused and that every day is a struggle, and that making tons of money, having tons of fans and friends and living the good life is, like, such an ordeal, batting those puppy-dog eyes for maximum impact, and the little girls will understand - and make it easier for you to afford another mansion.  These guys are about as punk rock as Phil Collins.  And their anguished frat boy shtick?  I'm buying it about as much as I would Colin Farrell joining a monastery.  This CD is a must to avoid.

reviewText:
Not since 1990, when a Broward County, Florida judge declared the 2 Live Crew album, "As Nasty As They Wanna Be" legally obscene, has a rap album stirred as much controversy as Eminem's Aftermath/Interscope Records release, "The Slim Shady LP."

While the use of graphic language and violent imagery is common in hardcore and gangsta rap, "The Slim Shady LP" pushes the envelope to extremes rarely heard on a commercial release. Surprisingly, many reviewers have given the album high marks, pointing to Eminem's rhyming skills and suggesting that his explicit tales of sex, violence, drugs and general depravity are simply examples of a warped sense of humor.

Humor? I doubt that any parent whose daughter has been raped or molested will find much humor in a track like "Guilty Conscience," in which Eminem gleefully narrates a date-rape scenario with an underage girl. Nor do I get the joke in '97 Bonnie And Clyde," in which an abusive husband murders his wife, dumps her body in the ocean, then tells his pre-adolescent daughter, "Nobody in this world is gonna keep you from me/I love you."

Here's the rub: rappers like Eminem cheerfully recount the most horrific scenarios (almost always from the first person point of view) in explicit detail, extolling some combination of violence, sex, drug use, or criminal behavior. When called to task for their lyrics, the usual answer is something like, "It was meant as a joke," or "I'm playing a character."  The latter reasoning equates a gangsta rapper with an actor who plays a villain in a film... It doesn't fly. No one in his right mind goes to the movies and actually believes Arnold Schwartzenegger is a cop-killing cyborg. On the other hand, rappers love to point to their "street credibility." They want fans to believe that they are the cheeba-loving, `ho chasin' playa who inhabits their raps.

Rappers often defend their devotion to these rap clichs because they're "keepin' it real" or because they're "just reflecting the way life is in the `hood." You can't have it both ways - either it's fiction, or it's fact. Either way, (c)rap music is influencing an entire generation of young people with a warped vision of life. Pop music is an art form geared primarily to young people.

Many of Eminem's CDs are purchased by pre-teens who have seen Eminem's videos - the "clean versions" of course - on MTV, and consider him, if not a hero, at least a celebrity worthy of their attention and admiration. Older teens and adults might know that Eminem is the embodiment of a sick, dirty joke - a lot of younger fans do not. Naturally, Eminem has a(n) (flawed) answer for that - good parents can monitor what music their children are exposed to, he says. At home, yes - but what parent can monitor a child at school or on the playground?

Read through the customer reviews, and time after time you'll read fans raving about Eminem's "skills." Since when is the ability to recite dirty tongue-twisters considered a musical talent? I doubt the guy could sing "Happy Birthday" on key, or play "Jingle Bells" on the piano. But hundreds of peer-pressured fans who equate samples with songwriting, and beats with music, love him.

There was a time when I would have found the idea of labeling a record album "pornographic" ridiculous. But when I read news reports about 14-year-olds gunning down their classmates at school, or 13-year-old boys raping 10 year-old girls, or the rise in drug use among children under 16, I have to believe that pop culture, with its ever-increasing focus on sex, drugs and violence, is partly to blame. The messages delivered in albums like "The Slim Shady LP" might not be the sole cause of these problems, but they certainly contribute to and aggravate them.

Without any redeeming social value, "The Slim Shady LP" is, quite simply, aural pornography. I'm not for censorship, but if "artists" like Eminem (and Interscope, his record company) choose to portray a sick, immoral, criminal view of human nature, then present it to teenagers (and teens, not adults, are the target audience) as something to be laughed at, they should be prepared for all the criticism, boycotts, and legal hassles that result. Adults who care about the moral message our children are being fed need to draw a line in the sand and say "Enough is enough."

Like any pop/rock fan, the words "Abbey Road" hold a special lofty place in music fans' hearts, mainly due to the Beatles and what their namesake LP title did for the history of rock music.  After much curiosity, I listened to the tracks after getting my hands on Kylie's latest offering.  My first reaction was:  "What a DUD".

These sessions add absolutely NOTHING to the original versions Kylie recorded, some going back to the mid to late-1980's.  Hearing tracks like "Locomotion" and especially her big crossover hit "Can't Get You Outta My Head" getting the makeover in London's Abbey Road studios to new instrumentation and vocals actually pale in comparison to their original versions.  If anything, Kylie's voice sounds noticeably WEAKER here than her original versions, maybe due to the inevitable onset of age.

So, save your wallets, Amazon folks, and skip this trashy money-making scheme from Kylie's recording label.  Maybe it SEEMED like a good idea at the time, but definitely wrong, wrong, and WRONG execution here.  Like some here have commented, a waste of money by Kylie and her handlers and a waste of our hearing time.  If Abbey Road Studios takes on more "DUD" projects like this, it could easily tarnish their lofty reputation in the music industry.  Perhaps Kylie and her music producers better head back to their drawing boards and cook up something more "original" than trying to make a quick buck off the name "Abbey Road".  Surely you CAN do better than this, Kylie!!

reviewText:
Meat Loaf is known to be emotionally disturbed, excentric, funny, loud, intelligent and over the top. A person who's able to get horribly depressed to the point of almost commiting suicide. Therefore, a person who's hard to cease, follow or comprehend. Musically speaking, this "bipolar" artist can give us two sides: With Jim Steinman and without Jim Steinman. As simple as that. You know it. I know it.

When he's doing a CD with Steinman, an exceptional songwriter who's equally just as manic-depressive (his words), he's elevating his music to a degree that is unequalled in the industry. Steinman & Meat Loaf are like Dr. Frankenstein and his monster. When he's not working with Steinman (how can he?), or when the two of them are (again!) fighting, he tries to either copy him with songs that are pale copycats but nevertheless catchy or he tries to deviate completly from that "Steinman touch".

With "Hang Cool teddy bear", it's the latter. He's getting away from Steinman and he's going either more heavy or more folk. Frankly, i don't see why he would want to do that. When you have the chance to sing words written by Jim Steinman along with music composed by him, how can you lower yourself with normal melodies and insipid lyrics? Diversity? Wanting to try something new? Ok then. At least, go with songwriters that are just as inventive or original. Do an album with the guys from Pink Floyd or with brian Eno or The Edge, or i don't know, Rob Zombie, Marilyn Manson, Hans Zimmer or Enya. Christ! Even go and work with Madonna who's always coming with something new. You know what i mean? You want to get away from the grandiloquence of Steinman? Go but with style and uniqueness. Don't go with popular songwriters that will never get higher than Jim Steinman's little toe in terms of creativity or uniqueness. It's like doing movies with the the likes of Fellini or Bergman and then doing a movie with the producers of "American Pie". And being proud of it.

"Hang Cool Teddy Bear" doesn't even have great classic songs in it. Ok, some of them are "fun" to listen and none of them are necessarily garbage if you're in the right state of mind but c'mon! How can an artist seriously be equally proud of songs like "Bat Out Of Hell" and, let's say the new "Love Is Not Real, Next Time You Stab Me In The Back"?

The only song that is truly unexpected is "Los Angelooser". The rest is just a collection of low rates, not so cool, not so bad songs that will never really make any Meat Loaf compilation album. Ok, if you have to force it, maybe you could underline "Living On The Outside" and "If I Can't Have You" that kind of stick in your head. But really, what song from this new CD would you put next to "Life Is A Lemon And I Want My Money Back"? or "A Kiss Is A Terrible Thing To Waste"?

It's simple and it is, of course, my humble opinion: when you work with Jim Steinman, you set the bar so high that you simply can't work with just anybody after that. Your work will ALWAYS suffer from the comparison. Always. Steinman is one of a kind. His words, his music, his quotes, his character. Some of his lyrics become poems, for crying out loud!

While we have to go through a normal CD like "Hang Cool Teddy Bear" (cause i remain a Meat Loaf fan- that is my own ambiguity), we have great Steinman songs that are lying there, waiting to be sang by The Loaf. Songs like "Braver Than We Are", "What Part Of My Body Hurts The Most" or "Speaking In Tongues". try to find them on the net and you'll see what i mean.

People, we have to wake up and put pressure for those two friends to come back together, make peace and give us what we truly are awaiting with anticipation: "Bat Out Of Hell IV". ALL DONE BY JIM STEINMAN AND HIS TEAM.

Not "Hang Cool Teddy Bear". What the hell?

Jim Steinman, where are you? Do something! Help your friend recover his musical nobility!

reviewText:
I've always considered these reviews to be a way to find new music: If I agreed with another reviewer about several CDs, I might try something they recommended. Reviewers like Lord Chimp and Wickerman were two of my early favorites. So when I write how this album completely sucked, I'm not being a fanboy or trasher, I'm trying to help other readers who might want to get an idea of what I like and don't like. If that helps someone out there pick up some great music - and avoid garbage like this - then my reviews are doing what they're supposed to, not gaining me more votes so that I too can be a Top x00 Reviewer.

Why is this DT's weakest album to date? Writing. It sucks. The only tracks that catch my interest are "These Walls", "I Walk Beside You", and "Panic Attack." "Never Enough" has moments, and "The Root of all Evil" has a great title and a brief instrumental passage before the middle break that's breathtaking, but the rest of this recording is just dreadfully dull. "Octavarium" (the song) is an outtake from Pink Floyd, as is much of "Sacrificed Sons;" not to insult PF fans, I just don't want that much of their style showing up in a DT release. And for the rest of the album, there aren't any hooks in these songs - I don't mean like in a pop formula, I mean something you find yourself humming right away or hours later. One reviewer wrote, back on 6DoIT, that there was nothing memorable about that music, and while I disagreed on that recording, I'll say it here: There's nothing memorable about this release. Except, that is, how it has so little to enjoy.

I agree with another reviewer that these guys are overextended on side projects. Their writing has deteriorated since SfaM, and now so has their performance. And those lyrics? Dreadful. Insipid. Boring. By comparison, the lyrics on this release make Lost Horizon look like e.e. cummings. They spent months writing and arranging this CD, so why does most of the material seem so weak and undeveloped?

Exceptions: "These Walls" sounds like an uptempo Journey number from the mid-80s; whereas songs like this normally strike me as appeasements for the record company, on this CD it's actually the best song. (That's scary.) "I Walk Beside You" is similar, very radio-friendly (even in length, at 4:29). "Panic Attack" is fast and has an echo of the work I expect from DT.

But that's all I can find here. 75 minutes of multitrack work and  I can only appreciate about 1/4 of it. And that title track - even worse than the last Royal Hunt album. It's so damned dull it makes me angry I looked forward to another epic DT track. Even Falling Into Infinity had better writing than this, and that was my least favorite in the DT discography before this. No doubt DT fans will buy this release anyway, but I'm warning anyone willing to read about my reactions: You *might* like this recording, but don't bet on it. Fates Warning's recent "FWX" spanks this CD from start to finish.

I give this two stars for a few decent tracks and glimpses of greatness on a couple others, but take away a star for putting out something that's overall this weak and dull. DT swings and misses by a LOT this time out...

This band, while solid, is nothing special.  They take the overdone formula of rock-rap and streamline it, but add nothing to it.
The lead singer sounds like an angry reject from a boy band.  He can sing well, but sounds too high pitched and nasily to be anything but whiney.  The rapper is solid, yet nothing special.
Lyrically, Linkin Park aims at the lowest common denominator by whining about relationships.  It's nothing new, and has been done better by other bands (early Tool, The Cure, Stabbing Westward, and others).
Musically, it's power chords for the chorus, unoriginal hip-hop for the verses.  They know that, for the most part, playing it safe ensures good record sales, so they play it incredibly safe.  Everything's trinary (AABA), and everything's formulaic.  The songs grow loud when expected, quiet when expected...it's paint-by-numbers.
Linkin Park isn't horrible.  They're just typical of the way mainstream rock has become.  Catchy, simple, but adding nothing to the art.  The fact that they won the Grammy for Best Metal Album does not bode well for the genre.  It was a notice to the world that rock is on life support.

reviewText:
With lyrics like "In Berlin, by the wall, you were [ I can no longer remember the exact measure, let's say ] 5 foot, 6 inches tall", or the equally banal "Since she lost her daughter, it's her eyes that flow with water" -  the listener should immediately sense trouble. Because when we finally hear the daughter start to scream  -  by the way, was it "daughter" singular, or "daughters" plural? there seem to be lots of 'em wailing in here - we know we've arrived solidly in the dark, airless basement of unadulterated, manipulative kitsch. And it gets worse: you'd better force yourself to nod knowingly during "Sad Song". If you laugh, giggle or snicker at the formula string arrangements you'll simply ruin it for the rest of us.

Together with its grade-school lyrics and haunting lack of imagination, "Berlin" delivers a degree of pretension exceeded only by the more recent "Drella".  What can I say? "Berlin" is easily as dumb as that other period trainwreck, ELP's "Tarkus". While the music is clearly unrelated, the two are joined by the vast and growing scale of their respective failures. Recall with me the appropriately weepy Moog that ushers us to the tear-filled end of ELP's pretend monster. ***Sigh*** I can't help but also remember the artifice of emotions bathing "Berlin" and shed a tear, too, for "The Kids".

"Berlin" is little more than a sometimes clever artist straining beyond all credulity. The album and ideas are pat, shallow and the whole thing tends to mope rather than reach any true depth of feeling. Skip it in favor of  "Transformer" and join Joel and the bots on the Satellite of Love.

LSO engineers have the Barbican to deal with (horrible sound space) and they seem to make it worse, turning out spectacularly bad sound.  At the start, at regular volume I could not hear a thing.  Had to crank it up to almost twice the normal level to hear the quiet (oh so quiet) opening.  The whole sound of the orchestra, and thereby Rostropovich's conducting is distorted.  Weird miking, flutes up front with a harp, mid sound level are the violins and timpani, in the next room perhaps are cellos and basses.  Then a drum major seems to go to the podium and thump, thump, thump.  Horrible!

Eleven minutes in and I was running to the player to turn it down.  5 minutes later, up... Then... you get the picture.

And the sense of air and space that SACD does so well, not here.  It's like a bad analogue recording - mushy, dead and ill focused.

Avoid the whole LSO Live line.  I have yet to hear good sound from any of the label's recordings.

Try Kondrashin on Meloydia/Chant Du Monde, or Mravinsky on Philips or Erato, or De Priest on Delos or Haitink on London.  All excellent performances.  Or try Rostropovich on Teldec.

Back it goes.

I heard Rostropovich play this live with the San Francisco Symphony and it was great.

The proper final album for the great Ray would have been one that recognized the sadness of his fading light.

Perhaps the most egregious misundersanding of Ray's talent and music was the Willie Nelson duet, It Was A Very Good Year.  A soft, quiet, low key duet with Willie and Ray would have been perfect.  But the producer, John Burk, went over the top, ruining all the potential with a Frank Sinatra or Sammy Davis Jr. type of production.  This was a disgrace, evidencing a fundamental misunderstanding by the producer of the song, the artists and the music.

I could go on and on.  The album is an abomination, spoiled not by the artists but by the idiots who conceptualized it.  Shameful.

'Fast car' was a remarkable single for it's time. We all talked ourselves into the rest of the filler on this cd, about which the best you can say is it's all extraordinarily average. If however art to you is didacticism, you will be in heaven. This has twee rhetorical questions ("Why are the missiles called Peacekeepers?"), exhausted imagery (I know somewhere in here a baby is crying) and worst of all an acapella sermon. All it lacks it some sort of "Save the bunnies" track. All of this gets filtered through Chapman's self-annointed "nobler than thou" suffering and humorless delivery, and of course that ridiculous all-purpose quaver. She doesn't exactly deliver a message subtly. Oh Tracy, won't you be my conscience?

This schtick had no future and noone bought her follow-up C.D.. But this garbage is still being pushed on us by "enlightened" radio stations, and I still hear the lesser songs from this cd all the time. It's a shame. I HATE these songs. To paraphrase the movie Bull Durham, "Aw, Tracy Chapman is as full of cr*p as anyone." You wouldn't know it from all of this unbearable condescension. I think her dream job would involve a cleric's collar and a pulpit.

Some liberals feel that music is just another place to be a drag. (And these remarks are coming from a massive liberal!) I don't subscribe to that hogwash. 10,000 maniacs, Midnight Oil and Tracy Chapman are the bottom of the barrell; a very humorless barrell.

DJ Shadow is reknowned for all sorts of innovative, unique use of samples, turntabling, hip-hop, and electronica. So how did he end up going from the brilliant "Endtroducing" and "Brainfreeze" to a piece of overprocessed, soulless dreck like "The Outsider"? Nobody can be really sure, but however it happened, it wasn't worth the ride.

From start to finish, this album is a ride through uninteresting rap and a schizophrenic array of different sounds. It feels as though Shadow was running out of time before a deadline, and hastily slapped together some songs that belonged to current trends and appealed to the radioslave crowd.

Things sound promising with the eerie, ambient "Outsider Intro," which spins up a mythic edge to the album. "In a twilight of a time, there emerges a need for man to comprehend his own bitter fate. Finally resigned to the inevitable beyond, he searches the ages, desperate for stories of insurance, redemption and hope..." It's a promising beginning.

Then it all falls apart. "This Time" stumbles over itself into a radio-friendly pop disaster, followed by an equally forgettable rap entry in "3 Freaks." DJ Shadow attempts to regain the turntablist edge with headache-inducing hyphy with its twangy electrobeats, and halfhearted synth over jagged, rambling raps that never really go anywhere.

As if that weren't schizophrenic enough, Shadow then decides to do a bluesy, acoustic "Levee Blues," reminiscent of the bluesy sound of Howlin' Wolf or Muddy Waters, and even some new-agey piano solos that sounds like something from a relaxation album. Then it's back to the generic rap and lifeless trip-funk, with Shadow apparently tiring of the sound himself by the end. He certainly sounds uninspired enough, to the point where the final song sounds like Super Mario Hip-Hop.

Don't bother looking for DJ Shadow of "Endtroducing" and "Brainfreeze" in this album. It's like someone using the name "DJ Shadow" has put out entirely different music -- not only is his "sound" gone except for a scrap here and there, but his creativity is as well. While every artist has to pursue new territory, Shadow isn't doing that.

It sounds like he is chasing whatever will go over best with the mainstream -- the current hip-hop trends, and generic rap from a plethora of guesting MCs. And the random, schizophrenic quality only makes it worse -- Shadow veers madly from pop to hard rap to blues to ambient piano to hyphy (the last of which ensures that this sound will be dated in about five minutes).

To make things worse, the only raps worth listening to are in the intro and Sergio Pizzorn. Other ones tend to be either incoherent or downright incomprehensible -- and even if you figure out what they are saying, it isn't anything too impressive. They're also some of the most soulless rap songs I've ever heard, with layers of synth and the odd beats to distract from the complete lack of soul or feeling.

Incoherent and all over the place, "The Outsider" is an unexpected stumble for a very talented DJ -- ultra-generic hip-hop, plus everything except the kitchen sink. A disastrous attempt to try something new.
label: negative

John's talents were wasted, with his vocals drowned in layers of instruments, which unfortunately destroyed the albums ambience.  The eighteen minute version of burn down the mission became panned out to the point of very overdone. As much as I love listening to Elton's Music, this album was a rapid fall to failure.  The modestly improved "madman across the water" and "Honky chateau", were released in 1971 and 1972 respectively. but it would be the release of "Don't shoot me, I'm only the piano player", and "Good-bye yellow brick road" in 1973, that would bring him back to his audible peak, and steer him well clear of this brief trench in his career.

reviewText:
Few bands have released live albums of such as high calibre as this one.  When it comes to slide guitar mastery and virtuoso old style jamming, the Allman Brothers Band had on peer in their prime and this album is a showcase of what they were like at their prime.  No weak tracks on this 7 track live album with "Statesboro Blues" and "Whipping Post" the stand outs."

This mlps version of the album though is a vast disappointment as the sound quality is very poor and is certainly not remastered. The old adage of judging the book by its cover certainly holds true here and therein lies the great waste. As far as mlps designs go, the packaging is first class as the gatefold design and workmanship plus the super quality cardboard used makes this one of the best mlps' that I've ever seen. An inner sleeve with all the lyrics in English and Japanese is included however, the most important part of the whole package, the cd sound quality, has been left unchanged making this version of the classic album a huge disappointment for the audiophile. Such a well done mlps design surely deserves a much better remastered sound quality to accompany it. The powers that be have let a great opportunity to produce a high-class reissue version of the album go by. Unless you are a great mlps design fan alone, I don't know why you would want to pay serious bucks for great-looking cardboard when there is no improvement sound-wise to the cd that you already own.

If you consider that Duane Allman together with Eric Clapton were probably the greatest blues guitarists of their time when Duane died (just hear their work together on Derek and the Dominoes' "Layla")the loss is truly great and one cannot but wonder at what might have been.

Alas, we'll never know but get this and "Brothers and Sisters" if you want to get the best of the Allman Brothers' work. If you are a guitarist and want to learn what great blues and slide work sounds like, get these two as well as the "Eat a Peach" albums as essential listening material.

Just don't get these mlps versions which sound exactly the same sound quality-wise as the versions you already have and hence waste a lot of money for good mlps design alone.

reviewText:
Oh wow, this is really kind of embarrassing. 77 people have reviewed this item as if there's anything new to be found. As if this isn't the umpteenth compilation of hits (mostly from the 60's and 70's) by Clapton and his handlers with a view to soaking up yet another dollar from his slavish and somewhat judgment impaired fan base. It's hard not to feel crapton when you've just handed down your money for something that's more or less identical to 55 other compilation ablums out there, save maybe a few newer songs who I'm sure no one is very interested in anyway. What is EC trying to tell us with this release, half of which is over 30 years old? That he has absolutely nothing left to say or contribute, but that of course should hardly be revelatory to any of us. As a guitar player, he's quite skilled. No one will dispute that. However, unless you are a guitar player, no one wants to hear his long winded solo's, particularly the blues derived ones, which is one of his sad fortes. Crapton is just another in the long line of aging British rock stars who plundered, stole, and fed the blues to a white audience without so much as changing a note. He is just another washed up wanna-be, who made his bones on blues derivative rock and roll. When I say blues derivative, I mean ripped off totally. Blues based rock, blues stolen rock if you will, is the most boring, inane waste of time in music rivaled perhaps only by Crapton's non-bluesy compositions and covers. He isn't any kind of a songwriter, which accounts for the inordinate number of covers he has released throughout his squalid career, many of which were released as singles as I'm sure his handlers advised him he had a much better chance of getting a hit with a carbon copy version of someone else's song than one of his own third rate compositions. Nothing of this kind can be as abhorrent as "his" version of Bob Marley's "I Shot the Sheriff". I've placed "his" in quotations because it can hardly be called his own as his chief goal seems to be to mimick this song to the point in which uninformed listeners might think Marley had an estranged English half brother. There is no point in covering someone's song unless you revamp it, turn it into your own. When you cover someone's song and go to great lengths to imitate the person, release the sad creation as a single, you are merely trying to make a buck. Not content to rip off blues alone, Crapton plunges deep in to the heart of Jamaica and brutally assualts reggae as well. Musically, it is a carbon copy of the original Wailers song. But the real disgrace is Crapton's pathetic and poorly conveyed Jamaican accent. I'm sure young Gordon Sumner aka Sting was taking notes. This is no longer just a case of a very untalented hack trying to make a buck, but now borders on offensive.

As for his orginal compositions, this collection contains all the 70's staples that the myriad others do. Many of them contain a common theme in Crapton's lyrics, that he's been dumped and made to look like a loser and an imbecile (by something other than his music). It contains of course the obligatory, pitiful "Wonderful Tonight" which I suspect is a much played anthem for married couples trying to reignite the passion of a decaying relationship just before an evening of disappointing sex.

I forever recall a picture of a wall somewhere in England with the words "Clapton is God" scrawled on it. I remember that the picture that I saw had a dog in the corner of it urinating on this wall. The object lesson obvious; even a dog shows more intelligence, taste, and judgment than your average Claptonian.
label: negative

reviewText:
As an old and ardent Stray Cats fan, I can only unhappily conclude that Brian Setzer suffers from arrested artistic development.  From his weird foray into mainstream rock, "The Knife Feels Like Justice," to his self-proclaimed "Guitar Slinger" stuff, to this omnipresent neo-swing monstrosity, it is painfully evident that he really never moved much past "Baby Blue Eyes."  And that was over twenty years ago folks.
It seems that while Setzer absorbed a LITTLE rockabilly and a LITTLE jump blues, he missed much more of it.  He is not a master of these styles, and it is evident no matter how he dresses things up.
He is a talented singer and fair (yes, only fair) guitarist, but he is not persuasive in any style.  His songwriting is passable at best.
"The Dirty Boogie" (a puerile title if there ever was one), was nearly the official soundtrack of the neo-swing dance craze.  This was the period during the late 90's when unsuccessful rock and ska bands decided that they could somehow channel the sophistication of jazz and swing by donning zoot suits and porkpie hats.  Setzer's overblown mix of rockabilly and big band was unique to be sure, but it was also an assault on the ears and sensibilities of those who actually were familiar with these idioms.
From this set, the mangling of "Jump, Jive, and Wail" emerged as a movement anthem.  I have to wonder whether Setzer actually sat through a listen of Louis Prima's version, or if he simply thought that taking a jack-hammer to the tune would improve it.  "This Ole House" wasn't exactly Rosemary Clooney's finest hour, but Setzer's cranked-out rockabilly vision didn't improve matters any.  The dopey "Let's Live It Up" sounds more than a little like "Something's Got to Give" on the chorus, and like non-descript Cats on the verse.  Setzer inflicts unforgivable butchery on "Sleepwalk", projectile-vomiting pointless guitar riffs at every cadence.  He really doesn't get it.  Finally, the bombast of "Rock This Town" takes weak material and grinds it into dust.
We are happily some years beyond this lame stuff.  Now, when "Jump, Jive, and Wail" is heard on the radio, it's the real Louis Prima deal.

There are a couple of guitar solos that start out clear and just disappear into the grinding noise that is the back up sound for almost every song.

"Do ya wanna ride in educated horses?" "Be an American. Witch. Foxy foxy." These are actual lyrics from the few songs that had more than one verse. I actually have listened to this album about ten times, trying to find one song that I could like. Even the worst albums that I have ever heard, had one or two halfway good songs. However, I can sincerely and honestly say that this is the dumbest bunch of songs I have ever heard. The guitar riffs are gone. It is just the same music from several years ago, remixed and muddled, with lyrics that he must have gotten from a room full of typing monkeys. Then there are the little snippets that get sampled, including western movies. I guess this is his western album. If you have money to waste, donate it to the homeless shelter. This album is the worst trash that I have ever heard.

reviewText:
I'm re-writing this review for "The Downward Spiral" because I now think my original review isn't that good, so here's a better one for you folks.

Here we go again, another mainstream release from the 90's that's been overrated beyond belief.  Even in my teenage years, when I had this extremely misguided belief that Tool and Rage Against the Machine were the best bands the music world had to offer, I wasn't impressed with Nine Inch Nails.  Now that I'm an adult who's listened to a ton of underground metal and industrial bands, my hatred for NIN and Trent Reznor has only escalated much higher than in past years.

FRAUDULENCE

Now you may be thinking "What does this have to do with the music?"  I'll tell you.  Reznor really wants you to believe that he's this dark and edgy musician, but when you compare this criminally overrated "classic" with the prime works of industrial bands like Front Line Assembly, Laibach,  and Godflesh, you'll know right off the bat that Reznor is nothing more than a pop musician in the disguise of a troubled, gritty musician.  The fact that Reznor is such a blatant egomaniac who thinks he can smash Front Line Assembly in a 1992 interview with Spin magazine doesn't help, either.

MUSIC STYLE

The way these songs on this album are executed ultimately proves that Reznor has absolutely zero respect for the industrial music artform, or for music in general.  What's ultimately worse is that Reznor is terribly diluted into believing that he's actually being "unique," when he's just taking excrement and serving it up in an aesthetically-pleasing fashion for gullible, angst-laden teenagers who haven't yet learned what real industrial music is.

The general music style for "The Downward Spiral" can be summed up in that Reznor dilutes mechanical industrial keyboards and beats, mixes them with corny "quiet" sections and distorted guitar riffs, and neatly arranges them in a pop song structure as to not lose the potential of giant record sales among mainstream music listener.

Reznor's vocals on this album are terrible.  They're either juvenile screaming or whiny singing.  I'm not joking, Reznor would be better suited for a run of the mill alternative rock band rather than an industrial band.  The vocalwork alone is terrible, but his lyrics futher damage this album.

What ultimately infuriates me is that Reznor has this stupid idea that it's the lyrics that are the main source of providing a certain atmosphere to music rather than the instrumental compositions.  Reznor sells the idea that he's a "dark musician" by penning extremely hammy poetry that you'd see in an "outcast" 15 year-old's notebook.  Reznor's lyrics are about as edgy as those written by Korn frontman Jonathan Davis.  No joke, in the song "Heresy," Reznor screams out "God is dead, and no one cares!!"  Seriously, that's such juvenile songwriting.  It gets even worse when in the song "I Do Not Want This," Reznor says "Don't tell me how too feel!!"  In "Piggy," Reznor whispers out "Nothing can stop me now, because I don't care."  Wow, I'm really feeling the genius in his lyrics.  This wouldn't be too bad if Reznor was in his mid-late teens when he wrote these lyrics, but he was in his late 20's when he wrote and recorded this album.  Reznor is proof that some people grow up while others just get old.

Now the bad lyrics would be forgivable if Reznor did what good musicians do when they realize their lyrics aren't that good, they bury them behind the instrumental work, and use the instruments to be the main source of atmosphere.  However, with this album, you don't get that.  Reznor, again, has a massive ego to where he thinks his juvenile lyrics are brilliant to where you have to clearly hear ever word that comes out of his useless mouth.

SONGS

To be fair, there are traces of potential here.  "The Becoming" is what comes closest to being a proper industrial song, as this actually has some deviance from the pop melodies that Reznor almost always confines himself to and actually amps up the darkness and aggression provided from the instruments.  However, his lame vocals keep this from being a masterful song.  "A Warm Place" is a decent instrumental that shows that along with "The Becoming," shows that Reznor has the potential to make decent music when he feels like it, but that's where any sort of praise ends.

The rest of this album is laughable at best, painful at worst.  "Mr. Self Destruct" is a ho-hum industrial metal hybrid, and that's really all I can say.  "Closer" epitomizes my point that Reznor tries to use "dark" lyrics to make up for the fact that the instrumental work on that song is really tepid, and this doesn't help that he tried to go even further by releasing a hokey music video with a shaved naked girl and a spinning pig's head.  "March of the Pigs" is another trying-too-hard "noisy" industrial-metal hybrid with that goofy "quiet" interludes (where he says "How does it make you feel?) in a bad attempt at showing dynamics.  "Big Man With a Gun" tries to sound like a proper industrial song mixed with some guitars, but it still falls flat, and it's hurt even more with Reznor's over-the-top whiny alt-rock styled singing.  "Piggy" tries to set itself apart from the rest of the album by being primarily drum and bass-driven with whispering vocals that eventually pick up in aggression later in the song, but these just show how untalented Reznor really is.  I think I made my point about the songs.

PRODUCTION

Like many overrated mainstream "classic" albums, the sound quality on this is too clean and sterile for an album that's supposed to be "dark and gritty."  It's made to be even more laughable that Reznor thought he was going to make this album even darker by recording it in the house that the Charlie Manson "family" murdered some of their victims.  This just shows that Reznor is trying everything to be "dark" besides crafting music that's actually dark.

FINAL WORD

"The Downward Spiral" is NOT the "dark and edgy" industrial-rock masterpiece that Trent Reznor or mainstream media outlets like MTV want you to think it is.  Reznor resorts to every gimmick to make his music seem "dark."  It's funny how respectable industrial bands like Front Line Assembly and Godflesh resorted only to making music that's actually dark to push this across.

Skip this counterfeit material and go for the genuine articles in industrial music.

Godflesh:  "Streetcleaner" and "Pure/Cold World/Slavestate" (this is one boxed set)
Front Line Assembly:  "Caustic Grip," "Tactical Neural Implant," and "The Initial Command"
Die Krupps:  "Stahlwerksynfonie" and "I"
Laibach:  "Opus Dei" and "Nova Akropola"
Skinny Puppy:  "Bites," "Too Dark Park," and "Last Rights"
Spahn Ranch:  "Anthology 1992-1994"
Swans:  "Filth/Body to Body, Job to Job"

Once you start listening to the above albums, you'll soon be throwing away any Nine Inch Nails and Marilyn Manson albums you might have.
label: negative

Sadly this one suffers from a common malady, no good songwriting. The words written out and FORCED over a sheen of noise. There is no thought on melody of flow. And there are multiple examples of generic stock 1 4 5 verses on multiple selections. The exception of course is a cover which is a perfect example of good songwriting but it's been butchered as one would expect from RZ. Listen to the word "rock" in "last night in Little Rock..." as an example of how out of tune his vocal is.

The voice is as always so over processed to hide the fact there's so little about it. When in doubt hide it in a wash of electronic processing. It's also a shame that you have some talented sidemen and this is the output of the endeavor.

Rather than rely on material the emphasis is the bad boy visual image that drives what is known of RZ. That's what makes this sell. That's what fans are drawn to as musically it's just a dismal mish mash. The look is the draw not the music. Elements are thrown up in the air and they fall where they fall. There's no artistry at hand. This is quite an inferior haphazard product.

This is another one destined to be one of the Sound Opinions guys November 2013 Turkey Shoot items.

For those of you who would like to hear a similar release but one that has higher-grade songs, vocals and musicality, check out Alice Cooper's Killer release. Compare the two and see what is real and what is inferior.
