reviewText:
Let me tell you something off the bat: I really try to like this recording. I have listened to it at least 10 times to try to convince myself that this recording is "not that terrible" and I am completely wrong. This is one of the worst opera recordings that I have ever heard.

Lets begin with the tempo, at times WAYYYYY too slow and at times frenetically paced, completely destroying whatever flow the music has. The orchestra is also WAYYYY too loud for the singers most of times. In fact the whole balance between singer and orchestra is non-existant. The lound passages are way to loud and the soft passages are way too soft. Amazingly there is no color to Wagner's masterful orchestration. You just hear wall and wall of sound and that is it.

Now the singers. Ludwig is fantastic, in fact there are NO ROLES that she does not excel at. Listen to her warning cries to Isolde in Act II, it is as if an angel calling from afar. Helga Dernesh should not be singing this role. Every note seems like a struggle for her and it is painful to hear how a once talented singer has completely sang herself out of her proper roles.

By far the worst part of this recording is Jon Vickers. His voice is reedy, hoarse, and totally devoid of any beauty. People knock WIndgassen but compared to Vickers Windgassen sounds like Pavarotti. Vickers literally has to chew up every single word and spits them out in the worst display of consonant popping I have ever heard. He is the worst Tristan on record. Just compare him to Ludwig Suthaus makes you want to cry. What do people see (or hear) in Vickers anyway?

THe fact that such a terrible recording merits an asking price of $52.99 is ridiculous. You can't PAY me $52.99 to listen to this one more time. Why this recording is still in circulation when you have Kleiber, Bohm, Barenboim, Bernstein, or any number of other acceptable alternatives out there defies belief.

Now you have been warned, buy at your own risk.
label: negative

reviewText:
I don't want to sound like I'm trashing this album just to be fashionably harsh, but neither am I willing to sugar-coat this review just to get lots of "Helpful" votes. To be perfectly honest this is the first Rush album since I started listening to them (around 1975,) that holds absolutely zero value for me. In spite of coming from a band that I've loved for a long time, this album is flatly unlistenable.
For context's sake: I've always regarded this band as matchless in rock music - even to the point of being beyond the scope of comparative classification. Their growth and "constant change" in musical direction have always seemed to echo the growth and change in my own life, and it is those qualities which have made them so enduring in a fickle and frequently superficial business.
Rush have always worked elements of passing trends into their sound as a subtle nod to the change around them, but always restructured through their own intensely individual stylization. Examples would be the excellent treatment they gave to the Police-type ska influence and stark Ultravox "Euro" feel on Signals, and the tongue-in-cheek rap breaks - mixed with stunning philosophical insight - in Roll The Bones' title track. But on T4E they seem to have completely subordinated every aspect of their style to that bastard offspring of the Decade of Ugly: "grunge".
"Grunge" is specifically NOT what I want to hear coming from Rush - what a waste. Give me an analogy here...ahh, Ellington plays 'BigMouth Bass'?
There is literally not a single memorable or even interesting moment here, unless you discard the actual disc and treat the release solely as a short book of Peart's ever-fascinating poetry. I would limit myself to a criticism of Lifeson and Lee for a creative block in songwriting exceeding even that of the dismal Presto - but what's really amazing with T4E is that even Peart's percussion has been dumbed-down to the point where it's unrecognizable as his. I went back and made myself listen to this album again, trying to imagine the percussion being the product of a subcontracted, generic studio drummer - and it was not difficult(!) Peart can be justifiably classified as the Frank Lloyd Wright or Nikola Tesla of rock percussion, but T4E is clearly the least-remarkable work he's done in his entire career.
In a negative sense, Test For Echo brings to mind something Billy Sheehan said awhile back about the importance of crafting "good songs" - a seemingly obvious point. In the course of putting this album together, Rush defaulted horribly on that core element. They found a way to drag themselves down to the level of 90s grunge - at the price of obliterating their own identity. Let's hope that with the Decade of Ugly fading into the haze of cultural history (along with that great calcified cultural hairball called "grunge",) Rush will discard any remnants of that trend, step back up to their own level, and get back to making great music.
The concept of a "good song" and the entire "grunge" phenomenon are perhaps irreconcilable polar opposites - and I acknowledge fully my cultural bias on this point.
But I think there is also wisdom in Huey Lewis' maxim, "Sometimes, Bad is Bad".
label: negative

reviewText:
As many people may know by now, Sony was recently caught with egg on their face when a security specialist found out that a recently purchased CD (Van Zant: Get Right With The Man) from Sony music not only installed DRM software (digital rights management, to limit and outright prevent copying music to certain devices), but it did so in such a sneaky way that it hid itself entirely from Windows, and opened the system up to security issues such as viruses.

This CD has the same copyright protection, called XCP. When installed, Sony hijacks your computer and installs custom software which:

1) Hides itself entirely from Windows by installing as a rootkit

2) Hides itself in such a manner that any files begining with $sys$ are also hidden. For example, if you install the XCP copy protection software on your machine, and rename "document.doc" to "$sys$document.doc" it then becomes invivisble to you forever.

3) Installs its own custom CD-Rom drivers to hijack your system. It also sneakily names these drivers "Plug and Play Device Manager" to seem as if it's a part of Windows. Trying to delete these drivers manually will disable your CD-Rom drive entirely.

4) Offers no uninstall option until you manually contact Sony

As of my writing this review, Sony has "apologized" for this incident, and claims they will "re-evaluate" this copyright protection software on their CDs in the future.

In the meantime, a virus is currently running wild, which names itself begining with $sys$ in an attempt to hide from the user and virus scanners.

Several class action lawsuits are also pending against Sony right now.

In summary, as you can tell from above, Sony's actions here are absolutely horrible. This is your music. You purchased it, and they should not have any right to dictate how you can use it, let alone install software which compromises your system security.

This is one of the CDs with Sony's XCP copyright protection software on it, and as a result, you should not buy it to send a message to Sony that this will NOT be tolerated in the future.

reviewText: In The Beatles' Anthology DVD, when discussing the Sgt. Pepper's album, one of them says that the whole album concept died right after 3 tracks, as the rest of the songs could easily fit in any of their previous albums. Still this fact did not stop the album from being ranked as the #1 best rock album of all time by Rolling Stone magazine, and probably many other similar rock music publications. Ever since that album appeared, there have been countless other albums by other artists trying to capture that imaginary inexistent essence of what amounts to unicorns and rainbows, the result of some unrestrained acid trip. And even then, these pale imitations yielded a few songs that could serve as a yearning vehicle for the rest of the album to be as good or better than the exceptional single. For the canny artist, this could be a showcase of their alter-ego, and a harmless gamble, as they could always say "it wasn't us" should the album prove to be an embarrassment (The 1978 soundtrack to the film "Sgt. Peppers'), or claim it as "the next step in the artist's development" should it be a COMMERCIAL success. Note I said "commercial" for this is what this album was: a success. Musically speaking it is an album of various musical styles wrapped in a "psychedelic motif" but the psychedelic part of the music is only present on a couple of tracks at most. The album has 3 good singles (America, Pop Life, Raspberry Beret), of which only one (Pop Life) is anything resembling "psychedelic". The other one is the opening track, which is passable, but not good enough to be a good song or a single. The rest of the album is full of pretentious funk and boring fillers. If you ever heard a similar themed album XTC - "Oranges And Lemons" after you were sold on the cover, you'd find pretty much the same pattern there: Psychedelic opening track, hit single, minor single, followed by 13 tracks of bad filler crap over the course of 2 LPs. Psychedelic albums are but a fad, a fake fashion statement not unlike the $100 Tiffany "Punk" Safety Pin, and yet another marketing ploy which still to this day evokes an illusory world but fails to deliver on its promise.

reviewText:
...they said that they wanted their music back.
There can be no doubt at all that Counting Crows probably played as a covers band for several years before they hit it big - you can just tell from listening to this album.  They have had four studio albums to create an identity of their own, but have failed to do so - they continue to crib from Van Morrison, Bruce Springsteen, Warren Zevon, John Hiatt, etc.  And now they're releasing a best of album only four albums into their career - that's either a sign of writer's block or completing a contractual obligation, but given their inexplicably hugely successful cover of Joni Mitchell's "Big Yellow Taxi" with young piano diva Vanessa Carlton, I would assume it's the former.  Doesn't surprise me too much - they shilled for a certain soft drink not too long ago, if I recall.
The shamelessly derivative Counting Crows would be better if they were consistent, but they shift gears between utterly pretentious ("Mr. Jones", "A Long December") and completely banal ("Hangin' Around", "She Don't Want Nobody Near").  In "Mr. Jones", frontman Adam Duritz blurts out "I want to be Bob Dylan", though the timbre of his voice and all the "sha-la-la-la's" in the song clearly indicate that he aspires to be Van Morrison.  "Hangin' Around" is but one of many songs that drives its chorus into the ground that by the time it's over you're on the brink of insanity.  You've heard all the songs on this album and know exactly what to expect - soft rock tunes with meandering (but occasionally interesting), self absorbed lyrics from Duritz, delivered with all the precision and passion of a covers band.
In summary: There are far worse bands out there than Counting Crows, but that's no reason to support these guys - they're derivative, unoriginal, and Adam Duritz is way too fond of Hollywood starlets for this band to be taken seriously.  And they released their "best of" album too early in their career.  Basically, this band's music has been done before, and it was written and executed better than anything these guys have put out.  Check those musicians out instead.

One star is far too generous a rating for this waste of shelf space at the record store, and waste of plastic and paper packaging. This is yet another example of the bottomfeeding record industry putting out product with a "beautiful" face. (beautiful is in quotation marks, because this is yet another case of trying to put out "black" music as performed by a white singer). And as usual, the powers that be and many facets of the media gush uncontrollably over how "great" she is, all the while ignoring the truly great singers out there who go unrecognized, and these singers just so happen to be "black." It's so sad because music today is all about image, "beauty," marketing, and TV and radio OVER-rotation and overexposure. There are plenty of great singers out there who only see ONE album (if they see one at all) and then they're shoved out the door because, first, they're not white, two, their albums don't sell enough on the first go-round to satisfy the mega-conglomerate record labels which are all owned by five or so mega-companies, and three, too many listeners have been brainwashed by commercialism and pop music overexposure to even know what is good, true, soulful music. Their eyes deceive them and play tricks on their ears. They equate their Eurocentric notion of beauty with what is good music. Black is ugly to them, so they will never ever give a black singer credit, while white artists playing black music forms are deemed geniuses while the black originators and truly gifted musicians/artists go unrecognized and wallow in obscurity. And since the big labels are solely concerned on immediate and mega-million returns on their dollar, artists are not being nurtured. All we receive are clones, recycled pop ideas and remakes. There are true artists out there, but they get one shot on big labels, or live in obscurity on independent labels, and such albums don't see the light of day in big chain stores that sell CDs.

If Joss Stone was black, and not a blonde Caucasian person, she'd be yet another lost singer without an opportunity. It's too bad people don't know what good music is anymore since the big labels don't care to get behind it as they are concerned with the flavor of the week. I just wish people would know there's more to music than what's on the radio, what's on TV or cable, and what gets the heavy marketing. Most people have the Internet now, go do a little looking beyond the superficial marketing. Some big labels do have good artists on them, but you have to search.

Here's some names you could look into.

Julie Dexter

N'Dambi

Conya Doss

Kem (he's on a big label)

Sandra St. Victor (was once on big label, but now is on independent)

Erykah Badu (on big label)

Jill Scott (on independent, but is rather well known)

There are more out there. Those who think Joss Stone is so great are just really missing on real soul, and are being suckered by the big labels to buy commercialism. Joss Stone is not a bad singer per se, but just very artificial, superficial and derivative. She's all style, no substance, all frosting, no cake. There's not much there once you get past her derivative style. My review here will probably get major negative opinions from the readers out there, but that only goes to show they don't know what true, good soul music is. Buy this CD if what flimsy pop-soul that imitates the real thing is what you like. But if you know and like true soul, you'll know where to look.

And if you just don't like to buy soul from black singers, then perhaps try Nikka Costa, (she reminds me of former Family Stand lead singer Sandra St. Victor), she's fun and not half bad. But still, hopefully, you'll open your eyes and ears to embrace all types of singers.
label: negative

reviewText:
Sigh...where to begin. I guess the best thing to do is start with the positive. I have seen lead vocalist and principal songwriter Sully Erna in various interviews in magazines and on television. I have to say, from what I've seen of him and read about him in his interviews, I really genuinely like the guy. If I ever met Sully, I wouldn't even doubt that we could be good buddies. Well, that is until I say what I'm going to say next.
This is just a TERRIBLE, TERRIBLE album. I'm not playing the part of your traditional music critic, because I am quite the fan of nu-metal...but, err...Well, in the land of uber-popular nu-metal bands Godsmack are just "Godawful."
I bought this CD some time ago after hearing "Moon Baby" and "Whatever." I really did enjoy those songs quite a bit. In fact, the first few tracks really got me pumped. Then, track number 4 kicked in. Now, I will admit (if this can be considered fault) that I have ZERO tolerance for a blatantly ripped off song. ZERO tolerance...I even gave Godsmack the benefit of the doubt until I heard them lift ANOTHER song from the same group on their "Awake" album. So what am I talking about? "Time Bomb." Anyone who thinks Godsmack is a great band needs to go to their local music store back catalog of early 90's heavy rock albums. You'll find EVERYTHING you need right there. In fact...if you burn a CD of various bands of that era, you will have one full Godsmack album. Sure, it may take more time...but it'll smell a whole lot fresher than this big pile of rotting musical flesh.
But I digress...back to "Time Bomb." This song is a BLATANT rip off of a "Nine Inch Nails" song called "Last" on the "Broken" EP. Not only is the riff COMPLETELY lifted...the song follows the same structure, and the lyrical delivery (and even some of the content) is almost identical. For example:
Time Bomb:
I AM IN A LIVING HELL, MAKES ME WONDER IF I'M ALIVE.
CAN'T SEEM TO BRING MYSELF TO FIGURE OUT WHY.
Last:
gave up trying to figure out my head got lost along the way
worn out from giving it up my soul i pi$$ed it all away
Last:
i know it's all getting away it comes to me as no surprise
i know what's coming to me is never going to arrive
Time Bomb:
LIE DOWN IN ALL THIS PI$$, YOU DRINK IT FROM ME EVERY NIGHT.
The best way to do this exercise is to listen to BOTH of these songs one after the other. Does anyone remember those Mad Magazine song parodies that said "sung to the tune of"? The same rule applies here. Just sing the lyrics of "Last" to the Godsmack song and vice versa...that alone should hopefully make up for the amount of money you spent on this CD. I spent a little over $6 on this garbage and I still feel ripped off.
As for the rest of the album, chugga-chugga-chugga, GRRRRR...chugga-chugga-chugga, grrrrr... The lyrics are absolutely terrible, I have heard all of this agony and pain before. Using lots of profanity does not make you look or sound more angry; it just makes you sound illiterate. As for the guitar playing, I'm not even going to criticize it because I am an avid fan of bludgeoning caveman riffs; chugga-chug 'til your arm falls off. Just write YOUR OWN RIFFS!
label: negative

reviewText: I'll keep this simple.  Smashing Pumpkins was a great band in the early 90's, but Melon Collie was their last good album.  Since then it's been a revolving door of musicians, different lineups on each album-even though Machina had the original lineup.  And the song quality and direction of the band has suffered ever since.  Now it's the Billy Corgan band and the songwriting is just dull.  there is nothing I can remember from listening to this album twice.  No melody, no guitar riff, no piece of music or anything stands out.  Billy's passion is gone.  The album sounds like a bunch of b sides at best, except Pices was a b side album and that was an awesome album.  A few of these songs, like 3 maybe aren't terrible, but they aren't good either.  And the rest are awful.  Billy loves the electronic music and he's not afraid to show it these days.  There are keyboards on here that sound like old bad video game music.  Run2me is the worst song to come out in 2014, and this is the worst album I've heard at least from 2014, probably in the last decade actually.  Though Oceana was bad too, so it has competition there.  Overall if you're hoping for the same pumpkins magic of the early days you won't find it here.  You won't even find an inventive new sound.  You'll find a guy trying desperately to hang on to relevance dragging a band name through the mud because his Zwan and solo albums didn't do as well as he would have liked.  Smashing Pumpkins should have retired after machina and their legacy wouldn't have been tarnished.  But instead Billy keeps releasing one bad album after another under their name.

reviewText:
I could go on about how 50 used to be nice on the mic(back in the How To Rob days) or how Banks used to kill it on the early G-unit mixtapes or how Tony Yayo used to bust a decent verse once in a blue moon but it makes no sense to do that now. On the advent of Game's departure and  Young Buck being dropped from the group(I don't care what coast you're from.... we all got agree that 50 made a big mistake right there), G-unit only had one thing to do: prove that they can still stay afloat after all this. Unfortuantely this is not the album that is going to do it. Straight Outta Southside is the best track on the album and it pretty much goes downhill after that. A lot of the beats here suck as well as the hooks. Both 50 and Banks rhymes are phoned in and even the Yayo's rhymes are trash, for some strange reason, he is the only one(out of the remaining members) who has a presense on the mic on this album. Young Buck appears on a few songs and brings some heat but even he cant save this album from being garbage. Piano Man, Rider Pt 2, Close To Me, Party Aint Over, Let It Go, You So Tough stink lyrically and production wise. The title track is flat out weak and anyone bumpin I Like The Way She Do It and Kitty Kat in their whips needs to be slapped senseless. Both of those tracks are straight garbage. Ready Or Not has some decent bars by Lloyd Banks but Yayo and 50 both bring the track down. Money Make The World Go Round has a nice beat but the track suck lyrically.
Bottom Line: Terminate On Sight is even worse than Beg For Mercy(at least that album had five passable tracks). The beats are weak and the rhymes are telegraphed in. Its safe to say that G-unit is on the downslide and this album will get them on the fast track to obscurity a lot quicker than they expected. Two thumbs all the way down
Standouts: STRAIGHT OUTTA SOUTHSIDE.

Well lets see, back in the day i use to love Skid Row, even there 1995 Subhuman Race with more of a Punk Edge was great compared to this train wreck. Bands never seem to get the idea that changing singers changes the whole overall sound of the band. As with Maiden(horrible), Anthrax(mediocre), Black Sabbath(all sucked but Dio), just to name a few. The only worth while change that only lasted one album was Judas Priest(Jugulator), i can't think of any other exceptions. This doesnt even remotely sound like Skid Row, it sounds like more modern bands such as Shinedown(whom are ok), Crossfade, Default, etc etc, even Creed at times. I'm more of a obscure metal fan myself anyways, bands such as Nevermore, Soilwork(older), At The Gates, Carcass, Testament, and Tad Morose. Bands like this keep the real metal torch burning bright, each differently in there own way. This is yet another failure of an 80's band trying to make a "come back", without Bach they are dead in the water. Also whats with this TWO stuff, unforgiven II, Operation Mindcrime II(coming from Queensryche in 2006), Helloween-Keeper Of The Seven Keys-The Legacy(why not just call it III)?, and so on, this is a trend that seems to plague older bands who are running out of fresh new ideas. Sad to say Skid Row has now became one of those bands. Heres a few good and bad come back albums, mostly bad.

1. Death Angel-Art Of Dying(Not totally horrible but pretty weak)

2. Kreator-Enemy Of God(One of the few GREAT COMBACK ALBUMS 10/10)

6. Anthrax-(Guess we will see, not much hope though i don't think)

So i would recommend staying with bands who still have it and never have let it go, or listen to these bands as they struggle to keep there head above the music industries polluted waters. Just like Metallican't, Skid Row have left the building.

reviewText:
Before the retard Peter Dolving returned to the Haunted, they had released their peak album "One Kill Wonder" which was flawless from start to finish. Nothing but sheer brutality, rhythmic technicality, and breakneck thrash going at 1000 MPH. This is the only thing that anyone who was once in At the Gates has ever done that was even close to achieving the greatness of the aforementioned band. Their second record was pretty damn good as well. Then, unfortunately, the frontman for this era of the Haunted (Marco Aro) left shortly after some shows for the OKW album and their original vocalist returned to the fold. While his style of vocals worked for their 1998 debut, he was still the weak link in the band. But, with them having been on the roll that they were on, I never would have imagined that it could have hindered them. Boy, was I wrong. In late 2004, they released the rEVOLVEr album and proved to be a shocking disappointment. They added in these boring, dragging, hicked out slow songs with some horrible and just dumb sounding vocal displays and all the thrashing that remained were lazy riffs with more bad vocals. The production was weak as could be, and all the anger and feeling was gone. The only tracks with any staying power were the two bonus tracks on the limited edition and even those had some annoying vocal parts. Peter Dolving just is not a good vocalist. He wants to be the next Phil Anselmo and it's so obvious. From his drug addict stories to some of his hicked out clean singing to his attitude on stage.

Due to the fact that he was 75% of the reason why the band had been brought down so drastically, I didn't really have any interest when I heard that the Haunted had been recording for a new album. With Dolving at the helm, there really isn't anywhere left for them to go. A source obtained the album before it's release so I decided what the hell? Might as well give it a listen....

It's like they thought of all the worst things they could possibly do, and went ahead and did them. First off, making all the songs start with "THE" has been done before and if it's not for a reason, it's quite stupid. Not only are the Haunted no longer a thrash band, but one can almost go as far as to say that the Haunted are no longer a METAL band. All the most terrible ideas on rEVOLVEr are the ones constantly exercised on this one. The whole thing practically is Dolving's clean singing accompanied by slow, boring, redneckish riffs. There is no technicality, no speed, no aggression, NOTHING. I cannot believe that this is what is left of At the Gates. (Not that Adrian Erlandsson is doing any better) It's so much worse than I could have even imagined. There is not one song that I didn't just want to hit the skip button so bad while hearing it. And that weak production from their last album remains as well.

If you enjoyed the real Haunted, stay away from their last release, and stay even farther away from this one. The Haunted are done. I'll just stick to the 2nd and 3rd records. After seeing what that moron has done to this band, I can't even enjoy the first album. Another once-amazing Swedish band down the crapper.

reviewText:
Their heydey behind them, their live shows moving in the direction of touring jukebox, the Beach Boys have in the past 25 years put out four albums of material, but sadly little of merit, "Keepin' the Summer Alive" and "The Beach Boys" are a good example of this.

"Keepin' the Summer Alive" actually isn't that bad of an album, its just that it moves between one uninspired and lackluster song-- the lifeless "Oh, Darlin'" with a horrible bridge vocal by Mike, a dead cover of "School Days" (that did much better live, interestingly enough), and a plodding Carribbean-styled song "Sunshine" are good examples.  Add to this digging into the barrel of leftovers and pulling out tracks like "When Girls Get Together" (with horrid lyrics) and "Santa Ana Winds" (with a horrid voiceover) from the early 70s.  Top this off with a bad Bruce Johnston self-referential nostalgia piece in "Endless Harmony" and there's not much to look forward to.

For all this dull material, there are a couple really strong tracks-- the title track, cowritten by Randy Bachman and Carl Wilson, is a great rocker, and the song "Goin' On" was Brian reminding us that he's a genius, its really the standout song on the record and sits amongst the best Beach Boys material, but its not enough to save the album.

Sadly, as bad as "Keepin' the Summer Alive" is, "The Beach Boys" is worse.  The opener, "Getcha Back" is actually pretty good, it owes quite a bit to Brian's '60s work, though written by Mike Love and Terry Melcher, and Brian's falsetto is great to hear, but the production is a bit clinical and the drums sound artificial.

Unfortunately, the rest of the album carries over that thread, but also adds way too many synthesizers to the mix, giving it a very dated, mid-80s feel, and quite honestly, the synth wash fails miserably for the Beach Boys material.  Adding to this are several of Brian's songs have lyrics by Eugene Landy, whose lyrics match the tacky production value on numbers like "Crack At Your Love" and "Male Ego".  Add to this a song by Boy George and one of his CUlture Club cohorts ("Passing Friend") and a not-so-great Stevie Wonder song further brought down by a synthesizser wash ("I Do Love You"), and you've a recipe for distaster.  Carl's contributions fare somewhat better, but poor production takes what should have been a great soulful song in "Maybe I Don't Know" and reduce it to a synthesized 80s glam pop disaster.  Even more horrifying is the bad attempt at a surf glory rewrite in "California Calling", which ranks among the most embarassing of Beach Boys tracks.  The only track that seems to really claw its way above the poor production is Carl's beautiful "Where I Belong", which keeps the synths way in the background.

Really, this isn't great for the casual fan, there's not enough material on here to make it worth having.
label: negative

There is something inherently prosaic in this dead dull "music of der future". Fortunately, man has still some sense of individualism, but barely, and Kraftwerk's fascist goal for music has not rendered vocals obsolete. Listening to this, it harkens back to the techno geek 1970's when Germans laden in neo-fascist uniforms with thin ties and a pound of grease on their hair, showed no emotion on stage, acting like machines. Most of them wore leather pants so tight that they froze while playing, hence the dumb and inarticulate Krautbot look. They copied architecture chic from the 1930's, added some 70's porn montage and called it "modern" 1970's and praised the revolution of robots and computers. Not only is that very idea horrifying, but it is also silly. "Kraftwerk" means "cheese plant" in German and they are very cheesy.

The CD is probably one of the most horrible things I've listened to. If you can get to the end of it, you'll find all sorts of unwanted electronic noise, Krautbot voice dubs, electro fuzz, beeps, computer konks, repugnant computer-generated vocals, static, repulsive synthesizers, and extremely unpleasant clamor that goes on forever, that you'll soon be reaching for a hammer to crush the CD. In my estimation, all crap. A few American bands at the time tried the stale trend with deadly results, Gary Numan The Pleasure Principle (1979), Styx Kilroy Was Here (1983) , both tossed their careers away because of it.

You'll be reminded of foolish telephone companies, lumbering computer screens, electronic wires and moronic techno cabarets in dark German cellars. This is the 2nd album by these Krautbots in 28 years, so be glad their production output has ceased.

reviewText:
After I came to this page, I had to pour myself some coffee, throw cold water on my face, and slap myself a bit because I couldn't believe what I was seeing.  As of this writing, the vast majority of the reviews here give teen actress / wannabe pop star Lindsay Lohan's latest album 5 stars - the highest possible review.  Hmmmm... apparently the promotions department at Casablanca Records is working feverishly to develop interest in this album.  Now, in my honest and fair opinion, 5 star reviews should be reserved for something that is an absolute masterpiece - a true work for the ages.  Can anyone who listened to this album honestly say that this belongs in the class of works by, say, Mozart or Beethoven, or perhaps Wilco or Radiohead?  But I digress...

On to the matter at hand, which is Lindsay Lohan's second album, A Little More Personal (Raw).  We are introduced with "Confessions Of A Broken Heart (Daughter To Father)", a track which may be semi-autobiographical to Lohan (who co-wrote four songs on this album), but is an off-putting, cliched, treacly mess of a song.  Lohan sings with such ham-fisted conviction that you honestly get this vibe from her that she thinks that she is the only person to ever have a dysfunctional family, to ever have his/her parents divorce, to ever become distant from his/her father.  And in light of who she really is (drinking, dancing on tables and partying until the wee hours with the Hollywood elite), you know the song is not genuine and she's just milking this situation as fodder for album sales.  And the lyrics themselves are pretty sorry - she sings about wanting "a daddy to hold [her]" as if she's about 8, and the way she wails lines like "Did you ever love me?" shows just how untrained and unpolished her voice is.  Lindsay, cheer up honey - you've lived a charmed life, which both of your parents have made numerous sacrifices to give to you ... besides, there's an exclusive party going on till dawn somewhere on the Sunset Strip and you're invited, that ought to cheer you up.

With this whole album, one kind of gets the feeling that Lohan is just trying to tap into the girl-next-door charm that helped make Kelly Clarkson a ubiquitous star this past year (those marketing geniuses at Casablanca are at it again!).  This commercial makeover is very calculated, given the fact that just a year ago Lohan was whining about being hounded by the paparazzi over lightweight bubblegum dance/pop and seductively cooing double entendres like "I wanna come first".  One can also surmise that Lohan put very little effort into this recording (chalk it up to either those kiddie flicks that really put the champagne and caviar on the table, or to the obvious - lack of talent) - as stated before, she has only four co-write credits on the album, as the bulk of the songwriting goes to studio songsmiths for hire like Kara DioGuardi.  The sound is rather generic as well, with producer John Shanks applying his usual glossy sheen to cover up any inadequacies on the part of the singer or musicians (hey, this guy produces Ashlee Simpson as well!).

Lyrically, at times Lohan tries to sound, as she would say "like, deep or something" on certain tracks, but often finds herself stumbling on some pretty awkward, clumsy lyrics - for instance, she sings about a "universe of missing stuff" on "Black Hole", and the words on tracks like "A Beautiful Life" are unbelievably cliched and irrelevant.  Then there's a song like "Fastlane", where Lohan tries to pass herself off as a world-weary, inhibited, troubled soul, which is only so convincing when the opposite is true.  In the hands of a more capable artist (and with some revised lyrics), this song could have worked - in Lohan's hands, it just falls apart.

In summary: A Little More Personal (Raw) is just the typical weak disposible mass-market fare that usually sees release this time of the year.  There's an attempt at reinvention here, but it just doesn't pan out.  Lindsay Lohan's first album was pure drivel, but at least it was a style that suited her fine - here, she just seems like a fish out of water.  She makes an attempt at relevance but only comes out looking slightly more credible than Ashlee Simpson, and that's not saying much.  Instead, I would recommend looking not to the major music video outlets, but to the left of the radio dial for inspiration - you're far more likely to find something with more substance and with a much longer shelf-life there than on this tepid, vacuous commercial pop/rock album.  My advice: you can do far better than this.

reviewText: Well, this was unexpected. Julian Lennon has put out a couple of albums-worth of excellent material since the mid-1980s. Count me in as a fan. Until now. Sheesh! You have to wonder how he could have taken a decade off from the music business and return with this utterly wretched effort. How could anyone write such infantile insipid lyrics, in his mid-40s for heaven sake? They completely destroy the sometimes palatable music. All would merit F's for failure in any community college course in songwriting. Incredibly, the lyrics of the songs are actually displayed in an accompanying booklet, two pages devoted to each song with different butterfly motifs across from the lyrics. That's indicative of how cliched and banal all of this is: butterfly images to illustrate change, as if we didn't get enough of that between kindergarten and high school. If this is what Julian does with help from several writing collaborators, I'd hate to hear what he'd write on his own. Yikes! I would prefer to spin this CD on my Walkman a few more times to give one or two almost-bearable tunes a chance, but I just can't force myself to do it. Life is too short. No wonder this CD found such limited distribution after a long-delayed release. It appears that brother Sean has officially donned the father's mantle. For Julian, a renewed career in the restaurant business beckons. This CD should be a mortifying embarrassment for all involved. What a pity.

reviewText:
Don't get me wrong, I enjoy Bruce Springsteen's music very much.  Many of Bruce's other CD's are filled to the brim with passion and emotion.  However, this Ghost of Tom Joad CD leaves me very cold.
There are twelve songs on this CD's and they all seem to move at the same lethargic pace. The bleak tone surely does not help. On many of them it is extremely difficult to make out what Bruce is singing or more appropriately, mumbling.
Worse yet are the songs themselves.  Most if not all of these songs lack a good melody.  Youngstown and the title track are the only ones which seem memorable after three listens. A few others catch me for a moment but then fade away due to an overly repetitive pattern and a strong lack of instrumental definition.  The guitar playing is way too quiet that it barely adds any impression to the disc.  The ocassional harmonica blasts are the only thing that keeps from dosing off from boredom.
It's not that I dislike it that Bruce decided to make another all acoustic recording.  Whereas Nebraska was bleak and limited to a guitar/harmonica instrumental accompanyment, at least Bruce actually put some creative stylings into those songs.  And each of those tunes moved at distinctive paces and several of them had strong melodies.  The Ghost of Tom Joad on the other hand is dull, dismal, and boring.

reviewText: The original audio CD released in 1990 was the best collection of Mamas and Papas long string of hits at the time.  This collection however was not mastered from tapes.  You can clearly hear vinyl hiss, crackles and pops and just plain distortion on many tracks.  If you compare the tracks on this collection to the same tracks on the 2001 collection "All The Leaves Are Brown, The Golden Era Collection", you can clearly hear the difference in quality between the vinyl sources and the tape sources.  Listen to "Monday Monday" on the "Greatest Hits" CD and you'll hear incredible distortion along with surface noise in the quiet passages. One track on the "All The Leaves Are Brown" collection still sounds like it was mastered from a vinyl source (I Saw Her Again Last Night) but it still sounds better than the "Greatest Hits" version.  The "All The Leaves Are Brown" collection will most likely cost you a little more, but you get 2 CD's of Mama's and Papa's gems containing 27 tracks on Disc One and 25 tracks on Disc Two. The improvement in sonic quality over the "16 Of Their Greatest Hits" collection makes it the better choice for fans of The Mamas and Papas.

This'll make you laugh: Chris de Burgh has a new album out.

My New Years resolution this year (or one of them anyway) was not to dish out so many derogatory one-star reviews on dear old Ammie, but when you've got some-one as plainly talent-less, charm-less and handsome-less as de Burgh, openly slapping my sensibilities with a shocking album of senses-numbing cover versions, I feel a responsibilty to act - and act decisively.

Chris de Burgh is the most boring man in the world by a country mile. Soaring above titanic drudges like Sting, Essex, McCartney and even the undisputed British heavyweight of dull, Phil Collins, like a proud eagle on the wing.
He is indescribably tedious on a previously un-plumbed level; cricket is more interesting than him; his very name induces catalepsy in previously incurable insomniacs, and now (and you're not gonna believe this), he's cast his snoozy, lack-lustre spell over some of the songs that 'inspired' him.

It'll come as no surprise that none of the stuff he's chosen for 'Footsteps' (do not laugh yet) is any good - so what this deluded twit thinks he can bring to songs that charging with 50,000 volts wouldn't enliven is anyones guess, and a classic example of his nauseatingly unjustified gall.

Y'see, Chris de Burgh, despite all evidence to the contrary, thinks he's good.
It's this mis-shapen, grotesque illusion he's under that hits my 'blow now' button every time.
He's as smug as only some-one who writes great songs and does good work on a regular basis should be. He truly believes that any-one, other than his family and friends, would be interested in what mediocre tripe has 'influenced' him, and be remotely intrigued to see the evidence slumped corpse-like on a post-mortem trolley.
I personally went Sherlock-like through the forensics of 'Footsteps' shaking with anticipation, tremblingly trying to uncover what somnambulant disaster ultimately inspired 'Lady in Red,' but found no answer.
Perhaps it was the fierce abstract of 'Where Have All The Flowers Gone' and I completely missed it.

I wasn't expecting Chris de Burgh's favourite songs to include 'God Save The Queen' or 'Complete Control' but even so, I have been stopped in my tracks by the stupefying tepidity of 'Footsteps' - an album that Night Nurse took legal action to stop the release of, for fear of plummeting sales.
High, wide and not paricularly handsome. These days, middle aged MOR has much to commend it and can be interesting, but this isn't a good example.

As for my resolution, remember: 'the slowest mule is nearest to the whip.'

reviewText:
At midnight, a light was switched on in the control room of the Tidbinbilla Deep Space Tracking Station, some twenty kilometres outside of Canberra.

"Your Grace," said Cato, the trusty man-servant of Father Melchizedek OP, the High Priest of Period Practice and Grand Inquisitor of SPECTRE (Sinister Period Practice Enacted to Counter Traditional Readings Everlastingly), "I thought we were coming to Australia to see some of the sites like Sydney Harbour or the Great Barrier Reef? Or, in the very least, to hunt down and burn those Luddites of the Australian Knappertsbusch Association. Instead, you've dragged me all the way out here and in the middle of the night too. Oh Terror and Doom of the Karajanists, illuminate me in my darkness and I shall be healed!"

At first no answer was forthcoming. The cleric was sitting at the main control and busily pushing many a button. Every so often he whinnied in falsetto. Five minutes later, he unveiled a copy of Jeggy's Brahms First Symphony with the Orchestra de  Revolutionaire et Romantique, inserted it into a CD-ROM drive and then turned to his man-servant with a look of triumph on his pale face.

"Know this Cato - you speak more truly than what you realise. While the pretence of our trip to the Penal Colonies was heresy and the extermination thereof, I had an ulterior purpose in mind. We have swept all before us. Nowadays, what conductor is not enthralled to the Cause, be it Rattle in Haydn or Nezet-Sequin in Mozart or Fischer in Bruckner? Victory in hand, it's time to convert the cosmos! I am accordingly beaming this august performance in the direction of the Andromeda Galaxy, some 2.5 million light years from Earth. May it bring purity and salvation to its indigenes, be they humanoid, blob-like or something in between!"

"Your Grace, is that wise?" Cato said warily. "I know the very performance in question. Some - not me of course - would question the scrawniness of its strings, repudiation of grandeur and Jeggy's unreflective manner wherein substance is invariably sacrificed to the God of Brisk Efficiency. Has there been a more underwhelming account of the titanic finale in history? Whatever happened to the innate heroism of the score? When played like this, the B1 could almost pass for one of those boring Schubert symphonies (the early ones!) Nor do the tit-bits matter in the least. Truly, the world has contracted thus!"

The cleric glowered at his man-servant.

"Cato, sometimes I wonder whether you could benefit from a session or two with the Iron Maiden! I am not interested in your thoughts! Leave the study of heresy to me while you focus on my . . . . 'hard-to-meet' needs! Now, we shall retire for the night. Tomorrow, we will visit the Sydney Opera House. Who knows - it could be staging a production of Hasse's Artaserse at the expense of confectionery such as Parsifal or Elektra!"

Some 2.5 million years later, the transmission reached the spiral arms of Andromeda. It was duly recorded by the scientists at the court of the Galactic Emperor Klendon Na-Fang Goldu, terror of the universe. Its source was promptly identified. Legions were assembled. Before embarking for earth, he addressed the soldiery in their common tongue.

"Relax boys - this is easy meat!"

reviewText:
Creed has always been something of a hollow band.  They take from their influences (Pearljam, Stone Temple Pilots, The Doors, Lynard Skynard), but add nothing.  Instead, they simply rehash the same old tune.  This CD is no different.
Stapp is once again at his ego driven, pretentious worst.  The key to any form of art is to know when to go from overabundance to subtlty.  Stapp, unfortuantely, only knows how to go full-speed ahead.  Even when singing quietly, the effort is so heavy handed that it smacks of "Look at how delicate I am.  Aren't I cool?"  In other words, his ego is the driving force behind his vocals.
Lyrically, he suffers from a Jesus complex.  He knows what no one else knows, he sees what no one else sees.  Thankfully for us (or so he'd like us to think), he's there to serve as the beacon we obviously so sorely need.  He's willing to make the sacrifices we aren't, for the good of us all.  Instead of leaving questions for the listeners to answer themselves, he tells us how it is, or how it ought to be.
As far as the music of the album itself is concerned, it shares the same clunky problems as its predecessors.  It's a wall of sound, with no subtlty or surprises.  It follows their trademark power ballad (haven't they been out of style for a decade?) formula.  Slow, muddy guitar builds to slow, distorted muddy guitar, then falls back again.  The guitar playing is especially horrible because it completely saturates the bass.  It's loud and distorted, but has horrible timbre, and the guitar player doesn't help himself at all by overplaying (he needs to learn that rests are okay).
In the whole, Creed once again supplies us with an irritatingly catchy, yet technically flawed, effort aimed at the lowest common denominator.  It's bubblegum for the ears wrapped in televangilist packaging.

reviewText:
Let me start off by saying that I do NOT buy into the Sammy Hagar vs. David Lee Roth garbage that I see being plastered all over these reviews. If any of you who are old enough can remember back to 1978 when that very first Van Halen album was released, it was a wonderful album to behold. Now, if you loved that 1st album and loved the Hard Rock music genre you'll remember what else you were listening to back then? UFO, Aerosmith, Black Sabbath, Blue Oyster Cult, Scorpions, Rush etc... Probably somewhere in your record collection there was some Montrose and possibly some Sammy Hagar. To us growing up back then, we liked all this music in this genre, including Sammy Hagar.

Now, I do agree, Van Halen is NOT Van Halen without David Lee Roth. Pure and simple. I loved the guy as much as anyone one else who listened to and went to see their concerts. When Sammy joined I was sad because I really loved Sammy solo and Van Halen with Roth.

When DLR released his EP of cover songs shortly after leaving Van Halen in 1985, there was some hope that a solo Dave was gonna be interesting. When "Eat 'Em And Smile" in 1986 was released, I ate it all up, loving the whole album. Then, in 1988, the ship started to sink with the release of "Skyscraper", and it wasn't just me, look at the chart history. Sure "Just Like Paradise" hit number one on the US rock charts, but it was more of a cheesy pop song that is still pretty bad today. It was evident that the song writing and overall quality of DLR's albums was going down hill.

Sure, DLR has released only 7 studio LP's since his split in 1984 with VH, but the quality of each just progressively gets worse. Just listen to them if you dare. Where were you all through these DLR years when he sold very few copies of his solo stuff?

What has my head spinning is the amount of reviews that state that David Lee Roth is back. Maybe with Van Halen, but he's never really been too far away. 2003 is a long time since his last LP, "Diamond Dave' but if you listen to it, you'd be glad that he didn't make another.

Jump on the bandwagon here....

With this new Van Halen album, "A Different Kind of Truth" the songwriting, especially the lyrics, which we all know is 100% Dave, is still pretty poor and at times very childish and almost unfinished, and embarrassing as hell...and don't give me that crap on how these are old songs, reworked. What kind of cop-out crap is that? It didn't work then, so let's push it on the public now? Dave's voice is unmistakable, but is showing BIG signs that he's not a kid any more. Just listen to the intro to "Stay Frosty". It's probably one of the worst vocals I've heard in years. Hey, I'm getting older too and can't do what I used to, but I do know when to quit.

And, when it comes to they music. I do admit that it is damned good on most tracks. The problem lies with the vocals though. I'm not going to listen to an album for the music if I cannot stand the vocals. Plain and simple, if I bought this CD, I'd never put it into my player again. I'm SO glad for Spotify, which allows me to preview the whole CD without having to buy it.

I read one review that said something to the effect of: "How can a TRUE Van Halen fan dislike this album?" and also, "You're not a fan if you don't like this album." Well, that's BS!

I really think that people who pre-ordered this CD or bought the digital MP3 version, had SO much faith vested in it, that they were going to like it no matter what. There's also the people who will buy anything from an artist, even if it is inferior to prior work. Then, there's the younger listeners who've listened to their parents old albums and are so excited to be feeling a piece of the excitement when a major band like Van Halen releases something. Not too many bands these days have stirred up the musical pot like this new CD.

And, my favorite fans...The ones who now go to concerts JUST to try and experience some old magic so they can brag about it. Yeah, these people know who they are. They never liked Van Halen back in the day. They were into disco or punk or new wave, and totally trashed Van Halen and all other bands in this genre. This goes for critics too, who hated thee types of bands back in the 70's and 80's. Now all of a sudden, these people have a change of heart and want to be part of the "Fun".

I'll live with my memories of days past when Van Halen was still relevant and the audience was filled with teens and young adults, my age THEN..Not people trying to re-live those days. I'll take my old Van Halen albums and close my eyes and remember how it was. To those of you, enjoy this record because there may not be another. Eddie's making tons of money off of it and if he goes on a bender when this tour is over, he may never return.

So, fellow and lady reviewers, this is my opinion. No one will change my mind or make me listen again. It's simple, some people like it and some don't. Respect those of us who believe that it's no good and that "Tattoo" song just may be one of the worst songs ever recorded....it was just fueled by all of the hype leading up to this release.

And, if you like this kind of heavy music and want to listen to a great "Comeback" album, give a listen to: "Anthrax - Worship Music" and enjoy a truly GREAT album.

reviewText: What horrible casting. I don't have too much to add to what's already been said. Some roles are not written for opera singers. The studio recording of "On the Town," for example, used opera singers for the role of Gaby and the various bass roles (Sam Ramey was wonderful singing "I Understand"), but wisely cast non-operatic singers in the other rolls. Kiri TeKanawa seems like a passable Nellie, if you've never heard Mary Martin. Jose Carreras is a out of his element playing a Frenchman as he was playing a New Yorker in "West Side Story." I liked Mandy Patimkin's "Younger Than Springtime," but "Youv'e Got to be Carefully Taught" is hurried. Rodgers and Hammerstein considered this the most important song in the score, and they wanted the message to get across. This version hardly does that. The worst, however, is Sarah Vaughn's Bloody Mary. She makes no attempt to get into the character--she sings it as if she was in a nightclub. Maybe this would be fine on a solo CD, but in a musical one should try to become part of the story, not impress us with her jazz interpretation. Listening to "Bali Hai," I was reminded of Bill Murray's hilarious send-up of Las Vegas lounge singers on "Saturday Night Live." But he was trying to be funny. I know this is an old recording, but if Amazon still has the nerve to sell it, then buyers should beware. In short, I have heard this show better sung in community theater productions.

reviewText:
I had heard in classical music circles that Russell Watson was this not very good tenor who had become very popular without being very good. Nothing had prepared me for the experience of listening to him myself. First of all, no comparison should be made between Russell Watson and a genuine classical music performer. Despite the fact that some of his tracks are adapted from great masterpieces (with wind chimes and things added), there is no more reason to consider him a classical musician than there would be to consider Jim Carrey a serious sportsman if he suddenly decided to throw a football around during half-time at a big game. But we live in an age of this kind of singing... There is a big difference between the cream of the crop having a bit of fun and making a few million dollars by putting on a popular show, and someone whose appalling vocal technique would not survive un-miked in an opera house for even one full season and whose musicality is next to nil. Watson misses the inconvenient step of being an opera singer and goes straight for the commercialism...There exists something in the world called kitsch. The idea of kitsch is that you take a great masterpiece of art, say for example the Mona Lisa, and you make a cookie jar out of it, or a plastic backlit reproduction of it. That's what this music is. No more than a glow-in-the-dark David or a [short story magazine] Dostoevsky should this be confused with the real thing. The art of singing opera requires discipline and great technical skill, as well as thorough musical training, and it is consequently very rewarding when done with care and genuine feeling. Thomas Allen, one of the premiere opera singers of the past thirty years, has described Russell Watson as a pub tenor. It's not a friendly description, but it's true. Go to the original. If you like the music Russell Watson sings - with his added sound effects and rewritten orchestration - hopefully you will like the real thing even more...
As an afterthought - I really have to say that to call this album 'The Voice' is an insult to whoever buys it, whether they genuinely enjoy the music or not. It's awful to have to put it like that, but he has a dreadfully inadequate voice which is very nasal and poorly placed... The present album is the musical equivalent of [hamburger restaurant] changing the name of their hamburger to a steak sandwich and expecting people to think it's prime corn-fed Iowa. It's amazing the things people do for money.

reviewText: Wilco was well on their way to establishing themselves as a truly great band. Their first four albums were all great! They followed up the Uncle Tupelo sound, but deviated slightly from the country alt sound and that was OK. I have never felt that Jeff needed to keep doing Uncle Tupelo, he should be allowed to evolve and grow. However, I questioned where that growth was going with "A Ghost is Born," an album that had an equal number of hits and misses. Then came "Sky Blue Sky," an album that had a lot more misses than hits. The problem with both of those albums was just an overall lack of energy or excitement. For the most part, they were dull albums. Yeah, yeah, they are a mid-tempo band, I have heard that. But something seemed to be missing. Now, some have argued that Jay Bennett had a stronger voice in Wilco than Tweedy would have you believe. That does have some credibility now, considering the fact that Jay's two albums with Wilco were great and the albums released after his departure were lacking. That is neither here nor there. Now we get "Wilco" the album. The terms syrupy, bubble-gum, cotton candy and crap come to mind. Look, I know I am going to get flamed by Wilco kool-aid drinkers in here, but I don't care. I am not one of these blind loyalists. Wilco's music is declining into an almost unbearable state. I still listen to the first four albums all of the time and always will, but it sure seems that this band has nothing new left to offer. The songs are no innovative, they are not interesting and they are about as deep as shot glass. If another band not named Wilco had released this album, I guarantee you that half of the people in here that profess to love it, would say it was not a very good band. I am hoping that Jeff will get it back somewhere down the road, but I am losing faith.

reviewText:
When I listen to Love Never Dies, I feel like I'm listening to a musical about the National Enquirer.

Really?  REALLY.  Don't believe me, just read what I have below:

The Phantom has teamed up with Madame Giry and Meg Giry (the box keeper/ballet mistress and her ballerina daughter) to flee to Coney Island.  Why?  I don't know.  Madame Giry was afraid of the Phantom, from what I gathered from the first musical, so why would she want to team up with him?  And now, Meg is sleeping around with men to give the Phantom money so that he can lure Christine (unknowst to them!) to Coney Island to have her sing in his musical.  Don't believe me?  That's exactly what is going on in this CD.  But let us continue!

There are new characters.  A trio of carnival misfits who work for the Phantom and act as his eyes and ears.  Who have no idea how insane their 'master' was when he was back in France.  To them, Phantasma (the ficitional carnival placed in Coney Island) is their weird home.  But the weirdest bit is what lies in the Phantom's room - a Christine Daae sex doll who he keeps in a cage and sings to.  Nobody else knows about this, except for the Phantom and Madame Giry.  Both of who pick at the Phantom for continuing to love this woman that apparently could never be his.

Christine gets the letter from the Phantom, asking her to come to Phantasma (and she doesn't put two and two together).  She also has a son, a 10 year old boy named Gustave.  Her husband, Raoul, has done a complete 180* since we last saw him - now a drunken gambling idiot who hates his wife and his son. Forget the equalities that lie between Phantom and Raoul - they don't exist anymore.  Forget the tension between the two men and Christine, because this was written so that you would dislike Raoul from the start.

When the Phantom and Christine finally meet up, you realize that Christine cheated on Raoul.  And when he ran away, she decided to go back to Raoul - not because she loved him, I'm assuming.  (Since she had sex with the Phantom.)  But she went back to support her poor butt, since the Phantom was nowhere to be found with his 50,000 francs.  Ha.

You also come to realise that Meg is in love with the Phantom.  And, is jealous of Christine's appearance with her husband.  You also learn that Christine's son likes the darkness and plays the piano like the Phantom... And just because of these reasons, the Phantom has deemed Gustave his son.  Talk about cliche!

So, throught the rest of this CD, you realize that the Giry's are ready to own the Phantom for his sick lusting for Christine (even though she's married) and Meg in particular wants to hurt them both.  Raoul, meanwhile, is totally forgotten about up until the part where the Phantom plays a bartender and sings to him (while he's drinking away) that Christine will never be his.  They make a bet over Christine - if she sings for him, she belongs to the Phantom.  If Christine denies singing for The Phantom, Raoul and Christine can leave Coney Island and The Phantom will leave them alone.

Christine DOES sing for the Phantom (because we all knew it was going to happen), and Gustave goes missing.  Christine and the Phantom discover that Meg has kidnapped Christine's son and is off to go drown him in the ocean. Meg also has a gun, which she stole from the Phantom (because earlier, the Phantom wanted to go and kill himself with the gun because Christine wasn't a part of his life).  The Phantom makes a slip of the tongue, compares Meg to Christine, Meg shoots Christine.  Christine dies, but not before she quickly tells Gustave that his father is the Phantom (because Raoul is no where to be found, he went back to France).  Phantom and Gustave cry. And Meg and Madame Giry, nobody cares about them since they stop singing (but it is assumable that Meg has gone insane).  And it ends.  It ends like that.

... Now tell me, who would want a musical of THAT?

Unfortunately, the songs did not help the plot.  The rhymes were simple (like rhyming mop with top) and the lyrics were wildly descriptive and slow down the plot.  (A wonderful torture device!)  The performers: Siera Boggess was too breathy and her portrayal of Christine makes her seem like a simpleton.  Joseph Milton's acting was better than his voice.  It wasn't reamarkable nor was it horrible.  And Ramin Karimloo's Phantom was FAR TOO YOUNG in voice and portrayal.  The Phantom has to be older than 30.  But since nowadways anybody can play the Phantom, nobody cares about the Phantom's age.

The entire plot can be summed up in Rick Astley's "Never Gonna Give You Up".  Which is sadly a lot better than this hokum that I just listened to.  I have not seen the musical, but since the whole show is almost preserved on this CD, I'm sure it'd be the same experience if I saw it live.  And reviews from many papers seem to agree that the score and the book are far more horrible than the sets and the production.

The original Phantom may not be the greatest achievement, but audiences keep coming to it...

When you put a story like that [Love Never Dies] on CD (and on stage) you're REALLY asking for it.

I'll stick to Sondhiem for now on.

No Doubt made inconsequential pop albums that at least worked as excellent ear candy (and their singles collection is as good as any 90's band that you'll find), but this is just egotistical preening. But the absolute bottom of the barrel is track three, "Hollaback Girl," where the woman who once declared her femininity and emancipation on "Just A Girl" seductively croons "This is my sh**" over and over. While loose religious plots worked well in "Jesus Christ Superstar" they failed miserably here. The music is grating and pedantic. It switches from genres of Broadway to those of country and calypso. While this might be enjoyable for the average "Raffi" aficionado it comes across as patronizing to the average listener of Broadway music. I attended a performance of this show recently and came to this conclusion: People like this show because it is big and flashy. It lends itself to brightly colored sets and powerful, belter-style singing. As with most of Webber's works, "Joseph..." gains respect not through its musical prowess, but through it's childish antics.

The lyrics are trite, stupid, and not representative of the darkness AIC is known for.  Take "Check My Brain" for example.  The song is about how Jerry Cantrell moved to California, was surprised that he actually likes it there, and is asking someone to check his brain because he can't believe it.  Look it up.  He said it himself.  What a dumb thing to write a song about.  Even the title track, which is supposed to be a tribute to Layne, is not respectful of him.  A closer look at the lyrics reveals a song that accuses Layne of not even trying to stop doing drugs and states that it was easier for him to keep using than to have to feel anything.  Anyone who read Layne's final interview would know this was not the case.  Layne stated he was no longer doing drugs to get high and it was no longer pleasurable for him.  His body was so sick and dependent on the drugs that he would be violently ill if he didn't use them.  He had tried to quit before but couldn't do it.  He also suffered from a broken heart from the death of his girlfriend.  Overall, this album is just wrong.  If they had changed the name and not attempted to sound like Layne, that would be fine.  The same people who are here praising this album would s@#$% a brick if Nirvana were to regroup with a replacement for Kurt Cobain; or how about Paul and Ringo assembling a new band with Lennon and Harrison impersonators called The Beatles?  What makes this any different?

WHAT'S WRONG WITH THIS ALBUM:  They have a punk feel, with a fast tempo for every song.  They can be a bit schizo and change it up, varying tempo and intensity with ease.  All well and good, until I listened to the next track.  Had I pushed repeat on accident?

I like the idea behind their formula, they're just not good enough to pull it off.  Okay, they turn from pop-punk (too much pop) to a fake metal sound (screaming over a hard rock riff is not metal).  The heaviness is what drew me in, however, it wore thin within ONE LISTEN of the album.

If you listen to the heavy part of each song, they are practically identical.  Same sounding riff combined with the same double-bass.  No changes in style, substance, and not much variety in tempo.  They have a fast or slow heavy style...still the same guitar...still the same double bass. Good for one song, until they do the same riff+double bass on the next song.  VERY BORING.  They don't spice it up or bring anything new past track 2.

Not worth my price of admission.  I'm not big on forumlas and repetiveness, this album has it in spades.

reviewText:
I hate Ryan Adams--everything about him, from his prissy onstage behavior to his movie star girlfriends to his boring inane lyrics to the fact that he can't boast of a single original idea. Rock 'N' Roll (very misleading title, that) is business as usual in the Adams camp.

In his previous band Whiskytown and past solo albums he was somewhat passable at doing the alt-country thing despite the fact that Uncle Tupelo, Son Volt, and even early Wilco were miles ahead of him. After the recording of the plastic, overproduced drivel of Gold he quickly became insufferable. Every one of Ryans' solo albums is full of undisguised Xeroxing from other artists (and often the worst parts, at that)--Bruce Springsteen, U2, Morrissey (bleh), Rolling Stones, Nirvana, Neil Young, Uncle Tupelo, and Paul Westerburg of The Replacements.

That last name is especially important, 'cause on this sh-tstew Ryan rides Paul's jock for all it's worth. Arena-rawk cliches are willingly recycled--the "soaring choruses" that allow for opportunities to make a Jesus pose (So Alive), the disposable pop hooks (Shallow), the "sensitive" piano ballads (ex. the title track--oh, how ironic!), and slick production. And lyrics that even a bunch of lamers like the Counting Crows would be embarrassed to write (witness the stupid profanity-laden chorus of Wish You Were Here; by the way, what an original title--'Floyd should sue).

And then for all his swiping, he has the unmitigated gall to diss Westerburg in the press. Ryan, the proctologist called a minute ago. He's just found your head.

I think I'll go to a Ryan Adams concert just so I can scream a  request for "Summer Of '69" and watch him have a strop. In the meantime, I'll entertain myself with something original and leave this crap on the shelf. I suggest you do the same.

As a true music lover who genuinely cares about sound quality, I honestly can't recommend this album for one simple reason: IT'S TOO BLEEPIN' LOUD!!! What do I mean by that, you might be wondering? Well somebody in the mixing room must've been asleep at the board because the EQ levels have been boosted way past what I feel are "acceptable" limits (even for a rock album, which is hard to fathom), with the differences between high and low range frequencies becoming less and less distinct on EVERY-SINGLE-TRACK! My heavens, if you're looking for a stereo reference CD to test how good your sound system is then this one clearly does not make the grade. For those who previously bought Metallica's 'Death Magnetic' album will know exactly what I'm talking about here.

This is a real tragedy because Robert Randolph and his band really brought their "A" game on this release. I haven't heard them sound this hot and inspired since their studio debut. I personally felt they could've done without their cover of the Ohio Players' 'Love Rollercoaster' since it doesn't quite surpass the original (might be on par with the Chili Peppers' version, come to think of it), but other than that it's a righteous return to form for them performance-wise. Still, all the better to just wait for a re-release where the volume levels are thoroughly back "in the green" where they should be.

reviewText:
I would consider myself big Brand New fan. I liked "Your Favorite Weapon" and I would rank their second album "Deja Entendu" in my Top 10 favorite albums of all-time, and I own over 1,000 CD's, so that is saying something. I was really looking forward to their new album, which seemed to take forever. For the longest time I heard nothing about the band and their website offered no information. Finally news came of "The Devil And God Are Raging Inside Me" and I was excited, to say the least. I expected nothing more than greatness from this album, but I allowed myself that doubt and understanding that there is no way they could top "Deja Entendu" musically or lyrically.

So I picked up Brand New's new CD on Tuesday morning and gave it a spin. I felt like a good friend of mine just died, because what I heard was a completely different band. But it wasn't a good kind of different. I have a very diverse musical collection and I like when bands change, for the most part. Brand New took such a huge nosedive on this release. I can sum up the new album with a few words; boring, groggy, spaced-out and dumbed down. The band seems uninterested and it shows in the music. They sound like they don't want to be there and they're only interested in noodling around on their guitars and trying very hard not to make a mainstream album. This will get ZERO airplay, unless that come out with a radio station geared towards the most boring music on the planet. If this gets played on the radio, there will be a rash of car crashes as a result, because drivers will be falling asleep left and right.

I hate to say it, but "The Devil And God Are Raging Inside Me" is the biggest musical disappointment of 2006 and perhaps off all-time. It's hard to imagine that there can be such a dropoff between albums, but Brand New managed to achieve it with this release. I can't believe this thing is getting 5 stars from some people, I can't give it any lower than the 1 star rating I gave it. It's horrid, a musical atrocity that numbs the brain and leaves you wondering what you're listening to.
label: negative

reviewText: Amazon's editorial review by David Hurwitz not only misses the mark, but is just plain factually wrong. First, for him (and all the others) who like to say that Semele is "really" an opera and not an oratorio, one has to question what criteria are being applied. Hurwitz seems to feel it's an opera because it requires spectacular voices, but ideally, all of Handel's vocal music should be sung by spectacular voices. If you think "oratorio" means only religious meditations like Messiah or Israel in Egypt, you might think that Semele breaks the mold, but most of Handel's oratorios are dramas portrayed through singing, and most could have been staged, if Handel had wanted to. Handel certainly didn't consider Semele an opera, and never staged it. It is true that it can be presented very effectively as an "opera," that is, fully staged with sets and costumes, but that doesn't mean anything. Other of Handel's oratorios have been staged by opera companies, including Samson, but that doesn't mean they aren't really oratorios. Even Bach's St. Matthew Passion has been staged by opera companies, but I don't think that means it's an opera. Conversely, in 1742 Handel gave a concert performance in Ireland of his opera Imeneo, but that doesn't mean Imeneo is "really" an oratorio. And even if Semele were an opera, it wouldn't be the "first" opera in English, as Hurwitz claims. Has he never heard Purcell's Dido and Aeneas (1685)? Not to mention forgotten opera seria composed in English as early as 1705. What I find most bothersome is the unstated assumption that dramatic oratorios are inferior to operas, that Semele is so wonderful (and it is) that it couldn't possibly be "just" an oratorio. That attitude does a disservice to the last decades of Handel's compositional career.

reviewText: Paavo Jarvi seems to be stepping outside of the composers his father, Neeme, favors, which is a good thing, but Paavo's conducting of Ravel is hardly impressive. Like his Debussy recording, Debussy: Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune; Nocturnes; Etc. [Hybrid SACD], there is just something missing here. I can't hear one bit of passion coming from Jarvi. The Cincinatti Symphony Orchestra play well, but there's just not much fire here. Am I missing something? I don't think I am. I own almost every recording of Ravel's orchestral music available. That said, the audio quality is top-notch, but this alone does not save this recording from mediocrity. Perhaps someone else will enjoy this recording, I just couldn't get into Jarvi's way with Ravel. I'll stick with Martinon, Boulez, Dutoit, and Tortelier.

Understand, I love Springsteen.  Born to Run is my second favorite album of all time.  I have seen him live over a dozen times.  I personally think he is the single most important American rock and roll artist ever (with apologies to Elvis, Chuck Berry and Dylan).  I even loved Nebraska, so don't tell me it's an E-Street band thing or a rock versus folk thing, but this album is unlistenable.

Some reviewers have called it beautiful and powerful.  That's rubbish.  There is a complete absence of melody on this record, as was the case with much of The Ghost of Tom Joad album (with a huge exception being "Youngstown" - a great song).  The apparently willful attempt to alter his singing style to sound like Woody Guthrie or Jimmy Rodgers is just frightening.  Dylan could pull it off, Bruce just disappoints.  But it's the songs and lack of anything remotely resembling melody that makes this record a failure.  Believe, I listened to Devil & Dust 10-15 times in hopes of finding what I am apparently missing.  I couldn't. I thought The Rising was a nice album.  I even liked the Devils & Dust solo tour (Bruce is a powerful performer, and maybe even more commading when it's just him on stage), but I doubt this CD will ever find its way back into the player.

That doesn't mean she's doing justice to these songs and it does not mean she delivers them with soul or sincerity. Quite the opposite; this record sounds like the marketing move of someone who's run a bit short on personal ideas and motivation. For example, her version of Willie and Laura Mae Jones is just awful; assembly-line country blues, indifferently jammed, with a lifeless PC reading of the lyrics, missing all of the naive charm that make Dusty's version so cool.

If you're buying this CD because you're a fan of Shelby and you've never even hear of Dusty Springfield, do yourself an incredible favor: skip this pointless, second-rate imitation (you can't even call it a tribute) and go find out about the real thing. You will be pleasantly surprised.

The lyrics are no better constructed than a simple dialogue or random thoughts in one's head.  The strumming is utterly boring and un-inventive. The banging on pots in the background is just that.  The recording technique is contrived.  If they were really serious about their music, the would spend an extra $[...] on a better tape recorder.

I'm pretty sure I understand what they're trying to do here, but then almost anyone could make this same noise.  It's simple sing-song jingles in nursery rhyme meter.  And if you don't fully believe that, and you like the hooks that much, then you should demand better production and musical accomplishment.  I mean, if they're that great, think how much greater they could be if they acted like a real band. But creepy has its limits when it comes to the soft confines of the (poorly titled) living room. For instance, a clown pulling a bouquet of flowers from behind his back with a smile so wide it looks painful is good creepy; but the same clown sawing off his arms in darkness while a midget tinkles (literally) onto a harpsichord is bad creepy.

It's the sort of thing you would have called bad for business before MTV jerked the Kennedy-Nixon debate credo off its axis, coming out in time for these dopes of mope to lather on the pancake batter, buckets of black lard and fried vaseline in lieu of hair.
