reviewText:
Just so you know where I'm coming from, I like all the Lou Reeds.  I like the jazz Lou Reed.  I like the gay Lou Reed.  I like the sexless-speed-freak Lou Reed.  I like the dry professor Lou Reed of "Magic and Loss".  I like the hateful Lou Reed of "Street Hassle".  I like the romantic Lou Reed from the Sylvia era. I've bought all Reed's studio albums, and never expected him to be anybody but who he was in that moment.

This was a dry, empty, and insecure "moment" for Lou Reed.

I personally suspect he was on antipsychotic medication (such as Thorazine), which would explain the lack of fresh material as well as his decision not to play guitar (I hate to mention this, but it would also explain his chubbiness in this period.)

Nothing can explain his appalling singing.  It's not just that he's cracked and hoarse -- he made that work on "Loaded", especially "Sweet Jane".  And what's his excuse this time, anyway?  It's not as if he'd spent the summer playing at Max's before recording THIS album.  Lou would be singing BEAUTIFULLY on his next album, "Transformer", so why in the blue blazes does he sound so awful here?  No excuse.

The instrumentation is awful.  The guitars are far too trebly.  The snare sounds like a garbage-can lid.  In a BAD way.  The musicians have no point of reference.  When they play "Ocean", they have no idea what they're playing.  Oh, I don't mean D, F, G -- I mean, they don't know what "Ocean" can be.  Was.  It didn't have to be the Velvets to be good.  Any number of musicians could have tuned into that vibe.  Hell, the great "Ocean" outtake on "Fully Loaded" just sounds like vintage Pink Floyd, anyway -- so why couldn't this disparate crowd of prog-rockers get into it?

"I Can't Stand It"?  Without the intense broken-down syncopated strumming Sterling Morrison provided, what was even the point?  Oh, yeah:  Chick singers.  Wow.  A 1970s album with chick soul singers on it, that's fresh.

"Berlin":  Without access to bootlegs, I can only guess it took until 1978's "Take No Prisoners" for this song to mature.  Here, it's irritatingly mis-arranged.  It doesn't even sound like the torch song it professes to be.  It sounds like it's made out of wood.  Dry, cracked wood.

"Lisa Says":  This was NEVER a good song, are the rest of you crazy?  But at least the lyrics for the VU version had a hint of real pathos in it.  Here, Mr. Bettye merely whines that he's neither a "California fool" or a "Good-Time Charlie".  And Lou Reed, of all people, should not whine.  Ever.

"Wild Child" hints at what Reed's problem was.  Whereas he'd once been a spectator to extreme people and lifestyles, here he's reduced to gossiping with his friends about them.  Lou Reed would NEVER again be this pathetic!

"Ride Into the Sun":  Points to the band for actually providing some energy.  Lou's singing still sounds awful (hadn't "producer" Richard Robinson ever heard of reverb?!?) but at least he's having fun with it.

"Love Makes You Feel":  Again, better energy from the band, and a basically decent song. (I'm also convinced this one inspired the Smiths classic "The Boy With A Thorn In His Side").  Lou's lyrics again illustrate his lack of true inspiration:  "I'm forever drifting into dreams . . . such a sad affair, to always be drifting into air".  As if we didn't already realize it, Reed warns, "It's not the proper thing".  Thanks for clearing that up, Lou.  Now I know why you shot speed all those years:  YOUR DREAMS ARE BORING.

"I Love You":  Having heard all the available versions, I'm confident in saying this one always sucked.  Was no one brave enough to tell him?

 . . . and, um, any other songs that are on here.  They're no good, either.

Happily, I can say Reed never made a (non-Machine) album this awful, ever again.  Sure, "Mistrial" comes close, but at least it has the catchy finger-poppin' "No Money Down" on it.  And "Sally Can't Dance" at least has attitude.  However you rate 'em, it says something about the man that he came back from such a disastrous debut album as this.

reviewText:
I understand that Springsteen is no longer in his twenties and will no longer produce the type of music that made me a fan (i.e. "Born to Run" and "Darkness") but his age is no excuse for making albums this poor.  I know that he has obsequious fans who would give him 5 stars for recording an album of late night snoring, but how can anyone other than the most blind follower defend lines such as "He robbed a bank in his diapers and his little bare baby feet" (sang in earnest no less) and "As the evening sky turns blue, a dream awaits in aisle number two"?  The former is from "Outlaw Pete, a song that the Chicago Tribune called a "genre exercise that ultimately feels silly".  I couldn't put it any better myself.

I realize that Springsteen is trying to replicate the melodic overtures and production aesthetics of Brian Wilson, but the problem with that is obvious; he is not Brian Wilson.  This is shown again and again in melodies whose attempts at being adventurous simply evince the man's lack of creativity in this style.  Though the sound on this release is much clearer than "Magic" it is still muddy and warrants the dismissal of Brendan O'Brien.

The two bright spots on the release are the last two numbers, "The Last Carnival" and "The Wrestler", but by the time one finally gets to them they are not enough to salvage your listening experience.

I'm not sure how to fix things for ya' Bruce, but I do know one thing for sure: Whoever was responsible for that contrived inner sleeve photo of you lying in the yellow field feigning sleep needs to be gotten rid of.  Talk about pretentious!

reviewText: It is my sad news to report to you that Mike Patton is not perfect.  He came down from Mount Olympus to give us a couple of solo efforts.  I now realize the emperor has no clothes.  This is the man who gave us Mr. Bungle, Fantomas, Faith No More, and he accentuated the Dillinger Escape Plan, Lovage and Tomahawk. It had escaped my attention that there were solo discs out there, and with this incredible genius I knew to expect the unexpected.  People talk about their unending love of Elvis, and I never understood how anyone could become so fixated on one artist with so much beautiful music out there...until I progressed beyond the great Faith No More to become a Patton head.  Now I am the one who basically gets mocked for becoming so fixated on one artist.  If you haven't heard the incredible Bungle alums Disco Volante or California; if you haven't heard the three stupendous Fantomas albums or any of the side projects mentioned above you will never regret the ride I hope these words are sending you on, but the road ends there.  My friends and I have an ongoing joke that Clapton and Petty could basically fart into a mic for 40 minutes and get three stars from major magazine publications, and the same holds true for the reviewers who give Patton's solo projects or Maldoror more than two stars.  I understand that experimentation for experimentation's sake can be honorable and noteworthy for the essence of daring, but these projects are not. If you are totally unfamiliar with Patton go in this order Faith No More>>Lovage>>Tomahawk>>Mr. Bungle>>Dillinger Escape Plan with Mike Patton>>Fantomas.  I'd say that 13 of these 16 albums make it into my top 50.

Juicy J might make a good guest appearance or group member, but he is not made to be a solo artist.  I didn't expect a lot of talent from Juicy J, since he only knows like 2 rhyme schemes, but I was expecting the talented people who seem to want to work with him, to carry this album.  Sadly, there is just too much Juicy J to drown out.  Besides every single verse having the same da da da da, dada or Dada, dada, da, da rhythm,  he is unable to rap any faster than one would normally speak. In fact, he actually raps slower than that.  These were things I already knew and expected from Juicy J, but with Wiz being one of the executive producers, I thought there was a chance of him rubbing off on Juicy.  No such chance.  It blows my mind that Wiz wants to work with him on so many projects.  Yes, I know we grew up with Juicy J when he was in 3 6 Mafia, so he's somewhat of a legend, but his lack of talent is ridiculously obvious.  Every single featuring artist out raps him on this album, with the exception of Project Pat.  Unfortunately, the featuring artists' parts are too short, then its right back to Juicy, just when you thought the song might be getting better.
I know theres a fair amount of repetitiveness in hip hop, but this album takes it to the extreme.  Repeating the same phrase over and over, isn't the only way to create a hook, and its just plain lazy, if you're doing it on every song.  It was embarrassing how much better Yelawolf was on  "Gun Plus a Mask", but his part was short, and the song couldn't be saved. That particular  song, encourages broke people to commit home evasion, straight glorifying robbing people of things they worked hard for....no joke.  I personally have had my home burglarized.  It was a nightmare filing my homeowners claim, because I didn't have receipts or serial numbers. I had to move in with family temporarily, until I could get a new place. And in the end my insurance company raised my $500 deductible, to $1000, so if I'm burglarized again, I'm automatically out a grand. That doesn't even include how violated you feel. .
Trey Songs and Wale do manage to break through all the trippin' Juicy's doing on this album, and make a high quality song with "Bounce It".  However, the subject matter is the same old, same old: doing drugs and using women.  In fact, every song, except for the home invasion theme song, is about drugs and sex, and the lyrics follow suit.  "Bounce It" was so much better than the other songs on the album, it made me think Maybach Music came in and produced that song themselves, to ensure they aren't associated with a crappy song. I felt the same way about Justin Timberlake's feature,  "The Woods".  I guess you have to expect his material to be drugs and sex, since 3 6 Mafia became a success using the very same M.O.  Still, there is very little creativity on this album.
Justin Timberlake also saves the song, "The Woods", later in the album.  And "Bands A Make Her Dance" with Lil' Wayne and 2 Chainz is very catchy, but I've already heard it a thousand times. Wiz is on two songs, but neither of them are of Wiz quality.  The album actually makes me wonder how much input Wiz actually had, because he is capable of amazingness, and Stay Trippy is far from amazing.  He may be the youngest producer on this, but he's certainly the most talented.  This is one of the worst albums I've heard this year. .

Listening to "Ironic" reminds me that Morrissette misunderstands the meaning of the word. Those reviewers here who recommend this product are doing the reputation of Everest Records as a top notch audiophile label during the golden age of early stereo, untold damage. I can only assume they are either stone deaf or are generalising the favourable impression they have gotten from respectable reissues on Vanguard or Classic Records, where the transfer to CD (or even SACD and DVD-A) has been achieved via the original master tapes and 35mm film masters, lovingly restored electronics and original playback equipment, by 16 bit or 20 bit SBM to the highest professional standards - not the crock of shXt we have presented in this product.

It is extremely aggravating to witness the investment in time and money, and the sheer enthusiasm, of such figures as Seymour Solomon of Vanguard, Bernie Grundman of Classic Records, to say nothing of the founders of the Everest line back in 1958, Bert Whyte and Harry Belock, undermined by yet another generation of rip off artists such as this crew based in the Netherlands.

An insult to the history of recorded sound. Not worth the trouble even if they were giving it away! Rubbish!

If you want this performance - and you should because it is very good - look elsewhere, specifically at the Vanguard disc.

Neither the stereo or mono versions, show any great step forward in sonics, over the already available abysmal transfers to CD format. The cheesy outside cover speaks for itself in terms of the packaging. It also serves as a good clue to what can be expected inside. The included booklet is no prize either for that matter.

If negative stars were an option, they would apply here. For a catalogue of work, as much a keystone of my generation as this is, this shabby treatment shoud not be forgiven, much less patronized.

reviewText:
I'm rewriting this review because I thought the original review I wrote for this album was rushed and poorly thought-out.  Here's a better review for you folks.

After a few years, I decided to give this album another whirl, thanks to YouTube.  Even with a more open mind and digesting a wider array of music since my last encounter with this trite sonic material, I still think it's very bland.  At best, this is inoffensive music, at worst, this will put you on the verge of screaming in pain.

In a way, I liken Kenny G's "Breathless" to James Cameron's Avatar.  Both are largely inoffensive media that puts all effort into style over substance and have raked in far more cash than they deserved.  I still think it's crazy that this album has sold over 12 million copies.  Anyway, on to my review.

STYLE

Kenny G's style of jazz can be easily classified as either "smooth jazz" or "easy listening."  In essence, the formula for most of the songs on this album are softly-played saxophone with minimal to non-existent percussion and airy keyboards in the background.  Two of the tracks on this album like "By the Time the Night is Over" and "Even if My Heart Would Break" feature guest vocalists in an attempt to mix things up, but they do much more harm than good.

FORGETTABILITY/LACK OF SOUL

One of the ultimate problems with this album is that it's a very forgettable one, and that so many of the songs I hear on it feel interchangeable.  Also, I guess because of the fact that this is supposed to be easy-listening, I hardly felt any creativity or soul poured in any of the songs on here.

SONGS

I guess if I were to choose a song on here that I would say that I came close to liking, that would probably be "Alone."  Since I think of all the tracks on here, this one shows the most effort and even a little creativity by diversifying the instrumental compositions a little, mainly with the inclusion of tastefully-done acoustic guitar in the beginning.

The rest of the songs, however, are either very boring or worse, cringe-inducing.

I'm not joking, I've had trouble distinguishing songs like "The Joy of Life," "Forever in Love," and "End of the Night" since there's really nothing interesting in these songs for me to latch on to.  I sometimes think for music that's supposed to be "relaxing," I don't even think it succeeds at doing that.  Sometimes, Kenny G will come up with a melody that can make you unwind, but then he'll throw in a sax solo that will break the mood, and you'll come out annoyed.

The two soul-pop songs, "By the Time the Night is Over" and "Even if My Heart Would Break," really got under my skin, but not in a good way at all.  The former features Peabo Bryson with backing vocals by Michael Bolton, Diane Warren, and Andy Goldmark.  Their vocal contributions are some of the lamest, most trite I've ever heard in music.  I'm not joking that it's they type of music you'd hear during an afternoon soap opera, and it doesn't help that the lyrics themselves are dime-a-dozen relating to romantic cheese (the theme itself isn't what makes it generic and cheesy, but rather the execution).  The latter features Aaron Neville, and his contributions don't fare much (if any) better than Peabo's.  Thematically and aesthetically, it's not much different from "By the Time the Night is Over," so I can't really comment much further on it, except that it's soulless, annoying music.

PRODUCTION

Much like Avatar, the effort in this album seems to have went to the production values.  Everything comes in crystal clear, even the backing instruments to Kenny G's sax, so I guess that's a plus.

FINAL WORD

Don't waste your time and money on this Kenny G record.  If you want jazz that'll give you a myriad of emotions while giving you music with effort and soul put into it, check out these albums instead.

Miles Davis:  B*tches Brew
Allan Holdsworth:  Sand
John Coltrane:  Blue Train
Herbie Hancock:  Mr. Hands
Return to Forever:  Where Have I Known You Before

Leave "Breathless" (and all other Kenny G albums) on the store shelves.

Finally, it should be noted that the album cover is begging to be desecrated with a Sharpie.

If you're going to recycle the same ideas that have been run into the ground a million times already (going to "war", hustlin', ballin', etc...  you know, the "typical" southern rappers lyrical content) at least try to make it clever.

reviewText: One of the blackest days in Metal history has to have been when Rob Halford left Judas Priest. I remember listening to this thing when it first came out...and thinking, "Judas Priest was disbanded so Halford could do this thing???!!" Seriously...in place of the great melodies, the back and forth guitar work, the fantasic songwriting found on any Priest album....Halford is now fronting a band that plays 2 or 3 guitar chords as fast as possible, and that's it. No songwriting, Halford's unique vocals are wasted. I mean during the 90's we could have gotten 4 or 5 more Priest albums, I mean real Priest albums with the original frontman...instead we are left with this forgettable mess. "Blowout in the Radio Room" is really the only stand-out song on the disk....and that's because it sounds completely different from everything else on the album. Other than the one tune, there is no reason to subject yourself to this thing. After listening to this you will understand why "Fight" only lasted two albums.

reviewText:
Just as the members of Faith No More may be kicking themselves for inadvertently influencing nu metal, the guys from the Buzzcocks must be giving themselves concussions for spawning one of the worst genres of music ever created alongside hair metal: pop punk. The fact that 20 years ago that name alone would have been considered an oxymoron is only further proof that this is musical cancer. However, unlike, nu metal, which is dwindling, pop punk is still in full force. It dominates the music scenes of Southern California, Florida and parts of Canada, truly horrible.
Where to start? Ok, first of all the legions of mall punk, which includes the abortion-worthy Blink-182, Simple Plan, New Found Glory, Good Charlotte, Something Corporate, Sum 41 and the like, are virtually indistinguishable. I have trouble telling them apart! C'mon how can you swallow this? Image wise, these bands are made up of preppie surf jocks in Dickies and finely spiked hair who have gone through the entire cheerleading squad at their high school. You have to acknowledged the fact that these people would have been considered the antithesis of what punk was during it's inception. Then we come to the subject matter: My blonde ditzy girlfriend, my boredom in high school, acting "punk" at the mall with all my other Vans-wearing buddies, and venting about the lows of living in white suburbia....wow. I may not have grown up in the 60's but the Stooges' self titled album speaks worlds more on teenaged summer boredom than any of these idiots. It's almost as disturbing as Dashboard Confessional singer Chris Carrabba's obsession with highschool grabass romance at the age of 27! Get over it. And the music? Well, it doesn't deserve any description of it's lousyness. Punk isn't a genre known for musical ability but this has gone too far.
Most fans of this crap would cover their ears in pain at mere listen of Minor Threat or Black Flag's vicious onslaught, or be completely unsure of what to think of Refused's wide palette of artistic expression. Hell, I'm sure some are even dumb enough to wonder why Fugazi are considered punk when their members don't look like J Crew models. This is a great evil in the world today and it needs to stop. Every teen comedy, every surfing film, every California frat party is layered with the poison that is pop punk. Fight the power.

reviewText: The Real problem with this recording as it is with many B'way recordings of the last decade is the micro-managing sculpturing of the sound. The voices play at the same level whether whispering or projecting. And when they belt, like Elaine Paige does at the end of "I'm Still Here", the sound becomes pinched, thinning out as if only certain frequencies were allowed to be recorded. And then there's the air around them: I guess the engineers are judging everything by their readouts instead of their ears because the singers sound like they're in an acoustically dead room, there are no harmonics floating in the air, the voices seem to have less than twelve inches before they hit an invisible dead wall. This doesn't sound like live music, this sounds like a museum recording, which is a shame because this could have been a real keepsake recording. Digital seems to be the bane of Broadway Cast albums. I wish someone would do something about it.

reviewText:
There is a danger to giving, heaping, too much praise on one so young.  A lot to what DGG gives us is excellent sonics.  But, there is no depth and no real excitement to this or the Mahler 5th by Dudamel.  These performances sound (tempo, balance, etc.) like retreads of earlier performances by some truly great conductors.  One may think that these performances sound wonderful, and to a certain extent, they do.  But remember that Szell, Bernstein, Karajan, Svetlanov and so many others did not have the technology we have today.
Now, you have the LAPO making the same mistake they made with Salonen.  Think about it; is there really any outstanding recording that you can remember from Salonen/LAPO?  One that distinguishes itself from any others?  You would think that a fine orchestra like the LAPO would be recording 2 or 3 discs a season.  One would think that they would have learned from their mistake.  Salonen is a fine technician, but there was nothing original about his performances.
Dudamel is about 28.  He has not lived with these works long enough to warrant recording them this young.  DGG must be really desparate to broaden their conductor roster to take on this one.
label: negative

reviewText: Tori Amos' Strange Little Girls is an interesting concept. It is an album of cover songs. The songs are all originally performed by men and in most cases they deal with women poorly. Ms. Amos has covered unusual songs before like a quiet, acoustic version of "Smells Like Teen Spirit". The problem with Strange Little Girls is that in reversing the perspective of the songs from male to female, they loose their meanings and power. "New Age" is an old Velvet Underground song about using a woman for pleasure. Ms. Amos' version loses the callousness that the Velvet's were trying to convey. "'97 Bonnie & Clyde" is an Eminem song where he dumps his ex-wife's dead body in lake. It sung to his daughter and he tells of how he will always be there for her. By singing it from the mother's point of view, it lessens the frightening lengths that a father would go to keep his daughter and turns it into a lament. "I Don't Like Mondays" was based on a true story of a girl who snapped and shot up her school in England. The Boomtown Rats' original had a sense of gravity underneath the airy arrangement. Ms. Amos' version reduces the violence to a cartoonish nature and you never get to the core of the song. Ms. Amos gets points for the idea of the album, but she fails in the execution.

reviewText:
One eventually learns to appreciate good stand up comedy... the audience interaction, the timing of the jokes, the overall charisma of the stage personality, the perceptiveness of some of the things he or she has to say...

...and good stand up this ain't.  Having heard most of disc 2 of this little collection, I had a hard time understanding what the point was... The guy starts out with the "humorously vulger"--which is only humorous if you have the maturity of a four-year-old--and then goes on to ... kinda sorta say five or six jokes but stretch them out over a good half an hour by repeating himself.

So he's already lacking in a lot of what makes stand-up comedy interesting, but let's not forget that this guy has NO idea of comedic timing.  By the time he would finally get around to the punchline... and they were not that good to begin with... I had to stop listening because I was tired of him repeating the same one or two words as build-up.

He also seems to think that weird sound effects make for hilarious comedy.  Not so: they make for overdignified fart noises.  This is the guy who sat at the back of the room in elementary school making farting sounds with his hands and blaming it on the girl who sat next to him.  Oh sure, we all laughed, but not because it was funny.  We laughed because he had the daring to do it in front of the Big Adult Teacher and risk getting into real Trouble and being Sent to the Principal's Office.  The messed up thing is that he never did get sent... but see, this isn't elementary school anymore.  And while the guy has some ideas I've never heard before (spaghetti out of the fingertips powers), he doesn't really seem able to coax anything out of them.

I have to say I did chuckle a couple of times, but they were always in expectation.  When he mentions relationships, or "that creepy guy you always know..." and those various staples of stand-up.  However then he'd go on being... him... and I was just left flat and disappointed.

--PolarisDiB

It's sad that CD singles don't really exist anymore, because several of the singles from this album have had promotional releases loaded with dance mixes--and I was HOPING some of those mixes might end up on this collection. Particularly mixes of You & I, since it hit #1 on the billboard dance charts--but most definitely not with any of the dreary mixes included here.

What we get is a predominantly experimental collection of dubs with barely any vocals. There are a few thumping dance beats thrown in that make you try to convince yourself that the particular mix makes the CD worth the purchase, but you soon realize that you'd much rather listen to the actual flawless version from GaGa's album. reviewText:
Made in CAN in 2001, Serial# 5-32320-2, Playing Time 73:32
Let me first say that my rating is not for the music, it's for the item as a whole. Why? Here you go: Syd Barrett only released 2 albums, both in 1970: "Barrett" (9 tracks selected here), and "The Madcap Laughs" (7 tracks selected here). Then, in 1988, the record company released "Opel", a collection of alternate takes (4 tracks selected here). As a "bonus", we get 1 track from the "Peel Sessions" CD, and finally, 1 previously unreleased track, "Bob Dylan Blues".
If you're avidly following SB's material, you probably already have 1992's "best of" compilation entitled "Octopus"; you might even have the "expanded" editions of the albums, which contain numerous bonus tracks, or the 3-in-1 box of these expanded albums called "Crazy Diamond".
So you want to buy this for the 3:14 "Bob Dylan Blues" track? Well you should if you're a collector; if you're new to Syd Barrett (either because he was in Pink Floyd, or simply because you've seen references about him), get either of his "official" albums, preferably in their "expanded" format, or go crazy and grab "Crazy Diamond": a complete discography in a single purchase!
label: negative

reviewText:
In a pop world dominated by prefabricated singers, plastic songs, or artificial appearances, Jessica Simpson has somehow always fallen by the wayside. It's hard for me to think of a more vanilla artist than Simpson, and it's a testament to her sheer blandness that the rest of America seems to have agreed with me, relegating her to the general pop background. When an artist is better known for their ignorance of tuna, you can be sure they are fairly irrelevant.

And so this entirely undistinguishable career of Christian pop and faux-gospel now brings us to Simpson's country experiment, Do You Know. Surprisingly there is no question mark to this album, as in Do You Know?, no question as to whether Simpson's Carrie Underwood-impression succeeds or fails. One listen is really all it takes; opener booty-call anthem "Come On Over" is about as generic as you can get in a genre that is nearly as fake as Simpson's previous arena, cheerfully bouncing along on a twangy guitar line and proclaiming "I need you now, I need you bad / I need you baby lookin' just like that." So it was these seductive longings that kept Tony Romo away from his teammates last season.

"Remember That" is your typical country-girl empowerment anthem in the vein of Underwood's "Before He Cheats," but lacking the fire of that admittedly guilty pleasure. The Simpson family has never produced any extraordinary singers of songwriters (just ask Ashlee), and Jessica's voice is mostly operating within one mode throughout Do You Know, from yearning note-stretching balladry on "You're My Sunday" to uh, more note-stretching country angst or declarations of love on "Still Don't Love Me," or "Still Beautiful," or pretty much any choice. The album's obvious highlight is the closing title track featuring Dolly Parton. When the two duet, it's almost painful to note the differences between the wannabe and the queen. Did I know that this record wouldn't be anything special? Sadly, yes.
label: negative

reviewText:
Unfortunately Kelly Rowland is another victim of the current trends in the U.S. Music Industry, specifically a victim of Universal Music and now departed executive Sylvia Rhone. For the past 3 years (2 or which she didn't have a record label after being dropped by her former label Columbia for low record sales of her 2nd CD Ms. Kelly) Kelly Rowland has recorded some memorable and catchy songs such as When Love Takes Over, (a huge worldwide hit), Choose (w Ne-Yo) and It's the Way You Love Me all with David Guetta for his CD One Love. More recently she was featured on another great song What a Feeling with Alex Gaudino (this song isn't on the CD, probably due to licensing issues). These songs were catchy, melodic and memorable. Well except for the Red One produced Down for Whatever (which most likely should be the 1st single in Europe)this collection of songs lacks melody and hooks that stays in your head. Today the music industry wants to turn what might be great songs into "urban music" with gratutious use of rappers on songs. Kelly falls into this trap here a few times using Li'l Wayne, Big Sean etc on songs. Recently Rowland said in an interview that she could include many types of styles for her fans who want Urban, Dance and Ballads. Not a good idea. She would have been better off to fuse urban and dance more like artists such as Chris Brown, David Guetta in the past and the Black-Eyed Peas. I expected that after the failure of Ms. Kelly, an urban-oriented project, Rowland would have taken her music in a different direction. I guess not. This CD lacks identity and seems to reflect Kelly's ongoing problem as a solo artist. In this recent interview she seemed to be trying to satisfy different fan requests instead of choosing her own musical identity/path and the music here reflects that problem.

As a result,  this CD lacks cohesion, is cluttered with too many different musical styles and leaves a person not wanting a 2nd listen. There is an A-list of writers and producers but many seem to lack the ability to write a catchy or memorable hook. The one David Guetta track Commander I believe is one of his worst songs. The chorus seems awkward and forced, unlike When Love Takes Over and What a Feeling (not a Guetta song) which are both glorious, lush and beautiful. Rodney Jerkins continues to turn out B-side type songs and is a mere shadow of the producer who had amazing songs in the mid to late 1990's and into the early 21st century (e.g., the songs recently done for Britney Spears CD Femme Fatale). Rico Love helped to craft a few songs here and they go nowhere despite Kelly touting him as "a genius". The hit song Motivation is included but again the song has no melody and I guess that's what urban music is about today. On a positive note, the artwork is beautiful and well done. The word on the internet is that when Kelly releases Here I Am in Europe and the U.K. later this year it will be a different version. I will wait and check that CD out and skip this one.

I've never been able to tolerate the 45 version ever since.

None of these other tracks are terribly great.  "Big City Miss Ruth Ann" by Gallery, "Daisy a Day" by Jud Strunk (what kind of name is that?), and "Tell Her She's Lovely" by El Chicano.  I could do without all these.

"My Maria" by B. W. Stevenson is still a popular playing one hit wonder, and though it charted pretty low, I really do like Albert Hammond's "The Free Electric Band."  This track is a great example of how Rhino can surprise us sometimes.  So, all and all, this disc is still a keeper to me, not only because I need to keep all the volumes because I'm a compulsive completist, but because it has "The Morning After" by Maureen McGovern.  I don't know why this song is important to me, but it is.  And "Funny Face" is easily forgettable.  I think Donna Fargo's voice was a little strange.  She definitely had a backwoods country kind of voice.

The best song of all on this volume is "Uneasy Rider" by The Charlie Daniels Band.  I love this song as I do with many of Charlie Daniels songs.  His greatest hits album "A Decade of Hits" is one of my favorite greatest hits collections.

So, as you can see, Volume 11 is pretty weak to me compared to the fabulous selections on volumes ten and twelve.  I'm glad this crappy stuff stayed together on this one CD instead of tainting the appeal of the other volumes.

And in the case of the marvelously talented vocalists Robert Plant and Alison Krauss, both the effort and the result is "NOT MUCH."

The music was chosen by someone else (T-Bone Burnett), and they may have had a chance to rehearse it a couple of times before laying down the tracks in the studio (probably separately, I suspect). Despite the superb credentials of the backing musicians, the fact that this is not and never will be a unified group is all too evident.

Everything about "Raising Sand" screams "artificial." It's a lightweight confection, concocted in the studio. But fancy engineering can't disguise the fact that neither Krauss nor Plant were really into the music, or even that familiar with it. Their expertise allowed them to fake their way through passably, but the absence of passion and live performance experience with it cannot be disguised.

Take a pass on "Raising Sand." Albums like this are the reason why CD sales are crumbling. Somebody is exploiting us here to raise some quick bucks by trading on famous names.

Then they disappeared. Fans wondered when we would ever hear from the band again. In 1986, we got Third Stage. More of that Boston sound. After and 8 year hiatus, Boston delivered again. We were happy and anxious for Boston Part 4.
It would be another 8 year in 1994 when Walk On is released. By now many fans have forgotten the band. Brad Delp and Barry Goudreau are gone, although Delp does contribute on the title track Walk On. Still the sound is there although changed and it is a very enjoyable album/CD.
In 2002, another version of Boston appears ... call it Boston 4.1. The sound is different. Its been another 8 years. It sounds like a CD made by a battle of the bands group, and not even the winner! reviewText:
It seems at the dawn of the new millenium we get a three greatest hits packages to the two most important bands in the history of rock'n'roll: Led Zeppelin and The Beatles.  With 1, we get 27 of the Fab Four's number one hits, all on one disc.  The funny thing is, it went to number one in a music scene dominated by Korn, Limp Bizkit, and other similarly uninspired or dreck bands (me, I prefer to stick with a little-known band in the US though they're huge in the Netherlands called Nevermore.  Check them out, they're great, hail from Seattle).  1 had a little criteria about it to defeat any arguments of tracks that should have been: its a collection of their number one hits, and quite generous at that -- clocking in at almost 80 minutes.  Also, The Beatles were birthed during a time when if you DID NOT play the singles game you were sunk.  Did Chuck Berry ever do a full album?  I don't know . . . if he did, it was probably just a collection of singles thrown together.
With this collection there's not that criteria of biggest selling or number one singles, and why?  Well, Peter Grant (Zep's manager) decided not to play the singles game, making it an album oriented art-form.  If you had to make a compilation disc of all the singles Led Zeppelin released, it'd be mighty slim pickings, though they did release a few singles.  So we have Led Zeppelin doing some really stellar albums, releasing no compilations until the mighty box set of 1990 (which, btw, is the best selling box set ever).  In 1993, the Boxed Set 2 shows up, catching all the stray tracks that have slipped through the cracks with the first one.  This is how this listener came to know Zeppelin, and to be honest I own only two of their albums, HOUSES OF THE HOLY and UNTITLED (not counting BBC Sessions), though I've listened to dubbed tapes of them. Although it may seem shocking to Zepheads, the first box set does a marvelous job staying true to the album spirit of Zeppelin, while the second one just is a necessity, though I like quite a few of the songs on that better than some of the material making the first box set.
That's two box sets.  But wait, there's more.  The Remasters with an interview disc thrown in there for good measure, and then a Complete Studio recordings with a reworked CODA (which I wish they'd release separately, and throw in "Girl I Love" and "Something" from BBC Sessions).
It just strikes this listener as odd that there's  been such a proliferation of these compilations when LZ's purpose has been album oriented rock.  It seems Page is trying to make up for lost time by over-releasing the Zep catalogue.  People may try to argue its a way to snag new listeners.  That's certainly true for The Beatles' disc, but with this it just strikes me as redundant.  There are several key songs missing throughout these two albums as well*, and the selections that did make it onto these discs simply don't get nearly as much radio play as a lot of other tracks.  Some would say by putting these lesser known songs (defined as heard on the radio regularly) it will help others go to the original albums.  But that goes against what a greatest hits package is supposed to be, doesn't it?  And considering the band, they used to want them to go to the original albums anyway
And while some may argue UNTITLED stands as their best work, there is an over-emphasis on this, though its hard to argue with their (or Page's) selections.  "Rock and Roll" has always been the most overrated song on that, and they should have eliminated that and put in "Going to California" instead.  And while "When the Levee Breaks" is a great recording, perhaps it shouldn't be on a greatest hits disc, considering all the tracks they did leave off that DO get lots of radio play (Ramble on, Heartbreaker, Living Loving, Hey Hey, etc).  Hey Hey should have been included just to have it in a relatively cheap package, and to this listener it stands as one of their best songs (listening to it now).
Bottom line: these albums are just product, and failed product at that.  By now, either you like Led Zeppelin or you don't, and no one will really care about these two albums anyway.  Even as greatest hits albums they don't work, because of the track selection includes material receiving little radio play while neglecting tracks that DO get a lot of radio play.  Only thing that makes these good are the album covers.  Other than that, ignore them, they're useless.  I'd have a little more sympathy if they did have their bigger radio songs.
*This is a list of songs that may qualify as "Should have beens".  The ones with the double asterisks are the ones I feel should have definitely put on instead of some of the other selections (such as "Since I've Been Loving You" and "Achilles' Last Stand) and get a lot of radio play.  You'll notice I have half of HOUSES on there, simply because those tracks do get a lot of radio play, and since this is aimed at the causal fan things like "No Quarter", which is a great song, and "Houses of the Holy" and "Trampled Under Foot" which don't get near as much as these do and should have been cut.  The other selections show my own tastes in the Zep catalogue.

Now, when I first heard that Oakey had included a slew of Dead Can Dance and Vangelis tracks on this particular CD, I was intrigued.  Had he remixed them?  That was the only possible explanation because otherwise (given their positions within the mix) they would completely halt any and all momentum.  And wouldn't you know, that's exactly what happened?
Granted, it's still a rather gutsy maneuver to veer so far into left field and mess with the expected format.  Unfortunately, other than a headache, this CD really didn't have anything new to offer.  Certainly there were a few choice tunes to be found on this mix, but any value they might have had was completely lost by the fact that Oakenfold seems to have staunchly refused to mix them.  Sure, a few tracks got beatmatched here and there, but then he would bring the tempo to a grinding halt, to get all "deep" on us with a touch of Vangelis or Dead Can Dance.  Consequently, there really isn't anyway to tell how Oakenfold would go from something like Tone Depth's "Majestic" into amoebaassassin's "Piledriver."
And as an added annoyance -- please, no one wants to hear sample after wanky sample of tottering, all-too-wealthy club goers flying from London to New York "especially for tonight" or any of the other (...) that breaks up the music.  "The music building gradually, it gradually builds..."  Yes honey, we know.
Overall, "Another World" missed its mark by miles.  Fortunately, Oakenfold very nearly redeems himself with the "Travelling" mix (of Australian release) which contains many of the same tracks but without the wanky nod to Vangelis or the self-referential samples (well... except for that on burst).  So if you feel the itch to purchase this, do yourself a favor and pick up "Travelling" instead -- more music, more longevity.  (But probably not much more.)

reviewText:
This compilation completely misses the point of ELO.

I've casually disliked this band for about 25 years, so I should know. They weren't real. Or significantly unreal, for that matter. Yet there was a time in the mid-to-late seventies when ELO meant something to me. When the songs and I were somewhere between boy and man . . .

"Live at Winterland 1976" shows that they were a studio band at heart and that Jeff Lynne wasn't a singer so much as a good in-the-studio vocals (and whatever else) manipulator.

Still, when in that studio and left to his own devices, manipulating whatever, wanking whenever, isolating the flotsam amid the gism (sorry, jetsam), and floating on his personal dream of music, he--like any boy in the same situation--sometimes hit the jackpot.

However messy, the first time was one of the best, as sometimes happens to the more fortunate of us. 'Do Ya' proved he was experienced, or experienced enough to convincingly sound like he was. Link Wray, Ray Davies and Dave Davies (with Jimmy Page looking over his shoulder), Lou Reed, Pete Townshend, and others could have cited paternity, but they had their own woodpiles to contend with.

Lynne really broke out in a sweat with "Eldorado": "A Symphony By The Electric Light Orchestra." A "symphony," no less. Although it expressed only too well the source of his inspiration, as well as the limitations of his performance ability, 'Can't Get It Out of My Head' is as romantic as a boy can get. 'Boy Blue' was the natural and, eh, deserved follow-up.

Lynne listened to his own tune and heard himself revealed . . . He wrote his best album as a result. "Face the Music" he did, and as many reviewers will tell you, dark it was. Yet that very personal confrontation, coupled with honest adolescent feeling (cf. 'Evil Woman'), produced an album of songs that a romantic seems to come up with only once in his lifetime (girls know better). 'Fire on High,' 'Waterfall,' 'Poker,' and 'One Summer Dream' are stand-out tracks, but, incredibly, the others are about as memorable. The story of a boy's night out.

Having revealed his soul, he didn't know what to do with it, so he sold it. "A New World Record" cashed in, with the best song, 'Do Ya,' being anything but new, or living. (He'd already did, I'd thought.) A trivial album covering up lost innocence with as much hoopla as the 20th century, or Leni Riefenstahl, could muster.

His soul gone, with nowhere to go, Lynne did what he knew best. He went back to that there studio, shut out the world, and wanked as hard as he could for a new revelation. And he was granted one: Home might as well be outer space, and rainy days are nice. In perhaps his best song of all, 'Summer and Lightning,' he's all alone, with no one else to mess things up. The title of the album, "Out of the Blue," isn't quite as honest as "Golden Shower of Hits" (Circle Jerks) would have been, but for an olio of boyhood remembered, the songs have their charms.

And that was it for the next few decades. There really was nothing left for Lynne to say.

(He sure did help other guys express themselves, though, boy howdy: 'Free Fallin',' 'Got My Mind Set On You,' 'Handle With Care,' 'You Got It' . . .)

"All Over the World: The Very Best of Electric Light Orchestra" includes none of the above-mentioned songs, except for 'Evil Woman.'

Instead, you get 'Xanadu' without Olivia Newton-John.

At least Rush made Xanadu seem important. But then Neil Peart had read Coleridge's poem, even if he is Canadian . . . Peart, that is. Not Coleridge. Who's British. Took laudanum, an opium derivative.

Speaking of which . . . Afghanistan is producing bumptious crops of the stuff these days. Flesh and blood must make good fertilizer. Perhaps Lynne could take a trip and refuel his personal fantasies. If you can't get out of your head, you might as well stay there. Enjoy the view. Write songs for the boy in so many of us. I'll relive my youth, or the part of it that I can half remember, with the tunes he's capable of writing--I'll give Lynne some credit. Which, really, is saying a lot.

And we're back to where we started.

reviewText:
An existential sci-fi drama written and directed by Duncan Jones (formerly known as Zowie Bowie, and son of rock icon David Bowie), Moon stars Sam Rockwell as Sam Bell, an employee of Lunar Industries who is coming to the end of his three year stint working at a gas production facility on the moon. As the sole employee of the lunar station, and with limited communication possible with Earth, Sam spends most of his time conversing with GERTY (voiced by Kevin Spacey), an intelligent super-computer programmed to attend to his needs. However, after Sam is knocked unconscious in accident, he awakens to find that he is no longer alone on the moon, and slowly begins to realize that his world is not what he thought it was.

The music for Moon is by the increasingly popular English composer Clint Mansell, who over the past few years has attracted positive press and numerous fans for his work with director Darren Aronofsky on scores such as The Fountain and The Wrestler. I have never bought into the hype about Mansell, having consistently found his music to be cold, mechanical, themeless, ambient nightmares which stand completely at odds with everything I love bout film music. Unfortunately, Moon is much of the same. Predominantly electronic with occasional interludes from a solo piano or a small string ensemble, the Moon scores groans and whines its way through 55 interminable minutes, with virtually no redeeming qualities; it was all I could do to sit through this score a couple of times to write this review.

The one track of note is "Memories (Someone We'll Never Know)", in which Mansell writes a simple piano theme filled with soothing chords which, despite remaining on the austere side, is a major improvement over pretty much everything else on the score. When it picks up a solo cello accompaniment in the second half of the cue, the effect is quite pretty. There are a few other moments in which Mansell introduces the piano; in the opening "Welcome to Lunar Industries", and later in "We're Not Programs, GERTY, We're People" for example, the piano acts as a kind of recurring metronome. There is also an unusual, dreamlike music-box theme in "The Nursery" that is unexpected. However, for the most part, the score is a nightmare, a thematic wasteland that just drones on and on, offering virtually no melody, no harmony, and nothing remotely tangible with which to connect.

As many people may know by now, Sony was recently caught with egg on their face when a security specialist found out that a recently purchased CD (Van Zant: Get Right With The Man) from Sony music not only installed DRM software (digital rights management, to limit and outright prevent copying music to certain devices), but it did so in such a sneaky way that it hid itself entirely from Windows, and opened the system up to security issues such as viruses.

This CD has the same copyright protection, called XCP. When installed, Sony hijacks your computer and installs custom software which:

1) Hides itself entirely from Windows by installing as a rootkit

2) Hides itself in such a manner that any files begining with $sys$ are also hidden. For example, if you install the XCP copy protection software on your machine, and rename "document.doc" to "$sys$document.doc" it then becomes invivisble to you forever.

3) Installs its own custom CD-Rom drivers to hijack your system. It also sneakily names these drivers "Plug and Play Device Manager" to seem as if it's a part of Windows. Trying to delete these drivers manually will disable your CD-Rom drive entirely.

4) Offers no uninstall option until you manually contact Sony

reviewText:
The sticker on the outside of this vinyl package states 'pressed on 180gram audiophile quality vinyl'

Don't let that trick you into purchasing this. This is a terrible master. It was done by Vlado Meller, who's mastered every Chili Pepper's album since 1999's 'Californication'. All of which have suffered from some of the worst mastering of all time. They're so loud they're clipped into the red. So good luck hearing any clarity or definition in his mastering through the waves of digital distortions shredding your ear drums.

Clearly by 2006, John Frusciante (he seems to have developed an increased interest in sound quality as years have progressed, using analog to record his solo ventures and mastering his 2009 solo album 'The Empyrean' very dynamically, which was a far cry from his Chili Pepper's world) had enough and Steve Hoffman was hired to master John's swan song, 'Stadium Arcadium' for vinyl. Steve Hoffman did a great job and the vinyl sounds rich and detailed, with lots of definition between instruments and most importantly the bass isn't drowned out in waves of static digital distortions.

But now with John gone, Warner Music have just resorted to having the lame, the deaf, the terrible, the anti music himself, Vlado Meller, make a vinyl master of this album to cash in on the vinyl sales boom.

What you're presented with when you drop the needle onto the grooves of this vinyl is very treble heavy thin sound, with no definition, very sharp, muddy and brittle sounding, with mostly inaudible bass, which in my opinion is sacrilegious considering the talents of Flea. It's not a pleasant listen and hurts your ears more than the commercially released loudness war CD.

I bought this vinyl after downloading a FLAC vinyl rip of a torrent site. I thought maybe i downloaded a bad rip. But nope.

Honestly Warner, enough is enough, fans have suffered through 4 RHCP albums mastered by Vlado Meller! What the f__k? Do you even listen to the music before you release it? reviewText:
I admit I was predisposed to dislike the album before I even listened.  That may seem unfair, but my predisposition was based on the fact that, with the exception of a few standout tracks, the past four Queensryche albums have been abyssmal.  As far as this album is concerned, Overall, I am a bit surprised.  Frequency Unknown is not as bad as I thought it would be, and there are more moments that I like than I would have thought.  But the ideas are not fleshed out well at times, the vocal melodies are frequently half-baked, and the vocal delivery is just outright painful and bad most of the time.  But most of all, this sounds like a Geoff Tate solo effort and not like something that should have the Queensryche name attached.  The three biggest problems I have with the album can be summarized as follows:

1.  Everything sounds rushed and underdeveloped.  There are some good ideas and some good melodies.  But nothing about the album feels like any amount of care or thought was put into making it sound and feel like a finished product.  Most of us know the facts behind how this album was put out.  We know that it was a rush job.  The problem is, it SOUNDS like a rush job, whether we are talking about the poor mix, the disjointed "cut-and-paste" sound of of the songs, or what have you.

2.  The singing is atrocious.  Geoff Tate was a key influence of mine, both in terms of getting into singing in the first place, and also in terms of pushing the envelope in my singing.  However, his singing has so badly deteriorated that it is painful to listen to.  Tate sounds strained, nasal, and off-key more often than not, and is far and away the weakest link on this album.  This is not a matter of personal taste.  He is objectively singing incorrectly and in a way that detracts from any positives these songs might have.  And that is a shame bacause, as mentioned above, some of these songs truly show promise and could have been decent.

3.  The album does not have the "Queensryche sound."  I do not mean to try to "put the band in a box."  One of the things I have always appreciated about Queensryche is that they have always changed and grown their sound.  Even in their earliest history, each album sounded very different from anything else in the catalog.  And yet, there was always a trademark complexity and depth to their sound.  I felt that Slater finally managed to capture that a bit on American Soldier.  However, with a few exceptions, it has largely been missing for several albums, and this latest Geoff Tate solo effort mislabeled as "Queensryche," that trend continues.

This is hands-down the worst Black Sabbath album ever. It starts on a sour note (oil and water have nothing on Ice T and Tony Martin for not mixing well), ends on a sour note (the only good thing about "Kiss Of Death" is that it means this horrible album is almost over), and has nothing but clinkers in between. Even the awful album Born Again has the saving grace of the excellent "Zero the Hero" and the so-so "Trashed."

There is not a single track on Forbidden that even qualifies as mediocre. You can almost hear something resembling good music under the mess that is "Sick and Tired," but trying to enjoy it is like trying to dig a penny out of a dumpster. "Get a Grip" tries to recycle the guitar riff from the aforementioned "Zero the Hero," but fails miserably. And tracks like "Shaking Off The Chains," "Can't Get Close Enough," and "Rusty Angels" will leave you feeling like you ate something you should have thrown away.

The god-awful production makes for an exhausting listen, and would have completely ruined the album had there been anything to ruin in the first place.

Forbidden is a joke, but it certainly isn't funny. If you want to hear some post-Ozzy Sabbath, pick up anything with Dio (Heaven and Hell, Mob Rules, or Dehumanizer). Barring that, at least get Eternal Idol or Cross Purposes, both far better than this. Forbidden is strictly for completists.

reviewText: The single most appealing piece in "The Year of Living Dangerously" original soundtrack (notice the lower case) would surely be Vangelis's "L'Enfant."  This is the beautiful instrumental music that accompanies the love scene where Sigourney Weaver (Jill) walks through the rain to Mel Gibson's (Guy Hamilton's) office where she wordlessly confesses that she is overwhelmed by her feelings for him.  If you're buying "The Year of Living Dangerously; Original Motion Picture Soundtrack," you may naturally expect this keystone piece to be included, because it is, indeed, part of the original soundtrack, i.e. the music that accompanies the film.  Bad news:  It's not there.  The rest of the music, while interesting, could best be described as "incidental."  The astute consumer may notice that a part of the sleeve announces "Original Music by Maurice Jarre".  I was extremely disappointed.  This may be a Vangelis problem since the week before, I had purchased what was advertised as the "Bladerunner Soundtrack," and was similarly disappointed to find it was NOT the original soundtrack (nothing on the CD itself claimed to BE the soundtrack), but instead, some pieces that had been featured in the film along with some other pieces, all recorded by Vangelis on a separate occasion, and in my opinion, disappointing.  I now believe that Amazon has the obligation to notify the consumer on their website advertisement of this product that these albums are not what they seem, and most certainly to drop the "O.T.S." and the word "Soundtrack" from the "Bladerunner" album.

reviewText: Here is what happened in 1976. They were putting together the Traviata to end all Traviatas. It was all done, passed off by the artists and management. It was superb. Of course, Domingo wanted to do the cabaletta "O mio rimorso, o infamia", since it is usually cut. And of course, he would have preferred to do the high C at the end (since Pavarotti always did) ... but it was utterly unrealistic for him. So he ended on the lower C (middle C), which after all is the note Verdi wrote, so he didn't consider it a terrible crime. Then after it was all passed off, some middle-management dude with an only superficial knowledge of music, mildly lamented there was no high-C to compete with Pavarotti. Being 1976, the middle-management dude was wearing a polyester suit with a clip-on tie, and had recently switched from horn-rimmed glasses to wire-rimmed. One of the lower-tier electronic engineers (with no knowledge of music whatsoever), said yes, he could arrange that. The electronic engineer had a big frizzy perm, bushy sideburns, a striped shirt, and plaid pants. The voice and orchestra were on different tracks, he said, so he could make the one higher and re-paste it over the other, and it would be all fixed up. He had excellent intentions and tried to do a good job, just like the little old lady working on the fresco of Jesus in the village church. So for example, when he noticed Domingo had a short portamento or scoop from G down to C, and he couldn't recreate that movement upwards, he artistically replaced it with a little gulp sound. And to help cover that up he also made the high C come in a hair early rather than a hair late. Finally it was perfect so he gave a little kiss to the master tape and sent it off to be processed. Now, thousands of sets were manufactured, shipped, and sold before anyone at DG heard any complaints. The artists all have a busy schedule and not in the habit of listening to their own records after being published, and anyway, they had already signed off on them. There was even a contract stipulation that DG couldn't change anything, so who cares? The best approach would be pretend nothing had happened, just keep quiet about it and wait it out. OK, it has been over 40 years now. The conductor has passed away and the 3 leads are pushing 80. I would humbly suggest it's time DG fixes this disaster as a belated gesture of goodwill to this distinguished cast. And they could do so without crawling around on the cutting room floor and turning over 40-year-old dustbins looking for tape fragments. Here is all they have to do: just cut the cabaletta already! For the benefit of newcomers, or anyone who gives a hot doggie-doo-doo, the defective cabaletta starts on CD 1, track 11, time 0:40. And the computer-generated note is at 2:03. So all the remasterers have to do, or all the end-user has to do while listening, to save their sanity, is hit the 'Next' button exactly at 0:39. The effect of this will be to simply skip the mess-pile. Now, if you are a completist and you really want the cabaletta, IT IS ALREADY RUINED! If you still want it anyway, for completeness, IT IS NOT EVEN COMPLETE! Domingo only recorded one verse, out of two in the score. (Pavarotti recorded both verses and hit the high C with no problems, FYI ... get it there!) As mentioned, it is a standard cut anyway; the majority of Traviata recordings don't include it, at least such important ones as Toscanini, or Moffo/Tucker, or Callas, off the top of my head. So if Domingo didn't happen to include it, he's still in very distinguished company. You can't tell me that if Domingo, with his immense stature in the world of opera today, asked DG to make that cut in future reissues, they would refuse. No way. So ... please just do it. Then they will have a far-above-average recording of Traviata, without any apologies (other than 40 years of pain and suffering for opera lovers). And no longer something that sounds like a bad SNL skit ... Humbly submitted ...

reviewText:
What can I say - I almost crapped myself after hearing this album. It's important to note that Damo's talents are by no means limited to wetting beds in Dublin, or arguing with a old woman - this guy can warble with the best of them.

One thing you should know about me is that I absolutlely love Mr. Rice. He has the fuzziest chest and prettiest eyes. Hearing his silky voice makes all my needs in the world go away. If, musically speaking, we are all cows grazing contentedly in the pasture of pop music, then Damien Rice is the barefoot redneck who tips us over with his unique brand of songwriting. . He overshadows Fred Durst's limp attempt at penetrating the public consciousness with his impressive voice. Some have even compared his voice to that of a llama getting strangled. I personally think it sounds like four orangutans dropkicking a midget.

When this CD came out, it wasn't just a half-hearted re-release of mediocre songs from an equally mediocre and cheesy former grunge singer; it was a watershed moment for all of music. The "folk" music phase had just started to abate, and people were craving bizarre patriotic songs about freedom from a singer who wets his bed. And sure enough, Damien R. was there. And boy, did he deliver.

From the hands clapping on butt0cks of "Volcano" to the thumping didgeridoo of "Eskimo," each song is a rhythmic testament to the immortal talent of Damien Rice The musical notes challenge one's hearing to the point of wanting to be deaf, and we are all grateful for that challenge. The lyrics engage and confuse like a gorilla in a bear suit.

A few words must be said about Damien's remarkable singing style. Damien Rice fills his hairy chest with all the air he can inhale and then screeches it out like two chimps getting pinched by a treadmill. As he howls out his kettle whistle, his lips form the words of the lyrics so that he's actually "singing." You have to hear it to believe it.

He hoists up the flag of freedom for folk music like an Irish Bono, gesticulatin' and syncopatin' like an epileptic mongoose. And wait till you hear his voice. That dang thing sounds just like three ostriches getting hit by a cement truck. His trademark "hooting" during violin and guitar solos secures Rice's spot in pop music history.

reviewText: As a big fan of Progressive Rock or "Art Rock," whatever you want to call the subgenre of rock n roll that makes people think of Rush, Genesis, Tool, ELP, King Crimson, Yes, Pink Floyd, Soft Machine, etc, I was told by some friends of mine that this was the album for me that would be perfect for my growing music collection. Nothing could have been further from the truth. I could not have been more disappointed. Disc 1, while heavy is quite pretentious especially the opening sone "Glass Prison"; here we have just a bunch of solos strung together in between the opening and closing singing parts. It would have been better if the each solo were part of a different song. The Great Debate is annoying because of the news recordings that take away from the music because they are way too intrusive; also, the song is way too preachy. The other three songs vocally make me think of a heavy Dennis DeYoung but more annoying. Overall, Disc One sounds as if Styx had a grandchild with Emerson Lake and Palmer. While I like the latter, the combo is unlistenable (if that's a word). Disc Two is even worse: the opening overture sounds like Chritsmas music!!! It sounds like the Trans Siberian Orchestra not like Rock music at all. Moments of War Inside My Head and The Test That Stumped Them All are tolerable but not in their entirety. The Grand Finale is anti-climactic and boring. In all honesty, I'd rather listen to Jethro Tull and Styx and for the most part I really don't care for these either but they are much better in comparison. It is so bad, I immediately, after listening to each disc twice, took it out of I-tunes and placed the CD in a shoebox in my closet so it will not be near my CD collection at all--it doesn't deserve to hold a place there. It is that bad!!!

reviewText: This being one of the infamous releases that fall pretty far from anything Hendrix or his associates had a hand in should in and of itself raise a big red flag. Many of the tracks came out on Cry of Love which Hendrix was working on prior to his death and which was finished by Eddie Kramer and Mitch Mitchel in 1970. The Cry of Love versions are far more solid and probably show far more connection and accuracy coming from the hand of one of the original band members. That many of the tracks on Voodoo Soup were concoctions of the producer mixing and adding overdubs by musicians who never knew Hendrix is highly alarming. Some of the differences between tracks on Cry of Love and this CD are indeed striking. The one exception is Peace in Mississippi. (understood here to be the actual version Hendrix recorded with The Experience in 1968 and left unadulterated) Peace in Mississippi is astonishing and if you can't hear the anger, anguish, struggle , and rightness of the civil rights movement in this track than you aren't going to get any deeper meaning from any piece of music. If you can cop Peace in Mississippi some other way, do it and make sure you are not getting the Crash Landing version which is doctored by this producer. As for this CD, buy Cry of Love. That is my view on it.
label: negative

You can even hear distortion resulting from this in some songs. Look up "Loudness Wars" on Wikipedia. This mastering effort is firing all of the weapons.

If you want compilation albums that are not fighting the "Loudness Wars", try "30 Years Of Maximum R&B box set", "Meaty Beaty Big & Bouncy", "Who's Better Who's Best", or "Greatest Hits" (although it's pushed a little). Don't pick "Odds & Sods", it has the same compression problems in the CD remastering. You can also get good dynamic range mastering of the original album formats in the individual album CDs, except the MCA version of "A Quick One". This good individual album mastering exists at least up to "Who's Next". I don't know about albums released after "Who's Next".

"The most exciting fourth" David Hurwitz called this on Classics Today, on the strength of which I bought this. Well, I don't know about that, because all I can hear is orchestral playing so bad (mainly in the strings; some fumbled passages in the cellos are really quite embarrassing) that I can't listen past it to see if I can find any redeeming features. Was it Barenboim's relative inexperience as a conductor (he was 29 at the time of recording)? Were the team at Deutsche Grammophon flown in from Germany suffering from jet-lag? Didn't the Chicagoans take to Danny used as they were to and spoilt by Reiner and Solti?
The seventh fares better, although here too the strings are ragged (beginning and ending of phrases) and more than once there is uncertain intonation (the adagio at 13:37 is a case in point; the finale at 0:22 another), unworthy of a great orchestra like the CSO. With so many releases of both symphonies available there is really no good reason to buy this twofer, even if it comes ridiculously cheap. Barenboim fortunately mended his ways in Bruckner some twenty years later with the BPO on Teldec and although perhaps the interpretations seem to divide opinions, the playing of the Berliners is uniformly great.

reviewText:
First, let me say I love this album. Its beautiful, lovely, piquant, quirky, ripping, gripping, insane, rock n roll. Yeah! redgrevillea's review got it right when he mentioned this is art and the rest of the Pink Floyd albums are architecture in comparison. Its one of the few records from this time that has stood, and will continue to stand the test of time. It lives and lives up to it's reputation.

Fans of the later big budget corporate albums will be confused by this record. Seek corporate rock elsewhere you niny brains, there is plenty of that stuff out there. Tons of it. You are obviously in the wrong place.

Unfortunately, REALLY UNFORTUNATELY, this is a textbook example of how to screw a reissue up. Its hard to understand their decisions.

FIRST off leave off the best cut on the original album "See Emily Play" which is a psychedelic classic and maybe THE psychedelic classic of the era!!! DUH! ??? Its the first song on the original and sets the tone for what follows. SECOND change the order of the cuts putting the long instrumental cut that is more like later corporate Pink Floyd RIGHT IN THE MIDDLE... for no apparent reason??? I like Interstellar Overdrive. But it is probably the song that most original Pink Floyd fans will skip EVERY TIME and it shouldn't be right in the middle. Sid got it right the first time when he put it last. It works much better that way. The idiot who decided to reorder the songs is just that, an idiot. You ding dong, you know who you are.

The inclusion of out takes "Bike" and "Flaming" which are not on the original is a good thing. I wish they had included more out takes. There is certainly room for more of the songs from that era. Oh well I guess I'll just have to DOWNLOAD them if I want to hear them. Dumb. The original order should have been preserved and as many of the outtakes as they could fit should have been included at the END after Interstellar Overdrive, to differentiate them from the originals. If they had done that this would be a 6 star CD. The music is great despite the production.

One last thing. Syd's problems, contrary to popular UNINFORMED opinion, were NOT due to drugs. If they were, EVERYONE in Pink Floyd, most of their original fans, and a good percentage of this generation would have succumbed too. Think about it, 90% of the people who built the personal computer industry dropped acid and listened to music like this. Syd had organic mental disease. Every review that mentions that Syd was taken out by drugs should be suspect, because it doesn't take much insight to understand that's just TOTAL NONSENSE.

One star for this reason - so people who are searching might be able to find this, one of the few reviews that makes sense. However its still a great album. I'd want to own a vinyl original before I'd want this but if you don't have a turntable, then buy this and DOWNLOAD "See Emily Play." Maybe just download it all.

I've been listening to Madonna for a long time, and as a fan, I can truly say that her best days are behind her. Beginning with 2000's Music, there has been a slow, steady decline in the quality of her music. Don't get me wrong, "Music" has some great songs, "Don't Tell Me" is probably one of my favorites from Madge, and even "American Life" and "Confessions..." had some decent moments. But with "Hard Candy", Madonna hit a turning point, essentially making a joke out of herself in the process. Why would you, The so-called "Queen of Pop" need to have featurettes of stars that the younger generation adores? It would be because you are no longer relevant....

MDNA made my stomach turn from the moment I knew it was going to be released. Let's start with the fact that she has airbrushed the hell out of herself in the artwork (Google "Madonna un-airbrushed to get an idea of what she's really looking like these days), and used a concept she ripped off from another artist for the cover (google "Sergio Lagos, Solo"). Hmmmmmmm thats really innovative, to plaigarize someone else's ideas, then turn around and diss Gaga for doing the same. I am no Gaga fan, but let's face it: A lot of Madge's career has been a rip off in the first place...

The actual music contained is a waste of time. "Give Me All Your Luvin'" is garbage. Again, if Madonna was relevant, there would be no need for guest rappers and cutesy-baby talk lyrics. "Girls Gone Wild" is a joke. C'mon? You know its bad when you have to start ripping off stuff from your own back catalogue. It's basically a remix of "Act of Contrition" from "Like a Prayer" album with a bunch of other crappy lyrics tacked on. "Gang Bang", "Superstar", "I'm Addicted" are all notable for their awfulness. It's all eurotrash dance mix garb, which Madonna has played out for going on six albums now. This music is tailor made for people with absolutely no mind of their own who will buy anything that their "idol" throws at them, for the sake of commercial appeal. At 40, with "Ray of Light", this act was fresh and innovative. At 54, it's played out as hell and we need you to stop, Madonna. You can make so much money off of your name in other ways, I wish that you would stop believing that your music is one of them. Fund your daughter's career. At least people won't be barfing when they see her dancing around on stage in hot pants (hint, hint)

Maybe there are people out there who still buy Madonna's music. Good for you! Im just glad I didn't spend any of my own money on this mess. Madonna: Im glad your album tanked, im glad you had the biggest 2nd week sales drop in chart history. Maybe you can take the hint and spend more time with your plastic surgeon (Who btw made you look terrible!)

That's right, pushing boundaries. Comparisons were made between Berlin and Sgt. Pepper because both albums push the boundaries of studio music. These days artists can pretty much reproduce the studio sound live but in the 70s you still had your musical career split in two.
As you can imagine Berlin has a dark subject matter, the streets, the drugs, cutting wrists, all the things that give Lou Reed's lyrics that extra bit of realism, the feeling that the artist has personally experienced these things. It would be interesting to compare this album to something modern like Tom McRae's debut. 'The Bed' Reed sweed voices "What a feeling" and you can consider this kind of singing quite normal on the McRae album but there's no point to it, there's too much indulgence and avoidance on McRae's effort while 'The Bed' is simply about a fateful night where a woman cuts her wrists. It's the simplicity, the daring quality of Lou Reed's lyrics, that carries across the music.
The layering is very impressive and it was a brave decision for Reed to release it after the commercially successful Transformer. Berlin is like the complete opposite of Sgt. Pepper's hip wanderings. But never forget that it's just rock and roll.

reviewText:
Some absolutely HORRIBLE, murderous versions of some beautiful Bacharach music. Chryssie Hynde does ok with "Baby It's You" but destroys "Message To Michael" by breathing in all the wrong places.
Elvis Costello proves he understands and can sing Bacharach, but he doesn't have the vocal chords to pull it off pleasingly. "God Give Me Strength" and "This House Is Empty Now" would sound wonderful if sung by Dusty Springfield (one of his idols, and Bacharach's choice to sing the original versions of "The Look of Love" and "Wishin' & Hopin")...but Costello just doesn't cut it here.
What we learn from this CD and the live show it was recorded from, is that Burt Bacharach is not for everyone to sing. In the 60's we had Dionne, Dusty and Gene Pitney. In the 90's we have who? All Saints???
But luckily, as the CD progresses, Luther Vandross shows us the right way to sing Bacharach, with a beautifully luscious medley of "The Windows of the World" and "What The World Needs Now Is Love." (in 4/4 time versus the original 3/4)
Then, lastly, his mentor, Dionne Warwick, gives a virtual Bacharach singing lesson armed with her 40 year recording career and her over 20 top 40 hits with Bacharach. I hope the other performers took copious notes.
Dionne makes it look so easy, but after listening to several "young" artists make feeble attempts,and almost destroy Bacharach's music, you realize it really takes some serious musicality to sing Bacharach's work. What makes him so wonderfully complex is his seeming simplicity.
Wynona, All Saints, Barenaked Ladies, and especially Sheryl Crow...all have a long way to go before they can reach the interpretive heights of Luther and Dionne. In the meantime, who wants to watch them learn??
I say skip this CD and invest instead in the classic Dionne/Bacharach/David collaboration LP's from the mid to late 60's.
Also, Dusty Springfield and Gene Pitney are essential chapters in the Bacharach saga. It seems hard to even compare Springfield's "The Look of Love" or Pitney's "The Man That Shot Liberty Valance" to some of the substandard stuff on this CD.
If you want to listen to Bacharach, go to the pros and don't waste your time with the uninitiated.
